en: O wielder of the stone, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, [I say] "canā"— this combination of two particles is to be applied by dividing them [as *ca na*]. Even for a great price (*mahe śulkāya*), I shall not surrender (*parā deyām*) nor sell (*na vikrīṇāni*) you.
O Vajrivaḥ, O Indra who holds the thunderbolt in your hand, we should not give him away for wealth amounting to a thousand—that is, for a sum numbering one thousand;
nor should we give him away for a price of ten thousand—that is, for a *śulka* amounting to ten thousand (*ayuta*).
O Śatāmadha, O Indra of abundant wealth, [we should not give him] for a hundred.
This is much more than enough;
even for immeasurable wealth, I shall neither give you away nor sell you. The meaning is: "Even for wealth exceeding the stated amount, you are most dear to me."

O Indra, you are more desirable to me than my father or even my brother who enjoys [wealth]; both mother and father please me, for you are a noble lineage for the sake of attaining riches and prosperity.

O Indra, you are more wealthy (*vasyān*) than my father; indeed, you are even more wealthy than my brother who does not protect us. O Vasu, dweller, both my mother and you are equal (*samā*). [The masculine form remains by Pāṇini 1.2.67. You two honor me—you grant me worship. For what purpose? For the sake of wealth (*vasutvānāya*) and for the sake of prosperity (*rādhase*); that is, for the possession of both.
What do you say? Where are you? For your mind is indeed far away among many people.
O warrior, stirer of the fray, shatterer of forts, you have been stirred; the Gāyatrī verses have indeed begun to sing your praises.

Where, O Indra, did you go in former times? And where are you now? For your mind wanders among many sacrificers. O warrior, O maker of battle, O shatterer of forts, come hither! Our singers, skilled in song, sing forth praises. [Note: *Alarṣi* is derived from the root *iyarti* with the prefix *ā*, and is irregularly formed according to Pāṇini 7.4.65. **Translation:** "Where, O Indra, have you gone in the past? And where are you now? For your mind indeed wanders among many [sacrificers]. O warrior, O maker of strife, O destroyer of fortresses—come hither! Our singers, skilled in chanting, sing forth [praises]. **Explanation:** The hymn addresses Indra, asking about his movements in the past and present. It notes that his attention is distributed among many worshippers. The poet then calls upon him—describing him as a skillful warrior, a creator of conflict, and a breaker of the demonic strongholds—to arrive. The singers, proficient in melodic praise, offer their songs of adoration. The grammatical form *alarṣi* is an archaic imperative derived from the root *iyarti* ("to come") with the prefix *ā*. The commentary cites Pāṇini 7.4.65 to justify its formation within the class of roots beginning with *dādhrṣi*.
Sing forth this Gāyatra hymn to him who is the breaker of forts, the beloved one;
may he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, come to sit upon Kaṇva’s sacred grass and shatter the strongholds.

Sing forth the *gāyatra* song for him; let it be sung for that Indra, the shatterer of forts (*puramdara*), who is the one to be desired (*vāvātuḥ*)—or rather, the one to be honored by the worshipper. With those verses by which the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), having come to sit upon the sacred grass (*barhis*) at the sacrifice of Kaṇva’s son Medhātithi and Madhyātithi, may he approach and may he shatter the enemy forts. Sing the *gāyatra* melody in those very verses. 1. *asmai*: for him. 2. *vāvātuḥ*: one who is desirable or to be honored; alternatively, one who honors or praises. 3. *puramdaraḥ*: the destroyer of forts. 4. *yābhiḥ*: with which [verses]. 5. *kaṇvasya*: of Kaṇva (referring to Kaṇvaputra Medhātithi and Madhyātithi). 6. *barhiḥ*: the sacrificial grass (*yajña*). 7. *upa āsadam*: to sit near or to approach. 8. *yāsat*: may he go or approach. 9. *vajrī*: the wielder of the thunderbolt. 10. *bhinat*: may he shatter. 11. *puraḥ*: the forts. The meaning is: "Sing the *gāyatra* Sāman in those verses by which Indra, being praised, approaches the sacrifice of Kaṇva’s sons and shatters the enemy strongholds."
1. To whom [belongs] kha, jha, ta, śa, ya;
2. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, va, vā, tuḥ.

Those horses of yours which are ten-fold, those which are hundred-fold, and those which are thousand-fold; those stallions of yours which are vigorous and swift-moving—with them, come quickly to us! O Indra, those horses of yours which travel ten leagues (*daśagvinaḥ*) exist; and those others which are hundred-fold (*śatinaḥ*) and thousand-fold (*sahasriṇaḥ*) exist. Those horses of yours (*aśvāsaḥ*) which are stallions (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*), capable of impregnation, youthful, and swift-moving (*raghudruvaḥ*)—with all of them, come (*ā gahi*) quickly (*tūyam*) to us (*naḥ*).

I invoke today, for the sake of abundance, Indra who is stirred by the Gāyatrī hymn—the well-yielding cow, the other nourishment that provides a wide stream and is ever-ready. I invoke him indeed today, the one who milks out the essence.

That Indra, who—by means of *abhiśriś*, a substance for joining through the act of binding—even without [the aid of] the *jatru* (collarbones) from the neck, before the piercing (*ātṛda*) that causes the flow of blood, becomes the *saṃdhātṛ*, the uniter of that which was to be joined (*saṃdhi*); he, the bountiful (*maghavan*), the possessor of much wealth (*puruvasu*), is the one who restores (*iṣkartā*) that which has been shattered (*vihuta*).
O Indra, let us not be like outcasts, nor like strangers to you;
O wielder of the thunderbolt, we have been difficult to approach, like forests abandoned by their owners.
O Indra, wielder of the stone, let us not become like outcasts, nor like strangers to you, nor like forests abandoned by their owners; we have been difficult to approach. 13.

O Indra, from you alone, through your grace, may the one who offers good praise be victorious; accept this well-spoken hymn of the generous patrons. May it protect you; may your own vigorous and well-uttered praise prevail. 16.

O Indra, come quickly now—come at once—to the joint praise (*sadhastutim*) of the one who desires you, the sharer, and the worshipper; that praise being performed together with other officiating priests. May the hymn of praise from the wealthy patrons, the other sacrificers as well, reach and satisfy you.
And now, I too desire to offer a beautiful hymn of praise directed toward you.
For he has pressed the Soma with the stones; run it through the waters!
Like secret fires, they clothe him in their forms, milking him from his flanks.
Press out the Soma with the stones; wash it thoroughly in the waters. Like men clothing a bridegroom in secret, the heroes have milked it from its udders. 17.
O Adhvaryus, press the Soma with the stones—the pressing-stones; "hi" is used for emphasis, meaning "press this very one.
Wash it thoroughly in these Vasatīvarī waters.
"Perform the shaking of this Soma.
The shaking of the Soma is performed in the *vasatīvarī* waters with the mantras beginning with "adābhyagrahe himādāsutaḥ" (O invincible one, pressed from the snowy mountain).
The meaning is: "Do that."

Like the skins of cattle that cover the fire, the Maruts—the leaders and followers of Indra—clothe the clouds. From the *vakṣaṇās*, the rivers, they milk out water for the sake of the rivers; they draw it forth and pour it out.
For this reason, press the Soma with the stones for the sacrifice to Indra;
let it flow forth in joy.
Whether from the earth or from the vast expanse of heaven, from the radiant heights, grow strong in body through this song of mine; as one well-born, fulfill all that has been created.
Whether from the earth or from the mid-region of the vast heaven, grow strong with this body through my song; O well-doer, fulfill the desires of those who have performed good deeds. 18.
O Indra, come now from the earth—
so called because beings move (*jamanti*) upon it—
or from the sky, or from the great luminous realm (*rocanāt*), that is, from the shining firmament or from heaven.
The prefix *adhi* restates the sense of the ablative case.
With this body of mine, stretched out and expanded, grow great—become increased—through my song of praise.
O Indra, performer of noble deeds, satisfy (*ā-pṛṇa*) those among our people who have been born, filling them with their desired fruits.
For Indra, press the most intoxicating Soma, the choice-worthy;
let him swell this bright juice, which is urged forward by every prayer like one seeking booty.
Press out for Indra the most intoxicating Soma, the most excellent; may Śakra cause it to swell, for he is urged on by every prayer like one seeking booty.
1. [The syllables] *kha-śa* signify "pressing.
2. From the [syllables] *kha-bha-śa*, which mean "shining forth":

O Adhvaryus, for Indra—for the sake of Indra—well press (*su sota*) and extract the Soma that is most intoxicating (*madintamam*), most exhilarating, most excellent (*vareṇyam*), desirable, and fit for mixing.
Why is this so? To this he says:

*śakraḥ* (the powerful one), *indraḥ* (Indra), by *viśvayā dhiyā* (with every mental act), that is, with all ritual actions characterized by the *iṣṭi*, *soma*, and other sacrifices; *hinvānam* (impelling), meaning pleasing [him]; *vājayum* (desiring booty), meaning desiring food for himself—*enam* (this) *yajamānam* (sacrificer).
*Na* is used here in the sense of "now" (*saṃprati*).
"Saṃprati" means he causes to swell or increase;
therefore, the meaning is: "Press the Soma for that Indra."
Let me not, with my song that ever yearns for Soma, provoke you like a wild beast among all men; for who would not entreat one who is powerful?
Never have I provoked you with my song, like one who angers a wild beast with the cry of Soma; for who would not entreat the Lord? 20.

O Indra, joined with you at the libations and sacrifices by the flowing of the Soma through the strainer and by my song of praise, come hither, O Indra, and rejoice with wondrous divine bounty! Fill your wide, swelling belly like a lake with the shared draughts of Soma.
O Indra, come hither; O God, rejoice with wondrous bounty! Like a lake, fill your belly with the shared draughts of Soma, wide and swelling. 23.
O Indra, come hither!
O radiant God, rejoice with delightful and beautiful wealth consisting of Soma.
Together with the Maruts who drink along with you, fill your own vast, abundant, and increased belly like a lake with the Somas being drunk.
The root *prā* means "to fill";
it belongs to the first class (*ādādika*).
On the twenty-fourth day, during the midday *brahmaśastra*, there is an optional verse beginning with "ā tvā. [The meaning is:

for the sake of drinking (*pītaye*)—that is, for the purpose of consuming—the sweet-tasting, desired, and praiseworthy (or alternatively, that which is to be carried and attained) *ambhas* (water), namely the Soma-form food (*anna*).

Drink of this pressed juice, O lover of songs, like the first drinker; of this refined, flavorful [juice], this beautiful draught is offered for exhilaration. 26. Drink! Indeed! Of this! O lover of songs! Of the pressed [juice]! Like the first drinker! Of the refined! Of the flavorful! This! The draught! Beautiful! For exhilaration! Is offered. 26.
O *girvaṇas*, you who are to be honored with songs and praised with hymns, O Indra, [partake] of this pressed-out soma.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because the object (karman) functions as the recipient (saṃpradāna), according to the rule: "The mention of 'action' (kriyā) must be supplied."
Drink this pressed Soma quickly;
there is an illustration for this:
"like one who drinks first."

Vāyu is called *pūrvapā* because, being prior to all the gods, he drinks first. Thus, in the principal cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*), the meaning is that [Vāyu] should drink before all the gods.
Of what kind of Soma?
Of that which is adorned, meaning refined by means of honorific expressions.
By the rule *samparyupebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.137), the augment *suṭ* is added to the root *kṛ* in the sense of ornamenting;
by the rule *parinivibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.70), the *s* of *suṭ* becomes *ṣ*.
*Vasinaḥ* means possessing flavor.
Moreover, this *āsutiḥ*, this *āsavaḥ*—the intoxicating, beautiful, and splendid Soma juice—is *patyate*, that is, it serves for *madāya*, for exhilaration, for the production of joy.
[The root] *pallu* means "to go."
Or rather:
the root *pati* has the sense of sovereignty;
he rules over, that is, possesses, intoxication.
The meaning is: "capable of producing intoxication."

He who alone exists by his wondrous power, the great and fierce one, comes with his hosts; may he, the fair-cheeked, come, for he does not fail to come; he does not avoid the offering. 27. He who is alone, by his wondrous power, the great, the fierce, [comes] against the obstructors. May he, the fair-cheeked, come; he does not fail to come; he does not avoid the call. 27.
Indra—who is alone (*v*ekaḥ), solitary, and indeed without companion (*asahāya*)—by means of his own deeds (*vṛtaiḥ ātmīyaiḥ karmabhiḥ*), prevails over (*abhy asti*) and overcomes his enemies.

And he who is great (*mahān*) and superior (*adhika*) by virtue of his wondrous power (*daṃsanā karmaṇā*), for that very reason is fierce (*ugraḥ*), of exalted strength (*udūrṇabalaḥ*), and fair-cheeked (*śiprī*).
*Śiprā* refers to the helmet (*śirastrāṇam*).
In the sense of praise:
"one with a beautiful helmet.
Or alternatively:
*Śipre* refers to the jaws or the nostrils; he who possesses these is *śiprivān*. May that Indra always come, arrive, and reach us.
May he be such; may he not depart, may he not become separate, may he not be disunited.
From the roots *gam* and *yauti*, there is the augment *ḍa* and the suffix *le*.
By the rule “*itaśca lopaḥ*,” there is the elision of the vowel *i*.
In the case of *gam*, there is the elision of the *śap* suffix by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*.”
From the root *yu* (to join), the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *sibbahulam*.
May he come to our invocation (*havam*) and our hymn of praise (*stotram*), may he reach it;
may he not avoid it, may he not exclude it, may he not abandon it.
In short, it means: "May Indra always receive us and our hymn of praise."

You crushed the moving fortress of Śuṣṇa with your weapons; you followed after the light, O Indra, when you struck him down twice, as he was fleeing. You crushed the moving fortress of Śuṣṇa with your weapons; you followed after the light, O Indra, when you struck him down twice, as he was fleeing.
O Indra, you [overcame] the wandering, mobile nature of the Asura Śuṣṇa, the witherer.
In the Vedic language, because the substitution of the preceding vowel (pūrvatva) is optional according to the rule "vā chandasi," there is the substitution of *yaṇ*.
*Puram* means the place of residence; *vadhaiḥ* means by weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and others; *samapiṇak* means you completely pulverized.
The meaning is that you shattered it.
This is the form of the root *piṣ* (to grind) in the imperfect tense (*laṅ*), second person singular.
And furthermore, there is light.

Shining forth, you followed after him; you went after Śuṣṇa to slay him. Or rather: then, following the light that shone within the breach of Śuṣṇa’s fort, you went after it; you reached it—this is the meaning. O Indra, when you became doubly worthy of invocation by the two kinds of worshippers—the singers and the sacrificers—then you crushed the fort of Śuṣṇa; such is the connection. [In the verb *bhava* (you become), the suffix *sip* takes the augment *aṭ* in the *leṭ* tense; the *śap* suffix is elided by Vedic rule; and because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "bhūsuvostiṅi," the *uvaṅ* substitution occurs. On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing during the Brahma-śastra, "mama svā" is the optional *anurūpa* verse; the Sūtra has already been cited. **mama tvā sūra udite mama madhyaṃdine divaḥ | mama prapitve apivare vasvā stomāso avṛtsata || 29 ||** At the rising of the sun, at the time of dawn, my hymns—O Vasu, O Indra who provides dwelling—turn toward you; let them bring you face to face with us. Likewise, at the midday of the day, may my hymns turn toward you. And at the *prapitva*, at the end of the day in the evening, may my hymns turn toward you. At *apiśarvare*: the time that has entered into the night (*śarvarī*) is *apiśarvare*; even at that time of night, may my hymns turn toward you. **stuhi stuhi idete ghā te maṃheṣṭhāso maghonām | ninditāśvaḥ prapathī paramajyā maghasya medhyātithi || 30 ||** Praise! Praise! Indeed, these here are the most generous among the wealthy for you—Ninditāśva, Prapathī, Paramajyā, and Medhyātithi, the giver of wealth. Āsaṅga, the royal sage, having given much wealth to Medhyātithi, urges him to praise his own gift: "O Medhyātithi, worthy guest of sacrifice, praise! Praise! Repeatedly extol us. Do not be indifferent. These indeed—we are the most liberal givers of wealth to you among the wealthy. Therefore, praise us. He describes what kind of praise: "Ninditāśva"—one by whose valor the horses of enemies are disgraced or rendered useless. "Prapathī"—one whose path is excellent; one who stays on the right path. "Paramajyā"—one whose bowstring is supreme; by this, weapons like the bow are indicated; meaning one possessing excellent arms. Or: "Paramajyā"—one who conquers (*jināti*) the most excellent enemies; from the root *jyā* (to lose vigor/decay), the suffix *vic* is added by the rule "āto manin. Being such a person, I am Āsaṅga—thus praise me. **ā yadaśvān vananvataḥ śraddhayāhaṃ rathe ruham | uta vāmasya vasunaściketati yo asti yādṛk paśuḥ || 31 ||** When, with faith, I mounted the horses that desire the woods onto the chariot, then he understands the desirable wealth—that which exists, whatever kind of cattle there is.

When I, Prāyogi, endowed with supreme faith and devotion, mounted the horses—those eager for the woods, seeking the woods, and sharing in the prize—upon your chariot, O Medhyātithi; at that time, praise me thus! And furthermore, this is a cumulative statement intended to emphasize the present subject: [praise him] who intends such desirable wealth (*vāmasya vasunaḥ*), for this Āsaṅga knows how to give it. He is one of the Yadu lineage—or rather, among the Yadus (men), he is well-known—as a "Paśu" (one possessing cattle, the term *paśu* here losing its comparative force); or else, *paśu* comes from the root *paś*, meaning a subtle observer. This is the construction: "He who exists as Āsaṅga, he intends [to give]."

He who, being impetuous, has bestowed upon me a great gift along with a golden skin—may he, whose chariot resounds, surpass all blessings as he approaches the assembly. 32. He who, being impetuous, has bestowed upon me a great gift along with a golden skin—may he, whose chariot resounds, surpass all blessings as he approaches the assembly. 32.
"Pray thus to me," says Āsaṅga to Medhyātithi.
He who is the self of Āsaṅga gave—along with golden skins (tvac) as coverings—to Medhyātithi, my own, great riches that are moving (ṛñja) and golden.
*Maha* is a root meaning "to give."
May this Āsaṅga, whose chariot resounds—his chariot being noisy—overcome all the extensive fortunes and riches belonging to his enemies.

Then Pḷāyogi surpassed others in giving; with ten thousand [cows] he went before them. Then ten bright bulls stood forth for me like reeds from a lake. 33. Then Pḷāyogi, surpassing others in his generosity, went forward with ten thousand [cows]. Then ten bright bulls stood forth for me like reeds from a lake. 33.

Moreover, Āsaṅga by name, the son of Pṛṣadhra and the king known as Prayoga, surpasses other givers by giving ten times ten thousand—that is, ten thousand—cattle and other such things. Immediately thereafter, ten [of each kind] of bulls capable of impregnation, brilliant and shining, given to me by Āsaṅga, are like *nalas*;
*nalas* are a specific kind of grass growing in ponds.
Just as they emerge from a lake or a pond in groups, even so, the cows and other animals given by me have emerged and remained outside from this Āsāṅga.
Having spoken thus to Medhyātithi, saying, "Praise me in this very manner," it follows that Prāyogī Āsaṅga is the seer (ṛṣi) of these four verses, and he himself is the deity.

His thick [thigh] was seen from the front; his thigh, standing firm and being supported, was like that of a woman. Having looked upon him, the eternal woman said: "O noble one, you bear a most auspicious nourishment. (34) *anu* | *asya* | *sthūram* | *dadṛśe* | *purastāt* | *anusthaḥ* | *ūruḥ* | *ava-arambyamāṇaḥ* | *śaśvatī* | *nārī* | *abhi-cakṣya* | *āha* | *su-bhadram* | *arya* | *bhojanam* | *bibharṣi* || 34 ||
This King Āsaṅga once became a eunuch due to a divine curse.
His wife, Śaśvatī, distressed by her husband’s lack of virility, performed great austerities. By that asceticism, he regained his manhood.

Having perceived that he had attained manhood, the king was constantly pleased; [he bestowed upon him] the status of being of the Śaśvata lineage (or: the state of being of the Śaśvata clan). He praised him with this [verse]: "They are mounted upon the *kha*, *ā*, *yoga*, *tva*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *ā*. [He was thus called] Prāyogi. By this means, he praised him.

In front of this Āsañja, in the anterior part—that is, in the secret region—the *sthūram* (thick, grown) male organ is seen following after it. That limb, being boneless (*anasthaḥ*), is the thigh (*ūru*), which is broad (*ūharva*) and hanging down (*avarambamāṇaḥ*) due to its extreme length, suspended with its face turned downward.
Or else:
*Ūruḥ*: By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the dual ending becomes *su*. He remains leaning upon his two thighs (*ūrū*).

Śaśvatī, the daughter of Aṅgiras, was a woman who became the wife of that Jaṣa. Having observed him at night—having seen his limbs to be of such a nature—she said: "O lord, husband, master, you possess (bibharṣi), that is, you maintain, most auspicious (subhadram), exceedingly excellent food, the means of enjoyment. Thus she spoke.
The second hymn, consisting of forty-two verses beginning with “*idaṃ vaso*,” is the seerly work (*ārṣam*) of Medhātithi Kāṇva and Priyamedha Āṅgirasa.
The two verses beginning with “*śikṣā vibhindo*” belong to Medhātithi alone.
The verse “*svādavaḥ somāḥ*” is an *anuṣṭubh*, while the remaining verses are *gāyatrīs*.
Indra is the deity.
The final two verses belong to Vibhindu, as they are praises of his gift; thus they have him as their deity.

Accordingly, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “*Idaṃ vaso*, [a hymn] of forty-two verses, by Medhātithi Āṅgirasa and Priyamedha; [the verses] *svāda-vaḥ* are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and with the last two [verses], Medhātithi praised the gift of Vibhindu.”
The application of the *sūkta* has been explained.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the first triplet of verses in the *Marutvatīya* is the *anucara*.
For it is stated: “‘*idaṃ vaso sutamandhaḥ*’ is the *pratipad* and the *anucara* of the *Marutvatīya*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.14).

In the second watch of the night, during the *brahmaśastra*, this very same triplet (*tṛca*) serves as the *stotriya*. And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "O Vasu, come here to this pressed soma; intoxicate yourself with the soma" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.4). This same triplet also serves as the *anucara* for the *marutvatīya* śastra on the fourth day.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘We implore you with sacrifices, O Vasu; here is the pressed soma-juice’—these two [verses] are the *pratipad* and the *anucara* of the Marutvatīya [śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
O Vasu, drink this pressed soma-juice until your belly is well-filled;
we offer these songs to you.
This, O Vasu, is the pressed juice; drink it until your belly is well-filled. O fearless one, we have offered it to you. 1.
O Vasu, O Indra, the bestower of dwelling, drink this present pressed juice, the food characterized as Soma,
so that your belly, your stomach, may become well-filled— that is, exceedingly full. O fearless one!
She who fears from all sides is *ābhayī*.
The suffix *ini* is applied to the root *bhi* (to fear) according to the *Uṇādi* rules. She who does not cause fear is *anābhayī*.
O such Indra, for you (*te*), for your sake, we offer (*ririma*) the Soma characterized by longing;
[the root] *rā* means "to give.
The *liṭ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Shaken by men, pressed by horses, and purified by the straining-cloths,
he is like a horse washed in the rivers.
Shaken by men, pressed out, purified by other means, and cleansed by the filters like a horse bathed in rivers. 2.

Shaken by men who are the leaders of the sacrifice, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), purified by the act of shaking—the *ādhvanya* cup being prepared through that shaking—pressed by means of horses, stones, and cows acting as instruments, extracted by the *adhvaryu* priests, and filtered through the fleece (*vāra*) of a ram or a ewe;
for Soma is indeed purified by a tuft of wool which serves as the center of the ten-strand filter (*daśāpavitra*).

This was stated by the venerable Āpastamba: “He gives a tuft of white wool to the sacrificer; he makes it the center of the *daśāpavitra* on the cart; the white filter of the *valakṣmī* remains unknotted. In rivers, in flowing waters, like a horse—like a horse that has been washed, rinsed, and purified—the meaning is that just as a horse bathed in water becomes radiant with its impurities removed, so too does the Soma, pressed with the *vasatīvarī* waters, become radiant.
Such is the Soma; its connection with the following verse is expressed as "that barley of yours."
Mixing that Soma for you like barley with milk, making it sweet as *arka*, O Indra, may we be with you at this communal feast.
Mixing that barley with milk like a sweet soma-juice, O Indra, we call upon you for this communal feast.
1. *jhay-avadhūtaḥ*; *tā1-2-4-adhūtaḥ*.

O Indra, for you (*te*), having mixed (*śrīṇantaḥ*) that aforementioned Soma with cows—meaning with products of the cow such as milk and other ingredients used for mixing—just as one prepares barley (*yavaṃ yathā*), that is, like the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) made of barley which is offered at the libations (*savanīya*), we have made it sweet (*svāduṃ*), meaning fit to be tasted by virtue of its flavor. Regarding the verb *akarman* (we have made), the *cli* suffix is elided after the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense according to the rule "in a mantra, [the *cli* of] *ghas* [and others is elided]."

Since this is so, therefore, O Indra, I call upon you—such as you are—to drink that Soma at this present *sadhamāda*, a sacrifice characterized by shared exhilaration; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

In the *niṣkevalya* of the *mahāvrata*, the remainder of the hymn beginning with “Indra it somapāḥ” (RV 8.2.1), consisting of three *gāyatrī* verses, is to be recited. Having omitted the other three [verses], and having also excluded the verse “svādavaḥ” from that [hymn], one should insert in its place the verse “na hy anyaṃ balākaram” (RV 8.2.4).
This is likewise prescribed in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*: “From the hymns beginning with ‘indra it somapā ekaḥ,’ he omits the last three [verses].”

The meaning is that hunters, reviling those sweet Soma juices through various means such as nets and the like, pursue them by force— just as one pursues a deer— as though they were unqualified [for the sacrifice]; the root *mṛg* is used in the sense of "pursuing."
And those people who, with "cows"—
"cow" being a name for speech—
approach [the teacher] with words and praises, they go toward him in a contemptible manner.
The meaning is that they are unable to praise him correctly.
The root *tsara* means "to go by guile.
The meaning is that such people do not perceive Indra.
On the third day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), the triplet beginning with "Three for Indra" (*traya indrasya*) is the *anucara* of the [stotra] addressed to the Maruts (*maruvatī*).

For it is stated: "The *pratipad* and *anucara* of the [stotra] addressed to the Maruts are 'Him for great bounty' (*taṃ tamidrādhase mahe*) and 'Three Soma-pressings for Indra' (*traya indrasya somāḥ')" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).

May there be three pressed Soma-libations for Indra, the god, in his own dwelling, for him who drinks the pressed juice. (7) "Three" (trayaḥ). "Of Indra" (indrasya). "Somas" (somāḥ). "Pressed" (sutāsaḥ). "May they be" (santu). "Of the god" (devasya). "In his own" (sve). "Dwelling" (kṣaye). "Drinker of the pressed juice" (sutapāḥ). (7) For the sake of drinking, may there be three—existing in a threefold manner as the three pressings—for Indra, the god endowed with qualities such as generosity, in his own dwelling, that is, in his own sacrificial hall; let them be "pressed," meaning prepared by extraction. "Drinker of the pressed juice" (sutapāḥ) is a descriptive term containing a reason: since this Indra is a drinker only of the pressed Soma, therefore let them be pressed. This is the sense.

Three reservoirs flow forth; three ladles are well-filled, upon a single support. Three reservoirs—meaning the three vessels known as the *droṇakalaśa*, *pūtabhṛt*, and *ādhavanīya*, which serve as the receptacles for the Soma—flow forth; they cause the Soma to stream out for the sake of Indra. Threefold are the ladles (*camu*), the *camasa* cups used during the three pressings, which are well-filled with Soma for the sacrifice to Indra. If one asks where all this occurs, it is said: "upon a single support" (*samāne... bhārman*), that is, within a single sacrificial performance (*bharaman*) being carried out by the officiating priests. The word *adhi* here expresses the sense of the locative case.

Pure art thou, resting in many places; mixed with milk in the midst; most gladdening for the hero with curds at the third pressing. O Soma, you are pure; you are cleansed by the woollen filter. You, who rest completely in many vessels—such as the *praśitra* and the *camasa* cups—are mixed in the middle with milk and other ingredients used for blending, such as milk and the like, during the drawing of the *maitrāvaruṇa-graha* and others. At the third pressing, you are mixed with curds. Being thus prepared, become the one who most effectively exhilarates the heroic and valiant Indra.

These Soma juices of yours, O Indra—sharp and pressed by us here—these pure ones beg for the milk-mixture. (10) O Indra, these Soma juices belonging to you are sharp—that is, providing intense intoxication—and have been pressed by us, the Adhvaryu priests. Being pure and clear, they beg you for the *āśira*, the mixing substance such as milk. "Mix them"—this is the connection with the following verse. (18)

Mix this milk-mixture, the sacrificial cake, and this Soma for Indra; indeed, I hear that you are wealthy. 11. That milk-mixture; the sacrificial cake; for Indra; this; Soma; mix; indeed; you; I hear; to be wealthy. 11.

1. *jña-ta1-2-4-adhiḥ* | 2. *kha-sthā*; *bha-sthāḥ*; *śa-sthāpitaḥ* | 3. *kha-śa-śrapaṇadravyaiḥ* | 4. *śa-śrapaṇadravya* | O Indra, "mix" (*śriṇīhi*) those aforementioned Soma juices with the "milk-mixture" (*āśiram*), that is, the curdling substances such as milk and the like, for the sake of the sacrifice.
Immediately thereafter, mix this "sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśam*)—characterized by parched grains, flour-cakes, and so forth—the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*, as well as this our Soma.

The meaning is that one should join the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which was eaten first, with the Soma, which is drunk afterwards. If it is asked what the reason is for your prayer, [the answer is]: "For" (*hi*) "because [you are] *revantam*, i.e., possessing wealth."
In the phrase "rayimantau bahulam," there is a vocalization (samprasāraṇa).
Since you are heard of everywhere as possessing abundant wealth—as it is said, "I hear of you as having much wealth" and "you have much wealth"—for that reason, we pray to you alone.

Having drunk [the soma] into their hearts, they fight like those intoxicated by wine; they do not age naked while standing upright. 12. In their hearts, having drunk, they fight; like those intoxicated by wine, they do not; standing upright, they do not age naked. 12.
O Indra, these Soma juices, having been drunk by you, fight within your own hearts;
they strike one another.
Therein lies the illustration.
The meaning is that, like "durmadāsas"— those who are evil-intoxicated— when liquor is drunk, they fight with one another to intoxicate you, just as such people intoxicate their drinker. Moreover:
"The meters are like horses;
because they do not abandon him, they are called 'unbared' (anagnāḥ).
And they 'serve' (jarante)—that is, they praise—you who are filled with Soma, just as one praises a cow or similar animal when it is full of milk."
The root *jarati* has the meaning of praising.
If on the sixth day the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* is to be accomplished with the *Raivata-sāman*, then the *anurūpa* verse for the *niṣkevalya* chant is "revāṃ id.
For it is prescribed: "The *stotriya* and *anurūpa* are 'revatīr naḥ sadhamāde' and 'revāṃ id evataḥ stota' respectively" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

May the singer of praise be wealthy indeed from one as bountiful as you, O Maghavan; may he truly be the first to hear of you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. 13. May the singer of praise be wealthy indeed from one as bountiful as you, O Maghavan; may he truly be the first to hear of you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. 13.
"He is *harivaḥ*, [meaning] *harivan*.
By the rule "the *ru*-substitute for *mat* and *vas*," the *n* is replaced by *r*. [Thus, *harivan* becomes *harivaḥ*; *hari* refers to the two horses.
In the same way, O Śibi, may the one who praises you—who are *arevataḥ*, possessed of wealth and endowed with much riches—be *arevān*, that is, wealthy;
the word *iccha* is used for emphasis:
he shall certainly become possessed of wealth and shall not fall into poverty.
He confirms the very point already stated by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic:

"Of one such as you, that is, of one who is similar to yourself. [The suffix] *-vatup* is applied according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, there is an addition [to the list of suffixes] for the sense of similarity after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."
"May he be the singer of Maghavan—the bountiful one, the wealthy one, the renowned, the famous, celebrated everywhere—and of any other as well.
The word "may he be" (*predu syāt*) is supplied [from the context].
May he be pre-eminent (*prasyāt*).
It will surely come to pass and shall not fail;
what need is there to say that your praiser shall surely become wealthy?

Even the hymn being recited, the non-cow has not perceived; nor the *gāyatra* being sung. 14. Even the hymn (*uktha*), being recited, the non-cow, the enemy, has not perceived; nor the *gāyatra*, being sung. 14.
The word *gauḥ* means "one who sings. 1. *Agoḥ* means "of the non-singer" (the one who does not praise).

*Ariḥ* means "the enemy," namely Indra. *Śasyamānam* means "being recited. *Uktham* refers to the *śastra*, the liturgical hymn being chanted by the Hotṛ priest. *Canā ciketa* means "he recognizes" or "he understands.
[The root] *kit* is used in the sense of "knowing."
The form *liṭ* is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The word *na* is used here in the sense of "not at present.
[The meaning is: "He does not even know the *gāyatra* sāman—which is currently being sung by the *prastotṛ* and others—or even that which is called the *gāyatrī*."
For this reason, we praise that very Indra; such is the meaning.

Do not give us up to the drinker, O Indra; do not deliver us to the arrogant one. O possessor of power, help us with your powers! 15. Do not [give] us, O Indra, to the drinker; do not deliver [us] to the defiant one. Teach [us], O powerful one, with your powers! 15.
1. From *kha*, *jñā*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* itself.
2. *Kha*, *jñā*, *ta*, *ña*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* form "cow" (*gauḥ*); *jñā*, *ta*, *la*, *ra*, *ga*, and *ṛ* form "cows" (*rgāḥ*).
3. By means of *kha*, *jñā*, *ta*, and the hymns (*stotra*) and so forth.
O Indra, do not abandon us to the one who hates us; for *pīyati* is a verb signifying the act of killing— do not forsake us to the enemy who is by nature murderous and intent on violence.
"Do not [be] defiant toward us; do not abandon us.
The root *śṛdhu* means "to be defiant" or "to overpower.
Rather, O powerful Indra, O possessor of might (*śacīvan*), instruct and guide us with your own powers (*śacībhiḥ*), that is, through your own deeds.
Alternatively, the root *śikṣ* has the sense of giving; [the meaning is:
"Give us the desired wealth."
Alternatively:

"Desire to train [yourself] to conquer the enemies," that is, desire to make yourself capable of conquering them. This is the form in the imperative (loṭ) of the root *śak* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), after the substitution of *i* for *śak* according to the rule "sani mīmā" and the elision of the reduplication.
In the first watch of the night, during the Brahmaśastra, the triplet for the stotra is “vayamu tvā” (We [choose] you).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “vayamu tvā tadidarthā vayamindra tvāyavo’bhi” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).

We, O Indra, seeking this very goal, as your devoted friends, we the Kaṇvas praise you with hymns. 16. We—indeed—O Indra, for that very purpose, as your followers, your friends, the Kaṇvas, chant with their hymns. 16.
O Indra, we—your friends, sharing the same station, desiring you for ourselves, and having that very praise concerning you as our sole purpose and goal—praise you.
The particle *u* is a filler.
And the Kaṇvas—our sons and others born of the Kaṇva lineage—extol you with hymns, that is, with the recited chants (*uktha*).

Never indeed have I praised another, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with newer hymns; only your own praise have I recognized. 17. Never indeed have I praised another, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with newer works; only your own praise have I recognized. 17.

O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, I— who abide in this most new (*naviṣṭha*) sacrifice belonging to you, who are *apasaḥ*, skillful and active in ritual works— do not indeed (*gha na*) praise (*ā papana*), that is, do not at all extol (*panateḥ* is a verb meaning "to praise") anything other than what concerns you. Rather, I recognize (*ciketa*) your own hymn of praise (*stoma*).
The meaning is: "I praise you alone at all times."

The gods desire one who presses the soma; they do not long for sleep. The dull-witted fall into negligence. 18. They desire. The gods. One who presses. Not. For sleep. They long. They go. To negligence. The dull-witted. 18.
The gods, Indra and all the others, desire to protect the sacrificer who is pressing the Soma;
they do not long for sleep. They do not wish for that state of sleep for him who is performing the libation.
The meaning is that they cause [the mind] to remain perpetually awakened.
The dative case is used for the object according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.4.36, *spṛherīpsitaḥ*.
The root *spṛh* means "desire."
The root *cur* begins with *d*.
For this very reason, the gods, being "atandras"—that is, free from sloth—go to, or obtain, his Soma, which is "pramādam," meaning it produces intense exhilaration.
O come forth with strengths; do not disregard us, like a great man seeking a wife. 19. O! Well! Come forth! With strengths! Do not disregard! Toward us! Like a great man! Seeking a wife! 19.
O Indra, come toward us with vigor—that is, with the foods that must be given to us—come well and pre-eminently; come quickly indeed.
Do not be angry;
for *haṇīyati* is a verb meaning "to be angry."
Or rather, do not feel shame;
the root *haṇīhū* is listed among the Kaṇva-class roots in the sense of "shame.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like a great man with a young wife": he whose wife (*jāyā*) is young is so described. The substitution of *niṅ* for the final member of the compound is applied by the rule "jāyāyā niṅ."
Just as such a great man, though superior in virtues, goes quickly toward his own wife while being shameless, so it is in this case.

May he not, being ill-disposed toward us this evening, cause [us] harm; may he stay far away from us like an unpleasant son-in-law. 20. *mo iti* (particle), *su* (well), *adha* (now/then), *duh-ṛṇāvān* (ill-disposed, difficult to deal with), *sāyam* (in the evening), *karat* (may he do/make), *āre* (far away), *asmata* (from us), *aśrīraḥ iva* (like one who is ungracious), *jāmātā* (son-in-law). 20.

Possessing the *duharṇa*—the *duharṇa* being a slaying difficult for others to endure—the Lord Indra, who possesses that, shall come from afar toward us this very day, at this moment. May he not make the evening—the end of the day, the time of twilight—exceedingly long; let him not cause it to be delayed. [In the word *mākarat*: after the root *kṛ* with the particle *mā*, in the *luṅ* tense, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cl* occurs according to the rule *kṛmṛdṛhibhyaḥ*. A son-in-law (*jāmātā*): one is born (*jāyate*) as offspring (*jā*), and its maker (*nirmātā*) is the husband of the daughter. "Without splendor" (*aśrīra*): splendor does not exist in him, thus he is *aśrī*; he who possesses that is *aśrīraḥ*. The suffix *ra* is used in the sense of possession. A son-in-law devoid of virtues, though repeatedly summoned, delays until the time of evening. The meaning is: do not you likewise cause such a delay in time. || 20 ||

The benevolent favor of this hero, who bestows much; the thoughts of him who is known in the three [worlds]. 21. vibhā | hi | asya | vīrasya | bhūridāvarīm | sumatim | triṣu | jñātasya | manāṃsi || 21 ||

We indeed know the auspicious and wise benevolent intention (*sumati*) of this heroic and valiant Indra, who is the giver of abundant wealth; for we truly know his mind and heart as he has manifested for the sake of his work throughout the three worlds, beginning with the earth. Therefore, the meaning is that we shall compose a hymn of praise such that pleasure may arise in that Indra.

Pour it forth indeed toward Kaṇvamant; do not withhold it from the powerful one, who is more glorious than Śatabhūti. 22. Pour it forth indeed toward Kaṇvamant; do not withhold it from the powerful one, who is more glorious than Śatabhūti. 22.

O Adhvaryu, pour out the Soma quickly for Indra, who is accompanied by the Kaṇvas—the word *kaṇ* meaning "to sound," so the Kaṇvas are either the singers (stotṛs) or the sages (ṛṣis) belonging to the Kaṇva lineage. Offer it to him. From this Indra, who acts with power (*śavas*)—that is, from the exceedingly powerful one whose manifestations (*bhūtis*) are a hundred; for "a hundred" signifies many—one whose protections (*ūtis*) are numerous, we truly do not know any person more glorious (*yaśastara*). Therefore, the meaning is: offer the Soma specifically for him.

O presser, bring the Soma with the best [effort] for Indra, the hero, for Śakra; bring it so that he may drink, for the noble one. 23. With the best. O presser. For Indra. The Soma. For the hero. For Śakra. Bring. Drinking. For the noble one. 23.

O *abhiṣotṛ* (presser), press [the soma] for *indra*: for him who is *sotaḥ* (the presser); for the *vīra* (hero); for the *vikrānta* (valiant); for the *śakra* (mighty) endowed with power; for the *narya* (beneficial to men); for the *nṛbhyaḥ hita* (beneficial to men); for *indra* with the *jyeṣṭha* (eldest or principal) *aindravāyava-graha*.
For he is indeed the eldest among the *dhārā-grahas* (stream-offerings).
Therefore, O Soma, bring it, carry it, fetch it;
cause him to attain heroic power. And let that Indra drink that Soma; let him drink it.

He who is most easily found, O you who are like a stranger, [grant] wealth consisting of horses to those who praise you, and booty consisting of cattle to those who laud you. 24. He who is most easily found; O you who are like a stranger; [grant] wealth consisting of horses; to those who praise; booty; to those who laud; consisting of cattle. 24.

That Indra who is most cognizant—most thoroughly aware and a knower of the hymn of praise—among those who do not falter, who cause no distress, and who bring happiness; that Indra bestows upon the *jaritṛ*s (the chanters), the *hotṛ*s and others, and the *stotṛ*s (the singers), the *prastotṛ*s and others, *vāja*—meaning food or strength—accompanied by many horses (*aśvāvantam*) and accompanied by many cows (*gomantam*). This is the sense of the verse.

In the *atirātra* sacrifice included within the *ahīna*, during the first *paryāya* of the Hotṛ’s recitation, the verse beginning with "apanthām" is the *stotriya*; for this triplet is praised by the *chandogas*.
Indeed, it is recorded in the tradition: "The *stoma* is the *stotriya* according to the conviction of the *chandogas*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.13).
The two carriers of the path have sped forth toward the Soma for the exhilaration of the heroic, brave hero.

O pressers, pour forth the Soma for exhilaration, for the Hero, for the Brave One! (25) O pressers—meaning the Adhvaryu priests who perform the extraction—for the sake of exhilaration, for the Hero, for the Victorious One;
we, the praisers, [invoke] the *sadhamāda*—that which is to be enjoyed together—with the thought that "he praises you, the Lord, face-to-face.
The sense is: therefore, come hither as well.

And those praises which, magnifying Indra—the doer of deeds—strengthen you for great bounty and for wealth. 29. And praised; and; which; thee; strengthen; for; greatness; for; bounty; Indra; the doer; strengthening. 29.
O Indra, those who increase you—the singers who perform deeds, the praisers, and their hymns of praise—strengthen you.
For what purpose?
For great wealth, for vast riches, and for power.
For the sake of obtaining both; the ellipsis to be supplied is "they obtain those two.
Or else:
The connection is with the words "In the future, they have truly established their powers."

And those songs which are for you, O you who are borne by songs, and those hymns—for you they have truly established these as powers. 30. And the songs which are yours, O you who are borne by songs, and those hymns—for you they have truly established these as powers. 30.

O Indra, these songs—praises worthy of being carried by hymns—are being offered for you; and these words in the form of praises are yours. Furthermore, the *ukthas*—the recited hymns and the spoken words—are being performed for your sake. All of these together have indeed bestowed strengths upon you; they have established power in you.

Truly, this one of many exploits, with the thunderbolt in his hand, alone bestows prizes from of old, being unimpaired. 31. Truly. Thus. This one. Of many exploits. Prizes. Alone. With the thunderbolt in his hand. From of old. Unimpaired. Bestows. 31.
Indra is truly active, performing many deeds;
*vi* is an expletive.

He is the sole one (*vikaḥ*), the chief among all the gods, with the thunderbolt in his hand and the thunderbolt in his arm. From of old (*sanāt*), for a long time, he has been unrestrained (*amṛktaḥ*), unoppressed by enemies. Such is Indra; he bestows (*dayate*) spoils (*vājān*)—that is, food or strengths—upon his worshippers.

Indra, the much-invoked, the great one with his mighty powers, slays Vṛtra with his right hand. 32. *Hantā* (slayer), *vṛtram* (Vṛtra), *dakṣiṇena* (with the right [hand]), *indraḥ* (Indra), *puru* (much), *puruhūtaḥ* (invoked by many), *mahān* (great), *mahībhiḥ* (with the great), *śacībhiḥ* (powers). 32.
This Indra, with his right hand alone, was the slayer (*hantṛ*) of Vṛtra, the Asura; he struck him down effectively.
The suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of one who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*).
The genitive case is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyaya... (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

*vpuḥ* means *puru* (much). By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision of the case-ending. In many places, he is *vpuruhūtaḥ* (invoked by many). He is *vmahān* (great), the most excellent among all, through *vmahībhiḥ* (great) *vśacībhiḥ* (actions or powers).
The meaning is: "O Indra, being such as you are, protect us."

In whom all people and even the mighty deeds abide; indeed, the wealthy one follows after him like a shaven-headed woman. 33. In whom... all... people... and... mighty deeds... indeed... the wealthy one... 33.
All people, all subjects, revolve around him, O Indra; they are dependent upon him. Moreover, there are also mighty deeds—this is a name for strength.
In that Indra reside the powers that effect downfall, the forces that conquer enemies and rival merchants—
the root *ji* meaning "to conquer in the pressing [of Soma]";
that Indra [overcomes] the wealthy patrons.
*Magham* is wealth characterized by sacrificial offerings (*havilakṣaṇa*). He becomes a *vanu*, one who desires that [wealth], and a *mandī*, one who rejoices in it.
*Cet* and *iti* are fillers.
1. Śa-havanīya-Indra. 2. That is this; or rather:
The meaning is that Indra, being exhilarated, favors those [praisers]; or alternatively,
"for that wealthy Indra, the praiser becomes favorable"— this connects with the subsequent sentence as a single syntactic unit.

Indra has performed all these deeds—he who is heard far beyond [all], the giver of booty to the wealthy patrons. 34. He; these; has done; Indra; all; he; beyond; is heard; giver of booty; of the wealthy ones. 34.
This Indra [performed] all these pervasive heroic deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra;
or else,
[he pervaded] the classes of beings, such as the earth and so forth.
He performed those deeds; he, Indra, who is renowned as preeminent in his powers and is praised everywhere,
moreover, that Indra becomes the giver of *vāja*— of food— to the *maghavan*s, the wealthy sacrificers who offer oblations.

He brings forward the chariot even from afar, which he drives toward the prize; for he, the mighty one, is the bearer of wealth. 35. He brings forward the chariot, even from afar, which he drives toward the prize; for he, the mighty one, is the bearer of wealth. 35.

Indra, the striker, whose nature is to strike, [drives] the chariot that rushes forward, seeking cattle. He protects—that is, he guards—the singer from one who is "apākāt," meaning from one whose wisdom is unripe;
the word *cit* implies a further inclusion:
he protects even from one whose wisdom is ripe. For that singer indeed, being a lord (*inaḥ*), becomes a carrier of wealth—a bringer of riches that flow well.
The suffix *tṛn* is applied to the root *vah* in the sense of one who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*).
By the rule *bhato 'na loka-avyaya-*, there is a prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*) when it follows a word ending in *bh* or *at*.

The winner, the sage, with his swift steeds; the slayer of Vṛtra with his men, the hero; the true protector of the one who serves him. 36. Winner, sage, with swift steeds; slayer of Vṛtra, with men, hero; true protector of the worshipper. 36.
That Indra is a wise sage; with swift horses serving as his vehicles, he is the winner and the one who reaches the goal.
Likewise, being a hero endowed with valor, together with the Maruts as his leaders, he is the slayer of Vṛtra, the obstructing Asura, striking him down effectively.
Furthermore, toward the sacrificer who serves him, that Indra—being truthful, virtuous, or of an unfailing nature—is the protector and guardian of the one who serves.
Since all rules are optionally applied in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply here for the object (*karman*).

O Priyamedhas, worship this Indra with a concentrated mind—he who has become truly worthy of honor through the Soma juices. 37. Worship him, O Priyamedhas; [worship] Indra with a concentrated mind; he who has become [so]; through the Somas; truly worthy of honor. 37.
"Priyamedhāḥ": those for whom the sacrifice (medha) is dear (priya) and favorable; they are so called. The plural number is used for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*) regarding the self.
The seer named Priyamedha speaks, addressing himself:
"O Priyamedhas, with a mind that is *satrāc*—that is, accompanied by Indra who is worthy of praise—worship, that is, sacrifice to, this very Indra with your heart;
that is to say, perform the sacrifice with deliberate intent."
In the phrase "yajadhvainam" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.43), there is the elision of the vowel due to the use of a particle.
That Indra, by means of the *soma* offerings serving as instruments, becomes one who truly eats—that is, one whose eating is not false.

O Kaṇvas, sing forth to the one renowned through song, the lord of the virtuous, who desires glory, the one of vast majesty, the possessor of strength. 38. O Kaṇvas, sing forth to the one renowned through song, the lord of the virtuous, who desires glory, the one of vast majesty, the possessor of strength. 38.
1. It is heard as *kha-śa-ta-i*; it is heard as *gha-na-śa-iti*.
2. The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is among the virtuous (*satsu*) [as] *jha-ta-na-śa*.
3. By means of those things which have become the causes (*kāraṇabhūtaiḥ*), namely *kha-ta-bha*.
O *Kaṇavāsas*, sons of *Kaṇa*, whose guests are the rams—
this is an address to himself using the plural form for the first person:
"O sons of *Kaṇa*, you who have rams as guests, [you have honored] *Gāthaśravas*, whose glory is to be sung, the lord of the virtuous (*satpati*), who desires renown."
Sing praises to that Indra who possesses a desire and longing for the sounds of the chants and the oblations;

to him who is "purumān"—the Brahman-Self—or rather, who extends widely and constantly through many regions; and to him who is "vājin," possessed of impetuous speed—to him endowed with such qualities, sing! Praise him!
The powerful one who, apart from the dwelling places of the waters, bestows everything upon men,
for those who find their desire and prosperity in him.
He who, though without tracks, is the powerful friend who gives cattle to men, for those who have fixed their desire upon him. 39.

When the cows had been carried away by the Paṇis, Indra—who is a friend, who is powerful, and whose deeds are praiseworthy—bestowed back the cows for the sake of the *nṛ*s (leaders), that is, the gods, even without the tracks (*padébhyas*) left on the path by the departing cattle which served as a means of discovery;
and to those gods who, in this Indra, cherished and attained their desire (*kāma*), he gave them [the cows]. This is the syntactical connection.
"Let him go to that Indra"—this forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding [verse].
Thus, O wielder of the stone, you have favored the wise Kaṇva, my guest; for, becoming a ram, you went toward me.
Thus, O wielder of the stone, [I have praised] the wise Kaṇva Medhyātithi; like a ram, he has come hither against the noble one. 40.

O wielder of the thunderbolt (adrivaḥ), having become a ram (meṣaḥ) and approaching (abhīyan)—that is, assuming the form of a ram—[you went] toward Medhyātithi, the son of Kaṇva (kāṇvam), the seer known by that name, who was endowed with wisdom (dhīvantam) and possessed of hymns of praise (stutimantam), in this very manner (itthā ittham) as described.
The word "yaḥ" (who) is understood from the context; due to its connection [with the verb], there is no suppression of the accent (nighātābhāvaḥ).
The meaning is: "We praise you, who brought him [Medhātithi] here.

A Brāhmaṇa passage, which serves as an explanation of a portion of the Subrahmaṇyā mantra—"medhātither imam" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.12.3)—is recited by the Chandogas: "For, having become a ram, he carried off Medhātithi, the son of Kaṇva" (Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 1.1).
It is with reference to this that the present hymn of praise was composed.
Śikṣā Vibhindu gave him forty thousand and eight thousand cities.
O Vibhindu, you have bestowed upon him four times ten thousand and eight thousand cities.
Having obtained wealth from King Vibhindu, [the poet] praises his gift with this first verse:
O King Vibhindu, you, being a giver (*dadat*), have bestowed (*śikṣa*—that is, *aśikṣaḥ*, "you gave") four *ayutāni*—that is, four times ten thousand, or forty thousand—to this great seer;
furthermore (*paraḥ*), even beyond that, you have given eight thousand.
And indeed, those two who increase the milk, the unaging ones,
have bestowed upon me the power of manly joy and the capacity for procreation.
And indeed, those two who increase the milk, the two who delight in joy, have been magnified by me as the wives of the one who brings forth.

1. The self of the person [is] the measure of *kha-bha-puta*; the self of the person [is] the crossing over of *jha-kṣa-tara* (twice, thrice, four times); the self of Brahman [is] the measure of *ta-na-puta*.
2. In *kha-na-bha-śa*, "hi" does not exist; in *ta3-pa.brā.*, it is "ha".
And moreover, those two well-known [deities], increased by milk—that is, to be nourished by water (*payas*)—are to be made manifest (*mākī*) for the delight (*raṇasya*) of the multitude of beings.
This is the name of the singer.

I have praised (*mamahe*) for the sake of manifestation and acquisition—the generation of the aforementioned wealth—for *dyāvāpṛthivī* (Heaven and Earth), who are never to be made to fail (*napyāu*, from *napātavyau*), whose nature is constant favor, and who are the source of progeny (*janivanāya*).
One should understand that this praise of the greatness of the gift implies that such a gift is obtained only when Heaven and Earth are pleased, and not otherwise.
"Pibā sutasya" (Drink of the pressed juice) is the third hymn, consisting of twenty-four verses, composed by Medhyātithi, the descendant of Kaṇva.

The odd-numbered verses are Bṛhatīs, and the even-numbered verses are Satobṛhatīs; the twenty-first and twenty-third verses are Anuṣṭubhs, and the twenty-second and twenty-fourth verses are Gāyatrīs; the twenty-fourth verse is a Bṛhatī.
These four [hymns] are praises of the gifts of King Pākasthāman, the son of Kurayāṇa;
therefore, they have him as their deity.
The remaining ones have Indra as their deity.
And thus it has been enumerated: "Drink [the soma]; the twenty-four [verses] are for the pure guest; the *pragātha* is in *anuṣṭubh* and *gāyatrī*, while the others are in *bṛhatī*;

it is a praise of the gift by Pākasthāman, the son of Kaurayāṇa. In the *niṣkevalya* section of the *mahāvrata*, this hymn is excluded from the *bārhatatṛcāśīti*, as are the seventh and eighth verses.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "In the hymn beginning with 'pibā sutasya rasinaḥ,' one omits the seventh and eighth verses" (*Ai. Ā. 5.2.4*).
In the *Niṣkevalya* section of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the first *rathantara-sāman-pragātha* is to be recited;
for it is prescribed: "'pibā sutasya rasinaḥ' is the *sāman-pragātha*" (*Āśva. Śrau. Sū. 5.15*).
This *pragātha* is also prescribed for the *niṣkevalya* chant on the twenty-fourth day;
for it is stated: "The [verse] 'ukto rathantarasya' is for the *rathantara*, and 'ubhayaṃ śṛṇavacca naḥ' is for the *bṛhat*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.3).
Thus, elsewhere as well, wherever the *pṛṣṭha* stotra consists of the *rathantara*, this *pragātha* is to be understood as applicable in all such cases.
On the fifth day, in the *prauga-śastra*, there is this *pragātha* addressed to Indra beginning with "Drink of the pressed [juice]":
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Pibā sutasya rasino devadevaṃ voḍvase’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
Drink of the pressed, flavorful juice; intoxicate us, O Indra, with the milk-mixed [draught]. Be mindful of us as your companions at the feast, for our increase. May your insights protect us. 1.
Drink of the pressed juice, O Indra; exhilarate yourself with our draught rich in cattle. Be mindful of us as our companions at the feast for our prosperity; may your thoughts protect us. 1.

O Indra, drink this our pressed (suta) Soma, which is rich in essence, full of flavor, and mixed with milk and other products of the cow used as mixing substances (śrayaṇa-dravya). The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because the object of the action is treated as a recipient, according to the rule "the mention of the action [as a verb] must be made. Drink such Soma as this.
And having drunk, be exhilarated;

moreover, as one who shares the feast (*sadhamādya*), who is to be gladdened together with us and to be satisfied by us, being our *āpi*—a kinsman who provides—be for our increase, that is, awaken yourself for our prosperity. May your thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*), your intellects characterized by grace, protect and guard us, your praisers.
May we, as victors, abide in your favor; do not abandon us to the malice of the enemy. Protect us with your manifold aids during our sacrifices, and lead us toward your gracious intentions.
May we, as possessors of strength, abide in your gracious favor; do not deliver us over to the adversary. Protect us with your manifold aids, and lead us toward your benevolence. 2.

O Indra, may we, possessing strength and offering oblations, abide within your auspicious favor—that is, within your benevolent intention. For the sake of the adversary—one who intends harm—we pray that you do not strike us; do not harm us.
The root *stṛṅ* means "to injure.
[In the phrase] *mā hiṃsi*, the *aorist* (*luṅ*) ending is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa-śleṣ*).
Rather, [it is used] with *abhiṣṭibhiḥ* (by means of invocations). *Abhyeṣṇī-*...
1. *ta-śa-medhātithe*; 2. *jha-ta1-2-4-kurayāṇasya*; 3. *kha-bha-yajñe*; 4. *jha-ta1-2-bhavema*.
With those desirable, wonderful (*citrābhiḥ*), or manifold (*bahuvighābhiḥ*) aids (*ūtibhiḥ*) of yours, protect (*avata*) us;
guard us. Likewise, lead us (*ā yāmaya*) toward excellent fields (*sukṣetreṣu*).
Always make them happy indeed.
O Lord of abundant wealth, may these songs of mine cause you to grow strong upon the mountain; the pure, wise ones, radiant as fire, have celebrated you with their hymns of praise.
These—Om!—may my songs, O Puruvasu, increase thee; these pure, purifying-colored, and wise words have sung aloud with hymns of praise. 3.
O Indra, possessor of abundant wealth (*puruvasu*), may these my songs—these words in the form of *śaśa*—increase and magnify you.
Likewise, may they, possessing a purifying color (*pāvakavarṇa*) with a brilliance equal to fire, and therefore pure (*śuci*), do so for you.

Indra by his might spread out the two great worlds; Indra caused the sun to shine. To Indra indeed all beings have submitted; to Indra flow the pressed drops. 6. Indra; great; the two worlds; he spread out; by his strength; Indra; the sun; he caused to shine. To Indra; indeed; all; beings; have submitted; to Indra; the pressed; drops. 6.
This Indra, by the greatness—the vastness—of his own power (*śavas*), caused the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), to expand; he spread them out.
Likewise, this very Indra caused the sun, which had been enveloped by Svarbhānu, to shine;
by slaying that Asura, he made it manifest.
Moreover, in this very Indra, all—the entire range of worlds, that is, all created beings—have taken their rest;
the meaning is that they are governed by Indra.
Likewise, the *indavas*, the Soma drops being pressed and purified, are also governed by this very Indra; the meaning is that they are contained within him.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, if the Rathantara-sāman is used as the *pṛṣṭha*, then men call after him with the *niṣka*;
they praise in regular succession.
"‘Pūrvathā’:
the suffix *thā* is applied according to the rule *apratnapūrva-* etc., in the sense of the word *pūrva*.
The meaning is: just as they praised in former times, so too do they praise now in that very same sequence."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, at the midday pressing during the Brahmasattra, the *pragātha* beginning with "tat tvā yāmi" serves as the *anurūpa*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The two *pragāthas*, 'tat tvā yāmi' and 'suvīryam', are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.16).
On the twenty-fourth day (*cāturviṃśika*) as well, at the midday pressing, this same *pragātha* serves as the *anurūpa* for that very [stotra].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘I approach that one of excellent heroism; [I praise] you, the most bountiful’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
I implore that heroic power and that sacred prayer for primordial awareness,
by which you helped the Yatis and Bhṛgu when wealth was at stake, and by which you rescued Praskaṇva.

I beg of you that heroic power; I beg of you that sacred prayer for the sake of first thought—that by which you helped the Yatis and Bhr̥gu when wealth was staked, and by which you protected Praskaṇva. || 9 ||
O Indra, I entreat you for that "su-vīryam"—excellent heroic power.
(The elision of the vowel is a Vedic [chāndasa] usage.
Likewise, I entreat you for that "brahma"—abundant food—for the sake of "pūrva-cittaye," that is, for prior wisdom or for obtaining it before others.

"When there is wealth that is beneficial and desired, by means of which heroic power you bring wealth from those who have ceased their ritual acts— the *yatayas*, people who do not sacrifice— and bestow it upon the great seer Bhṛgu;
or alternatively,
the *Aṅgirases* who are disciplined in their rituals are the *yatayas*."

You bestow wealth for their sake; the dative case is used here in the sense of "for the purpose of" (tādarthye). And with that Vedic knowledge (*brahman*) by which you protected—that is, guarded—Praskaṇva, the seer who was the son of Kaṇva and descended from Kaṇva.
The syntactical connection is: "I request both of those."
That by which you released the great waters toward the ocean—that, O Indra, is your manly power.
That greatness of his is not to be attained at once, he whom the two worlds have cried out after in praise.
That by which you released the great waters toward the ocean—that, O Indra, is your manly power. That majesty of yours has not been equaled; it is that after which the worlds have cried out. 10.
O Indra, by means of that power which is your own, you released—that is, you poured forth—the great, vast waters into the ocean.
The meaning is that in former times you created as much water as fills the great ocean with its waves.
That strength of yours is indeed *vṛṣṇi*, meaning "rain-bestowing" or "fecundating."
The meaning is that it bestows the desired fruit.
"His," that is, Indra's, "māhātmya" (greatness) "na saṃnaśe"—it is not to be fully grasped;
the meaning is that it is unassailable by others.
The suffix *ken* is used in the sense of a future passive participle (*kṛtya*) after the root *naś*. "That greatness which the earth—the earth being the world—*anucakrade*, that is, follows.
Here, the root *kad* has the meaning of "going" (*gati*).
The meaning is that [something] exists dependent upon that.
Be gracious to us, O Indra, as I seek you for wealth and heroic strength;
be gracious to the prize-winning hero who strives for the first place, and be gracious to our hymn of praise, O Primordial One.

Be gracious to us, O Indra, when I entreat you for wealth and heroic strength. Be gracious to the prize-winning power that strives first for the booty; be gracious to our hymn of praise, O Ancient One. 11.

1. *kha-tan-na-bha*: by our own; 2. *kha-samyamāsanīyaḥ*; *jña-ta1-2-na-bha*: to be properly removed; *ta3-śa*: to be completely pervaded. O *indra*, [bestow] *suvīryam*, that which is endowed with excellent heroic power.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the final member of the word according to the rule "ajir-vīryau ca.
The word *yat* refers to wealth (*rayiṃ dhanam*), which I (*svām*) solicit (*yāmi*).
The elision of a phoneme here is archaic (*chāndasa*).
"Give us that wealth"—
the root *śak* here has the sense of "giving";
therefore, in the imperative second person singular (*loṭ*), there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by Vedic license (*chāndasa*).
In the word *huśalbhyah*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs.

Likewise, in *sipāsate*, meaning "he desires to honor," from the root *san* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), there is optionally the absence of *it* by the rule *manī-vantardhaṃ*; consequently, by the rule *janasanakhanām*, there is the substitution of *āt*.
"Vājāya": *vāja* is a name for food;
by that, its acquisition is indicated.
O Agni, first of all— before anyone else— grant wealth to the sacrificer who possesses the oblation;
or rather,
for the sake of the person who desires to enjoy you through his ritual acts (where the dative *vājāya* functions as an accusative), grant and bestow food (*vāja*) upon him.
Afterwards, for the sake of praise—that is, for the hymn—O ancient Indra, who existed in former times, O nourisher, be gracious and grant [us]!
In the word *stoma*, the suffix *man* is applied after the root *stu* according to the rule beginning with "arti-tusi-".
Be pure for us, O Indra, since you have protected the prayer of this man who desires to offer worship;
be pure, just as you, O Indra, protected Ruśama, Iyāvaka, and Kṛpa, and favored Svarṇara.

Be gracious to us, O Indra, for you have protected Paura; be gracious to the prayers of him who desires to worship. Be gracious, just as you, O Indra, protected Ruśama, Iyāvaka, and Kṛpa, and [rescued] Svarṇara.

O Indra, grant— that is, bestow— upon us that wealth of this sacrificer who belongs to us, we who desire to perform *dhī*s (devotions), deeds, or hymns of praise. Indeed, with that very wealth by which you protected Paura—
the son of the king named Puru— you have preserved him.
Moreover, O Indra, just as you protected the three royal seers named Ruśama, Iyāvaka, and Kṛpa, so likewise grant power to Svarṇara— the leader and bringer of all oblations— or rather,
empower this sacrificer who is to be led toward heaven (svaḥ).
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that you become capable of performing sacrifices through the attainment of wealth and other resources according to your power.

Since *indra* is addressed as a vocative at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no application of the eighth [rule] which would cause its depression (*nighāta*); instead, the vocative accent prescribed by the sixth [rule] applies, whereby the first syllable is acute (*udātta*).

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), during the *brahma-śastra*, there is the *kadvat-pragātha* beginning with "akanvyaḥ. This is stated in the Sūtra: "The *kadvat* *pragāthas* are 'akanvyas,' 'atasīnām,' and 'syākṛtam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
On the second and subsequent days of the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices, this *pragātha* belongs to that very day;
for it is stated: "The *ārambhaṇīyā*s, the *paryāsa*s, and the *kadvat* *aharahaḥ-śastra*s—the *hotraka*s [recite these] on the second and subsequent days only" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.1).
The mortal who praises the swift one among the Kanvas shall eat of them;
now indeed, extolling his greatness and Indra-power, they have followed after him with songs.
The mortal who praises him—the swift one—shall indeed now proclaim his greatness, his Indra-power; chanting the light of heaven, they have sung his praise. 13.

"Who indeed, a mortal subject to death, a new one—meaning a contemporary of today—could praise Indra? Who, a singer, could extol him? The meaning is that Indra cannot be praised by those of little wisdom belonging to the present time. [The root] *gṛ* is used in the sense of "to sound" (to praise). *Atasīnām*: of praises; *atantīnām*: of those that are not stretched out (uninterrupted); *matatagāminīnām*: of those that proceed in succession; *turaḥ*: the impeller or prompter; *martyaḥ*: a mortal; *navyaḥ*: new, i.e., contemporary; *kaṅkuḥ*: who indeed; *gṛṇīta*: would praise. The sense is that Indra cannot be praised by those of limited intellect belonging to the present day. The root *gṛ* signifies "sound" (praise).
[The root] belongs to the *kryādi* class.
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "the vowels of roots beginning with *pū* are shortened.
*Nū*: formerly, even in earlier times; *svaḥ*: all; *guṇantaḥ*: praising, i.e., the singers.
Or rather:
people, praising— that is, extolling— Indra, who is *svaḥ*, meaning "well to be chosen" or "to be attained," [attain] *indriyam*.
The *indriya* is the mark of Indra; it belongs exclusively to Indra.
They truly did not attain his greatness, the majesty of this Indra.
In the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *abh*, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used by way of grammatical substitution.
By the rule "ata ādeḥ," there is the substitution of ā for the first letter of the reduplicated syllable;
by "abhoteśca," the augment nuṭ is added;
and by "hi ca," there is no prohibition of the nighāta (anudātta accent).

1. *jha-ta1-2-tvā* tvā | 2. *jha-ta1-2-4-śakya* | When praising, who among the seers strives for the gods? Which inspired poet (*vipra*) honors them? O Maghavan Indra, when will you come to the call of the one who presses the juice? When will you come to the one who praises? (14) *kat* | *ūm* | *stuvantaḥ* | *ṛtayanta* | *devatā* | *ṛṣiḥ* | *kaḥ* | *vipraḥ* | *ohate* | *kadā* | *havam* | *maghavan* | *indra* | *sunvataḥ* | *kat* | *ūm* | *stuvataḥ* | *ā* | *gamaḥ* || 14 ||
O Indra, who indeed are those people praising you, performing hymns of praise? "Devatā" is formed by adding the suffix *tal* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*);
the nominative case is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Aiming for you, O God, they have sought the truth; they desired the sacrifice of Truth.
Even the desire for your sacrifice is difficult to attain, let alone the prospect of reaching you.
Who is the seer, the observer, the wise sage—the singer who bears [the hymn] aloft?
It brings hymns of praise to you;
the meaning is that no one at all is able to praise you.
Since this is so, for that reason, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, you yourself must come as a bestower of grace.

As such, when—at what time—did you come to the invocation of the sacrificer who presses the soma? That is, when did you approach the call? And when—at what time—did you come to the invocation of the sacrificer who merely offers praise? That is, when did you approach the call?
In both instances, "of the one pressing" (*sunvataḥ*) and "of the one praising" (*stuvataḥ*), the case ending is acute according to the rule *śaturanumaḥ*.
In *gamerluṅi*, because it belongs to the *lṛdita* class, there is the substitution of *caleḥ*.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), during the Brahma-śastra, the *pragātha* "udu tye" is to be recited as the subsequent response (*anurūpa*).
This is stated in the Sūtra: "udu tye madhumattamā indraḥ pūrbhit" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.16).
In the Caturviṃśa sacrifice, at the same midday pressing and in that very same Śastra, this *pragātha* is an optional response.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, these most honey-sweet [Soma drops] have been poured forth" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).

These most honey-sweet songs, these hymns of praise, go forth—like chariots seeking booty, ever-conquering with their wealth, and possessing unfailing aid. 15. Out! Indeed! These most honey-sweet songs, these hymns of praise, go forth—ever-conquering with their wealth, possessing unfailing aid, and seeking booty like chariots. 15.

These well-known, most honey-sweet— that is, exceedingly sweet— *giraḥ*, which are unchanted utterances in the form of *śastra*s, and the *stomās*, which are chanted hymns such as the *Bahiṣpavamāna* and others,
arise; O Indra, they rise up directed toward you, spreading upward.
The root *īr* means "to go"; it belongs to the *adādi* class. In this regard, there is an illustration.

Satrājita, conquering his enemies along with them, and for that very reason *dhanasāḥ*, i.e., sharing wealth; [the root] *vana* and *ṣaṇa* are used in the sense of "sharing" (*saṃbhakti*). [The suffix] *viṭ* is applied after the roots *jan*, *san*, *khan*, *kram*, and *gam*.
The substitution of *ā* [for *u*] occurs by the rule “*viḍunnoranunāsikasyāt*” (Pāṇini 6.4.19).
"Those whose aids (*ūtayaḥ*) are undecaying" means those whose protections (*rakṣāḥ*) are undecaying (*akṣitāḥ*), that is, free from destruction.
The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) of the root *kṣi*.
Due to the exclusion [of this case] by the rule *niṣṭhāyāmaṇyadarthe*, there is an absence of lengthening;
for this very reason, by the rule *kṣiyo dīrghāt*, there is also an absence of the status of being a *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix.
*Vājayantaḥ* means seeking after *vāja* (sacrificial food or strength).
In the case of *kyac*, there is a prohibition against the substitution of *it* and lengthening by the rule "na cchandasyaputrasya.
Thus, they are like chariots distinguished by their excellence;
just as those [chariots] rise up here and there in various ways, so too do these [words] resound—this is the meaning.
Through the Kaṇvas and the Bhr̥gus, like the Sūryas, they have attained all that is to be attained;
the Āyus have urged Indra with their hymns of praise, and the Priyamedhas have raised their voices.

1. Kha, Na, Bha, Devatāmu; 2. Kṣa, Māhānam pratyā; 3. Ja, Pratigacchaḥ; Śa, Atigacchaḥ; 4. Kha, Pragāthaḥ vaikalpiko 'nurūpāntaram; 5. Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, Śa, Ādādikaḥ; 6. Kha, Ta, 3, Na, Bha, Sadaiiva.
Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhṛgus, like the Sūryas—they have attained all that was intended. Exalting Indra with hymns of praise, the Āyus, possessing dear splendor, have sung aloud. (16)

Like the Kaṇvas—ṛṣis born of the Kaṇva lineage—and like the Bhṛgus—ṛṣis born of the Bhṛgu lineage—who offer praise, they have attained (ānaśuḥ), that is, pervaded (viśvamit vyāptam), that very Indra with their meditative thought (dhītam ādhyātam). Like the suns: just as the rays of the sun pervade the entire world, so too [did they].

Moreover, the *priyamedhas*—those of beloved wisdom, or humans known by that name—the *āyavas*, praising and honoring that very Indra with hymns (*stomaiḥ*), sang his praises; [the root] *as* is used here in the sense of "to sound" or "to praise. It belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
Yoke, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, your two bay steeds from afar;
come hither, O Maghavan, for the drinking of Soma, O fierce one, accompanied by the seers.

O Vṛtra-slayer, most excellent among slayers, yoke your two bay steeds, O Indra, from the far distance! Come hither toward us— like the sun in the sky, rushing upward as it were, endowed with radiance and swift-moving.
The meaning is that it is the most excellent in beauty.

Pākasthāman has given me a red horse, well-yoked, filling out its girth, a bringer of wealth that awakens the mind. 22. Red. To me. Pākasthāman. Well-yoked. Girth-filling. Has given. Of wealth. Awakener. 22.
King Pākasthāman gave to me—me—to a red-colored bull or horse;
of what kind?
One with a beautiful yoke, that is, one with a beautiful place for bearing the burden.

The suffix *ak* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74). Furthermore, by the rule *ṛvādayaśca*, the initial syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is acute-accented. [Thus one says] *kakṣyaprām*.
*Kakṣyā* refers to the strap being fastened around the two *kakṣas*, that is, the armpits (*bāhumūla*). It means the one who has spread it out— that is, the one who has made it thick.
