*Prā* means "in filling. *Rāyaḥ* means "of wealth. *Vibodhanam* means "an awakener," specifically that which makes one aware;
the meaning is: "the cause for the attainment of abundant wealth."
By the rule beginning with "udidam," the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.

For whom ten other draft-animals draw at the yoke, as birds carry Tugrya to his home. 23. For whom; others; ten; toward; the yoke; they draw; the draft-animals; home; birds; like; the son of Tugra. 23.
The horse previously mentioned is further qualified: "for whom.
Here, the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

The yoke—that which is to be borne by a horse or a bull—refers to the pole of the yoke. Other than this subject at hand, ten distinct substitutes—either horses or oxen who are the bearers—being present, carry or sustain me.
This is an illustration of expressing plurality in the singular.
*Astaṃ*.

*As-tam* means "the house" because the collection of objects (*padārthajāta*) is cast or thrown (*asyate*) into it. *Prati-vayo-na-gantāraḥ* refers to horses that do not go back; just as [the gods] carried Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, from the shore of the ocean, even so [the horse carried me]. Such a horse he gave to me—this is the connection with the preceding verse.
And that [chariot] was carried by *bhujyu*, as should be understood from such passages as "O Nāsatyas, you carried Bhujyu" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.116.4).
Alternatively, the dative case in *yasmai* is used in the sense of the object;
the meaning is: "He gave me such a chariot as ten other draft-animals—ten horses—having gone toward the *dhur* (the yoke-end), carry their own burden."

The self of the father, the body, the garment, the giver of vigor, the ointment—this indeed is the fourth [portion] of the ruddy one: the matured state, the enjoyer, the giver, the food. 24. Self. Of the father. Body. Garment. Giver of vigor. Ointment. Fourth. Indeed. Of the ruddy one. Matured-state. Enjoyer. Giver. Food. 24.
Now, Pākasthāmā was himself the son (tanaya) of his father Janaka;
the meaning is that just as his father was praiseworthy for walking upon the path of the righteous, so too was he.
Likewise, he was a *vāsa*, one who causes others to dwell or provides them with shelter.
The suffix *asun* is applied to the root *vās* according to the *Uṇādi* rules. "Ojodāḥ" means one who bestows or sustains *ojas*, that is, strength;
or alternatively:
The self is the ever-moving;
"father" is a name for food;
by whom the food is pervaded when it is given.
I have found Pākasthāman, who gave a garment spread wide, an ointment, and the means for anointing such as clarified butter and oil;
who is a giver of vigor and strength;

who is the fourth (turīya) in relation to his own great-grandfather, or rather the one who overcomes (turvaka) and destroys enemies; the liberal one (bhoja) who causes his foes to suffer; the giver of the aforementioned red-colored horse (rohitasya); such is Pākasthāman, endowed with these qualities—him I have found.
I praised in the manner described.
The word "hither" (ita) is a filler.
The fourth hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with “yad indra,” is the seerly work (ārṣam) of Devātithi of the Kaṇva lineage.
The verse beginning with “vṛkṣāścin me” is a Purauṣṇih; the remaining uneven-numbered verses are Bṛhatīs, characterized by their metrical structure and the presence of the word *bhuja*.
Because the gift of Kuruṅga is praised in the three verses beginning with “sthūraṃ rādhaḥ,” those verses have him as their deity.

Preceding that, those beginning with the fifteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] belong to five deities or to Indra as their deity. 1. On both sides (kha-pārśvayoḥ). 2. ta3—indicative; śa—sublating. The Fifth Aṣṭaka.
The remaining [verses] are dedicated to Indra.

Thus it is stated in the *Ātānūka*: "O Indra, that one verse beginning with 'devātithi' is a *sati* [verse], while the others are *purauṣṇih* at their end; they are praises of the gift of Kurukṣa, preceded by [the word] *tapu*, and four of them are dedicated to Pūṣan."
In the Mahāvrata, fourteen verses from the Niṣkevalya hymn belonging to the Bṛhat-saṃhitā collection are to be recited by the Ādhvaryu.
Likewise, in the Pañcamāraṇyaka it is stated: "The fourteen [verses] beginning with 'yad indra prāg apāk udak' (AiĀ 5.2.4).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the first Pragātha in the Acchāvāka's Śastra is optionally the Stotriya.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, as [the bull] goes to the east, to the west, or to the north, so [is] the deed performed by the Gaura" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
O Indra, when you are invoked by men from the east, the west, the north, or the south—with your helmet on, urged by many heroes—you are for the Anu people; O bold one, you are for Turvaśa.

O Indra, whether you are invoked by men from the east, the west, the north, or the south—you are the one who bestows joy, impelled by many heroes; you belong to the Ānava, and you are the bold champion for the Turvaśa.
O Indra, [whatever is] by those situated in the east (*prāk*), in the eastern direction—

the *añc* suffix having been elided according to Pāṇini 5.3.30, *añceluk*, following the rule for the locative case ending (*astāti*) after words meaning "connected with" (*sasambandha*) such as *adhika*—
or by those situated in the west (*apāk*), in the western direction.
Or [the word *udak*] is used by those situated in the northern direction (*udīcī dik*);
or [the word *nyak*] is used by those situated below in the downward direction (*nīcī dik*).
In the case of *nyak*, the original accent of the prefix *ni-* is maintained according to the rule "nyadhī ca."
By the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the following unaccented (anudātta) vowel becomes circumflex (svarita).
By such men—by these worshippers—you are invoked; you are called for your respective tasks, O Sima, O most excellent Indra.
Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: "They call the most excellent one 'Sima'."
Even though you are thus invoked by many, nevertheless, O Ānava—
Ānu being the name of a king—
you exist as Puru, the royal seer, being impelled (*nṛṣūta*) among men, that is, urged on by his own human singers.
The meaning is that the praisers urge you toward performing what is beneficial for the king.
[This is derived from] the root *pū* in the sense of "urging";
from this, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed in the passive sense.

In the phrase "tṛtīyā karmaṇi," there is the preservation of the original accent (prakṛtisvara) of the preceding word. Furthermore, O *praśardha*—O Indra, you who are exceedingly bold and a conqueror—you are *nṛpūta*, impelled by men, for the sake of Turvaśa, the king known by that name.
Or whether you delight yourself with Ruma, Ruśama, Śyāvaka, Kṛpa, O Indra, or with Kaṇva—the Kaṇvas, bringing hymns of praise along with sacred prayers, invite you; O Indra, come hither!
Whether with Ruma, Ruśama, Śyāvaka, or Kṛpa, O Indra, you take your delight; the Kaṇvas, bringing hymns of praise along with their sacred prayers, draw you hither, O Indra—come!

Or rather: although, O Indra, you rejoice together with the four kings, Ruma and the others, nevertheless the Kaṇvas—the seers of the Kaṇva lineage who bring hymns—draw you toward them with their powerful mantras; that is, they cause you to come. Or else, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative.
With the *brahmā* verses they offer and give the *brahma*-oblations by means of the *abhisutya* [soma-pressing].
[The root] *dāṇ* means "to give. The substitution of *yaccha* is according to the rule beginning with *pāghrā*.
Therefore, come quickly; "ā gahi" means "come hither. The elision of the *śap* suffix after the root *gam* is a Vedic (chāndasa) irregularity.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the *pragātha* beginning with "yathā" serves as the *anurūpa* for the *acchāvāka* recitation.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘yathā gauro apā kṛtam’ is for the *acchāvāka*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
As the thirsty stag longs for water made clear by the clouds, come quickly to us at the beginning and at the end of the journey; drink well among the Kaṇvas.
As a thirsty bull goes down to a pool dug by royal seers, so come to us at evening and at dawn; drink well among the Kaṇvas, O Turya! Drink well together with them! 3.
The wild ox (*gauramṛga*) is thirsty, desiring to drink with its mouth [filled] with waterless [flesh].
There is a singular number used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is according to the rule beginning with *uḍidam*.
When the field has been prepared, made complete, cleared of weeds, and made free of grass, one understands by what means and in what manner the water flows;
the word *ava* is used in the sense of the word *abhi*.
Being directed toward it, he goes quickly. Thus, when the time for sowing, kinship, and the arrival of the rains has come, O Indra, do thou protect us swiftly.
This is a call for speed:
come quickly!
And having come, O Kaṇva, drink well all the Soma that exists among us—the sons of Kaṇva—with our shared effort and in unison.
O Maghavan, may these Soma drops exhilarate you, Indra, for the granting of wealth to the one who presses them.
You drank that pressed juice from the vessel; you have established yourself as the supreme subduer of power.
May they exhilarate you, O Maghavan!
O Indra, may these Soma drops, which are for you and are like cutting tools, exhilarate you, intoxicate you, and gladden you.
The *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of honorific address.
For what purpose?
For the sake of bestowing wealth (*rādhas*), that is, for the purpose of giving riches to the sacrificer who presses the Soma.
From the root *dadāti*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *aco yat*.

The vowel *i* [of the suffix] is substituted by the rule *indhī* (Pāṇini 6.4.25). Since the suffix is marked with *y*, it is udātta according to the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*; thus, the word retains the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).

In the word *śatrunamaḥ*, the case-ending following the word *śatru* is acute. Furthermore, having committed an act of seizing against that person—having forcibly snatched away even what was not given—you drank the *soma*. This is according to the Vedic text: "Having caused the destruction of the sacrifice, he drank the *soma* by force" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4.12.1).
What kind of Soma? Pressed (*suta*),
that is, extracted, upon the two *camū*—
the two pressing-boards.
The Soma has been pressed for you by the two aged ladles (*camasa*) belonging to the *hotṛ* and the *maitrāvaruṇa*, prepared by the flowing streams.
Because it is thus, O Indra, you possess the most excellent, most praised, or greatest strength (*sahas*).
Therefore, may even my own Soma-draughts exhilarate you—this is the prayer offered.
By his might he has created power; with his breast he has shattered the fury of the enemy.
O Indra, O youth, all those who sought to attack thee have been brought low, like trees that have been felled.
By his might he overcame might; with his breast he shattered the fury [of the foe]. O Indra, O Youthful One, all those who strove against you bowed down like trees. 5.
That Indra, by means of his own *sahas*—that is, by his overcoming power and heroic deed—has *pracakre*, performed pre-eminently the *sahas*, the overcoming of enemies;
likewise, by means of his *ojas*, his strength, he has shattered the *manyu*, the anger of others.
The latter half-verse is addressed in the direct mode (*pratyakṣakṛta*).
"he vyaho.
This is a name for the "Great One" (Mahat).
O Great Indra, all the *pratānāyavaḥ*—that is, all the enemies desiring battle—were *vni vyemire*, meaning they were held fast by you, like trees, like great growing trees.
The meaning is that the disciples became like trees standing motionless.
He indeed accompanies with a thousand those who are younger in battle,
who makes for himself a son, Prāvaga, of great heroism, and who, as a donor, honors me with his offerings.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Jha, Na, and Bha, the word *prapitve* does not exist.
2. [The rule applies] from the manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Ma.
3. [This is] because of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the initial syllable of *iti*.

He attends [the sacrifice] as if with a thousandfold [strength], he who, armed with weapons, has reached your praise; he makes his son preeminent and endowed with great heroism, for he, the giver, honors you with words of adoration.
O Indra, that person who attains (*ānaṭ*)—that is, reaches or brings you to—your *upastuti* (praise or hymn of praise), [he] accompanies (*sacate*) [you];

[the verb] *sacate* means "he comes together with" (*samavaiti*). [The present tense suffix *laṭ* is used here; the *parasmaipada* ending is employed by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the *ātmanepada*.]
"In the assembly.
"By a thousand" means by a force numbering a thousand; that is the sense.
And the sacrificer who, with "utterances of homage"—that is, with words of salutation and hymns—"offers," meaning gives oblations to you.
The root *dāś* means "to give.

That sacrificer, through the grace of the boon (*vara*), produces—that is, brings forth—“a son” who is “endowed with excellent heroism” (*suvīrya*) in battle and who is an “excellent avoider of enemies” (*aprāvargam*).
The meaning is that he obtains [this] by the favor of the boon.
From the root *dā* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
By the rule *upasargasya ghañyamanuṣye* (Pāṇini 6.3.122), there is lengthening of the vowel.
By the rule beginning with *thāthādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), the final syllable of the subsequent member bears the udātta accent.
Alternatively,
"possessing excellent vigor" (*suvīrya*) is an epithet of the son;
the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative.

The word *śobhanavīryam* means "a son of beautiful valor. In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule “*vīravīryoṃ ca*,” there is acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the final member.
Do not fear, do not grow weary in the friendship of you, the fierce one.
We have beheld your great deed, O Bull, worthy of being seen; we have seen Turvaśa and Yadu.
Let us not fear; let us not grow weary in the friendship of you, the fierce one. Great is the deed of yours, the bull, worthy of being proclaimed. May we behold Turvaśa and Yadu. 7.
O Indra, when there is your friendship—the friendship of you, the fierce one of exalted strength—we shall not fear;
let us not be afraid of any enemy whatsoever. Let us not be exhausted; let us not become weary or afflicted.

"O Vṛṣṇi, the showerer of desires, that great and abundant deed of yours—characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and other such acts—is 'abhicakṣyam,' meaning it is to be proclaimed on all sides and is worthy of praise.
Therefore, for those who have attained friendship with you, a being of such sublime power, neither fear nor fatigue arises; this is the sense.
If it is asked how this is known, it is said in reply:"

The meaning is this: "May we see the royal sage named Turvaśa and the one named Yadu living happily through your grace"—indeed, we have already seen them. Therefore, it is logical that fear and the like do not arise for one who has attained friendship with You.
Following the sound, the bull has settled upon his haunch; his gift does not provoke anger.
The cows are blended with honey from the bee-hive; come quickly, run hither, and drink!
Along the flanks he has spread himself; like a bull, his gift does not fail. The cows are blended with honey from the bee-hive. Come quickly, run hither, and drink! 8.
Indra, the showerer of desires, "along" (anu)—

the prefix *anu* being used in the sense of the third case— [covered] "the right other hip," that is, the region of the hip; he "clad himself" (*vavase*) with the left hip, using that very part of his body as a garment.
It covers the entire multitude of beings;
the meaning is that it exists having itself transcended the whole world. And there is another Vedic passage: "When you stood upon the earth with your other thigh" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.32.11).
Moreover, "dānaḥ" means "one who cuts off. [The root] "dān" is used in the sense of "cutting off" (avakhaṇḍana);
[the suffix] "ac" is added according to the rule for roots beginning with "pac" (pacādyac).
And he [Indra] does not harm or injure this person;
[the root] *riṣ* and *ruṣ* mean "to injure.
The meaning is that there is no one at all capable of harming Indra.
Alternatively:

the giver (*dānu*)—the sacrificer who offers oblations—does not provoke the anger of this Indra; that is to say, he does not generate wrath [toward him], but rather serves him at all times with oblations.
The second half-verse is addressed directly [to the deity].
"By the sāragha [honey]": *saraghā* means a honey-bee.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Ta1, Ta4, and Na, the term *parasmaipada* is absent.
2. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, and Da; and Bha, Dā. 3. In manuscript Kha, Da, and Ṣa, *riṣa*.

Through connection with that, [the phrase] "by honey" (*madhvā madhunā*) is an ellipsis of a simile (*lusopama*). Our Soma juices are like cows— producing joy like cows— because they are mixed, touched, and refined by a flavorful curdling substance such as milk, just as if by honey.
Alternatively, from the root *dhiv*, meaning "to please," *dhenavaḥ* means "those who please";
that is, the gratifiers.
Alternatively,
[the word *nābhi*] is derived from the root *ghed* (meaning "to drink") with the suffix *nap*, according to the rule *gheṭa iñ* in the *Uṇādi* list.
By virtue of that same connection, there is also the substitution of the vowel *i*.
The meaning is: "The Soma juices are to be drunk.
For this reason, O Indra, "come quickly" (*ehi*) to our presence.
And having arrived, [he says]: "O Soma, go quickly to that place characterized by the high altar (uttaravedi) where [the oblations] are offered. The verbal root is *du*, meaning "to go."
The lengthening of the vowel is according to the rule *avyādavadyād-dhruvāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.118).
Immediately thereafter, [the sacrificer says] "Drink" the Soma given by the Adhvaryu;
the meaning is: "Fill your own belly thoroughly with that Soma."

The charioteer with horses, the fair-formed one— Indra is indeed your friend here, O Indra. Accompanied by strengthening food that grants nourishment— O Adhvaryu, leader of the sacrifice, do you cause the Soma to flow.
Cause it to reach the location characterized as the *uttaravedi*;
or rather,
cause it to become fluid by its nature as *rasa*.
The meaning is "they press [the Soma].
If one asks for what reason, it is because Indra desires to drink— wishes to consume— this Soma.
If it is asked how this was understood by you, he says in response:
"The two *vṛṣaṇā*, the showerers (of benefits), or the two *harī*, the bay horses, have surely been yoked today;
having approached, the charioteer has harnessed them to the chariot."
And Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of Vṛtra, has indeed come; he has arrived.

The person who offers oblations considers himself to be acting on his own accord when you, O Citta, are satisfied with the Soma. This food of yours is suitable and well-prepared; come toward it, hasten, and drink!

He himself, that person who offers oblations, considers [himself] [as such]; where you, O Indra, are satisfied by the drinking of Soma—this food of yours, worthy and well-poured out, here it is; come toward it, hasten forward, and drink! *Daśuriḥ*: one who gives (*dāśvan*); from the root *dāś*, the suffix *urina* is added according to the Unādi rules. He, the person characterized as a sacrificer, the giver of oblations, "himself indeed" (*svayaṃ cit*)—that is, by his own self alone—"considers," meaning he knows everything; the sense is that his wisdom is not dependent on another. "Where"—in which person—you, O Indra, "are satisfied" (*tṛmpasi*) by the drinking of Soma. The root *tṛp* means "to be satisfied"; it belongs to the Taudādi class. The augment *num* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.1.59.1 (*śe tumpādīnām*). "This" (*idam*), your own (*te*), "worthy" (*yujyam*) or suitable, our Soma-characterized "food" (*annam*), "well-poured out" (*samukṣitam*)—meaning properly poured into the vessels—from the root *ukṣ* "to sprinkle," with the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*). The accent of the prefix remains as its original due to the rule "the preceding element retains its accent. Come toward (*ā ihi*) such Soma that has not set; "hasten forward" (*pra drava*), reach it quickly; immediately after that, "drink" (*piba*), perform the act of drinking.
O Adhvaryu, press the Soma for Indra, you who stand upon the chariot; while performing the sacred prayer, they look toward the one who presses the juice for the giver.

"Having mounted the chariot—O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra! Upon the broad surface of the skin placed for the pressing of the *brahmaṇyas* (the base or root), the pressing-stones shine forth as they themselves press the Soma, performing the sacrifice of the donor. (13) *Ratheṣṭhāya*: "Standing on the chariot" is *ratheṣṭhaḥ*. [The suffix] *kap* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*; [in the compound] *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, there is non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. For such an Indra, O Adhvaryus, press the Soma; that is, extract it by means of pressing (*puñ abhiṣave*). The substitution of *tanap* for the suffix occurs according to the rule *taptanaptanadhanāśca*. *Adhi brahmaṇya ardayaḥ*: "Upon the broad surface"—that is, upon the wide area of the skin (*adri*) placed for the pressing of the *brahmaṇya*, which is the base or root. "Upon" (*adhi*) means above. The other pressing-stones (*adrayaḥ*), situated in the four directions, while "pressing the Soma"—meaning they themselves press the Soma independently of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—which is the sacrifice (*adhvara*) of the donor (*dāśvat*), the sacrificer by which the rite is accomplished—"shine forth," that is, they manifest themselves preeminently. The meaning is that they proceed with great zeal in the pressing of the Soma. Alternatively, the construction may be joined thus: "O Adhvaryus, press the Soma with those stones (*adribhiḥ*)."
May the two beloved bay steeds, O bull-like Indra, bring you toward our sacred prayer;
may they carry you hitherward to this sacrifice, to the soma-pressing that adorns the rite.

The two beloved bay steeds, the showerers of benefits, shall carry Indra to the waters. May they, the ornaments of the sacrifice, bring you hither to the pressing of Soma so that you may hasten hither. 14.
1. *kha-yonā*; *śa-tathā*.
"The atmosphere is Brahman" and "the two favorites" (*vāvātā*) are those who have come into being.
This is a Vedic dual form derived from the root *van* (to desire); it features the elision of the suffixal *niṣṭhā*, the substitution of *ā* for the vowel, and the accent of the verbal root.
In the phrase "anyeṣām api dṛśyate," the lengthening of the vowel is according to the rules of the *saṃhitā* due to repetition (*abhyāsa*). Alternatively, *vāvātā* means she who goes again and again.
The root *vā* is used in the senses of "motion" and "smelling.
From this root, ending in *lu* and followed by *luk*, the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed in the sense of the agent.

"Vṛṣaṇā" means the two testicles or the two scrotums; "harī" refers to the two horses characterized by the aforementioned qualities, which have the nature of carrying [the chariot]. Being such, they [are employed] "in the waters," that is, in our own ritual actions.
The word *apaśabdaḥ* ends in *s* and denotes the object (*karman*).
According to the rule "In the Veda, the elision of [the *s*] of *pīvopasana* should be stated" (Pāṇini 6.3.109.6), the *s* here is elided.
Thus, they two shall "bring near" (*upa-vakṣataḥ*), that is, carry toward or lead up to this *Indra*.
The suffix *leṭ* is applied to the root *vahati*, with the augment *iṭ*. The suffix *sip* is added according to the rule "sibbahulam.

Furthermore, let the "steeds"—those who resort to the sacrifice (*adhvaraśriyaḥ*), meaning those who attend the sacrifice—your other horses, which are by nature swift-moving (*saptayaḥ*), bring you, O Indra, toward us, facing this way (*arvāñcam*), unto each and every pressing (*savanā savanāni*), such as the morning pressing and others connected to our sacrifice; that is, let them cause you to approach.
"It" refers to the inhalation (pūraka).
We choose Pūṣan, the possessor of many riches, for our alliance. O powerful one, invoked by many, O liberator, grant us through our prayer the strength to win wealth.
We choose Pūṣan for our alliance, the possessor of many riches. O Śakra, invoked by many, O deliverer, grant us through our prayer strength for offspring and wealth. 15.
Regarding this, they have said that because the characteristics (*liṅga*) of both Pūṣan and Indra are present, these [verses] are explained in two ways.
We choose—that is, we honor pre-eminently—the "Pūṣan," the nourisher who possesses much wealth (*puruvasu*), or rather, the god known by that name;
for what purpose?
For the sake of union; "yuk" means a companion (sakhā), and its state is "yujyā."

The meaning is "for the sake of friendship. O Śakra, O Puruhūta (one invoked by many), O Vimocana (liberator) from evil—whether you are Indra or Pūṣan—O Saḥ (He), do thou *śikṣa* (teach/instruct) us with thy own *dhiyā* (intellect), desiring to make us capable.
For what purpose?
"For wealth" (*rāye*) means for the sake of obtaining riches. "To strike" (*tuje*) means to conquer or to harm enemies; [it is derived from] the root *tuja* in the sense of "harming.
From this root, the suffix *ken* is applied in the sense of a gerundive (*kṛtya*).
Alternatively,
in the word *rāye*, the dative case is used because [the recipient] is treated as a *saṃpradāna* (indirect object) according to the rule "the mention of an action must be made [in such cases].
The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*).

O Śakra, being pleased by our prayer and hymn of praise, bestow—grant—to us riches and wealth; for you are one whose deeds consist of giving. In the word "udidam," the case-ending of "rāyaḥ" (riches) is udātta.
Sharpen us like a razor in the hands of a barber; grant us wealth, O Deliverer!
In thee alone is that well-known treasure of the dawn found, which thou bestowest upon the mortal man.
Sharpen us like a razor in the hands of a barber; grant us wealth, O Deliverer! That well-known, bovine treasure is with you, for you impel that mortal man [to prosperity]. 16.
O Indra, O Pūṣan, or [you two], "sam śiśīhi" means sharpen us thoroughly; that is, make our intellects sharp.
It is like "bhurij," which is a name for the arms.
It stands like the razor in the arm of a barber.
Moreover, O Vimocana—O deliverer from sin—grant us riches; bestow wealth upon us.
[The root] *rā* is used in the sense of "giving."
For what reason?
Because "ustriyam" indeed refers to you;
"ustrāḥ" means cows.

The construction is as follows: "That wealth" (*tat vasu*) connected with him, which is our "dwelling-place" (*nivāsaka*)—that is, our easily obtainable (*suveda*) treasure, not found among other gods—"which you impel" (*hinosi*) toward each mortal worshiper (*martyam martyam*), that wealth is [to be found] in you. Since this is so, the word "bestow it upon us" (*rāsva*) should be supplied.
I seek you, O Pūṣan, for protection; I seek you, O singer, for aid, O Āghuṇa.
I do not fear his hostility, for that is nothing to you, O Vasu; I praise you for progeny and for the Sāman.

1. *kha-bha-vavātā* | 2. *na-śa-uktalakṣaṇau* | 3. *kha-bha-śiśya*; *śa-tiśya* | 4. *jha-bāhoḥ* | I desire you, O Pūṣan; I desire to praise you, O radiant one. That [desire] is not for a stranger, O Vasu; I praise it for the sake of the sacrifice and the Sāman. 17.
O Pūṣan, nourisher, you who are known by this name, O God, I desire to propitiate you; I long for you.
O Āghṛṇi, you of radiant luster, I desire to praise you; I long to offer hymns to you.
I do not desire, nor do I long for the praise of any other deity besides you.
If one asks, "Why is that?"—
it is because *araṇa* means non-delight, which causes unhappiness;
therefore, the meaning is that I desire to praise you alone.
I praise that Vāsa, the dweller, for the sake of the one who praises him, for the wise one, for the sake of the *sāman* among hymns;
*sāman* here means a hymn (*stotra*),
which is indicated here by its functional equivalence.
"tad te" (that is yours);
or rather,
"pajña" is the name of Kakṣīvat.
For it is recited: "That which the Pañjras invoke over you" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.10).
"To him"—that is, to me, just as to Kakṣīvat;
the sense of comparison is obtained through the force of the context.
"Give the wealth that is required"—this is the ellipsis.
The cows go forth to the pasture, O glowing one; you are our eternal wealth, O immortal Pūṣan. Be gracious to us on our journey, most bountiful for the winning of booty.
Go far away, O glowing one, to some other pasture for the cattle! O immortal Pūṣan, be our constant protector and auspicious friend; be most bountiful for us in the winning of strength. 18.
O glowing one, O radiant one—whether you be Pūṣan or Indra—at some time or other, our cows go forth to graze upon the grass.
O immortal, deathless god, may that wealth consisting of them be forever secure for us;
let it not be harmed by thieves, fear, or other such dangers.
Moreover, O Pūṣan, nourisher, being our protector and guardian, be auspicious—that is, a bringer of happiness.
Likewise, for the winning of *vāja*—that is, for the acquisition of food or strength—be most bountiful, the greatest giver.
We consider the abundant wealth of King Kuruṅga, consisting of a hundred horses, at his celestial sacrifices; indeed, we celebrate it during the delights of this fortunate king among the Turvaśas.
We have meditated upon the abundant wealth of a hundred horses from Kuruṅga, during the divine rites of the king, the radiant and fortunate one, amidst the delights among the Turvaśas. 19.

With this first verse, Devātithi praises the gift of the king named Kuruṅga. [The word] *kuruṅga* [is derived from] *kurutām gacchati* (he goes toward the Kurus) or *kulam gacchati* (he goes to the family).

The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to the rule "it is seen elsewhere as well" (*anyatrāpi dṛśyate*), and it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* class. In the sacrificial rites (*diviṣṭi*)—meaning the seeking of heaven (*div*), which are the causes for its attainment—of such a king (one who is *eṣa*, radiant; *dīpta*, shining; *subhaga*, fortunate; and possessing *śobhana-dhana*, excellent wealth), and while there were delights and gifts in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) among the Turvaśas...
This is a name for humans. The locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Among humans, we have recognized—that is, we have known—the abundant, massive gift (*rādhas*) consisting of a hundred horses (*śatāśva*), joined with a hundred steeds. We have perceived it.
The meaning is "we obtained."
Through the prayers of the powerful Kaṇva, and through the far-reaching, beloved offerings,
the seer has won nourishment, thousands of cattle, and herds of kine beyond measure.
1. Kha-ma-etatsaṃjñaka;
2. To Pārjaka.

With [his] thoughts, the inspired Kaṇva won over the beloved, heaven-reaching [horses] of the prize-winner. Following the thousands, the seer drove forth the herds of cattle from the back [of the mountain]. 20.

I, the seer Devātithi, have driven out—that is, I have fully obtained—all sixty thousand herds of cows that are completely pure (*nirmajān*), which were acquired through the prayers (*dhībhiḥ*) of the wise Medhātithi, the son of Kaṇva, who was possessed of vigor (*vājinaḥ*) and offered oblations (*haviṣmataḥ*); these cows were won by the seers known as Priyamedhas, who were radiant (*abhidyubhiḥ*) and devoted to their worship. (The verb *aja* here means "to go" or "to drive.")
Just as herds of cows were given by the king to the Priyamedhas and the Kaṇvas and accepted by them, so too those given by him are being accepted by me; such is the meaning.

Even the trees rejoiced at my arrival; they shared out the cow with great bounty, they shared out the horse with great bounty. 21. Even the trees rejoiced at my arrival; they shared out the cow with great bounty, they shared out the horse with great bounty. 21.
When that aforementioned wealth had been obtained by me, even the trees themselves resounded; they made a sound. How so? To this he says:
these seers (*ṛṣi*) partook of—that is, they enjoyed and obtained—the cow that is worthy of praise and great.
"They obtained," that is, they acquired, "the great steed worthy of praise.
The singular number in the phrase "village and horse" (*gāmaśvam*) is intended to denote the class (*jāti*).
Alternatively:
*mehanā* is a single word consisting of three syllables: *me*, *iha*, and *neti*.
As Yāska said: “Regarding the verse ‘yad indra citram’: [it means] ‘whatever wonderful, praiseworthy, and great wealth exists;
or whatever is not mine here’—thus there are three middle words” (Nirukta 4.4).
Then it should be explained as follows:
"These sages sacrificed a cow and a horse;
here, in this king, there was no gift of excellent wealth for me, there was none for me"—this is the meaning of what all the people, headed by the trees, proclaimed.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the fifth book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the eighth [maṇḍala] begins to be explained.
In the first anuvāka of the eighth maṇḍala, four hymns have been explained.
The fifth hymn, consisting of thirty-nine verses beginning with "dūrāt," has for its seer Pragātha Ātithi of the Kaṇva lineage.
At the beginning are thirty-six triplets; then two Bṛhatīs;
the last is an Anuṣṭubh.
In the other five hymns, the gift of the Cedi prince named Kaśu is praised;
therefore, they have him as their deity.
The remaining hymns are dedicated to the Aśvins.

And thus it has been enumerated: "From 'dūrāt', forty-one [verses] for Brahmātithi; the Aśvina [śastra] consists of two Bṛhatīs ending in Anuṣṭubhs, with the last five half-verses being a praise of Kaśo’s gift.
In the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra of the Āśvina sacrifice, this hymn is used in the Gāyatrī metre, excluding the other two skins.
For it is stated: "'dūrād ihaiva'—one should omit the last three" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).
1. Kha-citra | 2.

Śa-atha pañcamasyā | From afar, as if from nearby, that which is well-guided, red-hued, and sharpened—[the Maruts] have spread their light in every direction. || 1 || From afar, as if from nearby, that which is well-guided, red-hued, and sharpened—they have spread their light in every direction. || 1 ||
From afar, indeed from a great distance, situated in the eastern region of the sky, she is as if "right here"—as if existing in close proximity.
[This is formed] from the root *ās* with the suffix *śatṛ*; after the elision of *ś* and *u*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*.
The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the feminine noun ending in *śatṛ* is established by the rule *śaturanumaḥ*.
When this Dawn, of ruddy form and shining appearance, has shone forth— that is, when she has caused [the world] to awaken—
she is "established in her color.
This is the form derived from the causative of that root (*varṇ*), in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.

Regarding the phrase "yaduttākṣityam," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent. Then, [the word] "bhānum" means "light" (*dīptim*); "viśvadhā" means "in many ways" (*bahuvidham*); "vy atatanat" means "she has spread out" (*vistāritavatī*).
The suffix *śap* is used by way of transposition (*vyatyayena*) from the root *tan*.
"O Aśvins, you attend to such a dawn"— this forms a single syntactic unit with the following verse.
Alternatively,
during the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), Dawn appeared after being praised by the section concerning Uṣas.
The sentence should be completed by supplying the ellipsis: "O Aśvins, as we are about to recite the hymn to the Aśvins, you two also appear in order to hear the ritual performance."

O Aśvins, destroyers of foes, come hither with your mind-yoked chariot of broad power; attend upon our sacrifice. 2. O Aśvins, destroyers of foes, come hither with your mind-yoked chariot of broad power; attend upon our sacrifice. 2.
"O Aśvins, you who are destroyers (*dastrā*), beautiful to behold, or the subduers of enemies— the form *ākāraḥ* [is used] according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
O Aśvins, you two who act in accordance with men, that is, like leaders (*nṛbhiḥ*)."
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*) according to the first rule [Pāṇini 5.1.117].
Alternatively,
it is *nuvatīm*.

The word *nṛ* [becomes] *nṛp* before the suffix *danta*, according to the rule "or due to similarity of sound" (*śrutisāmānyāt*). The substitution of *v* for *r* occurs by the rule "in the Veda, *iraḥ*" (*chandasīraḥ*).
The elision of the suffix *dīp* occurs by the rule "elision in the Veda" (*chandasoluk*).

The suffix *matup* is acute-accented by the rule "hasvanṅubhyāṃ matup. [The phrase] "idaṃśīm uṣasam" means that you two "sacethe," that is, you properly approach or accompany this Dawn with your own chariot as a vehicle.
[The root] *pac* is used in the sense of "coming together" (*samavāye*).
Alternatively,
the root *sac* has the meaning "to serve"; thus,
*sacethe* means "you two serve."
Regarding this, Yāska says: "Be with us for our well-being; attend to us for our well-being" (Nirukta 3.21).

By what kind of chariot? "Mind-swift," meaning swift by the mind alone, independent of any other operation, and capable of being impelled by mere recollection; and "broad-backed," meaning possessing extensive strength or a vast army.
Since the Aśvins are praised immediately after the Upasads, it is said that they go to the Upasads.

To you two, O possessors of wealth through your steeds, the hymns of praise have been offered; even as a messenger has brought forth his speech. 3. To you two, O possessors of wealth through your steeds (*vājinīvasu*), the hymns (*stomāḥ*) have been directed (*prati-adakṣata*). Even as a messenger (*dūtaḥ*) has brought forth (*yathā-ohiṣe*) his speech (*vācam*). 3.
"O you two who possess the wealth of booty (vājinīvasū)!
Vāja is food characterized by the oblation;
the sacrificial action associated with that is vājinī."
Those two in whom there is *vasu*, meaning wealth, are described as such. Alternatively, they are those who possess *vasu*— wealth consisting of food— to be given to the singers.

"O Aśvins, may the hymns—the praises composed by us for you—be perceived; that is, let them be beheld. The verb *adṛkṣata* is the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *dṛś* used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Vedic usage.
Due to the rule *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*, the suffix is *kit*; consequently, by the rule *sṛjidṛśoḥ*, there is the absence of the augment *am*."

The forms *ṣatvakatvaṣatvāni*. And I, being as I have been addressed—that is, as a servant (*preṣya*)—entreat the word of my master, his command; in that same manner, I shall utter a word full of affection for you both. There is a transposition of persons (*puruṣavyatyaya*).
"Yāce" means "to beg"; that is, the sense of requesting.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively:

just as a messenger conveys a message spoken by his master to another person located in a foreign land, even so do I carry (*ohiṣe*), that is, bear, this speech in the form of praise; I deliver it to you both.

The middle [person] occurs by way of transposition from *vah*. The vowel *samprasāraṇa* is Vedic; because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix according to the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the augment *iṭ* is added.
There is the absence of the *śap* affix and the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel;
furthermore, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to the rule "eki pararūpam."
1. Kha-bha: *viśvadhātṛtam*; Jha: *prātaranuvākam*. 2. Kha-bha: *tām upasthena*; Jha: *upase upasthena*; Śa: *upasena*.
4. [The group] beginning with *jha*, *ta*, and *śa* possesses a nasal (*netṛmatī*). 5.

Alternatively, [the group] beginning with *kha*, *bha*, and *ra* is so called due to the commonality of their phonetic intervals (*śruti*); or [the group] beginning with *ta* is so called due to the commonality of its phonetic intervals.

6. [The group] beginning with *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya* is "you who go correctly" (*samyagācchathaḥ*); [the group] beginning with *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa* is "you who go correctly" (*samyaggacchathaḥ*).
7. Kha jha jha ta² śa ūhe. Rigveda [Aṣṭaka 5, Adhyāya 8, Varga 2]: 556.
The Kaṇvas praise the Aśvins for their aid— they who are much beloved, most gladdening, and possessors of many riches.
The two who are most dear to us for our protection, the most gladdening, the possessors of abundant wealth—O Kaṇvas, I praise the Aśvins. 4.
"Beloved by many" means dear to many; "very delightful" means causing great exhilaration,
or alternatively,
intoxicating many to a great degree.

O Aśvins, possessors of many treasures and abundant wealth, such as you are, we of the Kaṇva lineage praise and extol you for our protection and aid. (The dual form *puruvasū* is used for the dual *puruṣavacanau*;
alternatively: [End of segment]
The plural form "kaṇvasaḥ" is used for the sake of honor. The seer addresses himself, saying:
"O inner self, you who belong to the Kaṇva lineage (Kaṇvasaḥ), praise—praise the Aśvins!"
Most bountiful, best at winning booty, hastening along, O Lords of Splendor,
you who go to the house of the donor.
Most bountiful, best winners of booty, impetuous, lords of splendor, you who go to the house of the donor. 5.
Most generous, most munificent, worthy of honor, or worthy of worship; or rather, the two best givers, the greatest winners of *vāja*.
*Vāja* means food or strength;
they are the supreme bestowers of it.
Alternatively, *vāja* refers to food characterized by the oblation (*havis*).
These two are the most excellent sharers thereof.
[The suffix] *viṭ* is applied to the roots *san* or *sanat* according to the rule "janasana-."
There is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal of the suffixes *viṭ*, *van*, and *an*.
[The two] who provide food (*iṣ*) to the praisers (*stotṛbhyas*).
From the word *iṣ*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "he causes to do" (*tat karoti*).

When the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would have occurred due to the suffix *ṇvul*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "not when [the word] is not a verbal root and is monosyllabic.
Alternatively,
they are "desiring" (*eṣayantau*), meaning they cause one to attain the highest goods (*śreyāṃsi*).
The root *iṣ* means "to go.
From this, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied; due to the fact that a rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably valid, there is no substitution of *uṇ*.
They are the two auspicious lords (patī) or masters of beautiful wealth or of prosperity.
[The *s* in *patī* occurs] because of the rule "ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputra" which changes the *visarjanīya* to *s*.
They are those who go to, or whose nature it is to go to, the house of the donor (*dāśuṣaḥ*), that is, the sacrificer who gives sacrificial porridge, cakes, and other offerings.
The suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tacchīlika*).
Consequently, by the rule "na lokāvyaya... (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the genitive case in the sense of the object is prohibited.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "We praise such Aśvins."
For the liberal donor Sudeva, you two have smoothed out a pasture rich in ghee, providing wisdom that does not fail.
To the liberal donor, Sudeva, grant wisdom that is unfailing; with clarified butter, cause his pasture-land to flourish. 6.
Those two Aśvins are such as they are; for you two, [act] for the sake of the *sudevā*—one by whom beautiful gods (*śobhanā devāḥ*) are to be worshipped is so called.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "not after *nañ* or *su*" (*nañsubhyām*), there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the latter member.
To that donor, to the sacrificer who has offered the oblation—
the dative case here expressing purpose—
to such a sacrificer, [the goddess grants] *sumedhām*, meaning one possessing an excellent sacrifice (*yajña*) that is never-ending.
*Vitaraṇa* means passing away or departure; *apāya* means the state of going away. *Anapāyinīm*:
in this negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent of the first member, which is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), is retained.
"Such a *gavyūti*. A *gavyūti* is a pasture-land where cows (*gāvaḥ*) "yūthante," that is, gather together; thus it is a place for the movement of cattle.
The substitution of *ava* [for *go*] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.79.2: "*gavyūtau chandasi*."
"Sprinkle" (ukṣataṃ) means "pour" (siñcatam) that [offering] with ghee and flowing waters;
[the root] ukṣa is used in the sense of "to sprinkle."
O Aśvins, come to our hymn of praise with your swift, winged, and eager steeds; come hither with these.
O Aśvins, hasten toward our hymn with speed; come hither with swift falcons and with horses. ||7||
May those two Aśvins [come] to our hymn of praise with their horses;
"adravat" and "tūryam" are both names for speed,
while "ekaḥ" is a filler word.
O Tūryas, come quickly; approach!
Or alternatively, "dravat" is an epithet of the *stoma*.
"Flowing" means moving swiftly; that is the meaning of *stoma*.
With what kind of horses? With "hawks"—those whose gait is worthy of praise, whose movement is like that of a hawk, and who are swift-moving.
1. *kha-bha-śa-*: [The substitution of] *ā* occurs when *as* follows. 2. *jha-ta-śa-*: *ṇic* is added after a root ending in *e*, *o*, or *ai* when a causal suffix (*tumun*) follows.

With those [horses] by which you traverse the three distant realms, all the luminous spheres of heaven, and across the three nights. ||8|| With those: *yebhiḥ*. Three: *tisraḥ*. Distant realms: *parāvataḥ*. Of heaven: *divaḥ*. All: *viśvāni*. Luminous spheres: *rocanā*. Three: *trīn*. Nights: *aktūn*. You traverse: *paridīryathaḥ*. ||8||

O Aśvins, with those horses by which you traverse— that is, you go around— the three heavens for three days and the three nights for three nights (the accusative case is used here to denote duration), [you travel] from afar to all the radiant dwellings of the gods, which are the stars pervading the entire expanse.
The root *dīyati* has the sense of "going.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "By them, our hymn of praise has been approached."
And may you grant us food accompanied by cattle, and gains that find the light of day; O Pṛthu, open wide for our acquisition. ||9||
Moreover, O you two who cause the day to be obtained;
or rather,
those who are to be known and praised at the time of daybreak.

"Give us (naḥ), for our sake, food-offerings (iṣaḥ) consisting of cattle—meaning, joined with many cows"—this is the ellipsis. "And also (uta)," give us wealth (rāyaḥ) that is to be honored (sātīḥ) or bestowed;
[the word *sātīḥ* is derived from the root *sanati* or *sanoti* with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of the object].
By the rule "janasanakhanām," there is the substitution of āt;

by the rule "uti-yūti" etc., the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *ktin* is prescribed as a nipātana. Furthermore, for our "sātaye"—that is, for the acquisition or the enjoyment of the aforementioned cows and other things—"pathaḥ," the paths which serve as the means thereto, "vi sitam," bind them open specifically.
