In the second Anuvāka there are seven Sūktas.
Among them, the first Sūkta, consisting of forty-eight verses beginning with "mahā~ indraḥ," is the Ṛṣi Vatsa Kāṇva's;
it is in the Gāyatrī metre and is dedicated to Indra, with the exception of the final triplet (tṛca).
In this [hymn], the gift of Tirindira, the son of King Paraśu by name, is praised;
therefore, that triplet has him as its deity.
Accordingly, it is recorded in the Anukramaṇī: “*Mahān indraḥ*: forty-eight verses; another triplet is a praise of the gift of Tirindira, the son of Paraśu.”
In the *Mahāvrata*, this hymn is [included] among the eighty *gāyatrī* triplets, with the exception of one other triplet.
Likewise, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: “One omits the last three verses of the triplet beginning, ‘Great is Indra by his might’” (*Ai. Ā. 5.2.3*).
At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), when there is an excess of Soma, these verses beginning with ‘Great’ are for the purpose of the *stomātiśaṃsana* (extolling the *stoma*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With the verses addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu, beginning with ‘Great is Indra who by his might,’ [he performs] the Stoma of the excess” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.7).
In the third round, the triplet ‘Great is Indra’ is the *anurūpa* for the Hotṛ’s *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Great is Indra who by his might... I honor all the people’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 36.4).
In the *asuryāma* sacrifice, when there is an additional *uktha*, this very triplet of verses serves as the *anurūpa*.
For it is stated: “Great is Indra who [is great] by might; now indeed, O Aśvins” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.11).
In the New Moon sacrifice for one who sacrifices to Mahendra, “Great” (*mahān*) alone is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *sāṃnāyya* offering.
For it is stated: "Great indeed is Indra who by his might became so; O Indra, you have become great through our prayer" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).

Great is Indra, who by his might has grown through the hymns of Vatsa, like Parjanya rich in rain. 1. Great is Indra, who by his might, like Parjanya possessed of rain, has grown through the hymns of Vatsa. 1.
Indra, who is great by virtue of his vigor and strength, being superior to all— like what? Like one who possesses rain.
The meaning is that he is like the great god Parjanya, who, endowed with rain, is the bringer of juices.
That Indra has grown, indeed is increasing, through these hymns of praise offered by Vatsa—the one named Vatsa, who stands in the place of a son—by means of such recitations.
When the many inspired singers (viprāḥ), carrying the oblation of Truth (ṛtasya vāhasā), bring forth offspring, filling them with the nectar of Truth (prajāṃ ṛtasya piprataḥ). || 2 ||

When the many, the carriers—the horses—filling the regions of the sky, bring forth or carry forward Indra, who is born preeminently from the sacrifice (*yajña*), the truth (*satya*), or the cosmic order (*ṛta*), then the wise ones (*vipra*) praise that Indra with a hymn of praise (*stotra*) which is the vehicle (*vāhasa*) that brings about the sacrifice or the truth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
1. Of Kha-na-bha-śa Kaṇva; 2. Of Kha-na-bha-ta; 3. Like Parjanya, the showerer of rain; 4. Just as one who brings rain; 5. Of the son Vatsa; 6. The praisers of the wise Śa.

When the Kaṇvas have praised Indra with hymns as the accomplisher of the sacrifice, they proclaim his kinship and his weapon. (3) The Kaṇvas [praised] Indra, when they celebrated him with hymns as the accomplisher of the sacrifice; they proclaim his kinship and his weapon. (3)
The Kaṇvas:
this is a name for those who offer praise;

that is, the singers belonging to the Kaṇva lineage. When they drew Indra toward them with hymns—that is, with songs of praise—as the means for accomplishing, as the producer of the sacrifice (yāga), then they performed [the rite].
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *kṛ*, the substitution of *ghas* occurs by the rule "in mantras, *ghas* [is substituted for *kṛ*] in the *luṅ*.
At that time, I shall consume (*vjam*) the weapon of the enemies—namely, arrows and the like—which is indeed a destroyer.
This is an example of an augment (*āgama*) having an excessive name.
They say—that is, they declare—that [the weapon] is superfluous, honored [in name], and devoid of purpose;
the meaning is that since every task to be accomplished by a weapon has already been performed by Indra, the weapon is useless. Indeed!
They call him Indra, whose nature is to wield weapons in battle, his kinsman, indeed his brother;
the meaning is that he behaves like a brother in all matters.
In the third sequence, there are forty-two verses beginning with "To his fury, [O people]" (*asamasya manyave*) in the *śastra* of the Hotṛ priest.
For it is stated: "The forty-two verses beginning with 'To his fury, O people' are for the one who has conquered the quarters" (*āśva. śrau. 6. 4*).

Before his wrath all the tribes, all the people, bow down together, as the rivers flow toward the ocean. 4. sam asya manyave viśo viśvā namanta kṛṣṭayaḥ | samudrāyeva sindhavaḥ || 4 || Before his wrath, all the tribes, all the peoples, bow down together, like rivers toward the ocean. 4.
All the clans (*viśaḥ*), all the peoples (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*), and all creatures enter into the wrath (*manyave*)—
or rather,
the hymn of praise (*mantraḥ*) which is the means of meditation— of that Indra.
For that purpose, they bow down; they incline perfectly by themselves.

This is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*) from the root *nam*. The prohibition of *yaṅ* and *ciṇ* applies here according to the rule: "Not for *duh*, *stṛ*, or *nam*."
They become humble.
Herein is an illustration:
just as rivers, by their very nature of flowing, bend down of their own accord toward the ocean, even so [do they bend] toward the ocean.

That was his vigor, by which he, Indra, brought both worlds together; he rolled them up like a hide. 5. *Ojaḥ* (vigor); *tat* (that); *asya* (his); *tiviṣe* (for vigor); *ubhe* (both); *yat* (when/which); *samavartayat* (he brought together); *indraḥ* (Indra); *carma-iva* (like a hide); *rodasī* (the two worlds). 5.
The vital power and strength of that Indra has shone forth intensely; [the root] *viṣ* means "to shine.
By which vital power this Indra has rolled together both worlds, heaven and earth, as if they were a hide—he causes them to revolve perfectly.
Just as someone at one time spreads out a piece of leather and at another time contracts it, so too those two were subject to that [leather]; this is the meaning.
With his hundred-jointed, virile thunderbolt, he indeed split asunder the head of the violently shaking Vṛtra. 6.
The word *cit* also has the sense of "even" (*api*), and it is displaced [in the sentence].

Indra split apart (*vi bibheda*)— that is, severed— the head (*śiraḥ*, *mūrdhānam*) of even (*cit*) Vṛtra, the obstructer (*āvaraka*), the powerful (*bodhataḥ*) Asura who excessively shakes the world, with his *vṛṣṇi*— that is, his potent (*vīryavatā*)— thunderbolt (*vajreṇa*), which possesses a hundred joints (*śataparvaṇā*), meaning a stream consisting of a hundred sections.
Among the Ābhilāvika hymns, at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the three-verse hymn beginning with “*imā abhi*” is praised as an optional *anurūpa* (corresponding verse).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘*imā abhi pra ṇonumaḥ*’—this is then for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.8).

We chant these prayers aloud at the forefront of inspired thoughts, like the brilliant flames of Agni, like double-flashing lightnings. (7) We chant these aloud; we, the poets, [chant] at the forefront of inspired thoughts; [we chant] the brilliance of Agni, like double-flashing lightnings. (7)
1. *jha-ta1-2-4-manyu*:
"In the presence (*agreṣu*) of the singers (*vipām stotṛṇām*), we repeatedly proclaim these our *dhītayaḥ*—that is, our *dhiyaḥ*, our hymns—toward [you] (*abhi pra*) with fervor (*jotumaḥ*).
The root *ṇu* means "to sound."
What kind of hymns?
"Of Agni," like the "flame" (śocis)—that is, like a radiance—shining and blazing, consisting of the form of the Vedas.
The Kaṇvas, with their hymns, have sent forth their radiant thoughts by means of the stream of Truth, like a well-formed child from within the cave.
The secret songs have come forth by themselves, as the inspired thoughts of Kaṇva shine brightly with the stream of Truth (ṛta).
When those prayers (*dhītayaḥ*)—which are truly existent within the secret cave (*guhā guhāyām*)—are approached by Indra himself (*ātmanā*), they shine forth (*pra śocanta*), that is, they blaze up.
Or rather:
approaching Indra of their own accord (*ātmanā*), they are kindled.
The ellipsis is that those praises—the seers belonging to the Kaṇva lineage—perform them "accompanied by the stream of Ṛta," that is, of water in the form of Soma.
O Indra, may we obtain that wealth consisting of cattle and horses; may we obtain the sacred prayer for the sake of first awareness.
O Indra, may we obtain that wealth consisting of cattle and horses; may our prayer be foremost for the sake of thought. 9.
O Indra, may we obtain—that is, may we attain—that well-known wealth of yours, which is rich in cattle, joined with cows, and endowed with horses;
likewise, may we obtain the exalted prayer for the sake of primordial knowledge, that is, for the sake of knowing even before others.
I have indeed received from my father the wisdom of the immortal nectar;
I have been born like the sun.
I have indeed received from my father the wisdom of the Eternal Order; I have been born like the Sun. 10.
"I alone have grasped—completely taken hold of—the wisdom, that is, the intellect characterized by grace, of my father, the protector, of *ṛta*, the truth, the non-false Indra.
For because it is so, therefore I was born like the sun; just as the sun appears while shining, even so was I born and manifested."
With a focused mind, I adorn my songs like Kaṇva,
by means of which Indra becomes powerful in his might.
I, with my extended mind, adorn these songs like Kaṇva, so that Indra may indeed bestow his strength.

Like Kaṇva, my father, and like Kaṇva, I adorn (*śumbhāmi*) my songs (*giraḥ*)—that is, my words—with this hymn (*stotra*), which is of the nature of the Veda, by means of this mental instrument (*manmanā*) directed toward Indra.
For when they are employed regarding Indra, they become adorned by virtue of their truthfulness.
Indeed, by that hymn, Indra surely *dadhé*—that is, he holds fast—*śuṣmam*, the power that withers the enemies.
The meaning is: "He who generates such a hymn for Indra—that is, such strength—by means of that mental prayer (*manman*)."
Those who have not praised you, O Indra, and those who have praised you—
be exhilarated by my excellent hymn of praise.
O Indra, those seers who have not praised you, and those who have praised you—be magnified by me as one well-praised! 12.

O Indra, those people who have not praised you and do not praise you, as well as those seers—the seers being the people who perceive the mantras—who have praised you and do praise you: among both these groups, being well-praised (suṣṭuta) by my own hymn alone, increase; that is, become great.

1. May we attain what is beyond this [world]. When his fury thundered, shattering Vṛtra limb by limb, he sent the waters toward the ocean. (13) When his fury thundered, shattering Vṛtra limb by limb, he sent the waters toward the ocean. (13)

When this Indra’s wrath (*manyu*), having enveloped Vṛtra—the demon or the cloud—stood there, rending him apart joint by joint (*parvaśaḥ*) and limb by limb (*paruṣi paruṣi*), and when he uttered his sound characterized by thunder, then that Indra sent forth the waters (*apaḥ*)—the waters of rain—toward the ocean, the place of gathering.

O Indra, you struck down the steadfast Śuṣṇa with your thunderbolt upon the Dasyu. O fierce one, you are indeed heard as a bull. 14. O Indra, you struck down the steadfast thunderbolt upon Śuṣṇa, the Dasyu. For you, O fierce one, are heard as a bull. 14.

O Indra, when the Dasyus were being withered by Śuṣṇa—O Indra, those Yatis and those Bhr̥gus who have praised you—among them, O fierce and powerful Indra, hear my very own invocation! (18) O Indra, those Yatis—who are self-restrained descendants of Aṅgiras—and those Bhr̥gus—who belong to the lineage of Bhr̥gu—have praised you; among them, O fierce and mighty Indra, hear my very own invocation, that is, my hymn of praise. (18)

These dappled cows of yours, O Indra, yield clarified butter and the milk-mixture; they swell with the draught of this Truth. O Indra, these dappled (pṛśni) cows of yours—variegated in color—yield clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which is characterized by flowing, and this milk-mixture (*āśira*), the liquid used for mixing. What kind of dappled cows are they? They are those that cause the swelling (*pipyuṣīḥ*) of *ṛta*—of the Truth, of the infallible Indra, or of the sacrifice (*yajña*).
O Indra, those who have swallowed you have made you their embryo,
as the sun is encompassed by the heat.
Those which, O Indra, are the sprouts.
Thee,
with the mouth,
as the embryo.
The worshippers have surrounded [him] like the Law.
The Sun.
O Indra, these *prasva*s;

they are called *prasva*s because they release the embryo while being impelled (*prasuvante*). [The suffix] *kip* is applied to the root *sū-* by [Pāṇini 3.2.61]: *satsūdviṣa-druha-duh-yuja-vida-bhida-chida-ji-rājām upasaṃkhyānam*.

Such cows as these, having eaten with their mouths your heroic power—which, after the slaying of Vṛtra, had been transformed into the form of plants and other things—conceived a fetus; that is, they retained your heroic power within themselves.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as the rays of the sun bear around the solar disc water that sustains and nourishes it in the form of a fetus, so too [did those cows].
Or alternatively:
like *paridharmā*, that is, like the sun which sustains [all] on every side;
just as the sun holds up the entire world on every side, so too [is he].
The meaning is that Indra’s virility is the sustainer of the entire world.

The holding of Indra’s virility—which has been transformed into the form of herbs and so forth—within themselves by the cows is clearly recorded in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], beginning with the passage "Of Indra who had slain Vṛtra... and continuing: "They gathered it from the herbs into their own selves; they milked it back" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.3.3).
The connection with the preceding verse is also this: these cows milk that virility, which has been transformed into the form of milk, for the purpose of mixing [with Soma].
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, during the *atiriktoktha*, the verse "svāmicchavaspate" is used.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "svāmicchavaspate taṃ pratnathā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9).

O Lord of Might, the Kaṇvas have magnified you with their hymn; the pressed Soma drops [magnify] you alone. (21) O Lord of Might, O Indra, the Kaṇvas—the singers or the seers of the Kaṇva lineage—have magnified, indeed do magnify, you alone with their hymn (*uktha*), that is, with their sacred teaching. And the pressed Soma drops (*indavaḥ*), extracted by the Adhvaryu priests, likewise magnify you alone.

O Indra, wielder of the stone, under your leadership alone is there praise; the sacrifice is one that must be extended across the warp. O Indra, wielder of the stone—O you who possess the stone as the means of striking—indeed, under your very leadership (*praṇītiṣu*), that is, in your established guidances and bestowals of wealth, there is *praśastiḥ*, excellent praise. Likewise, the sacrifice (*yajñaḥ*) is *vitantasāvyaḥ*, that which must be stretched out across the warp.

1. *Jha*, *ta1-2-4*, and *bhṛgugotrāsvā* read "tvāṃ"; *śa* reads "bhṛgugotrotpannāsvā tvāṃ". 2. *Śa* reads *pṛśnavarṇāḥ*. 3. *Jha*, *ta4*, and *śa* read *enaṃ*. 4. *Gha* and *śa* read *tvāmit tvāmeva*. *Tamaḥ*: This is derived from the root *tan* (to extend) according to Vedic usage. Alternatively, there is the suffix *tansi* belonging to the *kaṇvādi* group for the purpose of vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*). From that, the *āya* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. Thus, the non-sacrificial act (*ayajña*) is increased and performed by you alone.

O Indra, bestow upon us great nourishment, rich in cattle, like a fortress; and grant us offspring and heroic strength. (23) O Indra, for us—for our sake—be mindful of bestowing great nourishment, rich in cattle, like a fortress. The word *na* is used here in the sense of *ca* (and). Like a fortress (*puraṃ na*); a fortress is a place of protection. Be mindful of providing us with protection and preservation.

And that swift-moving force, O Indra, which you caused to shine forth among the Nāhuṣī tribes—O Agni, [grant] all that to us. (24) O Indra, among the Nāhuṣī tribes—the Nahuṣas being a name for humans, or referring to the subjects of a certain king named Nahuṣa—in all those people, O Agni, that force consisting of a multitude of swift-moving horses which you caused to shine forth (*pradīdayat*) from the front; "and" (*uta*) that too, [grant] it to us—this is the ellipsis. The particle *ā* is a filler.

O Indra, as you bestow [wealth] upon the pen, like the sun, you look upon that which is near at hand; when you, O Indra, show mercy to us. (25) The particle *na* here does not mean "not," but rather "now" (*saṃprati*). "O Indra, now, you who are wise (*sūraḥ*), you bestow [wealth] upon the pen (*vrajam*)—that is, the cow-stall—looking toward what is near (*upāka-cakṣasam*). *Upāka* is a word for 'near. You look upon it closely; you spread it out on all sides. The meaning is that you fill it with cattle. [This is derived from] the root *tan*, in the Vedic perfect tense (*liṭ*), where by the rule *tanipatyoś chandasi* there is the elision of the penultimate vowel. *Yat* means 'when'; O Indra, when you show mercy (*mṛḷayāsi*) to us—that is, you comfort us. (13)

When indeed, O Indra, you of great power, you rule over the peoples—great and boundless in your might. (26) *Aṅga* is used here for the purpose of addressing. O Indra, *yat*—you who are *tavipīyase*. *Tavipī* is a name for strength; it means "you act like strength. Just as an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth destroys every kind of enemy, so too you, being alone and without assistance, slay the entire host of enemies—this is the meaning. And you, who *kṣitīḥ*—this is a name for humans—*prarājasi*, you rule over humans preeminently. The root *rāj* denotes the act of sovereignty. Because of its connection with the preceding word (*yat*), it does not undergo the loss of accent (*nighāta*). That Indra, by *ojasā*—by his strength—is *mahān*, greater than all; therefore he is *apāraḥ*, boundless. The meaning is that he cannot be brought to an end by anyone whatsoever.

Thee, who art of wide-reaching power, the people, bringing oblations, address for protection with their drops of Soma. (27) O Indra, those "people" (*viśaḥ*)—the subjects—who possess "oblations" (*haviṣmatīḥ*), meaning they are endowed with sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and other gifts, approach and "address" (*upa bruvate*) thee, who art "of wide-reaching power" (*uruvyasam*), meaning thou who pervadest extensively, for the sake of "protection" (*ūtaye*). With what? With "drops" (*indubhiḥ*), that is, with Soma juices, for the purpose of satisfaction. Or alternatively: with Soma drops, they praise thee, who art of wide-reaching speed, for the sake of protection.
1. Kha-bha minati. 2. Kha-bha indra tvam.
3. Śa rakṣaṇāya.

In the shelter of the mountains and at the confluence of the rivers, the sage was born through inspired thought. (28) *Upahvare girīṇām saṃgathe ca nadīnām dhiyā vipraḥ ajāyata.* (28) In the *upahvare*—the sheltered slopes—of the *girīṇām*, the mountains; and at the *saṃgathe*, the confluence, of the *nadīnām*, the rivers—in such a place, through *dhiyā*, whether by the performance of sacrifice or by hymn of praise, the *vipraḥ*, the wise Indra, *ajāyata*, came into being. Therefore, the sense is: "We too shall sacrifice or offer praise in such a place. Regarding the word *girīṇām*, the acute accent on the first syllable is due to the rule *nāmanyatarasyām*.

From there, the wise one, looking down from the heights, beholds the ocean; from where the one who drinks deeply moves. (29) From there—from that world of heaven—wherein Indra, the "drinker" (*vipānaḥ*), meaning either pervading or endowed with excellent drinking, "moves" (*ejati*) or exerts himself; from those "heights" (*udvataḥ*)—the suffix *-vat* being used here in the sense of the verbal root according to Pāṇini 5.1.118—"the wise one" (*cikitvān*), that is, Indra, knowing [his way], "beholds" (*ava paśyati*) the "ocean" (*samudram*), the Soma offered by the sacrificers which has the nature of overflowing (*samundana-śīlam*). He gazes downward with his face turned below. Alternatively, Indra is praised in his aspect as the Sun: in whatever sky the "drinker" (*vipānaḥ*), the Sun-aspect of Indra, moves and abides; the "wise one," the knowing and learned Indra, from those "heights"—that is, from this atmosphere which rises upward—he "beholds the ocean. This is an elliptical expression; he beholds the entire world characterized by the ocean. With his rays extended downward, he illuminates it.

Then indeed they behold the light of the ancient seed, the daybreak which is kindled before the sky. Then indeed (*āt it*), they behold the light (*jyotiḥ*) of the ancient (*pratnasya*) seed (*retasaḥ*)—the daybreak (*vāsaram*)—which is kindled (*idhyate*) before (*puraḥ*) the sky (*divā*). When this Indra, in the form of the Sun, is kindled—that is, shines—beyond the sky, that is, above the world of heaven (*parastāt dyulokasya upari*), immediately thereafter (*ādit anantaram eva*), they behold the light, the shining splendor, of such an Indra in the form of the Sun, who is the "ancient seed. [The word *retas*] comes from the root *rī* (meaning "to go" or "to impel") with the suffix *asun* and the augment *tuṭ*, according to the rule *surībhyāṃ tuṭ ca*. Alternatively, *retas* is a name for water; thus it means "possessing water" (*retasvin*), and by implication, the possessive sense is indicated. Or, the accusative case in *vāsaram* denotes duration (*atyantasaṃyoge*); the meaning is that they behold the light throughout the entire day, from the beginning until the end. [The change of the visarga to *ph* in *vāsaram* occurs] according to the rule *isumoḥ sāmarthye*. 14.

O Indra, all the Kaṇvas increase your wisdom and your manly power; yea, O Mightiest One, your virile strength. (31) O Indra, all the Kaṇvas—whether the singers of the Kaṇva clan or the seers of that lineage—increase your *mati* (wisdom/intellect) and your *pauṃsya* (manly power); this is a term for strength, and they increase your strength as well. Regarding the form *vardhanti*: because the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* in Vedic, the *ṇi*-affix is dropped by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*. Furthermore, O *śaviṣṭha* (most powerful)—the suffix *-mat* is elided by the rule *vinmatorluk*, and the final *ṭi* is dropped by the rule *ṭeḥ*—O such Indra, the Kaṇvas indeed increase your *vṛṣaṇya* (virile strength), your leadership, power, and action.

O Indra, enjoy this beautiful hymn of mine; protect me well, and further increase my inspired thought. 32. This—me—O Indra—beautiful hymn—enjoy—forward—well—me—protect—and—further—increase—inspired thought. 32.
1. *Śa*: such a Brahmin; 2. *Kha-bha*: in the world; 3. *Kha-jha-śa*: powerful action; 4. *Jha-ta1-2-4*: they cause to increase—thus [it is said].
O Indra, graciously accept (*jupasva*) this, my own excellent praise (*suṣṭuti*) standing before you;
and having accepted it, protect (*pra ava*) me, the singer, most excellently (*su*).

And furthermore, increase our thought—that is, make our intellect grow—so that it may become a seer of many truths; this is the meaning. And, O possessor of the thunderbolt, we, the inspired poets, have fashioned this prayer for you, O mighty one, so that you may live. uta | brahmaṇya | vayam | tubhyam | pra-vṛddha | vajrivaḥ | viprāḥ | atakṣma | jīvase || 33 ||
Moreover, O exalted one, who has attained supreme growth through hymns of praise, O wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrin), Indra—[the suffix] *matup* is used here as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Or alternatively: [the text continues...]
"One who possesses a vajra is a *vajrin*; [the term] *hasta* [is used here] because he possesses that.
According to the rule *chandasīraḥ*, the *m* of the suffix *matup* becomes *v*."
By the rule *matuvaso ruḥ*, the *m* is changed to *r*.
O Indra, for you—on your account—the wise ones (*viprāḥ*), that is, the intelligent ones;
we [offer] *brahmāṇi*, meaning hymns of praise or food characterized by oblations.
The substitution of *yā* for the case-ending (*sup*) is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
For the sake of living (*jīvase*), meaning for the purpose of life, we have fashioned (*atakṣama*), i.e., we have performed;
[the root] *takṣū* (or *tvakṣū*) means "to make thin" or "to fashion."
The *śap* [suffix] is elided by Vedic license (*chāndasa*).

The Kaṇvas have sung forth toward Indra, as the waters flow down a steep descent; so does our winning prayer. (34) Toward him, the Kaṇvas have sung in praise, like waters flowing down a steep slope; the prayer that wins favor has gone toward Indra. (34)
The Kaṇvas—the sages of the Kaṇva lineage—have praised Indra; that is, they extol him.
The root √stu is used here in the sense of "praising."

From the *kuta* [wooden vessel] and so forth; moving along a steep, downward-sloping path like waters— so too the hymn (*mati*), being composed by the Kaṇvas, becomes a praise that possesses abundance (*vananvatī*), spontaneously full of devotion for Indra, the one worthy of praise.

The hymns have magnified Indra, as rivers swell the ocean—him whose wrath is unsurpassed, the ageless one. 35. Indra. Hymns. Have magnified. Like the ocean. Rivers. Whose wrath is unsurpassed. The ageless one. 35.
The hymns (*ukthāni*) and recitations (*śastrāṇi*) being chanted by us have increased, that is, they cause Indra to grow—
just as rivers, characterized by their flowing, increase the ocean, the receptacle of waters.
Of what sort is Indra?

*Anuttamanyu*: one whose *manyu*—meaning anger or indignation—is *anutta*, that is, not driven away by others and not overcome. The absence of the short vowel [in *anutta*] is due to the optionality provided by the rule *nudavidonandrāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.56).

"Aja" means free from old age (*jarārahita*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first syllable of] *nañ*, *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta* [is udātta]," there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the final member.
Come to us from afar with your two beloved bay horses; O Indra, drink this pressed soma! 36. Come to us from afar with your two beloved bay horses; O Indra, drink this pressed soma! 36.
O Indra, come to us from afar, from the distant world of heaven, with your two beloved, tawny steeds;
having arrived, drink this pressed Soma of ours.

Thee alone, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra, do the people who have trimmed the sacrificial grass invoke for the winning of booty. 37. Thee alone, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra, do the people who have trimmed the sacrificial grass invoke for the winning of booty. 37.

O best slayer of Vṛtras—most excellent destroyer of obstructing enemies—it is you alone that people, those characterized as officiating priests who have trimmed the sacrificial grass (vṛktabarhiṣaḥ)—meaning those for whom the sacrificial grass has been cut for the sake of the sacrifice and who have thus commenced the rite—invoke (hayante).
[Note: In the formation *dveḥ*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" in the context of the suffix *śap*.]
For what purpose?
For the winning of booty (*vājasātaye*).
[Note: The word "Indra" does not appear in the manuscripts marked kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa.]
For the sake of obtaining food or strength;
or rather,
this is a name for battle.
The meaning is that they call upon you for assistance in whatever battle there may be for the acquisition of booty (*vāja*).
Both worlds follow you as a wheel follows the driver; the pressed drops of soma follow you. 38. Follow you; both; the two worlds; like a wheel; the driver; follow; the pressed; drops; of soma. 38.
O Indra, both the worlds—Heaven and Earth—follow after you; that is to say, they remain dependent upon you. In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as the wheel follows the chariot wheel,
so too does this [wheel] follow the horse named Etaśa as he goes before; it revolves after him in that manner.
Moreover, the drops, the Soma juices being pressed by the officiating priests, follow after you.

Rejoice well, O Indra, hero among the sun-like men; and rejoice at Śaryaṇāvat with the hymns of Vivasvat. 39. Rejoice! Well! Among the sun-like men! And! O Indra! At Śaryaṇāvat! Be exhilarated! With the hymns of Vivasvat! 39.
Moreover, O Indra, at Śaryaṇāvat— Śaryaṇā being the name of certain regions situated in Kurukṣetra—
the lake located not far from them is Śaryaṇāvat.
In the word *madhvat*, the suffix *matup* is added by the rule *madhvādibhyaśca*;
the vowel lengthening occurs by the rule *mato bahvacaḥ*;
and the substitution of *va* for *ma* occurs by the rule *saṃjñāyām*.
While that lake exists, at this sacrifice which must be performed by all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) for Svarṇera, rejoice thoroughly—be exhilarated and satisfied.
Furthermore, through the *mati* (thought/devotion) of Vivasvat, the patron (yajamāna) who performs the service, be intoxicated—attain exhilaration. [Note:
From the word *mati*, the third case ending takes the long vowel *ā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*, resulting in the form *matyā*.]

Growing great toward heaven, the bull, wielder of the thunderbolt, has roared; he is the slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme drinker of Soma. 40. Growing great; toward; heaven; the bull; wielder of the thunderbolt; has roared; slayer of Vṛtra; supreme drinker of Soma. 40.

Having grown great, the mighty wielder of the thunderbolt, the possessor of the *vajra*, the slayer of Vṛtra—whether he be the cloud, or the Asura—Indra, the supreme drinker of Soma, the showerer of waters, roared loudly with a sound characterized by thundering in the sky, in the celestial realm, or in the atmosphere, just as it is heard by us;
that is to say, he caused this sound to be produced by means of the thunderbolt struck against the clouds.

For you are a seer born of old, the sole lord by your might; O Indra, you pour forth wealth. 41. For you are a seer, born of old; you are the one, the lord by your power; O Indra, you pour forth riches. 41.
O Indra, you are "born first," having been born or produced before all the gods;
or rather,
having appeared at the very beginning of the sacrifices.
For you are indeed a seer, an observer, and you are truly omniscient;
moreover, among all the gods, you alone are the preeminent one, the sovereign lord by virtue of your splendor and strength—
or rather:
Alone and without companion, you are the sovereign lord of the entire world through your own inherent power.
As such, you repeatedly bestow wealth (*vasu*) upon your worshippers;
the root *skuñ* here signifies the act of giving.
And so it has been said: "O Indra, while you were snorting, you gave much wealth; O Indra, you gave much that is worthy of being sought" (Nirukta 6.22).
May our hundred bay horses with smooth backs carry you toward the pressed juices and the offerings. 42. asmākam | tvā | sutān | upa | vītapṛṣṭhāḥ | abhi | prayaḥ | śatam | vahantu | harayaḥ || 42 ||
1. When *kha*, *sa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* are present;
2. *kha-bha* increases.
O Indra, regarding our, that is, our own, *somas*, [grant] nourishment.
This refers to food;

and having in view the sacrificial offerings characterized by parched grains, flour-cakes, and so forth, [the text says]: "May a hundred—meaning a number of one hundred—"bay horses," whose backs are "smooth" (vīta), that is, whose upper parts are excellent, "carry you," meaning they shall convey you [to the sacrifice].

The Kaṇvas have magnified with their hymn this most holy prayer, which overflows with honey and clarified butter. 43. This—well—holy—prayer—of—honey—of—clarified-butter—overflowing—the Kaṇvas—with—hymn—have—magnified. 43.

Now, the Kaṇvas—the sages of the Kaṇva lineage—have magnified with their hymns (*uktha*) this sacrifice (*dhī*), which is being performed well and excellently, which was performed by our ancestors such as the fathers, and which increases (*pipyuṣīm*) the sweet, flowing water of ghee—or rather, which has been augmented by sweet ghee and clarified butter—for the sake of Indra.
For indeed, by means of hymns...

And thousands of hymns were offered as praise to Sāji, who was known by this name and was a seeker; or rather, O Sāji, this hymn is for you—born of the Panis, Kakṣīvat—to whom the kings named Tirindara and others gave it.

The preeminent one has reached heaven; he gave away camels yoked in fours, along with such fame as belongs to that man. 48. Furthermore, the preeminent one has reached heaven; he gave away camels yoked in fours, along with such fame as belongs to that man. 48.
Then King Kakuha, being exalted and preeminent through his fame and renown, pervaded the heavens—the celestial realm—with his superior splendor.
What was he doing?
He was bestowing, that is, giving away, camels yoked with four, namely, harnessed to four loads of gold.
Likewise, by bestowing such a person as a slave;
The second hymn, consisting of thirty-six verses beginning with "pra yad vaḥ," is the seerly work of Punarvatsa of the Kaṇva lineage; it is addressed to the Maruts and is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Thus it has been enumerated: "pra yad vaḥ, thirty-six verses; [the seer is] Punarvatsa; [it is] Māruta.
In the expanded ten-night sacrifice (daśarātra), during the first Chandoma day, this hymn serves as the Māruta-nivid insertion within the Ābhīmāruta Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn beginning with 'pra yad vaḥ' and 'triṣṭubham dūtam vaḥ' is for the Maruts" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.9).

*pra yad vaḥ triṣṭubham iṣam maruto vipraḥ akṣarat | vi parvateṣu rājatha || 1 ||* O Maruts, when the inspired sage has poured forth for you this *triṣṭubh*-metered food, you shine forth across the mountains. || 1 ||
O Maruts, you who are measured in speech and measured in luster—these are the intermediate hosts of gods known by this name.

Because the word occurs at the beginning of a metrical foot (pādādi), the prohibition against being at the beginning of a sentence (apādādau) applies; thus, while the eighth-level *nighāta* (anudātta) does not apply, the first syllable of the vocative receives the sixth-level *udātta* accent.

To you (*vaḥ*), meaning for you, the wise (*vipraḥ*) singer, when he poured forth (*pra akṣarata*)—that is, sprinkled or cast into the fire—the *iṣ* (sustenance) characterized by Soma, which is worthy of praise at the three *savanas*, praised by the three gods, or connected with the *triṣṭubh* meter, specifically that belonging to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavanikī*). When he offered it, then [you were invoked].
Or alternatively: "Triṣṭubham" refers to the hymn having the Triṣṭubh meter; it should be construed with "food" (iṣam) and "Soma.
In that case, you shine forth upon the mountains—that is, upon the lofty peaks resembling mountains.
Having gained strength through that Soma, become especially radiant.

O brilliant ones, when you, seeking power, have prepared your course, the mountains have bowed down. 2. When, O brilliant ones, seeking power, you have prepared your course, the mountains have bowed down. 2.
*He tavipīyavaḥ*: *tavipī* is a name for strength;
[they are] those desiring that.
Or alternatively:
"endowed with strength. O brilliant (*śubhra*), that is, shining ones; O Maruts! The *yāma* is the chariot, so called because it goes to the journey (*yāna*).

When you—by means of horses and other instruments—have gathered it together, that is, when you have joined it together for the purpose of moving, then even the mountains and hills *ni ahāsata*: they go down completely; being terrified by the speed of your chariot, they move from their own places.
The root *ohāṅ* means "to go";
the elision [of the nasal] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Roaring with the winds, the sons of Pṛśni have raised their voices; they have milked forth swelling nourishment. 3. And they have raised [their voices] with the winds, the lowing ones, the sons of Pṛśni; they have milked forth swelling nourishment. 3.
The *vāśrāsaḥ* are those characterized by lowing, making sounds; they are the sons of *pṛśni*.
*Pṛśni* is the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*).
Those whose mother, their progenitor, is she, are thus described.
By the rule *ṛtacchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.4.158), there is a prohibition of the suffix *kap*. Such are the Maruts; they are called *vāyavaḥ* because they blow (*vānti*) or move, and they are *pṛṣvaḥ*.
With the spotted deer as their mounts, or indeed with the winds that constitute their own limbs, they drive forth—that is, they cause the clouds and other phenomena to rise.
Likewise, they milk—that is, they bestow—upon the worshippers nourishing food (*iṣ*) that causes increase.
1. *jha-ta1-2* read "Maruts, Maruts."

2. Or [the name] is *jha-ta-mitarāviṇaḥ*. 3. According to the *Nirukta*: "Or they roar loudly" (*jha-vā mahadravantīti*); at the end of *ta1*, it says "or they roar loudly" (*vā mahadravantīti vā*). The Maruts rain down mist; they cause the mountains to tremble. When they go on their course with the winds. They rain down; the Maruts; the mist; forth; they cause to tremble; the mountains; when; their course; they go; with the winds. (4)
The Maruts—gods of this name—scatter, disperse, and spread abroad the *mih*, that is, the rain;
likewise, they cause the mountains, the peaks, to tremble. If one asks, "When does this occur? [the answer follows].
The meaning is: "when," that is, at the time when they reach the path, the chariot, or the journey together with the winds.
The rivers have yielded themselves to your power, O Maruts, for your support, for your wide dominion, and for your great impetuous strength.
To you, the mountain has bowed down for your abode; the rivers have yielded to your great power for the sake of your vast dominion.

O Maruts, when the mountains— meaning the hills or mountains— yielded of their own accord for your journey or for your chariot (the *jas* case ending is replaced by *su* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*), then [you came].

Likewise, the *sindhus*—the oceans or rivers characterized by their flowing nature—have submitted of their own accord for the sake of your great, drying power (*śuṣmāya*), that is, for the sake of your mighty sustaining force (*vidharmaṇe*).
The meaning is that the mountains and rivers remain fixed in one place out of fear of your command.
At that time, the Maruts sow the mist; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The form *yameḥ* is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) used in the sense of the agent as the object (*karmakartari*). There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) by the rule: “After [a word] not ending in *yat*, [the verb] is always [accented].”

We invoke you by night for protection; we invoke you by day; we invoke you while the sacrifice proceeds. 6. You—verily—by night—for protection—you—by day—we invoke—you—while the sacrifice—is proceeding. 6.
O Maruts, we invoke you alone for protection by night;
and by day as well, we invoke you alone at the sacrifice.
A sacrifice is called *adhvara* because there is no obstacle (*dhvara*) in it;
according to the rule *nañ-subhyām*, the final syllable of the compound is accented.
While the sacrifice is *prayati*—proceeding or being set in motion—we invoke you yourselves for the sake of protection.

Yonder rise those red-hued, bright ones with their journeys; lowing, they move above the ridge of heaven. 7. Yonder rise those red-hued, bright ones with their journeys; lowing, they move above the ridge of heaven. 7.

Those Maruts of yours, possessing the previously mentioned qualities, having ruddy-colored forms (*aruṇapsavaḥ*), wonderful (*citras*)—meaning praiseworthy or marvelous—and lowing (*vāśrās*)—making sounds—such as these, by means of their journeys (*yāmaibhis*) or courses, rise up from above the sky (*divo adhi*), from the high ridge (*snuā*) or elevated region of the heavenly world.
The particle *u* is a filler.
By the rule "there is an addition [to the list] for *māṃsa* and others at the beginning of words," the substitution of *sn* occurs for the word *sānu*.
In the *kārīrī* sacrifice, for the oblation to Sūrya, the verse “They release the ray” (*sṛjanti raśmim*) serves as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
For it is stated: “They release the ray with power... the golden thread with the swiftest [horses]” (*sṛjanti raśmim ojasā vahiṣṭhebhir hiranyāsi tantum*; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.13).

They emit a ray with power, a path for the sun to travel; they have spread themselves out with their beams. 8. They emit a ray with power, a path for the sun to travel; they have spread themselves out with their beams. 8.
Because of the hearing of the word *tat* (that), there is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word *ye* (who).
Regarding "those Maruts for Sūrya"—that is, for the Sun—the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive, according to the rule: "The dative should be stated in the sense of the genitive."
For the purpose of *yātu* (going), [he extended] the *raśmi* (rein). According to the rule "aśe raśa ca," the suffix *mi* is added after the root *aś*, with *raś* as its substitute;
or alternatively:
They create— that is, they produce— the path by means of their rays, which are endowed with splendor, and by means of their vital energy (*ojas*) or power;
the meaning is that they generate the path of the sun by removing the obstructor, such as Vṛtra, which had covered it.
Those Maruts, with their splendors—that is, their radiant energies—have spread abroad; they remain pervading the entire dark world.
O Maruts, accept this song of mine; O Ṛbhukṣans, accept this hymn;
accept this my invocation.

O Maruts, accept this song of mine; O Ṛbhukṣans, accept this hymn of praise; accept this my invocation. O Maruts, accept (*vanata*)—that is, enjoy—this *giram* (song) of mine (*me*), which is present before you and consists of words in the form of verses (*śakharūpā*). O Ṛbhukṣans—this is a name for the great ones (*mahajjāma*); they are the "Great Ones" (*mahāntaḥ*). [In the formation of the stem] the vowel *a* is substituted by the rule *ito'ssarvanāmasthāne*; the absence of lengthening is according to the rule *vā ṣūparvasya nigame*. You all, accept this *stomam* (hymn)—the praise accomplished through chanted mantras—and this *havam* (invocation), which is my present call in the form of a sacrificial formula (*yājuṣa mantra*), accept and serve it.
The three streams have yielded honey for the wielder of the thunderbolt— the well, the swelling, water-bearing spring.
Three; the lakes; the speckled ones.
She milked the honey for the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The fountain, the wellspring, the watery source.

The cows, who are the mothers of the Maruts, yielded for Indra— the wielder of the thunderbolt (the dative case here denotes purpose)— sweet milk and other substances used for mixing; they yielded these at the three pressings, which are like three lakes filled with Soma, for the purpose of mixing during the three seasonal libations.
Alternatively:

[The poet says that] the *pṛśnayas*—the intermediate voices (*mādhyamikā vācaḥ*)—have milked, or rather, they milk through the medium of rain, the sweet *soma* for the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), the host of Maruts, into three reservoirs: the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhakṣaṇa*. Or else, by the word *pṛśnayas*, which denotes mothers, their sons are intended.

The Maruts, whose mothers are the earth, milked for Indra’s sake the well—the flowing, watery cloud—filled with honey, that is, with Soma, into the three reservoirs, such as the *droṇakalaśa* and others. [The verb] *duduhe* (they milked) is the perfect tense form of the root *duh* used in Vedic meter; the change to *rebh* follows the rule "irayo re."
There is no *anighāta* because it begins with the first syllable of a foot (*pādādi*).
O Maruts, when we, seeking your favor, call upon you from heaven, come hither to us quickly!

O Maruts, when we, desiring your favor, call upon you from heaven with hymns, do come quickly to us! O Maruts, whenever we—desiring *sumna*, that is, seeking happiness for ourselves—invoke you from the heavenly world (*divaḥ*) with praises, do indeed (*ā tu*) come immediately and swiftly (*upagantana*) to us. In the imperative form of the root *gam* (to go), the suffix *-tanap* is substituted according to the rule "tasanasanathanāśca."
For you, O bounteous Rudras, lords of the Ribhus, are indeed wise in our home and in the exhilaration of the soma-draught.

For you indeed, O bounteous givers, O Rudras, O lords of the *Ṛbhus*, are wise in the house and even more so when exhilarated by the soma. (12) Furthermore, O bounteous givers (*sudānavaḥ*), O possessors of excellent gifts; O Rudras, sons of Rudra—the absence of the *nighāta* accent on the vocative is due to its position at the beginning of a *pāda*; O great ones (*ṛbhukṣaṇaḥ*), or rather, O Maruts of vast splendor—such as you are, you indeed (*hi*) become possessed of supreme wisdom (*pracetasaḥ*) in the sacrificial hall (*dame*) when the intoxicating soma has been drunk (*made*).
O Maruts, send down from heaven wealth that is exhilarating, rich in food, and sustaining for all.
1. [The letters] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa are followed by ve.
2. There is no [letter] 'hi' following kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa.

O Maruts, bring to us from heaven wealth that distills exhilaration, abounding in food, and sustaining all; come hither, O Maruts! O Maruts, bring to us—our wealth—from heaven, let it come. From the root *ṛ* (to go), with the causative sense implied, in the imperative of the *juhoty-ādi* class, the suffix *-ta* is replaced by *-tana* according to the rule *tasan-asan*. By the rule *anudātte ca*, the first syllable of the reduplicated stem becomes udātta. What kind of wealth? That which distills exhilaration (*madacyutam*), meaning either flowing with joy or causing the pride of the enemy to fall away; that which is rich in food (*purukṣum*), providing many dwellings or praised by many; and that which is all-sustaining (*viśvadhāyasam*), sufficient for the maintenance and nourishment of all our people.

When, O radiant ones, you have set your course as if upon the heights of the mountains, you rejoice with the pressed drops of soma. O radiant Maruts, when you have prepared your chariot—equipped with horses and other means of travel—as if ascending to the summits of the mountains, then you exhilarate yourselves with the pressed drops of soma.

15. So much indeed of their favor should a mortal beg with his prayers—from the invincible one. A mortal, that is, a human being who is a singer, should beg—that is, request—with his *manma*s (prayers or hymns) for *sumna*, which means happiness or wealth, belonging to these Maruts. Now, he speaks in the singular to denote the group as a whole: "So much indeed" (*etāvatścit*)—he should beg for the favor of this invincible (*adābhya*) host of Maruts, whose extent is such that it cannot be harmed by anyone. From the word *etad* (this), the suffix *vatup* is added in the sense of measure according to the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ*; and the substitution of *ā* occurs according to the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. 20.

Those who, like drops, blow through heaven and earth with their rains, milking the inexhaustible spring. Those Maruts, like drops—that is, like water-drops—blow through (*anu dhamanti*) heaven and earth (*rodasī*, i.e., *dyāvāpṛthivī*) with their rains; they follow them, pervading them completely. Or rather, they "blow after" them in the sense that they cause their parts to rise up. What do they do? Milking the inexhaustible (*akṣita*) spring—the cloud—filling it and causing it to pour its contents downward. The present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used here in the sense of a causal motive according to Pāṇini’s rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ* (3.2.126). Thus, because they milk it in this way, they blow through heaven and earth; such is the meaning.

They rise up with their roars, they rise up with their steeds, they rise up with the winds; the praise-song rises up, O sons of Pṛśni. (17) With their roars—*svānebhiḥ* means with sounds or cries—the Maruts rise up, they emerge. [The root] *svan* means "to sound. Because of the rule *svanahasorvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.62), the suffix *ap* is optionally used; thus, in this alternative case, the suffix *ghañ* is applied. By the rule *karṣātvataḥ*, the word has an udātta accent on the final syllable. The form *svānebhiḥ* becomes *svānais* by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. The particle *u* is a filler (*pūraṇa*). Likewise, they rise up with their *rayaiḥ*—that is, with chariot-fronts or vehicles. "Sons of Pṛśni" (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*)... [refers to the Maruts].
1. Accumulated by *kha*, *bha*, and *sa*.
2. By the winds whose faces are like chariots, [namely] *jña*, *ta*, and *ra*.
3. By the hymns and praises that move with *ja* and *dī*.
4. The Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, are thus raised up by hymns and praises—sons of Pṛśni, the offspring of Pṛśni, they are indeed thus raised up and exalted in many ways by the hymns composed by us.

By which [protection] you protected Turvaśa and Yadu, by which [you protected] Kaṇva who was desirous of wealth—may we well meditate upon that [protection] of yours for the sake of riches. (18) By which [protection] you protected Turvaśa and Yadu, by which [you protected] Kaṇva who was desirous of wealth—may we well meditate upon that [protection] of yours for the sake of riches. (18) "By which" means by your own protection, "you have protected" (*āva*) Turvaśa and Yadu, these two royal sages; this is the form of the verb *ava* in the perfect tense, second person plural. And "by which" you have protected the sage Kaṇva who was "desirous of wealth" (*dhanaspṛtam*), "that" protection of yours, "for the sake of riches" (*rāye*), "we shall well meditate upon" (*su dhīmahi*), that is, we shall contemplate it beautifully. (18) These refreshments of yours, O bounteous givers, swelling like clarified butter—strengthen them with the hymns of Kaṇva. (19) O "bounteous givers" (*sudānavaḥ*), O Maruts, "these" (*imāḥ*) refreshments (*iṣaḥ*) of yours, "swelling" (*pipyuṣīḥ*) "like clarified butter" (*ghṛtam na*), [strengthen them] with the "hymns" (*manmabhiḥ*) of Kaṇva. (19) ...swelling like clarified butter... (19)
Together—*ūm*—these [gods] have brought together the great waters; together the two hips, together the sun, and together, from of old, they have fashioned the thunderbolt. 22.
Those Maruts, possessing those aforementioned qualities,
[poured down] the great,
abundant waters— the waters of rain.
They have milked; they continue to milk. They cause [the substances] to be joined with herbs and so forth.
Or else:
Struck by the rays of the sun at the time of dharma, they hold [the water] perfectly above.
By the rule "bṛhanmahator upasaṃkhyānam," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* following *mahat* is acute;
by the rule "uḍiḍam" and so forth, the nominative plural suffix *śas* is acute because it follows a word ending in a vowel other than *a*.
In that same way, those Maruts sustained the earth, the two worlds, and heaven and earth so that they remain established each in its own place;
for by means of Vāyu, whose nature is the thread (sūtrātman), the entire universe is supported.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "O Gautama, Vāyu indeed is that thread; by Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, this world and all beings are held together" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
Likewise, they have fastened—the particle *u* being used for conjunction—the Sun, the impeller of all, namely Āditya, in the intermediate space; they hold him firmly there.
In this scripture, the Maruts, by striking Vṛtra at every joint—that is, in connection with all his limbs—sharpened and joined their own weapon, the thunderbolt, at each and every joint.
They have shattered Vṛtra limb by limb; they have split apart the mountain ranges that offered no resistance, performing manly deeds of heroic power. 23.
"Arājanaḥ" means not presided over by any king or master;
alternatively, "arājendraḥ" means one for whom a king— that is, a master— does not exist.
Endowed with that [power], the Maruts— performing, that is, exercising, the virile heroism and strength of a bull—
went forth, section by section, to pierce Vṛtra, the obscuring Asura or cloud; they brought about his distinguished destruction.
Likewise, he brought about the destruction of the mountains and peaks in a most extraordinary manner.

They aided the strength and the will of Trita as he fought; they followed Indra in the slaying of Vṛtra. 24. They [aided] Trita's; [of him] fighting; the strength; they helped; and; the will; they followed; Indra; in the conquest of Vṛtra. 24.
The Maruts followed— that is, they went to assist— the vigor, the enemy-drying strength, of Trita Āpya, the royal seer who was fighting and striking down his foes;
or rather,
they protected it in accordance with its nature.
Moreover, they protected his resolve and his deed;
furthermore, in the battle for the conquest of Vṛtra—that is, the war for the sake of slaying Vṛtra—they followed and protected Indra.

With lightning in their hands, reaching toward heaven, with golden helmets upon their heads, the radiant ones have adorned themselves for glory. 25. Lightning in their hands; reaching toward heaven; with helmets; upon their heads; golden; radiant; they have adorned themselves; for glory. 25.
With lightning in their hands, their weapon-bearing arms flashing,
reaching toward the heavens with radiant splendor,
the beautiful and resplendent Maruts display, for the sake of glory, golden helmets upon their own heads.
They manifest;
that is to say, they sustain.

When Uśanas from afar caused the fissure of the bull to gape open, it roared with fear like the sky. 26. When Uśanas from afar caused the fissure of the bull to gape open, it roared with fear like the sky. 26.

O Maruts, being praised by Uśanas Kāvya—the first case here used by *vyatyaya* (syntactic transposition)—or rather, from the word *uśanas*, the *jas* ending is replaced by *su* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*; thus, "you who desire the worshippers of Uśanas," when you went from afar (*parāvataḥ*), from a distant place, to the opening, the middle, of the chariot of Āmīva, the showerer of desires, or of the atmosphere which is the cause of rain—that is, when you arrived.
In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *yā*, for the second person plural, there is the substitution of *tan* according to the rule “*tasan-asan-athanāś-ca*”.
At that time, even the sky did not [shine].
Here, by the word *śu*, the assembly of people dwelling there is indicated.

Like the assembly of people existing in the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), the entire terrestrial host of beings also *cakradat*—that is, they cried out or trembled—from fear, namely, from the terror generated by your impetuous speed.
Come to us for the giving of the sacrifice, O gods, with your horses that have golden hooves. 27. Come to us for the giving of the sacrifice, O gods, with your horses that have golden hooves. 27.

O gods, the Maruts, endowed with qualities such as generosity, come near to us for the giving of our sacrifice (*makha*); [the suffix] *vani* is used here in the sense of the action [of giving] according to the *uṇādi* rules. With horses that have golden hooves—meaning hooves made of gold, or adorned with gold, or beautiful and lovely hooves—come hither, approach, and reach us.
The form *gameloṭi* involves the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

By the rule *tasanasanathanāśca*, the suffix *tamap* is substituted [for the optative marker]. Precisely because of this, there is no elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*), as the suffix lacks the *ṅit* designation.

When their spotted mares and the ruddy steed draw at the back of the chariot, the bright ones go forth, letting the waters flow. 28. When—of them—the spotted mares and the ruddy steed draw at the back of the chariot; the bright ones go forth, letting the waters flow. 28.
When these spotted deer— yoked with white spots— are harnessed to the chariot of these Maruts and carry it, and when the swift-moving *pṛṣṭi* (the side-horse) is yoked at the front;
or rather,
[when it is] being yoked at the front.
The red-spotted deer, yoked with white spots, draws [the chariot] at that time; then the bright, shining Maruts go forth.
And as they travel, the waters—characterized by rain—flow forth;
they stream everywhere.
The root *rī* is used in the senses of "going" and "smearing.
It belongs to the *kryādi* (fourth) class.
According to the rule "pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ," its vowel is shortened.
The absence [of the suffix] is Vedic.

According to the rule, “In a single sentence, the *nighāta* accentuation and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must be stated” (Pāṇini 8.1.18.5), there is no *nighāta* here for the preceding word because it belongs to a different sentence, as per the rule “*ṅiti tiṅaḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
At Suṣoma, at Śaryāṇavat, at Ārnīka, at Pustyāvat, the heroes stayed their chariot-wheels. 29. At Suṣoma; at Śaryāṇavat; at Ārnīka; at Pustyāvat; they stayed; with their wheels fixed; the heroes. 29.

In the *suṣoma*, which is endowed with beautiful Soma; in the *ārnīka*, the regions named *ṛjīka*; in the *śaryāṇavat*, connected with that [region], a lake known as Śaryāṇavat situated at the lower end of Kurukṣetra; and in the *pastyāvat*. *Pastyam* is a name for a house.

Accompanied by the sacrificial hall, the Maruts—the leaders of men—go forth for the drinking of Soma with their downward-rolling chariot wheels; that is, they proceed with the chariot wheels turning face-downward. This is the periphrastic perfect (liṭ) used in the Vedic sense of the root *yā*.
Alternatively:

The men, the leaders, and the officiating priests, distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, went—meaning they proceeded—to Śaryāṇavat to fetch Soma on a cart with downward-turning wheels (*nicakrayā*), that is, a cart whose wheels face downwards.

When will you come, O Maruts, thus to the inspired singer who calls upon you, with your mercies, to him who implores you? 30. When? Will you come? O Maruts! Thus [to] the inspired singer (vipra) who is calling out; with [your] mercies (mārḍīka), [to] the one who implores (nādhamāna). 30.
O Maruts, when will you come—with your mercies, that is, with riches which are the cause of happiness—to me, the wise singer who thus, in this manner, calls upon you, praises you, and entreats you?
Do not delay; the sense is: "Come quickly!"

Who indeed is truly dear to you, that you have driven Indra away? Who among you dares to claim friendship? 31 Who indeed? Truly. Who is dear? That you have driven Indra away. Who? Of you. In friendship. Dares? 31
He is *kathapriyaḥ*, meaning those who are delighted by discourse (*kathā*) or praise (*stuti*). [The root] *katha* [is used] in the sense of "composing speech" (*vākyaprabandhana*).
From this root, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.105, *cintipūjītyādinā*.
Then [the form] *ṣṭāp* [is derived].
In the case of a following word (*uttarapada*), there is shortening according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.63: *aṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasoḥ*.
The change to *dha* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"O Maruts, did you truly abandon Indra as he was fighting with Vṛtra?"—"When indeed?
means "At what time?"—the sense being that it was never at all.
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "The Maruts did not abandon him, saying, 'Strike, O Blessed One! Slay! Show your prowess! (AiB 3.20).
And there is another Vedic citation beginning with: “*vṛtrasya tvā śvasathād īṣamāṇāḥ*” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.96.7).
For this reason, [the word] *vaḥ* means “in your friendship” (*sakhitve*);
here the locative case is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
Who, as a friend, praises and implores you?
Or rather,
who attains [you]?
The meaning is that such unfailing friendship with you is difficult to obtain.
Together with the Maruts, who hold the thunderbolt in their hands and possess golden axes, O Kaṇva, I truly praise Agni for our sake. ||32||

With those who have thunderbolts in their hands, with those who have thunderbolts for arms, with those who possess golden axes— that is, those who possess the golden axe which is the tool for carving—
[with] Agni, who exists together with the Maruts, [O] Kaṇvas, that is, the Kaṇvas, [addressing] us!
O you who are the praisers, belonging to the Kaṇva lineage, or [other] sages— you should praise;
or rather,
"na" is used in the second case for the sense of the first case.
We are of the Kaṇva lineage.
By the rule *asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59), the plural is used for the singular;
however, the prohibition *saviśeṣaṇasya pratiṣedhaḥ* (Kāśikā on 1.2.59) applies by way of exception.
Thus: *stuṣe*, *stuve*.
In the second person singular of the imperative, *sip* is substituted [for *si*] by the rule "asibbahulam."

May I bring hither the vigorous, ever-sacrificing ones, who possess wondrous strength, for the sake of manly welfare and prosperity. 33. O! Hither! The vigorous! Ever-sacrificing! Toward! For manly! Prosperity! May I turn hither! Possessors of wondrous strength! 33.

I shall most effectively turn toward me those Maruts—those showerers (*vṛṣṇaḥ*) who bestow desired fruits, those who are worthy of worship (*prayajyūn*), and those possessing wonderful speed (*citravājān*), or wonderful movement, wonderful strength, or wonderful wealth.
I cause them to come so that they approach in my direction.

Moreover, for the sake of the most excellent, the newest, the most recent, the most highly praised, and for the wealth that is well to be attained, I shall turn those [gods] hither; I cause them to return.

Even the mountains bow down before him; even the rocky heights, considering themselves [powerful], submit; even the mountains have yielded to him. 34. girayaś cid ni jihate parśānāso manyamānāḥ | parvatāś cid ni yemire || 34 ||
As the Maruts approached, even the mountains— even the great rocky peaks— were pressed down;
or rather,
they were touched by the Maruts.
Therefore, thinking thus, imagining [this], and being oppressed, they *ni-jihate*—they go down completely;
they are driven from their places by the force of the wind.
Likewise, even the *parvatāś-cit*—the mountain-like clouds—are *ni-yemire*—they are restrained by his movement.
Or rather: "Girayaḥ" refers to small heaps of stones, while "śiloccayāḥ" refers to great mountains.

Moving crosswise, they carry those flying through the mid-air; the creators bestow vital strength upon the one who praises them. 35. Moving crosswise, they carry; flying through the mid-air; the creators; for the one who praises; vital strength. 35.
1. I shall cause the syllables *kṣa*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* to revolve. Those who have mounted the axle are going toward the axle-pole;
or alternatively:
Because their eyes move swiftly, they are called *akṣayāvānaḥ*.
[The suffix] *vanip* is applied to the root *yāti* according to the rule "āto manin.
Such horses carry—that is, bring—the Maruts as they fly, that is, travel, through the *antarikṣa*, the path of the sky.
Alternatively,
"patataḥ" (flying) is an epithet of the horses: those flying, that is, moving, in the intermediate space, the sky.
The absence of the *num* augment is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
What are they doing?
They are praising (*vstuvate*), that is, performing hymns of praise for the people; they are bestowing (*vdhātāraḥ*) and providing (*vidhātāraḥ*) food (*vayaḥ*) while performing [these acts].

Agni, indeed, has taken birth as the ancient one; like the sun with its radiance, he is the meter. They have spread themselves out with their beams of light. ||36|| Agni. Indeed. Birth. Ancient. Meter. Like. Sun. With radiance. They. With beams. Have spread themselves out. ||36||
Agni is indeed full of splendor and brilliance; he is the foremost among all the gods.
He was born from the *ajā*.
According to Pāṇini’s rule 3.1.61, "dīpana" and so forth, the suffix *luṅ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and the substitution of *cleśriṇ* is applied.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

*vchandaḥ* (desire), *upacchandanīyaḥ* (to be enticed), *vsūraḥ* (the hero)—not like the sun (*sūrya*). Immediately thereafter, those aforementioned *marutaḥ* (Maruts) *vvi vtasthire*, that is, they stand variously (*vividham*) by means of their *bhānubhiḥ* (splendors).
For in the Agnimāruta [section], Agni is praised first and the Maruts afterwards;
with reference to that, Agni and the Maruts are praised in sequence in the preceding and succeeding passages.
The third hymn, consisting of twenty-three verses beginning with "ā no viśvābhiḥ," is the seer's work of Sadhvaṃsas, the son of Kaṇva; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
These three hymns, starting from this one, have the Aśvins as their deity.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "ā naḥ [has] twenty-three verses; [the seer is] Sadhvaṃsas; it is addressed to the Aśvins; it is in the Triṣṭubh [and then] Anuṣṭubh meters."
This hymn belongs to the *prātaranuvāka*, the *āśvina-śastra*, the *ṛtāvān* section, and the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
for it is stated: "‘ā no viśvābhiḥ’, ‘tyaṃ cit’, and ‘atriṃ’ constitute the *ānuṣṭubha* [section]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.15).
It is also used by the *praśāstṛ* priest in the *atiriktoktha* at the *asoyāma*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā no viśvābhiḥ prātaryāvāṇā" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.11).
On the fourth day, in the Prauga Śastra, the triplet for the Aśvins begins with "ā no viśvābhiḥ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā no viśvābhirūtibhir asya vo ahrāṇam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).

Come to us with all your aids, O Aśvins; you two, O wonder-workers who travel on golden paths, drink the Soma-sweetness. 1. Come to us with all your aids, O Aśvins; you two, O wonder-workers who travel on golden paths, drink the Soma-sweetness. 1.

O Aśvins, you two who are swift—either because you pervade the entire world or because you are yoked with horses—come to us together with all your protections (*vūtibhiḥ*), which are to be bestowed. Having arrived, O Dastras—you two who are beautiful to behold or who destroy the enemies—O you whose paths are golden (or whose chariots are made of gold), or whose conduct is most delightful, O Aśvins such as you, drink the honey-like Soma juice.
Come now, O Aśvins, with your chariot that has the brilliance of the sun; you who are enjoyers, adorned with golden ornaments, sages of profound intellect. 2.

O you two who enjoy the oblations, or rather, those who cause the horses to be fed by the singers, or the protectors of the entire world; O you two adorned with golden ornaments, or whose limbs are made of gold; O you two seers (kavī) who possess far-reaching vision, or who grant boons to the singers; O you two of profound mind and praised wisdom—such as you are, O Aśvins, come now, indeed, to us on your chariot that shines like the sun.
Come hither from the realm of Nahuṣa, drawn by our well-fashioned hymns; O Aśvins, drink the honey-sweet mead pressed at the sacrifice of the Kaṇvas. 3.
Come from Nahusha; come from the mid-air with our well-fashioned hymns. O Aśvins, drink the sweet mead pressed at the libation of the Kaṇvas.
"He [reached] the Aśvins from Nahuṣa.
*Nahuṣa* is a name for a human being;
by implication, however, the world connected with him is indicated here.
From that human world—
*pari* here restates the sense of the ablative case—

with well-fashioned hymns (*suvṛktibhiḥ*), meaning with praises that are perfectly free from defects or with those that are well-composed, acting as the cause [of your arrival], come hither! Come both of you!
Likewise, come from the intermediate space—from the midst of the atmosphere, even from the middle world.
Having arrived, O Aśvins, drink the pressed, sweet Soma at our sacrifice, during the morning libation and the other sessions, for us who belong to the Kaṇva lineage.
Come to us from heaven, passing through the intermediate space, you who are dear; here the son of Kaṇva has pressed the Soma-mead for you both.
Come to us from heaven, come from the mid-air, O beloved ones; here the son of Kaṇva has pressed for you the sweet Soma juice. 4.
O Aśvins, come from the sky, from heaven—that is, from the celestial world—to us. [The *s* in *divaḥspari* is due to the rule:
“The visarga becomes *s* when followed by *pari* in the sense of ‘from above’ (*adhy-arthe*) in the ablative case.
O you who are pleased by the Soma existing here in this lower world, [come to us].
Alternatively: *kadhapriyā*;
the elision of a syllable is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Pleased by the narrative and the praise, [the gods say:
"O Aśvins such as you, come even from the intermediate space!
Here at this sacrifice, the son of the seer Kaṇva has pressed out for you two—the sweet soma-juice consisting of soma—for your sake."
Therefore, come hither—this is the syntactical connection.
O Aśvins, having heard our call, come to us for the drinking of Soma; Svāhā! O sages, increasers of the hymn, O heroes, [come] with your inspired thoughts. 5.
Come to us within hearing, O Aśvins, for the drinking of the Soma; Svāhā! You who increase the hymn of praise, O sages, O heroes, with your inspired thoughts. 5.
O Aśvins, listen to us;
"śruti" means praise.
Come to this sacrifice where praise has been offered, for the drinking of Soma, that is, for the sake of consuming the Soma.
The two increasers, the two sages, the Ashvins who possess far-reaching vision— svāhā! Being properly sacrificed with the utterance of "svāhā," or rather,
"svāhā" being a name for speech.
With speech in the form of praise, through the act of praising with words, may you two be the instigators of the hymn for the worshipper.
Likewise, O leaders, O Aśvins, through our prayers—that is, through our ritual acts—may you two be the instigators of that which is to be attained.
Or alternatively:
The vocatives begin with "svāhā.

O Svāhā, you two who perform the *svāhā*-utterance; O you two who impel the hymn—that is, the praise or the singer; O you two impellers; O you two sages (*kavī*), who possess far-reaching vision; [you who are] augmenters by means of your own *dhītis*, that is, by means of your insights.

2. [The variants read: *na-yajñapravardhakau*; *bha-yaṣṭuḥ pravardhakau*; *śa-yaṣṭuḥ pravardhakau*. "O Heroes, by your deeds you are the leaders of all; O Aśvins, come for the drinking of the Soma"—this is the very meaning of the sentence.
In this interpretation, the absence of the suffix *-parāṅga* in the word *dhītibhiḥ* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, the connection with the action is: "Come hither together with those prayers (dhītayaḥ) that go toward you.
O Heroes, come for our protection, just as the ancient seers invoked you both with oblations in the past; O Aśvins, come to this path, to this my excellent hymn of praise.
For whatever the seers have sacrificed to you in the past for protection, O Heroes, come hither, O Aśvins; arrive at this well-spoken hymn of mine. 6.

Those two leaders, the Aśvins, whom indeed the seers— the singers who perceive objects beyond the senses— invoked with hymns for protection in former times; [the form *juhure* is derived from the root *hu* (to invoke) in the perfect tense,
where the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule "abhyastasya ca," and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "halaḥ"].
The change to *rebhāva* occurs in the word *irayo re*.
At that time, O Aśvins, come hither (*ā yātam*); you have arrived.
Therefore, come also to this my beautiful hymn (*suṣṭutim*), this excellent praise; come near (*upa ā gatam*).
Even from the luminous realm of heaven, come to us, O you who know all things, through our prayers—O you who are mindful of Vatsa, and who hear our invocations through our hymns. 7.
Even from the luminous realm of heaven, come to us, O finders of the light, through our prayers, O you who are wise in action, through our hymns, O you who hear our call! 7.

O all-knowing Aśvins, you who cause us to attain the light of the sun or the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), come hither from the luminous realm of heaven (*divaḥ*) and from the radiant mid-air (*rocanāt*);
here, as before, the preposition *adhi* expresses the sense of the ablative case.
O you of superior wisdom toward the calf—that is, toward the worshipper (*vatse stotari*).
Alternatively,
they are so called because they possess an excellent mind (*cetas*)— that is, knowledge— which is to be understood as "dwelling" (*vatsa*) or "abiding.
O you two, come together with your own intellects (*dhībhiḥ*).
O Aśvins, you who are the hearers of our invocation—the listeners of our call and our hymns—come hither, being joined with our unadorned songs of praise.
Why do others sit around us? O Aśvins, the seer Vatsa, the son of Kaṇva, has magnified you both with his songs. 8.
What others sit around? O Aśvins, with our hymns of praise, Vatsa, the son of Kaṇva, the seer, has magnified you both with his songs. 8.
Do other worshippers, distinct from us (*asmad*), sit around you with their hymns of praise (*stomaiḥ*), O Aśvins, the two gods?
The meaning is: "No others besides us are able to praise the Aśvins.
Vatsa, the seer (*ṛṣiḥ*) and son of the seer Kaṇva, a seer who perceives the sacred formulas, has magnified (*avīvṛdhat*) you both, O Aśvins, with his songs of praise (*gīrbhiḥ*).
O Aśvins, most excellent slayers of Vṛtra, come hither with your hymns for our protection; O destroyers of enemies, be the bringers of joy to us. 9.
1. In the manuscripts kha, jha, na, and bha, there is an absence of the word *atyaparāṅgatva*.
2. In manuscript kha and bha, it reads *āgatau*; in jha, ta-4, it reads *āgacchantī*; in jha and na, it reads *āgacchatantī*. 3. In jha, ta-1, ta-2, ta-4, and ya, it reads *ṛṣiḥ*.

The sage has invoked you both here for protection with hymns, O Aśvins, you who are stainless and the greatest slayers of Vṛtra. As such, be the sources of bliss for us. (9) When the maiden mounted your chariot, O Aśvins, possessors of abundant wealth, then you both attained all our intended prayers, O Aśvins. (10) Therefore, come hither on your chariot of a thousandfold splendor, O Aśvins. Vatsa, the son of Kaṇva, has recited a honey-sweet word for you. (11) O Aśvins, you who are greatly gladdening, possessors of much wealth, and the thinkers of riches—O bearers of the sacrifice, may you both respond to this my hymn. (12) *Note:* 1. *kha-bha* read "prāpayata" (cause to reach). 2. *Purumandrā*: greatly gladdening, or to be exhilarated by many Soma libations. 3. *Puruvasū*: possessing much wealth, or the dwellers of many [treasures]. 4. *Manottarā*: thinkers or bestowers of riches; the form is derived from the root *man* with the suffix *tu*, following the *pṛṣodarādi* rule.
