*Ṛgveda* [Aṣṭaka 5, Adhyāya 8, Varga 28]:
"They both responded favorably to this hymn of praise; they commended it, saying, 'It has been well-recited.'"
The root *ṇu* means "to praise. Alternatively, it is used in the sense of hearing the praises of a young woman (*yuvati*).
They both heard the sound of the arrow being drawn back.

O Aśvins, bestow upon us all gifts that are blameless; make us possessed of timely offspring. Do not deliver us over to reproach. O Aśvins, grant to us all those excellent riches which are blameless—that is, free from causes of infamy—and bestow them upon us. Furthermore, make us possessed of *ṛtviya*—that is, endowed with the procreative act performed at the proper time (*ṛtu*). Likewise, do not subject us to reproach, nor deliver us into the power of the reviler.

Whether you two, O Nāsatyas, are in the far distance, or whether you abide in the sky, come hither from that place, O Aśvins, on your chariot adorned with a thousand ornaments. O Nāsatyas—those whose nature is truth, leaders of truth, or born from the nose—whether you are in the *parāvati* (the far distance), or if you are in the *ambare* (the sky)—this word being a name for "near," meaning you are in close proximity—the particle *adhi* here serves as a locative marker. From all such places, O Aśvins, come hither on your chariot which possesses a thousand-fold splendor (*sahasranirṇijā*).

O Nāsatyas, to that seer who, as a calf, has magnified you both with his songs—grant him food dripping with clarified butter, adorned with a thousand forms. (15) O Nāsatyas, to that seer who, as a calf, has magnified you both with his songs—to that seer grant food dripping with clarified butter, adorned with a thousand forms. (15) O Nāsatyas, to that seer who, as a calf, has magnified you both with his songs—that is, has strengthened you with praises—to that seer grant food dripping with clarified butter, possessing a thousandfold splendor; bestow it upon him. (27)

O Aśvins, you two bestow upon him strength dripping with ghee—upon him who, for the sake of your favor, strives to win wealth from the giver, O Lords of bounty. 16. pra | asmai | ūrjam | ghṛta-śrutam | aśvinā | yacchatam | yuvam | yaḥ | vām | sumnāya | tustarvat | vasu-yāt | dānunaḥ | patī iti || 16 ||

1. O Aśvins, you two who flow through the sky, bestow upon this singer strength—consisting of nourishing food that provides vigor—accompanied by a stream of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). O lords of giving, may he who praises you with satisfaction [attain] your favor for the sake of happiness.
And whoever should desire wealth— that is, should wish for wealth (dhanam) for himself— the construction [of the sentence] is "to him" (asmai).
Come to us, O destroyers of enemies, to this hymn, O you who enjoy many things!
O heroes, being well-disposed toward us, grant us these gifts for our protection.
Come to us, O destroyers of enemies, you who possess much wealth; come to this hymn of praise made by us, O heroes who are firm supporters, and grant these [gifts] for our assistance. 17.

O destroyers of the destructive, you who repel the harmful, or rather, you who devour—that is, consume—the harmful; O you of many enjoyments, you who partake of abundant oblations or protect many; O Aśvins, come toward this our hymn of praise.
Having arrived, O leaders, make us well-established—endowed with beautiful prosperity.
For that purpose, these earthly [objects] present before us have been given for the fulfillment of the intention;
"dātum" is the imperative (loṭ) of the root *dā*, with the elision of the *śap* affix by Vedic license (*chāndasa*).
With all your aids, O Aśvins, the Priyamedhas have invoked you, you who rule over sacrifices at the calls of the journeyers.
With all your aids, the Priyamedhas have invoked you both, O Aśvins, who rule over the sacrifices, at the calls for the sacrifice. 18.

O Aśvins, at the invocations of the journey—those sacrifices wherein there is the calling, the invocation, of the traveling gods—the Priyamedhas, seers whose sacrifices are dear, [invoke] you two who are the sovereign lords of the rites (*adhvaras*). The root *rāj* signifies the act of ruling or sovereignty.
For the Brāhmaṇa states: "The two Aśvins were indeed the Adhvaryu priests of the gods" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.2.1).
Thus, they have invoked you two, accompanied by all (*viśvābhiḥ*) aids (*ūtibhiḥ*), that is, by all forms of protection; the meaning is that they have praised you.
Come to us, O Aśvins, you who are sources of bliss and bringers of well-being,
for Vatsa, the praiser, has magnified you with his prayers, meditations, and songs.
Come to us, O Aśvins, you who bring happiness and well-being! You two have been magnified by Vatsa with his praises, his thoughts, and his songs, he who is devoted to you. 19.
O Aśvins, you two who bring delight (*mayobhuvā*), who bring about well-being (*śambhuvā*)—you two, come to us!

O praiseworthy Aśvins, that calf—the worshipper—who has magnified you both with prayers (*dhītibhiḥ*), with ritual acts, with services, and with hymns (*gīrbhiḥ*), [magnify] those very ones for us; this is the connection with what precedes.
With those [powers] by which you [aided] Kaṇva and Meṣātithi, with which you [aided] Vaśa Darśatrāja, and with which you [turned back] Gośva Āvarta— O Heroes, protect us with those very ones.
1. Conjoined with gha, jha, ta¹, ta², and śa;
2. Kha and bha belong to one of great wealth; 3. Śa and pārthiva denote riches.
With those [powers] by which you protected Kaṇva and Medhātithi, with which you protected Vaśa Darśatraga and Goraśya—with those, O heroes, protect us. 20.
O Aśvins, with those aids by which you protected the seer Kaṇva and Medhātithi; with which you protected Vaśa, known as Etasa;
and with which [you protected] Gośarya.
One whose ox is worn out is a *gośaya*; *śayu* means the same.
Thus it is recited in the Veda: "O Nāsatyas, you strengthened the cow with your powers for the sake of the exhausted Śayu" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.116.22).
O [Nāsatyas], protect such a *gośaya*, one who is exhausted.
O leaders, O men, protect us with those aids; that is, guard us.
With those aids by which you two, O Heroes, protected Trasadasyu in the quest for booty—
by those same aids, O Aśvins, protect us for the winning of the prize.
With those [aids] by which, O Heroes, you protected Trasadasyu in the contest for wealth—O Aśvins, with those [aids], protect us well.
This is well known from other directions, as in *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 4.36.1: "He turns around... and so forth.
The two Aśvins are seers of transcendent vision; by means of those words which are the causes of *ṛta*—that is, truth, water, or sacrifice—they [reveal] the *pada* from out of living beings.

The sense of "from" (*pari*) is that of "separating from"; according to the rule "after the ablative case, when used in the sense of 'limit' (*avadhi*), there is *satva* (substitution of *s*)," the *s* is applied.
"Upon the living beings," that is, "toward us, the living beings, facing downward"; the ellipsis is "come.
The syntactical connection is: "those footprints are now perceived."
The fourth hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with "ā nūnam," is the seerage of Śaśakana and has the Aśvins as its deity.

Among these, four verses—the twentieth, the twenty-first, and the second and third—are *gāyatrīs*; five verses—the first, the fourth, and the fifteenth, repeated twice—are *bṛhatīs*, according to the definition and designation stated in [Anuvāka] 5.3 as "the middle foot being one syllable longer";
the tenth is a *triṣṭubh*, the eleventh a *virāj*, the twelfth a *jagatī*, and the remaining verses are *anuṣṭubhs*.

And thus it is enumerated: "Ā nūnam saikā, śaśakano, the other two Gāyatrīs, the first, fourth, and sixth [of the remaining] are Bṛhatīs, the fifth is a Kakubh, and the last three are Triṣṭubh, Virāj, and Jagatī.
This hymn, *Idam*, belongs to the Atiriktauthya at the Aśvamedha sacrifice for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
For it is enjoined: "Ā nūnam aśvinā, taṃ vāṃ ratham" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.11).

Come now, O Aśvins, you two, to the aid of Vṛta; extend to him wide and secure protection, driving away those who are hostile. Now indeed, O Aśvins, you two, come for the protection of Vṛta; bestow upon him vast and unassailable shelter, warding off those who are enemies.

O Aśvins, you two, come now—indeed, you must certainly come—for the sake of protection and for the praise of Vṛta. Having arrived, bestow upon this seer a broad, extensive dwelling—a home free from all affliction.
Likewise, keep those who are stingy, the hostile enemies, far away from the one who praises you.

Whatever manly strength is in the mid-air, whatever is in heaven, and whatever among the five tribes of men—bestow that, O Aśvins. 2. Whatever | in the mid-air | whatever | in heaven | whatever | among the five | human tribes | manly strength | that | bestow | O Aśvins. 2.
Whatever strength and wealth exists in the intermediate world frequented by Gandharvas and others,
and whatever exists in heaven, the celestial realm—
[all that] for the sake of the five classes of men.

The term *anu* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, by the rule "when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*," the second case ending is employed.
Wherever the fivefold humans—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—reside, whatever wealth (*nṛmṇa*) exists there in this world; [that is what is referred to].
O Aśvins, bestow upon us that threefold heroic strength and wealth; grant it to us.

O Aśvins, just as the inspired poets have fully contemplated your wondrous deeds, so indeed take heed of Kaṇva’s hymn. 3. O Aśvins, just as the inspired poets have fully contemplated your wondrous deeds, so indeed take heed of Kaṇva’s hymn. 3.

O Aśvins, those wise ones— the *vipras*, meaning the intelligent sacrificers— who have repeatedly touched upon (*parimamṛśuḥ*), that is, who perform and keep in mind, your *daṃsāṃsi*, your wondrous deeds consisting of service; even so, in that very manner, take note of and understand my own service, I who am the son of Kaṇva.
1. kha-bha: *tadānīṃtanāni*; jha: *tadādīnāni*; ta: *tadīnāni*; na: *tadānāni*.

This Gharma is poured out for you both with a hymn of praise, O Aśvins. This Soma, rich in sweetness, O lords of ample wealth, is that by which you take notice of Vṛtra. This [is] for you two; the Gharma; O Aśvins; with a hymn of praise; around; is poured out. This; the Soma; rich in sweetness; O lords of ample wealth; by which; Vṛtra; you two take notice of. ||4||

O Aśvins, this *gharma*—the Pravargya vessel belonging to you two—is being poured out and moistened by means of the *stoma*, that is, by the hymn consisting of *ṛc* and *sāman*. The meaning is that it is prepared in such a way as to bring about your satisfaction.
Or alternatively:
The *mahāvīra* vessel, which serves as the receptacle for the *gharma* oblation, is that *gharma*;
it is being poured around or poured into with the *stoma*, that is, with the hymn of praise, for the sake of you two.
Furthermore, O possessors of wealth consisting of food, this Soma of the third pressing, rich in sweetness, is offered to you both.
By means of which you two perceive Vṛtra, the obstructing enemy, as one to be slain;
this refers to both, namely, "this Gharma" and "Soma."

Whatever [work] has been performed by you in the waters, whatever in the tree, and whatever in the plants, O performers of many wonders—by that, O Aśvins, protect me! 5. Whatever [work] has been performed by you in the waters, whatever in the tree, and whatever in the plants, O performers of many wonders—by that, O Aśvins, protect me! 5.
O Aśvins, you of many wondrous deeds and many works, that medicine which was prepared by you in the waters, in the liquid elements—that you have made.
[The form] *akārṣṭam* is from the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense; by the rule "in mantras, *ghas*, etc.," there is the elision (*lup*) of the *cli*.
Likewise, *vanaspati* means the lord of the forests (*vanānām patiḥ*).
The augment *suṭ* is applied because [the compound] belongs to the *pāraskara*-class.

By the rule "in the case of *vanaspati* and similar compounds, both members [retain their original accent]," there is simultaneous preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for both the preceding and following words. Furthermore, this singular number is used because it denotes a genus (*jāti*).
Whatever medicinal power exists in the lords of the forest, the trees, you two have fashioned that;
for within these plants, both the burning heat and the ripening are deposited—thus "oṣadhayaḥ" refers to rice and other such grains.
In the rule "karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca," the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *dhā* when it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Because the compound is listed among the *dāsībhārādi* group, the original accent of the first member is retained.
Furthermore, by the rule "oṣadheś ca vibhaktau aprathamāyām" (Pāṇini 6.3.132), a long vowel is substituted [for the final *i* of *oṣadhi*] before a case-ending other than the nominative.
O Aśvins, whatever medicine has been prepared from grains and plants that you two have made—
by all that medicine, O Aśvins, protect me (aviṣṭam).
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood of the root *av*, the suffix *sip* is applied by virtue of the inclusion of the word "bahuḷam" (variously) in the rule *sibbahulam*.
Then this [follows]:

Whatever you two stir into motion, O Nāsatyas, or whatever you heal as gods, this calf of yours finds you through his prayers; for you go to him who possesses the oblation. yat | nāsatyā | bhuraṇyathaḥ | yat | vā | devā | bhiṣajyathaḥ | ayam | vām | vatsaḥ | mati'bhiḥ | na | vindate | haviṣmantam | hi | gacchathaḥ ||6||
O Nāsatyas, you two Aśvins who are of a truthful nature, since you both *bhuraṇyathaḥ*— that is, you nourish the entire world;
[the root] *bhuraṇ* means "to support" and "to nourish," and belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class.
The two gods are the Aśvins, who are endowed with qualities such as generosity;
the short vowel [in "devā"] is a Vedic (chāndasa) or Saṃhitā-form contraction.
Or rather, those two of you who heal—that is, who perform the healing of all living beings, the alleviation of disease.
The root *abhiṣaj* is used in the sense of "healing.
This [root] also belongs to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class.
"He"—that is, this calf, the praiser—does not find, does not obtain, you two by means of his *matibhiḥ*, that is, by means of his exclusive hymns worthy of being meditated upon.
The rule regarding the vowel lengthening is Vedic.
If it is asked why this is so, it is said:
for you two go toward the praiser who is possessed of oblations, that is, endowed with sacrificial offerings.
Therefore, the sense is: "May you two, being joined with oblations and hymns of praise, be gracious."
1. The two Aśvins; 2.
and the *stoma* consisting of one, two, four, and six verses.
When the milk-mixture (*gopayas*) is being poured into the *mahāvīra* vessel during the *pravargya* rite, the verse beginning with "ā nūnam" should be recited as the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*).
For it is stated: "Now indeed, the seer [addresses] the Aśvins; pour forth splendor upon the pressed [Soma] at the Ājya [laud]" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 4.7).
Now indeed the seer has perceived the hymn for the Aśvins with skill;
let him pour out the most honey-sweet Soma and the heated milk-oblation for Atharvan.
Truly, the seer has now perceived the hymn of the Aśvins with wisdom; let him pour out the most honey-sweet Soma and the Gharma-oblation for Atharvan. 7.

O Aśvins, when you two come hither, then the seer—the seer of the mantra—will surely, by means of his most excellent and desirable intellect, fully recognize the hymn of praise (*stoma*) addressed to you, O Aśvins.
[The root *kit* means "to know";
the form is the Vedic perfect.]

Thus, [the offering] most sweet—that is, exceedingly sweet—Soma, and the Gharma, the oblation called Gharma connected with the Pravargya rite, [were offered] into the Atharvan fire, the non-injurious Agni.

That which Kakṣīvat offered to you, and that which the seer Vyaśva, and that which Dīrghatamas, and that which Pṛthī, the son of Vena, offered to you in the sacrificial seats—even from there, O Aśvins, take notice. 10.
O Aśvins, you two—the seer Kakṣīvān invoked and praised you just as he did; and also the seer named Vyaśva invoked you just as he did;
and just as the seer Dīrghatamas invoked you both.
In the dwellings—that is, in the sacrificial halls—the royal sage known as Pṛthu, the son of Vena (Vainya), offered oblations to and praised you both in such a manner;
even so (*eva*) is this hymn of mine for me who praises in this very way.
After the word *idam*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the accusative case.
O Aśvins, take heed; know [this].
Go forth as our protectors from vomiting and as our protectors from afar; be the guardians of our moving world and the guardians of our bodies.
Come hither for the sake of our household and our offspring.
Go!
O drinkers of the *chardi*!
And...

When I should invoke the Aśvins for the winning of booty—that is, for the purpose of battle—then, it is implied, "come hither now. In battles, in combats, in the destruction of enemies, that power of the Aśvins which is the overcoming of foes and their protection—that protection is the most excellent, the most highly praised.
The sense is: "Therefore, I shall call him."
Come now, O Aśvins, for these invocations have been offered to you;
these Soma juices are radiant among the Turvaśas, and these are for your sake among the Kaṇvas.

Come now, O Aśvins! These [prayers] call you; awaken them, O Dawn! O Goddess, you of true bounty, awaken the two Aśvins! O great Hotṛ of the sacrifice, awaken them in due order! For exhilaration, awaken lofty glory! 17.
O Dawn, awaken the two gods, the Aśvins, for the sake of hearing our hymn of praise.
O Goddess, endowed with the qualities of generosity and other virtues; O Sūnṛtā, excellent leader; O Mahī, great one—you who are thus highly fortunate, awaken the two Aśvins.

O *yajñahotṛ*, the invoker of the sacrifices—that is, the one who summons the deities who are to be worshipped—awaken the Aśvins with hymns of praise so that they may be constantly and continuously present.
Likewise, for their exhilaration (*mada*), that is, for the sake of producing joy in the Aśvins, we have prepared the great (*bṛhat*) and glorious (*śravaḥ*) Soma, which is worthy of being heard.

O Uṣas, as you come with your radiance, you shine together with Sūrya; indeed, this chariot of the Aśvins comes toward us for our protection. 18. O Uṣas, as you go forth with your light, you shine together with Sūrya; truly, this chariot of the Aśvins comes hither for our drink. 18.

When you go forth together with the radiance of the Dawn, then you shine brightly along with the Sun. Moreover, at that time, this chariot of the Aśvins comes indeed to the sacrificial hall—the enclosure which is to be protected by men, that is, by the various officiating priests.

When the pressed stalks have been drunk like cows from their udders, or when the voices have resounded as the gods go forth toward the Aśvins. 19. When the pressed stalks have been drunk like cows from their udders; or when the voices have resounded as the gods go forth toward the Aśvins. 19.

When (*yat*)— that is, when (*yadā*)— the stalks (*aṃśavaḥ*), meaning the *soma* plants, having been drunk (*āpītāsaḥ*), that is, being entirely yellowish-green in color, yield (*duhre*) their juice (*rasam*) with the wooden vessels (*ūdhobhiḥ*), just as cows (*gāvaḥ*) yield milk;
[here] there is the elision of the *ta* suffix according to the rule "lopas-t-ātmanepadeṣu," and the augment *ruṭ* is added according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."

Or rather, when the priests, desiring the gods, have praised with their voices—that is, with hymns—then, O Aśvins, protect us! [The word *anuṣata* means "they praised" or "they performed. At that time, O divine Aśvins, grant us protection.

Forward for glory, forward for power, forward for protection consisting of heroic sons; forward for skill, O ye two of far-reaching wisdom! 20. Forward for glory; forward for power; forward for protection consisting of heroic sons; forward for skill, O ye two of far-reaching wisdom. 20.
O Aśvins, possessed of supreme wisdom (*pracetasā*), protect us for the sake of splendor (*dyumnāya*)—that is, for the sake of radiance, food, or glory;
the dative case here denotes purpose.
Protect us for the sake of splendor.
Protect us for the sake of *śavas* (vigor) and *bala* (strength);
protect us for the sake of *nṛpāhya*—that which is to be endured by men—and for the sake of *śarman* (shelter) and *sukha* (happiness);
protect us for the sake of *dakṣa* (skill) and for the sake of increase (*vṛddhi*).

Alternatively, in "yumnāya" and so forth, the dative case is used because the object [of the verb] is treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), according to the rule "the mention of the action [as a governing factor] must also be applied.
The meaning is: "Grant us wealth and the rest."
O Aśvins, worthy of praise, you sit upon the father’s sacrificial offerings with your prayers and through your auspicious favors.
1. *kha*—*saṃduhate*; *gha*—*duhate*; *jha*—*ta₁₋₄*—*asaṃduhate*; *na*—*saṃ*—*saṃduhate*. 2. *kha*—*jha*—*ta₁*—elision of *śa*; *ta₄*—elision of *la*. 3. *kha*—*nṛpāhyāya*; *śa*—*nṛpāhye*.
When indeed, O Aśvins, you have settled with your insights in the father’s womb, or when, O you worthy of praise, you are present with those of noble knowledge.
O Aśvins, if you two dwell—that is, reside—by means of *dhīs* (ritual actions) in every womb, that is, in every place belonging to the Father, the Protector, the Heavenly World;
or else, O ye two who are worthy of praise (*ukthyau*), if you dwell together with the well-known ones (*sujñebhiḥ*), that is, with happiness (*sukhaiḥ*);
then, being praised by us, come hither—this is the ellipsis.
Alternatively:

if you dwell together with prayers (dhī) and hymns of praise in the womb—meaning the sacrificial hall—belonging to the father, the protector, and the sacrificer; and if you dwell together with those who are well-informed and bringers of happiness, then come!
The word *nunam* is a filler (*padapūraṇa*).
And it has been said by Yāska: "Furthermore, it is also a word-filler:
'Surely that [favor] of yours is for the singer as a boon'" (Nirukta 1.7).
The fifth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "yatsthaḥ," is the seerly composition of Pragātha, the son of Kaṇva; it is addressed to the Aśvins.
The first verse is a Bṛhatī;
the second is a Madhyejyotis Triṣṭubh, according to the rule: "That which has eight syllables [in its middle] is a Jyotis."
This is because the existence of the characteristics thus described [in Anuvāka 9.8] is present.
The third [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh*, and the fourth is an *āstārapaṅkti*;
for its characteristic is stated as: "If another [verse] has the *āstārapaṅkti* [structure], it is an *āstārapaṅkti*" (Anuvāka 8.7).
The fifth [verse] is a Bṛhatī, and the sixth is a Satobṛhatī.
Thus it has been enumerated: "The six *pragāthas* beginning with 'yatsthaḥ'—the Bṛhatī, the Madhyejyotis Triṣṭubh, and the Āstārapaṅkti *pragātha*.
This hymn is used in the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) and in the *āśvina* ritual, within the Bārhata meter for the *āśvina-śastra*.
For it is stated: "The [verse] beginning with 'dyumnī vāṃ yatsthaḥ' is in the Bṛhatī meter" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).

Whether you two are in Dīrghaprasabhanī, or there in the luminous realm of heaven, or in the ocean, or in a constructed dwelling—from there, O Aśvins, come hither! 1. yat | sthaḥ | dīrghaprasabhanī | yat | vā | adaḥ | rocane | divaḥ | yat | vā | samudre | adhi | ākṛte | gṛhe | ataḥ | ā | yātam | aśvinā || 1 ||
O Aśvins,

you who are in that world where the *prasabhāna*s are long and extensive— the *prasabhāna*s being the sacrificial halls because the gods are pleased (*prasīdanti*) within them— if you two are present there, if you abide there.
Or whether you are there, in that shining place belonging to *div*, the heavenly world;
or whether you are in the ocean, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—
so called because "from it the waters flow forth."
In that fashioned house which has been built, you dwell;
therefore, from all three of these places, O Aśvins, come hither!

Or if you have prepared the sacrifice for man, then surely take notice of Kāṇva. I invoke Bṛhaspati, all the gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, and the Aśvins, with the speed of the swift hawk. yat | vā | yajñam | marnave | saṃmimikṣathuḥ | eva | it | kāṇvasya | bodhatam | bṛhaspatim | viśvān | devān | aham | huve | indrāviṣṇū iti | aśvinau | āśuṣerhasā || 2 ||

Furthermore, [invoke] Bṛhaspati, the lord of the great gods and the domestic priest of the deities; all the gods, beginning with Mitra; and Indra and Viṣṇu, for the sake of swift attainment.
Or alternatively: [the rest follows].
"In these sounds"— I quickly call upon, I invoke, the two Aśvins who are praised as the measurers of sound everywhere.

Those two Aśvins, of wondrous deeds, I now invoke, who have been made ready for our grasp; they whose friendship toward us and kinship among the gods are preeminent. (3) I now quickly invoke those two aforementioned Aśvins. Of what nature are they? They are of wondrous deeds (*sudaṃsasā*), performing beautiful acts; they have been "made ready" (*kṛtā*) for our "grasp" (*gṛbhe*)—that is, for the acceptance by them of the oblations offered by us, or for the granting of wealth to us—and they have manifested themselves among the gods. The particle *adhi* here merely restates the sense of the locative case. Of those two Aśvins, their kinship (*āpyam*) and their friendship (*sakhyaṃ*) toward us exist preeminently (*pra*); that is, it prevails and continues with excellence. Such are the two whom I invoke—this is the syntactical connection.

Upon whom all sacrifices depend, O Asuras, even as the sun; those two who are the wise overseers of the sacrifice and the rite, who by their own powers drink the sweet Soma juice—[those two Aśvins]. Upon whom, upon the two Aśvins, all sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others prevail and arise—because the severed head of the sacrifice was joined back together by the two Aśvins. Thus, beginning with "The head of the sacrifice was cut off," the Taittirīyaka Saṃhitā states: "Those two restored this head of the sacrifice when they take the draught for the Aśvins, for the sake of the sacrifice's restoration" (TS 6.4.9.1). Furthermore, even in a place devoid of praise (*asura*), where the sun is the singer of praises, those two Aśvins are the preeminent knowers (*pracetasā*) of the *adhvara*—the sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma that is free from injury or sin. [I invoke them] with *svadhābhiḥ*, meaning with praises that are the cause of strength; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Those two Aśvins who drink the Soma-like honey—the sweet Soma juice.

Whether you two, O Aśvins, possessors of wealth in horses, are in the west or in the east; whether you are with Duhyu, Anu, Turvaśa, or Yadu—I call upon you both; therefore, come hither to me! (5) O Aśvins, if today you are in the west, or if you are in the east, O possessors of wealth in horses; or if you are present among the four worshippers beginning with Duhyu—if I thus invoke you both who are everywhere present, then immediately thereafter, come hither to me! (5)

Whether you fly through the mid-air, O you who enjoy many things, or whether [you travel] along these two worlds, or whether you mount your chariot by means of your self-sustaining powers—from there, come hither, O Aśvins! 6. Whether you fly in the intermediate space, O you who enjoy much, or whether [you travel] along these two worlds, or whether you mount the chariot with your inherent powers—come from there, O Aśvins! 6.
1. In the seizing of *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *tara*, *na*, *bha*, and *gṛbha*;
2. it becomes *kha* and *bha*; 3. in *jha*, *duhya*, *anava*, *turvaśa*, and *yadu*.
O you who enjoy much, the protectors of many, or the consumers of abundant oblations— whether you travel along the paths in the mid-air,
or whether you proceed toward these two worlds, heaven and earth,
or whether you mount your chariot together with your own *svadhās*— that is, with your own splendors or powers, having taken your seat upon the chariot.
By the rule "adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām," the locus (ādhāra) receives the designation of object (karman).
Therefore, from every place, O Aśvins, come hither! Come!
The sixth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "tvam agne," is addressed to Agni; it is the seer Vatsa of the Kaṇva lineage, and it belongs to the Āgneya (Agni) deity class.
The first verse is a *pratiṣṭhā-gāyatrī* because it is endowed with eight syllables and six feet. The second verse is a *vardhamānā* because it is endowed with six syllables and eight feet.
And so it has been said: "The *pratiṣṭhā* [verse] increases by six and eight syllables, while the opposite is the *viparītā*.
The tenth verse is a *triṣṭubh*, and the remaining ones are *gāyatrīs*.

Accordingly, it is recorded in the *Anukramaṇī*: "In 'tvam agne,' there are ten verses; they belong to Vatsa Ābhreya and are in the *gāyatrī* meter; the last is a *triṣṭubh*; the *ādhā*, *pratiṣṭhā*, and *pādhā* are increasing [in syllables]."

In the Prātaranuvāka, during the Āgneya rite, in the Gāyatrī metre, and in the Āśvina Śastra, this hymn is used with the exception of the final verse. For it is stated: "One should recite the last verse, 'tvam agne vratapāḥ... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13). The first verse [of the hymn] is dedicated to Vratapati and serves as the invitatory prayer (anuvākyā).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows; whatever vows of ours we may violate" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13).

O Agni, you are the guardian of sacred vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices. O Agni, O radiant god, you are the guardian of vows (*vrata-pā*) among both mortals and gods; you are the protector of sacred rites (*vratāni*). For this reason, you are to be praised (*īḍya*) at the sacrifices.

You are to be praised in the assemblies, O victorious Agni; you are the charioteer of the sacrifices. O victorious Agni, subduer of enemies, you are to be praised in the assemblies—that is, in the sacrifices. You are the charioteer, the leader of the sacrificial rites.

As such, O Jātavedas, drive away from us our enemies; O Agni, drive away the godless and hostile forces. O Jātavedas, knower of all that is born, O Agni, you who possess the aforementioned qualities, separate from us those who hate us—drive them far away—and likewise separate from us the godless, demonic, and hostile armies of our foes.

O Jātavedas, even though you are present nearby, you do not approach the sacrifice of the mortal enemy; indeed, you have no desire for it. 4. Even though he is near—though you are present, existing in close proximity—you do not approach the sacrifice of that mortal, the enemy; the word *aha* is used for emphasis: you simply do not desire it. 4.

We mortals, the wise ones, meditate upon the many names of you, the immortal Jātavedas. (5) O Agni Jātavedas, knower of all that is born, we mortals—human beings who are sages and possessors of wisdom—meditate upon, that is, we know and celebrate, the many, extensive names of you, the immortal god who is free from death. (5)
The inspired poets call upon the inspired one for protection; mortals call upon the god Agni with songs for their aid.
1. You do not desire it.

The wise ones, the mortals—for the sake of help—we invoke with songs Agni, the god, for our protection. (6) The wise ones (*viprāsaḥ*) means the intelligent; the mortals (*martāsaḥ*) means we humans. We invoke with songs—that is, with hymns—the wise, intelligent god Agni, who is endowed with qualities such as generosity, in order to satisfy him with oblations (*avase*), and for the sake of our protection (*ūtaye*). In the *ābhiplavika* *ukthya* sacrifices, during the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the triplet beginning with "ā te vatsaḥ" is an optional *stotriya*. As it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘ā te vatsaḥ’, ‘mano yamadāt’, ‘āgne sthūraṃ rathi bhara’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

May Vatsa draw your mind hither, O Agni, even from the highest dwelling-place, with a song that longs for you. O Agni, may the seer Vatsa draw your mind toward himself, even from the most excellent dwelling-place—the heavenly world—by means of a song that yearns for you.

For in many places you are indeed the same; you are the lord over all the tribes. In battles we invoke you. (8) O Agni, for in many places you are indeed the same—identical in appearance. For this very reason, you are the lord and master over all the tribes, that is, over all the people. Such as you are, we invoke you in battles for the sake of protection.

In battles, seeking strength, we invoke Agni for protection—he who bestows wonderful wealth in the contests for booty. (9) In battles (*samatsu*), in the exhilarating conflicts, we—desiring strength (*vājayantaḥ*)—invoke Agni for protection (*avase*). Of what sort? One who possesses wonderful wealth (*citrarādhasam*) in the contests for booty (*vājeṣu*), that is, in the battles.

For you are ancient, indeed worthy of praise at the sacrifices; as the Hotṛ priest from of old, you sit as both ancient and new. O Agni, satisfy your own body with oblations, and through sacrifice, bestow prosperity upon us. He is ancient, indeed; worthy of praise at the sacrifices; from of old the Hotṛ, and yet new, you sit [in the rites]. O Agni, satisfy your own body, and through sacrifice, bring us prosperity. O Agni, at the sacrifices—those acts of worship—you are indeed ancient, for you are the one worthy of praise. The word *kam* is an expletive. Likewise, having been the Hotṛ—the invoker of the gods—from time immemorial, and being worthy of praise as something new, you sit down in the sacrifices. O Agni, carrying the oblations of the gods, satisfy your own body—that is, your own form—with your portion of the sacrificial offering. And for us, your worshippers, through sacrifice, grant us prosperity—that is, good fortune. The suffix *-añ* is applied after the word *subhaga* in the sense of "possessing," because it is listed among the words beginning with *udātta* in the rule *subhagānmantra*. 36. Translation complete.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may the Great Lord of the Supreme Holy Place (Yatīndra Maheśvara) bestow the four goals of human existence.

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the fifth book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Jha, Na, and Bha, "yajñeṣu" is not present.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, and Bha, it reads "subhagamantre.
Oṃ.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, having saluted whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones, at the commencement of all their undertakings, feel their purpose is accomplished and remain well.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.

Having thus explained the fifth Aṣṭaka, we now begin the explanation of the first chapter of the sixth [Aṣṭaka], preceded by a presentation of the seers, meters, deities, and ritual applications (viniyoga).
In the second Anuvāka of the eighth Maṇḍala, six hymns have occurred.
The thirty-third hymn, beginning with “ya indra,” is the seventh hymn; it belongs to Parvata of the Kaṇva lineage as its seer, is composed in the Uṣṇih meter, and has Indra as its deity.
And thus it is enumerated: "The [hymn] beginning with 'O Indra, you who are on the thirty-three mountains' is in the *auṣṇiha* meter.
In the *niṣkevalya* section of the *mahāvrata*, there are two hymns at the beginning of the *auṣṇiha-tṛcāśīti*.
Likewise, it is enjoined in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*: "The *auṣṇiha-tṛcāśīti* consists of the two hymns beginning with 'O Indra, greatest drinker of soma'" (*Ai. Ā. 5.2.5*).

On the tenth day, six verses at the beginning of the Niṣkevalya Śastra are to be recited; for it is stated: "The six Uṣṇih verses beginning with 'ya indra somapātama' [are to be used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.12). In the Brahmaśastra during the third pressing of the Ābhiplavika Pṛṣṭha days, the hymn beginning with 'āyāsya' serves as an optional *anurūpa* verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘O Indra, greatest drinker of Soma, come to us, O Indra’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.8).
In the third round, this same triplet is also the *anurūpa* for the Acchāvāka.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Indra [is the one] among the pressed Somas; he who is the greatest drinker of Soma, O Indra’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

O Indra, most powerful one, we implore that exhilaration which is the greatest drinker of Soma, which is conscious, and by which you strike down the devourer. We implore that very [exhilaration]. O Indra, most powerful one, we implore that exhilaration which is the greatest drinker of Soma, which is conscious, and by which you strike down the devourer. We implore that very [exhilaration].
O Indra, you who are the greatest drinker of Soma— the supreme consumer of Soma— O most powerful one (śaviṣṭha);
"śavas" is a name for strength.

Therefore, from the stem *vin*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied as a comparative (*ātiśāyanika*). By the rule *vinmator luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *vin*; thus, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
O Indra such as you, that intoxication (*mada*) produced by the drinking of Soma makes one conscious—that is, it enables one to correctly understand how to perform deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra.
Because the word *yaḥ* is also connected with the word *cetati*, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is not elided according to the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*.
Alternatively, this may be construed as a single sentence as follows: [he who is thus intoxicated...].
"O Indra, most powerful, greatest drinker of Soma, you who are the supreme drinkers of Soma—that exhilaration which is to be gladdened by Soma juices and is yours to win—[he] shall attain it.
There is a transposition of persons [in the verse]:
"you shall fully know in your mind."
In the word *mada*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *mad* according to the rule *‘mado ’nupasarge’*.

We seek from you that intoxication (*mada*) produced by the drinking of Soma—by which intoxication you strike down (*ni haṃsi*), that is, you cause the destruction of, the *atriṇ*, the sapless one belonging to the class of Rākṣasas. We implore you for such intoxication, for the purpose of making this request.
We entreat you;
or rather, [the root] *ī* means "to go."
It belongs to the *daivādika* class.
There is an elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
"Īyāmahai" means "we shall approach."
The meaning is: "We shall worship with hymns of praise."

With that [help] by which you protected Darśagva, Adhigu, the trembling one, and Svarvara; with which you protected the ocean—that we implore. 2. With that [help] by which [you protected] Darśagva, Adhigu, the trembling one, the lord of heaven; with which you protected the ocean—that we implore. 2.

O Indra, by that exhilaration born from drinking the Soma, [you protected] Daśagva—the Aṅgirasas known as the Daśagvas who, having completed their sacrificial session (*sattra*) in ten months, emerged [from it]. Of them, this [hymn] is for Abhrigu, one whose movement was unimpeded and who traveled eightfold; it is addressed to Varṣiṇ.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, and Na, the sequence *tara-4-na-bha-śa* is given as “Vāgīśādyāḥ... gajānanaṃ,” which is not present [in the other versions]. 2. In the manuscripts Ga, Na, Bha, and Śa, the sequence is *gatāni*; in Ta, it is *tāni*. 3. In Ga, the reading is *karmāṇi*. 4. In Ga and Na, it is *athavaitadeva*; in Bha, it is *athavaitadeka*. 5. In Ga, it is *balavan tvam indra*. 6. In Ga, it is *starpayitavyaḥ*. 7. In the manuscripts Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, it is *somapānāya janitena*; in Ga, it is *somapānena janitena*. 8. In Śa, it is *īk*. 9. In Bha and Śa, it is *īmahe*. 10. In Ga, it is *saṃbhajāma*. 11. In Ga, it is *metatsaṃjakaṃ vā ṛṣi*.
You protected the Sun—the shaker of darkness, the dispeller [of it], the golden-hued leader of all—by driving away the Dasyu Vṛtra and others;
and with that exhilarating power (*mada*), you protected the ocean, the waters, or the mid-air. We implore you for that exhilaration of yours, or for you who possess it.
"For when one is made joyful, Indra, being pleased, bestows much wealth;
therefore, a request for that cause—intoxication—is appropriate."

We pray for that [path] by which you impelled the Sindhu and the great waters like chariots, so that they might travel upon the path of Truth (ṛta). 3. By which [you impelled] the Sindhu, the great waters, like chariots; [that path] to travel upon the way of Truth—*for that we pray*. 3.
O Indra, with that exhilaration born of drinking Soma, you impel the great, vast waters—the rainwaters—toward the river, which is prone to flow, or toward the ocean;
therein the illustration is:
"as if [impelling] chariots."
Just as chariot-warriors urge their chariots toward their desired destination,
so do we entreat that exhilarating draught (mada) so that it may go— that is, reach— the path of *ṛta*, the way of sacrifice.

This hymn, purified like clarified butter, O wielder of the stone, for our protection—by which power indeed you have grown great among us. 4. This hymn... for our protection... like clarified butter... purified... O wielder of the stone... by which... now... together... with power... you have grown great. 4.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, like clarified butter—pure like ghee purified by mantras—be mindful of this our pure and stainless hymn of praise (*stoma*); [this is the ellipsis].
For what purpose?
For the sake of our desired aim (*abhiṣṭaye*).
The meaning is: "for our acquisition of desired wealth and the like.

By means of which hymn (*stotra*), being praised, you—by your own power (*ojasā*)—at that very moment, at the time of the praise itself, indeed quickly (*nu*) carry us (*vavakṣiya*) [to the goal]; that is, you cause us to attain our desire through this hymn (*stoma*). This is the syntactical connection.
Delight in this, O lover of songs; like the ocean, it swells. Indra, with all your aids, you have grown great. ||5||

O *girvaṇas*, you who partake of songs—that is, O Indra, who are to be honored by hymns—be pleased with and enjoy this *stoma* being performed by me. And that *stoma* swells, like the ocean which increases upon reaching the rising of the moon;
the meaning is that because of the abundance of the multitude of Indra’s qualities to be expressed, the praise that conveys them also becomes expansive.
The word "yena" (by which), joined with the verb "vavakṣiya" (you have carried) in the preceding ṛc, is connected here as well by virtue of its syntactic force;
for this very reason, there is no elision of accent (*nighāta*) for it according to the rule "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ."

O Indra, by whatever hymn of praise, by whatever cause, and by all your pervasive aids and protections you have grown great—that is, you carry [the worshiper] forward and lead them to what is better than that.

From the root *vah* with the suffix *san*, in the formation of the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*)—whereby the suffix *ām* is excluded by the prohibition "not in a mantra" (*amantra*)—this form occurs in the *thal* suffix of the *liṭ*.

The god who, from afar, has bestowed upon us friendship as our noble heritage—spreading it out like rain from heaven, you have carried us across. 6. He; us; god; from afar; with friendship; for our noble purpose; has bestowed; like rain from heaven; spreading it out; you have carried (us) across. 6.

1. *kha-gha₁-jña-ta₂₋₄-bha₂*: "in the removal of the two halves"; *na*: "not by the removals of the two halves"; *bha₁*: "by the removal of the position of ṛṭha"; *śa*: "in the removal of the two halves.
2. *ga*: "satisfied. 3. *kha-jha-ta₃*: "at the very moment"; *ga-na-bha*: "at the very moment"; *ta₄*: "at the very moment."
4. [The variants] *kha-ga-ta-bha-śa* do not contain the word *pinvate*.

The god Indra, endowed with qualities such as generosity (*dāna*), having come from the distant realm (*parāvataḥ parāvataḥ*)—that is, from afar, from the heavenly world (*dyuloka*)—has bestowed (*māmahe*) wealth (*dhana*) for our friendship (*sakhitvanāya*).
This is a form of the root *mā*, signifying the act of giving.
Or rather:
"It is worshipped by us," from the root *maha*, meaning "to worship."
In this verse, the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The second half-verse is addressed directly (*pratyakṣakṛta*).

O Indra, just like rain from heaven—spreading our riches as it were from the sky—you who have "wished to carry us" (*vavakṣitha*), that is, you who desire to bear us [to safety], I praise you; such is the ellipsis.
His banners have risen up, and the thunderbolt is in his two hands,
when he split asunder the two worlds like the sun.
His banners have grown strong, and the thunderbolt is in his two hands, when he, like Sūrya, has rent asunder the two worlds, heaven and earth.
The *ketavaḥ*— that is, the cognitions directed toward our hymns— of this Indra;
or else,
the *ketavaḥ* are the banners raised upon his chariot.
They have carried [us] forward;
they have brought us to superior states.
And moreover, from their two hands...

This refers to the arms. When this Indra, like the sun—the impeller of all—strengthened the two worlds, heaven and earth, by bestowing rain and other benefits, at that time the thunderbolt remained in Indra’s hands and carried [the burden]. This is the meaning.
O Lord of the Hundred, if a thousand great buffaloes were to swell with strength, then your great vital power would increase even further.
O Lord of the virtuous, when you, though but a child, devoured a thousand buffaloes, then indeed your great Indra-power increased. 8.

O *pravṛddha*, you who have grown exceedingly great; O *satapate*, O Indra, protector of the virtuous (*sat*); when you slew the thousand *mahiṣas*—this term "great" refers to the great Asuras such as Vṛtra and others—then [you became great].
This form of *han* is Vedic;
or else,
it is from the root *ghasla*, meaning "to eat."
In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule "ghasaḥ" [Pāṇini 2.4.37], there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*.
Immediately after that, O Indra, your *indriyam*—your heroic power—being *mahi*, great and abundant, *pra vāvṛdhe*, increases preeminently.
Indra consumes the food with the rays of the sun.
Victorious through his own inherent power, he has grown great.
Indra, with the rays of the sun, burns down the Arśāna; like Agni victorious over the forests, he has grown great. 9.
This *indra* [is] visible by means of the rays— i.e., the beams— of the *sūrya*, the impeller of all;
[the form] is derived from the root *ṛ* "to go" with the suffix *ānac* and the augment *śuṭ*, according to the rule "The quality of *ṛc* and the augment *śuṭ*" (Uṇādi-sūtra 2.245).
In this context, the prefix *ati* should be understood as signifying "excessive," even when used alone;
whereas the prefix *ā* is employed in the sense of "overpowering" or "subduing," as in the expression *ārtim ārchuḥ* (Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.2.4).
It utterly burns—that is, it completely consumes—the Asura Mandeha and others who cause the affliction of hemorrhoids;
[the root] *upa* here means "to burn.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as a forest fire reduces forests and jungles to ashes,
so too Indra— who is *sāsahiḥ*, characterized by the habit of overcoming his enemies— *pra vāvṛdhe*, increases exceedingly.
"This most recent [hymn] of yours, full of seasonal rites, with its prayers—
honoring you, much beloved— it is being measured out."
This newest prayer of yours, full of seasonal power, approaches; serving you, much-beloved, it measures itself out. 10.
O Indra, this *dhīti*—this hymn of praise being performed by me, standing here before you—goes toward you.
Of what sort is it? It is *ṛtviyāvatī*.
*Ārtvijyam* refers to sacrificial rites to be performed during the proper seasons, such as spring and others.
Possessing that [quality], she is *navīyasī*, most new [or excellent].

1. Ga: wealth and so forth. 2. Ga: of the best among the virtuous. 3. Ga: great and powerful; Gha: from greatness. 4. Ga: named Mandeha. 5. Jha-Ga: wealth, forests, and wildernesses; Ta: forest-dwellings.
This is a fresh praise [of Indra] in the form of a hawk.

"Worshipping" (saparyantī), meaning honoring him, and being "much-beloved" (purupriyā), meaning greatly pleasing, she "measures out" (mimīte) the qualities residing in Indra as if they were delimited objects;
the connection is that she thus proclaims his majesty.
Because of its connection with the word *anumīyamāna* and the word *yat*, there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the verb *mimīte*.
Alternatively,
*saparyantī purupriyā* should also be connected with this [verb] *eti*.

Therefore, since the preceding word resides in a different sentence, the rule "the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must be stated as occurring within the same sentence" applies; consequently, because there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) with respect to that [following word], the first syllable of the reduplicated form receives the udātta accent by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated forms [is acute]."
The divine one, the womb of sacrifice, purifies the season in due order;
she has grown strong through the hymns of Indra and measures them out.
The divine one, pregnant with the sacrifice, purifies the season in due order; she has increased through Indra’s hymns and truly establishes them. 11.

The wise ones (*viprāḥ*), the bringers of hymns (*ukthavāhasaḥ*)—that is, the carriers and deliverers of the *ukthas*, the recited liturgies—who are the *ātharvaḥ*, the human beings, have greatly exhilarated (*abhipramanduḥ*) that Indra with joy; [the verb *madi* takes the *parasmaipada* ending by way of grammatical substitution]. Of every sacrifice, [they have exhilarated him].
Due to the rule "In the Vedic language, there is optionally no doubling [of consonants] in the section concerning dual endings" (Kātyāyana 6.1.8.1), there is an absence of doubling.
*Āsani* means in the mouth (*āsye*) of that Indra; by the rule beginning with "padan," the word *āsya* is replaced by the substitute *āsan*.
I shall cause [the body] to grow by sprinkling it with pure *piṇya* (oil-cake), like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The form *pyāyate* is due to Vedic usage (*acchandasaḥ*); the substitution of *pī* for *pyai* occurs according to the rule "lidyahośca."
What is that? It is the oblation (*havis*).
The meaning is: that which exists as the oblation characterized by Soma, pertaining to *ṛta*, that is, the sacrifice (*yajña*).

And Aditi has generated a hymn for Indra, the self-ruling lord—the hymn highly praised for his protection—since it belongs to the Eternal Order (Ṛta). 14. And Aditi, for the self-ruling lord, has generated a hymn for Indra, highly extolled for his aid, since it belongs to the Eternal Order. 14.

Moreover, Aditi—the undepressed mother of the gods, or she whose hymns are unbreakable—has generated, has brought forth, has produced for Indra, who shines by himself (*svarāj*), a hymn (*stoma*) that is abundant and excellent, praised by many men, or rather, worthy of being praised by many;
for what purpose?
For protection (*ūtaye*).
That which is the hymn related to *ṛta*, to sacrifice, or to truth—that is the connection with the term "stoma.

The many have sung aloud for protection and for praise, as the two bay steeds of different courses [carry] the God, when that of *ṛta* occurs. (15) abhi | vahvayaḥ | ūtaye | anūṣata | praśastaye | na | devam | vi-vratā | harī | iti | ṛtasya | yat ||15||
The *vahvayas*, the officiating priests (*ṛtvijas*) who carry out the rites, have praised (*anūṣata*) Indra for the sake of protection (*ūtaye*) and for the sake of renown (*praśastaye*).
[The root] *nū* means "to praise";
it belongs to the *kuṭādi* class.
O Lord, Indra, endowed with qualities such as generosity; *na* here signifies "now.

Now, bearing your two bay horses (*harī*) while performing various deeds, they carry you toward that hymn or oblation which pertains to *ṛta*—whether it be the sacrifice or the truth. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Whether, O Indra, you rejoice in Soma with Viṣṇu, or indeed with Trita Āptya, or whether you delight among the Maruts with the flowing drops. || 16 ||

O Indra, if you drink the Soma together with Viṣṇu when Viṣṇu has come for the purpose of drinking at another person’s sacrifice; or if you drink the Soma while Trita Āptya— the son of the Waters, known by that name— is the royal seer performing the sacrifice as the patron—
*gha* being a particle used for filling out the meter.
Or if you rejoice (*mandase*)— that is, you take delight (*mādyasi*)— in the Maruts when they have come to another’s sacrifice for the drinking of Soma,
even so, rejoice thoroughly (*sam*) with our very own drops (*indu*),
that is, with our Somas. Or, O Śakra, if you rejoice in the distance, over the ocean, [rejoice] with our pressed drops, with our shimmering drops.
1. [The syllables] *kha*, *jña*, *ta* (3), and *pra* (4) signify praise; *ga* (1) and *bha* signify excellence; *ga*, *ra*, *ta*, *ra*, and *na* signify excellence.
2. *Ga* (1) signifies the drinking of Soma; *ga* (2) signifies the drinking of [other] juices. Or rather:
O Śakra, whether you rejoice in the distance or over the ocean, take delight only in our pressed juice along with the drops of Soma. 17.

O Śakra, lord of the Śakas, whether you are far away, having gone to a distant land, or in the ocean which is by nature surging, or in the *soma*— regarding these [places] as connected [to us] through our address: or if indeed you rejoice (*mandase*) and exhilarate yourself (*mādyasi*), even so, when our own *soma* has been pressed, join yourself completely (*saṃ raṇa*) with the drops, that is, with the juices of the *soma*.

Or if you, O Lord of the Truth, are the strengthener of the one who presses the juice and performs the sacrifice; or if you take delight in his hymn together with the drops. 18. Or if you are the strengthener of the one who presses the juice and performs the sacrifice, O Lord of the Truth; or if you take delight in his hymn together with the drops. 18.

O Indra, Lord of the good, protector of the virtuous, [be present] for the sacrificer who presses the Soma; or rather, you are the one who causes him to prosper (*vṛdhaḥ*). [The suffix] *ka* is used here with the sense of the root *vṛdh* being internalized, signifying the result of increase. And when the hymn (*uktha*) or the praise (*śastra*) of that sacrificer is recited, you take delight (*raṇyasi*) and rejoice.
Even so, drink well with our very own drops, that is, with our Soma juices.

For your protection, let us praise Indra after Indra, the god among gods; for the sake of the sacrifice and for victory, they have attained their goal. ||19|| God after god—for your protection—Indra, Indra, for the purpose of praising; for the sake of the sacrifice, for conquest—they have fully attained [their aim]. ||19||

O you priests and sacrificers, for your protection—that is, for your preservation—you [should worship] Indra, the God of gods, who is endowed with qualities such as generosity. Although Indra is one, he manifests as many, assuming numerous bodies in various places to accept the oblations at sacrifices performed simultaneously; thus, though single, he is present there in many forms.
Accordingly, another Vedic text states: "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.47.18).
In relation to that, this is a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
I praise—that is, I laud—that Indra who exists as everything divided into many parts. This form is a Vedic usage of the optative (*liṅ*) from the root *guṇāti*.
Or rather,
this is simply a verbal noun (kāraka):
[it means] "while desiring to praise," that is, when there is a desire to laud.
Immediately thereafter, my pressed juices have pervaded—indeed, they continue to pervade—the entire Indra.
For what purpose?
For swift enjoyment (*turvaṇe*), that is, for the sake of the sacrifice, for the performance of the ritual.
Alternatively,
because the object is treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) according to the rule "the mention of action must be made," the fourth case is used.
[The word *yajñam* refers to] a sacrifice that is to be seized, or one that overcomes enemies, or one that is quickly shared.
With sacrifices they have strengthened Indra, the bearer of sacrifice; with Soma-draughts, the greatest drinker of Soma; with invocations, they have increased him and attained their goal. ||20||

[We worship] with sacrifices—by means of various rites and offerings that accomplish the purpose of men—the "sacrifice-bearer" (*yajñavāhasam*), who is to be carried or brought by sacrifices, or rather, the one who brings about the fruit for the sacrificers of the songs of sacrifice.
Alternatively, he is the "sacrifice-bearer" because he is to be attained through sacrifice.
He says "with sacrifices" (*yajñebhiḥ*) to indicate that it is not merely by a single sacrifice, but by all of them.
Thus, with these Soma-libations, the singers have magnified Indra—the greatest drinker of Soma, the supreme drinker of all Soma—with invocations and hymns; they cause him to grow.
And those hymns being performed pervade him and reach Indra;
the verb *aś* takes the *parasmaipada* ending by virtue of the suffix *ti*.
1. Kha-tara-4-bha³-Śakreṃdra; Gha-jha-ta³-śa-Iṃdra.
2. Ga-adhiḥ. 3. Ga-ta¹-²-yajñavoḍhavyam.
In the sixteen-verse hymn, the triplet beginning with "yad indra pṛtanājye" is [the third].
For it is stated: "The two triplets 'yad indra pṛtanājye' and 'ayaṃ te astu haryataḥ' consist of uṣṇih and bṛhatī verses" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.2).
O Indra, when the gods placed you at their head in the battle for supremacy, then your two beloved bay horses carried you forward.
When, O Indra, the gods placed you in the forefront in the struggle for battle, then indeed your two beloved bay steeds bore you forward. 25.

"O Indra, in the *pṛtanājya*. This is the name of a battle (*saṃgrāma*). Alternatively, it is called *pṛtanājya* because the *pṛtanās*—armies—go (*ajanti*) toward it; or because one is conquered (*jīyate*) therein. Thus, *pṛtanājya* is a battle.

In that regard, when the gods placed you—*tvā*—in front (*puraḥ*) for the slaying of Vṛtra, holding you before them, immediately thereafter (*ādit*), [you became] the two beloved ones (*haryatā*), the two who are desirable. [The root] *harya* means "to move" or "to desire.
The suffix *atac* is added according to the rule beginning with *bhṛmṛdṛśi*.
Such were your two bay horses; they bore you and carried you along.
When you, O wielder of the thunderbolt, had slain Vṛtra who obstructed the rivers with your might,
then indeed your two beloved bay horses carried you forward.
When, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you slew Vṛtra who obstructed the rivers with your might, then indeed your two beloved bay steeds carried you forward.
"O Vajrin, cut through the river-encircled [obstacle] with the thunderbolt!
The waters are indeed roaring;
for it is heard in scripture: "When he roared in the two worlds after being slain, therefore you are named 'Nadyas' (the Roaring Ones)" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.1.2).
When, at that time, you slew with your might—that is, struck down—Vṛtra, who was obstructing [the waters], whether he be the cloud characterized by non-shining or the Asura;
the rest is the same.
When Viṣṇu strode out his three steps with his might, then indeed his two beloved bay steeds carried him forward.
When Viṣṇu strode forth with his might over the three steps, then indeed did those two beloved bay steeds carry him. 27.

O Indra, that god Viṣṇu, whose nature is pervasion, following after you with his vigor—that is, with his strength—at which time, in the form of three steps, traversed the three worlds, meaning he strode across and delimited them;
the rest has already been explained.
When those two beloved bay steeds grew stronger day by day,
then all the worlds submitted to you.
When your two beloved bay steeds have grown strong day by day, then indeed all beings have submitted themselves to you.

O Indra, when your two beloved, desirable, and seizing horses, the *hari*s, grew strong day after day—at that very moment thereafter, all beings, the entire multitude of creatures, were brought under control by you.
When the Marut clansmen restrained their musical instruments for you, O Indra,
from that moment all the worlds were brought under your control.
When those Marut clans submitted themselves to you, O Indra, then indeed all beings submitted to you. 29.
1. *gha*—they are yours.
2. *kha*, *jña*, *ta¹*, *bha*—they increased; *ta³⁻⁴*, *na*—they expanded; *śa*—they spread out.

O *indra*, for *tubhyam* (you), for your sake, when *mārutīḥ* (the Marut-related), i.e., those *viśaḥ* (clans) consisting of the Maruts, your own subjects, *niyemire* (restrained), i.e., when they restrained the multitudes of beings.
Anything else is false.
When you held up the sun, that bright light in heaven,
then all the worlds submitted to your command.
When you established yonder sun, that bright light in heaven, then indeed all beings submitted themselves to you. 30.

O Indra, when you sustained—that is, held fast—in the sky, for the illumination of the world, that distant, pure, stainless, shining light, the Sun, the impeller of all, the one of beautiful prowess, the Āditya;
[the rest is the same].
O Indra, this excellent hymn of praise the sage offers to you with his inspired thoughts; it carries him across, like a kinswoman carrying one to his station at the sacrifice.
This well-wrought hymn of praise, O Indra, the inspired singer sends forth to you with his meditations—like a kinswoman who brings him across to his goal at the sacrifice. (31)
O Indra, the wise sage, the singer, at the sacrifice, with his prayers, ritual acts, and services, sends forth this beautiful hymn—this present, fulfilling, and pleasing praise—to you;
just as one leads a kinsman to excellent steps and stations, so does he lead you forward.
When they, being well-united, sang aloud in his dear abode— at the navel of the sacrifice, at the milking during the ritual— then [the waters flowed].
When they sang together in his beloved abode, at the navel of the sacrifice, the milch-cows lowed forward at the rite.

When, at the sacrifice (*adhvara*), during the rite, in the abode (*dhāman*)—the place or the brilliance—of this Indra, which is dear and worthy of being gladdened, the singers, coming together in harmony, loudly sang forth their praise;
for there is a Vedic citation: "Now, indeed, the dear abodes of Indra" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.5.7.6). The root *svar* means both "to sound" and "to heat."
In what place?

At the *nābhi*, that is, at the navel; in the center which serves as the navel of the earth, at the milking of the Soma—the means of sacrifice—at the place of milking, that is, the site of the *abhivasti*;
in other words, upon the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).
The connection with what follows is: "then give the wealth."
O Indra, grant us great heroism, excellence in horses, and abundance in cattle, just as the Hotṛ priest does at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of first thought.
O Indra, grant us great heroism, abundance of horses, and abundance of cattle, just as a Hotṛ priest does for the sake of first thought at the sacrifice. 33.

O Indra, grant us— that is, give to us— wealth endowed with excellent heroism (*suvīryam*), joined with a splendid host of horses (*svaśvyam*), and accompanied by a magnificent herd of cattle (*sugavyam*). [The root *dad* in *daddhi* means "to give" and is anudātta.]
Thus, by this reasoning, the *parasmaipada* [is used].
1. *khanta-na-bha-śa-marutyaḥ*; 2. *khanta-na-bha-śa-prakāśamānāya*; 3. *gha-yajamāna-sādhanasya*; 4. *śa-dā*.
[In this form] there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ*).

And I, at the sacrifice (*adhvare yāge*), like a human Hotṛ-priest who praises as a knower (*vid*), have likewise praised [him] "for prior knowledge" (*pūrvacittaye*), that is, for the sake of knowing our hymn of praise before other worshippers; such is the sense to be supplied.
In the third Anuvāka there are eight hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, "indraḥ suteṣu," consisting of thirty-three verses, is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Nārada Kāṇva; it is addressed to Indra and is in the Uṣṇih meter.
Thus it is enumerated [in the Anukramaṇī]: "indraḥ suteṣu, [the seer is] Nārada."
Regarding the *niṣkevalya* hymn in the *mahāvrata*, the application (*viniyoga*) for the two *auṣṇiha* verses is stated together with the preceding *sūkta*.
In the third round (*paryāya*), the *stotriya* triplet for the *acchāvāka-śastra* is "indraḥ suteṣu" and so forth;
for it is stated: "indraḥ suteṣu someṣu... ya indra somapātamaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).

Indra purifies his praiseworthy resolve when the Soma juices have been pressed; for he is the great one who knows the increase of skillful power. When the Soma juices have been pressed, O Indra—O you who are worthy of being sought after through songs and hymns—for your sake, the gift belonging to the sacrificer who performs the pressing of the Soma flows forth; that offering given by the officiating priests goes toward the Āhavanīya fire.
And you, being thus exhilarated, rejoicing, and exulting, you shine forth preeminently over this sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
The root *rāj* has the sense of "to prosper.

"O Indra, grant us now that for which we, pressing the Soma, entreat you: bring us manifold wealth that finds the light of heaven. (5) Now, O Indra, give us that for which we, while pressing the juice, implore you. Bring to us wondrous wealth that discovers the light of heaven. (5)
O Indra, now—certainly—grant, that is, bestow, that wealth upon us.
[The root] *dad* means "to give.
The use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) here is by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
The *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Whatever wealth we, while pressing the Soma—performing the extraction—implore from you, furthermore, bring to us that wonderful, praiseworthy, and all-encompassing light, or rather, the knower of heaven, the believer; bring to us, as it were, a son, O Wealth! Bring it! Bring it! Bring it!

7 | When the far-seeing singer has boldly proclaimed your songs, he climbs up as if along branches, for you take pleasure in it. 6 || When the far-seeing singer has boldly proclaimed your songs, he climbs up as if along branches, for you take pleasure in it. 6 ||

O Indra, you who are the observer of men (*vi-carṣaṇi*), when the singer (*stotṛ*) especially intensified (*ati-praśardhayat*) his songs (*giraḥ*)— that is, hymns of praise— for your sake, making them exceedingly powerful for the subduing of enemies; [the root] *śradh* is used in the sense of "subduing" (*prasahane*).

When those songs delighted you, when they served you or sought your favor, then, just as many branches grow upward upon a single tree, so too do all virtues grow within you through praise. O ancient one, by your rejection [of the unworthy], hear the songs; hear the call of the singer. At every exhilaration, you have grown strong for the sake of the doer of good deeds. *pratnavat* | *janaya* | *giraḥ* | *śṛṇudhi* | *jarituḥ* | *havam* | *made-made* | *vavakṣitha* | *sukṛt-vane* ||7||
O Indra, just as in the past—just as formerly you generated praises by bestowing the desired fruits upon those who lauded you—even so now, generate and produce our songs of praise (*giraḥ*).
And hear, listen to the invocation (*havam*) of the singer, the praiser;
take it to heart.

Such as you are, when there is satisfaction after satisfaction with the exhilarating Soma, you carry—meaning you bestow—the desired fruit upon the well-doing sacrificer. His true words play like waters flowing down a slope; he who by this wisdom is called the Lord of Heaven. (8) His true words play, like waters going down a steep descent; he who by this prayer is called the Lord of Heaven. (8)
The *sunṛtās*—the words consisting of pleasant truth—of this Indra sport and frolic.
Therein lies the illustration:
like waters (*āpaḥ*) going (*yatīḥ*) along a downward-sloping path (*pravatā*).
Just as waters flow along a downward-sloping path, [the priests]—(1) *ga*-barhiṣi; (2) *kha-gha-ta-ja*-somābhiṣuṇvantaḥ; *ga-bha*-somān abhiṣuṇvantaḥ; *śa*-somābhiṣavaṃ kurvantaḥ.
3. "ga-ta-na-bha-śa-āhara" (Ṛgveda 3.39.61).
Just as they sport by flying up and swooping down, so it is here.

Indra—who is the protector (*pāti*) of heaven (*divaḥ*), that is, of the celestial realm (*svargasya*)—is addressed and propounded by this very hymn (*ayā dhiyā*), that is, by this praise; "of this Indra" is the grammatical connection.
