Moreover, he who is called Indra is the self-controlled one, the controller, the sole one, the very one who alone is the lord and protector of the *kṛṣṭī*s, that is, of human beings. By whom?
By those who increase him through homage—that is, by those who magnify him with praise or oblation—and by those seeking his protection, who desire his aid.
Therefore, you should take delight in that pressed Soma mentioned before;
or rather,
O singer, praise that Indra when the Soma has been pressed.
The root *raṇ* has the meaning of "sound."

Praise the renowned one, the wise, whose two bay steeds are ever-vigilant, who goes to the house of the donor—him who is worthy of our homage. 10. Praise! The renowned! The wise! The two bay steeds! Whose! Ever-vigilant! Who goes! To the house of the donor! Worthy of our homage! 10.
O singer, praise—that is, extol—that Indra who is wise (*vipaścit*), possessed of distinguished knowledge (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), learned (*śruta*), and renowned (*prakhyāta*).

Praise that Indra whose two bay horses (*harī aśvau*) are capable of overcoming enemies (*prasakṣaṇā*), who go to the house of the one who offers oblations (*namasvin*), who possesses sacrificial gifts (*haviṣmat*), and who is a liberal giver (*dāśuṣaḥ*)—that is, the sacrificer—and who are ever-ready to travel; such is the connection [of the verse].
The suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*ācchīlika*) when it follows a verbal root meaning "to play" (*div*).

Hastening with your horses that are dappled and swift, O you of great mind, come to the sacrifice; for indeed, peace is yours. 11. Hastening; O you of great mind; with horses; dappled and swift; come; to the sacrifice; with the fleet; for indeed, peace is yours. 11.
"O you of great intelligence! (*mahemate*): he whose mind (*mati*) or intellect (*buddhi*) is directed toward a great fruit (*phala*) is "one of great intelligence" (*mahemati*).
The absence of the *sandhi* elision (*aluk*) is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
O Indra, being thus impelled and hastening, come to our sacrifice with your swift-moving horses that are glossy and speckled;
for indeed, in that sacrifice of yours, there is found *śam*, happiness.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Come!"

O Indra, O most powerful one, O Lord of the virtuous, bestow wealth upon those who sing your praises; grant to the wise patrons immortal fame and abundance of riches. 12. O Indra! O most powerful one! O Lord of the virtuous! Wealth! Upon those who sing your praises! Bestow! Fame! Upon the wise patrons! Immortal! Abundance of riches! 12.

O most powerful (*v*śaviṣṭha), O lord of strength (*v*satapat), O protector of the virtuous (*v*satām pālayitah), O Indra (*v*indra), bestow (*v*rathi*) wealth (*v*dhanam*) upon us who are possessed of virtues (*v*guṇatsu); establish it (*v*dhāraya).

Furthermore, grant (*v*dehi)—this is the ellipsis—to the patrons (*v*sūribhyaḥ*), the singers of praise (*v*stotṛbhyaḥ), immortality (*v*amṛtam*), imperishable wealth (*v*vasutvanam*), pervasive fame (*v*śravah*), food, or glory.
At the rising of the sun, at the dawning of day,
O Indra, come hither with joy, taking pleasure in your steeds.
1. Bha-raṇa, praise!

I call upon you, O Indra, when the sun has risen; I call upon you at midday, in the middle of the day. O Indra, being pleased, come to us with your coursing horses. 13. O Indra, when the sun has risen—having reached its rising—at the morning libation (prātaḥsavana), I invoke you. Likewise, at midday—the middle portion of the day—at the midday libation (mādhyaṃdinasavana), I invoke you. O Indra, may you, being pleased and enjoying [the offering], come to us with your coursing horses (sasibhiḥ). 13.

Come hither quickly; run forth; rejoice in the pressed soma mixed with milk. Spin out the ancient thread, as you have known how. O Indra, come hither quickly; having arrived, run forth quickly toward that place where the Soma dwells. Having gone there, rejoice—be exhilarated and glad—by drinking the pressed Soma which is mixed with milk products such as milk and curds used for mixing. Thereafter, spin out—that is, properly complete—the ancient, extended thread of sacrifice, just as I perceive it; that is to say, make it capable of producing its fruit.

Whether, O Śakra, you are in the far distance, or whether, O slayer of Vṛtra, you are nearby, or whether you are in the ocean—of that Soma-juice, you are indeed the protector. O Śakra, O powerful Indra, if you are in the far distance; O slayer of Vṛtra, if you are nearby; or if you are in the ocean—that is, in the waters or in the intermediate space—from all those places, having come hither, you are indeed the protector through the drinking of the *andhas*, the food characterized by Soma. 15.

May our songs of praise increase Indra; may the pressed Soma drops increase Indra; may the people bearing oblations have found favor with Indra. (16) May our songs—our words in the form of hymns—increase Indra, cause him to grow. May the pressed Soma drops, the *indavas* extracted by us, also increase that Indra. May the people (*viśaḥ*), the subjects endowed with oblations (*haviṣmatīḥ*) consisting of sacrificial cakes and other offerings, have found favor (*arāṇiṣuḥ*) in that Indra. (16)
Him indeed, the inspired singers, seeking his protection, have magnified with their aids that flow forth like rivers; Indra, the worlds have magnified like branches. 17.

The wise (*viprāḥ*), the intelligent, desiring protection (*vavasyavaḥ*), the singers—those very ones—strengthen that same Indra with abundant, approaching, and satisfying offerings (*ūtībhiḥ*), whether these be oblations or hymns.
Likewise, they strengthen the two worlds (*kṣoṇīḥ*), the habitations.
“Kṣoṇī” is a name for the earth. All the worlds characterized by that [earth]—being dependent upon it like the branches of a tree—have increased and continue to increase.

At the Trikadruka rites, O gods, you performed the conscious sacrifice. May our songs of praise increase that very sacrifice which bestows excellent gifts. tri-kadrukeṣu | cetanam | devāsaḥ | yajñam | atanata | tam | it | vardhantu | naḥ | giraḥ | su-dāvṛdham || 18 ||
At the Trikadrukas—

where the Trikadruka days are the three Abhiplava days known as Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus— it was there that the gods, the divine ones, stretched out, wove, and fashioned the sacrifice for Indra, the conscious one, the impeller, the one to be worshipped.
In the word *tanoti*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) in the *laṅ* tense according to Vedic usage.
In the word *ambhasaḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In the verb *pibateḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Vedic usage.
By that Soma which you have drunk as the cause, may we overcome, cross beyond, and surpass all hostile enemy armies.
O Indra, lover of songs, when shall the singer become most blessed for you? When will you bestow upon us wealth in cattle and horses?
When, O Indra, lover of songs, shall your praiser become most blessed? When will you bestow upon us wealth in cattle and horses? 22.

O Indra, lover of songs (*girvaṇas*), who enjoys the praises (*gir*) of hymns—when, at what time, shall your praiser become most blissful (*śantama*), that is, most exceedingly happy? And when, at what time, would you establish us in wealth consisting of herds of cattle (*gavya*), in herds of horses (*aśvya*), and in other riches that serve as our dwelling (*vasu*)? Please sustain us in these.
And indeed, your two well-praised bay steeds, the powerful ones, carry the chariot of you, the ageless one, to that most exhilarating [soma] which we desire.
And indeed, your two well-praised bay steeds, the vigorous ones, carry the chariot of the undecaying one—the most intoxicating which we implore. 23.
Moreover, O Indra, let your two bay horses (*harī*), which are well-praised (*suṣṭutā*) and showerers of desires (*vṛṣaṇau*), now carry your ageless (*ajuryasya*) chariot to our vicinity.
You, whom we entreat for wealth that is most exhilarating (*maditamam*), belong to you—such is the syntactical connection.
We implore that one praised by many, the mighty one, with ancient aids;
may he sit down again upon the beloved sacred grass.
We implore him, the one praised by many, the youthful, with ancient aids; may he sit down upon the beloved sacrificial grass, for he has been established there from of old.

We implore that Indra—who is truly great, who is praised by many, and who is celebrated by many—with ancient, time-honored aids, namely with the means of satisfaction consisting of Soma-offerings. May that Indra sit down upon the beloved, joy-bestowing *barhis* (the strewn sacrificial grass), that is, the darbha grass, in order to accept the oblation. Furthermore, may he accept the oblations existing in a twofold manner, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, as well as those characterized by Soma; this is the understood sense.
Prosper, O you who are well-praised by many, with the protections beloved by the seers;
milk forth for us swelling nourishment and come hither to us.
Prosper, O you who are praised by many, with those aids celebrated by the seers! Pour forth for us swelling nourishment, and come hither toward us! 25.

O Indra, invoked by many, you who are praised by the seers with hymns composed by the seers—the visionaries of mantras—praised in ancient times; do thou increase well through these aids and protections; cause us to prosper.
Or rather:
do thou increase, attain growth, through these praises and aids offered by the seers.
For us, for ourselves, milk forth—pour down toward us—the swelling, abundant food that is desired; that is, grant it to us.
This is the meaning.

11. 1. Kha, Gha, Jha, Ta-1, 2, 3, Bha-1, 3, Śā: *śobhanastutī*; Ga: *śobhanaścatau*. 2. Bha: *vṛṣaṇā* (vṛṣaṇau). 3. Ga: *tara puruṣṭutam*. 4. Ga: *purāṇābhiḥ*. 5. Ga: *dvidhā*. 6. Ta-1, 2, Bha-3: *ṛṣistutābhiḥ*; Ga-2: *ṛṣibhiḥ stutābhiḥ*. 7. Ga, Na, Bha-1: *dhukṣva*.

O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, you are indeed the protector of the one who praises you in this manner. From the *ṛta* (the cosmic order), I send forth to you my prayer, yoked with thought. O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivaḥ*), you are indeed the protector (*avitā*) of the sacrificer who offers praise in this way (*ityā*). Since this is so, for that reason, from the *ṛta*—that is, from the sacrifice—I attain your *dhiyam*, your benevolent wisdom, which is "yoked with thought" (*manoyujam*), meaning it is to be meditated upon and reached through hymns of praise. Alternatively, from the *ṛta*—which is the truth—through praise, I attain the action that is joined with you and brings you pleasure.

O Indra, yoking here those two well-known bay steeds, the *sadhamādyas*, which possess far-reaching wealth, come hither for the drinking of Soma; call out to them! O Indra, yoking here those two well-known bay steeds, the *sadhamādyas*—to be gladdened and satisfied by you along with the oblations—which possess far-reaching wealth and have vast riches, come hither for the drinking of Soma; call out to them! (27) O Indra, at this sacrifice, for the sake of drinking Soma, come toward us. What are you doing? Yoking those two famous ones, the *sadhamādyas*—to be exhilarated and satiated by you together with the sacrificial offerings—the two bay horses (*harī*) that possess far-reaching wealth and extensive riches, joining them to the chariot.

Let those Rudras who follow you, O Indra, come toward us; let them attend upon this glorious sacrifice. And likewise, let the clans accompanied by the Maruts come toward our food. Let those Rudras who are your followers, O Indra—namely the Maruts—come toward us. Let them attend upon and reach this glorious sacrifice which is worthy of being resorted to. And furthermore, let the clans joined by the Maruts—other divine subjects as well—come toward our food; for "food" (prayaḥ) here refers to the oblation consisting of our sacrificial offering.

These, his swift-onrushing hosts, have taken pleasure in his station, when they have established themselves at the navel of the sacrifice, so that it may be known. (29) These aforementioned beings, consisting of the Maruts and others, who are his—Indra’s—*pratūrtayaḥ*, meaning those who violently strike down enemies, *juṣanta*, took pleasure in, or occupied, his *padam*, his place. That place in the sky (*divi*) which is difficult for others to discern is what is meant by "his station. Furthermore, they *sam dadhuḥ*, have established themselves, at the *nābhā*, the navel—the central point—of the *yajñasya*, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices; that is, in the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) or on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). *Yathā vide*: "so that it may be found," meaning in such a way that one obtains the desired wealth; or alternatively, "for the sake of knowledge" (*vide*), meaning so that we may possess superior wisdom and insight.

He—for far-reaching vision—toward the east, as the sacrifice proceeds, measures out the sacrifice in succession, having looked around. 3
1. *Kha-ta-na-bha-śa-yajñādetuḥ*.

2. *Kha-ta-na-bha-dakṣovaram*; *ga-pakṣe-varam*; *śa-dīkṣā-varam*. When the sacrifice—free from violence—is proceeding, moving forward, extending eastward in the eastern sacrificial hall (*yajñagṛha*), this Indra, having looked upon that proceeding sacrifice with special insight (*vicakṣya*) in due succession (*anuṣak*), measures it out—that is, he brings it to completion.
For what purpose? For long-lasting, extensive vision— that is, for seeing— or else:
For the sake of the fruit that is to be seen.

O Indra, your chariot is a bull; and your two bay steeds are bulls. You, O Śatakratu, are a bull; your roar is a bull. 31. This chariot of yours, O Indra, is a bull; and your two bay steeds are bulls. You, O Śatakratu, are a bull; your roar is a bull. 31.
O Indra, this chariot of yours is a bull (*vṛṣan*), a showerer of desires;
and moreover, your two bay horses (*harī*) are bulls, powerful showerers.
O Śatakratu, you of many deeds and great wisdom, O Indra, you too are a bull, a showerer of desires.
Likewise, "invocation" (havaḥ)—the calling directed toward you—is a showerer (vṛṣā);
even an invocation directed toward you showers desires.
What need is there to mention that your chariots and other [possessions] shower [them]? This is the intended meaning.

The pressing-stone is a bull, the exhilaration is a bull; this pressed Soma is a bull. The sacrifice which you impel is a bull, O Bull, for you are the one who brings joy. 32. The pressing-stone is a bull; the exhilaration is a bull; this pressed Soma is a bull. The sacrifice which you impel is a bull; O Bull, you are the one who brings joy. 32.
The pressing-stone (*grāvan*), the means for extracting [the juice], is a bull (*vṛṣan*), a showerer of desires.
O Indra, your exhilaration (*mada*) born from drinking the Soma is also a bull, a showerer. And this pressed Soma, extracted for your sake, is likewise a bull, a showerer.
The sacrifice which you promote—you reach—that sacrifice is a bull, a showerer of the desired fruit;
and your invocation is also a bull.

As a bull, I call upon you, the bull, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with your wondrous aids; for you, the bull, are worthy of praise, and you have accepted our hymn of praise. 33. Bull. You. Bull. I call. Wielder of the thunderbolt. With wondrous. Aids. For you are worthy of praise. Toward the hymn of praise. Bull. You have accepted. 33.

O Vajrin, wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, you who are the bull (*vṛṣan*), the showerer of benefits—I, the bull, the showerer of oblations, call upon you with various wonderful and praiseworthy aids that bring satisfaction; I invoke you with hymns. For since you, being worthy of praise, cherish and accept the hymn made in your honor, therefore my invocation is effective as a showerer of boons.
Or alternatively:
The meaning is: since you, the bull and showerer, accept the praise, therefore you are "hava" (to be invoked).
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "yad indrāṅhaḥ," is addressed to Indra; it is in the Gāyatrī metre and is the seership of Gopūkya and Aśvasūki of the Kaṇva lineage.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "yad indra, fifteen verses short [of sixteen]; Gopūkya and Aśvasūki, the two descendants of Kaṇva.
This hymn is recited at the Niṣkevalya section of the Mahāvrata rite.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "In the hymn beginning with 'yad indrāha yathā tvam pra samrājam carṣaṇīnām'" (*Aitareya Āraṇyaka* 5.2.5).
This same hymn also occurs in the *Brahmakhaṇḍa* during the third *paryāya*.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'yad indrāha pra te mahe'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.4).

O Indra, if I were the sole lord of wealth as you are, my worshipper would be a possessor of cattle. (1) If, O Indra, I were like you, the sole ruler of riches, then my singer of praise would be one who possesses herds of kine. (1)
1. gha-ta-na-cakṣase ca;
2. gha-tvā tvām;
3. śa-vāvaṃdha.

O Indra, just as you alone, being truly singular, rule over *vastu*—that is, over wealth (*vasu*) or treasure (*dhana*)—so too, if I were to possess such sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), then my worshipper would be "friend of cattle" (*gosakhā*), meaning he would be accompanied by cattle. The intention is: why should the worshipper of you, the Lord, not be accompanied by cattle? Indeed, he should be so. 2.
O Lord of Śacī, I would wish to learn from this wise one and desire to give [myself] to him.
I would learn; I would wish to give this to him; O Lord of Might, to the wise one—so that I might become a lord of cattle. 2.
O Lord of Śacī, O Indra, bestow power upon this wise singer; may I have mastery over my mind and desire to give this gift to the one who praises me.
Thereafter, may I teach—that is, may I grant—the wealth requested.
[The ellipsis implies: "If, by your grace, I should become the lord of cattle (gopatiḥ), the sovereign of cows."
O Indra, your generous bounty is like a cow; for the sacrificer who presses the soma, she yields milk, kine, and horses in abundance.
The verse "dhenuḥ te indra sūnṛtā yajamānāya sunvate" is the *paryāsa* triplet for the office of the *brahman* priest at the morning pressing on the twenty-fourth day.
For it is stated: "The triplets beginning with 'vyantarikṣamatiracchayāvāvasya sunvataḥ' are the *paryāsa*s" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.2).
On the second and subsequent days of the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices as well, this same *paryāsa* triplet belongs to that very same *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *hotrakas* recite the *paryāsa*s day by day from the second day onwards" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.1).

In the exhilaration of Soma, Indra extended the luminous realm of the intermediate space when he split Vala asunder. (7) In the exhilaration (*made*) produced by drinking Soma, this Indra extended (*atirat*) the shining (*rocanā*) intermediate space (*antarikṣam*). For he split (*abhinat*), that is, tore open (*vyadārayat*), Vala—the Asura or the cloud—standing there obstructing it. (7)

He drove out the cows for the Aṅgirases, making manifest those that were hidden in the cave; he thrust Vala downward. (8) He drove out the cows for the Aṅgirases, the seers, from whom they had been carried off by the Paṇis who dwell in Vala. Making what? Making manifest—bringing to light—those cows which were "hidden in the cave," existing in the secret place of the cavern so that they were not seen, being concealed by the Paṇis. Furthermore, he thrust Vala, the Asura and lord of the Paṇis, downward, driving him face-downward.

By Indra, the luminous realms of heaven were made firm and strengthened; they are steadfast and cannot be driven away. (9) By Indra, the luminous realms (*rocanā*) belonging to heaven (*divaḥ*)—those shining bodies consisting of the dwellings of the gods, namely the stars—were made firm (*dṛḷhāni*), having strong constituent parts, and were strengthened (*dṛṃhitāni*). The meaning is that they were made to abide in one place with immobility. Alternatively, since the roots *dṛha*, *dṛhi*, and *vṛhi* mean "to grow," the sense is that they were increased (*vardhitāni*). Furthermore, being steadfast (*sthirāṇi*) and solid, they are not to be driven away (*na parāṇude*); that is, they cannot be displaced from their positions by anyone. The root *nud* means "to impel"; from this, the suffix *ken* is applied according to the rule for the sense of gerundives (*kṛtyārthe*). 3.

Like a wave of the waters, O Indra, the hymn of praise speeds swiftly toward you; your exhilarations have shone forth. Like a wave of the oceans, like a surging billow that rises higher and higher in intoxication, so, O Indra, does this hymn of praise move with the speed of a swift runner. With the foam of the waters, O Indra, you struck off the head of Namuci, when you conquered all rival hosts. 13. With the foam of the waters, O Indra, you struck off the head of Namuci, when you conquered all rival hosts. 13.
In former times, it is said, Indra was unable to seize the asura Namuci, the lord of the asuras.
While fighting with that asura, he was captured by him.
Having been seized, Indra spoke to him in this manner.

"I release you at night and by day, with the dry or the wet weapon, provided that you do not harm me. Thus released by him, Indra, at the junction of day and night, severed his head with foam—which is characterized as being neither dry nor wet.
This meaning is established in this [verse].
O Indra, with the foam of the waters that had become the thunderbolt, you severed the head of the Asura Namuci from his body; you caused it to roll away—meaning, you cut it off. If one asks "When?"—
When you, O Indra, having slain Vṛtra and the Asuras, conquered all— the entire— contending hosts of the Asuras.

O Indra, you shook down the Dasyus who, by means of their magical powers (*māyābhiḥ*), were seeking to ascend to heaven. 14 O Indra, you shook down the Dasyus who, by means of their magical powers, were seeking to ascend to heaven. 14 — O Indra, you shook them down; you impelled them headlong.

O Indra, drinking the Soma and becoming superior, you utterly destroyed the assembly of those who do not press the Soma, causing them to go in all directions through mutual discord. 15 O Indra, as a drinker of Soma, becoming more excellent, you have completely destroyed the assembly of those who do not press the Soma—that assembly which goes in various directions due to internal strife. 15–16.

The third hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "tambabhi," is in the auṣṇiha meter and is dedicated to Indra; its subject matter is the same as that of the previously mentioned [hymns]. Thus it is enumerated: "tambabhi, [it is] with the *sasa* [refrain], in the auṣṇiha [meter]."
In the *niṣkevalya* of the *mahāvrata*, because it consists of *auṣṇiha* verses, this hymn is used in the *aśīti* [stoma], excluding the last verse.
For it is stated: "He sings 'tam abhi pra gāyata'; he omits the last verse" (*AiA* 5.2.5).
Among the options for the *ābhlava* days, in the *brahmaśastra* at the third pressing, the first triplet of verses serves as an optional *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Sing forth to him; we [sing] to you, the ancient one" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

Sing forth to him with songs; seek to win over with hymns Indra, who is invoked by many and praised by many—the radiant one. Sing forth to him; sing forth to Indra, who is invoked by many and praised by many. With your songs, seek to win over the radiant one.

Sing forth, O singers, toward that very Indra, who is invoked by many (*puruhūta*) and praised by many (*puruhūta*). Whose great strength (*bṛhat sahaḥ*), being doubly vast (*dvibarhasaḥ*), sustains both heaven and earth (*rodasī*), the mountains, the clouds, the waters, and the sun (*svar*) by his virile power (*vṛṣatvanā*). O you who are praised by many (*puruṣṭuta*), you alone rule (*rājasi*). O Indra, you strike down the Vṛtras (*vṛtrāṇi jighnase*) so that we may obtain the spoils of victory (*jaitrā*) and glorious fame (*śravasyā*) to be mastered. 4. Exulting in that intoxication, rejoicing, you shine forth (*virājase*)— that is, you rule preeminently— at this *barhis* grass, at the increasing sacrifice.
The genitive case "of this" (*asya*) is used in the sense of the instrumental.
With this sacrificial grass and with wealth, rejoicing, you shine forth; you blaze preeminently.

Therefore, the chanters of hymns follow after that exalted mind as of old; conquer the waters whose lord is the bull, day by day. Therefore, even now, the chanters of hymns follow after that [mind] as of old; conquer the waters whose lord is the bull, day by day.
O Indra, that well-known power of yours even now, as of old, the chanters—those who possess the hymns and the sacrificial verses—praise in succession.
As such, O Lord, win day by day the waters whose husband is the rain-god Parjanya, bringing them under your own control.

That great power of yours, your vigor, and your wisdom—the Dhiṣaṇā bestows upon you that desirable thunderbolt. 7. Your—that—power—great—your—vigor—and—wisdom—thunderbolt—bestows—Dhiṣaṇā—desirable. 7.

so too does praise sharpen your *śuṣma*—your drying, consuming strength—and furthermore, your *kratu*—your wisdom, power, or action—as well as your excellent *vajra*, the weapon to be chosen. Praise makes them keen.

O Indra, heaven and earth increase your manly power and your fame; the waters and the mountains incite you. 8. O Indra, heaven increases your manly strength; the earth increases your renown; the waters and the mountains urge you on. 8.

the earth increases your *śravaḥ*, your fame.

[In the formation of the verb], after the root *vṛdh* in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *śap*, because of the rule "in the Veda both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), there is the status of being an ārdhadhātuka; consequently, by the rule "after a verbal root ending in *g*, when followed by a suffix not having *iṭ*" (*geraniṭi*), there is the elision of the causative marker *ṇi*.
The waters, the intermediate spaces, the mountains—meaning the cloud-masses possessed of joints—or the hills, all these impel you, O Lord; they please you or attain you as their own master.

likewise, the host— the strength— belonging to the Maruts exults after you, following your joy, or rather,

O Indra, you, the bull, the showerer of benefits, are born as the most bountiful giver among all people, among the divine folk; therefore, you hold and bestow all things together with noble offspring, such as sons and others. O you who are praised by many, you alone truly strike down the Vṛtras; no other than Indra performs a greater deed.

O Indra, invoked by many, you alone, being without a second, utterly—this is a great thing—destroy all the vast Vṛtras, the hosts of enemies; or rather, "utterly" (*satrā*) means "with companions. Together with them, simultaneously, and with a single effort, you strike them down. *Tośati* is a verb meaning "to slay"; the sense is that they are incapable of acting [against you]. Furthermore, no one other than this Indra performs, nor attains, any greater deed, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and the like. The sense is that Indra alone is capable of performing [such deeds]. When, O Indra, those who praise your thought call upon you in various ways for aid, then, with our men, conquer the light of heaven here. (12) When, O Indra, those who praise your thought call upon you in various ways for aid, then, with our men, conquer the light of heaven here. (12)

O Indra, in whatever battle they invoke you with various hymns of praise and with their thoughts for the sake of protection, being thus summoned by our own men—the leaders and singers—conquer and overcome the enemy force, the light of heaven (*svaḥ*). Be ready for our great dwelling; entering into all forms, gladden Indra, the Lord of Might (*śacīpati*), for victory. (13) Be ready for our great dwelling; entering into all forms, gladden Indra, the Lord of Might, for victory. (13)
He, the praiser, has implored for our great dwelling— that is, for our house— for the sake of that [dwelling].
The dative case is used here in the sense of purpose (tādarthye).

For the sake of the house, [he approached] the Lord of Śacī— the protector of actions (for *śacī* is a name for action)— entering and pervading through praise all the pervasive forms, that is, the entire collection of qualities residing in Indra; [it is] sufficient, excellent, and complete.
Or rather:
by means of *śacī*, make *Indra*—who has become the husband of *Śacī*—rejoice; gladden that very *Indra* for victory, that is, for the sake of conquering what is to be conquered.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "either by praise or by service."
The fourth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "pra saṃnājam," is the ṛṣi-seer Irimbiṭhi Agni Kāṇva’s composition; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and addressed to Indra.
For it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Pra saṃnājam: twelve verses by Irimbiṭhi. This hymn is recited as the Acchāvāka-śastra during the second round (paryāya) of the Atirātra sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pra saṃnājam upa kramasvā bhara*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

In the Mahāvrata as well, these two hymns beginning with this [verse] are used for the Niṣkevalya, excluding the final *dvṛca* (pair of verses) from the subsequent section. Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: “In the hymn *pra saṃnājaṃ carṣaṇīnām*, one omits the last two [verses] of the latter [section]” (Ai. Ā. 5.2.5).
Let the praiser celebrate with new songs Indra, the sovereign of the people, the most bountiful among men, the protector of heroes.

1. *bha*: all riches. 2. *kha*: you bestow (*dadhiṣe*); *ta*, *na*, *śa*: you bestow upon the two most excellent praisers; *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *śa*: you bestow; you are born (*jajñiṣe*); you manifest (*prādurbhavasi*); for that very reason, *viśvā*: from all [directions]; *bha*: you bestow upon the praisers.
3. *ga*, *na*, *bha*: moreover, O Indra.

"Praise Indra, the sovereign of the peoples, the man of new songs, the most bountiful, the subduer. (1)
O singers, praise with excellence Indra, who shines preeminently among the *carṣaṇīs*, that is, among men; or rather, the sovereign lord of men.
How is he?

With songs—that is, with hymns of praise—he is the one to be praised anew (*navyam*), the leader (*naram*), the protector of men (*nṛpāham*), the overcomer of enemies and human beings, and the most bountiful giver (*maṃhiṣṭham*).
In whom all hymns of praise and all glorious deeds find delight,
as the waters find their rest in the ocean.
In whom all hymns of praise find delight, and all glorious deeds, like the descent of waters into the ocean. || 2 ||
In that Indra, all *ukthas* (hymns) and *śastras* (recitations) take delight; and all things worthy of renown—every kind of food characterized by oblations—also find their rest.
Therein lies the illustration:
like the protection (*ava*) of the waters (*apām*) in the ocean (*samudre*).
It is called *avastaraṅga-jala* because it descends or moves downward;
the meaning is that they roar just as [water] subsides within the ocean.
I seek to win him with a beautiful hymn— the eldest king, the one who acts according to his will, the mighty possessor of strength— for the sake of winning great spoils.
I seek to win him over with fair praise—the sovereign king, the most excellent, the one who acts with purpose, the mighty victor—for the sake of gaining great spoils.
I honor that Indra with *suṣṭuti*, with excellent praise; how so? As *jyeṣṭharāja*, shining among the *jyeṣṭha* gods, those who are most praiseworthy.
From the root *rāj* (to shine), the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule *asatsūdviṣa...*.
In the battle (*bharé*), [he praises] the one who is the doer (*kṛnúm*) of great deeds (*máhaḥ*) such as the slaying of Vṛtra, the possessor of food (*vājinam*) or the powerful one. For what purpose?
"From riches" means for the sake of obtaining wealth.
Whose exhilarations are unfailing, profound, wide, and rescuing, full of joy in the battle for heroes.
Whose exhilarations are unimpaired, profound, wide, rescuing, and full of joy in the battle for heroes. 4.

The exhilarations (*madas*) of that Indra, produced by the drinking of Soma—which are *anūnāḥ* (unfailing), *gabhīrāḥ* (profound in depth), *uravaḥ* (vast), *tarutrāḥ* (crossing over or overcoming enemies), and which, in the *śūrasātau* (battle frequented by heroes), become *harṣumantaḥ* (filled with joy and eager for combat)—belong to him; such is the connection with the preceding and following verses regarding that Indra.
For when the stakes are set, they call upon him for assistance;
those whose ally is Indra are victorious.
For when the spoils have been set out, they call upon him alone as their helper; those whose Indra is [their ally] are the victors. 5.

When wealth is at stake, when enemies are arrayed, and when prizes are to be won, the singers invoke that very Indra—possessing the aforementioned qualities—for the sake of speech, for the sake of proclamation, and for the sake of partisan advocacy. And in that regard, those on whose side Indra stands are the ones who conquer;
through victory they obtain those riches, and no others.
They drive him hither with flashes of light; they urge him on with sacred hymns.
This Indra is the creator of wide space.
Him they drive away with incitements; him they crush with their deeds. This Indra is the creator of wide space. 6.

With *yautana* hymns that bestow strength, men honor that very Indra; they make him noble, the omniscient Lord. Through their deeds, men honor him. This Indra, possessing such qualities, becomes the provider of wealth for his worshippers.

Indra is called Indra, Indra is the seer, Indra is much-invoked; great with his mighty powers. 7. Indra. Bruva. Indra. Rṣiḥ. Indra. Puru. Puruhūtaḥ. Mahān. Mahībhiḥ. Śacībhiḥ. 7.

He is worthy of praise, he is to be invoked, he is to be pressed [for libation], a warrior-hero of many deeds; though he is indeed alone, he is all-surpassing in power. 8. He. Worthy of praise. He. To be invoked. To be pressed. A warrior. Of many deeds. Being indeed one. All-surpassing. 8.
That aforementioned Indra is worthy of praise (*stomya*), that is, he is to be lauded;

he alone is to be invoked (*havya*) and is true (*satya*), meaning he is virtuous among the good or possesses an invincible nature; he is a warrior (*satvā*) who brings down his enemies, and one of many deeds (*tuvikūrmi*).
For this reason, although he is "one," being alone and without companion, he becomes "overpowering," a subduer and a scorner of his enemies.

The people, the inhabitants of the earth, magnify that Indra with hymns, with Sāman chants, and with Gāyatra verses. 9. Him—with hymns; him—with Sāmans; him—with Gāyatrīs; the people—the inhabitants—magnify Indra. 9.

The *carṣaṇayaḥ*—the seers who perceive the mantras—and the *kṣitayaḥ*—human beings—strengthen that Indra with *arkaiḥ*, that is, with Yajus-form mantras which serve as means of praise. Likewise, the Udgātṛ priests strengthen him with *sāmabhiḥ*, that is, with mantras distinguished by their chanting.
Similarly, the Hotṛ priests strengthen that very Indra with *gāyatraiḥ*, that is, with Śakvari-form mantras not sung, which are endowed with meters such as Gāyatrī and the like.

To the leader toward better fortune, the maker of light in battles, the conqueror of enemies in combat—[to him we pray]. 10. Leader; toward better fortune; hither; the maker; light; in battles; the conqueror; by battle; the enemies. 10.

"Vasyaḥ" means more excellent; "vasīyaḥ" means highly praised wealth or treasure. "Accha" means toward or in the direction of. "Praṇetāram" means the one who leads or causes to reach. "Samatsu" means in battles, by means of the destruction of enemies. "Jyotiḥ" means light, characterized by victory. "Kartrīm" means the one whose nature is to act or produce. [The suffix] *tan* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) from the root *kṛ*. Why is this so? He says:
"By means of *yudhā*, that is, through battle, [he is] *sasahāṃsam*, one who has overcome *amitrān*, the enemies;
the ellipsis is "they cause Indra, who possesses such qualities, to increase."

He, the protector, carries us across to safety by boat; Indra, invoked by many, leads us beyond all enemies. 11. He; us; protector; carries across; safely; by boat; invoked by many; Indra; all; beyond; enemies. 11.

He who has crossed over, the filler, the fulfiller, Indra, invoked by many—he, with a boat as a means of crossing, shall safely carry us across all enemies, our hating progeny, through well-being and security. May he deliver us.
As such, O Indra, favor us with strengths; grant us a path and lead us toward happiness. 12. As such, you, O Indra, [favor] us with strengths, and grant [us] a path, and lead us toward happiness. 12.
1. For the sake of the entire host (gaṇa).
2. May he cause us to cross over, may he protect us.
O Indra, such as you are, reveal yourself to us with strengths (vāja) and grant us wealth.

The root *daś* has the sense of giving as its function. And [the word] *gātu*: [it means] "desire for the path" (*mārga*). From the word *gātu*, the suffix *kyac* is applied in Vedic usage in the sense of "desiring another" (*parēcchā*).
There is no prohibition of the long vowel in *chandasyaputrasya*.
Likewise, lead us (*naḥ*), who are well-knowing, toward happiness (*sujñam*) and toward our purpose (*accha*).
The fifth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "ā yāhi," is addressed to Indra and composed by Imimbiṭha Darāṣa.
The fourteenth verse is a Bṛhatī and the fifteenth is a Satobṛhatī; the first thirteen are Gāyatrīs.
Indeed, it is enumerated thus: "ā yāhi [consists of] five fewer [verses], ending with a Pragātha."
Excluding another *pragātha*, the application (*viniyoga*) of the remainder has been stated for the *mahāvrata*.

In the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), six verses are to be recited as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the *brahmaśastra*; likewise, the subsequent six verses are also to be recited.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Ā yāhi supumā hi te’—these six are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses; the subsequent seven [verses]... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.10).

On the twenty-fourth day (*cāturviṃśika*), at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the first triplet in this very *śastra* is designated as the *ṣaḍaha-stotriya* for the purpose of insertion (*āvāpa*).
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'Ā yāhi supumā hi te', 'indram indrāthino bṛhat'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.2).
Come hither, for thou art truly full of power; O Indra, drink this Soma! Sit upon this sacred grass of mine.
Come, O Supuṣma! For this Soma is thine, O Indra; drink it. Sit here upon this sacred grass of mine. 1.
O Indra, come; do thou arrive.
For we have indeed pressed the Soma for thy sake.
Drink this very Soma that has been pressed.
For that purpose, sit down upon this my sacred grass (barhis) spread upon the altar; take your seat, settle yourself here.
O Indra, may your two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer, bring you hither;
hear our sacred invocations.
O Indra, let the two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer, bring you hither; listen to our sacred hymns. 2.
O Indra, may the two long-maned, tawny steeds, yoked by prayer and joined by the mantra, bring you hither toward us.
And you, having approached our sacrifice, hear our prayers; accept our hymns and hold them well within your mind.
O Indra, we, the Brahmans, possessing Soma and having pressed it, invoke you as our companion, O drinker of Soma.
O Indra, we Brahmins, accompanied by you as our ally, being Soma-drinkers ourselves and possessing Soma, call upon you with songs of praise.
O Indra, we Brahmins, as priests, invoke you with a fitting hymn of praise;
how so?
As the drinker of Soma, the one who drinks the Soma juice.

Of what sort are we? We are *sominaḥ*, possessed of *soma*; we are *sutavantaḥ*, having pressed the *soma*; and we are *abhiṣutaiḥ somair upetāḥ*, endowed with the *soma* juices that have been extracted by pressing.
Come to us who have pressed the juice; come to our beautiful hymns of praise. O fair-cheeked one, drink of the exhilarating draught.
Come to us who have pressed the juice; come to our beautiful hymns of praise. O fair-cheeked one, drink well of the soma-plant. 4.
O Indra, come toward us who have pressed the Soma;
having approached, then attend to and recognize our excellent hymns of praise.
O Indra, you with the beautiful helmet or beautiful jaw, drink your portion of the path of the food characterized by Soma.
Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object:
"O blind one, drink our Soma."
1. ga1-abhiprāyasi; gara-abhiprāyaḥ | 2.

ga-ta-bha-suṣumā | I pour it into your two flanks; let it flow through your limbs. May you swallow the sweetness with your tongue. (5) I pour it into your two flanks; let it flow through your limbs. May you swallow the sweetness with your tongue. (5)
O Indra, into those two flanks, your bellies, I pour;
I cause the Soma juices to flow in.
The meaning is: "I fill your flanks with Soma."
For Indra indeed has two bellies;
thus it is heard in scripture: "Fill both bellies with the soma-drink and with the sweet food.
Or else:
The duality [of the moon] arises from the distinction between the left and right sides, or the division of the two halves, of that very single belly.
Let that [moon], as the Soma, pervade—that is, occupy—all the limbs, the members of the body such as the hands and feet, one after another.
And you, with your tongue—the organ of taste—take up the sweet Soma being poured by me for the sake of enjoyment.
By the rule "chandasi śāyaj api," the suffix *bha* following the root *grah* is replaced by *śāyac*; its status as *bha* is established by the rule "hrasvād bhaḥ."

May it be sweet for your enjoyment; may the honeyed Soma be for your body; may the Soma be a blessing to your heart. (6) May it be sweet for your enjoyment; may the honeyed Soma be for your body; may the Soma be a blessing to your heart. (6)
O Indra, for you who bestow [blessings] perfectly and well, may this sweet Soma be pleasant and delightful;
may it be sweet for your body (tantra);
and may that Soma be auspicious (śam), a source of happiness, for your heart (hṛd).

O all-beholding Indra, let this Soma flow forth toward you, like a woman who has been embraced. 7. This one, O all-beholding one, like women gathered together, let the Soma flow forth toward you, O Indra. 7.

O Indra, most observant one, as a husband is [attracted] toward his wives, so let this Soma, covered like women by white garments, approach and flow toward us—covered, that is, enveloped by the path and other ingredients for mixing.
"U" is a filler.

With a thick neck, a pot-bellied form, and strong arms, Indra slays the Vṛtras in the exhilaration of the soma-juice. 8. With a thick neck; with a pot-bellied form; with strong arms; in the exhilaration of the soma-juice; Indra; slays the Vṛtras. 8.

Long-necked (*tuvigrīvaḥ*) means having a broad neck; "broad-bellied" (*vapedaraḥ*) means having a full belly, in the sense that his expanded stomach can contain many Soma drinks as if they were swallowed within. Having such qualities, Indra, with beautiful arms (*subāhuḥ*), when exhilarated by the joy (*made*) of the food (*andhasaḥ*) consisting of Soma, strikes down (*jighnate*) the Vṛtras, that is, the hosts of enemies.

O Indra, go forward at our head; you who rule over all by your might, O slayer of Vṛtra, destroy the obstacles. 9. O Indra! Forward! Go! Before us! You! Ruler of all! By your power! The obstacles! O slayer of Vṛtra! Destroy! 9.

O Indra, being the lord and master of the entire world by your power and strength, go forth before us, proceed, and reach our front. O slayer of Vṛtra—slayer of obstructing enemies—destroy the Vṛtras, that is, annihilate the hosts of our enemies.
In the eight [offerings] at the rise of the moon for Indra the Giver, "Long be your goad" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
For it is stated: "Long be your goad; auspicious be your hands, well-formed be your palms" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.13).

1. *ga-ta-bha*—this is *asik*. 2. *ga-ta-bha-a*—there is no *asik*. 3. *bha-gātrā*—the limbs. 4. *ya-sarvāny-anukrameṇa*—all of them in succession. 5. *ga-prahe*. 6. *ga-bha-somaḥ tvām*. 7. *ga-vapā-vudaraḥ*. (Maṇḍala 1.40)

Long be your goad, with which you bestow wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the Soma. Long be your goad, with which you bestow wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the Soma. O Indra, let your goad—the weapon used for drawing [objects] toward you—be long; let it be extended so that it may reach even a distant object. With that goad, you bring and bestow wealth (*vasu*) upon the sacrificer who performs the pressing of Soma. In the second round (*paryāya*), the triplet beginning with "This, O Indra, is your Soma" (*ayaṃ ta indra somaḥ*) serves as the *stotriya* for the Hotṛ’s recitation. As it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘This, O Indra, is your Soma,’ ‘This [is yours] among the human race’" (*āśva. śrau. 6. 4*).

This Soma of yours, O Indra, has been purified upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Come hither; run to it and drink! 11 This Soma of yours, O Indra, has been purified upon the sacrificial grass. Come hither; run to it and drink!

11 O Indra, for you—this word *te* (for you) undergoes the substitution of the augment *yugā* by nipātana (irregular rule)—whatever resolve (*kratu*) exists in this *Kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice, he has directed his own mind toward that.
In ancient times, the sages named Kuṇḍapāyins, performing [the sacrifice] on all sides, established it;
that is to say, they properly performed the ritual for the sake of the non-causal [state].
In the perfect tense (liṭ) of the root *dhā*, the substitution of *ra* for *ira* occurs according to the rule "irayo re."

O Lord of the Dwelling, you are the firm pillar, the protection of the Soma-loving ones; you are the drop, the breaker of eternal fortresses, Indra, the friend of the sages. 14. O Lord of the Dwelling! Firm pillar! Protection of the Soma-loving ones! The drop! Breaker of eternal fortresses! Indra! Friend of the sages! 14.
O Vāstoṣpati, O Lord of the Dwelling, may this pillar—the support of the house—be firm and stable.
May it be our armor, the protector and strength of our entire body as represented by the shoulders, for us who are worthy of Soma or drinkers of Soma.
Moreover, may it be possessed of the *drapsa*, the flowing Soma.
The suffix *tva* is applied according to the rule for the *arśas-* group.
May Indra—who is the breaker and destroyer of many eternal fortresses, the cities of the Asuras—be our friend, the ally of us sages and seers.

The son of Pradāku, the worshipful one, the seeker of cattle—being alone, yet overcoming the many—he shall lead forth the swift horse with his impetuous might and guiding power, so that Indra may drink the Soma. 15. *Pradākusānuḥ*, *yajataḥ*, *gaveṣaṇaḥ*, *ekaḥ*, *san*, *abhi*, *bhūyasaḥ*, *bhūrṇim*, *aśvam*, *nayat*, *tujā*, *puraḥ*, *gubhā*, *indram*, *somasya*, *pītaye*. 15.
*Pradākusānuḥ*:
*pradāku* means a serpent;
he is like that serpent in being highly elevated (*sānu*).
The meaning is that his head is likewise elevated; or alternatively, he has a ridge (*sānu*) that is worthy of being honored (*pradakva*), like a mountain peak.

Just as he is to be served by many—by means of jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth—and not by few, so too Indra is to be served by many efforts such as hymns of praise; this is the meaning.
He is "yajataḥ," one who is to be worshipped; "gaveṣaṇaḥ," the seeker of or the bringer of cattle.

Indra, who possesses such qualities, being *ekaḥ*—alone, without companion, and solitary—overcomes *bhūyasaḥ*, his many more numerous enemies. That *indraṃ*, the *bhūrṇim*—the one who is ever-active and pervasive like a horse—for the sake of drinking (*pītaye*) the Soma, *nayati*, he leads; that is, by implication, the singer leads him before us (*puraḥ*), brings him forward. By what means? [By means of praise.]
With a swift-moving *tuja* (impulse) and a *gubhā* (grasping instrument), that is, with a hymn of praise;
or rather,
this is an elliptical comparison [meaning "like a horse"].
Just as one leads a difficult-to-seize draft horse with a rope, so too, by means of praise in the manner described, the singer leads Indra of great power; this is the meaning.
The sixth hymn, consisting of twenty-two verses beginning with “*idam ha*,” has Iribheda Āṅgirasa as its seer and the *uṣṇih* meter.
The verse beginning with “*uta tyā*” has the Aśvins as its deity.
The verse beginning with “*śamabhiḥ*” has Agni, Sūrya, and Vāyu as its deities.
The remaining [verses] have Āditya as their deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “This [hymn], consisting of two more [verses] than the Āditya [group], is in the Auṣṇiha meter; with the last two verses, it belongs to Sūrya and Anila.
The application [of these verses] has been explained.

Truly, let the mortal now beg for this favor from them—the Ādityas—for their unprecedented bounty within their sovereign power. 1. This indeed; truly; from them; the favor; let the mortal; beg; of the Ādityas; unprecedented; in their impelling. 1.

Now indeed, at this very moment, surely, when there is the impulsion and instigation of these gods—the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, such as Mitra and the others—a mortal man, the worshipper, should beg for and request unprecedented, ever-new, and bliss-bestowing wealth;
not at some other time.
1. [The view] of those who maintain that [the fruit] is produced by the *saṃpāda* of the *soma*.
2. *Gha*- and *bha*-manuscripts: [The fruit] is produced as characterized by *maṃsa*.

For unassailable is the path of these Ādityas; undeceived are their protectors, who increase our well-being. (2) For unassailable (*anarvāṇaḥ*) indeed is the path (*panthāḥ*) of these Ādityas (*eṣām ādityānām*). Undeceivable (*adabdhāḥ*) are their guardians (*pāyavaḥ*), who increase our progress on the good path (*sugevṛdhaḥ*). The paths (*panthāḥ*)—meaning the ways or routes—of these Ādityas are *anarvāṇaḥ*: not assailed, not overtaken by others, and for that very reason *adabdhāḥ*, meaning unhurt. Since this is so, therefore those guardians (*pāyavaḥ*), as protectors, may they be *sugevṛdhaḥ*: increasers of easy passage and of happiness.

May Savitṛ, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us that wide-reaching protection which we implore. (3) May Savitṛ, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—these four gods—well and truly grant to us that wide-reaching (*saprathaḥ*), extensive, and broad protection (*śarma*), whether it be happiness or a dwelling, which we implore. "That" refers to the protection; "us" means for our sake; "well" (*su*) means most excellently; "grant" (*yacchantu*) means may they give; "which we implore" (*yat īmahe*) refers to the protection that we request.

O Goddess Aditi, endowed with the qualities of generosity and other virtues; O you whose sustenance is unassailable; O you who are beloved by many—come hither together with the gods, your own sons, who are wise and provide excellent protection. Come in a most auspicious manner! *Devebhiḥ | devi | adite | ariṣṭabharman | ā | gahi | smat | sūrībhiḥ | purupriye | suśarmabhiḥ || 4 ||* O Goddess—endowed with the qualities of giving and so forth; O Aditi, whose maintenance is unharmed (ariṣṭabharman); O you who are dear to many (purupriye)—O Aditi distinguished by such attributes, come (ā gahi) together with the gods (devebhiḥ), your own sons, who are wise (sūrībhiḥ) and possessors of great happiness (suśarmabhiḥ). *Smat* is a particle used here for the sake of excellence (*śobhanārtha*). Come in a beautiful and auspicious way.

For those sons of Aditi indeed know how to separate the haters; they, the wide-striding and faultless ones, [know how to] separate us even from distress. For those sons of Aditi—those gods, Mitra and the others—indeed know (*viduḥ*) how to separate (*yotave*) the haters (*dveṣāṃsi*), such as the Rākṣasas and others. The substitution of *as* for the suffix *jhi* after the root *vid* follows the rule "vido laṭo vā. Likewise, they—the performers of vast deeds (*uru-cakrayaḥ*) and the faultless protectors (*anehasaḥ*)—know how to separate us even from distress (*aṃhościt*), that is, from sin characterized by affliction.

May Aditi protect our cattle by day; may Aditi, free from duplicity, protect them by night. May Aditi, ever-increasing, protect us from distress. (6) May Aditi—unafflicted or indivisible, the Mother of the Gods—protect our cattle during the day. Likewise, may that Aditi, who is "free from duplicity" (*advayāḥ*)—meaning devoid of the two-fold distinction between external and internal, always of one form, and without guile—protect our herd of cows and other animals during the night. Furthermore, may she protect us as well from *aṃhas* (sin or distress). By what means? By her own ever-increasing protection.
And may that Aditi come to us by day with her thought and with her aid; may she grant us well-being and joy, and drive away our enemies. ||7||
Moreover, may that aforementioned Aditi— she who is to be thought upon, consulted, or praised— come to us by day with her protection (ūti).
Having come, may she, Aditi, grant us peace (śaṃtāti), happiness (mayaḥ),
and drive away our enemies (sridhaḥ) who cause affliction.
The root *sṛdh* has the sense of binding.
In the rule *śiva-śam-ariṣṭasya kare* (Pāṇini 4.4.143), the suffix *tāti* is applied after the word *śam* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
And may those two divine physicians, the Aśvins, grant us well-being; may they drive away evil from here and keep our enemies afar. (8)
Moreover, may those two famous divine physicians, the Aśvins who exist among the gods— such as they are— grant us well-being (*śam*), that is, the alleviation of diseases.
May they ward off from us evil (*rapas*) and drive away our enemies (*sridhas*).

May the god Agni, distinguished by his own powers through the fires such as Atya and others, grant us peace (*śam*); may he bring about the pacification of our diseases or happiness.
May Sūrya, the Aditya who impels all things, shine for us so that there may be peace and well-being.
And may Vāta, the wind, being free from harm (*arapāḥ*), blow so that there may be peace.
May these [deities], beginning with Aiṣāda, drive away the enemies of existence.
Drive away disease, drive away misfortune, drive away ill-will; O Ādityas, keep us far from distress. ||10||
O Ādityas, drive away from us disease and affliction;
drive away the adversary who seeks to harm us;
and drive away the evil-minded one who intends us misery.
Moreover, O Ādityas, Ādityas, separate us from distress—that is, from sin.
The verb *yu* is in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood; the *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ*). By the rule “*tasanasanathanāśa*,” its substitute is *tanap*.

Since the *pi* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains. According to the rule “a preceding vocative is as if non-existent,” because the preceding vocative is treated as non-existent, the word does not follow immediately after another word; therefore, the *syāḍāgama* (the augment *syā*) does not occur.
Ward off the arrow from us, O Ādityas, and likewise avert the curse;
O possessors of all wealth, make our enemies fail.
1. In manuscript *ga*, "ca" is absent.
2. In manuscript *ga*: "vardhatām"; in manuscripts *na* and *bha*: "vartām". 63. Ṛgveda: [Maṇḍala 6, Anuvāka 1, Varga 27]
O Ādityas, keep the arrow away from us, and likewise keep death far off; O you who possess all knowledge, drive away our enemies. 11.
O Ādityas, keep the weapon—the injurer—far away from us;
and furthermore, keep the immortal [hostility] and the evil-minded one far away.
O you who possess all wealth or all knowledge, drive the haters and their enemies apart, away from us.
Separate us from one another.

O Ādityas, you who are bounteous givers, grant us that protection which releases even the sinner from his sin. 12. That—well—grant us—that protection, O Ādityas, which shall set free even the one possessed of guilt from his guilt, O ye of liberal gifts. 12.
O Ādityas, grant—that is, bestow—upon us that protection which is bliss;
O you of noble gifts, grant that protection of yours which releases even the sinner, the singer of praise, from sin. This is the connection of the words.

Whosoever mortal seeks to harm us with demonic intent—may he himself be harmed by his own ways and by his own people. 13. Whosoever, whoever, seeks to harm us; this mortal, with demonic intent—may he himself be harmed by his own ways, by his own people. 13.

Whosoever mortal man seeks to harm us— meaning he desires to injure us through the nature of a *rakṣas* or with the essence of a *piśāca* and the like— the root *riṣ* meaning "to injure" being used here— that man shall himself be injured by his own very actions. He shall be harmed by his own deeds alone.
May that person be one who goes and comes;
or rather,
may that person, moving about by his own movements, be struck down.

Completely strike down that evil, ill-spoken mortal enemy who, full of malice toward us, seeks to seize our wealth. 14. *Sam ita tam agham aśvavad duḥśaṃsam martyam ripum / ya asmatrā durhaṇāvān upa drayuḥ //* 14. "Completely strike down that evil, ill-spoken mortal enemy who, full of malice toward us, seeks to seize our wealth. 14.
May that mortal man—the evil-doer, the one of ill-repute, the enemy, the adversary—be completely encompassed by sin.
That mortal who arises against us, intent on wicked slaughter, and who is possessed of two-fold guile;
this is the meaning.
One who speaks what is beneficial when face-to-face, but speaks what is harmful when out of sight,
is called a deceitful rogue (*kapaṭadrū*).
May that sin also afflict the rogue who acts deceitfully toward us.

O gods, you are aware of that man here; O Vasus, you know the one who is fickle and the one who is steadfast in his heart. 15. O gods, you are aware of that man here; O Vasus, you know the one who is fickle and the one who is steadfast in his heart. 15.
1. *ga-ta-na-bha-śa-martya* refers to a mortal human being, *ideva*.

2. *ga-pratyakṣakṛto* means one who speaks what is beneficial in one's presence but speaks what is harmful in one's absence; the connection with the preceding [verse] is that such a person is "an enemy" (*ripu*).

O gods (*devāḥ*), endowed with qualities such as generosity (*dāna*), you Ādityas, *pāktrā*—that is, among those who have matured (*vipaktreṣu*) as singers of praise (*stotṛṣu*)—*sthana*, meaning "be present."
Alternatively, the suffix *ā* is used in the sense of the first case ending (*prathamā*); thus,
*pāktrāḥ* means "those who have fully ripened knowledge" (*paripakvajñānāḥ*).

Therefore, for this reason, O Vasus—those who provide dwelling—having approached these mortals, men who are of two kinds among those living within their own hearts (the chest)—namely, the deceitful and the non-deceitful, that is, those characterized by such traits and those devoid of guile—you must recognize and understand them.
We choose for ourselves the protection of the mountains and the protection of the waters;
O Heaven and Earth, fashion for us a beautiful form.
We choose the protection of the mountains and also that of the waters; O Heaven and Earth, keep affliction far away from us. 16.
We choose—that is, we partake of—the shelter and happiness associated with the clouds, the mountains, and the peaks;
and also that of the waters.
O Heaven and Earth (dyāvākṣāmā), place our sin and the evil we have committed far away from us, in a distant place.
The meaning is: "Separate us from [this]."
O Vasus, with your auspicious protection, ferry us across all difficulties by means of your boat.
O Vasus, with your auspicious protection, ferry us across all difficulties by means of your boat. 17.

O Vasus, you who cause to dwell, O Ādityas, you who possess the aforementioned qualities—by means of your auspicious, beautiful protection and happiness, carry us across all difficulties and impassable paths by your boat; carry us across, lead us beyond!
O Ādityas, most glorious ones, grant us that for our offspring and ourselves— that we may live a longer life.
For our offspring, for ourselves—grant us that very long life to live, O Ādityas, you who are most glorious! 18.

O Ādityas, sons of Aditi, you who possess great majesty and beautiful splendor, grant to us—for the sake of our offspring, our children, our grandchildren, and our great-grandchildren, so that they may live—most long, indeed, that well-known life; make it truly excellent for us.
O Ādityas, the sacrifice is indeed within your reach; have mercy!
In you alone do we find refuge for our kinship.
O Ādityas, you are the sacrifice, the one who removes reproach, the one who is within; have mercy! It is through you alone that we abide in good birth. 19.

O Ādityas, *hīḷaḥ* means "to be approached" (*hīḍigatyartha*). The sacrifice performed by us is to be approached and attained by you; it remains within your reach, being close (*antara*) to you. Therefore, be gracious to us; bring us happiness.
O you, being of the same birth, of the same kinship, of the same lineage, and of the same family as you, we indeed abide among you; we always remain even within you.
[The form] *masi* ends in *id*.
We implore Bṛhadratha, the god of the Maruts, the protector, and the Aśvins;
we seek Mitra and Varuṇa for our well-being.
1. Kha-ga-ta-na-pāktrā:
We implore the vast protection of the Maruts, the divine savior, the Aśvins, Mitra, and Varuṇa for our well-being. 20.

We pray for well-being—that is, for non-destruction—to the Lord of the Maruts, the gods; to Indra, the divine protector and guardian; to the two Aśvins; to Mitra and Varuṇa; and to the vast, mature *varūtha*, a dwelling that wards off cold, heat, and other afflictions. We entreat them thus.
O Maruts, may Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, and Varuṇa grant us a praiseworthy, threefold protection that is free from distress. May you extend to us a shelter of triple defense.
O Mitra, Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Maruts, grant us a secure dwelling, worthy of praise, rich in men, and providing triple protection. 21.

O Mitra, O Aryaman, O Varuṇa, O Maruts—may you all grant us a dwelling (*chardiḥ*) that is free from harm (*anehas*), endowed with men (*nṛvat*) such as sons and others, praiseworthy (*śaṃsya*), providing triple protection (*trivarūtha*) against cold, heat, and rain—or alternatively, consisting of three stories—to us. "Grant" (*yanta*) means "give."
O Ādityas, you who are indeed the kinsmen of mortals from death—take heed!
Prolong our life-span that we may live.
For you, O Ādityas, are indeed the kinsmen from death for mortals; remember us well and prolong our life-span that we may live. 22.

O Ādityas, since both you who are gods and we who are *manu*s—human beings—are indeed "kinsmen of death," meaning we have become close to death as the kin of Yama, therefore, for the sake of our living, so that we may live for a long duration, do you graciously extend our life-span, increasing it beautifully.
The seventh hymn, consisting of thirty-seven verses beginning with “*taṃ gṛdhyā*,” is the seer’s work of Sobhari Kāṇva.
The first, third, and other odd-numbered verses are *kakubh*s; the second, fourth, and other even-numbered verses are *satobṛhatī*s.
The twenty-seventh verse, “*piturna putraḥ*,” is a two-line (*dvipadā*) *virāj* of known syllable count.
‘O Ādityas’—this is a thirty-four-syllable *uṣṇih* verse;
‘You are kings’—this is the thirty-fifth, a *sato-bṛhatī*;
‘He has given me’—this is a *kakubh* verse.
The thirty-seventh verse, beginning with "uta me," is a *paṅkti* meter.
Both the thirty-sixth and the thirty-seventh have King Trasadasyu as their deity, because they consist of his gift (*dāma-stuti*).
The twenty-fourth and the thirty-fifth have Āditya as their deity.

The remaining [verses] are addressed to Agni. Thus it has been enumerated: "He seized that vulture; thirty-seven [verses] for Sobhari, addressed to Agni, in the Kākubha Prāgātha metre; 'ha pituḥ' is not in the Dvipadā metre; in the Kakup and Uṣṇih metres there is a praise of Trasadasyu’s gift; the two preceding [verses] are in the Uṣṇih and Satobṛhatī metres; 'āvāditya' is addressed to Aditi. The application of the hymns (*sūktaviniyoga*) is concluded.
The gods have sent forth that golden-winged bird as the divine minister;
they have directed the oblation toward the gods.
Him, the manly hero among the gods, the divine one—the gods have set him in motion as their chariot-pole; they have brought the oblation to him among the gods.
O singer, strive toward that well-known one; praise him!
The root *gṛdh* means "to praise. Of what sort is he?
Svarṇaram: the leader of all, or one who has been led at the beginning of the ritual by all the sacrificers;
alternatively, the leader of the oblations toward heaven.
Devāsaḥ: the gods, so called because they shine or praise; here, the officiating priests (ṛtvijas).

They go toward— that is, they approach— the Lord (deva), who is endowed with virtues such as generosity (dāna) and so forth, who is the master of wealth (artha-svāmin), or rather, the one from whom desirable objects (abhiprasanna-dravya) are to be obtained; they run toward him, that is, they proceed by means of praise and other such acts to attain him.
The root *dhavi* has the sense of "going.
And having reached the gods (*devatrā*) by means of that fire—the suffix *tra* is used in the sense of the accusative according to the rule "devamanuṣya... and so forth.
They bring forward—that is, they present—the oblation (*havya*), characterized by the *caru*, the *puroḍāśa*, and so forth;
for the root *vah* undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group.
O sage Sobhari, invoke for this sacrifice the ancient Agni, who has overcome all enemies, who possesses manifold purifying flames, and who is the controller of this Soma-offering.
O sage Sobhari, praise Agni, who has driven away the enemy, whose purifying flames are manifold, the controller of this Soma-offering; praise him, the ancient one, for this sacrifice.
The seer, addressing himself, urges him toward praise:
"O *vipra*, O wise one, O *Sobhari*—seer of this name—for the sake of the sacrifice (*adhvara*), do thou praise (*prīḷiṣva*) this Agni.
Of what kind [is he]?"

He who possesses abundant wealth or bestows ample gifts; whose brilliance is wonderful or whose flames are diverse; the controller of this sacrifice performed with Soma, which is to be accomplished by Soma; the ancient one from of old.

In the *ābhiplāvika* days, during the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), within the recitation (*śāstra*) of the *praśāstṛ*, the two *pragāthas* beginning with "ayajiṣṭhaṃ tvā" are optional as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "yajiṣṭhaṃ tvā vavamahe yaḥ samidhā ya āhutī" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).
We choose you, the best of sacrificers, the immortal god among gods, the priest of this sacrifice, the one of excellent wisdom.
We choose you, the best of sacrificers, the immortal god among the gods, the priest of this sacrifice, the one of excellent wisdom. 3.

O Agni, we choose you—the most excellent sacrificer, the one most worthy of worship; we elect you, we honor you. Of what sort are you? Among the gods, you are the god preeminent in qualities such as generosity; the invoker of the gods; the immortal, imperishable one; and the one of excellent wisdom, the perfect performer of this sacrifice.
To Agni, the Son of Strength, the fortunate one of splendid luster, whose flame is most excellent—
to him may he sacrifice for our well-being in heaven, [the well-being] of Mitra, of Varuṇa, and of the Waters.

To the Son of Strength, the fortunate one, the beautifully radiant Agni of most excellent luster—to him may he sacrifice for our well-being in heaven, [the well-being] of Mitra, of Varuṇa, and of the Waters. 4.
The son of strength, that is, of food; or rather, the protector (naptṛ) who does not cause us to fall, or the descendant (nasāra) in the fourth case.
Water is produced from food characterized by the *havir* oblation, and fire is born from the *śuci*, the *vanaspati*, and others—thus [it is said] in the fourth [verse].
In the phrase "annānnapāt," there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the negative particle *nañ*.
"I praise Agni"—this is the ellipsis—[Agni who is] *subhagam*, possessing beautiful wealth; *sudīditim*, a splendid illuminator; and *śreṣṭhaśociṣam*, one whose luster is most excellent.
May that Agni, for our sake, perform sacrifice directed toward the favor and happiness of the god Mitra and of Varuṇa among the shining divine folk in heaven;
likewise, may that Agni perform sacrifice directed toward the favor of the waters and the non-divine beings.
Whoever has worshipped Agni with fuel, whoever with oblations, whoever with sacred knowledge in his mind, and whoever with reverence as a skillful sacrificer— [to him may he grant wealth].

Whoever has worshipped Agni with fuel, whoever with oblations, whoever with sacred knowledge, whoever with devotion, and whoever, being a skilled sacrificer, has honored him with reverence—[to that person may he grant wealth]. 5.
1. *ga-na-ma-tvām*; *gha-tvā tvā*. 2. *gha-na-ma-avināśinam*. 3. *bha-jāyata*. 4. *ga-gha-na-ma-dīpayantam*.
This [verse] was explained by the venerable Āśvalāyana as being intended for the praise of the *pākayajña* (cooked-sacrifice), by pointing to another Brāhmaṇa text (*Āśva. Gṛ. 1.1.4–5*).
The man (*yaḥ mataḥ manuṣyaḥ*) who, with fuel (*samidhā*) such as that of the *pālāśa* tree, honors (*dadāśa*) and serves (*paricarati*) Agni (*agnaye adhyartham*).

He who serves with oblation after oblation accomplished by means of clarified butter and other materials; he who serves with the Veda, that is, through the study of the Vedas and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*);

and he who, being endowed with a "good sacrifice" (*svadhvara*) such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, worships with reverence (*namas*)—that is, with offerings such as cooked rice and sacrificial cakes (*caru-puroḍāśa*)—serving for the sake of Agni.
The phrase "tasyedvantaḥ" is to be connected with what follows later.

His swift-running horses hasten; his glory is most radiant. No distress caused by the gods from any quarter, nor that caused by mortals, shall reach him. (6) Of him—the one previously mentioned—his very own swift-running horses hasten; they exert their speed, meaning they overcome the enemies. His glory and fame are most radiant, or else, *ghubhritama* being a name for wealth, his fame and food are most abundant in wealth. Furthermore, no distress (*ahaḥ*) caused by the gods, arising from any cause whatsoever, reaches him; nor does that caused by mortals.

May we be well-disposed toward you through your fires, O Son of Strength, Lord of Vital Energies! May you, possessed of noble heroes, be well-disposed toward us. (7) "May we be well-disposed toward you through your fires," [O] Son of Strength, Lord of vital energies! May you, accompanied by noble heroes, be well-disposed toward us. O Son of Strength, son of power—for fire is generated when churned with force—O Lord of vital energies, Lord of oblations characterized as food, O Agni: "toward you"—there is a shift in grammatical number; through those fires that constitute your own limbs, namely the Gārhapatya and others, may we be *svaprayaḥ*, those who possess beautiful fires. May we become so. And may you, endowed with noble heroes (*suvīraḥ*), be one who desires us (*asmayuḥ*).

Praising [him], like a friendly guest, Agni is like a chariot to be known. In you, there are indeed secure and effective dwellings; you are the king of riches. (8) *praśaṃsamānaḥ* (praising), *atithiḥ na* (like a guest), *mitriyaḥ* (friendly), *agniḥ* (Agni), *rathaḥ na* (like a chariot), *vedyaḥ* (to be known). *Tve* (in you), *kṣemāsaḥ* (secure dwellings), *api* (indeed), *santi* (are), *sādhavaḥ* (effective/proper), *tvam* (you), *rājā* (king), *rayīṇām* (of riches). "Praising" means extolling. "Like a guest" (*atithir-na*) means like a guest. Alternatively, by a grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*), the agent-suffix is used in the sense of the object: "being praised," that Agni becomes "friendly" (*mitriyaḥ*), beneficial to his friends, the singers. Likewise, "like a chariot" (*ratho-na*) means like a chariot, "to be known" (*vedyaḥ*)—either as something to be obtained or as something to be recognized as the means for attaining desired fruits. The second half-verse is addressed directly (*pratyakṣakṛta*). O Agni, "in you" (*tve*), "there are indeed" (*api santi*) "secure and effective" (*sādhavaḥ kṣemāsaḥ*) dwellings or supports. Likewise, "of riches" (*rayīṇām*), "you alone" (*tvam eva*) "are the king" (*rājā*), the sovereign lord.

Truly, O Agni, that mortal who offers the sacrifice is fortunate and is to be praised; may he be a winner through his inspired thoughts. 9. Truly, [he] who offers the sacrifice, O Agni, that mortal, O fortunate one—he is to be praised; may he be a winner through his inspired thoughts. 9.
1. ga 1-dīptamam; ga2-gha-ta-na-bha-śa-dīptitamam | 2.
gha-na-bha-na va | O Agni, that mortal man who is a giver of oblations and whose sacrifice is offered—verily, he [is such].
This is a true name;
may it bear true fruit.
O Subhaga—O Agni of beautiful wealth—may he indeed be praśasyaḥ: praiseworthy and worthy of praise.

Likewise, may he be a winner (*sanitā*) through his insights (*dhībhiḥ*), his deeds (*karmabhiḥ*), or his hymns of praise (*stotrair vā*), being one who is disposed toward bestowing gifts (*saṃbhajana-śīla*).
He for whose sacrifice you stand upright, O dweller among heroes, he prospers;
he wins with his swift steeds, he wins with those who sing hymns, and he wins the prize with his heroes.
He for whose sacrifice you stand upright, O ruler of heroes—he succeeds; he wins with his horses, he wins with his singers, he wins the prize with his warriors. ||10||

O Agni, that sacrificer for whose sacrifice (*adhvara*) you stand upraised and prepared, being established [in his rite], that sacrificer—possessed of heroes, whether as dwelling men or as sons and others—accomplishes everything that is to be done; he succeeds. He explains this very point:
such a person becomes one who wins and enjoys the victory and other fruits accomplished by means of swift horses (*arvadbhiḥ*).
Such a person becomes a winner through those who are wise and through those who are heroic.
In whose house the all-pervading one accepts the hymn with pleasure, or he who, as the bearer of oblations, zealously performs the service.
In whose house Agni, the one who belongs to all men, shall take pleasure in the hymn of praise, or shall zealously attend to his oblations—[him] you, O Viṣas, [should protect]. 11.
In the house of that sacrificer, Agni— whose form is desirable by all,
for this is a name for beauty;
he who is beautiful and radiant— should maintain the *stoma*, the hymn of praise, and the *canaḥ*, the food characterized by the oblation.
And for whom the oblations (*havyā*); the word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction;
and may he cause the offerings (*havīṃṣi*) to reach (*veviṣt*) the pervasive gods (*vyāsān*).
The root *viṣ* means "to pervade.
This form is derived from it with the suffix *heṭ*.
The word "that sacrificer" (*sa yajamāna*) is to be connected with the preceding passage.
O Son of Strength, at the gifts of the praising Brahmin who most swiftly approaches,
O Vasu, place that god upon the highest [heaven] and bestow splendor upon the one who has found [thee].
Of the praising Brahmin, O son of strength, at the gifts of the most prompt one—make divine favor superior to that which is human, O Vasu; bestow splendor upon the one who has found [thee]. 12.

O Agni, son of strength (*sahasa*), you who are the offspring of power; O Vasu, O dwelling Agni, make the speech of the wise, meditative, praising, or lauding one—of him who is most swift in the offerings of oblations, or rather, of the one who knows, the learned and discerning one—protect the gods from below and surpass mortals from above;
that is to say, pervade the entire expanse of the sky.
Whoever seeks to win over Agni— the one of excellent skill— with oblations, with offerings, or with hymns, [he wins] the one who possesses the brilliance of a steed.
1. *ga-martya*: | 2. *kha-nā-ta-na-bha-śa* ‘agne’ does not exist: | 3. *kha-ta-śa* becomes: |
4. [The letters] ga, gha, na, and bha are for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice (yāga).
5. [The letters] ga, ta, bha, and the word nibasa are used by the Īśvaras.
6. [The letters] kha, ga, jha, ta¹⁻², na, bha, and śa are exactly this same [set].
7. By those who praise—by the *vipanyus* (stotṛbhiḥ)—he becomes the winner (*sanitā*); [the word ‘sa’ is absent in the Kha, Ta, and Śa recensions].

And by the heroes (*śūraiḥ*), those endowed with valor, by the *mṛtyas*, he becomes the winner (*sanitā bhavatu*—Śa recension). 8. Of the one most swiftly perceived (*makṣūtamatasya*)—[Ga, Jha, and Śa recensions].
Whoever seeks to win over Agni—the one of great skill—with offerings of oblations, with salutations, with song, or with praise, he wins the one of swift-purifying flame. || 13 ||

The sacrificer, with offerings—the giving of oblations—and with salutations, or with speech—that is, with praise—serves Agni, who is "well-skilled" (sudakṣa), meaning possessed of excellent power; he serves that Agni whose radiance is swift-moving (ajiraśociṣam). The ellipsis is: "he becomes prosperous."
He who, with kindled fuel and sharpened devotion, serves according to his laws among mortals—
he, the fortunate one, shall by his prayers and through your protections cross over all people, even as Rudra does.

He who, with sharpened [devotion], serves Aditi through his duties toward mortals—he, blessed with good fortune, shall by his prayers pass beyond all people like a fish across the waters. O Agni, that mortal man who, with good intentions, has established you—the wise one who beholds men—among his own abodes (the sacrificial fires), those wise ones, O God, have established you of excellent will.
O Agni, those very ones indeed become well-studied (*su-adhyāḥ*), meaning possessed of beautiful meditation (*śobhana-adhyāna*).

O wise (*vipra*) and radiant (*deva*) Agni, those wise (*viprāsaḥ*) and intelligent (*medhāvinaḥ*) priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*) establish (*nidadhire*)—that is, they place you by means of the consecration of installation (*ādhāna-saṃskāra*) in the Gārhapatya and other locations for the sake of sacrifice—you who are the beholder of men (*nṛ-cakṣasam*), the doer of good deeds (*sukṛtam*), or the one of excellent wisdom (*sukarmaṇam*); such is the syntactical connection with "those very ones" (*te gha*).
They have prepared this oblation for you, O fortunate one, and they have made the Soma-pressing in heaven for you;
those who have offered their desire unto you have won great wealth through the impetuous powers of the *iḍā*.

They have made this for you; O fortunate one, they have prepared this oblation for you and this soma-pressing for you. May they, through their strengths, win great wealth from heaven. O Agni, conqueror of Vṛtra, in battle, make our mind auspicious and beautiful—that mind by which you utterly overcome the enemies in the conflicts.
