Moreover, "stretch down"—that is, cast downward—the many, even the firm and stubborn forces of the "proud," the enemies who seek to overcome us;
that is to say, render them defeated.
And may we, through our "invocations"—meaning by means of oblations and hymns—attain you, O Lord, and enjoy your favor.
Or rather:
through your grace, may we obtain—that is, may we attain—the desired fruits by means of our prayers.

I praise with song the one established by Manu, whom the gods have sent forth as messenger and minister, the most excellent sacrificer, the bearer of oblations. 21. I praise with song; the one established by Manu; whom; the gods; as messenger; as minister; have sent forth; the most excellent sacrificer; the bearer of oblations. 21.
With speech—that is, with praise in the form of words—I laud that Agni who was established by Manu, by Prajāpati, or by the sacrificer.
Of what kind is he? Most excellent in sacrifice, the bearer of oblations, the steward or lord, and the messenger of the gods, acting as their envoy.
That Agni whom the gods impel most strongly forward.

To the one with sharp fangs, the youthful, the radiant Agni, you offer food; to him who, being invoked with clarified butter, bestows heroic vigor through his beautiful and truthful songs. (22) To the one with sharp fangs, to the youthful, to the radiant Agni, you sing forth food; to him who, Agni, being invoked with clarified butter, [bestows] heroic vigor through his beautiful and truthful songs. (22)

O singer, you sing—that is, you offer praise—unto Agni, who has sharp fangs, whose flames are keen, who is ever-youthful, eternally free from old age and death, and who shines resplendently; [you offer] *prayaḥ*, food characterized by oblations.

The meaning is: "Grant him prosperity. That Agni, when praised with *sūnṛtābhiḥ*—words consisting of pleasant truth—and when offered oblations of *ghṛta*, that is, clarified butter, bestows excellent heroic power (*suvīrya*) upon the singers; he imparts it and unites them with it.
The root *piś* means "to divide" (*avayave*).
Therefore, the grammatical connection is with the word *apraya*.

In the *ābhiplavika* *ukthya* rites, when the *pragātha* "yadābhro naḥ" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.19.19) is the *stotriya* in the *praśāstṛ*'s recitation, then the *pragātha* "yadi ghṛtebhiḥ" is the *anurūpa*.
The *sūtra*, however, has already been cited previously.

If, invoked with offerings of clarified butter, Agni brandishes his axe upward and downward like an Asura displaying his garment. 23. If... with offerings of clarified butter... invoked... his axe... Agni... brandishes... upward... and... downward... like an Asura... his garment. 23.
When this Agni, invoked and offered with clarified butter,
bears aloft and downward the voice— this being a name for speech— the sound— producing it.
Or rather:

he draws upward—that is, causes to rise with its face turned upwards—the *vāśī*, which is so called because it is habitually blowing or making sound, namely the flame; and he bears downward—that is, carries away or withdraws with its face turned downwards.

Just as the Sun, the thrower of rays like a sovereign lord (*asura*), causes his own form (*nirṇij*) to rise upward through its luminosity in the upper worlds and causes it to go downward in the lower worlds, even so Agni causes his brilliance to rise by means of this high-and-low manifestation.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "we praise him."
1. Those that are stable among the *gha* and *na* [consonants] are stable.

The god who, established by Manu, has sent forth our oblations with his fragrant mouth—the immortal, radiant deity, the invoker of the gods and performer of the excellent sacrifice—seeks to win for us desirable treasures. (24) He who, established by Manu—that is, appointed by Manu Prajāpati—the shining god Agni, with his fragrant mouth, sends forth our offerings toward the deities; he who is the performer of the beautiful sacrifice, the invoker of the gods, the radiant and immortal deity—he seeks to win, that is, he bestows upon the sacrificer, desirable treasures worthy of being chosen. (The word "bestows" is to be supplied as the sense.)

O Son of Strength, O Agni invoked with oblations, O you of friendly luster, if at the beginning I, a mortal, were to become you—an immortal—then I would indeed be immortal. "O Son of Strength (*sahasaḥ sūno*), O you who are invoked with clarified butter (*āhuta*), O Agni of friendly luster (*mitramahaḥ*): if (*yat*) I, a mortal subject to death (*martyaḥ*), were to become you (*tvam syām*) through my worship of you—attaining your very form, according to the Vedic revelation that "in whatever way they worship, they become that"—then I would become an immortal (*amartyaḥ*), a god indeed. (Verse 25)

O Vasu, I would not cause you to be reviled for the sake of false accusation, nor for the sake of evil-doing, O Holy One. May my praiser not be one of evil speech, nor may he be ill-disposed toward you, O Agni, nor may he be overcome by sin. O Vasu, O Agni, the dweller, I would not cause you to be reviled (*abhiśastaye*)—for the sake of false accusation or injury—with cries of abuse. [The root] *rās* means "to sound. O Holy One (*santya*), O Agni worthy of worship, I would not cause you to be reviled for the sake of evil-doing (*pāpatvāya*). Let my praiser not revile you with words of displeasure; therefore, let him not be one of evil mind (*amatīvā*). *Amati* is an unwholesome intellect; may even such a person not exist among us, O Agni, as an enemy (*duhitaḥ*). Therefore, let him not afflict us with that evil, unwholesome intellect (*pāpayā*).

Like a son well-nourished by his father in the home, may our oblation go forth toward the gods. (27) "Like a son of his father"—just as a son is well-supported by a father, so this Agni is our "well-nourished" one, meaning he is properly sustained by us with offerings, or nourished by the oblations like a son by a father. This Agni, well-nourished like a son for us, "in the home" (*duroṇe*)—that is, in the sacrificial hall—let our oblation go forth toward the gods; or rather, let it approach them. And let our oblation reach the gods.

1. ma-yaṃ | 2. In ta-bha-'te', [the word] does not exist. 3. jha-ta1-2: one who is devoid of the nature of death. 4. kha-gha-ta-na-śa: for this very reason, by means of sin; bha: what kind of praiser?

May I, as a mortal, ever enjoy thy favor through thine most near aids, O Vasu, O God. (28) O Agni, may I, as a mortal, always enjoy thy favor through thine most near aids—those that are closest or most direct—O Vasu, O God. (28) O Agni, O Vasu, the bestower of dwellings, may I, the mortal singer, always and at all times, through thine aids—that is, thy protections which are most near, or which proceed straight forward—enjoy thy favor; may I serve thee who art well-pleased. (28) Through thy wisdom, O Agni, through thy gifts, and through thy praises, may I obtain [wealth]. They call thee alone my providence, O Vasu; O Agni, rejoice to give! (29) O Agni, through thy *kratu*—thy ritual action consisting of service—may I obtain thee; may I worship thee. He explains this very point: through thy gifts (*rāti*) and through thy praises (*praśasti*), O Agni, they call thee alone my providence (*pramati*), O Vasu; therefore, O Agni, rejoice in order to grant [boons]. (29)

Kindling thee, O Soma, thus making thee blaze, thy juice is taken up for the oblation by the Adhvaryu priest. Moreover, thou art the beloved friend of the great dawns—for indeed, in the dawns, all beings are kindled for the sake of sacrifice—and thou shinest among the objects belonging to the night, or rather, thou illuminest the various things that exist in connection with the night. We Sobharis have come for protection to him who possesses a thousand testicles (rays), the one of excellent aid, the sovereign ruler, the protector of Trasadasyu. O Sobharis, we Rishis have come for protection to that Agni with oblations and hymns of praise. Of what nature is he? He whose "testicles" (muṣkāṇi) are his rays—so called because they steal away or dispel the darkness—he who possesses abundant splendor, who is of excellent approach, the universal sovereign, and the protector of Trasadasyu (the royal seer). O Agni, those other fires of thine which dwell near thee like branches of a tree—I, among men, increasing thy sovereign powers through praise, win from thee radiant glories and fame, just as other singers do, meaning: by thy grace, I obtain them. O Adityas, you who are free from malice and of noble bounty, you lead that mortal man across to the further shore of his undertaking, O lords of all, among the wealthy patrons. O Kings, O subduers of the people, you overcome every single human being who dwells among mankind. May we, O Varuna, Mitra, and Aryaman, be the charioteers of the eternal Law (Ṛta). O shining Kings, O conquerors of the enemy hosts, you subdue every human being who seeks to rule over men. O Varuna, Mitra, and Aryaman, may we be the drivers of the chariot of Truth. (Note: The commentary clarifies that "testicles" refers to rays, "objects" refers to the darknesses to be covered, and "charioteers of Truth" refers to those who uphold the cosmic order.)
The rest:
Or rather,
"O you [Maruts], do not go toward any other singer among men who are sacrificers, [toward] anyone who dwells as the master of praises."
O Varuṇa, O Mitra, O Aryaman—such as you are, may we be yours, your own; may we be the charioteers, that is, the leaders, of the *ṛta*, the sacrifice.
Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, has given me fifty brides; he is the most generous noble, the lord of heroes. ||36||
With this first *pragātha*, the seer praises the gift of Trasadasyu:
"Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa (Paurukutsa), gave me fifty maidens as a bride-price (*vadhūnām*).
Of what sort was he?"
Most bountiful, the greatest giver, the noble one who is to be approached, the master or lord, the protector of the good—the best among the virtuous—of those who offer praise.
And for me, the son of Prayauviya, Suvāsva [reigns] over Turvaṇi. He is the dark leader of the three sleeping ones; Śveta is the lord of those who have attained immortality. 37.
The eighth hymn, consisting of twenty-six verses beginning with "ā ganta," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Sobhari Kāṇva; it is addressed to the Maruts.
The first and subsequent odd-numbered verses are Kakubh meters, while the second and subsequent even-numbered verses are Satobṛhatī meters.
Indeed, it is enumerated thus: "ā ganta, twenty-six verses, addressed to the Maruts."
The application is concluded.
Come hither; do not suffer harm. O you who are ever-moving, do not stand still, O you who are united in your course. Even that which is firm, you cause to bend, O you who are prone to bowing. 1.
O Maruts, you who set forth, you who advance, you who go forward, come hither; come unto us.
Do not fail us; do not harm us by not coming.

O you of equal splendor, or of equal wrath, you who are firm—indeed, you who are accustomed to bending even firm and solid things such as mountains—O you who cause them to tremble, do not stand away from us; do not remain elsewhere apart from us.
For this very reason, the meaning is "remain."

O Maruts, lords of the *ṛbhus*, Rudras with strong weapons and brilliant splendors, come to us today with food—ye who are desired by many, ye who are sought after by Sobhari. vīḷupavibhir maruta ṛbhukṣaṇa ā rudrāsaḥ sudītibhiḥ | iṣā no adyāganta puruspṛho yuṣmā ā sobharīyavaḥ || 2 ||
1. Among those who have gone to the humans;
2. O you who have come from elsewhere!

O *ṛbhukṣaṇaḥ*, O great ones, whose dwellings are vast or far-extending; O *rudrāsaḥ*, O Rudras, sons of Rudra; O such *marutaḥ*, Maruts, with your *sudītibhiḥ*, beautiful splendors, and *vīḷupavibhiḥ*, firm-fellied [chariots].
*rathanemayaḥ* means *pavayaḥ*. Come (*ā gata*) on such chariots as have strong, firm (*vīḷu dṛḍhāḥ*) wheels (*pavayaḥ*).
He explains this very point:

O you who are desired by many (*puruṣpṛhaḥ*), you who are longed for and sought after by the seer Sobhari (*sobharīyavaḥ*), come now with food (*iṣā*) toward our sacrifice (*yajñam*). (The word *ā* is used as a filler.)
For the power of the Rudras is indeed manifold, the fierce might of the impetuous Maruts,
and the abundance of the rushing Viṣṇu.

For the manifestation of the Rudra-powers, the fierce might of the Maruts who are full of vigor, and of the rushing Viṣṇu— O bounteous Maruts, the vast heaven yields wide space for your coming and your rapid movement,
where the heroes display their physical strength and the power of their arms.
O Maruts, the vast heaven yields far upward for you to pass, unswervingly, when the heroes, endowed with the strength of their arms, display their powers upon their own bodies.
O Maruts, for your onset, for your strength, and for your rushing forth, the vast sky and the intermediate space retreat to a higher, more elevated place;
having been stirred by your arrival, they abandon their own atmospheric station and flee upward—this is the meaning.

In whatever intermediate space (antarikṣa), those leaders, the Maruts, who possess strength in their arms (bāhvojaḥ), cause their radiant ornaments (tvakṣāṃsi) to shine upon their own bodies (tanūṣu); that is, they direct them [to be] displayed there.
Or rather:
upon their "bodies"—that is, the waters situated within the expanded clouds—they repeatedly direct their sharp weapons (tvakṣāṃsi), fashioned from lightning, for the purpose of shattering the clouds.
The grammatical connection is: "that Brahman went into the intermediate space (antarikṣa) within the heart."
According to their own nature, the men— magnificent, brilliant, impetuous, and bull-like in their vigor— bear along their glory, they whose heat is unassailable.
Following their own inherent power and glory, the men—mighty, brilliant, impetuous, with virile forms and unassailable forms—bear [the sacrifice]. 7.
The Maruts, the leaders (naraḥ), according to their own nature (svadhām anu)—
*svadhā* being a name for food— bearing in mind the oblation characterized as food, carry and maintain (*vahante*) a great, exalted beauty (*śriyam mahi*).
Of what sort are they?

Resplendent (tveṣāḥ), meaning shining; powerful (amavantaḥ), meaning strong; possessing the nature of showers (vṛṣapsavaḥ), meaning having the form of rain-givers; and possessing straight forms (ahutapsavaḥ), meaning not crooked in shape.
The arrow of the Sobharis is anointed with the products of the cow upon the golden seat of the chariot.
O kinsmen of the cow, well-born ones, grant us great nourishment for our enjoyment and touch us with your favor.

The arrow is sharpened by the rays of light; upon the chariot of the Sobharis, within the golden vessel. Kin to the kine, well-born, for the sake of food and enjoyment—may the great ones now touch us. 8.
The song (*vāṇaḥ*) of the *sobharī* seers is manifested—that is, it is revealed and made manifest—by means of "cows," which are sounds characterized as hymns of praise.
Where?
Upon the golden chariot, in the interior space encased like a sheath (*kośe*).
Alternatively, the arrow is sharpened— that is, made manifest— by the *gobhiḥ*, meaning by those who go (*gantṛbhiḥ*), or by the Maruts who are the mothers (*mātṛkaiḥ*).
The meaning is that it is sounded upon the chariot for the sake of the Sobharis’ vision of knowledge (*jñānāya-dṛśe*).

Moreover, may those Maruts—who are kinsmen of the cow, whose mother is the cow, who are well-born (of auspicious birth), great, and of sublime power—be present for us quickly for the sake of food, for enjoyment, for touch, for pleasure, or for strength; this is the ellipsis.
Bring forth offerings for you, the host of Maruts, the bull-like, whose banner is the rain-cloud,
for him who moves with bull-like speed.
Bring forth offerings for your Marut host, the bull-anointed, the vigorous one, who rushes forward like a bull. 9.
O Adhvaryus, you who sprinkle within with the showering Soma—the showerer—bring forth the oblations toward the showering host of Maruts, the troop-form of the Maruts;
present the offerings at the Āhavanīya fire.
The host is distinguished.

Regarding *vṛṣaprayāvaṇe*: it refers to that [hymn] in which the Maruts—the "vṛṣaṇaḥ" meaning "setters-in-motion," and "prayāvānaḥ" meaning "those who go forth toward their natural state"—are present.
To that [hymn].

O Maruts, O leaders, come with your chariot that possesses bulls, that is equipped with a rain-producing pole, and that has a bull-like nave—come like winged falcons at your ease to enjoy our oblations. O leaders, O Maruts, come with your chariot that is accompanied by bulls—that is, by bulls capable of pouring forth rain—possessing a rain-producing pole, and having a bull-like nave (the *nābhi* being the hole for the axle-pin; thus, one with a bull-like nave). Come to us, to our oblations (*havyā*), for the sake of enjoyment (*vītaye*). "At your ease" (*vṛthā*) means without effort. Therein lies the illustration: "like winged falcons"—just as falcons, whose flight is praiseworthy, arrive swiftly, so too come quickly and without effort. 37.
Equal is the splendor of these [Maruts] as the golden ornaments shine upon their arms; they possess spears and flashing daggers.
The same applies to *añji*.

[Maṇḍala 8, Anuvāka 3, Sūkta 20] **Verse 18:** O Maruts, you who are eternally youthful, having come from heaven and the intermediate space, in whatever manner you desire us, let this hymn be exactly so. (The absence of the *śap* suffix in *vaṣṭi* is a Vedic anomaly. Those bounteous Maruts who are worthy of honor, and those who move about as bestowers of blessings (*mīḷahuṣaḥ*), even from that state, O youths, turn toward us with a most excellent heart and favor us. **Verse 19:** O Saubhara, sing well with a most new song unto the youths, the showerers, the purifiers—the Maruts—just as a plowman sings to his young oxen that draw the plow. **Verse 20:** O Maruts, indeed, praise with a song those who are victorious like boxers, who are to be invoked in all battles among the challengers; who are showerers, radiant, and most glorious. **Verse 21:** Like cows, O Maruts, being of good mind, kin, and of noble birth, they lick each other’s flanks in mutual affection. 1. Ga—‘ca’ is not present. 2. Gha—*ataścidatopi*.

O Maruts, you who possess equal splendor and equal wrath, having reached the quarters—the eastern and other directions—which are like cows, being your mothers, and which are connected by common kinship (being of the same lineage), lick one another. *Gha* is a filler particle. O dancers, O you with golden ornaments upon your chests, even a mortal man approaches you for brotherhood and friendship. Therefore, O Maruts, look upon us; for your kinship is ever-present in our firm praise and sacrifice. O Maruts, O you of noble gifts, O friends, O swift-moving ones, bring to us the healing medicine belonging to the Maruts. With those aids by which you protect the river Sindhu, by which you overcome [enemies], and by which you bestow favor upon Krivi—O you who bring happiness, O you whose enemies are never persistent, be our protectors with those auspicious aids that grant us bliss. Or rather, "be" (*bhū*) means "attain"; cause us to attain it. O Maruts, you for whom the sacred grass is excellent, whatever medicine is in the river Sindhu, whatever is in the Asiknī, whatever is in the oceans, and whatever medicine is in the mountains—all that [is yours]. (This is to be construed with the following verse. 1. *Bha*: "By common birth," meaning born from the same source.

Beholding all things, you carry them within your bodies; with that [power], speak for us! O Maruts, forgive the offense of our afflicted one, and set right again what has been broken. 26 viśvam | paśyantaḥ | vibhṛtha | tanūṣu | ā | tena | naḥ | adhi | vocata | kṣamā | rapaḥ | marutaḥ | āturasya | naḥ | iṣkartā | vi'hutam | punariti || 26 ||

Perceiving—that is, knowing—all the aforementioned remedies, you must bring them to us within our own bodies; and with that, speak for us—meaning, provide medical treatment. Furthermore, O Maruts, [look upon] the affliction (*rapas*)—a term for evil—of the one among us who is diseased.

Just as patience (*kṣamā*) serves to cure the disease that has its fruit in sin and passion, so do you restore the afflicted limb—disturbed and oppressed—to its former state, making it whole and complete without exception.
The elision of the *n* in *niḥ* is Vedic;
likewise, the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) after the root *kṛ* in the imperative (*loṭ*) is Vedic.
In the expression "tasana-sanātha," the word *ta* undergoes the substitution *tad*. For this very reason, the collection of prefixes (*upasarga*) is not treated as a separate avagraha.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may the Great Lord of the Holy Fords (Yatīndra Maheśvara) bestow the four goals of human existence.

Thus ends the first chapter of the sixth book in the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa, a commentary on the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign of kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
In the fourth section (anuvāka), there are ten hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of eleven verses, begins with "vayamu tvām.
According to the Anvānukramaṇikā: "vayamu [is] two less; the other two [verses] are a praise of the gift of Citra."
According to the *paribhāṣā* rule "ṛṣiprānyasmāt," the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Sobhari Kāṇva.
Since it is stated that "the *kākubha* [metre] belongs to the *pragātha*," its odd verses (*ayujaḥ*) are *kakubh*s and its even verses (*yujaḥ*) are *sato-bṛhatī*s.
The subject matter of the final two verses is the gift of Citra.
The remaining [hymns] belong to Indra.
The application of the hymns is based on their indicative marks (liṅga).
In the Ukthya sacrifice, during the recitation of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the *pragātha* "avayam u tvām" is the *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "We invoke thee, O matchless one, who [knowest] 'this and that' before this"—these are the two Pragāthas (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.1).
This optional Stotriya Pragātha is also used in the Ābhiplavika Ukthya sacrifice at the third pressing for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
Thus the Sūtra has spoken.
In this very *śastra*, when the *pragātha* "tvam na indrā bhara" is the *stotriya*, then the first verse of the three-verse *anurūpa* hymn "vayamu tvā" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *anurūpa* is to be combined [as follows]: 'vayamu tvā', 'apūrvya', 'yo na idam-idam purā', and 'yāhīma indavaḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.8).

Seeking your aid, O matchless one, we call upon you for strength—just as those carrying a heavy burden call out—desiring various boons, we invoke you, the wondrous one. vayam | ūm iti | tvām | apūrvya | sthūram | na | kat | cit | bharantaḥ | avasyavaḥ | vājai | citram | havāmahe || 1 ||
1. Jha is Maheśvara.
Thus, the venerable Sāyaṇa, the lord of ministers, who was the sole bearer of the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Bukka,
the seer who had attained the majesty of omniscience,
[composed this commentary] on the sixth book of the *Ṛgveda* (the *Dāśatayī*).
In the first chapter of the Aṣṭaka, behold these mantras.
2. Jha is Maheśvara.
Thus, the first chapter of the sixth Aṣṭaka has been explained by Sāyaṇa; he will now explain the second.
3. Now begins the second chapter of the sixth Aṣṭaka.
In the fourth Anuvāka:
O "Apūrvya," O unprecedented Indra, who have manifested at the three libations; we, "bharantaḥ," supporting you with offerings characterized by Soma, [invoke you] in "vāja" (the battle for booty).

*Vājayan* means "they go to fight" or "wherein the warriors seek booty (*vāja*)," thus *vāja* refers to battle. In that [battle], we—desiring protection for ourselves and seeking aid—invoke you alone, you who are *citram*, wonderful, praiseworthy, or manifold in form. We call upon you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as people, filling their house with rice and other grains, carry a large, superior load (sthūram) for the sake of food (vāja), so do they favor one man over another.
Thus, O fierce one, you have come toward us for the performance of our work—O bold one, you who are courageous.
We, your friends, choose you alone, O Indra, as our protector and winner of the prize. For this deed, for our protection, may that youthful and fierce one, who is bold, come toward us.
You indeed—2. Toward you—for the rite—for help. He, our youth, the fierce one, has exerted himself—he who is bold, you indeed.
Sinking down like birds, we call out to you, O Indra, with songs of praise—just as one calls to a cow—for the sake of the exhilarating, intoxicating, and eloquent draught of honeyed Soma. 5.
"O Indra, [come] to that which is mixed with cow-products.
The root *śrīṅ* means "to cook. Here, the word *go* refers to curd and milk, which are products of the cow.

Sitting— that is, dwelling— in your exhilarating, intoxicating, and expansive Soma-mead, which is mixed with curds and milk as the ingredients for the Śrauta sacrifice and which has the nature of leading one to heaven; sitting like birds in a dwelling, gathering together in one place, we praise you repeatedly or celebrate you with loud acclaim.
We address you with clear and sincere adoration; why do you reflect upon us even for a moment?
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, our desires exist; grant them to us! We are here, and our prayers exist.

Toward you indeed, with this homage, we speak to you. Why do you ponder again and again? O Lord of the Bay Horses, our desires exist; you are the giver, and we are present. Our prayers exist as well. (6) O Indra, toward you indeed—with this homage, whether it be through praise or with the oblation characterized by food—we address you; we speak to you. [The first word does not lose its accent because of the conjunction *ca*. But why, for what reason, do you ponder again and again? The root *dīdhī* preceded by *vi* means "to reflect. You reflect. [The root *dīdhīṅ* means "to shine" or "to play"; here it is used in the sense of reflection, with a shift to the active voice (*parasmaipada*) and the absence of the suffixal elision. If you ask, "For what purpose do you speak?"—O Lord of the Bay Horses, O Indra, our desires regarding sons, cattle, and so forth exist; let these desires be fulfilled. If you say, "I do not give," [we reply: you are indeed the giver of wealth and other things. Therefore, we remain in your presence. Furthermore, our prayers—that is, our ritual actions—also abide near you. Thus, the meaning is that we speak to you for the sake of obtaining wealth and other such blessings.
Surely, O Indra, we have now come to be under your protection; for all our riches, O wielder of the stone, were not previously beyond your reach.

Verily, O Indra, we have become yours alone through your protection; for indeed, O wielder of the thunderbolt, we did not know all your fullnesses in former times. Now, however, knowing you as the Great One, we are yours to be protected. *Note:* The word *parīṇasaḥ* is derived from *parīṇas*, meaning "fullness" or "greatness. The phrase *nahi nu te* implies that previously they were ignorant of your magnitude, whereas now they acknowledge it. The term *adrivaḥ* is a vocative of *adri-vat*, meaning "O possessor of the stone (the thunderbolt). The particle *it* emphasizes the exclusivity of their devotion. The verb *abhūma* is in the first person plural perfect tense, meaning "we have become. The commentary suggests a shift in perspective: formerly they did not recognize your greatness, but now they do. Thus, they declare themselves worthy of your protection.
O Hero, we desire all thy friendship and thy bounty; O wielder of the thunderbolt, do not withhold these from us.
Furthermore, O Vasu, O fair-cheeked one, bestow upon us in this world a share of strength consisting of cattle.

O Friend! O Hero! We know all of your friendship and your bounty. O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, we implore those two from you. And furthermore, O Vasu, O fair-jawed one, sharpen us for strength in this very battle rich in cattle. O Hero, O powerful Indra, we recognize all your friendship—your state as our friend. Moreover, we recognize all your bounty—the wealth that is to be enjoyed. O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, O Indra, we implore those two—friendship and wealth—from you; we entreat them directly. And furthermore, O Vasu, you who provide shelter for all, O fair-jawed one with beautiful temples...
1. By means of speed;
2. by means of protection; or [by means of] preservation.

Or rather: O Indra, you who possess a beautiful helmet (*śobhanaśirastrāṇa*), sharpen us—that is, make us keen—within this *vāja*, which consists of cattle and other things, or within all this food (*anna*).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
the meaning is: "By this gift, make us famous.
In the word *śiśīhi*, there is the Vedic substitution of *bhlu* for the suffix.
In the *ukthya* sacrifice, during the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* recitation, the *pragātha* beginning with "yo na idamadam" serves as the *anurūpa*.
This is prescribed by the *sūtra*: "The two *pragāthas* beginning with 'yo na idamadaṃ purā' and all the *kakubhas*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.1).
In the *ābhiplavika* Ukthya sacrifices as well, this [verse] is an optional *anurūpa* for the *Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s *śastra* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.8).

In the *Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s *śastra* at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) during the *ābhiplavika* Ukthyas, when the *stotriya* is the *pragātha* beginning with "tvaṃ na indrā bhara," it is to be brought in as the *anurūpa*.
In that case, "yo na idamidam" is the second [verse].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘The verse “yo na idam-adaṃ purā” is the *anurūpa* [verse] for the *samāhārya* [stotra] with “yāhīma indavaḥ”’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

Him who in the past brought this and that better thing to us—him, O friends, I praise for your protection: Indra, for our aid. (9) He who in the past brought forth this and that superior wealth for us—him indeed I praise for you, O friends: Indra, for our succor. (9)

O friends, sharing the same station— ye priests and sacrificers— he Indra, who formerly brought us this most excellent wealth (vasyaḥ)— the term *vasyaḥ* being derived from *vasu* with the suffix *īyasun*, where the elision of the vowel *ī* is Vedic— this praised treasure (*praśastaṃ vasu*), has led us, living beings, forward. That very Indra, the bringer of riches, I, Sobhari, praise for you, for the sake of obtaining wealth and for protection (*ūtaye*).

The lord of bay horses, the protector of the good, the subduer of peoples—he indeed is the one who has rejoiced. May he, the bounteous Maghavan, bestow upon us, his praisers, hundreds of cattle and horses. The lord of bay horses, the protector of the good, the subduer of peoples—he indeed is the one who has rejoiced. May he, the bounteous Maghavan, bestow upon us, his praisers, hundreds of cattle and horses.

He who possesses bay-colored horses (*vāryaśvam*), who is the lord of the good (*satpatim*)—the lord of the stars (*satām*) by virtue of his preeminent self-luminosity, or the lord of the excellent (*satām*)—who overcomes the people (*carṣaṇīsaham*) as the subduer of hostile men; indeed, that person praises him. That person who has been gladdened (*yamandata*) by him, having obtained wealth and being thus praised, he (Indra) becomes pleased with him.

This being so, may that Indra, the possessor of wealth, the Lord of the Hundred, swiftly bestow upon us, his praisers, a hundredfold multitude of cattle and horses; or rather, let him fulfill [our desire].
[The root] *vī* is used in the sense of movement and so forth;
here, the suffix *leṭ* is applied with the augment *iṭ*.
Therefore, having obtained the status of disputants, we shall praise him.

O Bull, with you indeed as our ally, may we address the one who pants against us in the assembly of people who possess cattle. 11. With you | indeed | even | as ally | we | toward | the panting one | O bull | may we speak | in the gathering | of the people | possessing cattle. 11.

O Bull Indra, worthy of increase, in the assembly—the place of battle—of the people possessed of cattle and other wealth, against the enemy who breathes heavily with excessive rage toward us, we shall indeed, by you alone as our ally (*vyuj*), speak back;
that is to say, we shall repel him.
1. That which is seen in *kha*, *ta*, *na*, and *śa* does not exist [in the other]; that which is seen in *gha* does exist [there].
2. It is the same for *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *ya*.

May we conquer in the battle, O much-invoked one, as doers of deeds; may we overcome the ill-disposed. With our men may we slay Vṛtra, and with our horses may we be victorious. O Indra, further our prayers. 12. May we conquer in the battle, O much-invoked one, as doers of deeds; may we overcome the ill-disposed. With our men may we slay Vṛtra, and with our horses may we be victorious. O Indra, further our prayers. 12.

O *puruhūta*, you who are invoked by many, O *indra*, [we say] "remembering in their minds the affliction caused by our various enemies who bring calamity. In that context, "those who cause harm" refers to the enemies who inflict injury; "in *kāre*"—*kāra* is battle, so called because weapons (*āyudhāni*) are scattered (*kīryante*) therein.
In that [struggle], may we conquer them;

may we overcome—stand superior to—even those of evil intent, the wicked-minded. Furthermore, together with the great men who lead with weapons, may we slay—the one who harms—Vṛtra, the enemy who obstructs the cattle.
Having slain [them], may we hear [of victory];
and, being free from enemies, may we prosper through our sons and grandsons and by means of rituals such as the *Abhiṣṭoma*.
Or else:
The root *śri* here contains an implied causative sense.
Since there is no harm from enemies, we would cause you to prosper with food characterized by Soma.
Therefore, may you thoroughly protect (*pra aveḥ*) our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*), that is, our ritual actions (*karmāṇi*).

In the *ābhilāvika* *uktha*s at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), during the *śastra* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, there are two optional *pragātha*s beginning with “*atrātavyaḥ*,” which serve as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*atrātavyo anā tvaṃ mā te amājuro yathā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

In this matter, O Indra, by birth you have from of old been without kinsmen and without friends; yet through battle alone you seek to win yourself friends. In this matter, O Indra, by birth you have from of old been without kinsmen and without friends; yet through battle alone you seek to win yourself friends.
O Indra, you are by very nature (*januṣā*)—that is, from birth itself—to be protected (*atrātavya*).
The suffix *vyat* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.1.145 (*vyan sapatne*).
You are *anā*, meaning "one who leads" (*anetaka*).
By the rule “ṛtacchandasi,” there is the suffix *kap*; this is a prohibition [of other suffixes].
The meaning is "one who does not restrain."
Though you have been without a patron and bereft of kinsmen from of old— for a long time indeed you have been devoid of brotherhood and the like—
and though you desire patronage and kinship, it is by fighting alone, by engaging in battle itself, that you become the friend of those who offer hymns of praise.

Never do you find one who is wealthy for friendship; they revile you, O possessor of noble horses. When you make the thunderer roar, you are summoned like a father when you gather [the waters] together. nakī revantam sakhyāya vindase pīyanti te surāśvaḥ | yadā kṛṇoṣi nadanuṃ samūhasyād it pitāiva hūyase || 14 || Never do you find one who is wealthy for friendship; they revile you, O possessor of noble horses. When you make the thunderer roar, you are summoned like a father when you gather [the waters] together.

O Indra, you do not find—that is, you do not accept or take refuge with—for the sake of friendship, that first man who possesses no wealth, who is destitute of riches, and who is devoid of the practice of giving and other virtues; for such a person does not perform sacrifices.
To the question of whether there are people who do not sacrifice, he says:
"those who possess fine horses."
The root *oṣ* means "to go" and "to increase. Those atheists (*nāstika*) who are intoxicated by liquor and likewise intoxicated [by pride] are consuming you;
for the root *pīy* has the sense of the action of harming.
They cause harm; the meaning is that you destroy them.
1. gha- summoned by the Rākṣasas; 2. ta-na-bhara-nā may we stand firm; bha1-3-bhitiṣṭhema; 3.

kha-ta-2-3-4-na-anā may he not lead us away; gha-anā may he not restrain us; jha-sapallarahitaḥ anā may he not lead us away; bha1-anā may he, being without offspring, not lead us away; bha2-3-anā may he, being without offspring, not lead us away (anekaḥ in bha3); śa-anā may you be many.
4. [The consonants] kh, ṭh, th, ph, ś, ṣ, and s.
5. [The consonants] kh, g, jh, ṭ, ḍ, n, bh, and any other [consonant] except m.

Let us not, O Indra, be like those who grow old at home, fools who, for the sake of friendship with one such as you, sit together by the pressed juice without offering. (15) O Indra, giver of cattle, let us not be excluded from your wealth; let us not fail to receive from you. Even the firm possessions of the enemy, I seize them; bring them hither, for no one can obstruct your gifts. (16) Whether it be Indra, or the auspicious Sarasvatī, or you yourself, O Citra, who has given this great wealth to me, the donor? (17) Citra indeed was the king, and others were but petty kings along the Sarasvatī. Like Parjanya with his rain, he spread himself abroad, bestowing thousands and tens of thousands. (18)

1. In the *gha* and *bha* manuscripts, [the reading is] *gṛhe*. 2. In the *kha*, *ta*, *bha*, *bhara*, and *śa* manuscripts, it is *nivasāmaḥ*; in the *ga*, *gha*, *ta¹*, *bha¹*, and *bha³* manuscripts, it is *nivasāmaḥ*. 3. In the *ga* manuscript, it is *tvahtadhanā*. 4. In the *gha* manuscript, it is *vikalpate*. 5. In the *bha* manuscript, it is *khalivayetāvata*. 6. In the *gha* manuscript, it is *iyadetāvahvanaṃ*.

Citra: Hither! O King! O petty kings! Hither! O others! O whomever! Along the Sarasvatī, like Parjanya with rain, Citra has indeed spread [wealth]. Giving thousands and tens of thousands, Citra by name alone, the king, has satisfied all those petty kings who dwell along the Sarasvatī; this very Citra has extended [his bounty] to them with wealth. He has stretched it out for them—this is the form of the root *tan* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* prefix, following the rule "the accent is optionally on the first syllable. Therein is the illustration: like Parjanya. Just as Parjanya satisfies the earth with rain, so does this Citra satisfy all with wealth. The second hymn, consisting of eighteen verses beginning with "Otyam," is the seerage of Sobhari Kāṇva. The first, third, and fifth verses are *bṛhatīs*; the second, fourth, and sixth are *satobṛhatīs*; the seventh is a *bṛhatī*; and the eighth is an *anuṣṭubh*. Following the rule "Kākubha is the *pragātha*," the remaining four are *kākubha* *pragāthas*. The deities are the Aśvins. Thus it is stated: "Otyam... the Aśvina hymn begins with three *pragāthas*, a *bṛhatī* and an *anuṣṭubh*, and the eleventh verse has the *kaku* and *madhya* meters with *jyotis*. In the morning liturgy (*prātaranuvāka*) during the Aśvina sacrifice, the first seven verses are used in the *bārhata* meter within the Aśvina recitation. It is prescribed: "Otyam... ā ratham... these seven" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15). 1. Otyam! That chariot, most wondrous, for aid, that which you, O Aśvins, easy to invoke, whose paths are like Rudra’s, mounted for Sūryā. O Aśvins, that chariot of yours—which is most wondrous (*daṃsiṣṭham*), exceedingly beautiful, or rather, the destroyer of enemies—I, Sobhari, invoke today for protection on this day of sacrifice. O Aśvins, you who are easy to invoke through hymns and recitations, whose paths are like Rudra’s (either prone to weeping in battle or whose paths are praised), that chariot which you two mounted for Sūryā when she chose her husband in the self-choice ceremony—that chariot I invoke. 2. The nourisher of the ancients, easy to invoke, much-desired, the protector, foremost in battles, accompanied by followers, with good thoughts, O Sobhari, hating the enemy, and peerless. O Sobhari, praise with auspicious hymns the chariot of the Aśvins. How characterized? The nourisher of the ancients by bestowing wealth upon previous worshippers; easy to invoke in sacrifices; much-desired by many; the protector (*bhuyum*)—from the root *bhuja* meaning to protect—the guardian of all; foremost in battles, going ahead in conflicts; accompanied by followers, possessing all enjoyments; hating the enemy, specifically hating foes; and peerless, unassailable by anyone or free from sin. 3. Here, those two most omnipresent gods, the Aśvins, with salutations, we bring hither for our own protection, they who go to the house of the donor. 1. *kha-ta-na-śa*: for you two; 2. *ta1-2-bhara*: nourishing.
Hither, O Aśvins, you who are most abundant in being, come with your aids; we make you turn toward us for the sake of the worshipper, you who go to the house of the donor. 3.

O you two who have become much (purubhūta), the nourishers of many enemies beyond measure; O two gods (devā), radiant and worthy of praise; you who go toward the house of the donor (dāśuṣaḥ), the sacrificer who has offered oblations, and who are ever-moving; O you two Aśvins, we shall well prepare (su karāmahe) you both here in this rite for protection (avase), with salutations (namobhiḥ)—that is, with oblations or hymns—so that you may come hither (arvācīnā), facing toward us.
One of you two has moved around the wheel of the chariot; the other here desires these [gifts]. O Lords of Splendor, may your benevolence hasten toward us like a milch-cow.

The wheel of your chariot moves around; the other [wheel] of yours speeds along the path. With that plough you two plough the barley—the grain called *yava*—and furthermore, you perform the furrowing for it.

O Lords of Splendor (*śubhaspatī*), O protectors of the waters, O Aśvins—those two of you endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics—we shall now, on this day of sacrifice, praise you both most excellently with beautiful hymns; we offer our praise.
Come to us, O lords of ample wealth, with those broad [steeds] of yours, by which you, O bulls, quicken Tr̥kṣi and Trasadasyu for great dominion.

Come near to us, O ye who possess abundant wealth; come by the broad paths of Truth, O ye powerful ones, by which you quickened Tr̥kṣi, O bulls, when he sought protection, and urged him on toward great dominion. 7.
O Aśvins, possessors of wealth consisting of food— those for whom food itself is their treasure— come hither to us by the paths of *ṛta*, the sacrifice that has become reality.

O Ashvins, you two bulls, the bestowers of wealth, [you who brought] Trasadasyu—the son of Trasadasyu—and Tṛkṣi, named thus, by those paths of steadfastness (*yebhiḥ dhairyamārgaiḥ*) for the sake of great sovereignty (*kṣatrāya*) and wealth (*mahe dhanāya*), you gladdened them (*jinvathaḥ*).
Thus, by those same paths, come to gladden us with wealth and other blessings; this is the meaning.
This Soma, pressed by the pressing-stones, O heroes, possessors of bull-like wealth—come hither for the drinking of Soma; drink it in the house of the donor.
This Soma has been pressed for you with stones, O heroes, O possessors of bull-like wealth; come hither for the drinking of Soma, drink in the house of the donor. 8.

O Aśvins, you two leaders of all, or rather, leaders of wealth for your worshippers; O possessors of rain-like riches (*vṛṣaṇvasū*), this Soma has been pressed—that is, extracted—by us with stones, namely the pressing-blocks, for your sake.
Therefore, come hither for the drinking of Soma, for the purpose of consuming the Soma.
And having come to the house—the place of sacrifice—of the donor who has offered the oblation, you two drink the Soma.
O Aśvins, lords of wealth, mount upon the chariot, upon the golden seat;
harness your plenteous refreshments.
O Aśvins, rich in rain, mount indeed upon the golden seat of your chariot; yoke your plenteous nourishments. 9.

O Aśvins, you two who possess the wealth of rain-giving nature, mount—ascend—this golden chariot, which is equipped with golden reins and the like, which serves as a repository for weapons and other gear, and which is by nature delightful.
(The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
You two alone must ascend it.
Then, O two, bestow upon us abundant, purifying, and substantial foods (viṣas). Join them to us.
With those aids by which you protected Paktha, with which you helped Adhigu, and with which you rescued Babhru from distress—O Aśvins, come quickly with those same aids; heal whatever is diseased.
With those [aids] by which you helped Paktha, with which you helped Adhigu, and with which you helped Babhru Vijobhasa—with those, O Aśvins, come quickly to us; heal that which is diseased. 10.
O Aśvins, by those aids with which you protected—that is, guarded—King Paktha, who bears that name; and by those aids with which you protected King Adhigu, whose movement is unshakable;
and by those aids with which [you protected] Babhru, who especially gladdens with Soma offerings.
With all those protections by which you two have guarded [us], come quickly, swiftly,
and at once to us for the sake of protection.
Furthermore, "toward that which is afflicted"—our son and others who are accompanied by disease and so forth—"heal them," that is, provide medical treatment.
[This is from the section beginning with] *bhiṣak-kṛtvā* and so on.
Whenever we, seeking to win over with our songs, invoke the two Aśvins—the two who bring us over—at this very day, O you who are far-famed. ||11||

"Adhigū" means those who go quickly; "aśatagamanāḥ" means those who move swiftly in their actions; "vipanyavaḥ" means wise. We, who are "adhigū"—those who go with speed in battle for the sake of slaying enemies—invoke you two, O Aśvins, at this very moment, at the dawn of the day, with our songs characterized by praise. The connection with the subsequent verse is: "When we invoke you both, then come to us with those aids."

With those [powers], O Bulls, come hither to my invocation—[the powers] all-nourishing and containing all that is desirable. O Heroes, most bountiful with food and most abundant in being, come with those [powers] by which you strengthened Krivi. tābhir ā yātam vṛṣaṇopa me havam viśvapsuṃ viśvavāryam | iṣā maṃhiṣṭhā purubhūtamā narā yābhiḥ kriviṃ vāvadhustābhirā gatam ||12|| With those [powers], O Bulls, come hither to my invocation—[the powers] all-nourishing and containing all that is desirable. O Heroes, most bountiful with food and most abundant in being, come with those [powers] by which you strengthened Krivi.

O you two bulls, O Ashvins, who are ever-showering [with benefits], come toward my invocation—which is manifold in form (viśvapsum), consisting of hymns and liturgical recitations; which is desirable by all (viśvavārya), being sought after by all the gods—having turned your faces toward it, approach us with those aids. Come hither!
With those aids by which, O Heroes, you two Aśvins— the leaders of all—

desiring the oblations with food (the root *iṣ* meaning "to desire"), being most generous (*maṃhiṣṭhā*), the greatest givers of wealth, most widely present (*purubhūtamā*), appearing in many ways in battles as the supreme overcomers of many enemies, strengthened the waters with those aids toward the well (*krivi*).
The plural number is used for two [deities] for the sake of honor.
Vandana, having fallen into a well, was indeed raised up by you two after the well had been filled with earth;
likewise, the mantra says: "You raised up Udañcana for the one who beholds the light" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.112.5).
With those protections, come hither—come for the sake of our protection.
Even now, at this very time of days, praising those two Aśvins, I address them; indeed, we seek those two with our prostrations. ||13||
Those two previously mentioned Aśvins, who spread out weapons or riches for their worshippers in battle—I, praising them at this very moment, at the break of day, speak to them as I offer salutation;
thus, with obeisances, oblations, or hymns of praise, we entreat those very two for wealth and other blessings.

Those very two at evening, those at dawn, the lords of splendor, they whose path is like that of Rudra—O Rudras, possessors of abundant wealth, do not let us be seen by the mortal enemy as we go forward. 14.

O Lords of Splendor (*śubhaspatī*), guardians of the waters, whose paths are like those of Rudra, or whose paths are characterized by weeping (or praised) in battle—those very two, the Aśvins, at every *doṣā* (the evening), at night, those very two at *uṣas* (dawn), and those Aśvins on the journey (*yāman*) during the day—at all times, we invoke the Aśvins.
This being so, O Aśvins, possessors of wealth and food, O Rudras, do not let us pass away beyond the reach of the mortal enemy; do not abandon us!
The meaning is: "Do not make us subject to the enemy."

For the sake of easy passage, I call hither at dawn the two Aśvins, the easy-passing ones, with their chariot—the two who are victorious, like a father calling his two sons. 15. ā sugmyāya sugmyam prātā rathenāśvinā vā sakṣaṇī huve piteva sormarī ||15|| For the sake of easy passage, I call hither at dawn the two Aśvins, the easy-passing ones, with their chariot—the two who are victorious, like a father calling his two sons. 15.

Moreover, O Aśvins, you two who possess swift feet and are worthy of being served—bring to me, for my well-being, that which is easy to attain, namely happiness, by means of your chariot at the break of dawn.
Therefore, I, Sobhari, invoke you both; I call upon you just as my father used to call upon me. In this matter, there is an illustration: just as my father invoked you, so do I invoke you.

O you who are swift as thought, O showerers of blessings, O you who pour forth exhilaration, come with these aids that reach even to the distant; be present for our protection from afar with your many ancient succors, O you who provide abundant nourishment. (16) *manojavasā* (swift as thought), *vṛṣaṇā* (showerers of blessings), *madacyutā* (pouring forth exhilaration), *maśumāmābhiḥ* (with those reaching even to the distant), *ūtibhiḥ* (with aids), *ārāttāccit* (even from afar), *bhūtam* (be present), *asme* (for us), *avase* (for protection), *pūrvībhiḥ* (with many ancient ones), *purubhojasā* (O you who provide abundant nourishment). (16)
O Aśvins, you who move with the speed of thought, as swift as the mind; you who are showerers of wealth (*vṛṣaṇau*);

you who cause intoxication to flow—where "intoxications" (*madāḥ*) refers to enemies, for they cause one to be intoxicated—you who cast them down; you who possess manifold nourishment, being the enjoyers and protectors of many, or rather, those who gratify many worshippers with wealth and other gifts; O Aśvins, come quickly with your swift-moving aids and protections, and be present for our preservation from afar as well as from near at hand.

O Aśvins, heroes who drink the sweet draught, come to us with a wealth of horses, with cattle, and with gold, O destroyers of foes. 17. Come to us, O Aśvins, with a wealth of horses; come, O heroes who drink the sweet draught, with cattle and gold, O destroyers of foes. 17.

O Aśvins, you who drink the honeyed Soma most excellently, you leaders, the Dastras who are all-seeing—having made our dwelling (vartiḥ) rich in horses, rich in cattle such as cows, and rich in gold such as ornaments, come hither! Or alternatively: [The commentary continues: *Madhupātamā* means the two drinkers of the honeyed Soma to the highest degree; *narā* means leaders; *dastrā* means those who see everything. O Aśvins, *naḥ* means "of us"; *vartiḥ* refers to a dwelling (*vartante'tra iti vartirgṛham*). That [dwelling] should be made *aśvāvat*, i.e., possessed of horses; *gomat*, i.e., possessed of cows and so forth; and *hiraṇyavat*, i.e., possessed of gold, jewels, and the like. Having done so, *ā yāsiṣṭam* means "come hither. Or else: [the rest of the verse follows].
"Turn your course—the path of sacrifice—toward us, having made it equipped with horses and other [vehicles], and come;
this is the form of the root *yā* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense."

May we obtain from you, O possessors of wealth, at this approach, all desirable things—abundant progeny, heroic strength, excellent wealth, and that which is unassailable by the Rakṣasas. 18. Abundant progeny. Heroic strength. Excellent. Wealth. Unassailable. By the Rakṣasas. At this. Toward you. At your approach. O possessors of wealth. All. Desirable things. May we obtain. 18.

1. *kha* called upon *ta*; *ga* called upon the two Aśvins; *na* offered oblations; *bhara* and *śa* offered many oblations. 2. With *ṛc*s preceded by *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *bhara*, and *śa*; with protections (*ūti*) and guardianships (*rakṣā*) preceded by *bha* 1–3.
66. Ṛgveda [Aṣṭaka 6, Adhyāya 2, Varga 9]

"Of the shining one"— *dīditih* is a word meaning "to shine. "Of the one being kindled," "of the one with heat-consuming jaws"— that is, of the one whose fangs cause torment— "of the well-shaken one"— that is, of the one with beautiful luster— "of the one possessing the splendor of his host."
He takes refuge in that host of sacrificers for the purpose of receiving the oblation;

of such an Agni as this, the "śociḥ"—the brilliance—has "arisen" (ut-asyāt), being exalted, because it is free from decay (ajara) due to being churned again and again, and because it has come into being (bhūtam) or exists (bhavam) through increasing with the oblations.

Arise, O you of fair sacrifice; shine for us with divine beauty, with great splendor, radiant with your light. 5. Arise! O you of fair sacrifice! Be praised with divine grace, looking upon us with great brilliance, shining intensely. 5.
"O Agni, you of the beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*),

being praised by the chanters (*stavānaḥ*), you who are radiant with a great, blazing light that approaches from all sides or is well-known, you whose nature is to shine (*śuśukniḥ*)— the root *śuc* meaning 'to blaze'— you, being luminous, are divine."

662. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all those who suffer. Śāriputra, if there are good sons or daughters who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, who will protect them from all misfortunes. For this reason, one should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great compassion, and that he is able to provide protection to all sentient beings. If there be any who, during their lives, hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall all be delivered from suffering. If one were to burn a lamp and offer it before an image of Avalokiteśvara, or recite his name, one would not fall into the three evil realms; even if one has committed the five grave offenses or the ten evil deeds, by hearing his name, one will be delivered from all such sufferings. If one were to be bound with fetters or shackles, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, the bonds will immediately loosen. If one were to be threatened by robbers, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, they will instead gain a compassionate heart. If one were to be swept away by a great flood, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will find dry ground. If one were to be surrounded by a great fire, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, the fire will be extinguished. If one were to travel through dangerous mountain passes and wildernesses, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will encounter no harm. If one were to be in the midst of a battle, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, the swords and arrows will not strike. If one were to be born as a woman, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, she will be transformed into a man and attain birth in the Buddha-lands. If one were to dwell in the Sahā world, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will never again be born in the states of woe. If one were to be reborn in the heavens, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will attain birth among the gods. If one were to be born in the human realm, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will attain birth among humans. If one were to be born among the asuras, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will be delivered from the asura state. If one were to be born among the various animals, by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, one will be delivered from the animal realm. Those seeking the *ṛta*, with their song, have approached this upholder of *ṛta*, the accomplisher of sacrifice, at the place of homage. (9) *ṛtāvānam* (upholder of *ṛta*), *ṛtayavaḥ* (those seeking *ṛta*), *yajñasya* (of sacrifice), *sādhanam* (the accomplisher), *girā* (with song), *upo* (towards/up to), *enam* (him), *jujuṣuḥ* (they have approached), *namas-pade* (at the place of homage). O sacrificers who desire *ṛta*, approach with a song characterized by praise this Agni—who is the upholder of *ṛta*, possessed of sacrifice, and the accomplisher of sacrifice—at the place of homage, that is, the locus of the oblation (*havis*) or a limb of the sacrifice. [Note on grammar]: According to the rule *tiṅāṃ tiṅo bhavanti*, the first person ending has been substituted for the second person. Thus, *jujuṣuḥ* (third person plural) is used in place of the second person imperative.

May our well-ordered sacrifices go toward the one most excellent among the Aṅgirases, who is the Hotṛ-priest, who exists as the most glorious of all. (10) "May our well-ordered sacrifices"—those rites performed by us through praise and other means—"go toward the one most excellent among the Aṅgirases," that is, toward the preeminent Agni. "Toward" (*accha*) implies directness. And may they go toward him. That Agni, who is the Hotṛ-priest for all men, who, as the performer of the oblation, is "most glorious" (*yaśastamaḥ*)—the suffix *-tama* being elided—the most renowned of all; toward that Agni, let them go. (10)

O Agni, ageless one, those rays of yours, being kindled, shine with great light; like stallions that are virile and swift, they move with power. (11) O Agni, O ageless one (*ajara*), those (*tye*) kindled ones (*indhānāsaḥ*), shining brightly (*bṛhat bhāḥ*), are yours (*tvadīyāḥ*). Being virile (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*), meaning showerers of desires, and moving with power (*taviṣīyavaḥ*), they become all-pervading. Therein lies the illustration: "like horses" (*aśvā iva*); just as virile horses, being shedders of seed, move with power, so it is with them.

As such, O Lord of Strengths, grant us wealth accompanied by heroic power. Protect our children and grandchildren in battles. (12) O Lord of strengths—that is, of foods—O Agni, you who are such, grant to us (*naḥ*) wealth (*rayim*) endowed with excellent heroism (*suvīryam*). Protect (*pra ava*) our children (*toke*) and grandchildren (*tanaye*); for "grandchild" (*tanayaḥ*) is so called because he extends or propagates the lineage. And in battles (*samatsu*), protect preeminently (*prāva*) that wealth which is to be guarded. By this, he makes a prayer for sons and grandsons.

Or indeed, when the Lord of the Sages is sharpened and well-pleased among the clan of Manu, Agni repels all the demons. 13. yat | vai | u iti | vipra-patiḥ | śitaḥ | su-prītaḥ | manuṣaḥ | viśi | viśvā | it | agniḥ | prati | rakṣāṃsi | sedhati || 13 ||

1. Kha-gha-1-tana-bha-1-2-śa—thus [is] Agni. 2. Ga does not have 'ca'. 3. Ga-ta-bha-tye—those [who are] all-pervading belong to you. 4. Kha-ta-na-bha-1-2—[the word is] *pum*; Ga—*kulam*. 5. By the soldiers of Ga, it is to be conquered.

The Lord of the people (*viṣpatiḥ*), the protector of the clans (*viśām*), sharpened by oblations (*aśitaḥ*), that Agni, being well-pleased (*suprītaḥ*), whenever he dwells today (*adya*) in the dwelling (*viśi*)—the home—of a human (*manuṣyaḥ*), then Agni pierces (*vedhati*) and destroys all (*viśvet*) the obstructing *rakṣas* demons. [From the root *vidhu* ‘to go,’ belonging to the *auvādika* class; *u* is used for emphasis. Hear, O hero (*vīra*), O Lord of the people (*viṣpate*), this new hymn (*stoma*) of mine. Burn down the deceitful *rakṣas* demons with your consuming heat! (14) Hear, O Agni, this new hymn of mine, O hero, O Lord of the people! Burn down the deceitful *rakṣas* demons with your consuming heat! (14) O hero, destroyer of enemies, O powerful one, O Lord of the people, O Agni, hear this new hymn of mine—which is "new" because it is being performed now—and having heard it, utterly consume (*ni daha*) with your burning splendor (*tapuṣā*) those deceitful *rakṣas* demons who cause obstacles to our work. [The form *śṛṇu* is derived from *śru* with the suffix *-nu*; the elision of *v* is Vedic. No mortal enemy shall prevail over him through his magic power (*māyayā*), he who has given to Agni with offerings of oblations (*havyadātibhiḥ*). (15) No mortal enemy shall prevail over him even by means of magic power, he who has given to Agni with offerings of oblations through the priests who present the gifts. (15) Vyashva, seeking cattle (*ukṣṇayuḥ*), the seer (*ṛṣiḥ*), gratified you, the finder of wealth (*vasuvidam*). For great riches, we kindle you, even you, with fuel. (16) Vyashva, the seer of my father, desiring cattle or desiring the sender of rain, gratified you, the finder of wealth, with oblations for the sake of obtaining riches. Likewise, we too, for the sake of great wealth, shall kindle you, even you, with the proper offerings of wife and others. (16) Ushanas Kavya established you as the Hotṛ priest with his mind; he established you, Jātavedas, as the sacrificer for Manu. (17) O Agni, Ushanas Kavya, the son of a sage, established you—the sacrificer facing toward the rite, the wise Jātavedas—as the Hotṛ priest, the performer of the oblation, in the house of Manu. (17) For all the gods, being well-disposed, have chosen you as their messenger. O god, you have become the first to be honored at the sacrifice. (18) For all the gods, being well-disposed, have chosen you as their messenger. O god, you have become the first to be honored at the sacrifice. (18)

For all the gods, being well-disposed and united, have chosen you alone as their messenger, thinking, "He shall bring our oblations. O God, you have become the first among those worthy of sacrifice; through your readiness (*śruṣṭī*), O radiant Agni, you have become the foremost, the one most fit for the sacrifice by virtue of being the giver of offerings to the gods.

Indeed, let the mortal hero make this immortal one his messenger—him who is purifying, whose path is black, and who moves through the vast expanse. 19. This; indeed; the hero; the immortal; the messenger; let him make; the mortal; the purifying; whose path is black.

With these, let us worship Agni with the most excellent, most bountiful hymns, like Vyaśva, for him whose flame is bright and pure. (23) With these—let us worship—Agni—with the most excellent, most bountiful—hymns—like Vyaśva—for him whose flame is bright and pure. (23) We, the Viśvamanasas, with these most excellent (jyeṣṭhābhiḥ), most praiseworthy, and most bountiful (maṃhiṣṭhābhiḥ) hymns in the form of sūktas, let us worship—that is, we shall serve—Agni, whose brilliance is bright and pure (śukraśauciṣe), whose luster is blazing. How so? Like Vyaśva; just as our father Vyaśva served Agni with hymns, even so may we also serve him.

Now, O seer Vaiyaśva, praise with hymns the vast Agni of the household, as Sthūrayūpa did. O seer named Viśvamanas, son of Vyaśva, now at this time, praise with hymns—characterized by the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and other such forms—the vast Agni who exists within the house (*damya*) through being churned by the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*), or rather, who is beneficial to the houses of the sacrificers by warding off obstacles. Praise him with hymns. In this regard, there is an illustration: "like Sthūrayūpa. That is to say, praise him just as Sthūrayūpa, by name, praised him with devotion.

The wise ones praise Agni for protection—the ancient guest of men, the son of the trees. (25) The wise ones—the intelligent sacrificers—praise with hymns Agni, who is the guest of men, the son of the trees (born from the wooden fire-sticks which are of the nature of trees), the ancient one, for the sake of protection—that is, for the preservation of the ritual act. (13)

O Agni, toward all the great ones who are present, and toward the oblations of men, sit down with reverence upon the sacred grass (barhis). O Agni, toward all the great beings who exist for the purpose of offering praise, sit down on every side with reverence upon the sacrificial grass; likewise, sit down on every side to accept the oblations belonging to men.
Grant us many desirable things, O Vasu; grant us wealth that is much-sought after—wealth consisting of excellent heroic power, abundant progeny, and glory. ||27||
1. Because it is being born (gha).
2. kha: of human beings; ga, ta, bha, śa: humans [are] of human beings; na: humans [are] of human beings. 3.
kha, ga, jña, ta-1, 2, bha, ni: sit down.
Furthermore, upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the sacrifice, sit down firmly with reverence (*namas*), praise (*stotra*), and the oblation (*havis*).
O Agni, grant us many desirable things (*vāryāṇi puru*) such as cattle and other wealth;
likewise, grant us riches (*rāyas*) that are desired by many.

Of what nature is it? Grant us wealth that is endowed with excellent vigor (*suvīrya*), accompanied by progeny such as sons and grandsons (*prajāvat*), and possessed of fame and renown (*yaśasvat*). O Agni, you who are the bestower of boons (*vara*), impel the people toward the one who offers good oblations (*suṣāman*); O most youthful one (*yaviṣṭha*), O Vasu, grant eternal delight (*rati*) to all for ever. tvam | varaḥ | suṣāmṇe | agne | janāya | codaya | sadā | vaso | ratim | yaviṣṭha | śaśvate || 28 ||

O most excellent one, worthy of being chosen by all; O dweller, who causes the enemies to dwell [in fear]; O youngest one—being born again and again, O most youthful Agni—you [grant protection] to Suṣāman (one who possesses beautiful chants);
[the *vat* suffix occurs here because of the rule beginning with *suṣāman*];
[grant it] to the many, to the perpetual one, through your grace, for the sake of one possessing beautiful chants.
O friends, let us instruct a sacred prayer for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt; I shall praise it well for you, for him who is most heroic and bold. 1.

O friends—meaning, O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have become our allies—for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), whose hand holds the *vajra*, we shall recite this hymn in the form of a boar as a sacred prayer (*brahman*); that is, we pray for it.
[The root] *śāsu* is used in the sense of "instructing. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, there is the substitution of *al* for *pal*.
In the case of *itva-paratve*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition.

Therein, for you all—*yuṣmākam arthāya*—for the sake of all of you; for the most excellent leader of all, or rather, for the most excellent leader of weapons and so forth in battles; for that Indra, who is bold (*dhṛṣṇave*), whose nature is to crush his enemies—I praise him well, indeed, I laud him excellently.

By thy might thou art renowned as the slayer of Vṛtra through the slaying of Vṛtra; O Hero, thou bestowest gifts upon the liberal patrons beyond all others. By thy might thou art indeed renowned; by the slaying of Vṛtra thou art the slayer of Vṛtra; with thy protections, O Hero, thou bestowest abundantly upon the wealthy patrons.
O Indra, you are renowned—famous—by virtue of your might and strength;
for [the particle] *hi* indicates renown.
He states that very point:

By the slaying of Vṛtra—that is, by the killing of the demon Vṛtra—you become renowned as "Vṛtrahan," the slayer of Vṛtra. O Śūra, O Indra possessed of heroism, from the *maghavan*—the wealthy, affluent man—you surpass [all others] with your riches (*mṛdhaiḥ*) and bestow them upon us, your worshippers.

Being praised by us, bring us wealth most excellent in renown—that you, O Lord of Bay Horses, are the giver of treasure even in the desert. 3. Being praised by us, bring us wealth most excellent in renown—that you, O Lord of Bay Horses, are the giver of treasure even in the desert. 3.

O Indra, you who are such, being praised—that is, being extolled by us—bring to us, that is, bestow upon us, wealth consisting of sons or riches endowed with the most excellent and manifold fame. Give it;
this is the meaning.
O Lord of the bay horses (Harivaḥ)!
The two bay horses.
Likewise, O Indra, you who are *vasu*—the one who causes the enemies to dwell [in fear]—even at the very moment of your departure;
indeed, from the mere departure of your life-force, the enemies flee.
Furthermore, you are a giver, a bestower of riches.

O Indra, disclose the secret treasure and that which is dear to men; O bold one, being praised, bring it hither with courage. 4. ā nirekam uta priyam indra darṣi janānām | dhṛṣatā dhṛṣṇo stavamāna ā bhara || 4 ||

O Indra, furthermore, satisfy our dear friend, the most beloved one; for "nireka" means wealth, so called because it is separated out or because it goes forth. Open up, tear asunder, and make manifest that wealth for us, the people who are your singers.
The root *dṛ* means "to split.
There is a Vedic elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

And having split it open—O bold (*dhṛṣṇo*), O you who are by nature courageous, O Indra—being praised (*stavamānaḥ*) by us, your praisers, bring (*ā bhara*) with a bold (*dhṛṣatā*) and daring mind that wealth; give it to us.
The Asuras do not ward off your left hand, nor your right hand; O Lord of the Bay Horses, they cannot obstruct you in the raids for cattle. ||5||

1. *sa-jñā-1-2-ma-āśāsmahe*: We pray for that which is accompanied by knowledge; or rather, we pray for the Brahman in the form of the oblation being offered by us. 2. *sa-ta-na -ma-śa-āsapādaya*: Accomplish [that] with *sa*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, and *śa*. 3. *sa-ga-ta-na-bhara-śatrūṇāṃ gharṣaṇaśīla*: Having the nature of crushing enemies through *sa*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*; *bhā-1-3-manasā śatrūṇāṃ gharṣaṇaśīla*: Having the nature of crushing enemies with the mind through *bhā*, *1*, and *3*.

O Indra, lord of horses, those who act as adversaries by facing you in battle—those combatants who, during the *gaviṣṭis* (the searches for the cattle of the Aṅgirases stolen by the Paṇis), do not restrain your left hand;
that is to say, they cannot ward it off with their weapons and the like.
Likewise, they do not restrain your right hand either.
Furthermore, the obstructors—the Asuras such as Vṛtra and others who harass from all sides—cannot restrain your left and right hands.
In battles, let all your enemies go away in every direction with their hands severed by you;
the meaning is that you remain unharmed by them.
O wielder of the stone, I draw you toward me with songs as one draws cattle into a pen; satisfy the desire and the mind of the singer.
O wielder of the stone, I close you in with songs as one encloses a pen with cattle; fulfill the desire and the thought of the singer! 6.

O wielder of the stone, O Indra, O possessor of the thunderbolt, I reach you with songs—words characterized by praise. For indeed, O Dancer, there exists for you an unimpeded power; O much-invoked one, your gift is uninjured for the donor. 9.

O Indra, you who cause all things to dance as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*), your power (*śavas*) is such that it remains unassailed— indeed, it is well known— that it exists as something not reached by enemies. Likewise, O Puruhūta, invoked by many, the gift (*rāti*) consisting of wealth and other boons given to the sacrificer who has offered oblations becomes *amṛktā*, meaning unharmed by enemies.
The wealth of the sacrificer obtained from you is not harmed by enemies;
the meaning is that just as you are the protector of your own army, so too are you the protector of that wealth.
Pour forth, O most magnificent one, for great bounty, O most manly one!
Even that which is difficult to milk, O Madhavan, you milk for the sake of our support.
Pour forth, O most mighty one, for great bounty; even the firm, the difficult-to-overcome, do thou, O Maghavan, make subject to our generosity. 10.
O most excellent leader, most worthy of worship by all, pour into yourself—that is, fill your belly with Soma—for the sake of great *rādhas*, the power that completely overcomes enemies;

O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, being exhilarated by the drinking of Soma, strike down even the most difficult fortresses of the enemies—those which are firm and unassailable by others—for the sake of obtaining riches (*maghattaye*). Strike them down!
The meaning is "to tear asunder."
Never indeed have they gone elsewhere from you, O Lord of the Stone;
O Maghavan, protect us with those aids of yours.
Nowhere else, O wielder of the stone, have our desires gone but to you; O possessor of the prize, take heed of this, and favor us with your protections. 11.

O wielder of the stone, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, you are known to us as one who possesses wealth and is a giver; yet, not fully realizing this, our hopes—our expectations and desires—never before, even in ancient times, went elsewhere than to you, such as to other gods.
There they obtained no fruit.
Now we have come to know that you are wealthy and of a generous nature.
Therefore, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, with your protections (*ūtibhiḥ*), grant—that is, give—to us that wealth of yours which was obtained by the shattering of the cities of our enemies.
*Śṛgdhi* is a verb meaning "to give";
it is the *loṭ* (imperative) form of the root *śak*, with the Vedic elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
For truly, O Lord of the song, I find no one other than you to grant us prosperity,
wealth, glory, and strength.
Not indeed, O Lord; I find none other than you for the granting of bounty, for wealth, for glory, and for strength, O lover of hymns. 12.

O dancer, O inspirer of dance, O lover of hymns, O Indra worthy of praise and worship through songs and laudations—for the sake of *rādhas* (the accomplishment of power), for *rāyaḥ* (wealth), for *ghumna* (splendor), for *dyotamāna* (the shining), for *yaśas* (fame), and for *śavas* (increasing strength) and *bala* (power)—I find no one other than you; indeed, I obtain none other. (*Aṅga*) is used here as a particle of emphasis.
Pour it out for Indra; let him drink the Soma-mead.
He shall impel [us] with bounty by means of his greatness.
Pour out the drop for Indra; let him drink the Soma-sweetness. May he impel us with his bounty through his great majesty. 13.
O priests, pour out the flowing Soma for the sake of Indra; that is, perform the pouring by mixing it with the liquid for blending.
The meaning is: press it out.
Then, let him drink the Soma-made honey, which is intoxicating and full of ambrosia.

And having drunk, Indra— by his own greatness (*mahitvanā*), that is, by his very majesty (*svamahatva*)— along with abundant food (*vrādhas*), impels (*pra codayate*) wealth and other gifts toward the worshippers;
or rather,
[the text implies] the sacrificer [impels them] by means of his greatness.
Its greatness arises from being offered to Indra.
Together with *rādhas*, which means food, he impels the worshippers.
The meaning is that he urges the worshippers forward with the thought, "Let this be an offering for Indra."

Come near to the lord of the bay horses, the skillful, the all-seeing, the swift one! Truly, hear now the praise of Aśvya as he lauds you. 14. "Come near"—to the lord of the bay horses, the skillful, the all-seeing, the swift one; truly, hear the praise of Aśvya as he lauds you. 14.
The protector (pati) of the bay-colored (harīṇām) horses, the skillful (dakṣam) increaser (vardhakam) of his own strength, who is full of offspring (puśvantam)—
[the root] *pṛc* meaning "to join"—
he who yokes [his steeds] among the Maruts.
Or rather:
[I have seen] you, Indra, such as you are, uniting your own strength with enemies by means of weapons and the like. I have beheld you thus.
I, Viśvamanas, shall perform the hymn of Vaśvya. Vyaśva is designated by his names through the word "aśva" (horse).
While that son is speaking—that is, while he is performing a hymn of praise—surely now hear, listen to my praise concerning you.

For never before has one been born more heroic than you; no one is equal to you in wealth, nor in such deeds, nor in glory. 15. Not indeed, O friend, was anyone born even in the past more heroic than you; none is equal to you in riches, nor in such ways, nor in renown. 15.

O Indra, before you, no one more heroic—that is, more powerful—was ever born; indeed, this is well known. The meaning is that you alone were born possessed of such power. Furthermore, there is no one who is more capable than you in terms of wealth (*vāyā*). Likewise, no one was born superior to you in *evathā*—that is, by approaching the cities of enemies or in battle. Alternatively, *evathā* [is derived from] roots such as *ava* (to protect) and so forth; the change of *a* to *e* is Vedic, and the suffix *-atha* is according to the *Uṇādi* rules. There is none superior to you in protecting those who have come for refuge or in praising singers. Moreover, in *bhandanā*—"bhand" being a root meaning to praise—no one was born superior to you in hymns of praise. Thus, no one other than you was born as a possessor of wealth, a protector, or one worthy of praise. 17.
The triplet beginning with "edu maghavaḥ" is an optional *anurūpa* for the previously mentioned *brāhmaṇacchaṃsin* recitation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "edu maghavo madantaram, eto nindraṃ stavāma sakhāyaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

O Maghavan, drink more deeply of this exhilarating soma; O Adhvaryu, pour forth the juice for you! For thus is the hero praised, he who ever increases our prosperity. 16. O Maghavan, drink more deeply of this exhilarating soma; O Adhvaryu, pour forth the juice for you! For thus is the hero praised, he who ever increases our prosperity. 16.

O Adhvaryu, leader of the sacrifice, O priest, O bounteous one, pour out—meaning, press for the sake of Indra—the most exhilarating Soma juice, which is the very essence of the intoxicating food characterized by Soma;
"idu" is used here as a particle of emphasis.
You are a hero, capable, and ever-increasing—that is, one who is always to be strengthened by the oblation.
Alternatively, this Indra is always the increaser of his own power; for he is indeed praised with hymns, recitations, and so forth.
To Indra who has been praised, Soma must be offered;
therefore, the connection [of the verse] is: "Pour it out."
