1. *gha* and *bha*: for the sake of Indra; 2. *bha*: O Indra, belonging to [thee]; 3. *gha*, *bha*, *na*: not born; 4. *jha*, *ta1-4*, *ya*: just as; *ga2*: thus. Indra is the lord of the bay steeds; no one has attained thy ancient praise, nor thy glory through power. 17 Indra. Lord. Of the bay steeds. No one. Thy. Ancient praise. Up. Has attained. Through power. Nor. Glory. 17

O Indra, you who stand over the bay horses, you upon whom they are placed; no one at all (*nakiḥ*) reaches (*udānaṃś*) with his might (*śavasā*) your ancient praise (*purvyā stutim*)— this term being illustrative— nor even the praise being performed by those of the present day.
The root *aś* is used in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "and [the augment *nuṭ* is added] after *aśnoti*.
The *mum*-augment is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The meaning is that no one transgresses [your command].
Furthermore, because you are to be praised by all and are worthy of being sought after, no one surpasses your praise— neither in wealth nor in renown—
meaning there is no one else who is more powerful, wealthy, or praiseworthy than you.

Desirous of hearing [our prayers], we invoke him for you—the Lord of Victuals—who is to be magnified by sacrifices that do not fail. 18. We invoke him for you—the Lord of Victuals—desirous of hearing [our prayers]; he who is to be magnified by unceasing sacrifices. 18.
Not being negligent in their duties through means that do not shorten life and are appropriate for human beings;
or alternatively,
those who are heedful perform their work while remaining focused on a single task.

The meaning is that they do not go to another region after having begun their work. With such sacrifices performed by men of this kind, or with such men themselves, we—desiring food (*śravasyavaḥ*)—have invoked (*ahūmahi*) that Indra, the lord and master of strengthening foods (*vājānām patim*), who is to be magnified (*vāvṛdhanya*) by you through the connection of the sacrifice; we have called him. In the *luṅ* tense of the root *hve*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occurs according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in the Vedic language, it is manifold).
In the aforementioned *śabda*, these two *taca*s, "eto nv indram" and "stuhīndraṃ vyaśvavat," serve as optional *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "eto nv indraṃ stavāma sakhāyaḥ stuhīndraṃ vyaśvavat" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

Come now, O friends, let us praise Indra, the hero worthy of hymns—he who alone surpasses all the peoples. 19. Come now; Indra; let us praise; friends; the one worthy of praise; the hero; the peoples; he; all; surpasses; alone; indeed. 19.
O friends, who share the same station or are like brothers—O officiating priests (ṛtvij)—come here quickly! For what purpose? He says:
let us praise, that is, perform a hymn for, that Indra—the one worthy of praise, the leader of all.
Indra, who, being alone and without any companion, overcomes—that is, addresses with defiance—all the *kṛṣṭis*, meaning all the enemy armies; him we shall praise—this is the remainder of the sense.

To him who does not obstruct the cattle, who seeks cattle, and who is worthy of praise—proclaim against the Dasyu a luster more delicious than clarified butter and [sweet] honey. [Word-for-word gloss: To him who does not obstruct the cattle; to him who seeks cattle; to him who is worthy of praise; the Dasyu; luster; more delicious than clarified butter; and honey; proclaim.
O priests! To him who does not obstruct the cows—meaning he who, by means of praises, causes the cows to be withheld [from the enemy]—he is a *gorudha*. One who is not a *gorudha* is an *agorudha*.
He does not destroy them; rather, he listens to them with reverence. This is the meaning.

To such an Indra—who is therefore a seeker of cattle (*gaviṣ*), who desires hymns (*stotrāṇi*), and who is radiant (*dhukyāya*)—speak a word in the form of a praise-hymn (*vacaḥ stotrarūpam vākyam*), which is more sweet than even the most delicious clarified butter (*ghṛtāt svādutarāt ājyāt*) and more exceedingly sweet than honey (*madhuśca svādīyaḥ*). Speak it, O Ṛṣis! Since the sacrificer also becomes the performer of the rite performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), speak my own word and speech concerning Indra.
(Note: *na-bha-ekākī* means "alone, without assistance.")
2. Kha, jña, 1, 2, na, bha: may it be exceedingly beautiful to behold! 3. Gha: may it be sweeter; he prays that the food with ghee shall become even sweeter.

Regarding this, the Blessed Āśvalāyana said: "This speech of mine is indeed sweeter than clarified butter and honey; [the child] says this, thinking, 'May my pleasure be sweeter! (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.1.5).

Whose heroic powers are immeasurable, whose bounty cannot be surpassed; his sacrificial fee, like light, extends over all. 21. Whose—immeasurable—heroic powers—[are there]; not—his bounty—to be surpassed; like light—over all—is his sacrificial fee. 21.

The heroic deeds of this Indra— characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth— are "unmeasured," meaning his capacities are not limited such that one could say, "His powers are only this many and no more.
Alternatively,
[the root] *mīṅ* is used in the sense of "to harm."
The short vowel is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
For [the cities] are destroyed by enemies.
Likewise, the wealth (*rādhas*) of that Indra, which cannot be encompassed (*paryantave*)—that is, cannot be reached or seized—by enemies.
For this very reason, he whose sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of the gift of wealth surpasses all those who offer praise;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
"like light" (*jyotir-na*).
Because it possesses the light of the *ayana*, this is "Jyotis" (Light); it is free from the equatorial line (*nirakṣa*).
Just as the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) stands pervading all the worlds, so too does he cover the people who offer hymns with the gift of wealth; such is the meaning.

Praise Indra, as Vyaśva did—him who is waveless, the prize-winner, the one who bestows wealth; him who distributes the house of the noble man to the donor. 22. Praise Indra, as Vyaśva did—him who is waveless, the prize-winner, the one who bestows wealth; him who distributes the house of the noble man to the donor. 22.
He whose mind pervades the universe;
"ūrmī" refers to a harmful action,
[and thus] he is one who cannot be harmed by anyone whatsoever.
Alternatively, one must not approach him with enemies;
therefore, praise Indra—who is powerful like a horse, who is well-restrained by his worshippers, and who is such as this.
The praise is illustrated by an example.
"Like Vyaśva":
the meaning is that you should praise [Indra] just as Vyaśva, the father of Viśvamanas, praised Indra.
And being thus praised, the noble lord Indra bestows upon the donor—the sacrificer who has offered the oblation—*gaya*, which means wealth that is highly esteemed.
Or alternatively: *gaya* is the house for the worship of the gods. If there is a house, the gods are worshipped with oblations (*havis*).
He bestows such a house;
therefore, the meaning is: "Praise [Him] for the sake of obtaining wealth and a home."

Thus, now indeed, praise Vairya, the tenth and the ninth, the well-knowing one, worthy of celebration among the Caraṇīs. 23. Thus. Now. Upa. Stuhi. Vairya. Ca. Daśam. Navam. Suvidvāṃsam. Carkṛtyam. Caraṇīnām. 23.
He is the son of Vyaśva, Vaiyaśva Viśvamanas. Among the nine vital breaths (*prāṇas*) residing in the bodies of human beings, he is the tenth, completing the number ten.
Regarding this, there is a mantra: "Nine indeed are the vital breaths existing in a person among men; Indra becomes their tenth, moving through the self of Indra in a tenfold manner.
He is such [a one], and for that very reason, he is *navaṃ* (praiseworthy) and *suvidvāṃsam* (well-knowing), because he is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*).
1. ga-bha-tathāha; 2. gha-°rūpāṇi;
3. na-bha-balāni.
4. For the purpose of reaching the end; for the purpose of falling into ruin.
5. Of this, it is known.
6. The meaning is: *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.

Alternatively, it means that by whatever [means] wealth is given, one overcomes all enemy forces; or, having taken the wealth given by that [means], one becomes surrounded by enemies from every side—from the non-existent (*asataḥ*), from the great (*mahataḥ*), from the existent (*sataḥ*), or from everywhere (*sarvataḥ*).
7. *ga* reads *°ranabhigantavyam*.

8. kha—He is to be well-restrained by praises; ga—na-bha—he is to be restrained by suppliants and by those who offer praise; gha—ta1-2—he is to be well-restrained by praises and by those who offer praise; śa—he is to be well-restrained by suppliants and by those who offer praise.
9. ga—vyaśva is your seer; gha—vyaśva is your name; na-bha1-2—vyaśva belongs to you both (va); bha3—vyaśva is your eloquent one. 10. ta-na-bha—of the people (carṣaṇīnām).
11. Kha praises the pure Indra; Ta praises the pure Indra; Bha praises the one worthy of pure praise; Śa praises the wise one.

The wheel that thoroughly knows everything must indeed be honored by all again and again in their undertakings; praise such an Indra now, praise him closely. For you know, O thunderbolt-handed one, how to avoid the *nirṛtis* (destructions) day after day, like a pure man avoids pitfalls. (24) You know, O thunderbolt-handed one, how to avoid the *nirṛtis*. Day after day, like a pure man [avoids] pitfalls. Now the seer, addressing Indra, says: "O thunderbolt-handed Indra, you alone know how to avoid the *nirṛtis*—the destructive demons who cause calamity. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. Therein lies the illustration: 'day after day, like a pure man'."
The first half-verse is composed in the indirect (parokṣakṛta) style:
"Indra, who protects..."; he harms (*kṣaṇoti*) men.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after *kṣaṇoteraigādi*.
Therefore, from that *rakṣas*, which is born as a wind in the form of evil (*ahaṃsa*), he releases or liberates [the person].
The meaning is: "The *rākṣasa* does not even afflict him; how much less does it kill him?"
Moreover, Indra is he who [dwells] among the flowing rivers, the Gaṅgās and other streams; or rather,
among the *sindhus*, those characterized by their nature of flowing (*sarpaṇa*).
The meaning is "even at that time," as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges.
He should impel the wealth and other goods from the noble ones toward those singers who abide in them.
The root *ṛ* means "to go" or "to reach.
In the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*) mood, the substitution of *guṇa* occurs according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.4.29: *guṇo’rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*.
Furthermore, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the augment *āṭ* is applied even in the benedictive.
Now, as for the direct [evidence]:
O Indra, possessor of many riches, O thou who art rich in horses, we bend down—that is, we humble—the weapon that is the means of slaying, the slaughterer of Dāsa, the oppressor, the Asura.
Just as you brought excellent wealth for the sake of Sanibha and Sushāman, O fortunate one, rich in prizes, [bring it] for the Vyaśvas.
For example:
*vare*,
*susāmne*.
From the merchants,
you have brought [wealth].
Wealth for the Viśvas;
O fortunate one!
O possessor of swift horses!
By this verse, the granting of a boon (*vara*) is praised.

O *vara*, O King named Varuṇa, for the sake of Supāman—your own father—you formerly brought wealth from the treasury to the *sanis* (those seeking alms), so that he might attain the highest world; even so, now bring wealth to us, the sons of Vyaśva. Because of the indicative mark of the word "vājinīvatī," this [verse] refers to the Dawn (*uṣas*).
Regarding this triplet, Śaunaka has stated: "The last [verse] of the *aupasada* hymns is 'yathā varo suṣāmṇaḥ'.
O fortunate one, endowed with beautiful wealth, O possessor of food—the suffix *matup* here serves merely for the sake of restatement.
Alternatively:
*vāja* means "the act of going" (*vājana*); that which possesses this is the "possessor of speed," namely the horse.
O *uṣas*, you who possess such [speed], bestow wealth upon us.
The praise of his generosity arises from his giving of abundant wealth;
or alternatively,
he speaks thus after addressing the excellent sage Viśvamanas.

O auspicious one, O possessor of beautiful wealth, O Dawn rich in horses: just as you, having given wealth to my father Suṣāman—named Susāman—obtained wealth through that very Suṣāman from those seeking it for their gains, and just as you caused him to give [it], so too, having given wealth to me, cause it to reach Viśvamanas, the son of Vyaśva—the plural being used for honor. Thus, through me, you bestow the gift.
He, the excellent one, spoke thus; Upasama replied.
May the sacrificial fee of the Soma-presser come hither with horses;
may there be abundant wealth consisting of hundreds and thousands.

May the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of Nārtha, the son of Vyāśva, come to us Soma-offerers—both the gift and abundant wealth consisting of hundreds and thousands. (29) He says this because he has received wealth through her: "Of Nārtha. *Narya* means one who possesses men (*nara*); his descendant is *nārtha*. From that, by the rule for expressing mere relationship (*tasyedam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Of that Soma-offerer, the possessor of Soma, the sacrificer; or rather, as an epithet of Vyāśvas. May the sacrificial fee—the gift—of such a Varu, belonging to the Soma-offerer, come to us, the sons of Vyāśva. Furthermore, may the gift (*rādhaḥ*)—abundant, massive, and accompanied by wealth numbering in the hundreds and thousands—also come to us.
O you who act with guile, what the seeker asks of you in secret—
this Vala, relying on the waters, stands obstructing the cow-pen.

When the sacrificer asks you, O Dawn, "Where, where is he?"—that Vala, having taken refuge [in you], stands down by the cow-pen. (30) Now, having awakened the Dawn, she is addressed: "O you who are made of mystery (*kuhyākṛte*), that Vala—where, where (*kuha*) does he stand?"—is thus questioned by those desiring to know, who have set out with the aim of seeking him. From the word *kuha*, the suffix *kyac* is applied. O Dawn, when (*yat*) the sacrificer asks you (*tvā*) such things... (Note: The commentary clarifies that the interrogative *kuha* takes the suffix *kyac* to form *kuhyā*, meaning "one who desires to know where," and that the Dawn is addressed as being of such a nature.)
2. *ga-bha3-vyaśvasya*; *ta-na-bha1-svavyaśvaḥ*; *ya-suvyaśvaḥ*. 3. *kha-gha-ta-na-bha2-ya-śa-āgacchati*; *bha1-agacchati*. 4. *bha-tyetyecchayā*.
[Maṇḍala 8, Adhyāya 4, Sūkta 25] In the sixth book: 675.

Someone, having performed a sacrifice (*ījānaḥ*), being a suitor (*varaḥ*), asks (*pṛcchāt*—he asks): "Where does she stand with her guile (*kuhayā*)? When he asks this, then [the answer is]: "She is *apaśritaḥ*—resorted to by all.
Or else: [it means she has departed].
"With doors wide open" means that when supplicants arrive, the gatekeepers do not obstruct them. Such is the "vala," meaning a chosen one who is a restrainer of enemies by his own power.
Or rather:
she was won over by the monks through the gift of wealth and other such things;
"this," namely this boon, [is directed toward] the river named Gomati.
The accusative case is used here according to the rule "kālādhvanoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
You say that at that time he was standing on its bank.

The fifth hymn, consisting of twenty-four verses, begins with "tā vām. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "tā vām [is] the twenty-fourth [hymn]; it is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; the first three verses beginning with the tenth are addressed to the Viśvedevas; the penultimate verse is an Uṣṇih-garbha. The seer (ṛṣi) is Viśvamanas, the son of Vyaśva.
The metre is *uṣṇih*.

Because it possesses the defining characteristics stated in [Anuvāka 4.3], "The penultimate [syllable] is heavy; that which contains an *uṣṇih* has six, seven, and eleven [syllables]," it is an *uṣṇiggarbhā*.
The tenth, eleventh, and first [verses] have the Viśvedevas as their deities; for the remaining ones, Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities.
The application of the hymns is written down.
Those two of you, the guardians of the universe, gods among gods, worthy of sacrifice, upholders of cosmic order, and pure in will—I worship you both. || 1 ||

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two who are the guardians (*gopā*) of the entire world (*viśvasya*), the two gods (*devā*) characterized by luminosity, worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyā*) among the gods— such as you two, I assign the sacrificer to you for the purpose of offering oblations. Therefore, O Viśvamanas, you two who possess *ṛta* (*ṛtāvānā*), being truthful or possessed of sacrifice, and whose will is purified (*pūtadakṣau*)—
you do not become powerful merely by the statement "we two are powerful," but rather you are truly endowed with capability.
You worship Mitra and Varuna with oblations; you honor them.

Mitra and Varuṇa, who is of noble wisdom, are like two chariot-steeds joined by a common bond; they are well-born from of old, their offspring firm in their vows. 2. Mitra and Varuṇa, who is of noble wisdom, are like two chariot-steeds joined by a common bond; they are well-born from of old, their offspring firm in their vows. 2.
Varuṇa, who is of good wisdom (*sukratu*) and beautiful deeds (*sukarman*), and Mitra— these two, Mitra and Varuṇa— of what sort are they? [They are] *tanā*.
They extend crowns, bracelets, and so forth; thus, "tanāni" refers to riches (dhanāni). In the sense of "naśra," riches are the "rathyā," meaning the two leaders (netārau).
Alternatively, since wealth depends upon the performer of the ritual action, it is connected [to the verse] as "bestowing wealth.

Such are the two chariot-borne ones (*rathyau*), possessing chariots (*rathavantau*), who from of old (*sanāt*), that is, from long ago, are well-born (*sujātā*), meaning they possess a beautiful birth.
He says that very thing:

"The two sons" (tanayā) are the two sons of Aditi; "of firm vows" (dhṛtavratau)—that is, those whose actions are steadfast—those two you should worship; thus is the connection with the preceding verse.

The great Mother Aditi, the observer of Truth, brought forth those two all-knowing ones for divine sovereignty, they who are exceedingly glorious. 3. *tā* | *mātā* | *viśvavedasā* | *asuryāya* | *pramahasā* | *mahī* | *jajāna* | *aditiḥ* | *ṛtāvarī* || 3 ||
He clarifies his very nature as a son of Aditi:
"viśvavedasā" means "viśvavedasau," those who possess all wealth; or alternatively:
"Viśvavedasau" means those two who know—that is, perceive—all things consisting of both the stationary and the moving.
"Pramahasā" means the two of great splendor. Such are Mitra and Varuṇa; they were born, brought forth by Aditi, the divine mother, the vast and truth-abiding "Mātā.
For what purpose?
To Sūryā, the daughter of the Asuras, the slayer of the Asuras, [and] to Bala;
the meaning is that she was produced for the purpose of slaying the Asuras.
Great are Mitra and Varuna, sovereign gods and lords of wealth; observers of Truth, they are the highest, proclaiming the lofty voice.
1. *Uṣṇik* as before, preceded by *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *ta*, and *bha*.
2. The twenty-third [meter] consists of *ta*, *ta*, *bha*.
3. *Dyotamānaśīlau* consists of *ta*, *na*, and *bha*.

4. You two do not become strong merely by the words "you two are strong. Rather, you two are strong because of your power for the sake of sacrifice, or because you possess sacrifice, being of purified skill (*pūtadakṣau*), that is, of pure strength—not merely by the words "you two are strong.
O Great Ones! O Mitra and Varuṇa! O Sovereigns! O Gods! O Asuras! O Upholders of Cosmic Order (*ṛtavānā*)! You proclaim the Great Cosmic Order (*ṛtam*). 4.
*Mahantau*: great by virtue of an abundance of qualities; *sannājāu*: well-shining; *asurāu*:
powerful, or alternatively, the two impellers by virtue of being the inner controllers (*antaryāmin*) of all.

The two gods Mitra and Varuṇa, who possess the cosmic order (*ṛtāvānau*) and are truthful (*satyavantau*), proclaim—that is, illuminate through their own splendor—the great *ṛta*, the sacrifice, by means of the *stotra* (hymns of praise), the *śastra* (recited liturgies), and so forth.
This is a form derived from the root *ghuṣ* in the present tense (*laṭ*).

The two grandsons of great power, the two sons of Dakṣa, of noble intellect, of liberal gifts, dwelling in the abode of nourishment. 5. The two grandsons; of power; of the great; the two sons; of Dakṣa; of noble intellect; of liberal gifts; of nourishment; in the abode; dwelling. 5.
The two grandsons, the sons of the grandson, of great and mighty power—
meaning the two grandsons produced from strength—
of such [a one], of Dakṣa.

According to the rule "the root *dakṣ* is used in the sense of growth and speed," *dakṣa* means speed (*vega*). Their two sons are the offspring (*sūnu*) of that [speed]; they are called the sons because they arise from that speed by force (*balāt*).

Those two of noble intellect (*sukratū*), of auspicious deeds (*śobhanakarmāṇau*), and of excellent bestowal (*supradānū*)—givers of wealth and other gifts—Mitra and Varuṇa, dwell (*adhikṣitaḥ*) upon (*adhi*) the dwelling-place (*vāstu*) of the ignorant man;
for the word *vāstu* is designated as the object (*karman*) by the rule "adhi-ṣīṅ.
[The form] *kṣitaḥ* is derived from the root *kṣi* in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) according to Vedic usage.

You two who have gathered together the gifts, both celestial and terrestrial nourishments; may rain-bearing showers come toward you both. 6. You two who have gathered together the gifts, both celestial and terrestrial nourishments; may rain-bearing showers come toward you both. 6.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two who have gathered together the gifts—wealth that is to be given—bestow them upon us. Likewise, bestow the celestial foods that exist in heaven and the earthly foods produced on earth.
If it is asked how food is obtained in the absence of rain, it is said in response:
let the rains, full of water and accompanied by clouds, come toward you both and attend upon you.
When it is the time for rain, then it means "it rains."

Those two who look down from the vast heaven like herds [of cattle], the upholders of cosmic order (*ṛtāvānau*), the sovereign rulers (*samrājau*), established for our delight—7. *adhi* | *yā* | *bṛhataḥ* | *divaḥ* | *abhi* | *yūthā-iva* | *paśyataḥ* | *ṛtāvānā* | *sam-rājā* | *namase* | *hitā* || 7 ||
Just as Mitra and Varuṇa look down from the great, shining heavens upon the gods;
therein is the illustration: "like herds."
Just as a bull looks toward the herds of cows to sport with them, so too do these two look upon the gods to gladden them, having slain the Asuras by their own prowess—this is the meaning.
Of what nature are they? They are *ṛtāvānā*, possessors of truth; *samnājā*, well-shining; and *namase*, for the sake of the oblation, *hitā*, beneficial or dear—look upon them thus.
The two possessors of truth, of noble will, have sat down for sovereign rule;
the two Kṣatriyas of firm vows have attained dominion.
1. *ga*-samya-prājāmānau;
2. *gha*-mitrāvaruṇā, [i.e.,] Mitra and Varuṇa; 3. *ga*-balenotpā°; *tara*-balotpā°; *bha*-śabalavatotpā°.
4. Support the dwellings, the habitations.
5. [It is] from the root *kṣi* (to destroy).

6. O you two, Ga and Ya, you have firmly established (*saṃ yemathuḥ*) the gifts, the riches to be given; you both bestow perfectly the celestial and terrestrial refreshments—the foods of heaven and earth. May the rain-clouds, full of water, come and attend upon you.

The two seekers of Truth, of noble intellect, have sat down for sovereign rule; the two of firm vows, the Kṣatriyas, have attained dominion. (8) The two possessors of Truth, the two truthful ones, of noble intellect—meaning those of beautiful deeds or excellent wisdom—Mitra and Varuṇa, have sat down for the sake of sovereign rule. Thus says the mantra: "Varuṇa, of firm vows and noble intellect, has sat down upon the waters for sovereign rule" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.25.10). The two of firm vows, whose actions are steadfast, the two Kṣatriyas, the powerful ones, have attained *kṣatra*—that is, they have pervaded power. (9) Even before the eye, the two finders of the path, with their far-reaching vision, though closing their eyes, have perceived clearly; the two keen-sighted ones have beheld. (9) Even before the eye, the two finders of the path—meaning those who know the way exceedingly well—with their far-reaching vision, though closing their eyes, the two keen-sighted ones have perceived. (9) Even before the eye, the two finders of the path—meaning those who know the way exceedingly well—[with their far-reaching vision... [Note: The provided text fragment for verse 9 ends abruptly.]

The first half-verse is composed in the indirect (parokṣakṛta) mode. Being unharmed—because we are protected—we remain unoppressed by anyone; thus, for the sake of Viṣṇu, the one who bestows excellent gifts (*sudānu*) and is the benefactor of both the singers and the sacrificers, we offer praise with a loud call to that all-pervading deity named Viṣṇu. Now follows the direct (pratyakṣa) mode.
He is *svayāvān*:
he who goes by himself, alone, to heaven or to battle, is *svayāvān*.
O Viṣṇu, you who are accustomed to sending wealth toward your praisers, O Sindhu, for the sake of first thought!
"Intelligence is action," for it is heard likewise in another mantra: "She, by her insights, indeed made the mortal [immortal]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.29).
O you who were previously engaged for the sake of the sacrificer's commenced rite, listen to that end; hear the praise being performed by us.

We choose that most excellent, desirable thing worthy of protection, which Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman guard. (13) That desirable thing we choose; the most excellent, worthy of being guarded—whatever Mitra guards, whatever Varuṇa, and whatever Aryaman. (13)

We choose—that is, we partake of—that wealth which is most excellent, most expansive, worthy of being guarded, the protector of all, that which is to be protected by the self-controlled, desirable, and worthy of praise by all.
That wealth which Mitra—the friend of all—Varuṇa—the warder-off of enemies—and Aryaman—the one who moves everywhere, the deity so named—protect and preserve;
that wealth we choose.
The meaning is that they are the protectors of our wealth.

And may Sindhu, the lord of waters, grant us that; so too the Maruts, the Aśvins, Indra, and Viṣṇu—those who are bountiful and full of vigor. 14. And may Sindhu, the lord of waters, grant us that; so too the Maruts, the Aśvins, Indra, and Viṣṇu—those who are bounteous and full of vigor. 14.
Furthermore, he prays specifically for the protection of wealth:
"Moreover, may Parjanya, the flowing river of waters, protect that wealth of ours;
and may the Maruts likewise guard it."
May the Aśvins—the two gods—protect that wealth.
Likewise, may Indra and Viṣṇu, who are bounteous bestowers of desires, and all these gods, being united and full of joy, protect our wealth.
The meaning is that these gods, having bestowed wealth upon us, shall guard it.

For those impetuous heroes indeed strike down the hostility of even an active man, as a fierce torrent [sweeps away] its banks. 15. For those, indeed, O impetuous ones, the heroes, strike back against the adversary, even of one who is active, just as a sharp torrent [strikes the bank]. 15.

The *vunuṣaḥ*—the desirable, those worthy of being honored, the leaders (*naraḥ*)—for they indeed, O gods, being impetuous (*bhūrṇayaḥ*) and swift-moving (*kṣipra-gamanāḥ*), strike down the arrogance (*abhimātim*) of any and every enemy; that is, they destroy it in a hostile manner.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as sharp (*tigmam*) water moving with speed uproots a tree standing before it, even so do they strike down that arrogance. This is the meaning.

This one, the lord of the people, thus looks upon many things; we follow his ordinances according to your will. 16. This one, the lord of the people, thus looks upon many things; we follow his ordinances according to your will. 16.
1. *na-śa-ariṣyanto māhataḥ*; *bha1-2-ariṣyanto mahataḥ*. 2. *jha-ya-sarvaiḥ*; *bha2-stavaiḥ*.
He speaks of the deeds of Mitra.
The lord of the people (*viṣpati*), one of these two [deities], this Mitra, having beheld many and vast objects, gazes thus with his own splendor;
we follow— that is, we perform— the sacred laws (*vratāni*) and deeds of that Mitra for your sake.
We follow the ancient, familiar ordinances of universal sovereignty; we observe the long-renowned laws of Mitra and Varuṇa.

Of *sāmrājya*: the state of being a sovereign (*samrāj*) is *sāmrājya*. One who possesses *sāmrājya* is *sāmrājyaḥ*; the suffix *ac* is applied here according to the rule "from *arśas-* and so forth. Of Varuṇa, who possesses sovereignty, we [sing] his ancient *okyā*: *okaḥ* means a dwelling or home; the deeds beneficial to that [dwelling]. We...

That [splendor], O Sūrya, I invoke both heaven and earth at evening and at dawn; always rise up toward us among the liberal givers. (21) O Sūrya, that splendor of yours which belongs to Varuṇa and Mitra—[I invoke] both heaven and earth (*ubhe rodasī*) and both night and day (*doṣā vastauḥ*). By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the accusative case-ending is elided; by the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*, the accusative is used for time and distance. At night and during the day, I praise you. Being thus praised, O Varuṇa, rise up toward us among the liberal givers (*bhojeṣu*); always move toward us. The meaning is: "Among these givers, make us the foremost recipients of their gifts."

We have obtained a straight-moving, silver-colored, harnessed chariot from Suṣāman, the son of Varuṇāna, at Ukṣaṇyāyana’s [gift]. (22) *ṛjram*, *ukṣaṇyāyane*, *rajatam*, *harayāṇe*, *ratham*, *yuktam*, *asanāma*, *suṣāmaṇi*. (22) Varuṇāna was the son of Suṣāman and a king. When he gave a gift to Viśvamanas, the seer Viśvamanas describes that event with this verse. Regarding *ukṣaṇyāyane*: there was a certain elder brother of Harayāṇa named Ukṣan. The word *ukṣaṇa* denotes his descendant; from that base, the suffix *phak* is added. The *gā* and *chāndasa* rules apply. Even though the rule for vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) would normally apply, it does not take effect here because "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory. In *harayāṇe*, which is the descendant of that [Ukṣan], meaning one whose nature is to seize the life-force and sovereignty of enemies—at such a *suṣāman*. By the term "father" (*pitṛ*), the son is indicated. While the son of Suṣāman, the king Varuṇāna, was giving [the gift], what happened? We have obtained (*asanāma*) a straight-moving (*ṛjram*), silver-colored (*rajatam*)—meaning exceedingly white or resembling silver—and harnessed (*yuktam*) chariot (*ratham*). Through the favor of these [gods] beginning with Mitra, we have become partakers and have received it.

May those two [steeds] of mine, the bestowers of horses, the tawny ones—nay, even the bestowers of those skilled in action, the swift carriers—[be granted]. (23) May those two steeds of mine, the tawny ones among the multitudes of horses, be the "bestowers" (*nitośanā*). The root *toś* signifies the act of harming; thus, they are the extreme tormentors of enemies. And furthermore, may they be the "bestowers" of those skilled in the work of battle, acting as the destroyers of their own [enemies'] skill. May those two "swift carriers" (*nuvāhasā*), the bearers of men who lead the weapons, be quickly given to me by Varuṇa and Sūṣāmaṇ. (23) The Seer is Pratigṛhītāśvavāha. Among the "tawny ones" (*harīṇām*), meaning those of golden-yellow color, and the "multitudes of horses" (*aśvyānām*), they are the "bestowers" (*nitośanā*). The root *toś* has the sense of harming; they are the absolute obstructors of enemies. And also, they are the "bestowers" of those "skilled in action" (*kṛtavyānām*), meaning those proficient in the work of war. They are the "swift carriers" (*nuvāhasā*), the bearers of men who carry weapons. May those two horses be quickly given to me by Varuṇa and Sūṣāmaṇ. (23)

With reins held fast, equipped with whips, the two wise ones—possessing great strength and speed—have been harnessed together by my newest hymn. (24) "With reins held fast" (*smadabhīśū*): *smat* means "well-held"; the elision of the vowel *u* is a Vedic archaism. It means "yoked with beautiful reins," or alternatively, "possessing beautiful bodies. "Equipped with whips" (*kaśāvantā*): meaning "possessing whips. "The two wise ones" (*viprā*): meaning "the two sages," as is fitting for the wise. Just as a wise singer pleases the deity worthy of praise with hymns, so too these two are sources of satisfaction. "Of the great" (*mahaḥ*): belonging to the great Soma-vessel. "Possessing strength" (*vājinau*): meaning "endowed with swiftness. "The two running ones" (*arvantā*): the two horses. "Together" (*sacā*): simultaneously. Now the seer speaks of the two horses as if they were being released from the chariot: "With reins held fast... and so forth. They are joined with beautiful reins—or rather, with beautiful forms—and provided with whips. They are the two "wise ones" (*viprā*), fit for the intelligent; like a sage who delights the god to be praised through praises, these two likewise bring delight. Belonging to the "great" (*mahaḥ*) vessel of Soma, they are the two "possessors of strength" (*vājinau*), swift in their movement, the two "running ones" (*arvantā*), the two steeds, harnessed "together" (*sacā*).
1. The faults of *kha*, *ta*, *2*, *3*, *4*, *na*, *bha*, *1*, *2*, and *doṣāṃ*; the faults of *gha* and *śa* in the state (*avasthau*).
2. In the state (*'vastau*) of *kha*, *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, there is none.
3. Of the gods such as *na*, *bha*, Mitra, and others.
4. *bha*-pragṛhītā.
5. *kha-ta-na-bha* read "possessing the beauty of their own excellent bodies"; *śa* reads "possessing excellent beauty.
Praising Mitra and the others simultaneously with a most new, that is, a very recent, *matī*, that is, a thought or hymn of praise, [he attained] *asanam*.
"I, Viśvamanas, have shared [it] out"; the meaning is "I accepted."

The sixth hymn consists of twenty-five verses beginning with "yuvoru ṣū. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "'yuvoḥ'—consisting of five more [than twenty]; Vyaśva Āṅgirasa is the seer; it is dedicated to the Aśvins. From the twentieth verse onwards, however, they are dedicated to Vāyu. The first four are Gāyatrīs; the others are Triṣṭubhs; the twenty-first and twenty-second are also Triṣṭubhs; and the last is an Anuṣṭubh. The seer is Vyaśva Āṅgirasa, or Vaiśva Viśvamanas.

The sixteenth verse is an *aśastra* (without a *śastra* recitation); the first twenty verses are *gāyatrīs*, and the twenty-first and twenty-fifth are also *gāyatrīs*. The remaining verses are *uṣṇih*s as before.
The deities are the Aśvins.
The five verses beginning with the twentieth have Vāyu as their deity.
In the Prātaranuvāka of the Āśvina Śastra, within the Auṣṇiha metre, there are fifteen verses beginning with the Āśvina Śastra.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Auṣṇiha [section] consists of fifteen verses beginning with 'yuvoru ṣū rathaṃ huve'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).
O Aśvins, let your most swift chariot come hither; O heroes, it is renowned. Come to the hymns of the zealous one for the sake of glory. 4.
O heroes, leaders of all, O Aśvins—may your most excellent, most swift, renowned, and far-famed chariot come toward our sacrifice.

Having arrived by that chariot, you two behold—that is, you perceive through knowledge—the hymns (*stomān*) of that Turu who quickly performs praise, such as the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and other *stomas*, for the sake of his glory, which is to bestow sovereignty upon him. The root *paś* signifies the act of knowing; thus, "behold" means "know."
In the case of *dṛś* with the suffix *laṭ*, there is the substitution of *āṭ* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

O Aśvins, possessors of rain-like wealth, even though you are far away, take heed; for you, O Rudras, shall carry us across our enemies. 5. Even though you are far away, O Aśvins, take heed, O possessors of rain-like wealth; for you, O Rudras, shall carry us across our enemies. 5.

O Aśvins, possessors of rain-giving wealth (*vṛṣaṇvasū*), you who are of a raining nature and endowed with riches, even though you are *juhurāṇā*—the root *hurch* meaning "to be crooked" (*kauṭilye*).
The suffix *anac* is applied according to Ṛgveda-Prātiśākhya 2.248: *duhaḥ sano luk chalopaśca*.

O Rudras, you two Aśvins— those who are prone to weeping or who cry out in battle— you should recognize, that is, know, even those crooked enemies who create obstacles to one's actions through deceit;
"hi" is used for emphasis.
"O you two, cross over—meaning, overcome and afflict—those enemies who cause hatred; that is, destroy them. The root *pṛ* belongs to the Bhvādi class, meaning 'to injure' and 'to afflict'."

For you two, O Dastras, quickly rend everything in succession with your swift [powers], O inspirers of the intellect, honey-colored lords of splendor. 6. O Dastras, indeed, you two rend everything continuously and swiftly; O inspirers of the prayer, honey-hued, lords of beauty. 6.
The *dastrā* are those who destroy; they are worthy of being seen by all. Alternatively, [the root] *dasu* means "to perish."
The Aśvins are the destroyers of enemies; of what sort are they? They are "dhiyaṃjinvau," those who invigorate the intellect.
The root *dhav* has the sense of "pleasing.

[The term] *madhuvr̥ṣaṇau* means "pleasing in action" (*karmaṇi prīṇayantau*), [and] *madhuvārṇau* means "having honey-colored forms," that is, possessing bodies and splendors that have the nature of delighting everyone.
The meaning is that those who behold your form become delighted right there.

O you two such lords of auspiciousness (*śubhaspati*), protectors of the waters, such as you are, with your swift-moving horses, come in rapid succession so that it may be continuous; [come] toward our sacrifice alone, which is pervaded by all the offerings mixed together— *hi* being used for emphasis— you two open wide [the way] toward it.
His activity is to move with radiance;
come from all sides!

Come to us, O Aśvins, together with wealth that sustains all people, O bounteous lords, rich in heroes, and unshakable. 7. Come to us, O Aśvins, together with wealth that sustains all people, O bounteous lords, rich in heroes, and unshakable. 7.

O Aśvins, you two who possess all nourishment (*viśvapuṣ*), come to our sacrifice together with wealth (*rāyas*). The sense is: having arrived at the sacrifice, bestow wealth upon us. To the question, "What wealth do these two possess? he says:
The two *maghavantau*— possessors of great wealth (*mahanīyadhanavantau*)— are the two *suvīrau*, endowed with excellent capability;
or alternatively, *vīrāḥ* refers to capable enemies.
Therefore, go!
Nevertheless, you two shall not be made to fall from the forest by them, nor are you to be caused to fall;
you two shall return to the sacrifice.
Come hither to this our offering, O Nāsatyas;
come to us today with your help, O gods most glorious among the gods.
O Indra and Nāsatyas, O gods among gods, come now to this my offering, you who are most worthy of praise. 8.
He [is] Indra, the Nāsatyas, Indra, and the Aśvins, most worthy of being associated with.
[The root] *vac* means "to join together. By the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
"You two, who are to be approached with great intensity by all [beings] as they gather together and serve you—
[the word *pratīvyam* is derived from the root *vī*, meaning 'to go' and so forth;
the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the *uṇādi* rules]."
The prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Since the gods consume the oblations here again and again, it is called *pratīvy-ijya*.
That [sacrifice] belongs to him who stands before [the altar].
Come today to my sacrifice, which belongs to me, together with the gods;
or rather,
come toward it with favor, so that you may be present for the sake of this hymn being performed by me.
For we indeed invoke you two, like Vyaśva, seeking to cause [you] to grow;
come hither with your favors, O you who are rich in wisdom.
For we indeed invoke you two, like Vyaśva, nourishing you with our hymns; come hither with your benevolences, O you who are distinct in power. 9.
"Sprinkling" means bestowing wealth and other blessings; "desiring for ourselves" means we desire [these things].
For we indeed invoke you two alone as the spreaders of wealth and other such gifts; we call upon you for the sake of obtaining them.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like Vyaśva—
just as our father obtained wealth by praising you both, so too [may we obtain it].
O wise Aśvins, together with our *sumatibhiḥ*— the auspicious hymns being performed by us.
Or rather:
together with those of good mind— that is, with those possessing auspicious, benevolent intentions— come hither, come near on this day of sacrifice.
O seer, praise the Aśvins; will they not hear your call?
They will surely drive away the Paṇis who dwell closer than the banks of the river.
O Aśvins, O sage, praise them well! Will they not hear your call? They will surely drive away the Paṇis who dwell closer than even the furthest banks. 10.

O seer Viśvamanas! Praise the two Aśvins, the gods; praise them beautifully. Then may those two Aśvins, having heard your invocation many times—*kuvid* being a word for "much"—listen to your call. Thus praised by you, may the two Aśvins destroy (*kūḷayātaḥ*) the enemies who are very near. And furthermore, may they destroy the *paṇis*, those Asuras known by that name who remove the disease of fire. [The root] *kuḍi* means "to burn"; the suffix *syan* takes the augment *leṭ-yaṅ*. 27.
O men, hear this from Vainyaśva; may the sons of Vidatha listen to me—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, who are well-pleased.
Of Vainyaśva. Listen, O Heroes! And you two, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, who are well-disposed toward me, acknowledge this my prayer. 11.
May the two leaders, the Aśvins, sons of Vyashva, hear the invocation of Viśvamanas, the son of Vyaśva.
And furthermore, may you two know this my call; may you understand it as coming from me.
Then may Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—the god so named—being in harmony and united, having heard my invocation, bestow upon me wealth and other blessings.
O you who are worthy of praise, of that which is given by the young and brought by the patrons,
bestow great gifts day after day, O showerers of blessings!

O you two who are worthy of praise, [bestow] that which has not been given; O you two who are established in wisdom, [bestow] that which has been brought by the wise; day after day, O showerers of blessings, grant us great gifts! 12.
1. [The syllables] gha-ta-na-bha preceding the present one; jha-ta-ya preceding the sacrifice (yāga); ta-bha-ga preceding the present one.
O *dhiṣṇyā*, O *dhiṣṇyau*, O you two who possess wisdom (*dhiṣaṇā*), who are worthy of praise (*stutya*), O *vṛṣaṇau* (the showerers), O Aśvins, [be joined] with the *sūribhiḥ*.
By the rule "supāṃ supo bhavanti," the third case ending is used for the fourth case.

O You Two, bestow upon the wise singers—that which is given by You both to the praisers—and likewise that wealth and so forth which is brought by You both to the praisers; day after day, grant these to him who, being wise and possessing a discerning mind, performs hymns of praise for You.

He who has turned toward you with sacrifices, like a bride over her garments—those two, being honored, have made him beautiful, O Aśvins. 13. He who [has been] turned toward you by sacrifices, like a bride [adorned] over her garments—honoring [you], they two have made [him] beautiful, O Aśvins. 13.
Now, the first half-verse is composed in the indirect (parokṣa) mode:
that man who is surrounded by *yuvayoḥ*—by you two—with *yajñebhiḥ*, i.e., with sacrifices, acts of worship, or alternatively, with hymns (*gāthā*) directed toward you;
therein is the illustration.

When the bride is covered with a garment placed upon her—when she is thus veiled by another cloth—the Aśvins, providing for him by granting his desires and attending to him, made that man "bright" (śubhre), that is, they endowed him with auspicious wealth;
the meaning is that they made him possessed of riches and the like.
The sense is: "Make him who offers oblations to you both possessed of wealth and other blessings."

Whoever takes heed of you, the most wide-extending protection for men—O Aśvins, come around to provide him with a dwelling, O you who are free from malice! 14. Whoever | of you two | the most wide-extending | takes heed of | the protection for men |—the dwelling | O Aśvins | come around | to [provide], O you who are free from malice. 14.

O Aśvins, that mortal who thoroughly knows—that is, clearly understands—the Soma which is most widely pervasive (*uruvyacastama*) in the dwellings, which is to be protected by you (*nṛpāyya*), and which is to be drunk by you both (*yuvābhyām*)—for him there is protection.
*Vartiḥ* means a dwelling, as it is where one dwells (*vartate*).
[The word] *asmīyu* means "us."
The plural number is used for the sake of honor.
Desiring me, whose mind is directed toward all [the gods], do you two come around; come back to his house for the purpose of drinking the Soma.
He perceives; this is from the root *kit* meaning "to know," with the suffix *bahulac*, and the augment *leṭ*.

O you two who possess excellent, rain-bestowing wealth, come to us with protection that guards our men; like those who destroy the wicked, you have carried the sacrifice forward through our song. 15. To us! Well! O you two of rain-bestowing wealth! Come! Protection! Guarding our men! Like those who strike down the enemy! The sacrifice! You have carried it! By means of our song! 15.

O Aśvins, possessors of rain-like wealth and lords of abundant riches, come well toward us for our sake; come well toward our home for the sake of the Soma that is to be drunk and protected by leaders. Through song—that is, through speech characterized by praise—you two have furthered the sacrifice; you cause the completion of the sacrifice among men.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*Viṣudruh* [is derived from] *druh*, meaning "to desire to harm. A *śara* (arrow) is called *viṣudruh* because it strikes down all enemies.
The meaning is that, just as a hunter leads a deer to a desired location, so too, through praise, you bring the sacrifice to completion despite its deficiency.

In the Prātaranuvāka of the Āśvina Śastra, within the Gāyatrī metre, there are four verses beginning with "avāhiṣṭho vāṃ havānām. This is stated in the Sūtra: "The four verses beginning with 'avāhiṣṭho vāṃ havānām,' and [the verse] 'udīrāthāmā me havam' are in the Gāyatrī metre" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).

May this most excellent hymn among invocations, brought as an envoy, call upon you; O Aśvins, be present for the two of you. 16. Most excellent; for you; among invocations; the hymn; as a messenger; let it call; quickly; for the two of you; be present; O Aśvins. 16.
1. The constellation Gha-varṣa; 2. like a bride (gha-vadhūḥ); 3. with a new flute (bha-navaveṇa); 4. the completion of the sacrifice (ta-bha-yajñaṃ samāpti).

O men, O two heroes, leaders of all, among the invocations of the singers and their hymns, let my praise be the most pervasive (bāhiṣṭhaḥ), reaching you most excellently. Let my praise, acting as a messenger, call upon you.
May this my praise be a source of pleasure to you both.

Whether you rejoice there in the ocean of heaven, or in the home of food, O immortal ones, listen to me! 17. Whether you are there in the ocean of heaven, or you rejoice in the home of nourishment, O immortals, listen indeed to me! 17.

O Aśvins, if you two rejoice— that is, if you take delight— in that ocean, in that place of the waters belonging to *div*, the heavenly world (where *divaḥ* becomes *adaḥ* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*); [then come hither].

Moreover, if you two rejoice in the house of the sacrificer who desires the *iṣ* (sacrificial food), then, O immortal ones—O Aśvins, free from the nature of death—hear my hymn; indeed, hear it. The meaning is:
having heard my hymn alone, may you two rejoice.
Alternatively,
in the case of the animal sacrifice to Vāyu, this verse "O Vāyu, yours... is the *anuvākyā* for the omentum (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The lofty prayer goes forth toward Vāyu; O Vāyu, Lord of the Ṛta... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

O Vāyu, Lord of Truth, wonderful son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ, you have granted us [this]; we choose [you] for ourselves. 21. O Vāyu! O Lord of Truth! O Son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ! O Wonderful One! You have helped us; we choose [you]. 21.
O Lord of Truth, O Lord of the cosmic order, O Lord of sacrifices!
[The suffix] *suk* is added according to the rule "after words meaning 'all' and 'pratipadika', in the sense of longing" (Kāśikā 7.1.51.4).
You are the son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ, the son-in-law of Brahmā.
This story is to be understood through narratives, histories, and the like.
O Vāyu, you whose great and wonderful deeds are manifold, we choose for ourselves your protections (*avāṃrsi*); we partake in them at this animal sacrifice.

We pray to the son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord of wealth; we, possessing pressed Soma, like people seeking glory, pray to Vāyu. 22. Tvaṣṭṛ’s | son-in-law | we | the lord | of wealth | we pray to | possessing pressed [Soma] | Vāyu | for glory | the people || 22 ||

These people—we, these very people—having pressed the Soma, have extracted [the juice] for Vāyu, such as he is: the son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ, the Brahman, the Lord, and the Sovereign of all. We pray for wealth; we beg for riches.
With that which is given by him, may we be possessed of splendor and wealth—this is the sense.
For the Vāyavya [offering], there are two verses beginning with "O Vāyu, come from heaven, auspicious one," which are the second and third [verses].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two beginning with 'O Vāyu, come from heaven, auspicious one'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).

O Vāyu, come from heaven as a bringer of auspiciousness; bring hither the excellence of good horses. Bring upon your chariot the two great, broad-winged steeds. 23. O Vāyu! Come! Auspicious one! From heaven! Bring hither! Well! The excellence of good horses! Bring hither! Great! With the broad-winged pair! Upon the chariot! 23.
O Vāyu, auspicious one of heaven—that is, of the celestial world;
[here the accusative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*].
Come hither, bring about auspiciousness and well-being.

Since you are the support of all luminaries, it is prayed that you, having become their support, establish them in the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). Therefore, you possess sovereignty. A "herd of horses" (*aśvya*) is a collection of horses.
O chariot, carry us well and most excellently; convey us to all directions.

Now, bring forth for them even more capable horses. O great one, you who possess broad wings—that is, you who are joined with two broad flanks—carry the horses upon your own chariot and yoke them for the purpose of slaying the enemy.
For the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu, there are two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), namely: "tvāṃ hi supparastamam" and [the second].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'tvāṃ hi supparastamam'—these two; and 'kuvidaṅga namasā ye vṛdhāsaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

For we call upon you, the most excellent leader, in the contests for men; with magnificence, like a pressing-stone or a horse-backed steed. 24. You. For. Most excellent leader. In the contests for men. We call upon. Like a pressing-stone. Or a horse-backed steed. With magnificence. 24.

O Vāyu, you who possess the most beautiful form—*supma* is a name for "form" (*rūpa*), and *ra* is the suffix denoting possession—possessing an exceedingly beautiful form; by *maṃhanā*, meaning by your own greatness, [you are] one whose back is like a horse’s back, pervaded on all sides. The word *pṛṣṭha* indicates every limb; the meaning is "one whose entire body is pervaded. You—*hi* is used for emphasis—only you indeed we invoke in the *nṛsadaneṣu*. Since the men (*naraḥ*), the leaders of the sacrifice, the priests, sit here, these sacrifices are called *nṛsadana*. In them, we call upon you. How so? Like the pressing-stone (*grāvāṇam na*). Just as they call upon the pressing-stone with hymns for the purpose of pressing the Soma, even so do we call upon you with hymns.
1. One whose entire body is pervaded by the syllables Kha, Gha, and Śa; 2. one for the purpose of the moon’s extraction from the syllables Ta and Bha.

In the *Śunāsīrīya* sacrifice, the verse "sa tvaṃ no deva" is the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for Vāyu. It is also stated in the Sūtra: "‘sa tvaṃ no deva manaseśānāya... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.20). **sa tvaṃ no deva manasā vāyo mandāno agriyaḥ | kardhi vājān apo dhiyaḥ || 25 ||** O God, O Vāyu, shining one—or rather, you who are worthy of praise—you are the foremost leader among the gods. Being such, and being exhilarated by our mind, rejoicing of your own accord, grant us food (*vājān*), waters (*apaḥ*) through the piercing of clouds, and mental insights (*dhiyaḥ*) when both are bestowed upon us. That is to say, perform the rites of the Agnihotra and other ceremonies. The seventh hymn consists of twenty-one verses beginning with "agnir ukthe. The index (*Anukramaṇikā*) states: "‘agnir ukthe’: there are two more [verses]; Manu Vaivasvata [is the seer]; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas, and it is in the *Pragātha* meter. The seer is Manu, the son of Vivasvat. The first, third, and other odd-numbered verses are *Bṛhatīs*, while the second, fourth, and other even-numbered verses are *Satobṛhatīs*. The deities of these four initial hymns are the Viśvedevas. The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn is indicated by its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*). **agnir ukthe purohito grāvāṇo barhir adhvara | ṛcā yāmi maruto brahmaṇaspatiṃ devān avo vareṇyam || 1 ||** Manu makes his request: In this sacrifice (*adhvara*) consisting of hymns and recitations, free from violence, Agni has been placed as the priest (*purohita*) at the front upon the northern altar. Likewise, the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) have been placed in front for the purpose of pressing the Soma, and the sacrificial grass (*barhiḥ*) has been spread out in front. Thus, all being prepared, I, Manu, with a verse in the form of a hymn, seek—meaning I pray for—the protection (*avaḥ*) that is desirable and worthy of worship from the Maruts (the forty-nine hosts), Brahmaṇaspati (the god named so, the protector of the hymn), and the gods (Indra and others). The form *yāmi* is the present tense of the root *yā* (to go/seek); the loss of the nasal is a Vedic archaism. **ā paśuṃ gāsi pṛthivīṃ vanaspatīn upāsā naktamoṣadhīḥ | viśve ca no vasavo viśvavedaso dhīnāṃ bhūta prāvitāraḥ || 2 ||** By the first half-verse, Agni is addressed because of the presence of the word "ā" (come). O Agni, come toward the animal (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni-Soma in our sacrifice. [The root] *gā* means "to go"; here it is used in the Parasmaipada by metrical license. Likewise, come toward this seat of the gods, the earth; toward the trees (*vanaspatīn*) used as tools for churning; toward the dawn (*upāsā*) as the time for offering; toward the night (*naktaṃ*) as the time for sacrificing; and toward the plants (*oṣadhīḥ*). [The root] *uṣ* here means "to delight. *Oṣaḥ* is Soma, that which delights; those in whom it is placed are the *oṣadhayaḥ*. Come toward them. Or, *oṣadhyaḥ* refers to creepers that end with the ripening of fruit; come toward them. Alternatively, O singer, [come toward] the animals and so forth. 1. bha-saṃbhajanīyaṃ | 2. kha-tan-tī ca; śa-gamlṛ | 3. ta-bha-upasā |
Sing forth from all sides; praise!
The verbal root is *gai* (to sing) in the sense of "sound.
Therefore, O Vasus—those who cause to dwell—O Viśvedevas, possessors of all wealth or all knowledge, you who are all indeed the gods, become the protectors (*prāvitāraḥ*) of our ritual acts.
Together with this [Agni], may you be excellent protectors.
Let this most excellent one go forth for us among the gods as the ancient one—
among the Ādityas, among the Maruts who shine everywhere, and among the Varuṇas who uphold their vows.
May our sacrifice proceed well toward the immortals among the gods, foremost among the Ādityas, toward Varuṇa of steadfast vows, and toward the Maruts who shine with universal splendor. 3.
"Pūrvya" means ancient or primordial.
Because it is performed for the sake of the ancient gods such as Indra and others, the sacrifice (yajña) is also called "pūrvya.
Such a primary sacrifice, our own (naḥ), is the "adhvara. It is immortal (amrā).
The substitution of *ḍā* for the locative case ending is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[The forms] *amrau*.
Because Agni is the foremost among the gods, he is mentioned first.
In that [sacrifice], while all other gods are bowed down, let it proceed most excellently; let it go forth with pre-eminence.
He distinguishes the gods:

among the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi such as Indra and others—who possess steadfast action (*dhṛtavrata*), and among Varuṇa, and among the Maruts, who possess rays of light pervading everywhere (*viśvabhānu*), let it proceed.

For all you gods, possessors of all wealth, have indeed become the sustainers of man and the destroyers of enemies. O possessors of all wealth, with your unassailable protections, grant us a secure dwelling.

For all you gods, possessors of all-knowledge, have indeed become the protectors of Manu against the destroyer; O possessors of all-knowledge, with your unassailable guardians, grant us a secure dwelling as our leader. 4.
"Viśvavedasaḥ" means those whose wealth is spread everywhere; that is to say, those possessing abundant riches.
Such are the "riśadasaḥ," the destroyers or the exhausters of the "riśataḥ," the harming enemies. For indeed, all the gods together [act] for Manu.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
"For the increase of Manu" means for his growth;
he offers this prayer: "May they become [benefactors] by bestowing wealth upon the human singer, and may they cause him to prosper."

Then, O all-knowing gods, possessors of all wealth (or omniscient ones), with your unimpaired protections—meaning, protections that are not harmed by others—[grant us] that which is free from the wolf;
"wolf" here means a thief; [grant us that which is] devoid of such.
The meaning is "free from affliction. Grant us—that is, give to us—such a *chardiḥ*, a house;
that is to say, having slain our enemies, cause us to perform our rites within our homes.

The form *yantā* is derived from the root *yam*; the suffix *loṭ* is used, with the elision (*luk*) of the verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*) by Vedic rule (*chāndasa*). There is the substitution of *ta* for that [suffix], and because of this, there is no elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).
Come to us today with one mind, all of you in perfect harmony;
O Maruts, Goddess Aditi, come with our hymn and song to the great dwelling, the home of the waters.
Come to us today with one mind, all of you together in harmony; O Maruts, O Goddess Aditi, come with our hymn and song to this great dwelling, this home. 5.
O all you gods, being of one mind in all hymns, with equal thoughts, and being in harmony with one another, come to us— meaning, come through this song which is to be heard with eager attention—
with that *ṛc* together, on this day of sacrifice, come to us, the sacrificers. Immediately thereafter, O Maruts, O shining goddess, O great one among the gods...
1. Of us who possess the *bhaṃ* [syllable], [of those] dependent on it.
2. Of the actions dependent on the *gha* [syllable].
O Aditi—O Great One endowed with greatness, O Goddess named Aditi, who are not distressed—sit down in our dwelling, in our home, as one worthy of praise.
Due to the difference in sentence structure in the passage beginning with "marutaḥ," there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).
In the subsequent instance, because the preceding vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as non-existent, the following word constitutes the beginning of a sentence, and thus there is no *anighāta*.
O Maruts, come to our dear offerings; O Mitra, come to the oblations that are pleasing to you.
May Indra, Varuṇa, and the Ādityas—the swift heroes—sit upon our sacred grass.

Come toward our dear offerings, O Maruts; come toward the oblations consisting of horses, O Mitra, as you set forth. May Indra, Varuṇa, the swift heroes, and the Ādityas sit down upon our sacred grass.

O Maruts, whatever dear things are yours—whatever horse-like things are dear to you—come toward them without fail; bring our food to us. The meaning is: "Come hither, even though you are not yet yoked. Now, O Mitra—the word "Mitra" here also denotes Varuṇa and the others.

The meaning is: "O gods, Mitra and the others, come to accept each of the oblations (havyāni)—the sacrificial offerings fit for invocation. Come while being praised. [This is derived from] the root *ghā* preceded by *pra*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), with the substitution of *than* according to the rule *tasan-asan-athanāś-ca*.

And having arrived—Indra, Varuṇa, Indra and Varuṇa, the swift ones, the heroes who are leaders hastening for the sake of slaying the enemy in battle, the Ādityas, those sons of Aditi, and the gods such as the Maruts—may they sit down, may they take their seats, may they enter upon our sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which has been spread;
[the absence of the *sīdādeśa* for the root *sad* is a Vedic anomaly].
We, having spread the sacrificial grass and prepared the offerings, calling upon you in succession with pressed Soma, invoke Varuṇa like Manus, O wise and foremost ones.

We, having trimmed the sacrificial grass, having set forth the offerings, and having pressed the Soma in due order, invoke you, O Varuṇa—just as Manu did of old, we, the foremost, call upon you both. 7.

O Varuṇa, O Varuṇas, O gods, we the priests who have spread the sacrificial grass (vṛktabarhiṣaḥ), having offered the oblation (hitaprayasaḥ)— the term *prayas* meaning that which is to be enjoyed— we invoke you, calling upon you to accept these offerings, so that it may be continuous (ānuṣak) and uninterrupted in our successive rites. Thus, being those who have placed the oblations before you, we call upon you.
Of what kind are they?
Having pressed the Soma (*sutasomāsaḥ*), having offered the first oblations (*idvāgrayaḥ*), and having kindled the foremost fires (*samiddhāgrayaḥ*), we invoke them.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
O lords of men! Just as Manu invoked you in the sacrifice, so [do we].
Come forward, O Maruts and Viṣṇu, with your horses and with Pūṣan through this inspired prayer!
May Indra come first with those who desire to win—the Bull who is celebrated as the slayer of Vṛtra.

Come forward, O Maruts and Viṣṇu, with your horses and Pūṣan, with our own inspired thought! Let Indra come first with those seeking to win booty—he who is praised as the bull, the slayer of Vṛtra. || 8 ||
O Viśvedevas, come forth—approach our ritual with excellence.

O Maruts! O Viṣṇu—the god so named who is pervaded everywhere by his own power! O Aśvins—the two Aśvins! O Pūṣan—he is called Pūṣan because he nourishes the worshippers with wealth and other blessings.
O gods, Marut and the others, who bear these names: O gods, by means of *mākīnayā*—from our word "asmad" [the form is derived] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 4.3.1 (*yuṣmadasmadoḥ*)—[with the variants:

1. in the place of *sadanam*, *kha*, *jha*, and *śa* read *tara-*, *ṭa*, *ṣada-*; *na*, *bha*, and *ni-* read *ṣadan-*; 2. *gha* reads *indrāvaruṇau mitraśca*; 3. *śa* reads *dattāni*; 4. *bha* and *śa* read *mākīnayā māmakīnayā*]. Ka. 3-44.
Thus, [the suffix] *khañ* is applied as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*).
In the singular number, there is the substitution of *mamaka* according to the rule "ekavacane 'tavaka-mamako'";
the elision of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"May you, being praised with the devotion performed by me, come toward us today.
Because there is a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*) regarding the vocatives beginning with "O Maruts," they do not undergo the *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).
Furthermore, let that "Indra," the first—that is, the chief—of the gods, also come hither.
Indra, the bull who sprinkles desires,
is praised— that is, extolled— by the singers who desire that "gain" (sani), meaning acquisition, as the slayer of Vṛtra, the demon who obstructed the waters.
The suffix *liṭ* (perfect tense) in the sense of the object (*karman*) applied to the root *gṛ* "to sound" is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) irregularity.
O guileless gods, grant us a flawless protection, such that no one, O Vasus, shall ever overcome our shelter from within or from without.
O gods, free from malice, grant us a flawless protection, a shelter which no evildoer, O Vasus, shall ever overcome, even when he is close at hand. 9.
"Adruhaḥ" means those who do not deceive the praisers;
or alternatively,
it is derived from the root *duh* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the object (karmaṇi).
They are not to be harmed by enemies.
O gods—Maruts and the other deities—[grant] "acchidram," meaning a flawless or excellent "śarma.
*Śarma* is a dwelling, so called because it wards off (*śrṇāti*) suffering and the like.
"Grant that [protection] to us.

O Vasus—those who cause the enemies to dwell in fear, such as the Maruts and others—whether from afar, from a distant place, or from nearby, from a close place, may some person coming hither never at any time (*nū cit*) violate (*ādharṣati*) our home—that is, do no harm to it. Grant us that house which is desirable (*varūtham*), worthy of being chosen, and worthy of being enjoyed. This is the syntactic connection. Regarding the root *dhṛṣ* (meaning "to overcome"), because it optionally takes the causal suffix (*ṇic*), when the *ṇic* is not present, this is the resulting form (*rūpam*).
For there is kinship among you, O destroyers of enemies; O gods, there is also a bond of friendship.
Proclaim for us [a way] toward former prosperity, and quickly [grant] blessings for our new well-being.
O gods, destroyers of enemies, you possess kinship with us; you possess our friendship. Proclaim for us an ancient path toward prosperity, and swiftly grant us your newest favors for our well-being.
O destroyers of enemies, you who ward off injury, O radiant gods—the Maruts and others—there indeed exists among you a common descent (*sājātyam*), a state of being of the same lineage.
Furthermore, there exists kinship (*āpyam*); *āpi* means a relative.
The state of being that [relationship] is "attainability" (*āpyam*).

Because there is a connection among the praisers through the characteristic of being praised, there indeed exists a state of kinship between you and me, Vaivasvata Manu, as one who praises. Therefore, for the "first-occurring" (*pūrvasmai*), that is, for the first-bestowal of prosperity (*suvitāya*).
That which is well-traversed—that is, well-attained by all—is *suvita*, meaning prosperity.
For that most recent, ever-newer, and newest *sumna* (favor), proclaim it clearly and swiftly for us;
that is to say, bestow upon us the riches of prosperity.
For now indeed I have sent forth this hymn of praise to you, for the enjoyment of your wealth—
O possessors of all knowledge, may I, bowing in reverence, draw near to you as if to a cow.
Now indeed, for the praise of you; now, for the enjoyment of your wealth—O possessors of all knowledge, I, bowing down, have sent forth this [praise] toward you, as if toward another [deity]. 11.
O all-knowing ones, O gods who possess all wealth, I, Manu, desiring food, offer to you this other kind of praise— something that has never been seen before, as it were,
meaning something not performed by anyone else.
Such praise I offer now.

1. [The word *ta-*] is due to the connection with the characteristic of being praised among the praisers; [the word *bha-*] is due to the connection with the characteristic of praising the praisers. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. "Right now" (*idānīm eva*), I "have sent forth" (*upa ā asṛkṣi*)—that is, I send forth or perform. For what purpose? "For you" (*vaḥ*), belonging to you, "of the desirable" (*vāmasya*), that which is worthy of being sought; "right here" (*iha*), right now, "for the sake of devotion" (*bhaktyai*), meaning for the sake of worship or for the sake of obtaining it. *Asṛkṣi* is the form of the root *sṛj* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Because it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *nighāta* (lack of accentuation).
This Savitṛ, the excellent leader, has risen on high for you; he is most worthy of choice. Bipeds and quadrupeds, seeking their goals, have settled down, as have the birds ready to fly.
Om! May that Savitṛ, the excellent leader, stand up for you; he is the one to be chosen. Bipeds and quadrupeds, seeking their goals and eager to fly, have settled down. 12.
They are *supraṇītayaḥ*.
*Supraṇīti* means beautiful praise.

O Maruts, you who possess beautiful leadership and beautiful hymns of praise—among you, he who is upright, ascending, most excellent, desirable by all, and worthy of worship, that god Savitṛ, the impeller of all toward their respective tasks, when he has risen up, exalted by his own splendor, then the bipeds—men endowed with two feet—and the quadrupeds—horses and others endowed with four feet—as well as the winged birds, the flyers, have settled down to their respective duties.
When the sun has risen, some men perform the Agnihotra and other rites, while others offer hymns of praise directed toward the deities;
afterwards, they roam everywhere for the sake of grazing on grass and other fodder.
They entered. After the root *viś* preceded by *ni*, the *luṅ* suffix takes the *parasmaipada* ending by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The augment *ruṭ* is added because of the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [grammatical operations] occur abundantly."
On the fifth day, in the *prauga-śastra*, there is the triplet dedicated to the Viśvedevas beginning with "devadevam.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "devadevaṃ bṛhadu gāyiṣe vacaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.12).
We invoke the God of gods for your protection; we invoke the God of gods for our success;
we invoke the God of gods for the winning of booty, praising him with divine thought.
The god of gods, for your protection; the god of gods, for our desired aid; the god of gods, we shall invoke for the winning of booty, praising him with divine devotion. 13.

We, praising—that is, extolling—with the shining *dhī* (inspired thought) of the Goddess, call upon the God of gods, the radiant deity, for protection—that is, for the preservation of our ritual acts—among you.
He speaks in sequence:
we also call upon the God of gods for the sake of attaining our desired objects (*abhiṣṭaye*).
Therefore, for the sake of winning booty—that is, for the acquisition of food—we shall invoke him; we call upon him.
For all the gods, being of one mind with Manu, have granted their gifts together;
may they today, and may they hereafter, be finders of wide space for our progeny.
For all the gods, being of one mind, have been bounteous together for Manu; may they be so for us today and for the future, and may they be finders of wide space for our progeny. 14.

Being of one mind (*samanyavaḥ*), that is, having a common purpose—or perhaps being endowed with equal wrath for the sake of slaying the enemy in battles—all (*viśve*) these gods (*devāsaḥ*), namely the Maruts and the other deities, indeed (*hi sma*) shall be together (*sākam*) and simultaneously (*yugapat*) with me, the seer named Manu, accompanied by gifts of wealth and the like (*sarātayaḥ*). This is further entreated: may those gods be givers of wealth to us (*naḥ*) today (*adya*), and moreover, on all other days as well—what need is there to say more? May they be so.
Not only for us alone, but also: 1. that which belongs to *gha*;
2. when *na* and *bha* have arisen.
3. We invoke you, O Tābhā.
*Tuce*:
"tu" is a name for offspring.

"Tuji-piji" refers to the dwellings of violence and giving; he "tojayati" (torments) and "hinasti" (destroys) his father’s sorrow and so forth, thus he is called "tuja," a son. May they be "varivovidaḥ"—bestowers of desirable wealth—for "naḥ," our "putrāya," for the son.
I proclaim before you, O guileless ones, this gathering of hymns of praise;
neither deceit nor harm reaches that mortal, O Varuṇa and Mitra, who has honored your divine ordinances.
I proclaim you, O guileless ones, in this assembly of hymns of praise. No harm, O Varuṇa and Mitra, reaches that mortal who has honored your divine ordinances.

I praise you— the Maruts and others who are free from guile (adruhaḥ) or non-injurious (adroghāḥ)— preeminently in this sacrifice which is the assembly (saṃsthe) of those who offer hymns (upastutīnām), for it is performed as their place of enjoyment;
O Varuṇa and Mitra, that mortal man whom Dhūrti—
meaning injury or harm— [assails].
For that man whom harm from enemies does not afflict— he who has honored you according to your *dhāmas*, that is, your splendors;
for *dhāma* is that in which something is placed, namely the body—
from those [splendors] he has offered worship.
The root *vidh* means "to ordain" (*vidhāne*). It ordains—that is, it offers—the oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
By this, it is understood that even the luminaries possess the status of being oblations.
He extends his dwelling and increases great nourishments who offers to you according to your desire.
He is born preeminent through offspring by the Law; unharmed, he prospers in every way.
He extends his dwelling and spreads forth great nourishments—he who offers to you according to your desire. He is procreated through offspring by the Law; unharmed, he prospers with all things. 16.
He—that man—[causes] the Maruts and others [to dwell]; "he" refers to that human being.
"Kṣayam": a dwelling place (*kṣaya*) is a house, because they "dwell" (*kṣiyanti*) or reside therein.
That man "pranirate"—he causes it to increase pre-eminently.
*Tirat* means "to increase.
He alone increases *mahīḥ*, the great things, and *iṣaḥ*, the foods—that man who, for the sake of *varāya*, desirable wealth, offers *vaḥ*, to you, *dāśati*, presents oblations.
The syntactical connection is that he causes [them] to increase through wealth and other such means.
Furthermore, "by means of *dharma*.
That which is maintained by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is *dharma*, meaning ritual action (*karman*).

From that ritual action directed toward you, that man is "born forth" (*pra jāyate*)—that is, he is preeminently manifested—on all sides and in every way "with offspring" (*prajābhiḥ*), such as sons, grandsons, and so forth.
According to the Vedic scripture, "The self, indeed, is the name of the son" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.9.4.26).
Therefore, being *ariṣṭa*—unharmed by others—every person prospers through the offering of oblations to you all, increasing in wealth and other blessings.
Without a fight he obtains [booty]; he travels his paths by easy ways—he whom Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa, acting in concert and with like purpose, protect.
Without fail, he finds booty in battles; he travels his paths by easy ways—Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa, who are bounteous givers—whoever they protect with one accord. || 17 ||
That man, the giver of oblations to Aryaman and the other gods, is a warrior;
[the root] *yudh* means "in combat," with the suffix *kvip* used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
Even without war—that is, even apart from it—he acquires and obtains riches.
Furthermore, together with horses that have "good paths" (sugebhiḥ)—meaning those with beautiful gaits or those that go well—he traverses the roads;
that is to say, the regions to be traveled.

He goes toward—that person whom Aryaman constantly approaches; Mitra, who becomes a friend to the singers and the sacrificers by bestowing wealth; Varuṇa, the restrainer of enemies, or rather, the one who is to be chosen (varaṇīya) and honored. Or [the suffix] -tara-3-na-bha-°mi.
2. Bha: *haviṣpradātā* (the giver of oblations).

3. Kha: *atanan vāñchan*; Na: *atatatvācchan*; Śa: *atastatvācchan*. The connection of the meaning is as follows: those gods called *saratyaḥ*, who are designated by the common name of "givers" (*samānadāna*), being *sajoṣasaḥ*—that is, united with one another—protect and preserve with their own safeguards that giver of oblations (*havyapradātā*) whom they shield; he, [being thus protected], finds wealth and other blessings.
O Agni, even for this man, provide a horse-stealing [booty] and a safe passage even in difficult terrain.
Let this very arrow, failing its mark against him, perish as it strikes his fortresses.

O Agni, you make even this man famous; you provide a safe passage even through difficult terrain. May even that bolt of lightning, which previously pursued him, vanish from him now, never to strike again.

O gods, O Agni, even for this man— though he is not to be overcome by others— you must effect his complete entry into the enemy's fort, which is otherwise invincible. You yourselves must bring it about.
Or rather:
O Agni, proceed on a straight path;
likewise, even on difficult ground that ought not to be traversed, provide an easy passage.
‘Sa’ means in motion.
Perform a beautiful movement ‘ā’ on all sides.
This being so, may this ‘eṣā’ thunderbolt, as a weapon against enemies, quickly ‘nu’ pass ‘paraḥ’, beyond, from this ‘asmāt’ Manu who moves everywhere.
Afterwards, let that thunderbolt, not striking—that is, not harming anyone—perish; let it be destroyed.
When the sun rises, O you who delight in sovereignty, establish the cosmic order;
when at dawn upon awakening, O possessors of all wealth, or when at midday of the sky.

When today the sun rises, O you whose dominion is dear, may you establish the cosmic order (*ṛta*); when at sunset, or at awakening, O you who possess all knowledge; or when at the midday of heaven. || 19 ||

O gods of pleasing power (*priyakṣatrāḥ*), when the sun (*sūrye*), the impeller of all beings toward their respective duties, rises today— on this day— at whatever time you established (*dadha*) the auspicious home (*ṛtam*),
[the form *dadha* being the perfect middle voice plural of the root *dhā*];
at that time, O gods who possess all wealth (*viśvavedasaḥ*), in the act of wiping away [evil] (*nimṛci*).
The root *mṛc* has the sense of "going.
"At the setting of the sun" means at its complete departure; that is to say, in the evening.
"Maintain it at that [time];
or rather, at its awakening—that is, at the time of dawn;
or rather, at midday, in the middle of the day shining with the splendor of the sun of heaven—bestow wealth upon Manu. This is the connection with what follows.
Or when, O Asuras, you uphold the cosmic order (*ṛta*) at the place of rest, granting protection to the donor— O Vasus, possessors of all wealth, may we abide in the midst of that [protection].
