Whether at the close of day, O Asuras, you bestow the light of Truth as a shelter for the donor—may we stand within that protection of yours, O possessors of all knowledge, in the very midst of your dwelling. 20.

O *asuras*—the wise ones, the gods who are the masters of weapons in battle—or rather, when you have arrived at our sacrifice (*abhipitve*), for the one who goes toward the *ṛta*, the sacrifice that has become reality;
the form is from the root *iṇ* in the present participle (*śatṛ*).
For the sacrificing patron (*dāśuṣe*) who has offered the oblations, [grant] protection (*chardiḥ*).
‘Chardiḥ’ [is used] in the senses of ‘shining’ (dīpti) and ‘giving’ (dāna). That by which one shines is *chardiḥ*, namely, splendor (*tejas*).
Or else:

*Chardi* means a house, because they vomit [light] or play therein; that *haṃ* (house) is the brilliance (*tejas*). *Vyema* means "you bestow. If you do so, then we—O *vasavas*, who cover the singers with wealth and the like, or rather, who drive away the enemies—being *viśvavedasas*, possessing all wealth or being all-knowing—[shall be so].

1. After *kha*, *ta*, *na*, and *śa*, it flows; after *ga*, it flows; after *gha*, *bha-ra*, and the third [consonant], it flows; after *bha* (the first), let it flow. 2. After *jha*, *ta* (the second), *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, it perishes of its own accord.
3. *Ga* is vomited up and shines.
O gods, may we dwell— that is, may we abide— within that auspicious house belonging to you, which has been bestowed by you; here, the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
May we worship you with oblations.
In the case of the root *sthā* in the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "the suffix *aṅ* occurs after a root in the benedictive."
Whether today at sunrise, or at its departure, or at midday, or in the evening, you who possess all-knowledge bestow desirable wealth upon the man who offers oblations and is wise. || 21 ||
O all-knowing gods, you whose wealth pervades everywhere: whenever today— at this very moment—
or when the sun has risen,
or when at midday, in the middle of the day.
Or rather, it refers to the *āturci*; the root *āturci* has the meaning of "going.
[It occurs] at the setting of the sun.
The meaning is "in the evening.

To the one who offers oblations into the fire (*juhvānāya*), to that very one who is *pracetase*—possessing preeminent knowledge—to *Manu*, the seer of this name, for me, you bestow (*dhattha*) desirable wealth (*vāmaṃ dhanaṃ*). "We praise that," is the connection with what follows.

We choose that protection of yours, O sovereign ruler, like a son who provides many means of sustenance. May we, O Ādityas, as we offer the oblation, obtain that through which we may attain greater prosperity.

We choose that sovereignty of yours, O Universal Kings, as a son chooses a father who provides much protection. May we, O Ādityas, while offering oblations, attain that through which we may reach greater prosperity. 22.
O *samrājs*, the gods who shine perfectly, we are like your sons— the singular number being Vedic; just as sons are to be nourished by their fathers, so are we to be nourished by you.
May we obtain that wealth of yours which is rich in means and to be enjoyed by many;
by means of that wealth, may we attain a state of greater prosperity, becoming exceedingly wealthy.
In the case of the root *aś*, the suffix *śnam* is applied by way of transposition (vyatyaya) in the *laṅ* tense.
The eighth hymn consists of five verses beginning with "ye triṃśati.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "The [hymn] beginning with 'ye triṃśati' has five verses; the penultimate [verse] is a Pura-uṣṇih. Manu is the seer (ṛṣi).
According to the previously stated *sa-prīya* convention, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī;
the penultimate [verse] is Purauṣṇih;
and as before, the deity (*devatā*) is the Viśvedevas.
In the third *chandoma*, within the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, the hymn beginning with "ye triṃśati" is the *vinidhāna* for the *vaiśvadeva*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *vaiśvadeva* [is performed] with 'ye triṃśati'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.11).
The thirty-three gods who have sat upon the sacrificial grass, they have found the day and have taken their seats.
The thirty-three gods, the highest ones, have sat upon the sacrificial grass; they have found the day and have obtained it in two ways. 1.
Manu said: "Beyond thirty"—that is, after the number thirty—"are three";
the meaning is that there are thirty-three deities.
O gods, may those deities sit upon our sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of accepting the oblation; thereafter, may those gods know us as the givers of the offerings.
Then, in two ways—that is, in a twofold manner—may they grant us wealth, cattle, and so forth.
Or alternatively:
*Dvitā* means "twofold. By this, repetition is indicated;
the meaning is: "Give us wealth and so forth again and again."
Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the Agnis who bestow gifts together— may they, accompanied by their wives and observers of the eternal Law, [protect us].
1. *ga*-tasya; *gha*-dattasya; *bha*-pradattasya | 2. *śa*-sarvatra | 3. *ga-bha*-yadyadā; *gha*-tana-yadvā | 4. *kha-ta-na-bha-ya-śā*-etena | 5. *ga-gha-na-śa-aha*—*atha*:
Varuṇaḥ | Mitraḥ | Aryamā | Smadrātisācaḥ | Agnayaḥ | Patnīvantaḥ | Vaṣaṭkṛtāḥ || 2 ||
Varuṇa is the one to be chosen, the one to be honored.

Mitra is the friend who becomes a benefactor to the singers and the sacrificers by bestowing wealth and other gifts. Aryaman is the deity of that name who either brings wealth to the performer of praise or who moves constantly.
*Smadrātipācaḥ*:

Those who possess a *smat*—that is, an excellent (*su*) and beautiful (*sumat*) gift (*rāti*), namely the offering of oblations (*haviṣ-pradāna*)—are called *smadrātayaḥ*, referring to the sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*).
They are so described because they "accompany" (*sacante*) [the gods] by serving them through the bestowal of wealth and other gifts.
Or alternatively:
they attend upon the givers of oblations in such a way that it becomes auspicious;
such are the *patnīvantaḥ*, accompanied by the wives of the gods.
The fires are those that move about; they are various kinds of fires.
They have been consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ* call and offered with the *svāhā* call by me, beginning with the formula: "O Agni, partake of the Soma, *vauṣaṭ*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
The meaning is "well-sacrificed."
May they be our guardians from the west, from above, and likewise from below; may they protect us from the front with their entire host. || 3 ||
Those gods, Varuṇa and the others;
with all, that is,
with the entire host of followers.
The southern ones; the southern and the western ones. From there, may they be our protectors, our guardians.
These very ones are the waters of the north;
[they are so called] because of the elision of the suffix *at* prescribed in the sense of the ablative by the rule "añjer luk.
May they, moreover, be our protectors.
By the word *itthā*, he indicates the upward direction and the southern direction.
In this manner— that is, by the previously mentioned method— of the upward and southern directions,
may those gods be our protectors.
Likewise, "nyak" means from the downward direction;
here too, as before, there is the elision of the suffix *tasi*.
May they be our protectors even from below.
Furthermore, may those gods from the eastern direction be our protectors.

As the gods desire, so shall it be; no one can thwart that will of theirs—not even a hostile mortal. 4. As the gods desire, so indeed shall it be; no one at all can diminish that [will] of theirs—not even a stingy mortal. 4.
The gods are all shining ones;
"as they wish" means as they desire. [The root] *vaś* [is used] in the sense of longing.
Because of the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca," the substitution of *yaṇ* for the preceding form is optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
Thus, it is exactly as they desire; it is just so, in that manner.
He says that very thing:
No one at all—nothing whatsoever—diminishes or harms this desire of these gods.
[The root] *mīh* means "to harm";
this is a form in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood.
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "mīnāter nigame.
If it is asked how that which is desired by the gods comes to be so, he says:
"arāvā" (the non-giver).
If the gods should desire any man who is a non-giver, then even an enemy—a non-giver—[is acceptable];
*cana* has the sense of "even.
Even such a mortal, a man, when desiring [to worship], offers oblations to the gods.
Therefore, the meaning is that whatever they desire occurs exactly as such.

Of the benevolent ones, there are seven spears; seven are their splendors. They have all assumed glories upon themselves. 5. Of the benevolent ones. Seven. Spears. Seven. Splendors. Of them. All. Upon. Glories. They have assumed. 5.
In this regard, there is an ancient story:
because the embryo of Aditi—who desired a son equal to Indra—was divided into seven parts by Indra for a certain reason, that embryo became composed of seven groups;
from these, the Maruts were produced.
This is based on the Vedic scripture: “The Maruts indeed consist of seven groups” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.11.1).
This narrative was explained in detail within the hymn-group beginning with “This word is spoken for the Father of the Maruts” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.114.6).
And thus, the meaning of this ṛc is as follows.
Of the seven hosts of Maruts, there are seven distinct spears (*ṛṣṭi*), which are specific types of weapons;
likewise, there are seven radiant ornaments such as earrings (*dyumna*),
or *dyumna* may mean foods.
The readings of these groups are as follows:
1. Ga₁—*adhastādapya°*; Ga₂—*atasyādepya°*; Ta-Bha—*adhastādepya°*. 2. Gha—*āminat*. 3. Ga—*eṣorthaḥ*.
Then those hosts of Maruts, each with their respective forms and all their various splendors, took up [their positions] together, surpassing one another in excellence.

The ninth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “babhru-rekaḥ,” has Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, or Manu Vaivasvata as its seer. Thus it is enumerated: “Babhru-daśa: Kaśyapa or the son of Marīci; two pādas.”
The *dvipadā* verses consist of ten feet of twenty syllables each;
their deity is the Viśvedevas, as before.
In the third *Chandoma*, during the *vaiśvadeva-śastra*, the *dvaipada* hymn should be recited immediately prior to the *vaiśvadeva-sūkta*.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: “The two-footed hymns beginning with ‘Babhru ekaḥ’ are placed before the Vaiśvadeva hymns” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).
[The verses are: “Babhru is the one, Viṣṇu, the noble, the youthful; he holds the golden [disk] in his arm.”
Tawny-hued, alone, Viṣṇu, the noble man, the youth—on his body he anoints himself with gold. 1.
In this [section] of ten verses, there are separate deities for some of the words due to their indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Here, in the first verse, Soma is denoted by the word *babhru* ("tawny"),
as seen in such passages as "One should offer a tawny animal to Soma" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.1.3.3).

*Babhru* means brown-colored; it refers to one who is fully matured in qualities such as variegatedness (*śabalatā*). Alternatively, [it derives from] the root *ḍubhṛñ*, meaning "to sustain" or "to nourish."
The suffix *ku* is applied according to *Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.22, *kupraśca*.
When the moon has risen with all its nectar-filled rays, the alleviations of suffering are indeed nourished.
Such is *Viṣṇu*, the one who pervades the world (*viśvagandhana*), the *sūnara*, the excellent leader of the nights.
The nights are indeed led by the moon.

Such a youth—the singular god Soma—is young because he manifests day after day. He [adorns himself with] an *aṅki*, that is, an ornament; for an *aṅki* is so called because it is manifested or made visible by it. This [ornament] is golden (*hiraṇyaya*), meaning made of gold.
The means of manifestation—such as earrings, crowns, and so forth—adorns and makes manifest one's own body.
One [Agni], the radiant and wise, has taken his seat within the womb among the gods.
The one, the radiant, the wise, has sat within the womb among the gods. 2.
In this context, the word *yonim* is used [in the accusative] by virtue of its grammatical gender (*liṅga*),
as it is observed in such passages as "to Agni Gṛhapati.
Among the gods— that is, in the midst of the gods— he is *dyotanaḥ*, shining with his own splendor, and *medhiraḥ*, wise.
Alternatively, he is "endowed with wisdom" (*medhāyukta*) because he bestows wisdom upon the worshippers who desire it.

Such a one, the *unique* (*eka*) Agni, has "settled" (*ā sasāda*) in his "womb" (*yoni*), that is, in the Āhavanīya and other fire-places which serve as his abode, for the purpose of accepting the oblations.
He holds an axe of iron in his hand, steadfast among the gods.
One, steadfast among the gods, bears an iron axe in his hands within the divine assembly.

"Among the gods," that is, shining in the midst of the gods; "steadfast" (*nidhruvi*), meaning existing in an immovable place. Or alternatively, "steadfast" means "possessing constant movement," that is, moving perpetually.
Alternatively, he is one who possesses exceptional steadfastness in battles before his enemies;
such a "one" is the god named Tvaṣṭṛ, [who fashioned] the "āyasīm," made of iron, "vāśīm.
[The root] *vāś* means "to sound."
A *vāśī* is an axe, an instrument for carving, so called because it "makes sound" (*śabdayati*) or "causes enemies to cry out" (*ākrandayati*).
He bears—that is, holds—that [axe] in his own hand.
He bears a single vajra placed in his hand; with it, he strikes down the Vṛtras.
He alone bears the thunderbolt placed in his hands; with it, he strikes down the Vṛtras.
In this context, Indra is the deity because of the vajra-linga.

The singular Indra bears—that is, holds—the *vajra*, the weapon so named, which was placed within his own hand. That very Indra, by means of that placed *vajra*, violently strikes down (*jighnate*) the *vṛtras*—the obstructing demons or evils.

1. *gha-ta-na-bha* are held [as the *dhruvā*]. 2. This [is used] in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*; and it is stated in the *sūtra*: "The hymns consisting of two-footed verses begin with *imā nu kaḥ*, *babhruḥ*, and *ekaḥ*. 3. *śa* refers to ornaments such as earrings, golden crowns, and so forth. 4. *ta-bha* refers to that which is shining. 5. *kha-ta-na-bha*—in this manner, [the first and second *dhruvās* are formed].

One alone bears a sharp weapon in his hand—pure, fierce, and possessing healing medicine that soothes. (5) *Tiṅgam*, *ekaḥ*, *bibharti*, *haste*, *āyudham*, *śuciḥ*, *ugraḥ*, *jalāṣabheṣajaḥ*. (5) In this context, by the term *jalāṣabheṣajaḥ*, Rudra is designated. *Śuciḥ*: from the root *śuc* meaning "to shine"; blazing everywhere with his own splendor. Or alternatively, from *śuc* meaning "to grieve"; the one who causes grief and suffering to his enemies. For this very reason, he is *ugraḥ*, possessed of exalted power, and *jalāṣabheṣajaḥ*, the possessor of healing medicine that brings happiness by removing disease. Or alternatively, he is the one whose form is the physician (*bhiṣaj*) who brings happiness by cutting away the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for his worshippers. His status as a physician is heard in such Vedic texts as, "The first divine physician," and so forth. Such a one, the sole Rudra, bears a *tigma*—sharp-edged—*āyudham*. An *āyudha* is that by which one fights or strikes at enemies; it is the *pināka* bow.

*Sarpirāsutī*: because *sarpiḥ* (clarified butter) and *ghṛtam* (ghee) were pressed out (*āsūyata*) from these two, they are called *sarpirāsutī*. [The two] who have ghee as their oblation, Mitra and Varuṇa, "sat" (*asadaḥ*) in heaven, in the world of light. A *sadaḥ* is a place where one sits; that [place] they "made" (*cakrāte*), they performed.
Some sang the great Sāman; through it, they caused the sun to shine.
Chanting, some have conceived the great Sāman; by it they caused the sun to shine. 10.

"The Atris, some of them, 'conceived'—that is, they understood—the 'great,' that is, the vast Sāman consisting of the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, and other stomas. Praising—that is, honoring—that very [Sāman], those Atris, by means of that Sāman thus spoken, 'kindled the Sun.
They themselves are the deities here."
The tenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "nahi vaḥ," has the following meters:
the first is Gāyatrī, the second Purauṣṇih, the third Bṛhatī, and the fourth Anuṣṭubh.
Manu Vaivasvata is the seer (ṛṣi).
As before, the Viśvedevas are the deities; thus it has been enumerated: "Nahi vaḥ śrutam... ending in Purauṣṇih, Bṛhatī, and Anuṣṭubh.
The application (viniyoga), however, is understood from the indicative mark (liṅga).
"And may you become possessors of wealth and other riches. Furthermore, O gods, from Manu—
Manu being the father of all.
Therefore, do not lead us away from that path—the way which Manu, the father, fashioned from the place where he came; do not remove us from that path.
The meaning is: do not take us away.
Always lead us along that very path by which [the sages] proceed, namely, the path of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), and so forth.
But since there is a distant path far removed from this, lead us beyond it— that is, further away from it.
O all you gods who are here, and you Vaiśvānaras as well,
grant us wide-reaching protection for our cattle and our horses.
O gods who are here, you all, belonging to all men, grant us wide protection for our cattle and our horses. 4.

O gods, you deities; and furthermore, O Vaiśvānaras— the sacrifice is called Vaiśvānara because its "all men" (viśve naraḥ), namely all the leaders of the ritual such as the Adhvaryu and others, belong to it.
The forms "bhavāḥ" have appeared in order to accept the oblations, such as Soma and others, in that [sacrifice]. The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-arthe*).
Alternatively:

Agni is Viśvānara because he is the mouth of the gods; [the word] belongs to him. O all you gods, whatever you are, stay here at this our sacrifice to take the oblations; therefore, be far-reaching (saprathas).

The root *prath* means "to become manifest. *Śarma* is that which is well-known everywhere or extended everywhere; it is called *śarma* because it consumes (*śrṇāti*) or destroys all suffering—namely, happiness.
Grant that to us;
likewise, bestow protection—happiness—upon our cows, which are the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, and upon the horse.
In the fifth section (anuvāka), there are twelve hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the hymn beginning with "yo yajāti," consisting of eighteen verses, is the first hymn.
Vaivasvata Manu is the seer (ṛṣi).
The ninth and fourteenth [verses] are *anuṣṭubh*s; the remaining four, beginning with the fifteenth, are *paṅkti*s.
The tenth is a *pādanicṛt*, according to its definition: "Three [feet] consisting of six syllables each is a *pādanicṛt*" (*Anuvāka* 4.4).
The remaining eleven [verses] are *gāyatrīs* according to the previously stated definition.
In the first four, the sacrifice and then the praise of the sacrificer are heard;
therefore, they have those as their deities.
In the five [verses] beginning with "yā daṃpatī," the husband and wife are praised; therefore, they are the deities of those [verses].
In the remaining nine [verses], blessings for the husband and wife are set forth;
therefore, they alone are the deities.

And thus it is enumerated: "He who sacrifices... [the praise of the sacrificer]... these five [verses] beginning with 'ya' are for the husband and wife; the remaining [verses] are their blessings; [the first] nine are Anuṣṭubhs ending in Catuṣpaṅkti, and the tenth is a Pādanichṛt Anuṣṭubh."
Whoever sacrifices, causes others to sacrifice, presses the Soma, and cooks the oblation—
may he find pleasure in the Brahman of Indra.
Whoever sacrifices, sacrifices, or shall sacrifice; whoever presses the soma and cooks the oblation—that Brahmin alone shall find favor with Indra.

The sacrificer who performs the sacrifice once— worshipping the gods with oblations— having obtained wealth and other blessings from the gods, indeed sacrifices again, offering oblations to the gods for the attainment of his further desires; likewise, that same sacrificer presses the Soma and also cooks the animal-offerings, the sacrificial cakes, and so forth.
In all instances such as *yajati* and the like, there is the augment *aṭ* in the *leṭ* mood. That sacrificer [is] "of Indra" the "brahmans"—that is, the sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*).
"It" (*it*) is used for emphasis.
He repeatedly desires (cākanat) the hymns related to Indra;
from the root *kan*, meaning "to shine," the form is derived with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, where the reduplication is Vedic;
thereafter, the augment *aṭ* is added in the *leṭ* mood.
In this sacrifice, the sacrificer obtains wealth and so forth; this is the praise of the sacrifice.
That very sacrifice, being one that yields visible results, leads the sacrificer to perform the pressing of the Soma and other rites; this is the praise of the sacrificer.

1. *ga*—from afar; *gha*—let [it] flow from afar; *ta-na-bha*—from afar. 2. *bha*—"all" is not present. 3. *kha-ta-na*—the characteristic of *tala*; *bha-śa*—the characteristic of *tala*. 4. *ga-ta-na*—is praised. 5. *ga-ta-na-bha-śa*—the remaining final ones. 6. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa*—wealth and so forth. He who offers to him the sacrificial cake (*puroḷāśa*) and the pressed Soma with milk-mixture (*āśira*), him indeed Śakra shall deliver from distress. *puroḷāśam* | *yaḥ* | *asmai* | *somam* | *rarate* | *āśiram* | *pāt* | *it* | *tam* | *śakraḥ* | *aṃhasaḥ* || 2 || The sacrificial cake. He. To him. Soma. Offers. With milk-mixture. May he drink. Indeed. Him. Śakra. From distress. || 2 ||

The sacrificer who offers (*rarate*)—that is, bestows—to this Indra the animal-cake (*paśupuroḷāśa*) as well as the *āśira* (the mixture of Soma with milk) at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), [namely] the Soma mixed with cow’s milk; [the form *rarate* is derived from the root *rāti* in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the elision of *śap*, and the addition of the augment *aṭ*]: that capable (*śakra*) and powerful Indra shall protect (*pāt*) that sacrificer from distress (*aṃhas*), or from such a demon (*rakṣas*). The particle *it* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*): "he surely protects" (*apādeva*); he indeed protects. [The form *pāt* is the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *pāti*.]

His radiant chariot, impelled by the gods, has come forth; may he hear us and drive away all hostile powers. 3. His radiant chariot, impelled by the gods, has come forth; may he hear us and drive away all hostile powers. 3.

For that sacrificer who worships the gods, there comes—impelled by the gods such as Indra, radiant, and swift-moving—a chariot; through the sacrifice consisting of the offering of oblations to the gods, it exists, that is, it arrives. Then, by means of that chariot, he overcomes all hostile oppressions caused by enemies;
for Yāska states that the root *van* has the sense of "injuring."
By harming [the enemy], he indeed hears [of his success] and prospers through his sons and others.
In this regard, "by whom my chariot was protected" is a praise of the sacrifice; "by whom the well-worshipped gods gave the chariot" is a praise of the sacrificer.
In his house, the inexhaustible Iḍā, rich in offspring and accompanied by milch-cows, yields her milk day after day. || 4 ||

"Prajāvatī" means possessed of offspring such as sons and so forth; "asaścantī" [is used here] because "saścati" is a verb meaning "to go"—thus it refers to one whose nature is to come. "Dhenumatī" means she who nourishes (dhinoti) and delights all with milk; "dhenū" is a cow.
Accompanied by that, *iḷā*—food—is present in his house day after day; it is milked daily, being milked by the gods.
Or rather, *iḷā* is the deity of the cows.
She is firm and rich in milch cows; because she is the mistress of cattle, she is "rich in milch cows" through her cows. Iḷā is the deity of the cow.
Being impelled by the gods, she is the milker in the house of this sacrificer;
the meaning is that she bestows upon him sons and so forth.
In the *laṭ* (present tense) of the root *duh*, there is the elision of *ta* according to the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu."
Herein is the praise of sacrifice.

The two householders, being of one mind, who press [the Soma] and pour it forth with a constant mixture for the gods—5. The two householders, being of one mind, who press [the Soma] and pour it forth with a constant mixture for the gods—5.
In this [verse], there is praise of the husband and wife at the sacrifice:

"O gods, O gods, those two spouses, husband and wife, who perform the sacrifice with *samanasā*—that is, being of one mind (*samanasau*) regarding the ritual—who press the Soma, performing the extraction of the juice;
and those two spouses who then cleanse that pressed Soma, purifying it with the two filters."
The root *dhāv* is used in the senses of "flowing" and "purification.
Thus, it is performed constantly.
Where there is Soma in the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), there the substance for the mixing (*āśrayaṇa-dravya*) must indeed be cow’s milk.
Therefore, the connection with what follows is that those two who offer Soma joined with cow's milk—by means of its constant relation and its being drawn into [the vessel]—attain food and so forth.

Having eaten their fill from here, they, possessing good horses, have reached the sacrificial grass; they do not falter in the contests for booty. 6. Having eaten their fill from here, they, possessing good horses, have reached the sacrificial grass; they do not falter in the contests for booty. 6.

1. *Gha*: mixed with cow’s milk. 2. *Kha*, *Ta*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Śa*: [he gives] *soma* to him. 3. *Ga*: *laṃṭi*; *Ta*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Laṃṭi*. 4. *Ga*: endowed with sons and so forth. 5. *Ga*: “of a nature to come” means steady; *Ta*: “of a nature to come”; *Na*, *Ma*: “that which has the nature of coming. 6. *Ga*: such a one. 7. *Ga*: accompanied by that. 8. *Ga*, *Śa*: of the sacrificer and his wife. 9. *Kha*, *Ga*, *Ta*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Śa*: those who are husband and wife.

May those two—the husband and wife who are the givers of oblation (*havis*) to the gods—cause [the sacrificer] to eat. [The root] *aś* means "to eat. From the prefix *pra-* and the root *aś*, the suffix *uṇ* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva*), forming *prāśu*, which means "eating. They go toward the food and so forth that is beneficial or good for that eating; that is, they go toward it. Or alternatively, [they are] those who are to be eaten (*prāśitavya*); here there is an elision of a vowel. Those very two, being well-directed (*samyañcā*)—that is, well-aligned and united—have reached (*āśāte*) or attained (*ānaśāte*) the sacrifice externally. Therein they pervade the sacrificial materials. Therefore, those two—the sacrificers, or the husband and wife—do not fail (*na dhāyataḥ*) amidst the spoils (*vājeṣu*), that is, the foods given by the gods. The root *vayati* has the meaning of "going. They do not depart; the meaning is that they should always remain together with the gods.

Not even among the gods is there one who, when invoked, would fail to desire his goodwill, nor one who would not bestow great renown upon him who strives for it. 7. Not even among the gods; even when invoked; [he does not withhold] his goodwill; nor [does he withhold] great fame from the one who seeks it. 7.

This couple does not deny the gods, beginning with Indra; *apalāpa* means denial. Having promised, "We shall offer oblation (*havis*) to the gods," the failure to give it again is denial. [The root] *huḍu* is used in the sense of "removal. How is it known that they do not deny? To this he says: *sumatiṃ na jugukṣataḥ*. They do not wish to conceal (*jugukṣataḥ*) your excellent thought (*sumatiṃ*). *Saṃvaraṇa* means covering; the meaning is "they do not hide it. Rather, they offer praise. [The root] *guhū* is used in the sense of "concealing. By the rule *sanigrahaguhośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.12), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. There is an absence of the substitution of *bha* for *ha*. At the time of *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *bha* does not occur because of the Vedic nature (*chāndasatvāt*) of the text. Furthermore, *bṛhat* means great, because it is offered to the gods. *Śravaḥ* is a name for food. They desire to win (*vivāsataḥ*) great food—that is, they bestow it upon you. *Vivāsati* is a verb whose action is service (*paricaraṇa*). Giving is indeed a form of service. The meaning is that, having mixed the food given by the gods with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and other substances, they sacrifice again and again.

Possessing sons and possessing daughters, they enjoy a full span of life; both are adorned with golden ornaments. 8. Possessing sons, those two, possessing daughters, enjoy the full span of life; both are adorned with golden ornaments. 8.

Possessing sons through one who has sons, and even therein possessing young sons about sixteen years of age, adorned with golden ornaments (*hiraṇyapeśasā*), may both of them—that couple—attain a full span of life, a complete longevity.
The meaning is that through sacrifice, their progeny, wealth, and long life are brought into being.

Performing the office of the Hotṛ priest, bestowers of wealth, showing favor for the sake of immortality—strike down the hairy summit [of the enemy] and create a path among the gods. 9. vītihautrā (performing the office of the Hotṛ), kṛtadvasū (bestowers of wealth), daśasyantā (showing favor), amṛtāya (for the sake of immortality), kam (well), sam (together), ūrdhaḥ (the summit), romaśam (hairy), hataḥ (strike down), deveṣu (among the gods), kṛṇutaḥ (they create), duraḥ (paths). 9.
*vītihotrā* and *vītihotrau*:
those two for whom the *hotrā* (sacrificial invocation) is *vīti*, that is, dear and pleasing.
By means of this sacrifice, their offspring and so forth come into being.
Such [are they].
Or alternatively,
the root *vī* has the meaning of "splendor."
"Hotṛ" is a name for speech.
Thus, they are two whose praises are individually desired by the gods, with the request: "Perform praise directed toward us.
For this very reason, they are the "bestowers of wealth" (*kṛtadvasū*), granting the food in the form of oblations that bestows happiness (*kaṃ*) to the gods.
The addition of the syllable *ta* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "One who has made wealth by begging" means one who has acquired wealth from worthy recipients.
Such a couple, for the sake of immortality—that is, for non-death—and for the increase of their progeny, join together the hairy testicles and the womb; thus they engage in sexual union.
Thereafter, accompanied by their sons and others, the two perform *duvas*, which means service consisting of praise and offerings, among the gods.
Let the couple be praised with five [verses].
We choose the protection of the mountains, of the rivers,
and of Viṣṇu who dwells with them.
1. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa* means "going to sleep"; *ga-gacchataḥ* means "rising. 2. *kha-ga-jha-ta-ra* is "concealment"; *ta1* is "non-concealment. 3.
*kha-ga-ta-na-ma-śa* is "one's own."

4. *Śam* means "may he bestow food upon the gods," that is, may he give. 5. *Śam* refers to sons, grandsons, and so forth. We choose the auspiciousness (*śam*) of the mountains, of the rivers, and of Viṣṇu who dwells together with them. 10.
We choose the blessing of the mountains, of the rivers, and of Viṣṇu who dwells together with them. 10.
These are the blessings for the couple at the beginning [of the rite].

We choose—that is, we partake in—the same happiness that belongs to the mountains (*parvatānām*), characterized by stability or the pleasure derived from creepers laden with fruits and flowers; and the happiness that belongs to the rivers, which arises when sages or humans dwelling on both banks perform recitation (*japa*) and other rites; and the happiness characterized by being the enjoyer of all objects while remaining in one place through the performance of ritual acts. We pray for this.
We choose even that happiness characterized by the slaying of enemies which belongs to Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by the gods and whose presence is true;
the meaning is that, due to the absence of affliction, we abide together with the gods through the administration of poison.
May Pūṣan come, may Wealth, and Bhaga, the bestower of all prosperity, for our well-being;
may the broad path be auspicious, and the chariot of the god-favored one swiftly reach its goal, as do the heroes in whatever battles they may face.
The sacrificer who desires to worship these gods becomes swift in his course toward them.

Swift is the chariot of the one favored by the gods; or rather, [swift are] the heroes in whatever battles there may be. That sacrificer who seeks to win the mind of the gods shall surely prevail over those who do not sacrifice. 15.

Devavataḥ: He for whom the gods exist as those to be worshipped is "devavān" (one who has the gods). His chariot is "devadattaḥ" (given by the gods). It enters even difficult paths quickly and swiftly; its movement is unimpeded everywhere. Regarding this, there is an illustration: the word *vā* here expresses a comparison (*upamāna*). Just as a heroic warrior [acts] in certain battles (*pṛtsu*), so too [does this chariot]. *Yathaḥ*: Of the gods. *It* is used for emphasis. He alone desires to honor them with hymns (*iyakṣati*). Or rather, he desires to worship the mind of the gods with oblations (*havirbhiḥ*). That sacrificer (*yajamānaḥ*) surely overcomes (*abhivuvata*) those people who do not sacrifice (*ayajvanaḥ*), those who do not perform the ritual, by means of his own power. Regarding *iyakṣati*: from the root *yakṣa*, meaning "to worship. From *yaja*, meaning "to worship the gods," etc. The vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable in both cases is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the former case, the letter *k* is elided according to the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*.
O sacrificer, you do not suffer harm; neither does the one who presses the Soma, nor he who loves the gods.
He who, as a sacrificer, desires to worship the gods with this intention—he becomes swift in his course toward them.

No, O sacrificer, you do not suffer harm; no, O presser of soma; no, O lover of the gods—yes, the lover of the gods! He who, as a sacrificer, strives to win the mind of the gods, shall surely prevail over those who do not sacrifice. 16.
O sacrificer, you who seek to win the favor of the gods through your mind, you shall not come to harm;
you shall not perish, but rather shall increase with sons, grandsons, and so forth.
O Soma-presser, performing the extraction of Soma, you who seek to win the favor of those who press the juice through your mind—you too shall not come to harm.
O divine one, you who desire the gods and who seeks to worship the gods—such as you do not come to harm; rather, you increase through wealth and other blessings.
That sacrificer who desires to worship the gods with his mind overcomes those people who do not perform sacrifice.
No one shall escape him by his ritual act; he who seeks to flee shall not succeed in fleeing.
The sacrificer who desires to worship the mind of the gods—he indeed becomes swift as an arrow.

No one by his ritual act reaches him; he shall not be left behind, nor does he leave them behind—the sacrificer who strives to win the mind of the gods. Indeed, let the non-sacrificers fall short. 17.

Whosoever is a sacrificer who desires to worship the gods with his mind, no one at all—no one whatsoever—can reach him (*naśat*) by means of his own action; "to reach" (*naśati*) here has the sense of "to overcome. Furthermore, he shall not be separated from his own place; he shall not be divided or set apart.
Furthermore, he does not "yoṣati," meaning he is not separated from his sons and so forth, nor from his wealth and so forth;
for the root *yu*, meaning "to mix" or "to separate," takes the suffix *leṭ* with the augment *thaṭ* applied in both senses.
The rest has been explained.

1. Ga: "Presided over by the gods. 2. Kha, Jha, Ta, Tha, Dha, Bha: Just as one who is unimpeded in his movement enters into armies and battles for the purpose of slaying the enemy, so [is he]. Furthermore, the sacrificer [is one] whose mind is fixed upon the gods, Indra and others; Ga: "In battles, his mind is fixed upon the gods"—this is for emphasis; Ta³, Ta⁴, Na: "In battles, his mind is fixed"—this is for emphasis.
3. With *gha*-[suffixes] and oblations (*havirbhiḥ*); with *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* [suffixes], it means "you are" (*bhavān*).
4. With *gha* and *sa* [suffixes], it means "one who does not sacrifice" (*ayajvanaḥ*).
5. With *gha*, *iyakṣati* means "he desires to sacrifice" (*yaṣṭum icchati*).

Therein shall be great heroic power, and that which is worthy of swift steeds; for the sacrificer who strives to win the mind of the gods, he indeed becomes a conqueror over his enemies. 18. Therein. Great heroic power. And. That. Worthy of swift steeds. Of the gods. He. Indeed. Mind. The sacrificer. Strives to win. Over. Indeed. The enemy. He becomes. 18.

That sacrificer who desires to worship the mind of the gods—within that sacrificer there shall indeed be *suvīrya*, offspring and other blessings endowed with excellent heroism; and moreover, *āśuśravasyam*, that very renown associated with swift-moving horses, shall belong to him. Whatever person desires to worship or honor the mind of the gods with oblations, that person surely surpasses all those who do not sacrifice.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may the Great Lord of the Holy Tīrtha bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the second chapter of the Sixth Aṣṭaka in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the bearer of the yoke of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the third chapter of the sixth book begins.
"Pra kṛtnu" is the second hymn, consisting of thirty verses.
Regarding this, the table of contents (Anukramaṇikā) states: "Pra kṛtnu; thirty [verses]; Medhātithi [is the seer]."
The seer (ṛṣi) is Medhātithi Kāṇva.
According to the technical rule (paribhāṣā), "That which follows [the name of] Prāvatsapra is in the Gāyatrī metre," the metre (chandas) is Gāyatrī.
By the technical rule regarding the lack of specific instruction, Indra is the deity (devatā).
This hymn is prescribed for the Niṣkevalya Śastra of the Mahāvrata when it is chanted in the Gāyatrī meter;
likewise, it is sūtra-ed by Śaunaka in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "pra kṛtānyujīṣiṇa ā ghā ye abhimandhate" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.3).
In the first Paryāya of the Atirātra, this triplet beginning with "pra kṛtāni" serves as the Anurūpa for the Maitrāvaruṇa Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘pra va indrāya mādanam’ and ‘pra kṛtānyujīṣiṇaḥ’" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
In that very Śastra, there are fifteen verses beginning with "prati śrutāya.
For it is prescribed: "'prati śrutāya vo dhṛṣat'—these fifteen [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
On the morning pressing of the tenth day, during the recitation of the Acchāvāka, the triplet beginning with "apraśrutāya" is used in place of the verses for the wife and the sacrificer.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'apraśrutāya vo dhṛṣat'—these two triplets" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.12).
In the first round of the Atirātra included within the Ahīna sacrifice, the verse "panya idupa gāyata" serves as the anurūpa for the Hotṛ.
O Kaṇvas, you who possess the pressed residue, proclaim with a song of praise for Indra at the exhilaration of Soma.
The deeds of the one who possesses the soma-residue have been performed.
The Kaṇvas [sing] with a song of praise to Indra.
Speak forth of the pressed soma.

O Kaṇvas, you who possess the *ṛjīṣa*, proclaim aloud the deeds of Indra performed by means of the Soma that possesses the *ṛjīṣa*; speak them forth when the exhilaration of this [Soma] has arisen through the song—that is, the voice—of Indra.
He, the fierce one, who slew Suvinde, Anarśani, Pitu, Dāsa, and Ahīśuva, and released the waters.
1. The triplet beginning with *prati śrutāya* is addressed to Tanūnapāt. And it is stated in the Sūtra:
"The two triplets beginning with *prati śrutāya vaḥ* and *dhṛṣat* [are for Tanūnapāt]."

2. The Kaṇvas [speak]: He who—Indra, the fierce one, the uprooter, the brilliant one—releasing the waters, slew Subindu, Anarśani, Pipru, the Dāsa, and Ahīśubha. He who is Indra, the fierce one, the uprooter, the brilliant one, releasing the waters, slew the enemy named Subindu, the enemy named Anarśani, Pipru by name, the Dāsa, and the enemy Ahīśubha.

O Indra, strike down the abode of the great Arbuda, that which obstructs the rain; perform that celebrated deed of manly prowess. O Indra, strike down the abode of the great Arbuda, that which obstructs the rain; perform that celebrated deed of manly prowess. O Indra, pierce and destroy the dwelling place of the vast Arbuda, the cloud that withholds the water; perform that well-known act of heroic strength.

Boldly, for the sake of hearing your praises and for protection, I call upon the fair-cheeked Indra—who is bold against his enemies—for aid, as one calls for water from a mountain-cloud. O singers, for you—to hear your hymns and for your preservation—I boldly call upon Indra, the one with beautiful jaws, who is daring against his foes. "As for *tūṇīśam*": just as a man oppressed by heat calls for *tūṇīśam*, which is water; thus says Yāska: "Water is called *tūṇīśam*, because it flows quickly" (*Nirukta* 5.16). Just as one calls toward a cloud from a mountain—"mountain" (*giri*) being among the names for clouds—the meaning is that he calls out to him in that manner.

Intoxicated by the Soma, O Hero, you burst open the stall of cattle and horses for those who offer the Soma, as if shattering a fortress. 5. He; of the cow; of the horse; apart; the stall; being exhilarated; for the Soma-offerers; like a fortress; O Hero; you burst open. 5. O Hero Indra, you—the one well-known—being exhilarated and rejoicing, [open] the stall, the dwelling place, of the cow and the horse for the Soma-offerers; like a fortress, you burst it open, as if [attacking] the city of enemies, making its gates wide open. 1.

If you, O Indra, take delight in my pressed soma or in my hymn of praise, and if you bestow food upon me, then come hither from afar with your own power and nourishment. If you, O Indra, take delight in my pressed soma or in my hymn of praise, and if you bestow food upon me, then come hither from afar with your own power and nourishment. O Indra, if you rejoice in my pressed soma or in my hymn of praise, and if you grant me food, then come near from afar, bringing your own power and nourishment.

We indeed are yours, O Indra, lover of songs; you, O drinker of Soma, quicken us. We indeed are yours, O Indra, lover of songs; you, O drinker of Soma, quicken us. O Indra, lover of songs—worthy of praise through hymns—we truly are your singers. O drinker of Soma, you, Indra, quicken us; that is, you gladden us.

And bring us nourishment, O Maghavan, in your delight—nourishment that is inexhaustible; for abundant is your wealth. 8. And bring us nourishment, O Maghavan, in your delight—nourishment that is inexhaustible; for abundant is your wealth. 8.
1. kha-gharmābhitaptaḥ; ga-ma-śa-gharmābhitaptaḥ; ta-na-gharmābhitaptaḥ | ṚV 3.45.
Furthermore, O Maghavan, being well-disposed (*saṃrarāṇaḥ*), that is, rejoicing, [bestow] upon us food (*pituṃ*) that is unassailed (*avikṣitaṃ*), that is, inexhaustible.
Because the word *pṛkṣaḥ* is listed among the names for food in the passage "pṛkṣaḥ pituḥ," [the meaning is as follows]:
*ā bhara*—bring to us (*naḥ*), that is, bring hither;
for *te*—your—*vasu*—wealth—is indeed *bhūri*—abundant.

And make us possessors of cattle, possessors of gold, and possessors of horses; may we be united with nourishing offerings. 9. And for us, make [us] possessed of cattle, possessed of gold, and possessed of horses; may we be joined together with nourishing oblations. 9.
Moreover, O Indra, make us possessed of cattle—that is, provide us with cows;
make us possessed of horses, that is, make us eloquent;
and make us possessed of gold, that is, make us wealthy.
May we join together with offerings and foods; may we be united.

We invoke him of the great hymn, the one who bestows excellent gifts, for our protection; we call upon him who makes us successful, for our aid. 10. We invoke him of the great hymn, the one who bestows excellent gifts, for our protection; we call upon him who makes us successful, for our aid. 10.

We invoke Indra, who possesses excellent hands—the arms that are the extenders of actions, according to Yāska’s statement: “The two hands are the arms, because they are the extenders of deeds” (Nirukta 6.17)—who brings forth [his power] for the protection of the world; we call upon the one of great hymns (Bṛhaduktha), who performs what is right for the preservation of the world.
And thus Yāska says: "Bṛhaduktha means 'one whose hymn is great'; the hymn is to be recited for him" (Nirukta 6.4).

He who, even in the midst of battle, the performer of a hundred rites, the slayer of Vṛtra, the possessor of abundant wealth, makes [us] his own for the sake of those who praise him. 11. He who, even in the midst of battle, the performer of a hundred rites, the slayer of Vṛtra, the possessor of abundant wealth, makes [us] his own for the sake of those who praise him. 11.

He who is renowned as Indra in the assembly of battle is the one of a hundred powers (*śatakratu*), the performer of many deeds; moreover, immediately after that, he indeed performs this—such acts as the slaying of enemies. Furthermore, this Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of foes;

and moreover, for the sake of the singers (*jaritṛbhyas*)—that is, for the sake of those who praise him—he becomes the possessor of much wealth (*puruvasu*), meaning he possesses abundant riches, not for his own sake.

May he, the powerful Indra, the possessor of wealth, the bringer of bounty from within the ocean, come to us with all his aids. 12. May he, the powerful Indra, the possessor of wealth, the bringer of bounty from within, come to us with all his aids. 12.
May Śakra, that capable Indra, empower us as well; may he make us strong.
Moreover, Indra, with all his aids—that is, with all forms of protection—is the one who fills the gaps, meaning he is the one who covers over our deficiencies.

Sing forth to that Indra, who is a great river of wealth, easy to cross, and the friend of the one who presses the soma. 13. [He who is] a river of wealth, great, easy to cross, the friend of the one who presses [the soma]—sing unto that Indra. 13.
He who is Indra, the channel for wealth and riches, the great and most excellent protector, and one whose further shore is beautiful;
he who is the dear friend of the sacrificer who presses the Soma—
sing unto that Indra, praise him!

There is no restrainer of his powers, nor of his gracious gifts. No one says, "He does not give. Of this Indra’s *śacīnām*—of his excellent deeds (for *śacī* is listed among the names for action)—*nakiḥ* no one at all is a *niyantā*, a restrainer or controller. *Nakir vaktā na dād iti*: no one says, "He does not give. Rather, the meaning is that every person says only, "He bestows [gifts]. 15. 3.

Surely there is no debt to the Brahmins for those who are swift and press the Soma; nor has the Soma been drunk by one who is destitute. (16) *Prāśūnām*: those who reach the Soma are the "swift ones" (*prāśavaḥ*). For them, who are pressing the Soma, there is indeed no debt to the Brahmins—that is, the debt to the gods (*deva-ṛṇa*)—surely not; it truly does not exist. And thus it is heard in scripture: "He indeed is free from debt who has a son, who sacrifices, or who has lived as a student of sacred knowledge" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5). Furthermore, the Soma is not drunk by one who is *apratā*—one whose wealth is not extensive. The meaning is that the Soma is drunk only by one who possesses abundant wealth.

Sing unto the praiseworthy Indra; recite hymns to the praiseworthy one. Offer prayers to the praiseworthy one alone. (17) O singers, sing in accompaniment to the praiseworthy Indra alone. Furthermore, O chanters, recite hymns of praise to the praiseworthy Indra alone. And, O worshippers, offer other prayers to the praiseworthy Indra alone.

The praiseworthy, powerful Indra, who tears open hundreds and thousands [of enemies], is the one who is praised by the steeds; he who is the strengthener of the sacrificer. He, the powerful one, who tears open toward himself hundreds of heroes and thousands as well—he, this Indra, becomes praiseworthy by the enemies through his horses; and he is the strengthener, the increaser of the sacrificer who performs the ritual according to the injunctions.

Go forth freely according to your own will, following the invocations of the people; O Indra, drink of the pressed juices. 19. Go forth; freely, according to your own will, following the invocations of the people; O Indra, drink of the pressed juices. 19.
1. Kha–ta–bha: "Facing toward" means leading [them] forward; ga: possessing length; gha: the restrainer from all sides.
2. Jha–ta1–2: In that Indra, there are the *sāmans*.
3. In the *kha-ta-bha* recension, [the word] *panye* means "to be praised.

4. In the *gha* manuscript, there exists only a commentary on this mantra: "O singers (*upagātāraḥ*), praise the *sāmans* for that very Indra who is *panye*, meaning 'to be praised' (*stutya*). O *hotṛ*s, recite the *ukthas*, the hymns of praise, for that same Indra who is *panye*."
O Adhvaryus, perform, carry out, and offer the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*) for that very Indra who is worthy of praise.
O Indra, you who are to be invoked, move forth excellently according to the *svadhās*— the oblations— of the *kṛṣṭīs*, the human beings.
Second:
O filler, drink after the pressed-out Soma juices.

Drink, O Indra, that which is mixed with *svadhā*-milk, which is for you in the water; and also this, O Indra, which is yours. 20 Drink, O Indra, that which is connected to the *svadhā*-milk—the milk belonging to the cow, meaning the Soma purchased with a cow; for thus it is heard in scripture: "He purchases [the Soma] with a cow" (*Tai. Saṃ. 6.1.10.2*). And also that Soma which is in the water—for "water" (*tubhya*) is listed among the names for water—and which is mixed together with it, drink that Soma as well. And also that Soma which is yours, taken for your sake—that too is to be drunk by you; this is the sense. 4.

Pass by the one who presses [Soma] out of anger; pass by the one who has pressed it in a place where [the Brahmins] do not find delight. Drink this offered, pressed [Soma]. Pass by the one who presses [Soma] out of anger (*manyuṣāvinam*). Pass by the one who has pressed it (*susuvāṃsam*) in a place of distress (*upāraṇe*)—that place where the Brahmins, having approached, do not find pleasure. Pass by him. Drink this offered (*rātam*), pressed (*sutam*) Soma given by us in a place free from the harassment of Brahmins.

Come from the three distant realms; come beyond the five peoples. O Indra, may you behold our prayers. O Indra, you who have beheld our prayers (*dhenāḥ*), come from the three distant realms (*parāvataḥ*)—for "distant" (*parāvat*) is listed among the names for "far away"—come from the front, the back, and the sides. By this, the arrival of Indra from the front, rear, and flanks is invoked. Furthermore, come beyond the five peoples (*pañca janān*); that is, pass over them. Alternatively, the five peoples are the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Devas, the Asuras, and the Rakṣases. Thus Yāska says: "Some say they are the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Devas, the Asuras, and the Rakṣases; Aupamanyava says they are the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth" (Nirukta 3.8).

O Indra, as the sun emits its rays, so may my songs restrain you; like waters flowing together toward a low-lying place. As the sun emits its rays—its beams or the reins of its horses—so do thou release wealth for me. Furthermore, may my songs—my praises—restrain you together, in unison. Just as waters encompass a low-lying region together, such is the meaning.
