O Bull, when the Soma has been pressed, I pour out the pressed juice for you to drink; be satisfied and overflow with exhilaration. 22. O Bull (Indra), since the Soma has been pressed, I pour forth the pressed juice for you to drink. Be satiated and overflow with intoxication. 22.
1. Like a gift from Jha-Ta1-2-3-Dāta; 2. O Indra, at Gha-Pate; 3. Rambhā at Ga-Ta-Bha; 4. Smema, which causes intoxication, at Kha-Jha-Ta1-Bha.

Let not the foolish, seeking to harm you, nor those who mock you, deceive you. Do not favor those who hate sacred knowledge. O Indra, let not the fools—the deluded men—nor those desiring to harm you, deceive you; let not those intent on mocking you prevail. Do not associate with those who hate the *brahman* (the Veda or the priest).

Here, let them exhilarate you for great bounty with Soma mixed with the abundance of milk; drink like a wild buffalo at a lake. (24) O Indra, here at this sacrifice, let men exhilarate you for the sake of great wealth with Soma mixed with the abundance of milk—that is, with cow's milk. And you, drink that Soma just as a wild buffalo drinks from a lake.

Those ancient and new deeds which the slayer of Vṛtra has performed in the distance—proclaim them in the assemblies. (25) The slayer of Vṛtra, Indra, who in the distance—that is, far away—has impelled both ancient and ever-new treasures; proclaim those treasures in the assemblies, whether at sacrifices or in gatherings. Thus do the wise declare. (46)

Indra drank the pressed juice of Kadru at Sahasrabāhu; therein he displayed his manly prowess. Indra drank—the pressed soma belonging to Kadru, the one named Kadru—at Sahasrabāhu, who strikes down thousands of enemies (the remainder of the sense). On this occasion, he displayed—manifested—the manly prowess, the heroic might of Indra.

Knowing that truth for Turvaśa and Yadu, I called out [the enemy]; I have pervaded the *śarmi* in the conquest of Turvaṇa. (27) Knowing that well-known deed characterized by sacrifice and the like for Turvaśa, the king, and Yadu, the king named Yadu—that is, the *śami* (action), as it is listed among the names for action in the phrase "śacī śamī"—and knowing that truth in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), I, for the sake of pleasing those two, called out the one named Ahvayadhya, their enemy; I have pervaded him in the battle for the conquest of Turvaṇa. (27)

I have praised him, the common one, who is the deliverer of people and the protector of strength consisting of cattle. 28. taraṇim | traḥ | janānām | tradam | vājasya | go'mataḥ | samānam | ūm iti | pra | śaṃsipam ||28||
1. In manuscripts *ga*, *jña*, *ta4*, and *na*, [the reading] is *manuṣyāṇām aviṣyavaḥ*; in *gha*, *manuṣyāṇām aviṣyavaḥ*; in *ta1*, *ta2*, and *ta3*, *manuṣyāṇām maviṣyavaḥ*.

2. In manuscript *ga*, *pālakāmād abhan*; in *jha*, *ta1*, and *ta2*, *pālakāmā ādabhan*; in *ta3*, *ta4*, and *na*, *pālakāmā mādabhan*; in *bha1*, *pālakāmām ādabhan*. 3. In *ta* and *na*, the word *'mā'* does not exist.
4. Those [are] the gha-tā.

I praise that very same Indra, who is common to us all—he who is our savior, the deliverer of you people, including your sons and grandsons; the piercer of enemies; and the giver of cattle and wealth to the one who possesses them. (1.51.2) Like the Lord of the Rbhus, whom no one can restrain during the hymns, I praise Indra, who increases your strength, when the Soma is pressed along with the song of praise. (1.51.2) [The Lord] of the Rbhus, the great one, who increases the waters—*tubhyā-vrdham* being read among the names for water—Indra, when the Soma is pressed, I praise him during the hymns and recitations so that he may choose wealth [for us]. (*Na* is used here in the sense of "now" or "indeed. He who, for Triśoka, fashioned a separate dwelling and brought down the broad mountain, making a path for the cows to go forth. (1.51.3)

Do not, O Hero, slay us for one offense, nor for two, nor even for three; do not slay us, O Hero, for many offenses. O Hero Indra, do not slay us for one offense—that is, for a single transgression; do not slay us even for two offenses; and furthermore, do not harm us even for three offenses; and do not slay us for many—meaning for countless—offenses.

For indeed, I am afraid of you—of you who are like yourself, O fierce one, the crusher of enemies, the destroyer of evils, and the overcomer of assaults. 35 O Indra, I am indeed afraid of you—who are like yourself, the fierce, the impetuous, the crusher of those who strike at us, the destroyer of wickedness, and the one who endures the violence wrought by enemies. 48 *Note: Verses 35 and 48 refer to the same verse with different commentary traditions.*

May I not suffer the loss of my friend, O Lord of Abundant Wealth; may I not suffer the loss of my son. Let your mind be turned toward us. O Lord of Abundant Wealth (prabhuvaso), let me not experience the loss (śūnam) of your friend—let me not cause such loss to be known—and let me not experience the loss of my son. Let your mind be "āvṛtvat"—that is, turning back toward us; let it be so that you repeatedly bring us happiness.

Who indeed, O men, being unprovoked, has spoken thus to his friend: "Whom have I slain? Who flees from us in fear? (37) Who indeed, O men (*maryāḥ*), being unprovoked (*amaithitaḥ*)—*medhati* meaning "to revile"—that is, one who is not provoked by Indra, a friend speaking to a friend: "Whom have I slain? And who, terrified of us, flees away? Thus he speaks; the intention is that Indra alone is the speaker of such words. Accordingly, Yāska says: "*Medhati* means 'to revile. 'Whom have I ever slain? Who flees from us? (Nirukta 4.2). By the Śruti passage beginning with "Not for a single offense against us," it is understood that Indra surely seized the Ṛṣi. Thus the meaning is remembered.

O Vṛṣabha, showerer of desires, O Indra, when this Soma has been pressed, you have brought much wealth here, moving like a gambler toward his winnings. O Vṛṣabha, showerer of desires, O Indra, when this Soma has been pressed, you have brought much—that is, abundant—wealth into this [sacrifice], like a *śvaghnī* (a gambler) who, moving toward his winnings (*nivata*), has not lost. A *śvaghnī* is a gambler; thus Yāska says: "A *śvaghnī* is a gambler, for he destroys his own [wealth]" (Nirukta 5.22).

I grasp these two bay steeds of yours, yoked by our word, for the sake of your benevolence and your chariot—so that you may grant them indeed to those who offer prayers. 39. I grasp these two bay steeds of yours, yoked by our word, for the sake of your benevolence and your chariot—so that you may grant them indeed to those who offer prayers. 39.
1. ga-ta-na-bha—“I... indeed” does not exist.
2. ga-gha-ta-na—anuntracted. 3. na-bha-pālayata—protect!

4. *ga*-ta-na-bha read *abhipūte*; *jñāta*-*2-3* read *abhisute*. 5. *gha* reads *ababhran*; like a gambler, that Soma has reached you alone. Being visible with the *āvayas*, all the gods moved out, having gone down into the *nivata*s with their faces turned downward.
*kha* reads *saṃhate*; *ga* reads *sahante*; *ta-na* read *saṃhate*; *bha1-3* read *svaṃ haṃ*; *bha2* reads *svaṃ haṃtīti*; *śa* reads *saṃhateti*.
[Maṇḍala 8, Anuvāka 6, Sūkta 46] O you two, your two auspicious-horsed (sumadrā), beautiful-rayed steeds, yoked by the mantra— these two white horses (vetā harī)—
I draw forth with my two hands so that they may come toward us; this is the meaning.
Since you, O Vīti, bestow this wealth upon the *brahmans*, that is, upon the *brāhmaṇas*.
Shatter all enemies, strike down those who oppress us, and slay our mockers;
bring to us that which bestows wealth.
Shatter all enemies; drive away all oppressors; slay the mockers. Bring us that wealth which is desirable! 40.
O Indra, you, split apart— tear asunder— all these various hostile enemy armies;
[drive away] the harmful *mṛdh* enemies,
for *mṛdh* and *spṛdh* are listed among the names for battle.
Drive away and push aside [the enemies].
Therefore, bring to us that well-known, desirable wealth of theirs. Bring it to us!
O Indra, whatever wealth is hidden in the thickets, whatever is in firm places, or whatever has been carried away to the distant pastures—
bring that desirable treasure here to us.
O Indra, that desirable wealth which has been brought forth in the stronghold, in the firm place, or in the mountain—bring that hither! 41.

O Indra, bring that wealth which has been set apart for you—wealth placed in a firm and solid stronghold, unshakable by others; wealth deposited in a stable place, immovable by itself; and wealth brought forth even in a discerning place, capable of withstanding scrutiny. Bring that treasure to us.
O you whose entire human world knows the wealth bestowed by you,
bring that desirable treasure here.
O you whose wealth is known by all men, bring hither that desirable treasure which was given by the Bhr̥gus. 42.

O Indra, bring that desirable wealth (*vasu*) which you have given—given by you, the many, of that vast wealth; [the word *dattasya* is used for *dattam* due to a shift in case endings]. Every human being (*viśvamānuṣaḥ*) knows it; [the genitive case is used in the sense of the object]. Bring that desirable treasure. 49.
May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, who dispels the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the goals of human existence upon those who have heard his teachings.

Thus ends the third chapter of the sixth book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having explained the third chapter in the sixth [book], the illustrious Sāyaṇārya, son of Śrīmatī, now summarizes and explains the fourth chapter.
In this context, the fourth hymn, consisting of thirty-three verses beginning with "tvāvataḥ," is also the seer's own composition, belonging to Uttara Vaśalya.
According to the rules previously established regarding the *vatsapra*, the first four verses are *gāyatrīs*.

Among them, the first is a *pādanicṛt*, because it possesses the defining characteristic stated in the *Anuvākānukramaṇī*: "Three [verses] with six syllables each constitute a *pādanicṛt*" (Anu. 4.4).
The fifth [verse], "dadhāno gomadaśvavat," is a *kakubh* because it is endowed with feet consisting of eight, twelve, and eight syllables;
for its definition is: "If the middle [foot] is [longer], it is a *kakubh*" (Anuvāka 5.3).
The sixth [verse] begins with "tam indram."
1. There is no *ga*, *ta*, *na*, or *te*.
2. *kṣa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* [occur] when facing *ad*; *gha* [occurs] when facing *ad*. 3. *tā*, *l*, *3*, *n*, *prāta*, and *rābhṛtaṃ*.
4. *ga-tvam*; *jñāta-1-3-tvā*; *ta-4-na-bha-1-2-tvā*. Gāyatrī.
“*tasmin hi santi*” is a Bṛhatī in the locative case.
‘yaste madaḥ’ is the eighth [verse], an anuṣṭubh;
‘yo duṣṭaraḥ’ is the ninth, a satobṛhatī.
For it has been stated: “The odd-numbered verses are jāgata, and they are satobṛhatīs” (Anuvāka 8.4).
The tenth verse, “gavyo yuṇaḥ,” is a Gāyatrī;
the eleventh, “nahi te śūra,” is a Bṛhatī;
and the twelfth, “ya ṛṣvaḥ,” is a Viparītā Satobṛhatī, having eight syllables in the first and third quarters and twelve syllables in the second and fourth.
Because it has been stated, “If the two yujas are reversed” (Anuvāka 8.5),
the thirteenth verse, “sa no vājeṣu,” is a dvipadā consisting of twenty-four syllables.
The fourteenth verse, “abhi vo vīram,” is a pipīlikamadhyā bṛhatī.

The eighth verse, "In the midst of the thirteen," is called *pipīlikamadhyā*, because it is stated [in the Anuvāka]: "The eighth among the thirteen is the *pipīlikamadhyā*" (Anuvāka 7.7). The fifteenth verse, "He gave wealth," is the *kakubhyaṅkuśirā*, because it is stated [in the Anuvāka]: "The four [verses] consisting of *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* are the *kakubhyaṅkuśirā*" (Anuvāka 5.4).
The sixteenth verse, "To the people," is the *virāj*.
The seventeenth verse, beginning with “mahaḥ su vaḥ,” is a Jagatī.
The eighteenth verse, beginning with “ye pātayante,” is an Upariṣṭādbṛhatī because its fourth quarter consists of twelve syllables.
The nineteenth verse, beginning with “prabhaṅkam,” is a Bṛhatī.

The twentieth verse, “*sanitaḥ susanitaḥ*,” is a *bṛhatī* with uneven feet, because it has been stated [in the Anukramaṇī]: “Those with nine, eight, eleven, and eight syllables [respectively] are *viṣamapadā*.
The twenty-first and twenty-second verses, “*ā sa etu*” and “*ṣaṣṭiṃ sahasrā*,” are *paṅkti*s.
The twenty-third verse, “*daśa śyāvāḥ*,” is a *gāyatrī*.
The twenty-fourth verse, beginning with "dānāsaḥ," is a *paṅkti*;
the twenty-fifth and twenty-seventh are *bṛhatīs*;
and the twenty-sixth and twenty-eighth are *satobṛhatīs*.
The twenty-ninth is a *gāyatrī*.
The thirtieth, “*gāvo na yūtham*,” is a twenty-syllable *dvipadā virāj*.
The thirty-first is an *uṣṇih*.
The thirty-second verse is a *paṅkti*;
the thirty-third is a *gāyatrī*.
With the four verses beginning with “ā sa etu,” the gift of Pṛthuśravas, the son of Kanīta, is praised.
Therefore, they have those as their deities.
Of the four [verses] beginning with "ā no vāyo," Vāyu is the deity for thirty-two;
the remaining [verses] have Indra as their deity according to the rule regarding unspecified cases.

All of this has been stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: "The thirty-third [hymn] consists of eight verses beginning with 'tvāvataḥ'. The first is a praise of the gift (*dānastuti*) of Pṛthuśravas, son of Kānīta; it begins with a *pādanicṛt*. From the fifth verse onward, there are *kakub*, *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, *anuṣṭubh*, *satobṛhatī*, and *gāyatrī* verses. The subsequent *pragātha* is *viparīta*. Then there is a *dvipadā*, a twenty-four-syllable *bṛhatī*, a *pipīlikamadhyā*, a *kakub*, an *aṅkuśirā*, a *virāj*, a *jagatī*, an *upariṣṭādbṛhatī*, a *bṛhatī*, two *paṅktis* with unequal feet, a *gāyatrī*, and a *paṅkti*. There are two *pragāthas* addressed to Vāyu, a *gāyatrī*, a *dvipadā uṣṇih*, a *paṅkti* addressed to Vāyu, and a *gāyatrī*."
In the *niṣkevalya* section of the *mahāvrata*, one should recite this very hymn beginning with "O winner, O great winner" (*asanitaḥ susanitaḥ*).

Accordingly, Śaunaka has prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "The hymn beginning with 'Of one such as you, O possessor of many riches' (*tvāvataḥ puruvaso*) and ending with 'O winner, O great winner' (*sanitaḥ susanir*) [is to be used]" (AiĀ 5.2.5).

O Indra, Lord of many riches, O Leader, we are yours—such as you are—to guide us, O Upholder of the modest. tvāvataḥ puruvaso vayam indra praṇetaḥ | samasi sthātar hrīṇām || 1 || O Indra, Lord of many riches, O Leader, we are yours—such as you are—to guide us, O Upholder of the modest. || 1 ||
O Indra, possessor of many riches, leader of deeds, you who bring us to the further shore with excellence—O Indra, we are yours, belonging to one such as you;
for since there is no station equal to that of Indra, the meaning is "belonging to you.
We are yours by our very nature.
O you who stand as the presiding lord over those known by the name Hrīṇā.

For you indeed, O wielder of the stone, are the true giver of all refreshments; the giver of all riches. 2. You indeed—O wielder of the stone—are the true giver of all refreshments; the giver of all riches. 2.
O wielder of the stone, you who possess the thunderbolt,
we all know you to be the true and certain giver of food (*iṣ*) and the giver of riches (*rayi*). Thus, O Śakra, we all recognize you as such.
O Śatakratu, whose greatness the singers celebrate with hymns when it has manifested a hundredfold.

1. *ga-ta-bha-śa* is *bṛhatī*; 2. *kha-ga-ta-bha* is *uṣṇih*; 3. *kha-gha-ta-na-bha-śa* is *kanīnā*; 4. this ends with *ga*; 5. *kha-gha-jha-ta-2-bha-śa* is *praṇetṛ* (variant: *ga-prāṇetṛ*); 6. *na-ja* we do not know.
O Śatakratu, you of a hundred powers, whose greatness the singers praise with hymns—you, O Lord of infinite protection—[we call upon you] for our desired goal. || 3 ||

Truly, that mortal is well-guided, whom the Maruts, Aryaman, and Mitra—those who are free from malice—protect. (4) That mortal, that sacrificer, is indeed well-guided (sunīthaḥ)—meaning one who performs good sacrifices or possesses excellent guidance. The particle *gha* indicates what is well-known. To the question "Which one? he replies: "Him"—the sacrificer—"whom the Maruts, the gods, protect" (*pānti*), meaning they guard him, being "free from malice" (*adruhaḥ*). Likewise, "whom Aryaman protects," and "whom Mitra protects"—he alone becomes such [a person].

Bestowing wealth in cattle and horses, along with heroic strength, the son of Aditi prospers; he ever increases through riches desired by many. Bestowing (dardhānaḥ), possessed of cattle (gomat), possessed of horses (aśvavat), and endowed with excellent heroism (suvīryam), the son of Aditi (ādityarjataḥ)—that is, impelled and favored by the Ādityas—the sacrificer prospers (edhate), increasing (vardhate) at all times (sadā). Furthermore, he ever prospers through wealth (rāyā) that is longed for by many (puruṣpṛhā). 5.

We pray to that Indra for a gift; we pray to the powerful, the fearless, the lord of wealth. (6) We pray to that well-known Indra for a gift—that is, for wealth to be given. What kind of Indra? The one who displays power (*śavasānam*), the fearless (*abhīrvam*), and the sovereign lord (*īśānam*) of all.

For in him are all aids, together with all fearless companions. May his swift, tawny steeds bring him, the possessor of much wealth, to the pressed Soma for our exhilaration. In that Indra indeed are all aids; together with him are all fearless [companions], the hosts in the form of Maruts. Or rather, in him all protections exist together. May his swift, tawny horses, who are ever-moving, bring that Indra—the giver of much wealth—to the pressed Soma for our exhilaration.
That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent, O Indra, which is the greatest slayer of Vṛtra,
which with the sun-like [rays] has seized the light and is invincible in battles— [that exhilaration we desire].
1. Followed by *kha-ga-ta-āditya*; not followed by *āditya*. 2. In *kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa*, "arāyaḥ" is absent.
That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent, O Indra, which is most effective against Vṛtra, which you won the light with [your] men, and which is invincible in battles. 8.
In the preceding mantra, "for exhilaration, for the bay horses" was stated; that exhilaration is now praised.
O Indra, that exhilaration of yours which is *vareṇya*, meaning worthy of being chosen;
and that exhilaration which, in battle, is *vṛtrahantama*, the supreme slayer of enemies.
And he who is the first-taker, the seizer of wealth that resounds through heaven, for men from their enemies;
and he who is difficult to overcome and invincible in battles and conflicts— for that exhilaration, O bay steeds, carry him to the one who possesses the vehicle.
O possessor of all boons, he who is difficult to overcome, worthy of renown, and the victor in battles—he, O most powerful Vasu, come to our libations; lead us to a stall full of cattle.

He who is difficult to overcome, O possessor of all boons, who is worthy of renown and the victor in battles—O most powerful one, O Vasu, come to our libations; may we find a path to the stall filled with cattle. 9.

O Viśvavāra, O Indra, who art worthy of choice by all, in battles for booty, he who is *duṣṭara*—difficult to overcome—and a *tarutṛ*, a deliverer of enemies, exists; O *vaso*, O dweller, O most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*) Indra, as such, come to our *savanāni*, come to our libations. And may we go to a stall full of cattle, may we reach a pen abounding in kine.
Protect us as you did of old; let the chariot-horses speed forth. O most magnificent one, grant us wide space.
O most generous one, protect us as you did of old with your gift of horses and your gift of chariots; grant us wide space, O most mighty one! 10.
O Great Indra of the great sacrifice, you are approachable.

[The form] *gamyā* is a noun due to the status of being a particle (*nipāta*) resulting from the initial-like treatment (*ādivadbhāva*) of the combination of the two particles *gam* and *yā*. [The phrase] *asmākaṃ gām icchayā* means "by our desire for a cow" or "to give us a cow. Just as formerly (*purā*), in the past, you served us by granting cows and other gifts, even so today, serve us well (*su*) and attend to us.

The meaning is "come. Not only with the desire for cattle (*gavecchayā*), but also with the desire for horses (*aśvayā*)— that is, the desire to give horses— and furthermore, with the desire for chariots (*rathayā*), he shall serve you.
O hero, I truly find no end to your bounty;
O Maghavan, wielder of the stone, you have always been gracious to us, and with your strengths you have protected our prayers.
No, O Hero; I find no end to your bounty. Therefore, O Maghavan, wielder of the stone, grant us gifts evermore; clothe our prayers with spoils of war. 11.
O hero, O Indra of great prowess, I have not yet found—that is, I do not obtain—the limit of your *rādhas*, your wealth; indeed, I find it to be truly inexhaustible.
Since this is so, therefore, O Maghavan, possessor of riches, O wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivat*), Indra, grant us—that is, give us that wealth—most swiftly.
Furthermore, with strengths—that is, with foods—protect and nourish our prayers, our sacred rites.
He who is lofty, worthy of praise, and the consumer of all—much-invoked, he knows every birth.
All human generations, with uplifted ladles, invoke that powerful Indra.

1. [In the versions] kha, ga, ta, na, bha, and śa, "tava" (your) is not present. 2. [In version] gha: "tārakaḥ śravāyyaḥ śravaṇīyaḥ dayāḥ. 3. [In version] gha, na: "asmākam" (our). 4. [In versions] kha, gha, ta, na, bha, and śa: "yathāsmākaṃ yāgam" (as our sacrifice). 5. [In version] gha: "labhe khalu" (indeed, I obtain). 6. [In version] ga: "rakṣita" (protected).
He who is lofty, the one who makes [us] famous, the friend—he, the much-praised, knows all generations. All human ages invoke that powerful Indra when they are eager for wealth. 12.
Indra, who is lofty, beautiful to behold, and a friend who makes [his name] heard— O friends,

the officiating priests who cause him to be heard, he is such a friend who makes [himself] heard. Indra, who is invoked by many and praised by numerous sacrificers, he knows— that is, he understands— all *janimāni*, all the births of living beings.

All the Adhvaryus and others, having taken up their oblations and being zealous, invoke—that is, they call upon and praise—that powerful and mighty Indra at all times, throughout every human age (yuga) associated with mankind.

May he, the possessor of abundant wealth, the Maghavan, the slayer of Vṛtra, be our protector and our leader in the contests for booty. O Indra, you who carry off all treasures—that is, you who are the lord of all riches—may you be the overcomer of this enemy who withholds and obstructs the battle; [we] praise you as the one who protects us.
May you now swiftly grant us even a small portion of wealth.
We praise you greatly so that you may be well-disposed toward us—you who are bountiful, ever-approaching, and swift-moving.
With sacrifices and songs, you worship the Maruts who are followed by all men; I sing to you with reverence and with my voice.

Great indeed is your power; we praise you who are ready to grant boons, the bounteous one who comes at our call. With sacrifices and songs, you seek to win the favor of the Maruts, who are present with all men; I sing to you with reverence and with song.
"O Indra, [this is] for you, the great one"— that is the meaning;
the plural number is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
I desire swift movement toward our domain;
"araṃ" is the form used here.

For that purpose, for the one who bestows abundance (*mīḍhvuṣe*), the one who sprinkles (*sektre*), the one who moves swiftly (*araṃgamāya*), the one whose movement is complete (*saṃpūrṇagamanāya*), the one who goes (*jagmaye*)—to such a god, who is by nature ever-moving toward the sacrifice, we offer praise.
The meaning is: "We praise you.
By what means? That is stated:
by sacrifices (*yajñebhiḥ*), that is, by oblations which are the means of sacrifice, or by sacrifices themselves; and by songs (*gīrbhiḥ*), that is, by hymns of praise.
O God, you who desire to sacrifice for all men—that is, for all human beings who perform sacrifices—you are worshipped by these [sacrifices].
You belong to the Maruts;
furthermore, I praise and sing to you with reverence (*namas*) and with song (*girā*), that is, with hymns of praise.
They who cause the rivers to flow with their courses over the ridges of the mountains—
[we invoke] the sacrifice of those who roar mightily, the favor of those who thunder loudly, at the rite.
They who descend with their courses upon the ridges of the mountains—[we invoke] the sacrifice of these who roar mightily, the favor of those who roar loudly, at the solemn rite. 18.

Those who, with the great mountain-like clouds raining down from their heights, and with their rushing paths—that is, their powerful, strength-bestowing waters—cause [all things] to fall, or themselves fall and move along; for these Maruts, who possess abundant sound (*mahiṣvarṇīnām*), we perform sacrifice—the ellipsis being "we perform sacrifice.
And having performed it, may we attain the bliss (*sumnam*) created by those of many sounds (*tuvisvarṇīnām*) at the *adhvara*, the sacrifice.
Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
May I obtain the oblation characterized by the granting of bliss from those of abundant sound during the sacrificial rite.
O Indra, most powerful one, shatter the evil-minded; bestow upon us appropriate wealth, O you who impel our thought, impelling the highest thought.
O Indra, most powerful one, drive away those of evil thoughts! Bring us wealth that is worthy of our alliance, O you of impelling mind; bring the most excellent wealth, O you of impelling mind! 19.
We entreat you—the one who utterly destroys (*prabhañjam*) the evil-minded and wicked-hearted ones such as Vṛtra and others—to do so, is the ellipsis.
O Indra, most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*), being exceedingly strong, you who are praised, grant us wealth (*rayi*), that is, riches (*dhana*) which is suitable (*yujyam*), appropriate for us.

1. [The variants] *ga-bha* read *kṣipam athāpi*; *gha* reads *kṣipam idānīm*; *atha cit* means "also immediately thereafter. 2. *kha-jña-ta-1-2-araṃgamāya* [is glossed as] *araṃ*. 3. *jha-tṛ-4-na-bhara-śa* read *araṃgamanāya*. 4. *kha-ga-ta-na-śa-sa* read *evaṃbhūtāya*. 5. *ga-gha-ta-na* read *yajamānasādhanaiḥ*; *jha* reads *yajñasādhanaiḥ*. 6. In *ga-ta3-4-na-śa*, the word *ajmabhiḥ* is absent. 7. *ta-śa* read *bahudhvanīnām*. 8. *kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa* read *balavanniṣṭha*.

Bring wealth, bring it hither! O you whose mind is inciting!—that is, O God, you whose intellect impels and drives forth wealth. Furthermore, O you whose mind is inciting, bring that most excellent wealth hither! O winner (*sanitar*), O well-winner (*susanita*), O fierce one (*ugra*), O wonderful one (*citra*), O most wise one (*cetiṣṭha*), O truthful one (*sūnṛta*), O overpowering one (*prasahā*), O sovereign ruler (*samrāṭ*), bring to us in battles that victorious (*sahuri*) and conquering (*sahantam*) Bhujyu, the foremost (*pūrvyam*). May he come, that godless man who has taken such full wealth, just as Vaśa Aśvya took [wealth] from Pṛthuśravas Kānīta at the breaking of this dawn. [Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "When Pṛthuśravas Kānīta gave to Vaśa, that gift is praised here with these words beginning 'May he come'. May he come; may he, that non-god—a human being named Vaśa—who has taken full wealth consisting of moving cattle and the like, come here. Even if he were a god, he would be able to come; therefore, let him come by way of light. How did he come into possession of this wealth and on what occasion? That is stated: just as Vaśa, the son of Aśva, took it from King Pṛthuśravas, the son of Kanīta, at the dawning of this Dawn—at that cause, for that reason, let him come. Thus speaks the horse, or the circle of kinsmen. I have received thousands of mares, tens of thousands of horses, twenty hundreds of camels, ten hundreds of dark-brown mares, ten [thousands] of those with three red spots, and ten thousands of cows. That Vaśa, having arrived, says: I have received thousands of mares belonging to the horse [of Pṛthuśravas], and tens of thousands of horses. I have received twenty hundreds of camels. I have received ten hundreds of dark-brown mares. I have received ten thousands of cows that have three shining, beautiful white marks on their foreheads, backs, and flanks. 1. *gha* reads *saṃbhaktaḥ susanitaḥ suṣṭhu saṃbhaktardātā*. 2. *gha*, *ta3*, *ma*, *śa* read *sahanaśīlaṃ sahaṃtaṃ putrādiyuktam*. 3. *ma1-3*, *śa* read *śrūyate*. 4. *gha*, *ta3*, *ma*, *śa* read *prakāreṇa*. 5. *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa* read *prakāreṇa*.

Ten dark-brown, wealth-increasing, swift horses with flowing manes have turned the felly downward. (23) Ten—ten in number—dark-brown (*śyāva*) in color, swift horses, with flowing manes (*vītavāra*), rapid, and powerful, have turned the felly (*nemi*) downward; that is, they draw the chariot. These are "wealth-increasing" (*ṛdhaddrayaḥ*), meaning those whose speed has increased; "with flowing manes" (*vītavārāsaḥ*), meaning those whose strength has spread or whose power is extended; "swift" (*āśavaḥ*); and "churning" (*mathāḥ*), meaning those whose nature is to crush or overcome.

The gifts of Pṛthuśravas, the son of Kanīta, who is most bountiful—giving a golden chariot, he has become the most generous patron (*sūri*), the bestower of fame. (24) *The gifts of Pṛthuśravas, the son of Kanīta, who is most bountiful—giving a golden chariot, he has become the most generous patron, the bestower of fame.* The riches mentioned in the preceding mantras were previously indicated as belonging to his kinsmen or his father. [He belongs to] "Pṛthuśravas," the "son of Kanīta" (*kānīta*), who is "most bountiful" (*surādhas*) because his wealth is so abundant that he is thus called *surādhas*. These are "his gifts," these riches. And that Pṛthuśravas, "giving" (*dadat*) a "golden" (*hiraṇyaya*) "chariot," has "become" (*abhūt*) "the most generous" (*maṃhiṣṭha*), an exceedingly great giver, a "wise one" (*sūri*)—one who impels all or is possessed of wisdom. He "has made" (*akuruta*) "fame" (*śravaḥ*), a most exalted renown; he makes it, or may he make it. This verse, "Come to us, O Vāyu," is the third in the triplet dedicated to Vāyu for the *prauga-śastra* on the fifth day. For it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘Come to us, O Vāyu, for our great [offering],’ and ‘With a chariot of broad splendor’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).

O Vāyu, come toward us for great wealth, for sacrifice, and for power; for we have prepared much for you to give, even now, for the giving of great wealth. O Vāyu, come toward us—come hither—for the sake of great wealth, for the sake of sacrifice, and for power (pājaḥ). That is to say, in order to bestow both of these. What is there [to offer]? It is said: "We indeed have prepared much for you to give"—that is, praise or the oblation—for the giver of abundant wealth. "Even now" (sadhak), that is, immediately upon your arrival, we have prepared [this] for the giver of great wealth. 25.

He who brings [gifts] with horses, goats, and oxen—three times seven times seventy—with these Soma-pressers and Soma-offerings, O Soma-drinker, you are purified by the bright [Soma] for the sake of the gift. 26. He who brings with horses, with goats, and oxen—three times seven times seventy—with these Soma-pressers and Soma-offerings, O Soma-drinker, you are purified by the bright [Soma] for the sake of the gift. 26.

He who is Pṛthuśravas has himself, by his own intellect alone, delighted—that is, he has resolved—to give this wonderful and praiseworthy wealth, such as cattle and horses, which is present before me, for the sake of bestowing it.
And that king, a performer of auspicious deeds, [resided] at Araṭṭa, Akṣa, Nahuṣa, and Sukṛtvan;
these were the overseers of that king.
He commanded them, "Join these [gifts], such as cattle and so forth, to him. Alternatively, *araṭṭa* and others refer to other kings.
Among them, Mandadī is the daughter of Sukṛtarā.

In the lofty body, he who is the self-ruling lord—O Vāyu, you who are bathed in ghee—this very thing, impelled by purpose, impelled by passion, impelled by the dog, has now been driven forth. 28. In the lofty body; he who; the self-ruling lord; and; O Vāyu; you who are bathed in ghee; impelled by purpose; impelled by passion; impelled by the dog; forth; it has been driven; that; this; now; that. 28.
In the case of *ucathyā*, meaning "to be spoken," "to be praised," or "in the body" (*vapuṣi*); he who is *svarāṭ*, shining by himself.
Or alternatively:
the two kings, *ucathyā* and *vapuṣmant*.

Of those two, he who is *svarāṭ* exercises sovereignty (*svārājyam*), meaning he exists in preeminence. O Vāyu, he who is *ghṛtasnāḥ*—pure like clarified butter—that king [attains] *artheṣitam*, that which is obtained by means of horses, and *rajeṣitam*.
By the word *rajaḥ*, the camel and the donkey are meant.
He brought that which was impelled by the dog and gave it as a goatless goat;
that food brought by the horse is seen here before you—this is the meaning: "It is solely through your grace."
Alternatively, there is one verse for the purpose of completion:
"That which was brought by the horses—this indeed is it."

Just as cows go toward and enter their herd at the time of gathering (saṃgava), so too do these castrated bulls (*vadhrayaḥ*), given by Pṛthuśravas, approach and come near me. "Let not the castrated bulls approach me"—this repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

And when he slaughtered a hundred camels in the troop of Caratha, and twenty hundred among the Śvitnas. 31. And when... in the troop of Caratha... a hundred camels... slaughtered... and... among the Śvitnas... twenty hundred. 31.
"Vadha" means when one moves;
"caratham" means movement, walking, or going; [it refers to] that which is being moved in relation to such movement.
The meaning is "being urged toward the forest.
In such a herd, he offered up a hundred camels—a hundred of camels—to be given to us.
Moreover, for our sake alone, he offered twenty hundreds—that is, two thousand—or perhaps twenty groups of a hundred—in the white-colored herds of cattle.
A hundredfold is your great bounty for the donor, O Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman. Whom you Ādityas protect from malice, no evil shall reach him. Your aids are faultless; your aids are excellent. 1.
O Varuṇa, O Mitra!
This pair alone is also indicative of the entire group [of Ādityas].
O Varuṇa and the others, your protection (*avaḥ*)—that is, your guardianship—is great (*mahi*).
For whom?
For the donor, the giver of the oblation, the sacrificer for whom [the rite] is being performed.
Furthermore, O Ādityas, that sacrificer whom you protect from the presence of the malicious—him, this very sacrificer, no evil or sin shall reach; it does not attain him.
Why is this so? It is stated therein:
"Your *ūtayaḥ*—that is, your protections (*rakṣaṇāni*)—are *anehasaḥ*, meaning faultless (*apāpāni*) and free from affliction (*anupadravāṇi*).
Your *ūtayaḥ*, your protections, are *suūtayaḥ*, meaning excellent protections."
To whomsoever they have granted a dwelling and life, these wise Ādityas indeed rule over all the wealth of Manu. Unassailable are your aids; excellent are your aids. 4.

To whichever man they—the wise ones of exalted intellect—bestow a dwelling, a means of sustenance, and food, for that sacrificer and for his sake, these Ādityas have bestowed [their power] over all; they become the masters of the wealth of every wealthy human being, having seized it to bestow it upon the sacrificer.

May you carry us around, avoiding evils and difficult paths, as chariot-drivers do. May we indeed abide in the protection of Indra and in the favor of the Ādityas. Your aids are faultless; yours are the well-aiding aids. pari no vṛṇajanaghā durgāṇi rathyā yathā | syāmedindrasya śarmaṇyādityānāmutāvasi | anehaso va ūtayaḥ sūtayo va ūtayaḥ || 5 ||
"May they *pari-vṛñjantu*—that is, may they completely avoid—*naḥ* our *aghā* sins.
Therein is an illustration:
just as one avoids *durgāṇi*—difficult-to-traverse places such as pits, precipices, and the like—in that same manner."
May we abide in the protection of Indra;
moreover, may we also abide in the shelter and guardianship of the Ādityas.

O gods, O swift-moving ones, that sacrificer whom you have reached—he, that person, obtains (vāyati) abundant, not small, wealth; such is the connection [of the words].

"O Ādityas, you abandon that man—even though he be *tigma*, meaning sharp—here referring to a weapon employed out of anger; [the word] *tyajaḥ* is a synonym for anger. He does not *drāsat*. [The root] *drā* means 'to go with contempt'; thus, it means he does not approach in a contemptuous manner, i.e., he does not harm him. Likewise, you do not let *drāsat*—that is, you do not let *go*—that person toward *guru*, meaning heavy, increased, and unavoidable suffering. O Ādityas, you who are far-extending (*saprathaḥ*).

1. In the case of *manu*, there is no *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, or *śa*. 2. [The syllables] beginning with *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* are excluded. 3. *Gha* signifies the swift-moving Ādityas; *kha*, *ta*, *na*, and *sa* signify wealth (*dhana*); *śa* signifies the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). 4. [One who possesses] *na* and *śa* goes.

May he not suffer for it. The word *uśat* is a filler. *Śarma* means happiness. "May he not suffer for that which I have bestowed upon him. **Verse 8:** O Gods, we are indeed among you, like warriors in their armor. You [protect us] from great sin; you protect us from near [sin]. You protect us from great sin; you protect us from even small sin. **Verse 9:** May Aditi protect us; may Aditi grant us happiness. She is the mother of Mitra, the wealthy Aryaman, and Varuṇa. Yours are the aids; yours are the good aids; yours are the aids. *ādityāḥ | ava | hi | khyata | adhi | kūlāt'iva | sparaḥ | sutīrtham | arvataḥ | yātha | anu | naḥ | neṣatha | sugam | anehasaḥ | vaḥ | ūtayaḥ | su'ūtayaḥ | vaḥ | ūtayaḥ || 11 ||* 1. *ta-na-tana*; *bha-na-bha1-2-pāpa*; *śa-tena*. 2. *ta-śa-pāpa*; *na-bha1-2-pāpa*. O Ādityas, look down [on us] as one looks over the edge of a bank from a distance. Like a horse [reaching] a good watering place, come to us; lead us along a good path. Your aids are without fail; your aids are excellent; your aids are excellent. (Note: Regarding the variants, *ta-na-tana* refers to the reading *tena*; *bha-na-bha1-2-pāpa* refers to the reading *pāpa*.)
O Ādityas, descend indeed; like a touch from the riverbank, lead us along a good path, as one leads a horse to a fair ford. Without fail are your aids; excellent are your aids. 11.
O Ādityas, you must indeed protect us; look down upon us as we stand below.
Therein lies the illustration:
from the bank, the touch [of the water] on the bank is clearly perceived.
The meaning is "they stand.
Just as a man standing on a bank, desiring to know whether water has flowed downward or wishing to observe the people situated there, would look down;

in that same way, having done so, just as horse-guards lead swift horses to a *sutīrtha*—an excellent place for descent—so do you lead us, *anu nepatha*, that is, guide us along a *suga*, a good path.

There is no blessing here for the demon, nor for the one who seeks to harm, nor for the one who approaches with malice. Yet there is blessing for the swelling cloud, for the milch-cow, and for the hero who strives for glory. Your aids are free from fault; your aids are well-bestowed; your aids are indeed effective. 12.
O Ādityas, let there be no prosperity, welfare, or happiness here on this earth for the one possessing *rakṣas*— that is,
for the powerful one who hates us;
let there be no prosperity for him who comes to harm us.
Likewise, may it not come upon those who approach with harmful intent.
If so, for whom shall it be? It is said: may there be well-being for the cattle, and may that which belongs to you also be yours.
The word "ca" (and) refers to the cow and other items that will be mentioned later.
Furthermore, may there be prosperity for the cow that has recently calved;
may there be prosperity for the hero, our son and others.
To what kind of hero?
To one seeking renown (*śravasyate*), that is, desiring food (*anna*).
Furthermore, the word "not" (*na*) also carries over into the latter half [of the verse].
Its meaning is: "May there be no welfare for the bodies of cows and others who are opposed to us."

O gods, whatever evil deed exists, whether manifest or hidden—may Trita Āptya carry all that far away from us. Your aids are faultless; your aids are well-bestowing; your aids are indeed well-bestowing. Whatever evil deed exists, O gods, whether manifest or hidden—may Trita Āptya carry all that far away from us. Faultless are your aids; well-bestowing are your aids; your aids are indeed well-bestowing.
O divine Ādityas, whatever evil deed has become manifest, whatever misdeed exists that is hidden or concealed—
*apīcya* being a name for what is concealed—
may all that, both of these, not exist within me, in Trita Āptya.
But rather, place it far away from us; set it at a distance.
One should worship the Sun with the remainder of the hymn beginning with "And that which [is evil] among cows," after having seen a bad dream.

Accordingly, having commenced with "Having seen an unpleasant dream," the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* (3.6.6) prescribes: "One should worship the Sun with the five verses beginning with 'And that which is evil in cows.'"

3. In manuscript gha, it reads *asmadīyam* ("our").
Whatever evil dream is among the cattle, and whatever is against us, O Daughter of Heaven—O Radiant One, carry that away to Trita Āptya. Your aids are unfailing; your aids are well-bestowing. 14.
O Uṣas, daughter of heaven, O goddess, whatever evil dream— indicative of misfortune— that has been seen regarding our cows (the word *duṣvapnya* here having the suffix *yat* used reflexively),
and furthermore, whatever evil dream has been seen among us; [all that, drive away].
The meaning is: "O Vibhāvarī, remove all those bad dreams that we see which have the cowherds as their cause and which have us as their cause."
O goddess who shines forth, swell for Trita and carry him away; cast him far off.

Whether they wear a golden ornament or a garland, O Daughter of Heaven, you entrust all evil dreams to Trita Āptya. Your aids are faultless; your aids are excellent. Whether they wear a golden ornament or a garland, O Daughter of Heaven, you entrust all evil dreams to Trita Āptya. Your aids are faultless; your aids are excellent. 15.
O Dawn, daughter of heaven, may [the goldsmith] fashion a *niṣka*—or indeed some other kind of ornament—for the goldsmith, whatever bad dream was seen;
that is to say, whatever was seen by the goldsmith at the time of its manufacture.
The word *vā* is used for emphasis.
The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and).
Or, alternatively (*atha vā*), they shall make a garland for themselves today;
the meaning is "they are making."

Furthermore, whatever bad dream was seen by that garland-maker at the time of making the garland—that evil dream concerning both [the king and the maker], which rests upon Trita, the son of the Waters (*apām putra*), you place far away; you cast it off.
The meaning is: "We, as Tritas, abandon it.
Or alternatively:
Whatever bad dream has been seen by me while in the third state [of sleep], that you entrust to the goldsmith or the garland-maker;
having extracted it even from us, we place it upon those two.

To him who has approached that food, who has approached that labor, who has approached that portion—for Trita and for Dvita—carry away the evil dream! Your aids are unassailable; your aids are well-aiding; your aids are [well-aiding]. To him who has approached that food, who has approached that labor, who has approached that portion—for Trita and for Dvita—carry away the evil dream! Your aids are unassailable; your aids are well-aiding; your aids are [well-aiding].
To him whose food is that very thing which is well known as fit for consumption during the waking state— such as honey, milk-porridge, and so forth— even in the dream state;
to such a one.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of eating what is directly perceived, there is likewise a "consumer" (bhoktṛ) even in a dream. Likewise, regarding the refutation of that [position]: he whose action in the dream state is the very same censurable action that is performed during the waking state is "one who possesses that action" (tatkarmā).

To such a god, [I offer] that portion: the evil dream (duḥsvapna)—[variants: *duḥsvapna* (kha, na, bha 1–3), *duḥsvapnam* (ta, na, bha-ra), *duḥṣvapnyam* (śa)]. [The variants for the verb are: *paridadhasy upari* (kha, ta, bha, pa); *paridadhasi pari* (gha, na, śa).
3. ga-niṣkṛṣṭayoḥ; tara-2-śa-niṣkṛṣṭayoḥ; na-niṣkṛṣyetayoḥ | 4.

kha-gha-ta-bha- devāha; na-tadevā | O Goddess Uṣas, for Trita and Dvita who have approached this portion—that is, who have attained it—carry away the evil dream, which pertains to the sphere of harmful actions, and place it elsewhere.
The meaning is: may that which was seen in the dream—the eating of honey and so forth—be as pleasant as what is experienced in the waking state.
Just as we pay back a sixteenth part, an eighth part, or a debt, even so do we pay back all evil dreams to Āptya. Your aids are never-failing; your aids are well-performed.

Just as we pay back a sixteenth part, just as we pay back an eighth part, just as we pay back a debt, so do we pay back all evil dreams upon the Āptya. Your aids are free from danger; your aids are truly effective. 17.
They have prepared the consecrated animal for the purpose of giving; "just as" (yathā) in whatever manner they transfer a "portion" (kalām)—meaning a hoof—to another place, so [they do].
Now, the other word "yathā" is a filler.
Or alternatively:

Just as they collect the portions of the heart and other limbs for the sake of the sacrificial cuttings (*avadāna*), and just as they collect the *śapha*—that which is characterized by the hoof, such as the hoof-bone and so forth—for the sake of that which is not a sacrificial cutting, or just as they gradually pay off a debt, even so do we collect—that is, we remove—all evil dreams while they are still present within the reach of the Āptya. We have conquered; we have risen above this [evil]; we have become sinless.
O Uṣas, from whatever evil dream we have been afraid, may that shine away, for your aids are unfailing; your aids are for those who perform good deeds.

We have conquered; we have cast off evil; we have become sinless. O Uṣas, may that bad dream from which we were afraid fade away. May your aids be free from danger; may your aids be excellent; may your aids be good. 18.
May we, as the three, conquer evil; may we be victorious; may we obtain and enjoy happiness or well-being;
and may we become sinless and free from evil.
O Uṣas, may that evil from which we were afraid—that bad dream—shine away; let it depart.
(10) The sixth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "I have partaken of the sweet," is composed by Pragātha of the Kaṇva family; its deity is Soma, and it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The fifth [verse] is in the Jagatī meter;
Soma is its deity.
Thus it has been enumerated: “*Svādoḥ* [begins] with five fewer [syllables], a *pragātha*; it belongs to Soma, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and the fifth [verse] is in the Jagatī.”
The application of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics:
"I have eaten of the sweet food, being wise; I have partaken of the well-prepared [oblation] that finds wide space.
All the gods and mortals approach it, calling it honey."

From the savory [Soma], I have partaken with wisdom, being well-disposed and a finder of wide space. He whom all the gods and mortals approach from every side, calling him "Honey. 1. From the savory [Soma], I have partaken with wisdom, being well-disposed and a finder of wide space. He whom all the gods and mortals approach from every side, calling him "Honey."

I am Pragātha, the wise one of excellent intellect (*sumedhāḥ*), well-versed in study (*svādhyaḥ*), and of good deeds (*sukarmā*). [I praise] these [deeds] of *vayas*, that is, food—of that which is highly honored (*varivovitta*), of that which is delicious (*svāduḥ*) and worthy of being well-eaten. These are genitive forms [governing the preceding words]. (Note: Regarding the variants: 1. kha, ta, and sa read *saṃstuvanto*; ga reads *stuvanto*; na reads *saṃstuvanto*.)
2. In manuscripts kha, ga, ta, na, bha, and śa, the word ‘ca’ is absent. 3. In manuscripts kha, ga, ta, na, bha, and śa, it reads ‘apāgacchatu’.
[The meaning is: "May I consume—that is, may I not exhaust—the food characterized by the syllable *u*, which is the age and the Soma."

That state which all the gods, including Indra and others, as well as mortals, human beings, approach and reach, calling it "honey"—meaning they declare, "This is delightful"—that food he has eaten. At the leading forward of the two fires, this verse beginning with "antaśca" is used.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "antaśca prāgā aditirmavāsi śyeno na yoniṃ sadanaṃ dhiyā kṛtam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.10).
And within, Aditi has extended the eastern quarters with the splendor of divine power;
enjoying Indra’s friendship, may you, like a draft-ox following the yoke, prosper toward riches.
Within, you have gone forth; may you become Aditi, the deliverer from the divine fury. O Indu, enjoying the friendship of Indra, may you succeed toward wealth like a draft-ox following the yoke. 2.
O Soma, you have gone within;
you enter into the heart or into the sacrificial hall.
And having entered, you become the one who is subject to Aditi, the one who separates—that is, the one who keeps apart—the divine *haras*, which is anger.
"Hara" is a name for anger.
O "Indo," Soma, you, "juṣāṇaḥ"—that is, serving—the "sakhyaṃ," friendship, of "Indrasya," Indra, are "śrauṣṭhī.
"Śruṣṭi" is a name for speed.
The daughter of Śr̥ṣṭi is related to him.
And like a "yoke" for the swift [chariot], may you "prosper after" (*anv-ṛdhyāḥ*)—that is, you follow—for our acquisition of wealth (*rāye*).
Or rather, just as a horse brings one to the desired destination by means of the yoke, so likewise bring us there.
The meaning is that they are to be performed in successive order.
The two verses beginning with "We have drunk Soma" (*apāma somam*) are respectively applied to the touching of the chest and the touching of the heart after the drinking of Soma.

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the words 'We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; be auspicious to our heart, O Indu, when drunk,' they should touch their mouths and hearts" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.6).
We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have found the light, O gods.
What can hostility now do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do?
We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods. What can hostility now do to us? What, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do? 3.
O immortal Soma, we drink you; we shall drink you.
Thereby, we have become—indeed, may we become—immortal.
Since you are immortal, therefore we, who were drinking [the Soma], shall also become immortal.
Afterwards, we have gone to the "light," the shining heaven;
we have found, that is, we have come to know, the gods.
What indeed could an enemy, a foe, do now to us who have become such as we are?
And what, moreover, could the malice of a mortal, one who has become a mere human, do to me now?
O Indu, be a source of well-being to our heart when drunk; O Soma, be very gracious like a father to his son.
Like a friend to friends, O wise one of wide renown, prolong our life-span, O Soma, that we may live.

Be auspicious to our heart when drunk, O Indu; like a father to his son, O Soma, be very gracious. Like a friend to a friend, O wise one of wide renown, prolong our life-span, O Soma, that we may live. (4)

1. *ga-śabdayantaḥ* (those making the sound *ga*). 2. *kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa-tvam*. 3. *ga-bha-dhṛtvā*. 4. *kha-ta-na-bha-1-2-praya*; *ga-naya*; *śa-rāya*. 5. *kha-ta-1-2-amṛta avida*. 6. *kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa-artha tathābhūtān*. 7. *ta3-na bha1-cā*; *śa-ca*.
O *indu*, O Soma, being drunk by us, may you become *śam*—happiness—for our *hṛde*, that is, for our heart.
Regarding the arising of happiness, there are two examples.

Just as a father is for his own son, his offspring, so as to bring him happiness; or just as a friend, who establishes one in one's own welfare rather than in what is harmful, is "suśevaḥ"—meaning very kind or very pleasant—toward his own harvest; even so, may you also become [such]. *Śeva* is a name for happiness. Be like that.
Furthermore, O Soma, you who are praised in many ways by many or who possess great fame—O wise one, extend our life-force for our living, so that we may live. Increase our longevity.
These drops, when drunk, protect me—bringing wide renown—just as oxen fasten together the joints of a chariot.
May they guard me from the slipping of my foot, and may these drops preserve me from my own self today.
These [are] not drunk.
of fame; glorious; renowned; illustrious; having a good reputation; famous.

O Soma, O King, be gracious to us for our well-being. We are your devotees (*vratyāḥ*); know that. Our strength (*dakṣaḥ*) and our spirit (*manyuḥ*) are failing, O Indu; do not surrender us to the will of the enemy. O Soma, O King, be gracious to us for our well-being. We are your devotees (*vratyāḥ*); know that. Our strength (*dakṣaḥ*) and our spirit (*manyuḥ*) are failing, O Indu; do not surrender us to the will of the enemy. For you, O Soma, are indeed the guardian of our bodies. You sit within every limb, watching over men. Even though we may violate your sacred laws (*vratāni*), be gracious to us, O God, as a good friend, for our ultimate welfare. May I be united with the companion who has a soft belly—the one who, when drunk, shall not harm me, O Lord of Bay Horses (*hari-aśva*). This Soma which has been placed within us—for its sake, I go to Indra to prolong our life. Those ailments have departed; diseases have vanished. They have fled far away from us. Soma, the pervasive one, has ascended into us. We have gone to where they prolong life. (Notes: 1. *gha-iva*: Just as he causes growth by raining, so too [does Soma]. 2. *khata-na-bha-śa-eṣaṇena*: By driving away. 3. *bhara-hiṃset*; *bha1-hiṃsat*: May he harm.)

May those irresistible and powerful afflictions depart; may the female spirits of disease flee in terror. Soma has ascended upon us with wide-striding vigor, reaching the place where they prolong our life-span.
(11) Those aforementioned irresistible and powerful afflictions—may they go away.
Those powerful *tarmiṣīcī* waters, which terrified us, reached us, and thus made us tremble; they were afraid.
He states the reason for their departure:
because Soma, being vast (*vihāyas*), has ascended to or come upon us, they have therefore departed—this is the sense.
When that Soma has been drunk, in which men prolong—that is, increase—their lifespan, to that Soma they have gone.
O Fathers, that immortal drop which, when drunk from the heart, has entered into mortals—that Soma we shall worship with an oblation; may we abide in his favor and in his goodwill.

O Fathers, that immortal drop of ours which, when drunk within our hearts, has entered into mortals devoid of thought—to that Soma we would pay worship with an oblation; may we abide in his favor and his benevolence. 12.

O Pitṛs, that immortal drop (indu) which, having been drunk within our hearts and being devoid of thought, has entered into us mortals—to that Soma we shall offer worship with an oblation; we shall serve him.
May we abide in the favor of this Soma, in his bliss and in his benevolent disposition.

In the Mahāpitṛyajña, regarding the offering "to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, a cake," the *yājyā* is "O Soma, you... This is also formulated in the Sūtra: "O Soma, in agreement with the Pitṛs... the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass [grant] wide spaces" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19). Furthermore, this is also the *yājyā* for the *saumya* oblation at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
For it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the verse 'O Soma, in agreement with the fathers,' [one offers] the libation to Soma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.19).
O Soma, in harmony with the Fathers, you have extended yourself across heaven and earth. To you, O Indu, we pay worship with this oblation; may we be masters of riches.
O Soma, being in harmony with the Fathers, you have extended yourself across heaven and earth. To you, O Indu, we pay worship with an oblation; may we be masters of riches. 13.
O Soma, you, being in harmony with the ancestors and uniting with them, have extended yourself across heaven and earth; you spread them out in succession.
To that Soma let us offer worship with oblations and serve him.
May we become masters of riches and treasures.
O protecting gods, speak for us; let neither sleep nor idle chatter have power over us.
May we, ever dear to Soma, with noble heroes, proclaim our wisdom at the assembly.
O protecting gods, speak for us! Let not sleep master us, nor idle chatter; may we, ever dear to Soma, with noble heroes, proclaim our wisdom in the assembly. 14.
O gods, you who are our protectors and guardians, speak for us; grant us your favor.
Furthermore, let not sleep and slumber have power over us—that is, let them not be able to afflict us—and likewise, let not idle chatter.

1. In the versions *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, there is no "suffering" (*apīḍāḥ*). 2. In *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *ra*, *śa*, and *apa-rāme*; in *gha*: "may they abandon the offense" (*tyajaṃtu aparādhe*). 3. In *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*: "at death" (*martau*). 4. In *kha*, *ta*, and *bha*: "only this" (*apīyameva*). May the reviler not revile us.
May we be dear to Soma—dear ones—at all times, throughout all days.
The meaning is "at all times.

Being *subīrāsaḥ*, that is, possessing excellent sons, may we address the *vidatha*, the hymn of praise; that is, may we speak toward it. Alternatively, being possessed of good sons, may we address the *vidatha*, the house.
Addressing his sons and grandsons, he enticed them with wealth.
"O Soma, you [are] for us from every side"—this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation in the animal sacrifice to Soma.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Soma, you who bestow vital strength upon us from every side; those abodes of yours which are in heaven and those which are on earth" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
O Soma, you are the bestower of vital strength upon us from every side; you, the beholder of men, enter into us with heavenly light.
O Indu, being of one mind with us through your aids, protect us from behind and also from the front.

O Soma, you are the bestower of vital strength upon us from every side; as the finder of light, enter us, O beholder of men. O Indu, being well-disposed, protect us with your aids from behind and also from the front.
O Soma, you are the bestower of vital strength (*vayodhāḥ*) and the giver of food for us from all directions;
likewise, as the finder of heaven (*svarvit*), the beholder of men (*nṛcakṣas*), do you enter into us.
O Indu, being well-pleased (*sajoṣaḥ*), come with your aids (*ūtibhiḥ*).
Or else, the Maruts are those who go;
accompanied by them, protect us from behind, and also from the front.
Or else, the Vālakhilya [Sūkta].
The first hymn.
Sing forth to Indra, the bounteous giver, as is known;
he who, possessing many riches, bestows gifts upon his singers even by the thousands.
1. By means of the vowels *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *ūti*.
2. *Gha*: protect, guard. Commentary on the Vālakhilya Hymns.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. May Hari, who dwells within the solar orb and whose bliss is like that of the moon, protect us—he who causes the Lakṣmī of the meaning of the Vedas to blossom within the heart. The first hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "Abhi pra vaḥ," is the seer's own composition (*ārṣam*) by Praskaṇva and is dedicated to Indra. It is cataloged thus: "Abhi pra daśa; Praskaṇva; it is a *pragātha*. The meter of the odd-numbered verses is *Bṛhatī*, and the meter of the even-numbered verses is *Satobṛhatī*. The specific application (*viniyoga*) is to be understood from the ritual manuals (*sūtra*). (Verse 1) The Seer speaks of himself: "O Praskaṇva, *vaḥ*—[for] you [plural used] with reference to your sons and grandsons—directly worship Indra, who is your master. Therein is an illustration: just as you worship your own learned teacher (*vidvāṃsam*), so [should you worship him]. Of what nature is he? *Surādhasam*: one whose wealth (*rādhaḥ*) or gift is excellent. Who is this Indra? He who is *Maghavā*, the possessor of wealth..."
In a manuscript designated as "Jha" obtained from the Government Sanskrit Pathashala in Varanasi, a commentary on the Vālakhilya hymns is found to have been written.
However, because it is not found in any of the other manuscripts and because its style of exposition differs, it is clearly perceived that this was not composed by Sāyaṇācārya.
Nevertheless, thinking that it might be of use to scholars, it is provided here.
Regarding this matter, the authorities of this Pathashala, when questioned by us, have written as follows: "This manuscript was purchased for the Pathashala in the city of Revā;
it is heard that its transcription took place in Puṇyapattana itself.
It is impossible to state with certainty who composed the commentary on the Bālakhilya-sūkta contained in this manuscript."
It is certain that this was not composed by any scholar residing in Vārāṇasī.

Sing forth your praise to Indra, the most bountiful, as he is known to be—he who, as a liberal lord possessing many riches, bestows gifts upon his singers as if with a thousandfold wealth. (RV 8.97.1)

Like Śatānīka, he advances boldly; he slays the Vṛtras for the sake of the donor. Like the streams from a mountain, the gifts of him who possesses abundant nourishment flow forth abundantly. Like Śatānīka, he goes forward with courage; he slays the obstacles for the one who offers oblations. Like the juices from a mountain, the gifts of him who provides much sustenance overflow.

O Indra, lover of songs, may the pressed drops, the exhilarating juices, come to you; O wielder of the thunderbolt, O hero, they fill you for the sake of bounty, as waters fill a lake that is their own home. 3. *ā tvā sutāsa indavo madā ya indra girvaṇaḥ | āpo na vajrin anvokyaṃ saraḥ pṛṇanti śūra rādhase || 3 ||*

O Maghavan, drink this most sweet, faultless, furthering, and eloquent draught; for as you, being exhilarated, scatter [gifts] upon us, so may you boldly bestow them yourself like a shower of rain. 4. Faultless, furthering, eloquent, O Maghavan, most sweet—drink this! So that, being exhilarated, you may scatter [wealth] upon us; bestow it boldly by yourself, like a shower of rain. 4.
Puruvasu, the dweller of many, bestows and gives to the singers—the chanters of praise—an immeasurable amount, indeed by the thousands; "wealth and so forth" is the implied sense.
Here, the word *vā* serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
By a thousand alone (the word *iva* has the sense of restriction;
[it means] by a thousand alone).

(2) Indra, who by nature is bold and subdues his enemies, goes forth with force against the enemy armies as if they were countless, like [the leader of] a hundred hosts; he completely overcomes them and brings them under his control.
Furthermore, that Indra destroys and annihilates the *vṛtra*s—meaning evils or enemies—of the sacrificer who has offered oblations.
The gifts—gold and other riches—of this Indra, who possesses much food and many protectors;
for "gift" (*datra*) here refers to gold, as it is listed among the names for gold in the passage "the gift of the Maruts.
These gifts cause the world to swell—that is, they exceedingly gladden and satisfy it.
Here is an illustration:
just as the juices or waters belonging to a mountain or a cloud refresh the world, so it is in this case.

(3) O *girvaṇas*, O Indra worthy of praise with songs; those exhilarating drops, the pressed-out *soma* juices which exist as pressed libations—they, O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), O hero endowed with valor, fill you completely on every side, filling you so that you may dwell together [with them]. The meaning is that they satisfy you by the offering of their own essence.
How?
Like waters filling a lake; just as they fill a great reservoir of water, so it is. For what purpose?
For the prosperity of the sacrificer, that is, for the acquisition of wealth.
(4) O Indra, drink this Soma at the proper time, which is free from blemish;
what kind? That which promotes and causes growth.
The root *stṛ* preceded by *pra* has the meaning of "increasing.
*Vivakṣaṇam* means that which is to be praised with excellence; *maghavaḥ* means the most delicious, even sweeter than honey (*madhunaḥ*).
[This refers to] the object of desire (*kame-tam*).

By drinking of which you become exhilarated, O Haviṃdhin, and while partaking [of it], you scatter— that is, you bestow— the fruit fully and appropriately for us, the sacrificers. To whom, as it were?
O *dhṛṣat*, you who are the subduer of enemies, just as you yourself (*ātmanā*)—that is, by your own self—bestow [wealth] upon those who are wretched and miserable, so [do you bestow it here].
The prefix (*upasarga*) is to be supplied with the action of the verb (*yogakriyādhyāhāra*).

Run toward our hymn of praise like horses urged on by their drivers—O Indra, Lord of Self-Sovereignty, that which the milch-cows sweeten for you as gifts among the Kaṇvas. 6.14.5 Run toward our hymn of praise like horses urged on by their drivers—O Indra, Lord of Self-Sovereignty, that which the milch-cows sweeten for you as gifts among the Kaṇvas. 6.14.5 [Note: The Sanskrit text provided contains a repetition of verse 5.]

We have approached with homage the fierce hero, the pervasive one whose wealth is undecaying. O wielder of the thunderbolt, like a well for one who thirsts, our prayers flow forth toward you, O Indra, like streams of water.

Whatever indeed is present now, whatever is in the sacrifice, or whatever is upon the earth—from there, O great-minded one, O fierce one, come to our sacrifice with your swift and fierce steeds. || 7 ||

(5) O Indra, may you come toward and approach this specific hymn of praise (*stotra*) performed by our pressers—the *adhvaryu*s and others who perform the extraction of the *soma*—just as horses, being urged forward, reach their destination. Like what? Like horses being driven.

He reaches the place exactly as described; in that same way, O Indra, possessor of *svadhā* (food), your own cows—the *rātayaḥ* (gifts) consisting of offerings—which exist among us Kaṇvas, satisfy you (*svadayanti*). The meaning is that having entered your belly, they gratify you.
The phrase "you, sir, run toward" is to be connected with what precedes it.

(6) O Indra, we have approached you for refuge with reverence—that is, with oblations characterized by the *namas* offering—or else with a humble disposition (*namas*). Like what? Like a hero who especially puts his enemies to flight. We approach you thus. Like what? [Like a hero.]
Like one who has raised his fierce strength;
just as certain wretched people seek refuge in him, so [do they seek refuge] in you. Of what sort are you?
Endowed with various manifestations (*vibhūti*) and divine powers (*aiśvarya*),
or else having the nature of various abodes (*bhavana*),
according to the Vedic scripture: "By means of *māyās*, Indra moves in many forms."
This is because of another Vedic text: "He assumed a form corresponding to every form.

*Akṣitavasum* means one whose wealth is undiminished. Furthermore, O *vajrin*, O Indra who wields the thunderbolt, for you—unto you who sprinkle the fruits such as heaven and so forth—our *dhītayaḥ*, that is, our fingers, flow and pour out the Soma juice.
Like what?
Like a well (*udapāna*) that possesses water (*udakavat*). That is, like a pit or a well.
It flows just as water flows for one who sows grain and the like;
here, the word *iva* is redundant.
(7) O Mahemate, O Indra whose intellect is intent on worship, wherever you may certainly (*nūnam*) abide in some particular place.
Whether you abide at some sacrifice or ritual,
or whether you abide upon the earth,
from that particular place, O fierce one of uplifted power, come with your fierce, swift-moving horses to our sacrifice. Come hither!

(1) The seer speaks of himself:
"O Puṣṭigu, for the sake of attaining your desired goal (*abhiṣṭaye*), worship—that is, honor with excellence—the powerful Indra (*śakram*), who is capable in all deeds, in the most perfect manner.
Of what kind [is he]?"

[I praise] him who is renowned, famous, and endowed with beautiful wealth; that Indra who, for the sacrificer who presses the soma and offers praise, bestows— just as if by the thousands, though indeed beyond counting— the desirable, coveted treasure.
The root *mahi* has the meaning of giving (*dāna*),
because it occurs in that sense within verbal roots denoting the act of giving.

(2) When the pressed-out Soma juices have exhilarated this Indra—that is, when they have gladdened him—then his missiles, the weapons that accomplish power, overflow toward the *maghavan*s, the sacrificers who possess wealth in the form of oblations.
The meaning is that his [Indra’s] weapons bestow the wealth of his enemies upon them, thereby pleasing them. Like what?
*Bhujmā* means one who protects like a mountain or like a cloud;
just as that [cloud] satisfies the earth by bestowing waters, so too does he.
Furthermore, the seizing of the wealth of enemies is well-known from such Vedic scriptures as: "Bring forth the foods for those who act as enemies" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 5.4.5).
Of what kind are the weapons? They are "śatānīkāḥ," meaning those whose faces or points (anīkāni) are measured by a hundred.
The meaning is "facing in all directions.
For this very reason, they are difficult to cross and difficult to ward off.
They are called *samīpaḥ* because this food is perfectly (*samyak*) present within them.
Mahīḥ means great ones.
(3) O Indra, when the pressed drops, the *indavas*, the Soma juices—which are dear and beloved—have gladdened you, having exhilarated you with them;
then, O *Vasu* (Indra, from the root *vas*, "to cause to dwell"), for me, who have offered oblations to you, this sacrifice (*savana*) has been performed for my sake and brought to completion by you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
It is like water. Just as that [water] is rendered fruitful through bathing, drinking, and so forth, so it is in this case.
There is another illustration.
"Like milch-cows":

just as cows that yield the oblation (*havirdughā*) are made fruitful by the preparation of the *sānnāyya* offering and so forth, in the same way, the sacrifice is rendered fruitful by the drinking of Soma and other rites; this is the meaning.

The prayers flow toward you, the peerless one, who hastens for our protection; they pour forth the sweetness of the honeyed draught. O Vasu, the Soma drops, hastening toward you, have been placed within the hymns of praise. anehasam | vaḥ | haryamāṇam | ūtaye | madhvaḥ | kṣaranti | dhītayaḥ | ā | tvā | vaso iti | haryamāṇāsaḥ | indavaḥ | upa | stotreṣu | dadhire || 4 ||

O Soma, come to us at the well-performed sacrifice; hastening like a steed, you speed toward us. Forth [I praise] the hero, the fierce, the far-reaching, the winner of the bow, the distributor of great wealth. Like a well, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you have ever caused the waters to swell with abundance for the donor.
(4) O Ṛtviks, your *dhītis*—your fingers—flow with the sweet-tasting Soma for the sake of protection (*ūtaye*), directed toward Indra who is being invoked and praised;
what kind [of Indra]?
One who is faultless (*anehasam*).
"Anāhanas" means "not struck down";

the meaning is that he cannot be overcome by enemies. O Vāsu, O Indra, the bestower of dwelling, the *indavas*—the Soma juices—being praised and invoked, have placed you in their presence, having established you face-to-face during the hymns of praise.

(5) When there is a beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*) belonging to us, the sacrificers, and when the drinking of Soma (*soma-pāna*) has become the occasion, Indra—moving like a courser (*atya*), that is, like a horse characterized by constant motion—*ātośate*: he strikes down our enemies. The root *tośati* signifies the act of killing, as it is listed among the words for killing in the passage: "He strikes down (*nitośate*), he slays (*nivarhayati*)."
Having brought Indra before his very eyes, [the poet] says:

O Indra, skilled in tasting (*svadāvan*), those *gūrtayaḥ*—your own exalted hymns of praise—which please you, that is, which cause you to taste yourself, you, being such, do desire (*chandayase*) the invocation (*havam*), the praise of yourself, among the *pauraḥ*, the multitude of city-dwellers;
the meaning is that you long for your own praise to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
(6) O Indra, O hero, I especially implore and request from you the great wealth— the riches— that impels the enemies. (The fifth case ending is used in the sense of the object.)
Due to the force of the prefix (*upasarga*), an appropriate verb must be supplied.

Of what kind are you? You are *ugram*—vigorous and powerful; *vivicim*—the distributor of merit and demerit; *dhanaspṛtam*—the bestower of wealth; *vibhūtim*—endowed with various sovereign powers (*vibhūtis*). Therefore, O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, [you are for] the *dāśuṣe*—the giver of oblations.
The fourth case is used for the object (*karman*).
"Always" (*sadā*) means at all times; "with wealth" (*vasutvanā*) means by the giving of riches. "You satisfy" (*pīpetha*) means you cause to swell; the sense is that you cause [them] to increase.
Like what? Like a well (*udra*)— that is, a water-holding pit—
as it nourishes the world by the giving of water, so too does he.

Whether you are indeed in the far distance, or on the earth, or in heaven—O Indra, yoking your bay steeds, O great-minded, lofty one, come hither with your lofty companions. (7) Whether you are indeed in the far distance, or on the earth, or in heaven—O Indra, yoking your bay steeds, O great-minded, lofty one, come hither with your lofty companions. (7)

O chariot-borne ones, those bay steeds of yours which, never failing, surpass the vigor of the wind—with them you strike down the Dasyu for Manu, and with them you go around the celestial realm. 8. O chariot-borne ones, those bay steeds of yours which, never failing, surpass the vigor of the wind—with them you strike down the Dasyu for Manu, and with them you go around the celestial realm. 8.

O Vasu, O Hero, we shall provide for you as much as you require, more even than a man’s need, so that you may protect Etaśa in the struggle for wealth, and Vaśa at Darśavrja. 9. As much as this—of you—O Vasu—we shall provide—O Hero—more than a man’s [need].

As at Kaṇva’s, O Maghavan, at Medhya’s sacrifice, at Dīrghanītha’s, at Darbūnasa’s; as at Gośarya’s, O wielder of the stone (Adrivat), you sought to win for me the stall of kine adorned with bay horses. Now the third hymn: Just as you drank the pressed Soma, O Indra, at Manu Sāṃvaraṇi’s, so drink it now at Nīpātithi’s, O Maghavan, at Medhyātithi’s, at Puṣṭigu’s, and at Śruṣṭigu’s, together. The son of Pṛṣadvān restored Praskaṇva, who had been cast down and was lying exhausted. The seer sought to win thousands of cattle from the Dasyu Vṛka, who possessed the sword. Pārṣadvāṇa restored Praskaṇva, who was lying prostrate, exhausted and cast down. He sought to win thousands of cattle; the seer [sought them] from you... [the Dasyu] Vṛka.

He who does not fail when praised with hymns, he who is wise and the inspirer of seers—to that Indra speak with a manly thought, as one who desires to provide for the enjoyment of the non-injuring [worshipper]. 3.

He to whom they have sung the sevenfold hymn, three-layered, in the highest station—he indeed has roared through all these worlds; then indeed was manly power born.
