Him who is the giver of riches to us, that Indra we invoke; for may we obtain all his most recent favor in a stall full of cattle, O thou whose thoughts are on the kine. (5) He who is the giver of riches to us—that Indra we invoke; for may we obtain all his most recent favor in a stall full of cattle, O thou whose thoughts are on the kine. (5) || 18 ||

(3) The seer speaks of himself: "O you who hear! That Indra, when praised with hymns—by means of *ukthas*, that is, songs of praise—is not [merely] praised; being conscious (*cikit*), he perceives the knowledge of the praiser; he attends to it.
The root *vidh* has the sense of attending."
He speaks thus, declaring that you possess perfect knowledge:

"Addressing that Indra—the Supreme Lord who is the impeller (*codana*) of the sages, or the impeller and instigator of the *ṛṣis*, the mantras, and those who have seen them—speak, with a newer [or most recent] thought (*mati*), a hymn of praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"You do not nourish one who is not harming; just as someone might utter a newer hymn for the sake of protecting their own master who is not harming—that is, who is non-violent—so it is here."
(4) For that Indra, for that Supreme Lord, they have praised—the Sun, the one worthy of worship, who abides in the highest station, the most excellent place known as the heavenly world;
all praise him.
His essential nature has been perceived through such scriptural passages as: "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6).
The meaning is that all worship the sun. Of what sort is the sun?
It is the one with seven rays.
He is one whose rays are seven in number and preeminent like heads;
he is the nourisher of the three realms—the sustainer of the three worlds beginning with the earth.
Indeed, the Sun’s role as the nourisher of the three worlds is well known through his activities such as sending rain.

He whom they worship with oblations so that they may attain their true nature is indeed the Supreme Lord. Addressing all these visible worlds (*viśvā bhuvanāni*)—the entire multitude of beings in the form of gods, asuras, and humans—he has cried out; he roars with the voice of the intermediate region, using sounds expressive of restraint, compassion, and generosity.
Immediately thereafter, he brings forth, generates, and manifests his manly strength (*pauṃsya*), characterized by skill and power.
This is the meaning:
at the beginning, the Supreme Lord instructs those dwelling on earth for their benefit by means of His own speech, characterized as the thundering of clouds;
and when that is not heard, He subsequently manifests the instruction characterized as the lightning and so forth.
The meaning stated here has been elaborated upon in the *Khilakāṇḍa* of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (5.2) by the passage beginning with, "Three indeed were the sons of Prajāpati."
(5) We, the worshippers, invoke—that is, we call upon—that Indra, the Supreme Lord, who is the giver of *vasūni*—that is, of riches which are the causes of dwelling—for us.

For we know—that is, we recognize—the most recent (*navīyasī*), never before performed, auspicious favor (*sumati*) and benevolent mind of Indra; therefore, we invoke him. This is the connection with the preceding [verse].

By which good intellect we may go to—that is, obtain as our own mastership over—this pen rich in cattle, protected by a cowherd, and containing a multitude of animals such as elephants, horses, and so forth.

To whomsoever you, O Vasu, grant for the sake of giving, he attains the increase of wealth. As such, O Maghavan Indra, lover of songs, we, pressing the Soma, call upon you. 6. He who has reached out toward Krivi with his might, making *Śuṣṇa* resound with his blows; when he propped up and spread out that heaven, then indeed was the earthly one born as the first. He for whom this entire world—the Ārya, the Dāsa, and the enemy who guards the treasure—is subject;
even across the Ārya Ruśama Pavīru, that wealth is driven forth.

(6) O Vaso, O Indra, you who provide dwelling, for whichever sacrificer you exert yourself—that is, you command—for the sake of giving, for the purpose of bestowing wealth, that sacrificer attains and enjoys the increase and abundance of riches (*rāyas poṣam*).
It is marvelous that the sacrificer whom you impel to give wealth becomes enriched with treasures through the attainment of wealth by virtue of his hope in you.
Therefore, O Girvaṇas, O Maghavan, O Indra worthy of praise with songs, we, desiring the pressed Soma, invoke you, such as you are.

(7) O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, let the gift—the offering of the oblation—be quickly and certainly presented; indeed, it becomes ever more abundant for you, the radiant God, the Supreme Lord. It is brought right into your presence and becomes united with you.
The intention is this: even a very small amount, when swiftly offered into the true vessel, increases and becomes joined with the Lord.
Therefore, O Indra, O Supreme Lord, you are never—not at any time—a *starīḥ*, that is, a destroyer or injurer, toward the donor, the sacrificer who has presented the oblation.
Rather, you associate with him;
the meaning is that you establish friendship with him.
According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.1.6, "prasamupohaḥ pādapūraṇe," the doubling of the word *upa* is for the purpose of filling out the meter.

(8) Indra, who with his lethal blows—the strikes of his weapons—utterly making the nameless Asura Śuṣṇa, the deformed Krivi, resound by means of his might and strength, has thoroughly and pre-eminently pervaded [the world].
The meaning is that having slain the Asura, he manifested his own power everywhere. To the question "When? he replies:
As soon as that Asura, expanding himself and making himself wide, propped up—that is, made firm—the sky, the celestial world visible in the distance;
immediately thereafter (ādit), the terrestrial fire was born, it manifested.
The meaning is: at the very moment when Agni was produced by the obstruction of the breaths of the worlds.
(9) This entire visible host of Āryas, belonging to the Asuras, is the enemy and adversary of that Indra.
Of what nature is he?
He is the Dāsa, the destroyer of the beginningless [world], the guardian of treasures.

He protects—that is, guards—the treasure-trove. Likewise, he belongs to the Asuras and others. This one is the All. By the Aryas, the Dāsa is the guardian of the treasure-trove; he is the enemy. Even beyond that, for the sake of the noble Ruśama Pavīru, wealth is indeed driven forth for you alone. 9.
The inspired singers have sung the hymn, sweet with honey and dripping with ghee;
for us wealth has spread abroad, and manly strength; for us the pressed drops flow.
The wise ones have sung the hymn, dripping with ghee and rich in sweetness. For us, wealth has spread forth; for us, manly strength and power. For us, the drops of Soma are being pressed. 10. 9.
Now begins the fourth hymn.
Just as you drank the pressed soma, O Śakra, when Manu Vivasvat was king; just as you, Indra, took pleasure in Trita Chandra, so do you rejoice together with Āyu.
As you, O Śakra, drank the pressed Soma in the presence of Manu Vivasvat; as you, O Indra, take pleasure in the hymn of Trita, so do you rejoice together with Āyu.
The meaning is: he who takes away the wealth of others while protecting his own. By that Indra, against the Ruśamas—those inauspicious enemies—that *pavīravī* [weapon] was indeed hidden within;
for *pavī* refers to the chariot-felly, and those whose ends are within it are called *pavīrās*.
That wheel is "pavīravi. Regarding this, the Nirukta should be consulted, starting with the passage: "The *pavī* becomes [manifest] through chariots" (Nirukta 5.5).
Such a wheel is cast forth, that is, hurled.
Having made it manifest, it is stated in the fourth quarter:
"O Indra, for you alone, for your sake, that wealth—characterized by its totality, a mass of riches existing among the host of Asuras—is being cast forth (ajyate) by the host of enemies.

The intention is this: if even the gift of a discus hidden among the host of Asuras became a bestower of treasure for Indra, then what need is there to mention that a gift of wealth hidden within the seven [sages] would yield great fruit?
(10) *tuṇyavaḥ*: hastening;
the wise (*viprāsaḥ*), that is, the intelligent sacrificers, have followed after, i.e., they praise, Indra, who is worthy of praise (*arkam*). Of what kind [is he]?
"Sweet" means endowed with sweet nectar; "distilled from ghee" means pouring forth water by breaking open the clouds—that is, causing rain. With what intention do they worship? It is said:
"May wealth"—a mass of riches—"be spread abroad among us."
Likewise, may there be virility (*vṛṣṇya*), meaning the power to procreate, and strength (*śava*).
Furthermore, may the *indavas*—the Soma drops—be pressed out for us.
The meaning is that, with the intention that all this may be accomplished within us solely through the favor of Indra, [may it be so].

The hymn beginning with "yathā manau vivasvati," consisting of ten verses, is the fourth [hymn] of the [fifth] maṇḍala; it is addressed to Āyu and Indra. It is cataloged as: "yathā manāvāyuḥ. The seer (ṛṣi) is Āyu Kāṇva. The deity (devatā) is Indra. The metre (chandas) of the odd-numbered verses is Bṛhatī, and the metre of the even-numbered verses is Satobṛhatī. The ritual application (viniyoga) is to be understood from the Sūtra.
(1) O Śakra, O powerful Indra, just as you drank the Soma—pressed for the sake of Vivasvat’s son, Vaivasvata Manu—in whatever manner;
and just as you, O Indra, O Supreme Lord, greatly enjoy (jujoṣasi) the Vedic collection (chandas) existing within the seer named Trita;
so too, having partaken together with me, Āyu, of both that Soma characterized by the meters and that [other essence], you exhilarate (mādayase) both me and yourself.

O Pṛṣṭha, Medhya, Mātariśvan, Indra, when the Soma was being pressed, you rejoiced, just as [you did] at Darśiśva, Darśoṇya, Syūmaraśmi, and Arjunasa. 2. Pṛṣṭha, Medhya, Mātariśvan, O Indra, when the Soma was being pressed, you rejoiced, just as [you did] at Darśiśva, Darśoṇya, Syūmaraśmi, and Arjunasa. 2.

He who milks the exclusive hymns of praise, he who boldly drank the Soma—for him Viṣṇu strode out his three steps according to the ordinances of Mitra. 3. He who is our giver is our father—great, fierce, and the maker of sovereign power.
May that formidable Maghavan, rich in many cattle, grant us the gift of kine and horses.
(2) O Indra, just as you rejoiced— having drunk the Soma present with the seer named Pṛṣṇi while the Soma was being pressed—
and just as you rejoiced having drunk the Soma present with Medhya, Mātariśvan, Darśiśra, Darśoṇya, Syūmaraśmi, and Ṛjūnas— all these seers—
in that same way, you gladden me; such is the connection with the preceding verse.
(3) That Indra who milks—that is, receives or heeds—the exclusive, exclusive *ukthas*, the hymns that have him as their sole master.
(The meaning is "he hears.
(He hears.)
Just as Indra, being bold and the subduer of enemies,
having become triumphant, drank the Soma; for that Indra’s sake,
Viṣṇu— the pervasive one, also known as Upendra— acted.
Of Mitra. Mitra is the deity presiding over the day; for the Śruti states: "Mitra is indeed the day, Varuṇa is the night" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 4.10).
Characterized by his own attributes—
namely, the activities of rising and setting— he strode across the three worlds with three steps, having specifically traversed them with three feet.
"May that Indra exhilarate us"—this is the prayer for blessing.

(4) O Vājin, possessor of food; O Śatakratu, performer of many deeds, O Indra: you who take delight (*cākanaḥ*) in the hymns (*stomeṣu*)—that is, in the praises serving as the cause—and in the *vāja*, the food characterized by the oblation, when these serve as the occasion for that sacrificer—him, such a one as you, O Indra, [we approach] desiring glory (*śravasyavaḥ*). "Glory" (*śravaḥ*) is a name for food.
Desiring food, we, the sacrificers, offer oblations; we present the sacrificial gift. In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like cowherds [approaching] a cow that yields milk well;
just as those who attend to milking give green grass and the like to a cow that gives good milk.

We implore you, O Maghavan Indra, the peerless among the wealthy, the eldest among the bulls, the breaker of forts, the finder of cattle, and the sovereign lord of riches.
Listen!
Furthermore, O Vasu, O Indra, the dweller, listen to our beautiful hymn of praise.
Moreover, just as you heard the invocation of Kaṇva, so too hear our invocation.

(9) O Ṛtviks, that ancient (*pūrvya*) and venerable (*manman*) prayer (*brahman*), which has been poured forth (*asāvi*)—that is, offered as a hymn (*stotra*) by you—proclaim (*vocata*) that prayer to Indra, the Supreme Lord, for his sake. For you belong to *ṛta*, the Truth, which is Indra; [proclaim] those many (*pūrvīḥ*), numerous (*vahīḥ*), and great (*bṛhatīḥ*) [forms]. By implication, this means the many great incarnations (*avatāra*) of Indra’s qualities.
They have praised [him], having made him the object of their hymn. Furthermore, they have created for me, the singer, the *medhās*—that is, intellects endowed with retentive power.
Therefore, I pray: "Speak forth to the great Indra."
(10) That Indra who thoroughly gathered together— meaning he perfectly fashioned— the vast and great riches, such as gold and other forms of wealth;
and that Indra who thoroughly fashioned— meaning he perfectly arranged— the two worlds,
heaven and earth (*kṣoṇī* being a designation for heaven and earth).
This is because the names "rodasī," "kṣoṇī," and "andhasī" are listed among its synonyms.
Furthermore, that Indra who generated— that is, produced— the auspicious self in the sun,
him Indra, the bright, radiant, pure, and purified waters— characterized as the *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhana*— have thoroughly exhilarated (*samamandiṣuḥ*), causing him perfect joy.
Furthermore, the cows, the heads of the cows, the cow’s milk, the Soma plants, and their juices have exhilarated that Indra.
Thus, "O you of such great majesty, you are Indra"—in this way the Brahman spoke for your sake; this is the connection with what precedes.
The fifth hymn, beginning with "upamaṃ tvā," consists of a single ṛc; it is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Medhya Kāṇva.
This is indicated by the statement: "'upamaṃ tvā' etc., [the seer is] Medhya.
The meter of the odd-numbered verses is Bṛhatī.
The metre of the *yuj* verses is *satobṛhatī*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is to be understood from the Sūtra.

The destroyer of enemy cities beyond measure, and therefore the bestower of cattle (*govidam*); the Lord (*īśānam*) of all sciences, as stated in the Śruti:

(2) O Indra, you who day by day—every single day—increasing exceedingly and being worthy of praise, have afflicted Āyu, the Ṛṣi of that name, and Atithigva, the Ṛṣi of that name, by granting boons;
they, considering themselves sufficient [to resist], ward you off.
But you, having said, "He begs for his desired boon," distress them by force; this is the meaning.
We, the sacrificers desiring food (*vājavantaḥ*), invoke you—such as you are, O Indra (*haryaśva*), whose horses are bay (*hari*), the performer of a hundred rites (*śatakratu*)—we call upon you.

(3) *viśveṣām* means "of all"; *naḥ* means "our," referring to those related to us. By the principle that a word may denote what originates from something else (*tādātmyāt tādṛśyāt*), *adrayaḥ* refers to the Soma juices produced from the pressing-stones (*adri*). *Madhvaḥ* means "sweet."
The word "karmāṇi" (actions/deeds) is in the genitive case.
May they pour out their own essence, their liquid, completely;
that is, may they flow forth entirely for the sake of Indra—this is the ellipsis.
Who are they?
They are the drops of Soma, which, while existing in a distant land,
are pressed by the officiating priests toward [the sacrifice] among the people characterized as sacrificers.
And those drops (*indavas*) which are being pressed—that is, extracted—nearby, in the vicinity; let all of them together pour forth their own juice for the sake of Indra. This is the meaning.
(4) O Indra, strike down and destroy all, every single one of our hostilities and enemies; furthermore,
protect us and bring us to a state of universal renown.

Furthermore, may all people together bestow (*āsanvantu*) wealth (*vasu*) upon us; that is, let them give it directly to us. Moreover, in those excellent heads—namely, among us—in which you find satisfaction through drinking the Soma, may the stalks (*aṃśavaḥ*), that is, the Somas residing there, belong to you alone, being intoxicating (*madirāsaḥ*).
Not of any other whatsoever.

O Indra, the poets celebrate this heroic power of yours with their songs;

This heroic power of yours, O Indra, the poets celebrate with their songs; chanting praises, they have brought forth strength rich in clarity; the Pauras have attained it through their inspired thoughts.
They have approached Indra for protection with their skillful work—those at whose pressed juices you rejoice;
as you were exhilarated at Saṃvarta and as you were at Kṛśa, so, O Indra, be exhilarated among us!

They come to Indra for protection with their skillful work—those at whose libations you rejoice. Just as you were exhilarated at Saṃvarta, just as at Kṛśa, even so, O Indra, be exhilarated among us. 2.
May all the gods, being of one accord, come toward us;
may the Vasus and Rudras come to us for our protection; may the Maruts hear our call.
This is well known. "I come together with you alone" means that in battle I take refuge in you alone, and not in anyone else; the particle *eva* is an expletive. || 23 ||
The sixth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with “*etatte*,” is the *ṛṣi*-composed work of Mātariśvana Kāṇva and is dedicated to Indra.
It is recorded in the Anukramaṇī: “*etatte*... *mātāriśvā*; *no viśve* is a *pragātha* addressed to the Viśvedevas.
The third and fourth verses have the Viśvedevas as their deities.
For the other six [verses], Indra is the deity;
for the odd-numbered ones, the *bṛhatī* is the metre, and for the even-numbered ones, the *satobṛhatī* is the metre.
The application (*viniyoga*) is to be understood from the Sūtra.

(1) O Indra, those singers who are your praisers extol with hymns—i.e., with words in the form of praise—this visible power of yours characterized by the *pṛṣṭha* chants and so forth; those praising singers, while chanting, have obtained (*āvan*) nourishment (*ūrj*).

Furthermore, those praisers dwelling in the city (*paurāsaḥ*), through their mental faculties (*dhītibhiḥ*)—that is, their fingers—reach (*nakṣan*) the flow of clarified butter (*ghṛtaśrutam*), the milk-yielding cow and other livestock.
The meaning is that, through your favor, they constantly milk the cattle and other animals with their fingers.

(2) O Indra, those sacrificers in whose connection you rejoice—that is, you take delight—when the Soma juices have been pressed, poured out, and drunk; those sacrificers, for the sake of aid (*avase*) or for food (*annāya*), reach toward (*nakṣante*) you, the Supreme Lord Indra, by means of a "good performance" (*sukṛtyayā*), that is, through the excellent ritual act of pressing Soma.
The root *nakṣ* signifies "to pervade," as it is listed among the verbs meaning "to pervade" in the passage "it moves, it reaches.
In the sense of "for food," the meaning is that they take refuge in you.

Therefore, O Indra, just as you rejoiced (*amadaḥ*) when Saṃvarta—the sage of that name—was the sacrificer, and just as you rejoiced when Kṛśa—the one of that name—was the sacrificer, even so, in this manner, rejoice (*matsva*) among us, the Kaṇvas; [the ellipsis implies] "be delighted by the drinking of Soma and so forth."
(3) "Sajoṣasaḥ" means being in agreement; "viśve devāsaḥ" means all the gods. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "with reference to our sacrifice."

(4) Pūṣan, the nourishing god; Viṣṇu, the pervasive god; and Sarasvatī—the word *sara* means "water," and thus she is the goddess who possesses it—all these [deities] are the invocation and invitation for me, the seer Mātariśvana.
"Stotra" means a hymn of praise. "Avantu" means may they hear; here, the root *ava* has the sense of hearing.
Because the root *ava* is heard [in the sense of] "protection" and "motion" in this sūtra;

furthermore, may the seven rivers—the Gaṅgā and other streams—meaning the waters or the deities presiding over them, as well as Vāta (the wind) and the mountains—the deities presiding over Meru and the other peaks—hear my invocation.
Moreover, may Vanaspati—the protector (or protectors) of the forests—and the goddess Pṛthivī hear my invocation, that is, my hymn of praise.

The meaning is: through the granting of that wealth, know how to make us prosperous.
Of what nature are you?
You are *sadhamādhaḥ*, one fit for shared exhilaration, and *bhagaḥ*, the one worthy of being honored.

The meaning is: "With your assistance, we are eager to go to battle for the sake of wealth.

Together with *hotrās*, that is, with words characterized by praise.
The meaning is: "Vītī" refers to the oblation (havis) which is accompanied by food and encouraged by hymns of praise;
and furthermore, "sasvāṃsaḥ" refers to the sacrificers who possess food characterized by the oblation.

(8) The great heroic power of Indra has been manifested; it reaches out toward the noble one. Thy bounty, O Dasyave-vṛka, [is vast]. (1) By the "devavītibhiḥ" (feasts for the gods)—that is, by the enjoyments created by the gods—they are heard far and wide. For when the gods, such as you, partake of their oblations, then they become renowned; this is the meaning. (7) O Supreme Lord, since the life-span belonging to us, the people and sacrificers, as well as the food consisting of sacrificial porridge and cakes, and the blessings consisting of cattle, horses, and other riches, all exist and are offered unto thee, Indra, the Supreme Lord and Master of the world; therefore, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, come near to us sacrificers and reach us; that is to say, accept us as thine own and keep us near. Furthermore, for our protection, be bold and grant us nourishment that is overflowing—that is, which protects us exceedingly. (8) O Indra, we sacrificers are thine; and thou art ours, according to the Vedic text: "Thou art ours, and we are thine. Therefore, O Śatakratu, O Indra of many deeds, let us serve thee with hymns and praises. Since we are thine, therefore, O Indra, bestow wealth regularly upon me, Praskaṇva, the son of Kaṇva (or Mātariśvan). He describes that very wealth: "great" (mahi), meaning vast and worthy of honor; "solid" (sthūra), meaning mature and substantial; "enduring" (śaśaya), meaning lying within the bodies of gods and Brahmins, thus to be enjoyed by them; "irrepressible" (ahrya), meaning free from shame. Wealth obtained by sinful means is accompanied by shame, but this is not so, because it is obtained through the grace of the Lord. (25) "Bhūrīt"—this seventh hymn of five verses is by Kuśa, the descendant of Kaṇva; its deity is the gift of Praskaṇva; the meter is Gāyatrī. It is stated: "Bhūrīt... five verses; Kuśa praises the gift of Praskaṇva; it is Gāyatrī, but the third and last are Anuṣṭubhs. Thus, the meter of the third and last verses is Anuṣṭubh, while the others are Gāyatrī. The application (viniyoga) is to be understood from the Sūtras. (1) The heroic power of the capable Praskaṇva, characterized by his generosity, being "bhūrīt" (abundant), reaches out toward [the noble one] on all sides; I have perceived this. Even a small act performed by the Lord becomes great. 1. Anu.-"The third and fifth are Anuṣṭubhs."
Truly great is the heroic power of Indra; the serpent-like Dasyu hastens toward your bounty, O Vṛka. 1.
A hundred white bulls shine like stars in the sky; they have propped up the great heaven as if it were the sky itself.

A hundred bamboos, a hundred dogs, a hundred well-tanned skins; for me, a hundred balbaja-grass mats and four hundred ruddy mares. 3. A hundred bamboos, a hundred dogs, a hundred well-tanned skins; for me, a hundred balbaja-grass mats and four hundred ruddy mares. 3.

O descendants of Kaṇva, you are well-favored by the gods; moving from age to age, you pace about like horses. 4. O descendants of Kaṇva, you are well-favored by the gods; moving from age to age, you pace about like horses. 4.
From the very beginning, they have celebrated the rays of this [Sun]; his great glory has spread far and wide.
Even a mortal man cannot overtake his path as he speeds along.
The meaning is that it becomes manifest.
Now the seer, having perceived it directly, says:
"O Vṛka, O destroyer of enemies, the wealth (*rādhas*) belonging to you, O Praskaṇva, is capable of slaying the Dasyu; this is the ellipsis."
(2) O Praskaṇva, the hundred white-colored bulls (*ukṣan*), capable of impregnating, which were given by you, shine resplendently. Like what?
Like stars (*tārā*) in the sky (*divi*).
The meaning is that they shine upon this earth just as those stars shine in the sky.
Furthermore, by their great splendor (*mahattejaso mahattvena*), just as the stars do not pervade the celestial realm (*dyuloka*), so these wrestlers pervade the earth by the greatness of their fame.
(3) Praskaṇva [saw] a hundred *parimāptas* of bamboo reeds (*maskaras*).
The word "gave" (prādāt) is to be understood as the remainder in all instances.
He gave a hundred—that is, one hundred in number—dogs, meaning *sārameyas*. Likewise, he gave a hundred—that is, many—*mlātāni*, meaning softened or supple hides, that is, *ajināni* (skins).

Furthermore, he gave me, the seer Kṛśānu, bundles of *balbaja* grass—a hundred in number—and also four hundred shining, radiant cows. (4) O Praskaṇvas of the Kaṇa clan, descendants of Kaṇva: you are like birds, exceedingly swift as birds.
This is an example of an elliptical simile (luptopamā).
Wandering—that is, moving through the sky—you are *sudevāḥ*, meaning you become auspicious deities.
Therefore, by our blessing, move about and sport like horses.

(5) Immediately after [the giving], they did not wish to celebrate— that is, they did not desire to perform— the great, vast *śravaḥ* (glory or fame) belonging to Sāma, the son of Kaṇva, who was *anūna* (unfailing), that is to say, unsurpassed and most excellent.
The meaning is that some are not able to achieve such fame.
Furthermore, you would become a wretched man, falling excessively low from the path—that is, from the way of Dharma.

Truly, they have established this truth: the fame of the Perfect One is great. Even as the two dark mares traverse the paths, they cannot be seen by the eye, yet they are well-disposed. [The Eighth Hymn] 1. O Vṛka, your bounty has been seen against the Dasyu; like the sky, your power is wide-extending. Even with my eye, I am not able to fully encompass or behold the tawny cows; how much less can one describe the accomplishment of such glory? [Commentary: ‘Prati te’ is the eighth hymn, consisting of five verses. It is the seer’s work of Pṛṣadhra, son of Kaṇva, and is in the Gāyatrī meter. As it is stated: “*Prati te*; Pṛṣadhra [is the seer]; the last [verse] is addressed to Agni and Sūrya, in the Paṅkti meter; the remaining [verses] are addressed to Indra, in the Gāyatrī meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is to be understood from the Sūtras. (1) O Vṛka—Indra, the cutter of enemies—your inherent bounty (*rādhas*), which is wealth, has been seen as adverse to the Dasyu, the wasting enemy. Being taken away by the enemy, it does not serve his benefit, but rather results in his harm. What kind of bounty? *Ahyaṃ*: free from shame, meaning bold in slaying the enemy. Furthermore, your power (*śavas*) in its vastness (*prathinā*) is like the heavenly world (*dyauḥ*). Therefore, the intention is: "I praise you, who are supreme over all. (2) O Pautakrata—Indra, whose footstep is placed in the pure place (*pūta*)—for my sake, you, as Vṛka, have struck down ten thousand Dasyus, those wasting enemies. (3) Furthermore, O Indra, terrified of you, they gave to me, the seer Pṛṣadhra, a hundred donkeys (*gardhabha*), a hundred woolly ewes (*ūrṇāvatī*), and a hundred slaves (*dāsa*) along with garlands (*mālā*) surpassing them. Such is your power that I praise you. Alternatively, the meaning of these two verses is as follows: *Pautakrataḥ* refers to Aditi, whose footstep is placed in the pure place (*pūta*). It is fitting for Aditi to place her foot in a pure spot, according to the saying: "One should set down a foot that has been seen and purified. Her offspring is *Pautakrata*, Indra. *Dasyave*: the Dasyu is a mass of darkness that wastes away ritual action (*karman*). To slay him, being Vṛka—the Moon—he has bestowed ten thousand riches from his inexhaustible treasury upon me, Pṛṣadhra. Moreover, he has given me the hundreds of donkeys, ewes, slaves, and garlands. Yāska says: "Vṛka is the Moon" (*Nirukta* 5.20). (Note: Regarding verse 1, the phrase *pṛṣadhro 'ntyāmisaurī paṅktiḥ* should be read as *pṛṣadhro 'ntyāgnisaurī paṅktiḥ*. Also, the mantra reading is *dasyave*.)

There too she was led forth, clearly manifest for the sake of Pūtakratu; like a mare belonging to a herd of horses. 4. *There*, *too*, *forth* she was *led*, *clearly manifest* for the sake of *Pūtakratu*; *like* a *mare* from a *herd* of *horses*. 4.

He has come to mind, the conscious one, the bearer of oblations, he whose chariot is auspicious. Now begins the ninth hymn.

O divine ones, joined with the holy *ṛta* upon your powerful chariot, O worshipful Nāsatyas, come hither with your wondrous powers; drink all of this third [libation]. yuvam | devā | ṛtunā | puṇyeṇa | yuktāḥ | rathena | taviṣam | yajatrā | ā | agacchatam | nāsatyā | śacībhiḥ | idam | tṛtīyam | sarvam | pibāthaḥ || 1 ||

(4) Furthermore, Indra, moving about and traveling through various regions in many places, brought even his own mother—named Pūtakratāyī—who was residing there in heaven, to her own field. What did he bring?
A herd, a gathering of mares belonging to the stallion.
The sense is that this praise is sufficient, implying that he did not bestow [the gift] upon me alone, but also caused a herd of mares to be given to his own mother.
Here, the two particles *ita* and *na* are meaningless (*anarthaka*).
(5) Now, by this [verse], both [Agni] and the Sun are praised.
That well-known Agni belongs to the *cikituḥ*, that is, the conscious sacrificer; the genitive case is used in the sense of the object of the action.
He perceives—that is, he knows—the conscious sacrificer.
Of what nature is he?
He is the carrier of oblations (*havyavāṭ*), the bearer of sacrificial offerings; he possesses a good chariot (*sumadratha*), being himself by nature swift-moving.
Yāska [states]: “‘Sumat’ means ‘by himself’” (Nirukta 6.22).
The meaning is that he is one whose nature is to move without a companion.
Furthermore, the great Agni, being a *sūra*—an excellent impeller or mover—by means of his *śukra*, i.e., his bright glow or splendor, shines upon the earth at night.

And furthermore, while his own world shines day by day in the sky, the Sun—the well-impelling Āditya—shone, that is, he blazed. The intention is that by these two, all time consisting of day and night has been pervaded.
The ninth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “yuvaṃ devā,” belongs to Medhya Kāṇva; it is addressed to the Aśvins and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
It is enumerated thus: “‘yuvaṃ devā’—this group of four is by Medhya, addressed to the Aśvins, in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The application (viniyoga) is to be understood from the Sūtras.

(1) O you two worshipful, adorable, and radiant Aśvins, endowed with merit from ancient times through your being, through your ritual action, or through your benevolent intent—you two, by means of a chariot whose nature is speed, with horses harnessed thereto, carry [you] along with great strength; this is the sense of the ellipsis. Therefore, O Nāsatyas, you two who are true to truth, come, come toward this third libation together with your powers, characterized by acts of grace.
And having arrived, drink; "drink" is the understood sense of "sobham."

You two, O gods, are the three who consist of eleven; you are the true ones, seen at the forefront of truth. Accepting our entire sacrifice with favor, O Aśvins, drink the Soma for a long duration. 2. You two. O gods. Three. Consisting of eleven. True. Of truth. Seen. At the forefront. Our. Sacrifice. Entire. Accepting with favor. Drink. Soma. O Aśvins. For a long duration. 2.

That which was made for you to purify, O Aśvins, was performed by the bull of heaven, the straight path, and the earth—a thousandfold praise, as well as those who are present at the quest for cattle; come to all of them from here to drink! 3. That which was made for you to purify, O Aśvins, was performed by you—the bull of heaven, of the straight path, and of the earth—a thousandfold praises, and those who are at the place where cattle are sought; come hither to all of them to drink! 3.

This portion has been set out for you two, O worshipful ones; come hither to these songs, O Nāsatyas. Drink the honeyed Soma; protect the donor with your wondrous powers. 4. (2) O Aśvins, you two; and the other three, the eleven-fold [groups], the thirty-three gods—namely, as established by the Śruti:

"The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, Prajāpati, and the Vaṣaṭkāra"—all of you, being true and real, appear visible in the presence, in the eastern region, of the sacrifice which is true and not false.
Therefore, [O you two] who delight in—
that is, who enjoy and frequent— our *savana*,
that sacrifice (*yajña*) or *adhvara* worthy of worship wherein Soma is pressed (*sūyate*) or extracted (*abhiṣūyate*), drink (*pātam*), that is, consume, the Soma, the juice of the pressed plant.
What are you two like? You are *dīdyamī*: those whose internal fire (*jaṭharānala*) is *dīdi*, meaning an exceedingly blazing fire.
The sense is that even this [act] is appropriate for you two physicians, as if it were something blazing.

(3) O Aśvins, the fact that there is a Sun—the showerer of rain—from the sky (divaḥ), for the sake of the earth (pṛthivyāḥ), from the realm of space (rajaḥ), which is water—that entire deed of yours both is praiseworthy and worthy of hymn.
It is solely through your favor that your father, the Sun, rains upon the earth.
If water has not been drawn up from the earth by those solar rays,
how could they be the attractors of rain?
Therefore, the intention is that this action belongs to you two alone.

Since this is so, therefore: when there is the seeking of cattle (*gaviṣṭhau*) as the cause, those well-known thousands of *śaṃsās*—whereby sacrifices (*yajñāḥ*) are praised (*śasyante*) or extolled—are commenced; such is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"Go near all those sacrifices, all of them without exception; approach them.
The change in verbal number is Vedic.
For what purpose?
"pibadhyai" means for the purpose of drinking Soma;
"uta" is used here as a meaningless expletive.
(4) O worshipful Aśvins, worthy of sacrifice, this portion before you—this share to be enjoyed, characterized by Soma—is "nihitaḥ," meaning established or placed there according to rule.
Therefore, come to seize him—this is the ellipsis (*grahītu*).
Furthermore, O Nāsatyas, you two Aśvins who are true to truth (*satyabhūtau*), approach these nearby *giras*—words characterized by praise—to hear them;
and furthermore, drink the honeyed Soma, which is endowed with sweetness.

Furthermore, with your powers—characterized by the bestowing of desired fruits—protect and preserve preeminently our own relative, the donor, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation. (28.1) [Note:
The mantra reading is "ye"].
Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda 3.51.

Him whom the priests, being of one mind, fashion in many ways as they carry out this sacrifice—since that learned Brāhmaṇa was already engaged [in it], what indeed can be the specific contribution of the patron of the sacrifice there? yam | ṛtvijaḥ | bahudhā | kalpayantaḥ | sacetasaḥ | yajñam | imam | vahanti | yaḥ | anucānaḥ | brāhmaṇaḥ | yuktaḥ | āsīt | kā | svit | tatra | yajamānasya | saṃvit || 1 ||

A single fire alone is kindled in many ways; the sun alone has pervaded the universe. Dawn alone shines upon all this; indeed, this one alone has become the entire universe. One alone is the fire, kindled in many ways; one is the sun, pervading the whole. Dawn alone illumines all this; truly, this One has manifested as everything.

I invoke for you that radiant, bannered, three-wheeled chariot, easy to ride, comfortable, and of many boons— the one by whose union the wondrous wealth was born— for you to drink the overflowing draught. 3.
The tenth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “yamutvijaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Medhya Kāṇva; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
It is cataloged thus: “‘yamutvijaḥ’—[it is] for the Viśvedevas, or rather, a praise of the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
This means that the first [verse] has the officiating priests as its deity.
The application (*viniyoga*) is to be understood from the *Sūtra*.

(1) The conscious priests (*ṛtvij*), who possess equal wisdom, while fashioning and arranging this sacrifice—a specific ritual act to be performed—in many ways or diverse manners, carry it forth, bringing the gods to it.
Performing this sacrifice, the Brahmin—the wise one characterized as a priest—should remain engaged and concentrated in the specific sacrificial rite.
In that regard, what indeed is the ritual action?
The word "svid" expresses deliberation;
or rather, what is the *saṃvit*—the wisdom—of the sacrificer?
The meaning is that they do nothing at all.
Where the officiating priest alone is attentive in a ritual act, what purpose is there for the patron’s proficiency in wisdom?
The sense is: none whatsoever.
What kind of person is a Brāhmaṇa? One who is *anucāna*, having studied the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*) from the presence of a guru.

(2) The single, absolute Fire—the deity endowed with qualities such as giving—becomes thoroughly ignited (*samiddha*), blazing perfectly in many ways, such as the submarine fire (*vāḍava*), lightning (*vaidyuta*), and other various forms.
Likewise, the Sun, the single, solitary god who is the excellent impeller of the actions of living beings, having entered into the entire universe—
according to the Vedic scripture, "Having created that, he entered into it very same" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6)—
is present as the abundant one, manifested through manifold forms.
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The Sun is the self of that which moves and that which stands" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.115.1).
Furthermore, the goddess Uṣas, being alone—even while solitary—dispelling the darkness, shines forth, illuminating specifically this entire visible world.
Therefore, it is logical that Brahman alone—indeed, the one without a second—has come forth as this world, from the smallest atom down to the elephant; this is the implied conclusion.

The intention is as follows: if even deities such as Agni and others, being solitary, are capable of assuming many forms, then what need is there to mention that the Supreme Brahman, which is truly one, must be manifold?
(3) "O Viśvedevas, you two"—the change in number is due to Vedic license (*chāndasa*).

Among you, I invoke—that is, I call upon—for the purpose of honoring as a father and drinking the Soma, that Supreme Self (Paramātman) denoted by the word "That" (tat), who is the most excellent and unsurpassed.
Who is He? That Supreme Self, in whose connection (*yoga*)—that is, in the relationship between the served and the server—the wondrous bounty (*citramagha*) [manifests].

She whose wealth (*magha*)—consisting of cattle, horses, and other such things—is wonderful and praiseworthy, she is *Citramaghā*. (RV 10.85.20) 1. This is not found in the *Anukramaṇī*; see Macdonell, p. 31. 2. These portions of yours flow forth, O Indra and Varuṇa, for the great occasion when the juices are pressed;
at every sacrifice you exert yourselves with all your might, as you bestow your favor upon the sacrificer who pours the libation.

These portions of yours, O Indra and Varuṇa, flow forth for the great [sacrifice] when the juices are pressed. At every sacrifice, you two indeed stir yourselves with all your power, when you bestow your favor upon the sacrificer who presses the soma. 1.
Restraining the plants and the waters, Indra and Varuṇa have attained greatness;
they who have sped across the path at the far limit of the mid-world, for whom no enemy at all dares to stand as an adversary.
The worshipful Lakṣmī, endowed with manifold wealth, was born—that is, she appeared preeminently—to Yudhiṣṭhira and the others.
Of what sort was he?
He was "possessing light" (*jyotiṣmantam*), meaning that the sun and other luminaries exist as the objects of his illumination.
"By its light all this shines," according to the Vedic scripture. "Possessing a banner" (ketumantam): that which has banners—namely, cognitions (prajñā)—as its objects.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
*Ketu* is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*), because it is listed among its synonyms in the passage: "*Ketuh*, *ketaḥ*."
"Tricakram" means one whose wheel—his movement—is in the three worlds, beginning with the earth, as in his incarnation as Trivikrama;
this is according to the Vedic revelation beginning with "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.23.17).
Alternatively, it refers to one who possesses the unimpeded discus named Sudarśana in the three worlds.
The face consists of unsurpassed bliss, according to the Vedic scripture: "Oṃ, Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ.
The chariot has the nature of moving swiftly.
That is to say, it has the nature of moving;
for the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3.19) states: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper.
It is the excellent abode.
He who sits—that is, resides—in the beautiful nature of the Self is "supat," meaning well-established;
for the Śruti says, "Wisdom is the foundation; wisdom is Brahman.
He is "bhūrivāraḥ," meaning he who is to be chosen (vāraḥ) many times (bhūri) by many (bhūribhiḥ) living beings.
Because it is the self of all, it is fitting that it is dear to all;
for the Śruti says: "Everything becomes dear for the sake of the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
‘Imāni vām’: this eleventh hymn consisting of seven verses is by Suparṇa Kāṇva; it is addressed to Aryaman, Indra, and Varuṇa, and is composed in the Jagatī meter.
This is because it is cataloged [in the Anukramaṇī] as: ‘Imāni vāṃ sapta suparṇa aindrāvaruṇaṃ jāgatam’.
The specific application (viniyoga) is to be understood from the Sūtra.

(1) O Indra and Varuṇa! These sacrificial portions (*bhāgadheyāni*)—the oblations such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, which have now been prepared and constitute your respective shares—flow toward you both, desiring to reach you. Therefore, while the Soma juices have been pressed, I entreat you both for the sake of great honor (*mahe*). (The verb "I entreat" is supplied in accordance with the prefix.)
Since, at every sacrifice, you hasten to each libation— you indeed go to all three pressings—
and furthermore, you bestow what is desired upon the sacrificer who performs the pressing of Soma.
The root *śikṣ* has the sense of giving (*dāna*), because it is listed among the roots whose meanings are "giving" in the statement: "He bestows (*praṇāti śikṣati*)."

(2) O Indra and Varuṇa, when you two were present as the agents of plants and other things, then the plants—rice and the like—and the waters attained your greatness, that is, they pervaded your majesty; indeed, those plants which are of an exceedingly auspicious nature, and also the waters. Furthermore, [you two who are] connected to the paths of *rajas*, the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*).

The two who are masters of the settling, the plants, and the waters; Indra and Varuṇa have attained greatness. They who have sped forth beyond the realm of space, for whom no godless enemy dares to stand as an adversary. (2)

Truly, O Indra and Varuṇa, the seven voices of Kuśa milk for you both the wave of honeyed mead. With these, O Lords of Splendor, protect the donor who, unassailable, guards you with his thoughts. Truly, that is so. O Indra and Varuṇa, the seven voices of Kuśa milk for you both the wave of honeyed mead. With these, O Lords of Splendor, protect the donor who, unassailable, guards you with his thoughts.

Dropping ghee, gentle, quick-giving, the seven sisters dwell in the seat of Cosmic Order (Ṛta). O Indra and Varuṇa, with those [streams] of yours which drip with ghee, bestow [wealth] upon the sacrificer and grant him aid. ghṛtapṛṣaḥ (ghee-dropping), saumyāḥ (gentle), jīradānavaḥ (quick-giving), sapta (seven), svasāraḥ (sisters), sadane (in the seat), ṛtasya (of Cosmic Order), yāḥ (which), ha (indeed), vām (of you two), indrāvaruṇā (O Indra and Varuṇa), ghṛtaśrutaḥ (dripping with ghee), tābhiḥ (with those), dhattam (bestow), yajamānāya (upon the sacrificer), śikṣatam (grant aid). || 4 || 30 ||
We have proclaimed the true majesty and Indra-like power of these two for great good fortune.
O Indra and Varuṇa, lords of splendor, may we be sprinkled with the drops dripping with ghee according to our vow.
Flow across the path, to the further shore; move about as you desire.
For you two, no enemy—a destroyer, a godless one who opposes the gods, such as an asura—is found (*nakiḥ ohate*);
that is to say, there is no enemy whatsoever within the range of thought who can obstruct your movement as you roam according to your own will.

(3) O Indra and Varuṇa! Those voices—whether numbering seven, or characterized by movement, or consisting of the hymns of the seven *hotṛ*-priests—which, belonging to the sacrificer named Kuśa, milk out—that is, fill you both with—the wave of the sweet Soma, or the essence indicated by that wave; since this is indeed the unfailing truth, therefore, by means of those voices acting as the cause, protect and preserve the liberal giver, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation. [The text] further qualifies the sacrificer:

O Śubhaspati, O Indra and Varuṇa, the two protectors of the waters—that sacrificer who, being unharmed by anyone and free from malice, protects you both on all sides through his mental insights (*cittibhiḥ*), that is, through actions characterized by wisdom—protect him;
this connects with the preceding verse.

(4) In response to the inquiry as to which those truthful speech-entities are, he says: In the seat—that is, the place—of *ṛta*, the sacrifice, there are seven sisters, numbering seven, who move by themselves. Of what nature are they?
*ghṛtapṛṣaḥ*. "Ghṛta" is a name for water; by it, the Soma juice is indicated.
And thus, the meaning is that they flow with the juice of Soma.
"Saumyāḥ" means belonging to Soma; "jīradānavaḥ" means those that give quickly.

Furthermore, O Indra-Varuṇa—O Indra and Varuṇa—those [fingers] which, directed toward you both, flow with clarified butter (ghṛtaśrutaḥ), that is, they flow with the juice of Soma or flow with ghee (ājya).
"Het" is a well-known term for cause. By means of those causes, nourish the sacrificer with clarified butter;
and for that purpose, bestow—that is, grant—to the sacrificer what is desired.

(5) O Indra and Varuṇa! O Indra and Varuṇa! We have proclaimed—that is, we shall describe—for the sake of great and sublime fortune and sovereignty, the greatness consisting of a distinguished glory accomplished by you two through your radiant splendors.
Of what nature is that greatness?
It is true, that is, unerring.

We have spoken to you both for great good fortune. Truly, from those two brilliant ones, [we receive] greatness and Indra-like power. O Indra and Varuṇa, protect us well—[us who are] dripping with clarity—with threefold gifts, O pure ones. 5.

O Indra and Varuṇa, when you first bestowed upon the seers inspired thought, the wisdom of speech, and sacred learning; when the wise, performing the sacrifice, created those various stations through their ascetic fervor—I beheld all that. 6. O Indra and Varuṇa! When [you gave] to the seers inspired thought, the wisdom of speech, and sacred learning, O Agni; those places which the wise created while extending the sacrifice—through ascetic fervor, I beheld them. 6.

O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon the sacrificers goodwill worthy of honor and the increase of wealth. Grant us progeny, nourishment, and prosperity; extend our lifespan for the sake of long life. (7) O Indra and Varuṇa! Goodwill! Worthy of honor! Of wealth! Increase! In the seventh section (*anuvāka*), there are ten hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twenty verses beginning with "O Agni, come hither" (*agna ā yāhi*), is addressed to Agni; it is the *ṛṣi*-seer Bharga, son of Pragātha.

The first, third, and other odd-numbered verses are *bṛhatī*s; the second, fourth, and other even-numbered verses are *sato-bṛhatī*s. Thus it has been listed [in the Anukramaṇī]: "O Agni, there are twenty [verses]; Bhaga [is the deity]; it is a *pragātha*; it belongs to Agni; it is indeed a *pragātha*. This hymn is used in the *prātaranuvāka*, during the *Āgneya* ritual, in the *bārhata* metre, and for the *Aśvina-śastra*.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, come hither, being well-disposed" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
O Agni, come hither; we choose you as the Agnihotra-priest.
Let the extended ladle, filled with oblation, anoint you, the most excellent sacrificer, to sit upon the sacrificial grass.

O Agni, come hither with the fires; we choose you as the Hotṛ-priest. Let the extended ladle full of oblation anoint you, the most excellent sacrificer, so that you may sit upon the sacred grass (barhis). 1.
O Agni, come hither together with those fires that are to be sacrificed to;
for that purpose, we choose you as the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods.

You, having arrived, let the Adhvaryu, with outstretched hands, anoint you—the most excellent sacrificer—with the sacrificial ladle full of clarified butter, upon the sacred grass (barhis) which has been spread for your seating. Let him anoint you on all sides.
For indeed, O Son of Strength, O Aṅgiras, the ladles move toward you at the sacrifice;
we pray to Agni, the Son of Vigor, whose hair is ghee, the foremost in the sacrifices.
Truly, O son of strength, O Aṅgiras, the ladles move toward you in the sacrifice. We seek Agni, the offspring of vigor, whose hair is ghee—the foremost one in the sacrifices. 2.
O "Sahasas," son of strength—
you being churned by strength—
O "Aṅgiras," one among the Aṅgirases.
Alternatively, he whose function is to go to the highest goal (aṅgiras) is present everywhere;
the ladles (srucaḥ) move toward you (tvā) in order to reach you (accha) at the sacrifice (adhvare).

Therefore, in our sacrifices, we praise Agni—the protector who does not cause [us] to fall, the offspring of strength (ūrjas) and food (annasya), the leader of power, whose hair is ghee (ghṛtakeśam)—meaning he whose flames stand in place of hair—ancient (pūthyam), or rather, the filler (purakam). I laud him.

O Agni, you are a sage, a disposer, a purifying invoker worthy of sacrifice; you are delightful, the best of sacrificers at the rites, to be praised by the inspired poets with pure hymns, O radiant one.

O Agni, you are the sage, the ordainer; you are the purifying priest, worthy of worship, delightful, the best of sacrificers, to be praised at the rites by the inspired poets with their pure hymns. 3.
O Agni, you are the sage, the wise one; you are the ordainer (*vedhāḥ*), the dispenser of fruits.
O Purifier (*pāvaka*), you are the invoker of the gods (*hotā*), the summoner, or the performer of the oblation; you are worthy of sacrifice (*yakṣyaḥ*).

O Radiant One (*śukra*), you are the effulgent, the exhilarating, the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*). In the rites (*adhvareṣu*)—that is, in the sacrifices—you are to be praised with hymns (*manmabhiḥ*) by the inspired ones (*viprebhiḥ*), the wise officiating priests. You are the one to be lauded.
O most youthful, tireless god, bring the gods here for the feast, you who do not harm those who offer;
O Vasu, come toward the well-prepared offerings; rejoice, being well-disposed through our prayers.

1. [This verse belongs to] Bharga, the son of Gaṇaśa-Pragātha. 2. Bha1-2: "Possessing clarified butter" (ghṛtavatī) is *suk* (well); Bha3: "Endowed with oblations" (havirbhiryuktā) is *suk*. 3. Ga-Ta-Śa: The word "barhis" (sacrificial grass) is absent. 4. Ya: "Anaktu" means "let him enjoy. 5. Ta3-4-Na-Śa: "Sapūrvya" (ancient). 6. Gha: "Pāvaka" means "purifier. O most youthful one, O unceasing one, bring hither the longing gods for the feast. O Vasu, accept the well-prepared offerings; rejoice in our prayers, being well-disposed toward us. ||4||
O youngest one, O eternal one, bring hither— lead toward me, who am harmless and harmless toward others— the desiring gods who long for my unequalled purpose. For what purpose?

For the sake of enjoyment— that is, for the consumption of the oblation— O *vaso*, you who desire to dwell, approach (*abhigāhi*) the well-placed (*sudhitā*) offerings (*prayāṃsi*). Having arrived, being established (*hita*) by means of *dhītayaḥ*— that is, by hymns of praise— rejoice (*mandasva*).
Or rather,
the connection is with the words "rejoice with the prayers" (dhītibhiḥ).

You alone, O Agni, are far-famed, the protector, the seer of Truth; you, O kindled one, the radiant one, the inspired singers and the wise ordainers seek to win over. You alone, O Agni, are far-famed, the protector, the seer of Truth; you, O kindled one, the radiant one, the inspired singers and the wise ordainers seek to win over.

O Agni, O protector, O guardian, you who are Ṛta—truth itself—and a seer (kavi) of far-reaching wisdom, you alone are saprathas, vast on every side. O Samidhāna, being kindled, O Dīdivas, shining one, the vipras—the wise ones—and the vedhasas—the ordainers and worshippers—strive to win over and serve you.

O most radiant one, shine forth; bestow joy upon the people. Grant it to the singer, for you are great. May the gods be in my protection—Sūrya, the subduer of enemies, the noble lord. 6. Shine forth! O most radiant one, shine forth with exceeding brilliance;
illuminate us.
Bestow happiness upon the people, the progeny, and the singer.
You are great.
May the Sun be the refuge, the protection, and the happiness belonging to the gods for me; may our wise sons and others be our praisers;
and may they be subduers of enemies and possessors of noble wealth.

Just as you, O Agni, utterly consume even dry brushwood upon the earth, so, O you whose greatness is Mitra, burn him who harms us, the evil-minded one, and whoever seeks to deceive us. Just as you, O Agni, utterly consume even dry brushwood upon the earth, so, O you whose greatness is Mitra, burn him who harms us, the evil-minded one, and whoever seeks to deceive us.
O Agni, just as you completely consume—that is, you burn thoroughly—a large piece of dry wood lying upon the earth, so do you [consume this].
(The root *jūr* signifies injury;
thus, it means "you burn completely.")

"O you who are thus burning, O Mitra-mahas— O you who honor our friends, or whose splendor is like that of Mitra— who is it? Whosoever is an enemy of ours, and whosoever is an evil-minded one who desires to harm us, burn him!"

1. By the actions of *jha*, *bha*, and *dhīti*. 2. *Gha*: they cause to shine forth (*āvivāsanti*). 3. *Kha*, *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, *mu*, *tvaṃ devānām*. 4. *Kha*, *jha*, *ta* (1–2): *tejo vāryaka*; *ga*: *tejo vā*; *ta* (3–4), *śa*: *tejovāka*. 5. *Ta*, *na*, *bha* (1–2): *dahateti*; *bha* (3): *dahati*. *Ṛgveda*: [Aṣṭaka 6, Adhyāya 4, Varga 34]

Do not deliver us over to the mortal enemy, to the one possessed by demons, nor to the speaker of evil. Protect us with your auspicious guardians—those who do not harm, who are victorious, and who are wise. Do not deliver us (mā naḥ) to the mortal (martāya), to the enemy (ripave), to the one possessed by demons (rakṣasvine); do not deliver us to the speaker of evil (aghaśaṃsāya). With those who do not harm (astedhadbhiḥ), who are victorious (taraṇibhiḥ), who are wise (vipraiḥ), and who are auspicious (śivebhiḥ)—with these guardians (pāyubhiḥ)—protect (pāhi) us, O protector. [Note: The commentary explains that "wise" (vipraiḥ) refers to the guardians themselves, characterized by youthfulness, non-violence, the power to cross over difficulties, and the capacity to grant happiness.]

Protect us, O Agni, with one [verse]; protect us also with a second; protect us with three hymns, O Lord of Strength; protect us with four, O Vasu. 9. Protect us. O Agni. With one. Protect. And. With a second. Protect. With hymns. With three. O Lord of Strength. Protect. Four.

Grant us, through your excellent guidance, wealth that is highly desirable by many and most glorious in its own renown; bestow it upon us. By which we may overcome the defiant enemies in battles, crossing over the commands of the foe—O Lord of Power (*śacīvaso*), increase us with nourishment and quicken our thoughts that find riches. (12) By which wealth we may overcome the defiant enemies who exert their force in battles, crossing over the commands of the foe and slaying them—O Lord of Power, increase us with food; quicken our thoughts that find riches. (13) Like a bull sharpening his horns, Agni shakes his head like a wooden ladle; his jaws are sharp and cannot be withstood. He has beautiful teeth and is the mighty son of strength. (14) O Bull, Agni, your jaws cannot be withstood when you stand forth in various ways. O Hotṛ, offerer of oblations, make our offering well-sacrificed; grant us much desirable wealth. (15) You lie within the woods; mortals kindle you from your two mothers. Unwearied, you carry the offerings to the gods; indeed, you reign among the divine powers. (15) *Note on variants:* 1. *śardhataḥ*: "exerting force" (various editions). 2. *śṛṅge sthānīyā*: "standing in place of horns" (various editions). 3. *tigmāḥ*: "sharp" (omitted in some manuscripts).
In the forests, the two mothers together kindle you with their thoughts; unwearied, you carry the oblations prepared by the sacrificers; then indeed, you reign among the gods. 15.
O Agni, you lie within the two mother-wooden blocks (*araṇī*) that abide in the forests; you dwell there, nourishing yourself well.
Men, such as the *adhvaryu* priests and others, having produced you by friction while you are in that state, kindle you.
Thereafter, being tireless and unwearied, you carry the oblations—the sacrificial offerings—of the sacrificer who has prepared them toward the gods.
From the very beginning, immediately thereafter, you reign and shine resplendent among the gods.
The Hotṛ-priests, having fallen asleep, praise you, O Agni, who are worthy of sacrifice and easy to invoke.
You cleave the rock with your heat and your flame; O Agni, rise up above all people.

The sacrificing priests invoke you alone, O Agni, the one most worthy of sacrifice, the one to be summoned. With your heat and with your flame, you split the mountain asunder; O Agni, rise up above all people. 16.
O Agni, the seven hotṛ-priests praise and laud you alone—just you—who are easy to invoke at the Soma-pressing.
What kind of you?
One who is easily invoked at the Soma-pressing.

The meaning is "bestowing what is desired. *Ahūyam* means unexhausted and increased. Furthermore, [he shatters] the cloud (*adri*) by means of heat (*tapas*), that is, by the burning flame (*śocis*), which is his splendor (*tejas*).
Or rather, it should be construed as "he shines by means of austerity and radiance.
You cleave asunder.
O Agni, having surpassed us people, go forth—proceed toward the gods, taking the oblation with you.
Or else, disregarding those who oppose us, take your stand.
We, having spread the sacrificial grass, invoke Agni after Agni as your overseer;
we, with prepared offerings, call upon Agni, the Hotṛ of all peoples, throughout the eternal ages.
Agni and Agni, we invoke for you the one who dwells among men; we whose sacrificial grass is trimmed and whose offerings are prepared call upon Agni as the eternal Hotṛ-priest of all peoples. 17.

"Agni, Agni. [The repetition] is for the sake of emphasis. "O sacrificers, let us invoke *agni* alone for you (*vaḥ*), for your sake. Or alternatively, it may be explained as: "O gods, [let us invoke him] for you (*vaḥ*). Of what sort are we? "Vṛttabarhiṣaḥ," those who have trimmed the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Of what sort is Agni? "Adhigu," whose movement is unimpeded, remaining always in the house. "Abhimam" (the beloved). "Hita-prayasaḥ," we who have placed the oblation (*havis*)—[the phrase] "let us invoke" is to be supplied. Of what sort is Agni? The "Hotṛ," the performer of the sacrifice, residing in many lands (*śaśvatīṣu bhūmiṣu*). For what purpose? "For the sake of *carṣaṇīnām*," i.e., for the sake of human beings; for when Agni exists, the benefit to living beings is accomplished through rain, and thus his being for the sake of living beings is established. Or alternatively, [he is] the Hotṛ of human sacrificers, the accomplisher of their sacrifice.
O Agni, he who is wise brings this [offering] to you, O fair-armed one;
with your swift-moving power, O much-invoked one, bring us nourishment and strength most near for our protection.
O Agni, you who possess beautiful praise, the wise one attends to your protection; with a desire for us, bring to us food of many forms, the nearest strength for our aid. 18.
1. Kha, ta, śa, vā: *yo*; na, vā, vo. 2. Kha, ga, ta, *adhṛtakarmāṇam*; na, bha, *adhṛtagamanakarmāṇam*. 3. Kha, ta, na, bha, ra, 1, śa: *prāṇyupakārasiddham*.

May Indra hear both these [prayers] of ours; may he, the most powerful Maghavan, come hither toward this splendor, with his mind directed toward us, for the sake of drinking the Soma. May Indra hear both—this twofold speech consisting of hymns and recitations—directed toward us. Having heard it, may the most powerful Maghavan, joined with our focused thought, come hither for the drinking of the Soma.

For the two worlds (Heaven and Earth) have fashioned him, the self-ruling bull, for the sake of strength; indeed, you sit as the first among those who are comparable, for your mind is desirous of Soma. For them—the two worlds, Heaven and Earth—have fashioned him, Indra, the self-ruling (*svarāja*) one who shines by himself, the bull (*vṛṣabha*) who bestows rain that benefits the world, for the sake of power (*ūrje*). Indeed, they have fashioned that very Indra for the sake of strength. And because this is so, O Indra, you sit down as the foremost (*prathamaḥ*), the chief, among those who are comparable (*upamānām*), namely the other gods; for your mind is truly desirous of Soma.

In the aforementioned *acchāvāka* recitation, the *pragātha* beginning with "ā vṛṣasva" is an optional *anurūpa*. The Sūtra has stated it thus: ā vṛṣasva puruvaso sutasyendrāndhasaḥ | vidmā hi tvā harivaḥ putsu sāsahimṛṣṭaṃ cidadhṛṣvarṇam || 3 || O *puruvaso* (possessor of much wealth), O Indra, pour down [upon us] the pressed juice, the *andhas* (the Soma). For we know you, O *harivaḥ* (possessor of the two bay horses), as the conqueror in battles; you who are unassailable even by the fierce, yet the one who boldly assails others. O *puruvaso* (one who possesses abundant wealth), O Indra, do thou *vṛṣasva*—that is, pour down or bestow. What? The *sutasya andhasaḥ*, the pressed juice, the Soma, into thy belly. O *harivaḥ* (one accompanied by the two bay horses), O Indra, we indeed *vidma*—we know—*tvā*, thee. Of what sort? As the *sāsahim* (conqueror) of enemies in *putsu* (battles); as the *adhṛṣṭam* (unassailable) even by the *dhṛṣṭam* (bold ones); and as the *dhṛṣvarṇam* (the bold-colored one), the one who daunts others.

You have filled [the worlds], O truthful Maghavan; thus you are, O Indra, by your wisdom, as is your splendor. May we win booty through your aid, O fair-cheeked one, O wielder of the stone, even as we hasten swiftly toward it. You have filled [the worlds], O truthful Maghavan; thus you are, O Indra, by your wisdom, as is your splendor. May we win booty through your aid, O fair-cheeked one, O wielder of the stone, even as we hasten swiftly toward it.
1. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa-kiṃca*; *ga-ki tat*. 2. *ga-vidyāmahī*; *jha-tara-vibhmahi*; *tā3-4-na-śa-vidyāmahi*; *bha1-vidyāhi*.
O you whose truth is unassailable, O you whose truth is inviolable, O bounteous Indra, that which you have said shall be exactly so.
O Indra, may we perform this deed with wisdom in such a manner that I may have my desire fulfilled.
O thou of beautiful jaws, through thy protection as our cause, may we obtain and enjoy strength by thy grace.
Of what sort are we?
