O <sup>v</sup>Adrivah—O wielder of the thunderbolt (O you who know the thunderbolt)!
"Cutting that off":
"O Indra, Lord of the Śacīs, may we follow you with all your aids— just as we follow Bhaga— since you, O Hero, are glorious and a finder of wealth."
Be able! Oṃ! O Lord of Might, Indra, with all your aids! For we follow you, O Hero, as one who is glorious like Bhaga and a finder of wealth. 5.
O Lord of Might (*śacīpati*), O Indra, grant us favor and bestow what is desired, together with all your protections and the Maruts.
O Hero, we follow you—just as one follows fortune (*bharga*)—you who are glorious, renowned, and the finder of wealth, the bringer of riches. We follow you; we attend upon you.
"Paricarāma" means "let us serve.
O divine one, you who possess golden wealth, come with great joy to the purpose of the people.
No one indeed will consume this gift; whatever I place here, bring that back.
O God, you are the source of wealth, fashioned by many, of cattle, and of gold. For no one can ever exhaust your gift. Whatever I now beg of you, bring that to me. 6.

O Indra, you are the fulfiller (*paura*) of the horse; you are the one who fulfills (*pura*). Likewise, O God, you are the manifold-maker (*purukṛt*) of cattle. O golden-hued (*hiraṇyaya*), you whose body is made of gold, you are like a fountain (*utsa*).
O Indra, no one at all can exhaust the gift (*dāna*)—the wealth to be given—that resides in you for our desired purpose;
therefore, whatever I implore, bring that to me.
If the *bṛhat* sāman is used in the *ādhiṣṭoma*, then the *pragātha* is the corresponding verse for the *niṣkevalya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘tvaṃ hohi cerava’—these are the *pragāthas* [Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.15].
In the *niṣkevalya* section of the Mahāvrata, this *pragātha* occurs in the latter part.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: "‘tvāmiddhi havāmahe’ and ‘tvaṃ hohi cerava’ are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* *pragāthas* of the *bṛhatī* [Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.2]."
Be a finder of light for the pious singer, so that he may obtain wealth;
pour forth the rain, O Maghavan, for the sake of the cow, O Indra, and for the sake of the horse.
Come indeed to the pious man; find wealth for the granting of riches. Pour it forth, O Maghavan, for the seeking of cattle, and pour it forth, O Indra, for the seeking of horses. 7.
O Indra,
since it is understood from the context that you alone are indeed the one who bestows power, therefore come here; arrive.
Having come, O Bharga, bestow upon us wealth that is worthy of worship; obtain it and give it!
For what purpose?
For our prosperity, that is, for the granting of riches to us.

O Maghavan, for the sake of seeking cattle, for me who desires cattle, pour forth—pour out the cow; this is the sense. Likewise, O Indra, for the sake of seeking horses—for me who possesses wealth in horses—pour forth, pour out, and bestow the stone.
1. kha-jha-ta1-2-vā *yadyathānena*; gha-ta3-4 *yadyathānena*; bhara-vā *yadyathā yena*; na-śa *yathānena*.
2. Kha, jha, ta¹⁻², su, and ūti are [attested] by the protectors (rakṣakas); gha is [attested] by the protectors. 3.
Kha, gha, jha, ta¹⁻², and garva are [attested] by the citizens (pauras).
4. Kha, ga, ta, and śa do not have "utsa."
5. Kha, ga, ta, na, bha¹⁻², śa, and nakir dānam; bha³ and nakir hi. 6.
Kha, ga, ta, na, and śa: the Aṣṭoma-Bṛhatsāman.

O Indra, you consider hundreds and thousands of herds for the sake of giving to the donor; we, with inspired speech, singing praises for protection, bring Indra, the shatterer of forts, hither. O Indra, you (*tvaṃ*) consider (*maṃse*) many (*puru*), indeed numerous (*purūṇi*), thousands (*sahasrāṇi*) and hundreds (*śatāni*) of herds (*yūthā*)—herds of cattle and the like—for the sake of giving (*dānārya*) to the sacrificer (*yajamāna-viṣayāya*). Or rather, you bestow (*maṃse*) them upon the giver, the sacrificer (*dātre yajamānāya*). The root *mā* has the sense of "giving. Now, he speaks in the third person: we, possessing inspired speech (*vipra-vacasaḥ*)—that is, those with various excellent words—singing praises (*gāyantaḥ*) for the sake of protection (*avase*) or joy, bring (*cakram*) Indra, the shatterer of the forts of enemies (*puraṃdaram*), hither (*ā*) for his arrival or to face us.

Whether it be one who is not a sage (*avipra*) or one who is a sage (*vipra*), O Indra, whoever has performed your praise—let him rejoice exceedingly through you, O Śatakratu, O Prācāṃmanyu, O Ahaṃsana. Whether it be one who is not a sage—that is, one lacking wisdom or unskilled in hymns—or one who is a sage, that is, wise and skilled in hymns, O Indra, whoever has performed (*avidhat*) your praise (*varcaḥ*), meaning whoever praises you; let that singer rejoice (*pra marmandat*) exceedingly through his devotion to you (*tvāyā*). O Śatakratu, possessor of many deeds; O Prācāṃmanyu, whose wrath is directed forward—that is, whose anger is irresistible, for no one can withstand the wrath of Indra; O Ahaṃsana, so called because in battle he proclaims his own greatness as "I" while confronting the enemy, such is Indra.

If Indra—the one with mighty arms, the slayer of the Mṛkṣa, the shatterer of forts—should hear my invocation, then we, seeking wealth, call upon Indra with hymns of praise: the lord of riches, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, the master of boundless wisdom. *Ugrabāhuḥ*: possessing powerful arms; *mṛkṣakṛtvā*: the destroyer, the slayer of enemies; *purandaraḥ*: the breaker of strongholds, Indra. *Yadi me śṛṇavad dhavam*: if he should hear my call; *vasuyavaḥ*: desiring wealth; *vasupatim*: the lord of riches; *śatakratum*: the one of a hundred powers (or infinite wisdom); *indram*: Indra; *stomaiḥ*: with hymns of praise; *havāmahe*: we invoke. [Verse 37]

We do not consider ourselves sinners, nor misers, nor stingy; for now, at the pressing of the juice, we shall make the bull Indra our companion. (11) We do not consider ourselves sinners, nor misers, nor stingy; for now, at the pressing of the juice, we shall make the bull Indra our companion. 1.
O Paśupati, we do not consider ourselves *pāpāsaḥ*—sinners, those who have performed no merit, being devoid of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other observances—we do not so regard ourselves.
"Likewise, we do not think of the *arāyas*—the stingy ones, the poor, or those who offer no oblations;
nor do we think of the tongueless, the flameless, or the unrenowned.
We praise him who possesses the wealth of those who have performed vows, observances, and other meritorious deeds. Thus the Dawn speaks of herself.
Because at this very moment we shall make Indra—the showerer—our companion when the Soma has been pressed, therefore we think ourselves free from evil and the like;
for it is impossible for those characterized by evil and such to provide assistance to Indra.
In this regard, the Nirukta passage beginning with "We do not think ourselves evil" (Nirukta 6.25) should be consulted.
I have yoked the fierce one, the conqueror in battles, the destroyer of enemies,
the subduer. O you who bestow wealth, for you indeed are the increaser of great riches, of wealth, and of the dwelling.
This is understood by implication alone:
of what house or wealth is he said to be the "increaser"?
Of the sacrificer who "serves" or attends upon him.
O Maghavan Indra, O lover of songs (girvaṇas), we—having pressed the soma (sutāntas)—invoke you, such as you are, with our hymns (giras). We call upon you.

Indra is the observer, the slayer of Vṛtra, our protector from afar, and most excellent. May he protect us at the end; may he protect us in the middle; may he protect us from behind and from the front. (15) Indra is the observer—*spaś* meaning one who knows all. *Uta* (also) this slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahā*), the destroyer of Vṛtra, the protector from afar (*paraspāḥ*), is the one to be chosen (*vareṇyaḥ*) by us. May that Indra protect us—[the word] "son" is to be supplied—he shall protect our son. Thus may he protect the youngest son; may he protect the middle son; may he protect us from behind; may he protect us from the front. (15)

O Indra, protect us from behind, from below, from above, and from the front—from every side. Drive far away from us all divine fear; drive far away the non-divine weapons. O Indra, you—protect us from behind, from the front, from below (this being indicative of what is above), and from above (this being indicative of what is to the south). What need is there to say more? Protect us from every direction. O Indra, place divine fear far away from us; likewise, place the non-divine weapons—the weapons of the Asuras—far away.

Day after day, tomorrow after tomorrow, O Indra, protect us; and on the day beyond, protect us as well. O Lord of the virtuous, you shall guard all of us, your singers, throughout every day—by day and by night. (17) Day after day—that is, on every such day denoted by the word "day"—protect us in that very way; likewise, protect us on the "morrow," that is, on the third day. O Lord of the virtuous, protector of the good, you shall guard (you do guard)—all of us, your singers, throughout all days; and you shall guard us by day and by night as well. (17)
Pervasive, heroic, Maghavan, possessor of abundant wealth, he is united for valorous deeds.
O Śatakratu, both those arms of yours are virile, which have grasped the thunderbolt.

1. In manuscripts ga, ta, and śa, "of the house" (*gṛhasya*) is absent. 2. In manuscripts kha, ga, ta, na, bha¹·², and śa, "thou art" (*asi*) is absent. 3. In manuscripts kha, ga, ta, and śa, "and" (*ca*) is absent. 4. In manuscripts kha, ga, ta, na, and śa, it reads "he touches" (*sparśati*). 5. In manuscripts kha and ta, it reads "that son" (*putraṃ sa*). [Maṇḍala 8, Anuvāka 7, Sūkta 62] The Sixth Aṣṭaka, 817:

He who is prone to breaking, the hero, the bounteous giver, the one of many gifts, the one who bestows all together—for the sake of heroic power—both those arms of yours, O Śatakratu, are virile; they are those which have firmly grasped the thunderbolt. ||8||

Indra is the possessor of wealth (*maghavan*), the breaker (*prabhaṅgin*), whose nature is to shatter, the hero (*śūra*), the one of abundant wealth (*tuvīmagha*), and the mixer (*saṃmiṅkṣa*) who thoroughly unites [all things].
For what purpose? For valor (*vīryāya*), that is, for the display of prowess against enemies.
*ṣam* is a filler for the verse-foot.
Thus great is his majesty.
Now follows the statement of direct perception.
O Indra, both of your arms are indeed rain-givers, showering down desires; O Śatakratu, you of great wisdom, those two arms which have firmly grasped the thunderbolt as a weapon.
The third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "pro asmai," belongs to Pragātha Kāṇva.
This Indra, who is quick in giving (*jīradānuḥ*), desires to bestow (*sipāsati*)—that is, he wishes to share—with even an untrained, unyoked, and stray horse.
Therefore, O Indra, your greatness shall be proclaimed as you perform heroic deeds through your power.
The meaning is that it is worthy of praise.

Come hither, O Indra; let us perform for you strengthening prayers, by which you, O most powerful one, may take pleasure. May there be good fortune here for the seeker of glory; auspicious indeed are the gifts of Indra.

Come! Let us perform for you, O Indra, strengthening prayers, by which, O most powerful one, you may take pleasure. Here, for the seeker of glory, may there be blessings; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. 4.

O Indra, come hither! We shall perform for you *brahmāṇi*—mighty deeds characterized by praise. Of what kind? Those which are *vardhanā*, increasers of enthusiasm. O most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*) Indra, with those deeds you take pleasure (*cākanaḥ*). What? To do what is auspicious (*bhadra*). For whom? For the singer who desires glory (*śravasyate*), who longs for renown.
O Indra, when you make even the bold-minded more bold,
as the Soma is pressed with strong juices and they honor you with prostrations, the gifts of Indra are auspicious.
O Indra, you make even the bold man’s mind more bold when you, with the sharp Soma juices, honor him who serves you with prostrations and attends upon you—the auspicious are the gifts of Indra. 5.
O Indra, you make even the mind of one who is already bold more bold than the bold;

you make it exceedingly daring. For, when you—by means of the sharp, intoxicating Soma juices, by the honors of the worshipper, and by the adorning acts of those who embellish [the rite] with prostrations—you desire to grant the intention of the sacrificer; this is the sense.
The one who desires the hymns looks down like a mortal [upon those] who have turned away;
having taken pleasure in the skill of the Soma-presser, he makes him his friend and ally—blessed are the gifts of Indra.
He beholds, like a mortal, the waters; he who is equal to the seers, having enjoyed the soma-presser’s skill, makes him his companion and ally. Auspicious are the gifts of Indra. 6.
This Indra, being measured (*ṛcīṣamaḥ*) by the hymn—that is, defined and delimited by the praise of the *ṛc*—looks down upon us with favor.
Therein lies an illustration:
like a human (*mānuṣaḥ*), who looks down at wells (*avatān*) and pits.

And having seen [him], being pleased (*juṣṭvī*), he makes him a *yuj*—one who is joined—and a *sakhi*, a friend, for the sacrificer who possesses Soma and whose skill (*dakṣa*) has increased. The meaning is that he fulfills his intention.
Or alternatively:
Like a thirsty man who, upon being praised, sees wells full of water as if they were the Soma to be drunk, he—
having observed that Soma being prepared and having partaken of it— makes himself a friend to the skillful Soma-presser.
All the gods, O Indra, have yielded to your heroic power and to your will;
you have become the lord of all, O much-praised one. Blessed are the gifts of Indra.

1. By that which is impelled, joined with *kha*, *jña*, *ta* (1st, 2nd, and 3rd), *bha*, *ra*, and *aya*. 2. From *gha*, *tat* (that), and *tasmāt* (from that), [he] goes (*eti*). 3. O *gha*, come here to this sacrifice (*yajñe*). 4. O *gha*, [this is] yours (*te*). 5. By *ta*, *na*, and *pūjataḥ* (the two who worship). 6. By *kha*, *gha*, *ta* (1st, 2nd), and *diśasi* (you direct). 7. By *kha*, *gha*, *ta*, and *śa*, [he is] to be praised (*stutyaḥ*). 8. By *kha*, *jña*, *ta* (1st, 2nd), and *kṛṇute* (he makes), *kurute* (he does). All the gods, O Indra, have granted you heroic power to perform. You have become the lord of all cattle, O much-praised one; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. (7)

"O Indra," all the gods, following after "your" (te) "heroic power" (vīrya)—that is, capability—and "will" (kratu)—that is, wisdom—(anu) "placed" (dadhuḥ) them [in you]. They maintain both heroic power and wisdom.
The meaning is that by means of your strength and your wisdom, they too become strong and wise.
Such as you are, you are the "Lord of Cows" (*gopati*), meaning the lord of the well-known cows, or of waters, or of words of praise;
you "become" (*bhavaḥ*).
This is a qualification of the word *go*, even though it occurs within the compound *viśvasya*.
The syntactical connection is: "O Indra, invoked by many, you become [the object] of many praises."
O Indra, that power of yours is supreme among the gods;
for with your might you slay Vṛtra, O Lord of Might. Blessed are the gifts of Indra.
That power of yours, O Indra, is for the sake of the divine assembly; it is most near when you slay Vṛtra with your might, O Lord of Might. Blessed are the gifts of Indra. 8.
O Indra, I praise that supreme power of yours for the sake of the gods, for the sacrificer, or for the purpose of the sacrifice;
because you, O Lord of Might, slay Vṛtra with your vigor and strength, therefore that power of yours is praised.
Making human generations flourish as if with a garment, Indra—famed for his half-share—attained that consciousness; auspicious are the gifts of Indra.
As if with a pleasant voice, making the human generations beautiful, Indra—the one renowned from afar—has attained that consciousness. Blessed are the gifts of Indra. 9.

Just as a woman of equal mind makes men who are otherwise formless appear beautiful, and being herself self-controlled, brings them under her power, so too this Indra causes human beings to obtain their respective ages—the periods of time consisting of years, seasons, months, and so forth. Having performed that act of fashioning the ages, Indra made himself the "conscious one," the knower and director of all; this is the sense of the verse. And having done so, he became "famous," renowned everywhere.
O Indra, your power is renowned; your deeds are exalted on high.
Abundant indeed have they increased in your protection; auspicious are the gifts of Indra.

O Indra, your power is known; they have raised you up and raised your many deeds on high, O possessor of many cattle. O lord of the Maruts, under your protection, the bounties of Indra are auspicious. 10.
The word *indra* here is connected with the word *avāvṛdhuḥ*, even though it is separated [by intervening words]. They cause him to swell with Soma.
What?
Those horses are his strength;
not only are they strength, but they also "exalt" you through praise and other such acts.
Afterwards, they cause "your" "kratu"—that is, your wisdom—to "grow up" according to their own favor.
The word "bhūri" (much), which was previously set aside, is connected here;
the meaning is that they cause it to increase exceedingly.
Who are those who act in this way? It is said:

O *abhūri-go* (possessor of many cows), O *bahu-paśu* (possessor of many cattle), O *maghavan* (generous one), O *dhanavat* (wealthy) *indra*, those who abide in *tava śarman*—that is, in your happiness—they too act thus.
1. In the *kha-gā-ta-na-bha* [recension], "dadhuḥ" is absent.
2. In the *gha* [recension]: "O Indra, you are the lord of the universe.
3. In the *jña-na-bha* [recension], "vavṛdhuḥ" [is present].

Both I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra, shall join together for the sake of the Sūnīs. Even the stingy man, O wielder of the stone, shall yield to us, O Hero; for auspicious are the gifts of Indra. (11) O slayer of Vṛtra, Indra, both you and I shall join together—we shall become united—for the sake of the Sūnīs, for as long a time as it takes to obtain wealth. O wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, even a stingy person—one who does not give—shall yield to us, even to us who have joined together; he shall grant his consent to our wealth. (11)

Truly indeed do we praise that Indra, and not falsely. Great is the destruction for him who does not press [the Soma]; abundant are the lights for him who presses. Blessed are the gifts of Indra. (12) Truly indeed do we praise that Indra, and not falsely; we do not praise him with untruth. The meaning is: may the qualities spoken of by us be truly real and not false. Regarding the one being praised, Indra, the destruction of the one who does not press—that is, the non-sacrificer—is great and powerful. For the sacrificer who presses many *soma* juices—that is, performs the extraction—the favor bestowed by Indra is great. (41)
The fourth hymn consists of twelve verses beginning with "sa pūrvyaḥ.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "sa pūrvyaḥ; [the meter is] Gāyatra; the first [verse], the fourth and following two, and the seventh are Anuṣṭubhs; the others are Gāyatrīs; the last is a Daivī Triṣṭubh.
Thus, the first, fourth, fifth, and seventh—these four—are Anuṣṭubhs; the verse beginning with "asme rudrāḥ" is a Triṣṭubh; and the remaining verses are Gāyatrīs.
The remaining deities are the gods;
those prescribed for the sixth day of the Marutvatīya [śastra] are the first eight verses addressed to Indra.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘sa pūrvyo mahānām’ and ‘traya indrasya somāḥ’ are the introductory verse (pratipad) and the following verse (anucara) of the Marutvatīya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

He, the ancient one, the beloved of the great, has been anointed with the seasonal rites; through whose doors Manu, the father, anointed the sacred thoughts among the gods. He, the ancient, the chief of the great—the worshipful sacrificers—has been anointed with the seasonal rites as their instrumental cause; he, the beloved (vena), desiring their oblation, comes (ānaje). Through whose doors—that is, having reached the means of access—Manu, the father and protector of all, anointed the sacred thoughts (dhiyaḥ) among these gods. *Ānaj* is a verb meaning "to reach" or "to attain."

May the pressing-stones, with Soma upon their backs, rise up like the measure of heaven; may the hymns and the sacred prayers be recited. May the pressing-stones, with Soma upon their backs—the makers of the Soma-pressing—rise up like the measure of heaven, [releasing] Indra, the creator of the heavenly world. Furthermore, may the hymns (ukthā), the ritual recitations, and the sacred prayers (brahma), the songs of praise, be recited.
2. Indra is [denoted by] the letters kha, jha, ta (first and second), na, bha, and sa.
3. Indra is the foremost [denoted by] the letter gha.
The remainder [of the verse] implies that these are "to be praised" (śaṃsyā), meaning they are worthy of praise.
Alternatively, the construction is as follows:
"May those hymns and recitations that exist not abandon Indra."

That wise Indra disclosed the cows for the Aṅgirases; he drove them forth. I praise that manly deed of his. 3. He, the wise one, Indra, disclosed the cows for the Aṅgirases; he drove them forth. I praise that manly deed of his. 3.
That wise Indra, knowing the means, opened up for the sake of the Aṅgirases the cows that had been carried off and hidden by the Paṇis;
I praise such manly power and capability as his.

According to the ancient way, may Indra, the increaser of the sage, the destroyer of Vaka, the auspicious one at the invocation of the hymn, come hither to us for our protection. He, according to the ancient way, the increaser of the sage, Indra, the destroyer of Vaka, the auspicious one at the invocation of the hymn—may he come hither to us for our protection.
That Indra, as in the ancient times, even now—increasing the wise, the singers; the bringer of speech for the singer; the auspicious one who brings happiness;

[the lord] of the *arka* (the soma), so called because it is worthy of worship and the means of worship—let him come for our protection (*avase*) for the sake of the offering (*home*) of such soma, while we are present as the cause [of the rite].

Now indeed, O Indra, according to your will, may those who sacrifice to you with the cry of *svāhā* follow the desire of the worshipper; may the singers follow after your strength for the giving of the stall of cattle. 5. Now indeed, O Indra, according to your will, may those who sacrifice to you with the cry of *svāhā* follow the desire of the worshipper; may the singers follow after your strength for the giving of the stall of cattle. 5.
Or rather, the connection is: "O Indra, immediately after that, they follow after your *kratu*—your action—in due order.
They praise in succession. Who? [The answer follows:]...
"O Svāhākāra, O Svāhā-devī, [and] of the lord Agni, the *yajyavas* are those who sacrifice;
that is to say, those performing the sacrifice in the fire for your sake.
Such are the *arkas*, the worshippers and praisers."
*Śvātram* is a name for "quickly.
The intention is that they praise very swiftly and without prolixity, without making a delay in the form of praising other deities.
For what purpose do they praise? It is said:
For the bestowing of the lineage, for the giving of wealth.

In Indra all heroic deeds have been done and are yet to be done—he whom the singers know as the sacrifice. 6. In Indra | all | heroic deeds | have been done | and | are yet to be done | him | the singers | the sacrifice | know. 6.
In this Indra, all—meaning every—heroic deeds (*vīryā*) that have been done, those yet to be done, and those currently to be performed, exist; this is the ellipsis.
That Indra whom the *arkas* (praisers) know as the *adhvara*, the non-violent one—in him [all these powers reside].
On the fifth day, the *pratipad* of the *marutvatīya* [śastra] is the triplet beginning with "yat pāñcajanya yā.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The *pratipad* and *anucara* of the *marutvatīya* are 'yat pāñcajanya yā' and 'viś indra it somapā ekaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).

When the shouts of the fivefold people rose up toward Indra, he strewed forth his inspired songs with power; such is the dwelling of the noble one. When the shouts of the fivefold people rose up toward Indra, he strewed forth his inspired songs with power; such is the dwelling of the noble one. (7)
1. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ta, bha, ra, śa, and 'ca' do not exist. When [the word] *pāñcajanya* occurs, the five people (*pañcajana*) are the four castes together with the Niṣādas as the fifth.
There, with his own power and progeny, Indra’s roar was released;
they were struck down and scattered. Then this Indra, by his own greatness—meaning without any other assistance—overthrew and destroyed his enemies.
Such a one, Indra, is the object of praise; he is the dwelling place and the abode of the wise, of the hymns of the inspired poets, and of honor and hospitality.
This is your hymn of praise; you have performed those manly deeds for the sake of Cakṣu’s turning-point.
This [is it]. "Ūm"—thus [you spoke]. To them, you performed the *anuṣṭuti* (praise). You have performed those manly deeds; you have furthered the turning of the wheel. 8.
This praise (*anuṣṭuti*), being performed now as a favorable hymn of praise, belongs to you. To the question "Why is that so? it is said:

Since you have performed those well-known heroic deeds (*pauṃsyā*), such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others; that is the meaning of "those. O Indra, you have protected (*prāvaḥ*) the track (*vartanim*), the path of the wheel (*cakrasya*), which is the support of the chariot.
The meaning is that she protects [us] so that no obstacle created by a *rakṣas* may arise against our coming to the sacrifice.
The wide stride of this bull has been taken for the sake of living; he has seized it like a boar seizing barley.
For this bull, at the devouring of the grain, he has strode out widely so that he may live; he has seized the barley like a gathering beast. 9.
When various foods have been obtained for this showering Indra, the bull, every person makes a wide stride for the sake of life—that is, he sets out upon his path.
Or rather, when food belonging to Indra has been obtained or is to be obtained, he makes his footfall.
Having done so, everyone takes [it] from him who is praised, just as cattle take up barley.
O Maruts, sons of Dakṣa, may we, seeking aid through you, be possessed of such wealth for our increase.
Holding that [wealth], seeking your favor, O fathers of skill, may we be yours for the sake of the increase of the Maruts. 10.

"Maintaining that hymn," meaning holding it fast; "seeking aid" (*avasyavaḥ*), meaning desiring protection; we, O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), [should be understood as being] accompanied by you—or so the construction should be joined.
Such are we, "those whose father is Dakṣa."
The skillful one is food.
May we be its guardians, protectors, and masters.
For what purpose?
Of Indra, who possesses the Maruts—that is, who is accompanied by the Maruts—for the sake of increase, that is, for the strengthening [of him] through sacrifice.
O Hero, we praise you with hymns for your seasonal abode;
may we conquer with you as our ally, O Indra.
Truly! To the seasonal power, with hymns we praise you, O Hero. May we conquer, O Indra, with you as our ally. 11.

Truly, O Hero Indra! We praise you exceedingly with hymns—that is, we laud you with sacred verses—for you who exist at the proper season for the rite; the word *ṛta* indicates the time of sacrifice. To you, the manifestation of auspicious splendor (*dhāman*) who has appeared at that sacrificial time, we offer our highest praise.
O Indra, with you as our praised ally and companion, may we conquer—may we defeat—the enemies.
May the Rudras, the liberal ones, and the mountains be united with us in the slaying of Vṛtra when the call to battle is raised;
may those gods, with Indra as their chief—those who are established as a firm support for him who recites and praises—protect us.

1. kha ga ta na śa anya; 2. gha jña arthaḥ svāmī; 3. kha jña ta 1-2-3 yajamānasya; 4. kha ga ta na bha śa kutastava; 5. ta na śa yojye; 6. kha ga ta na bha śa kāle; 7. kha ga ta na bha śa ^atiśayena stumaḥ^ nāsti asme iti rudrāḥ mehanā parvatāsaḥ vṛtrahatye bharahūtau sujoṣāḥ yaḥ śaṃsate stuvate dhāyi pañjaḥ indrajyeṣṭhāḥ asmān avantu devāḥ || 12 || 1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ta, na, śa are "other" (anya). 2. [The syllables] gha, jña, arthaḥ, svāmī. 3. [The syllables] kha, jña, ta, 1, 2, 3 belong to the sacrificer (yajamāna). 4. From where (kutaḥ) is yours (tava), [the syllables] kha, ga, ta, na, bha, śa. 5. To be joined (yojya) [are the syllables] ta, na, śa. 6. At the time (kāle) [of the syllables] kha, ga, ta, na, bha, śa. 7. [The phrase] "we praise exceedingly" (atiśayena stumaḥ) is not present [in this context]. [The verse: "To us (asme), O Rudras, the Parvatas, with great bounty (mehanā), at the slaying of Vṛtra (vṛtrahatye) and at the call of battle (bharahūtau), being well-disposed (sujosāḥ)—those who have been established for him who recites and praises (yaḥ śaṃsate stuvate dhāyi)—may the gods, with Indra as their chief (indrajyeṣṭhāḥ), protect us! (pañjaḥ asmān avantu devāḥ) || 12 ||

May the Rudras, who are endowed with the power of pouring forth water, and the mountains—that is, the clouds—along with Indra, who is of one accord (*sajoṣāḥ*) with us in the slaying of Vṛtra and in the call to battle, protect us. That Indra, who is powerful (*pañjaḥ*)—meaning forceful or swift—and who goes toward the sacrificer who praises him, recites his name, and offers hymns of praise; may he, together with these gods of whom Indra is the chief, protect and guard us. The word "us" (*asmān*) is used for emphasis. Or rather, it may be construed in this way: [the Rudras, etc.,] protect us.

The Rudras, sons of Rudra, who are endowed with the power of pouring forth and sprinkling; who are like mountains, possessing mountain-like solidity, or rather, full and pleasing—according to the Nirukta (1.20), "A *parva* [is so called] from the root *pṛṇāti* or *prīṇāti*" [meaning to fill or to please].

At the slaying of Vṛtra and at the call for battle, may the Maruts, the gods who are in harmony and have become our allies, together with Indra as their chief—the Indra characterized as described above—follow after us.
The fifth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “urvā mandantu,” belongs to Pragātha.
According to the rule regarding the *prāgvat* suffix, it is in the Gāyatrī meter and dedicated to Indra.
This is stated in the Anukramaṇikā: “‘urvā’ [is the first word].”
The application is based on the conventional sense.

May the hymns of praise gladden you; bestow bounty, O wielder of the stone! Strike down those who hate the sacred word. And may the hymns of praise gladden you; bestow bounty, O wielder of the stone! Strike down those who hate the sacred word.
O Indra, may these hymns of praise gladden and exhilarate you most highly.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, bestow wealth upon us;
furthermore, strike down those who hate the sacred word.

With your foot, trample down the stingy Panis; you are great, for there is no one at all who can withstand you. 2. With your foot, [trample] the Panis, the ungenerous ones; trample them down. You are the Great One; indeed, no one whatsoever is a match for you. 2.
Trample down with your foot those who are stingy, ungenerous, devoid of sacrificial offerings, and possess wealth for themselves alone;
indeed, there is no one at all—be it a god, an asura, or a human—who can stand as your equal match.

You rule over the pressed juices, O Indra; you rule over the unpressed; you are the king of the people. 3. You. Rule. Over the pressed juices. O Indra. You. Over the unpressed. You. King. Of the people. 3.
O Indra, you are the master, the lord, of the pressed-out Soma juices that have been extracted;
likewise, you are the master of those not yet pressed out, which exist in the form of beautiful [unmanifest] states.
You are the king of all people.

Come hither, go forth; thy dwelling is in heaven. Let the cry of the people resound; thou fillest both worlds, O Heaven and Earth. 4. Come! Go forth! Thy dwelling is in heaven. Let the shout of the people rise up. Thou fillest both worlds, Heaven and Earth. 4.

O Indra, come here; come forth. Likewise, go forward from heaven—that is, from the celestial world. What? To your dwelling. Doing what? Making a sound, proclaiming yourself. For what purpose? For the sake of the people, that is, for the benefit of human beings. Or alternatively: having accepted the oblation, go forward and proceed happily; proclaiming [yourself] in heaven, praising the sacrificer. You fill both worlds—heaven and earth—with your splendor or with rain.
1. Having transcended Kha-Ta-Na-Śa.
2. Indeed, therefore you are great (Gha-Khalu-Atas-Tvam-Mahān-Asi).
3. Come from Kha-Gha-Ta-Na-Bha; come (Śa-Āgaccha).

Even that mountain, the cloud, possessing hundreds and thousands [of waters], you shattered apart for the sake of your worshippers. (5) O Indra, even *tyam*—that very one; *cit* is a filler particle. *Parvatam* means the mountain, the cloud. Since both terms refer to the cloud, one should understand them as a combination of etymological derivation (*yogarūḍha*). Possessing hundreds—that is, possessing hundreds of waters—and likewise possessing thousands, meaning a cloud of immeasurable rain, you shattered it apart (*vi rurojitha*) with your thunderbolt for the benefit of your worshippers.

We indeed call upon you by day at the pressing of the Soma; we call upon you by night. Fulfill our desire! O Indra, we call upon you by day when the Soma has been pressed; likewise, we call upon you by night. Having come when called, fulfill our desire.

Whose is this bull, the youth, with the powerful neck, never bending? Which priest honors him? (7) Who is he? That bull, the showerer [of benefits], the youth, eternally young, with the powerful neck, the broad-throated, the unbending—never once bowing down—who knows where Indra dwells? Which priest, which singer, honors you, worships you?

Whose libation, indeed, does the bull, having enjoyed it, go toward as a steed? And who, indeed, has fashioned Indra for himself? (8) Whose libation—*svit* being used here in the sense of inquiry—does the bull, Indra, the showerer of benefits, approach with pleasure as he hastens? And who, indeed, has made Indra his own—that is, who knows how to praise him? *Svit* is an expletive used for emphasis. *Arvā* means "steed" or "one who goes swiftly. *Jujuṣvān* means "having enjoyed" or "being pleased. *Ā cake* means "has fashioned" or "has recognized" in the sense of knowing how to praise. *Ū* is an emphatic particle. *Kasya svit savanam*—"Whose libation?"—expresses doubt or inquiry. *Vṛṣā* refers to Indra, the rain-giver. *Ava gacchati* means "he goes down toward" or "he approaches. *Ka u*—"Who indeed"—refers to the sacrificer. *Indram ā cake*—"has fashioned Indra," meaning he knows how to worship or praise him. *Svit* is a filler word (*pūraṇa*).

Whom have thy gifts reached? O slayer of Vṛtra, whom have thy heroic powers reached? Whom do the hymns reach? And who indeed is the nearest [to thee] in battle? [Thy] gifts, given by the sacrificers, have reached (*asakṣata*) and serve thee. O slayer of Vṛtra, O Indra, what kind of thee do the hymns (*ukthe*) reach with their recitations? And what heroic powers (*suvīryā*), those praises of excellent valor, have reached thee? And who indeed is the nearest (*antamaḥ*) in the fray? In the second turn of the rite, in the *śastra* of the Hotṛ, the triplet beginning with "This one for thee among men" (*ayaṃ te mānuṣe*) serves as the *anurūpa*. It is stated in the Sūtra: "‘This one for thee among men... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

1. In manuscripts *kha*, *ta*, and *ābhūta*. 2. In manuscript *ga*, *na* and *śa* lack the word ‘vistīrṇakandharaḥ’. 3. In manuscript *gha1*: ‘stotāraṃ vā’; in *ca*: ‘stotā-taṃ tvāṃ’; in *ya*: ‘stotā taṃ’. 4. In manuscript *ga*: ‘asevanta’. 5. In manuscripts *kha*, *ta*, and *śa*: ‘yuddhe dvitīye yuddhe’.

This Soma of yours is pressed among many men in the human race. Come to it; hasten forward and drink it. (10) This Soma is for you—either belonging to you or produced for your sake—pressed among many men, within the human race, or indeed among the Pūru kings. "Of this" means *of that*. "Come to it": having arrived, hasten toward the house; having done so, drink that Soma.

This [Soma] of yours, most intoxicating, is dear upon the Śaryaṇāvat, on the Suṣomā, and in Ārjīkīya. (11) This Soma, pressed by us, O Lord, is most intoxicating—that is, most exhilarating—for you. It is "resting upon" (āśrita), that is, supported by [certain places]. Where? That is stated: on the Śaryaṇāvat, the lake situated at the lower part of Kurukṣetra, which is possessed of autumnal waters. Where does that lake exist? It is stated: on the Suṣomā, the river bearing this name. And where does she exist? That is stated: in Ārjīkīya, the region bearing this name. The Soma which exists in those aforementioned places—this very one has been pressed. "Drink it"—this is the connection with what follows.

Come today for great bounty, for the lovely exhilaration that is impetuous; O Indra, run hither and drink this! (12) [The word] *tam* [refers to] that Soma described in the preceding mantra—him who flows in five streams and moves in five courses. Drink him for our great *rādhase* (bounty/wealth), for your *madāya* (exhilaration) which is *ghṛṣvaye* (impetuous, crushing the enemies). O *indra*, for that purpose *drava* (run/hasten) toward the Soma-vessel; for that purpose, *ehi* (come) now! The sixth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "yadindra prāk," is by Pragātha, in the Gāyatrī meter, and addressed to Indra. This is indicated by the *Anukramaṇī*: "yadindra. The application (*viniyoga*) is determined by its indicative marks.

O Indra, since you are invoked from the east, the west, the north, or the south by our men, come quickly with your swift steeds. O Indra, since you are called from the east, the west, the north, or the south by our men—the leaders of the ritual—come quickly with your swift-moving horses. Come hither at once!

Or whether you rejoice in the outflow of heaven, O Svarṇara; or whether you rejoice in the ocean of the soma-juice. Or whether you rejoice in the outflow of heaven—that place where the nectar flows—or whether you rejoice in Svarṇara (the one who leads to heaven), that is, on the earth at another place of sacrifice; or whether you rejoice in the ocean of the *andhas*—whereby the word *andhas* (food) indicates its cause, water—in the atmosphere which is the source of that overflowing; wherever you may be situated, [we call upon you]—this is to be connected with what follows.
1. *ta* is pronounced as *na*; *śa* is pronounced as *śru*. 2.
*gha* [is pronounced as *ja*] when followed by *ya*. 3.

With songs (*gīrbhiḥ*), I call upon you, the great and vast one, like a cow for the sake of nourishment, O Indra, for the drinking of Soma. (3) *Ā tvā gīrbhir mahām uruṃ huve gām iva bhojase indra somasya pītaye.* (3) O Indra, I call upon you (*tvā*) with songs (*gīrbhiḥ*), that is, with hymns of praise. Of what kind are you? Great (*mahām*), meaning immense; vast (*urum*), meaning abundant. For what purpose? For the drinking (*pītaye*) of Soma. As for the illustration: "like a cow for the sake of nourishment" (*bhojase*).

O Indra, let your bay horses, bearing your greatness upon the chariot, bring it hither; O God, let your bay horses, bearing your majesty upon the chariot, bring it hither. (4) O Indra, let your bay horses (*harayaḥ*), bearing and supporting your greatness (*mahimānam*)—your majesty—upon the chariot, bring it hither. Likewise, O God (*deva*), let the horses, bearing your majesty (*mahaḥ*)—your splendor—upon the chariot, bring it hither. Since it is impossible for the greatness and the majesty to be brought separately, the meaning is that they bring [the chariot] distinguished by both. Alternatively, the construction may be joined thus: "Let them bring you, who are bearing your greatness, upon the chariot; and let them bring you, who are bearing your majesty."

O Indra, you are praised; indeed, you are extolled as the Great, the Fierce, the Maker of Sovereignty. Come hither and drink our pressed juice. (5) O Indra, you are praised (*guṇīṣe*); indeed (*u*), you are extolled (*stuṣe*). [The particle] *u* is used here in the sense of "and. Of what nature are you? Great (*mahān*), increased by virtues; fierce (*ugraḥ*), possessed of formidable power; the Maker of Sovereignty (*īśānakṛt*), the creator of lordship. Such as you are, come (*ehi*)! Having come, drink (*piba*) our pressed Soma.

Possessing the pressed [Soma], we, providing sacrificial food, invoke you; for you to sit upon this *barhis* of ours. (6) "Possessing the pressed [Soma]," "you," "we," "providing sacrificial food," "invoke," "this," "of us," "*barhis*," "for sitting. (6) We—possessing the pressed [Soma], meaning possessing the Soma that has been extracted, and providing sacrificial food, meaning possessing the sacrificial pap (*caru*), the cake (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth—invoke you; we call upon you. For what purpose? For the sake of sitting upon this *barhis* of ours; that is, for the sake of being seated upon the *barhis* at the sacrifice, or upon the sacrificial grass itself. (46)

For since you indeed, O Indra, are common to all the many [sacrificers], as such we invoke you. (7) *Yat* (since); *cit* (indeed); *hi* (for); *śaśvatām* (of the many); *asi* (you are); *indra* (O Indra); *sādhāraṇaḥ* (common to all); *tvam* (you); *tam* (that); *tvā* (you); *vayam* (we); *havāmahe* (invoke). (7) O Indra, because you indeed (*yaccidhi*) are common (*sādhāraṇaḥ*) to many (*śaśvatām*) sacrificers—*cit* being a filler particle and *hi* indicating well-known fact—we (*vayam*) invoke (*havāmahe*) you (*tvā*), who are such a common one. The sense is that we call upon you even before others. At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), "This Soma-draught is for you" (*idaṃ te somyam*) is the *hotṛ*'s *prasthitayājyā*. It is also stated in the Sūtra: "This Soma-honey is for you; we invoke Mitra" (*āśva. śrau. 5. 5*).

Men have milked this Soma-like honey for you with the pressing-stones; O Indra, being pleased, drink it! 8. This—for you—Soma-like—honey—they have milked—with stones—men—enjoying—O Indra—that—drink! 8.
1. Bearing [the vessel] from Kha-Ta-Na-Śa;
2. for the sake of sitting down at Kha-Jha-Ta-1-2-Bha-1-2.

O Indra, for you (te), for your sake, they have milked this honey connected with Soma (somya) belonging to Soma—by the Atris, by means of the pressing-stones (grāvabhiḥ) which are the instruments of attainment; [they are] the men, our own officiating priests and others.
O Indra, enjoying and being pleased by that honeyed draught, drink!

For you surpass all noble sages; come quickly, O You who are praised! Bestow upon us great renown. 9. [All] the noble [sages], the wise ones—surpassing them, indeed, come quickly! Bestow upon us great renown. 9.
O Indra, you are the master of the noble ones; look beyond all the wise singers of praise.
For that purpose, come quickly!
Having arrived, bestow upon us—among us—abundant food, glory, or fame.

May the King, the giver of spotted deer that bring gold, be my provider; O gods, may the bounteous Indra not come to harm. The King, Indra, shall be the giver to me of spotted deer (*pṛṣatī*) that bring gold (*hiraṇyavī*). O gods, may the bounteous Indra (*maghavā*) not suffer injury.

Upon a thousand spotted cows, I have received a great, broad, bright, and pure piece of gold, radiant as the moon. (11) Upon a thousand spotted cows, I have received a great, broad, bright, and pure piece of gold, radiant as the moon. (11) I accept—that is, I take possession of—the gold brought by Indra, which is placed upon a thousand spotted cows, which is vast, extensive, moon-like in its brilliance, and pure and stainless.

The descendants of my protector Durgaha, through a thousandfold wealth bestowed by the bountiful one, have achieved renown among the gods. (12) O descendants of Durgaha, my protectors—having become possessed of excellent wealth (*surādhas*) through a thousandfold, immeasurable riches such as cattle granted by Indra—and while the gods are pleased (meaning, when Indra is pleased), they have won *śravaḥ*—that is, food or glory—among the gods; that is to say, they have obtained it. (12)
The seventh hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “tarobhir vaḥ,” is the seerical composition (ārṣam) of Kali, the son of Pragātha.

The first, third, and other odd-numbered verses are Bṛhatīs; the second, fourth, and other even-numbered verses are Satobṛhatīs; and the fifteenth is an Anuṣṭubh. Thus states the Anukramaṇikā: “tarobhiḥ pañconā kaliḥ prāgāthaḥ; prāgātham antyānuṣṭup. (Kali, the son of Pragātha, [composed] fifteen verses minus five [i.e., ten]; it is in the Prāgātha meter, with the final verse being an Anuṣṭubh.)
This hymn is included in the Bṛhat-trca-aśīti of the Niṣkevalya at the Mahāvrata.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: "He removes the last verses [of the preceding hymn] with the words, 'tarobhir vo vidadvasum' (Ai. Ā. 5.2.4).
In the Acchāvāka-śastra of the Agniṣṭoma, this Pragātha serves as the Stotriya.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two Pragāthas, *tarobhir vo vidadvasum* and *taraṇir isipāsati*, are the Stotriya and Anurūpa [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.16).
On the twenty-fourth day, this very Pragātha serves as the Stotriya.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "*tarobhir vo vidadvasum taraṇir isipāsati*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).

1. Who are those attacking with weapons of iron (gha-sādhana)? 2. [He protects] all the singers (stotṛn). 3. Of the spotted antelopes (pṛṣatīnām akṣṇām). 4. The word "great" (mahat) is absent in manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ta, na, and śa. 5. Indeed, the moon (candram) in manuscripts kha, ta, na, bha, and śa. 6. Indeed, the delighter (āhlādakam) in manuscripts kha, gha, ta, na, and bha. 7. "Of me" (me mama) in manuscripts kha, gha, jha, ta₁, and me. 8. O son of Pragātha (pragāthaputra) in manuscripts ga, ta, na, and śa. 9. Pragātha in manuscripts kha, ga, ta₁₋₃, and na. 10. Pragātha in manuscripts kha, ga, and bha.

With your speeds, O priests, [invoke] Indra, the finder of wealth, for our protection; singing the *Bṛhat* [Sāman], at the sacrifice where Soma is pressed, I call him as one calls a skilled provider who brings bounty. O priests, with your speeds—either possessed of speed or by means of speed itself—invoke Indra, the discoverer of riches (*vidadvasum*), for our aid. Being those who chant the *Bṛhat* [Sāman], attend upon him. Where? At the sacrifice where Soma is pressed, in the ritual of the Soma-offering. And I, too, call that Indra; like what? Like a supporter (*bharam*) who nourishes his family and is habitually beneficent (*kāriṇam*), whom sons and others call for their own welfare—even so do I call such an Indra.

Neither the fierce ones nor the steadfast gods can restrain him, O fair-cheeked one, in his exhilaration from the soma-juice—he who bestows upon the one who exerts himself, who presses the juice, and who praises him, that which is worthy of hymns. Neither the fierce ones (*dudhrāḥ*)—the Asuras and others—can restrain him in battle; nor do the steadfast gods restrain him. Furthermore, the mortal men (*suraḥ*), whose nature is to die, cannot restrain him. In his exhilaration (*made*) produced by drinking the soma-juice (*andhasaḥ*), he becomes the giver to the one who exerts himself (*śaśamānāya*), to the one who presses the juice (*sunvate*), and to the one who praises him (*jaritre*). What does he give? That which is worthy of hymns (*ukthyam*), wealth that is fit for praise. He causes [the earth] to tremble—this is the connection with what follows.

He who is the powerful Indra, the cleanser, who belongs to the horses, or he who is the one praised by the singers, the golden one—he, Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, makes the opening of the vast stall of cattle tremble. He who is the powerful Indra, the cleanser, who belongs to the horses—*aśvya* means "skilled with horses," or the suffix *-ya* is used here in its own sense; thus *mṛkṣa-aśvya* means he exists like a horse that has been washed clean. Or he who is the one praised by the singers—the word *kīja* expresses praise: "What is this? How was he born? And he who is the golden one, whose body is made of gold—that Indra, such a marvelous being, the slayer of Vṛtra, makes the opening of the vast stall of cattle—that is, the multitude of cows—tremble; the meaning is that he causes it to shake.
He who rends apart even that which is buried and well-accumulated for the sake of wealth for the donor—
Indra, the fair-cheeked one with bay horses, shall act by his own power according to his will.

1. In the *ghana-abhiṣuta-somaka* [manuscripts]. 2. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa*: for the sake of "you" (*tvad-artha*). 3. *kha-ta-na-śa*: the instrument (*karaṇa*) is accompanied by; *bha*: it is for one's own benefit (*sva-hita-karaṇa*). 4. *kha-ta-ma-śa*: there is no [mention] of food (*anna*) or Soma. 5. *kha-ta-na-bha-1-2*: lack of fortitude (*mā-dhṛti*).

Even that which is buried, even that wealth which has been gathered and accumulated—sacrifices, gifts, and the like—the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), the fair-jawed one (*suśiprāḥ*), the lord of bay horses (*hariaśvaḥ*), Indra, brings forth for the donor, the sacrificer. He indeed causes it to rise up. By what means? By his will (*kratvā*), by the performance of ritual action; in whatever way he desires, in that very manner he acts. Even that which is buried, having been dug into and placed in the earth, even that wealth (*vasu*) which has been gathered and collected—sacrifices, gifts, and so on—the wielder of the thunderbolt, the fair-jawed one, the lord of bay horses, Indra, brings forth for the donor, the sacrificer. He indeed causes it to rise up. By what means? By his will, by the performance of ritual action, by the means of sacrifice; in whatever manner he desires, in that very manner he acts.

Or whatever you desired, O much-praised hero, even from among men in the past—O Indra, we bring all that together for you: sacrifice, hymn, swift luster, and splendor. (5) O Puruṣṭuta, O Indra praised by many, O Śūra, O valiant one, from among men—the leaders, the singers—even as of old, so now also, whatever you desired, O Indra, that very thing we bring together for you: swift sacrifice, hymn, and splendor. What is that? It is said: the oblation fit for sacrifice, the recitation (*uktha*), and the speech (*varcas*) to be spoken; the meaning is: we bring together for you the oblation most dear to you and the hymn of praise. (48)

O much-invoked one, wielder of the thunderbolt, drinker of Soma, come together with the pressed Soma juices for exhilaration; O bestower of desirable wealth, you indeed become the most generous giver to the one who prepares the prayer and presses the juice. *sa-cā someṣu puru-huta vajri-vaḥ madāya dhṛkṣa soma-pāḥ tvam it hi brahma-kṛte kāmyam vasu deṣṭaḥ sunvate bhavaḥ.* O *puruhūta* (much-invoked), O *vajrivaḥ* (wielder of the thunderbolt), O *somapāḥ* (drinker of Soma), may you *dhṛkṣa* (drink) together with the *someṣu* (Soma juices) for the sake of *madāya* (exhilaration). For you alone, O *deṣṭaḥ* (bestower), become the one who grants the *kāmyam vasu* (desirable wealth) to the *brahmakṛte* (composer of prayers) and the *sunvate* (presser of Soma). On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing during the *acchāvāka* ritual, "vayamenam" is the optional *anurūpa* verse. Even the wolf, though belonging to Varuṇa and a harasser of sheep, finds favor in Indra’s paths or acts of wisdom; may he, enjoying this our hymn of praise, come hither, O Indra, with wondrous thought. Even the wolf, though a thief and belonging to Varuṇa—the restrainer of all—even he, being a harasser (*urāmathi*) of enemies traveling on their path, finds favor (*bhūpati*) in Indra’s *vayunāni*—whether meaning paths or acts of wisdom. The sense is that even one who is exceedingly cruel becomes favorable to Indra. Alternatively, the genitive *asya* is used in the sense of the object: "Even the wolf, in the form of a thief, finds favor in Indra’s *vayunāni*—that is, in his hymns of praise. May he, being pleased by this our hymn (*stoma*), come hither; O Indra, with wondrous thought—that is, through the act characterized by praise—come forth and arrive swiftly. On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, in the *Acchāvāka-śastra*, the *Kadrupragātha* beginning with "kadū nu" is recited. For it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *pragāthas* end with the *kadrū* verses, such as 'kadū nvāsya akṛtam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).

What indeed is there now that remains unaccomplished of this Indra’s manly deed? By what glorious renown has the slayer of Vṛtra not been heard of from his very birth? (9) What indeed, *kad ū nu*, is there of this *asya* Indra’s *pauṃsyam*—manly deed—that *akṛtam* remains unperformed? The meaning is: everything, including the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth, has already been done by him; there is no further manly task remaining. In the world, even one who performs a small act of manliness is praised for it; yet this one has not been praised [in that limited way]. By what *śromatena*—by what glorious, praiseworthy manliness—has he *na śuśruve*—not been heard of? Not merely by deeds performed in a few days; to this he replies: this *vṛtrahā*, the slayer of the exceedingly powerful Vṛtra, has been heard of *januṣaḥ pari*—from his very birth onwards—through the powers displayed. This mention of the slaying of Vṛtra is intended to illustrate the manifestation of that manliness. The sense is: just as the slaying of Vṛtra is heard of by all, so too are his other deeds.

The word *ve* is an Apabhraṃśa corruption for *dviṣat-ardha*.

When giving one *kārṣāpaṇa* to a debtor, they show by way of calculation that two great [coins] ought to be given; thus, because they act out [this performance] with the words *dviṣat* and *eka*, they are called *be-knāṭāḥ*. They are the "half-days" (*ahar-ddhāḥ*).

By the word "day" (ahaḥ), the Sun, who is its producer, is denoted. Those who see him are "day-seers" (aharddhāḥ). Now, it may be asked: since everyone sees the Sun, what is the distinction? It is said in reply:
O Sūrya, they behold [the results] in this very life, not in another birth;
the greedy who do not perform sacrifices sink into blinding darkness.
Or rather, they see only worldly days, not the unseen matters pertaining to the world beyond.
For atheists hold sensory perception as the primary authority.
The word "uta" has the sense of "only. [They regard] the Īśānas as mere merchants—similar to merchants and like Śūdras.
The ellipsis is that he overcomes them through his power (*ṛtva*) and indeed through his ritual action (*karman*), specifically by means of the transgression of beating and so forth.
Or alternatively:
"He conquers the Paṇis," meaning he overcomes only the Paṇis themselves, not the sacrificer.
The censure of merchants is recorded in the Smṛti: "One should treat cowherds, merchants, as well as artisans, actors, servants, and usurers like Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas" (Manu 8.102).

O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, O much-invoked wielder of the thunderbolt, we, your most frequent [worshippers], bring forth these unprecedented prayers for you, as if bringing a tribute. 11. We indeed, O Indra, O slayer of Vṛtra, O much-invoked wielder of the thunderbolt, bring forth these unprecedented prayers for you, like a tribute. 11.

O Indra, we indeed bring forth for you these unprecedented, new, and strengthening prayers and hymns; we, the most numerous, offer them up to you, O Vṛtra-slayer, O slayer of Vṛtra, O much-invoked one, O wielder of the thunderbolt! What is it like?
It is like a wage, as it were.
Just as they bestow her according to a fixed rule, so too,
because of the intent to bestow her according to a fixed rule, the analogy of wages is not contradictory.

For even many prayers, O thou of mighty deeds, Indra, call upon thee for aid. Even past the libations of the enemy, come hither, O Vasu; O most powerful one, hear my invocation! 12. For even many prayers, O thou of mighty deeds, Indra, call upon thee for aid. Even past the libations of the enemy, come hither, O Vasu; O most powerful one, hear my invocation! 12.

O Indra, you who are of mighty deeds and many actions, in you alone rest many prayers and hopes; likewise, protections and aids are established in you. Therefore, other worshippers invoke you to obtain these things. O Vasu (the dweller), O Indra, passing over the libations of the enemy—or rather, passing over the enemies themselves—come hither toward our own libations. Therefore, O most powerful one, listen to my call.

Verily, O Indra, we inspired singers belong to you alone; for there is no one other than you, O much-invoked Maghavan, who is our protector. 13. *vayaṃ gha te tve id indra viprā arpismasi | nahi tvad anyaḥ puruhūta kaścana maghavan asti marditā* || 13 || Indeed, O Indra, we inspired ones belong to you alone. For there is no one other than you, O much-invoked Maghavan, who is our protector. 13.

Moreover, through your aid (*ūtī*), with wondrous wisdom and marvelous action, grant us what we desire. O most powerful one, you are the knower of the path and the knower of the means.

The eighth hymn consists of twenty-one verses beginning with "tyā nu. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "tyā nu; [it has] one more [verse]; Matsya, the son of Sāmad, a Maitrāvaruṇi, or a descendant of Manyu, or many fish caught in a net;
but the first verse is addressed to Anu."

The son of the great fish Saṃmada is Matsya; or else, Mānya, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa; or rather, many fish, having been caught in a net, praised the Ādityas for release from their bonds. Therefore, from that [lineage], the Ṛṣis [arose].
According to the paribhāṣā rule, "The Gāyatra [meter] follows the Vatsapra," the meter is Gāyatrī;
the deity is Āditya;
and the application of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics (laiṅgika).
We implore those Kṣatriyas, the Ādityas, with our prayer— those who are most gracious— for our protection and for our desired goals.
Now we entreat those Kṣatriyas, the Ādityas, for their favor—those who are most gracious—for our protection. 1.
We entreat, we beg for protection from those Ādityas who are by birth Kṣatriyas—Kṣatriyas in their very lineage.
Of what kind?
Those who are *sumṛḷīkān*, that is, those who grant excellent happiness.
For what purpose?
"For the sake of attainment" (abhiṣṭaye), meaning either for approaching or for that which is desired.
The distinction is that in the case of the fish, entering the net is sought, while in the other case, it is the desired object.

Let not this snare bind us; may it spare us for a great task. For Indra alone is renowned as the sovereign controller. (8) Let not this snare bind us; may it spare us for a great task. For Indra alone is renowned as the sovereign controller. (8) Let not this snare—the binding net—bind us. May it spare us for a great deed, setting us free from the net. Who? Indra alone; he who is renowned everywhere as the sovereign controller, the master of all. May he spare us.

O gods, you who desire to protect us, do not let us be caught in the snare of our enemies, those who act with crookedness; do not touch us with harm. (9) O gods, you who desire to protect us (*aviṣyavaḥ*), do not let us be caught (*mā... abhi pra mṛkṣata*) by the snare (*mṛcā*) of our enemies (*ripūṇām*), those who act with crookedness (*vṛjinānām*). The word *mṛc* denotes the act of harming, as seen in such passages as "with that which harms, well-fashioned" (*yacchreṇa marcayatā supeśasā*, Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.17.15). Do not let us be touched by that harmful snare; do not cast the snare over us. Or alternatively: may there be no affliction for us reached by the snare. O gods, you yourselves must cleanse [us] and ward it off. In the *pavamāna* offerings at the *ādhāna* (fire-laying), this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) beginning with "And thee, O Aditi" (*uta tvāmadite*). It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "And thee, O Aditi, the great one... the great mother" (*uta tvāmadite mahi mahīm ū ṣu mātaram*, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.1). This same verse is also the invitatory verse for the omentum (*vapā*) offering in the sacrifice to Aditi. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "And thee, O Aditi, the great one... do not lead us into distress, O wide-pasture" (*uta tvāmadite mahaneho na uruvraje*, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).

And I, O great goddess Aditi, address you for the sake of my desired goal—address you who are most gracious. O great Aditi, mother of the gods, O goddess, I—Matsya, with Matsya at my head—approach and praise you. Of what nature are you? You are *sumuḷīkā*, one who brings forth excellent happiness. For what purpose? *Abhiṣṭaye*, for the attainment of my cherished wish.

O Aditi, protect us from all sides in the shallow and the deep—that is, in the water, for "deep" (*gabhīra*) is among the names for water as it is listed in the *Nighaṇṭu* with the gloss "the unfathomable" (*gahana*). O you whose sons are fierce, rescue us from the one who seeks to kill us in that water. Let no harm come to our offspring, nor to our children; let none of them suffer injury. O wide-ranging one, grant us freedom from harm so that we may spread forth; make it possible for our progeny to live. (12) O *anehas* (one free from harm), O *uruvraje* (you whose range is vast)—for this Aditi, the Earth, has gone far because of her extreme extensiveness—O wise one, O *ūruci* (you who shine widely), grant us the power to move forth and spread out for the sake of our offspring’s life. (12) [Note: *Urucī* is derived from *uru* (wide) + *ci* (to shine); *anehas* means "without harm" or "sinless"; *uruvraje* refers to the Earth (*aditi*) which is "far-reaching" due to its vastness.]

Act for whom? For our offspring, for our son, for our life—for his living. Act so that we, along with our sons, may live; thus, O you of vast power, act. Those who are the heads of the peoples, undeceived, possessing celestial glory, who guard the sacred laws, being free from malice—(13). Those who are the heads of the peoples, undeceived, possessing celestial glory, who guard the sacred laws, being free from malice—(13). Therefore, O Ādityas, grant us that new [favor] for our ancient [deeds], which shall release us from bondage like one bound, O Aditi. 18.
"May that bond of ours be well-praised as something new for the sake of our enjoyment;

by our liberation, it shall become worthy of praise for the sake of your continued presence. O Ādityas, sons of Aditi, and O Aditi, through your favor, may that which binds us—which previously acted as an obstacle—be released from us by your grace."
Alternatively, it should be construed thus:
"May that protection of yours which releases us be truly worthy of praise and lead to our devoted service."
O Ādityas, we possess no such power to leap over that [obstacle]; do you therefore have mercy upon us. 19. [We] do not; [our] is; that; power; O Ādityas; to leap over; you; for us; have mercy. 19.

O Ādityas, that speed (*taraḥ*) produced by you, the Ādityas, does not exist for us—that speed which is capable of leaping over (*atiṣkaḍe*), for our own leaping-over, the snare of the binder. Therefore, O you, have mercy upon us; the meaning is: provide us with such speed as that.

O Ādityas, let not the weapon of Viśvavat, nor the fashioned arrow, strike us down before old age. 20. O Ādityas, let not the missile of Viśvavat, nor the crafted shaft, slay us prior to our reaching old age. 20.
O Ādityas, [protect] us, who belong to Viśvavat—that is, to Yama, the son of Viśvavat;
for the word "father" (*pitṛ*) is used here [for Yama] in reference to his son.
His *heti*—meaning his weapon, which is "unfashioned" (*akṛtrimā*), produced by action (*kriyā*), and his *śaru*, the piercing missile—is his *prasiti*.
‘Purā’ means formerly; ‘anu’ means now; the sense is “at all times. ‘Jarasaḥ’ means from the aged; ‘mā vadhīt’ means do not harm.

O Ādityas, drive away hatred, drive away distress, and drive away every compacted affliction; utterly cast away all injury. 21. Drive away! Well! Hatred! Away! Distress! O Ādityas! Away! Compacted! Everywhere! Away! Cast away! Injury! 21.
O Ādityas, Ādityās, utterly (*su*) uproot (*vi-vṛhat*), that is, destroy, our enemies (*dveṣaḥ*,
those who hate us). Likewise, uproot (*vi-vṛhata*) our distress (*aṃhati*), that is, sin and evil.
In the phrase "hanteraha ca" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.502), the suffix *atip* is applied. Likewise, "tear asunder the compact net. Likewise, "tear asunder all evil (*rapas*) in every direction and everywhere."
"'Rapaḥ' and 'ripam' are names for evil," says Yāska (Nirukta 4.21).
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may the Great Lord of Dvārakā bestow the four aims of human life.

In this regard, the ninth hymn consists of nineteen verses beginning with "ā tvā ratham. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "ā tva ekonā: Priyamedha; the first is an Anuṣṭubh; the next four are Triṣṭubhs; the others are six Ṛks praising the gift of Ṛkṣa and Aśvamedha.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Priyamedha of the lineage of Aṅgiras.
The first, fourth, seventh, and tenth verses are *anuṣṭubh*s; the remaining verses are *gāyatrī*s according to the metrical rule "the rest are *gāyatrī*.
Within the six middle verses, the giving of *ṛkṣas* and *aśvamedhas* is praised;
therefore, they have those as their deities.
The remaining [verses] belong to Indra according to the paribhāṣā rule regarding what has not been explicitly stated.
The application of the hymn is based on its indicative marks (liṅga).
The first three ṛcs constitute the *pratipad* of the Marutvatīya [śastra].
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘ā tvā rathaṃ yathotaye’ and ‘idaṃ vaso sutamandhaḥ’ are the *pratipad* and *anucara* of the *marutvatīya* [śastra]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.14).
Furthermore, in the Mahāvrata and other rites, wherever another ṛc is not specifically prescribed, this very [pair] serves everywhere as the *pratipad*.
We turn you hither for our protection and for our favor, like a chariot—
O Indra, most powerful Lord of the True, you who possess many deeds and subdue the mortal foe.
We bring you hither for our protection and for our favor, even as one turns a chariot—O Indra, most powerful Lord of the virtuous, you who perform many deeds and prevail in battle. 1.

O Indra, we turn you toward us; we cause you to return. For what purpose? For our protection (*ūtaye*) and for our happiness (*sumnāya*). Like what? Just as they turn a chariot toward them for protection and happiness, so [do we turn you]. Of what nature are you? You who are "much-active" (*tuvikūrmim*), performing many deeds, and "overcoming assailants" (*ṛtīṣaham*), the subduer of those who seek to harm. O Indra, most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*) one, O Lord of the virtuous (*satpate*), protector of the good—such is the syntactic connection.
O you of many powers, O wise one, O lord of might, whose mind encompasses all things,
you have filled [the world] with your greatness.
O you of swift impulse, O you of swift wisdom, O possessor of power, whose mind encompasses all—through your greatness, you have filled [the world].
O Turviśuṣma, you of abundant strength; O Turvikratu, you of many deeds— or rather, of much wisdom, since "deed" is mentioned separately from "wisdom"—
O Śacīvas, you whose mind is endowed with many actions, O worshipful Indra, you have filled [the world] completely with your universal greatness.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of distinction, everything [would follow].
By whose greatness, O Mighty One, your two hands have reached around the golden thunderbolt as it moves across the earth.
By whose greatness, O Mighty One, your two hands have encompassed the golden thunderbolt as it courses around the earth. 3.
"O Great One"—
the word *yat* (of whom/which) refers back to what has been previously mentioned;
the subject under discussion is the hymn (*sūkta*), which is not a substance (*adravya*).

The meaning is: "of you," who possess the characteristics previously described, such as being capable of enduring the *turu* and *kūrmi* [demons]. The sense is: "May it always ward off fear from us."

Protected by you, with you as our ally, may we win great wealth in the waters, in the sun, and in battles, O wielder of the thunderbolt. (9) O Indra, protected by you (*tvotāsaḥ*), with you as our ally (*tvā yujā*), for the sake of bathing in the waters (*apsu*) and beholding the sun (*sūrye*)—that is to say, for performing activities such as knowledge when the sun has risen, and for performing activities such as traveling—we would win (*jayema*) great wealth (*mahad dhanam*) in battles (*putsu*). O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrivaḥ*), having conquered the enemies in battle, may we obtain their wealth; this is the meaning.
On the fourth day, at the Mahānāmnī rite, the triplet beginning with "taṃ tvā yajñebhiḥ" serves as the *pratipad*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The *pratipad* and *anucara* of the Marutvatīya are 'taṃ tvā yajñebhir īmahe' and 'idaṃ vaso sutaṃ andhaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).

We entreat you with sacrifices; we entreat you with songs, O most fond of songs, O Indra, just as you have indeed protected Purumīḍha in the battles for booty. (10) We entreat *you*, who are renowned as one worthy of praise, with *sacrifices*—that is, with the means of sacrifice such as Soma and the like. We entreat that very *Indra* with *songs*, that is, with hymns of praise. O *gīrvaṇastama*, O Indra, most worthy of being praised by songs—this is the connection of the words. O *Indra*, *yathā cid āvitha*: in whatever manner you have indeed protected me; *cit* is an expletive. Where? It is said: *in the battles for booty* (*vājeṣu*), meaning in conflicts. Of what sort am I? *Purumāyyam*, meaning one of great wisdom; that is to say, one who offers much praise. (2)

O wielder of the thunderbolt (adrivas), O Indra, that which is yours is truly sweet; your guidance is most pleasant, and your sacrifice is to be extended far and wide. O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, that [glory] of yours, renowned as worthy of praise, is indeed sweet and exceedingly delightful to experience. Moreover, your guidance—the leading forth of wealth and other blessings—is sweet and brings great joy. Likewise, both your subjects' sacrifices are to be extended far and wide.
