O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths for you to traverse, O wielder of the thunderbolt, neither the suns nor the two worlds could ever equal you for even a moment after your birth. 5.
O Indra, even if there were as many heavens as there are to serve as a counterpart for you, they would not equal you;
nor even if there were a hundred earths to be the reflections of your form, they would not equal you. O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, even a thousand suns—even countless suns—do not equal you.
The meaning is that they do not illuminate it, according to the scriptural text: "The sun does not shine there" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15).
What more need be said?
"Nothing whatsoever that was born, that arose previously, has reached [thee];
likewise, the two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasī), do not reach thee.
The meaning is: "Thou excellest all."
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
O Bull, your greatness and manly powers have spread forth in every direction by your might;
O Maghavan, wielder of the thunderbolt, protect us with your wondrous aids in the cattle-filled stall.
O Bull, your greatness and manly powers have spread forth; with all your strength, O Maghavan, protect us in a cow-filled stall with your wondrous aids, O wielder of the thunderbolt. 6.
O Bull, O Lord who rains down desired boons, you have filled— you fill and pervade—
what? All, that is, every heroic power belonging to the enemy.
By what means? By greatness, that is, by his own mighty power (*śavas*),
or else *vṛṣṇyāya* is an adjective qualifying this *śavas*.
This being so, the meaning is: "With your great force, which rains down [boons] as desired, you fill our armies.

Then, having done so, O wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin), O Indra, protect us—when there exists a cause related to the enemy—in the cow-pen (vraja) rich in cattle (gomati), that is, endowed with many cows.
By what means?
With various and manifold aids—that is, with diverse forms of protection.
Sīmadeva has not attained this abundance of life among mortals, O long-lived one;
even Etagva has harnessed the two Etaśas, and Indra has harnessed his two bay steeds.

1. *ga*—They praised correctly. 2. *kha-tara-vā*—the heavens; *ta1-yā*—the heavens. 3. *gha*—after the sun, our birth. 4. *kha-gha-jña-ta1-2-śaviṣṭha*—O most powerful one, O mighty one, O bountiful one, O possessor of wealth, O bull! 5. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa-tvam*—you are the bull. 6. *kha-ta-viśvāni*—all things. 7. *kha-gha-ta-bha-1-2-śa-vajre*—in the thunderbolt. [Maṇḍala 8, Adhyāya 8, Sūkta 70] Sixth Aṣṭaka, 849.

No, O long-lived one! That godless mortal does not obtain any nourishment at all. Even that man who yokes the two swift steeds, Etaśa and Etargu—to Indra, who yokes the two bay horses (Haris)—[that man alone attains it]. O long-lived one, that godless mortal—one devoid of the deity named Indra—does not obtain any nourishment whatsoever. That mortal who yokes for himself the two steeds, Etaśa and Etargu—the very ones that serve as his horses for traveling to his desired destination—and who yokes the two bay horses (Haris) to the chariot in order to go to the sacrifice; [only he attains it]. He who does not praise that Indra does not attain it. This is the syntactic connection.

Worship that Indra for you—the great one worthy of great honor, the conqueror who bestows gifts—who is to be invoked in shallow waters and who is to be invoked in deep waters; who is to be invoked in battles for the sake of booty. (8) O priests, you who are great, worship that Indra for you—the great one worthy of honor—for the sake of giving, as one who is ever-present and to be served. That Indra who is to be invoked in shallow waters, and who is to be invoked in deep waters or on dry ground, and likewise who is to be invoked in battles for victory—he is indeed to be called upon. (8)

Lift us up well, O Vasu, O Hero, for the sake of great bounty. Lift us up well, O Maghavan, for the sake of great wealth; lift us up, O Indra, for the sake of great renown. (9) O *vasu*, O dweller, O *śūra* (Hero), O *indra*, do thou *su udu mṛśasva*—lift us up well, indeed! For what purpose? For *mahe rādhase*—for great nourishment. Likewise, O *śūra*, O *maghavan*, O *indra*, do thou lift us up for *mahe maghattyai*—for the giving of great wealth. And likewise, O *indra*, do thou lift us up for *mahe śravase*—for great fame. (9)

O Indra, you who desire the *ṛta*, you satisfy yourself with those who revile us—those who revile you. O you of abundant valor, clothe yourself between our thighs; with your blows, utterly crush the Dāsa. O Indra, you who are devoted to the *ṛta* (cosmic order) and desirous of sacrifice, you take full satisfaction from those who revile us—that is, those who revile you. Since such reviling is itself a lack of sacrifice toward you, you satisfy yourself by taking pleasure in depriving that non-sacrificer of his wealth; this is the sense. Having thus caused him distress, O you of abundant valor (*tuvinṛmṇa*), clothe yourself between our thighs—cover us for the sake of protection. With your blows, utterly crush the Dāsa—the one who oppresses us, our hater, or the wicked one; you slay him. Or else, you utterly crush the Dāsa-Sura, the adversary of yours, with your blows. 10.
1. gha-yaḥ | 2. kha-ta-śa-vaitaśā; na-bha-caitaśā | 3. kha-ta³-dā-yojayati |
May the mountain, our own friend, shake off the man who follows another’s vow and seeks neither gods nor men; may the mountain shake off the Dasyu for the sake of our well-being.

One who observes no vows, one who is not human, one who is hostile to the noble, one who does not seek the gods—let the mountain, our own friend, shake him down; let the mountain shake the Dasyu for the sake of well-being. 11.

O Indra, [drive away] "one of another vow," that is, one whose actions are different; for this very reason, "non-human," meaning one who is disliked by humans who sacrifice to Indra; "a non-sacrificer," meaning one who does not perform sacrifice; "one who does not seek the gods," meaning a sinner whose actions do not concern the gods—"from heaven" (svaḥ), "shake him down," meaning cause him to fall.
Who? "The friend," Parvata—the sage Parvata, who is your friend.
Even if one attains heaven by worshipping another deity, the seer [Vasiṣṭha] nevertheless causes him to fall.
It is not merely a shaking; rather, the remainder of the sense is that "the mountain impels the *dasyu*—characterized as described above—toward *sumnāya*, toward death that strikes well.
Therefore, the remainder of the sense is: "Worship Indra alone with necessity."
O Indra, you are our protector; O Indra, you are one worthy of equal honor—
meaning you are to be honored by all.
By many, by numerous rishis—those priests who have transcended the senses and who possess sacrificial grass and perform the sacrifice—you are praised; you are extolled.
O Indra, you who give away one by one—that is, each single calf—to those many praisers, you bestow them as gifts.
O Śara, O destroyer of the enemy!
Here, the word "vatsa" (calf) is indicative of the cows that are the mothers of the calves;
[the meaning is] "you give the cows."

Maghavan, the son of Śūradevī, brought back our calf from the three [regions] as he who seizes with his ears [seizes] a goat for the sake of nourishment, like a wise sage. 15. Karṇagṛhā; Maghavā; Śauradevyaḥ; Vatsam; Naḥ; Tribhyaḥ; Ā; Anayat; Ajām; Sūriḥ; Na; Dhātave. 15.
This Vamaghavā is Indra; [he is so called] because of the *vaśīra-devas*, who are the "devourers" (*vatr*) from among the harmful ones.
They are called *devas* because they play (*divyanti*) and sport;
being both brave (*śūra*) and *devas*, they are the *śūra-devas*.
Their welfare consists in a battle with Śauradeva;
the cows belonging to him [are the object].
The meaning is that, having slain the enemies in battle, they belong to him.
She brought them here together with the calf, having seized them by the ear.
The particle *vā* is used in the sense of "and" (*ca*).
Having seized them by the ear along with the calf, she brought them to us.
He is the impeller of the Vasus, like a master; just as one brings cattle to a drinker by seizing them by the ear, so does he [bring them].
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with "tvaṃ no agne.
Sudīti and Purumīḷha are the seers, or either one of them.
Of these, the first nine are *gāyatrīs*; the tenth, twelfth, and fourteenth are *bṛhatīs*; and the eleventh, thirteenth, and fifteenth are *satobṛhatīs*.
Agni is the deity.
Thus it is enumerated: "Tvaṃ naḥ sudīti... purumīḷha; of these two, either one [is used], but the portion ending with the three *pragāthas* belongs to Agni.
In the *prātaranuvāka* of the Agni-sacrifice, in the *gāyatrī* metre, and in the *āśvina-śastra*, the first nine verses [are recited].
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "'tvaṃ no agne mahobhiḥ'—these nine [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).

O Agni, protect us with your greatness from every misfortune, and also from the hatred of mortal man. 1. You—us—O Agni—with greatness—protect—from every—misfortune—and also—from the hatred—of mortal man. 1.
O Vāyu, you who possess the power of speech, protect us with your days, with honors, or with riches of oblations; guard us.
From every kind of stinginess—either from a non-giver or from the act of not giving—protect us.
The meaning is: by yourself, having bestowed great wealth, protect us from the stinginess of the non-giver.
Or rather,
it should be construed as "endowed with greatness" (*mahobhir yukta-svam*).
Furthermore, protect us from the hater, from the mortal man.
The sense is: "having bestowed incomparable strength.
Alternatively, the connection is: "the mortal [is protected] from the enemy (dvipaḥ) out of hatred (dveṣāt).
In the case of the interpretation beginning with "from the non-giver" (arāteḥ), there too it should be connected as: "from the non-giving of the mortal."

For wrath, born of man, has no power over you, O you who are dear by birth; for you alone are the lord of the night. For wrath, born of man, has no power over you, O you who are dear by birth; for you alone are the lord of the night.
O Agni, that wrath of yours born of man—that anger pertaining to human beings—is not able to overcome you;
the sense is that you are protected by those such as ourselves.
Since men indeed move about during the day, the implication is that there is no loss for you during the daytime.

Now, as for the night-walkers, such as the *rākṣasas* and others—it is said that there is no affliction even from them. For you alone are indeed the protector of the quarters; you dwell as the possessor of the night.
For at night, he becomes especially radiant.
O Ṛjunapāt of brilliant luster, together with all the gods, bestow upon us wealth that contains every desirable thing.

1. You grant [the syllables] kha, ga, ta, bha, and śa. 2. In the versions marked kha, ga, ta, na, bha, and śa, the phrase "unpleasant things" (apriyajāta) is absent. 3. Ga: [The purpose is] to afflict us. 4. Gha: You are indeed [the one who grants these].

He—O Son of Strength, O Agni of auspicious luster, together with all the gods, grant us wealth that contains all boons! O Agni, you who are worthy of praise, you bestow upon us (*naḥ*) wealth (*vasu*). O Son of Strength (*ūrjo napāt*), O Dispeller of power, O you of auspicious luster (*bhadraśoce*), you whose light is praiseworthy! To emphasize this very point, he speaks again: "Grant us wealth (*rayi*) that contains all boons (*viśvavāra*). Or rather, there is no tautology: what kind of wealth you bestow upon us to give—that wealth characterized by houses and the like—and that which is worthy of being given, such as cattle and gold, grant that as well.

O Agni, the enemies do not deprive that mortal of his wealth whom you, as a protector, guard—the one who offers oblations. O Agni, the enemies (arātayaḥ) do not (na) deprive (yuvaṃta) that mortal (martam) of his riches (rāyaḥ)—him whom you protect (trāyase), the donor (dāśvāṃsam). O Agni, those of ill-will (arātayaḥ), being stingy and hostile, do not separate (na yuvaṃta) that singer from his chariots (rāyaḥ); or rather, they do not deprive him of his wealth (rāyaḥ). For you protect (trāyase) and preserve (pālayase) him who is a giver of offerings (dāśvāṃsam).

O wise Agni, that mortal whom you impel toward wealth at the winning of the sacrifice, he, through your protection, shall go among the cattle—he shall become possessed of cattle. 5. O wise Agni, that mortal whom you impel toward wealth at the winning of the sacrifice, he, through your protection, shall go among the cattle—he shall become possessed of cattle. 5. O wise Agni, that mortal whom you impel toward wealth at the winning of the sacrifice—that is, for the acquisition of wealth such as cattle—he, the sacrificer, through your protection (ūtī), meaning by your aid and preservation, becomes one who goes among the cattle; that is to say, he becomes a possessor of cattle. 5.

O Agni, you bestow wealth consisting of many heroes upon the mortal who offers oblations; lead us forward toward greater prosperity. (6) O Agni, you grant wealth accompanied by many heroes to the mortal who has offered the sacrificial gift; therefore, lead us forward so that we may attain even greater wealth. (6)

Protect us; do not deliver us over to the one who seeks evil, O Jātavedas, to the mortal of wicked intent. Protect us; do not deliver us over to the one who seeks evil, O Jātavedas, to the mortal of wicked intent. O Jātavedas—whether that means "knower of all beings" or "possessor of all wealth"—protect us; guard us. Yāska states [in Nirukta 5.23] that "uruṣyati" is a verb meaning "to protect. Do not abandon us. To whom? It is said: to the mortal man who seeks evil—that is, who desires harm—and who is of wicked intent, whose thoughts are evil, and who possesses a murderous mind.

O Agni, let no godless one deprive you, a god, of your delight. You alone rule over riches. (8) O Agni, let no godless mortal whatsoever deprive you, a radiant deity, of your *rati*—your gift or the wealth bestowed. May he not separate you from it. You alone rule; over what? You are the lord of *vasūni*, of riches, to bestow them. By this, the arising of the delightful gift (*rāti*) is expressed.
As such, O Son of Strength, you who are free from guile, bestow upon us wealth and nourishment,
O Vasu, friend of those who sing your praises.

1. *gha-jña*: for us, with all the gods. 2. *kha-ga-gha-ta-na-bha-śa*: possessing wealth (*rayivantaḥ*). 3. *gha*: the mortal sacrificer, the protector (*'rttāraṃ martyaṃ yajamānaṃ*). 4. *gha*: O wise one (*vipra prājña*). 5. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa*: divine gift (*devarātiḥ*); *gha*: your gift (*tava rāti*). [The verses: To Agni, for you, through the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajyā*). To Agni, at the commencement of the rite (*prayati adhvare*). To Agni, as the first among prayers (*dhīṣu prathamam*). To Agni, for the swift [chariot] (*arvāta*). To Agni, for the successful attainment of the field (*kṣetrāya sādhasē*). || 12 ||
O sacrificers, for the sake of your sacrifice to the gods—that is, by means of the sacrifice to the gods and for the purpose of that sacrifice—I praise Agni; this is the ellipsis.
Likewise, when the *adhvara*—the sacrifice—is proceeding, meaning when it has commenced with excellence, I praise Agni first, before the other gods.
Similarly, when the *arvāt*—the kinsman who causes obstruction—has arrived, I praise Agni for the purpose of averting obstacles to the sacrifice.
Likewise, I praise for the sake of the field (*kṣetra*), for the purpose of the field, for the acquisition of the field, for the means of attainment, and for the attainment of the field;
I praise for the fruit consisting of the acquisition of the field at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
The meaning is that I praise thus always—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
May Agni, who is the lord of desirable things, grant us wealth together with progeny; we ever implore Agni for our children and grandchildren—the Vasu who is the protector of our bodies.

May Agni grant us nourishment for our well-being; he who is the lord of all desirable things. O Agni, we constantly implore you—the possessor of wealth and the protector of our bodies—for our children and grandchildren. 13.
May the god Agni, for the sake of our common purpose, loosen for me the bond of friendship—
either toward him or within that [bond].
May he grant us food upon food—
that Agni who rules over and desires desirable riches;
that very Agni we repeatedly entreat for abundant wealth, both for our offspring and for their offspring.
This is understood precisely because he is called "the Lord of desirable things.
Of what nature is this Agni?
He is *vasum*, the dweller who is ever-present; and *tanūpām*, the protector of those who are ignorant.
Worship Agni with songs for protection, him whose flame is fierce;
O Purumīḷha, men worship Agni for wealth, and Agni for a well-shining dwelling.
Praise Agni with songs for his protection, him of the piercing flame; O Purumīḷha, praise Agni for wealth, you who are renowned; O men, praise Agni for the granting of a secure dwelling. 14.
O Purumīḷha, you should invoke Agni for our protection and for our aid; praise him with *gāthās*.
*Gāthā* is a name for a meter;
[praise him] with *gāthās* in the form of mantras.
Of what sort?
Of one whose radiance is directed toward the head (*śīraśociṣam*), that is, whose light has the nature of resting upon the head.
Likewise, invoke him for the sake of wealth (*rāye*).
Other men who are sacrificers also praise this Agni for their own sake;
therefore, Sudīti says to Purumīḷha, "For my great splendor, ask Agni for a dwelling, a house."
We praise Agni so that he may drive away our hatred; we praise Agni so that he may grant us peace and well-being.
Known by all, like a master of all wealth, may he be the one to whom the swift ones offer oblations.

We praise Agni so that he may keep hatred away from us; we praise Agni so that he may grant us well-being and peace. May he be invoked as a protector among all the people, the one who brings light to the sacrificial flames. 15.

1. *ga*-vo: yours. 2. *gha*-staumi: I praise; thus, among those of excellent intellect (*subuddhi*), I praise the foremost one first, prior to the other gods. 3. *ga-gha-ta-na-bha*-yajñe vighnam; *kha*-yajñair vipa°. 4. *gha*-tathābhi. 5. *kha-ga-gha-ta-na-śa*-“*kṣetrāya*” does not exist. 6. *bha*-“*kṣetrāya*” does not exist. 7. *gha*-purumīḷha: one who sprinkles much. 8. *gha*-tathābhi. 9. *kha-gha-ta-na-bha*-agniḥ. 10. *ta-śa*-purumīḷha.
We praise Agni so that he may separate—that is, set apart—from us our hatred, those who hate us.
Likewise, we praise him so that he may grant *śam*, which is happiness, and *yoḥ*, which is freedom from fear;
or rather, we praise him for the mingling of happiness (*śam*) and freedom from fear (*yoḥ*).
In this interpretation, the word expressing conjunction has the sense of "and" with the phrase *yotavā* (to shine).

That Agni is indeed the protector (*avita*) of all (*viṣvāsu*) creatures (*viśva*); like a king among the *ṛṣis*, he is our dweller (*vastuḥ*), the god who must be invoked (*havyo bhuvat*). Alternatively, among all creatures in the form of sacrificers (*yajamāna-rūpāsu*), he is to be invoked specifically by us, the *ṛṣis* who perceive the hymns (*sūkta-dṛśām*); he is the dweller (*vastuḥ*) of all, the god who provides habitation.
The third hymn consists of eighteen verses beginning with “haviṣkṛṇudhvam.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “Havirdvyūna; Haryata is the seer; it is a Prāgātha; or it is a praise of oblations.
Thus, the seer is Haryata, the son of Pragātha.
By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the Gāyatra [meter] is prior to the Vatsapra," the meter is Gāyatrī.
Because it is stated "but this belongs to Agni," the deity is Agni; alternatively, since the oblations are being praised, it may have that [Agni] as its deity.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
Prepare the oblation; may the Adhvaryu return to the sacrificial ground, for he knows its direction.

Prepare the oblation! Let him come! The Adhvaryu priest wins [the sacrifice] again, knowing his command. O you preparers of the oblation belonging to the Adhvaryu, prepare the oblation quickly, for this Agni has arrived; therefore, prepare it. The Adhvaryu wins—that is, he partakes of—[the sacrifice]; what is meant by "again" is understood from the context to be the sacrifice itself. What kind of Adhvaryu? One who knows the command, that is, the presentation, of this oblation.
He has sat down as the Hotṛ priest upon the mind, like a sharp-tipped arrow,
taking pleasure in his well-yoked chariot.

The Hotṛ sits down upon the sharp stalk; the Hotṛ, the officiating priest, sits down upon that sharp, piercing Agni. Of what nature is the Hotṛ? He is one who, within the mind of this Agni—that is, in the sacrificer—takes pleasure in his excellent chariot (or, in his well-guided course). The particle *adhi* here expresses the sense of the locative case.
People seek that Rudra within with their foresight;
they seize him with their tongue as his food.

Within, they desire him; they grasp with their minds that Rudra before them through their wisdom, seizing him with their tongue as he sleeps. That Rudra—"rut" means suffering (*duḥkha*); he is the one who causes that to flow away (*drāvayitṛ*). Alternatively, "rut" means praise (*stuti*); thus it should be understood as "he who is to be approached through praise," meaning he is worthy of praise. Such an Agni they desire to establish in the front, beyond [the ordinary], for the sake of the people—that is, for the sake of the sacrificer—by means of *manīṣā*, which is their own insight. They, subsequently, seize with their tongues—that word "jane" is derived from the root *jan*—that sleeping Agni by means of praise originating from the tongue; they seize him with their fingers. On this point, Yāska says: "In his own opinion, he is the middle light, whose dwelling is not perceived" (Nirukta 5.3).
He who bestows vigor drew his bow against Jāmyati; he ascended the ship and slew Duṣada, the crooked one.

He has heated the bow; the bestower of vitality has ascended the forest; with his tongue he has struck down the difficult-to-reach [foe]. The bestower of vitality (*vayodhāḥ*), the giver of food, standing in the central region, has heated—that is, intensely scorched—the *jāmi*, which is the atmosphere (*dhanuḥ* = *dhanvan*). Or alternatively, [he has heated] the bow. Yāska states that *jāmi* is a name for "excess" (*atireka*)—that which exists surpassing everything else (Nirukta 4.20). He has heated the *dhanuḥ*, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Or, [the word may mean] "to be invoked" (*havyaḥ*).
1. Kha, Ga, Ta, Śa: "viśva" is not present. 2. Gha: "havyaḥ" means "to be invoked."
3. *gha*—the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) from all sides. 4. *na*—*juṣāṇaḥ*: being pleased; *bha1*—*juṣāṇaḥ*: restraining. 5. *gha*—in the front region, within the interior of the sanctuary.
6. This sleep is the middle one of Kha-tar-nida; this sleep is the middle one of Jha-ta1; this sleep is the middle one of Na-bha.
I resort to Agni, who is prone to movement, whose bowstring is exceedingly heated, and who is the adversary of his own enemies.
And he, Agni, the bestower of vigor and giver of food, has ascended—indeed, he ascends—the wood and the water for the sake of liberation.
For that purpose, with his tongue as a flame, he struck—that is, he destroys—the cloud that has bitten;
in the case of the forest fire, he destroys the forest, which is a collection of trees.
With his tongue, he splits even the hard stone that has bitten.
Moving like a calf among the ruddy cows, he finds no one here to revile him;
he seeks the motherly breast of the praiser.
Moving here, the shining calf finds no one to restrain him; he seeks his mother to praise her.

The "calf" (*vatsa*) is so called because he is metaphorically designated as such due to his running about with the nature of a calf; or else, he moves like a calf—the word "like" (*iva*) being elided. Being "bright" (*ruśan*), that is, white, he does not find—that is, he does not encounter—an "obstructor" (*ninditṛ*), one who hinders him, in this world. Rather, being entreated by the ten fingers of the "Vivasvat," the sacrificer who serves [the gods], Indra [reaches] the "coffer" (*kośa*);
this is a name for the cloud.

He caused the water-showering cloud belonging to the sky—that is, related to the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—to fall down from that [sky]. The meaning is that he split it open. By what means? That is stated as follows:
By means of the threefold, threefold-turning cord of *kheda*,
or else,
in this context, the word "Indra" refers to either Agni or Āditya.
Because of the indicative mark "threefold" [found] in the word *khedaya*.

The newest flame goes around the threefold sacrifice; with honey, the Hotṛ-priests anoint it. 9. pari tridhāturadhvaraṃ jūrnireti navīyasī | madhvā hotāro añjate || 9 || The most recent flame goes around the threefold sacrifice; with honey, the Hotṛ-priests anoint it. 9.

This Agni is threefold, possessing three colors through the distinction of red, white, and black; he is *jūrṇi*, swift and impetuous. With his most recent flame, he goes toward the *adhvara*, the Pravargya rite. The *hotṛ*s—the Adhvaryu and others who perform the oblation—besmear him all over with honey, that is, with clarified butter and other offerings. Alternatively, Agni’s threefold, rapid, and swiftest flame encircles the Mahāvīra vessel.
"From that [comes] honey," so it is said.

They flow with reverence toward the well that protects, whose wheel is above, which encompasses the earth, whose opening is downward, and which is inexhaustible. 10. They flow; with reverence; toward the protector; whose wheel is high; encompassing the earth; downward-opening; undecaying. 10.

With reverence—that is, with bowing—they offer oblations into the *mahāvīra* vessel; [the vessel] which has its wheel raised, meaning its wheel is situated above; which is *parijamāna*, meaning pervaded on all sides; which has *nīcīnabāra*, meaning downward-facing openings; which is *akṣita*, meaning undecaying; and which is thus endowed with a remainder of milk.
With reverence, they pour [the offering] upon the *āvahaniya* fire. By means of the *mahāvīra*, the offering is poured into the *āvahaniya*.
The stones have indeed brought near the honey poured out upon the lotus-leaf at the release of the water-vessel. || 11 ||

The pressing-stones, being attended to by the officiating priests, having approached, pour out the overflowing honey into the *puṣkara*—the beautiful, expanded vessel for the *upayamana*. This occurs at the time of the release of the *avata* *mahāvīra* vessel;
indeed, after the oblation, they place the *mahāvīra* upon its stand.

O Cows, come hither; protect us, O great ones, you who bestow the essence of the sacrifice; for both your ears are made of gold. 12. Cows; hither; protect; protect; great; of the sacrifice; bestowers of essence; both; ears; golden. 12.
O cows who yield the warm oblation, protect the herd; come near, approach the great hero (Mahāvīra),
for you two are the givers of the fruit of the sacrifice,
the bestowers of the desired result upon the seeker.
Or it refers to the lips of the Aśvins, which are to be given;
or "rapaṇam" means sounding,
for "rap" is a mantra.
Therefore, it should be given well.
Alternatively, *pūda* means "to flow";
by means of the mantra, that which is to be flowed out—that is, to be milked—should be [treated].

"O you two, come hither for such milk as that of the cow and the goat—great, vast, and abundant; therefore, come near. The term "cow" (*go*) is also indicative of the she-goat (*ajā*), because the milk of the goat is likewise to be poured into the *mahāvīra* vessel.
Moreover, on both ears of this Great Hero—both being in the position of ears—there are two golden ornaments (*rukma*), made of gold; that is to say, they consist of gold and silver.
In the Pravargya rite, when the Mahāvīra vessel is being brought forward, the verse "ā sute" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With 'ā sute siśvata śriyam,' [one recites] at the Āji" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).

Let him pour forth beauty upon the pressed juice, the glory that encompasses both heaven and earth; may the River bestow the Bull. 13. (The variants noted: 1. *ga*-navatarā; *ta*-na-*śa*-bhavatarā | 2. *kha-ga-jha-ta1-2-na-bha-jha-mu* read *rapsude* | 3. *ga-kṣā-śaraṇīye*).

ā | sute | sisvata | śriyam | rodasyoḥ | abhiśriyam | rasā | dadhīta | vṛṣabham || 13 || Upon the pressed [Soma], let him pour forth the glory that encompasses both heaven and earth; may the River bestow the Bull. 13.
When the milk has been poured into the pressed [Soma], let the goat’s milk, the very essence of prosperity, flow together.
Flow, O Adhvaryus!
Of what kind is the goat’s milk?
Of the two worlds (rodasī); this is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative. [He is] "abhiśriyam," meaning one who rests upon heaven and earth.
The meaning is that it has increased through continuous connection up to its limit.
Alternatively, based on the Nirukta statement, "Some say the two Aśvins are heaven and earth" (Nirukta 12.1), the meaning is "the glory of the two Aśvins.
Immediately after the pouring, place—that is, establish—the bull, the showerer Agni, within the *ājya* and the milk.
Since the she-goat belongs to the fire-god (Āgneyī), it is appropriate to add her milk as well;
for the Brāhmaṇa states: "This she-goat indeed belongs to Agni" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.3.1).
Knowing their own dwelling place, like calves with their mothers,
they meet together with their sisters.

They, knowing their own dwelling place, have come together with their kinsmen, as calves do with their mothers. (14) Those cows—meaning they recognized it—or rather, the masculine designation "they" (*te*) is used in a general sense. What is it? Their own dwelling place (*okya*), namely the Mahāvīra vessel; the meaning is that they went there to be milked. He explains this very point: just as calves (*vatsāsaḥ*) come together with their mothers (*mātṛbhiḥ*), so too the cows, accompanied by their kinsmen (*jāmibhiḥ*), have each come together (*sam nasanta*) with the Mahāvīra.
Devouring the offerings, they establish a support in heaven;
to Indra and Agni be homage and light.

Upon the *srak* (spouts) of the *mahāvīra*, they provide a support (*dharuṇa*) in heaven for Agni as he devours with his flame; [they offer] homage (*namaḥ*) to Indra and Agni, and the light (*svaḥ*). As Agni devours—that is, consumes with his flame—the food within the *srak*s of the *mahāvīra*, they provide a support in the sky, that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for Indra and Agni, as will be stated later. When the *mahāvīra* is burning, they pour both kinds of milk over it; this is the meaning. Having thus poured [the milk] into the *mahāvīra*, they join together the "light" (*svaḥ*)—meaning all the cow-products and goat-products—as well as the "homage" (*namaḥ*), which is the food, for Indra and Agni; or else, [they join them] in the sky (*svar antarikṣe*). The words "they yoke" (*yojayanti*) are to be supplied.

When the *gharmaduh* has been milked during the *pravargya*, this [verse] is used: "He has milked" (*adhukṣat*). And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When it has been milked, [he recites] 'He has milked the swelling one' (*adhukṣat pippuṣīm*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).
This [verse] is also used for the *āva-stotra*, because it is stated in the Sūtra: "'He has milked the swelling one; food runs into the jars'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.12).
The swelling Pippuṣī milked the arrow; Muri swallowed it along with the sap, by means of the seven rays of the sun.
He milked forth the swelling, nourishing, and strengthening sap, the seven-stepped [speech], from the sun with its seven rays. 16.

The *ari*, the wind whose nature is to move, has caused the swelling of the nourishing food (*iṣ*) and the strengthening essence (*ūrj*) by means of the seven rays of the sun; he has milked (*adhukṣat*) the seven-footed speech—the intermediate voice that flows by its very nature—which exists as the smoke of the heated offering (*gharma*).
Although the Adhvaryu priest milks the cow with a vessel, she is here conceived in this manner.
That the intermediate speech yields honey is well known from such passages as "Uttering 'hiṅ', the cow lowed" (*Ṛgveda* 1.164.27, 28).
O Mitra and Varuṇa, the risen sun has taken up the Soma;
that is the medicine for the sick man.
Of Soma; O Mitra and Varuṇa; up has this risen; at the sun; I have taken it; that is the medicine for the sick. 17.
Of Soma; O Mitra and Varuṇa! Up has this risen; at the rising of the sun, I have taken it; that is the medicine for the sick man. 17.

1. For it is "na-bha". 2. Those [letters] kha, ga, ta, na, and bha come together. 3. kha-^merame; gha-^me; jha, ta, 1, 2, 3, śa, ^merame. 4. kha, ta, śa—thus from this very [source]; ga—from this, him. 5. kha, gha, jha, ta, 1, 2, 3, ^mājya.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, when the sun has risen, at the rising of the sun, he offers or accepts the Soma of Soma.
He states the reason for that:
That action, consisting of acceptance, is the medicine—the remedy—for us and others;
that is to say, it is beneficial.

And indeed, his footprint, that place of the beloved one worthy of being stored away—he has extended it all around the sky with his tongue. 18. And indeed; now; his; which; footprint; of the beloved one; worthy of being stored away; around; the sky; with his tongue; he has extended. 18.

While the Soma is being purified, I, desiring the gift of the beloved Soma-giver, have reached the *vyatpad*, the place of the offerings where the oblations are deposited; standing there upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*), I have pervaded the sky all around with my tongue, that is, with my flame.
The fourth hymn, consisting of eighteen verses beginning with “udīrāthām,” is composed by Gopavana Ātreya or Saptavadhri; it is in the *gāyatrī* meter and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
Thus states the Anukramaṇikā: “udīrāthām: Gopavana Ātreya or Saptavadhri [composed] this Aśvina [hymn].
This hymn is used in the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), during the *āśvina* ritual period, in the *gāyatrī* meter, and for the Aśvina-śastra.
This is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘udīrāthāmā me havam’—this is a Gāyatra [verse]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).

Rise up, O you who follow the Eternal Law; yoke your chariot, O Aśvins! Let your help be near at hand for us. 1. Rise up! For him who follows the Eternal Law, yoke the chariot, O Aśvins! Let your aid be present before us. 1.
O Aśvins, for him who desires the sacrifice—that is, for me—arise and come forth!
For that purpose, to reach the invocation and the sacrifice, yoke your chariot with your horses.
Your protection reaches us; O Bhūtas, be present here in our vicinity.

Come hither, O Aśvins, on your most swift chariot even in the twinkling of an eye; let your food be near at hand. 2. Even in the twinkling of an eye, come hither, O Aśvins, on your most swift chariot; let your nourishment be close by. 2.
O Aśvins, come to our sacrifice with a chariot that is faster than even the blink of an eye, moving with exceeding speed or impetuosity; O you who are unwinking!
The rest has been explained.
O Aśvins, spread out the heat with cold for Atri; let your aid be near at hand. 3. Spread out! For Atri. With cold. The heat. O Aśvins. Near. Let it be. Of you two. Aid. 3.

For the sake of that great seer Vasiṣṭha, who was being tormented even by the Asuras, [the Aśvins] spread out and provided a cooling covering of snow and water for his benefit—a dharma that wards off burning heat.
The Vedic citation is: “With snow and waters, you two warded off the scorching heat” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.8).
Where were you two? Where did you go? Where did you fly like two hawks?
Your nourishment was close at hand.

1. *gha-na-bha-he* [read as *mitrāvaruṇā*]. 2. *gha1-vyāpnotu nu śārṅga*; *ya-vyāpnoti*. 3. *jña-ta1-2-bha-* [the syllable] *vā* does not exist. 4. *ta-bha1-2-śa-udaka*; *bha3-udake*. Where are you two? Where have you gone? Where have you flown like hawks? Your chariot is near; let it be present for you. || 4 ||
O Aśvins, where are you two now?
Where have you gone at your own will?
Or where do you fly, moving as swiftly as falcons?
Thus, the ellipsis is: "May you two, whose natures are inconceivable, remain present through compassion.
May protection be near for such as those.

If you should hear this invocation today from anywhere at all, may your horse be near you, O Aśvins. 5. If you should hear this invocation today from anywhere at all, may your horse be near you, O Aśvins. 5.
Since it is determined from this [source], therefore today—at this time—in whatever place and at whatever time—may you both hear this our invocation.
O Aśvins, your course is most rapid; your kinship is closest. May your steed be near at hand. 6. O Aśvins, your journey is most swift; your friendship is nearest. May your horse be close by. 6.
I go to the two Aśvins, who are to be approached at the time of the final watch;
I go to them as my closest, most immediate kinsman and friend.
O Aśvins, you two have made a stall for the courser for Atri; the courser was indeed near you. 7. O Aśvins, you two have made a stall for the courser for Atri; the courser was indeed near you. 7.
O Aśvins, you two—you who for Atri, while he was burning in the house of Atri, created a horse to protect his dwelling;
may there be such protection from you both.
[The masculine form *avantam* is used by way of grammatical substitution.]

In the conflict against the scorcher of enemies, you two turn toward Vṛtra for the sake of Atri; may your horse be near at hand. 8. In the conflict. Against the scorcher of enemies. You turn. Toward Vṛtra. For the sake of Atri. Near. May it be. Of you two. The horse. 8.
May those two Aśvins, who are beautiful and captivating, bestow protection upon the praising Atri; may they ward off the heat from the scorching sun for him in the midst of his labor.

May the sevenfold stream, with its expectation, flow forth from the fire; may it be near you, O swift ones. 9. May the sevenfold stream, with its expectation, flow forth from the fire; may it be near you, O swift ones. 9.
The great seer Saptavadhi, through his prayer and praise for you two, O Aśvins, emerged from the chest and caused the stream of Agni to enter that chest;
that is to say, he burnt away that which obstructed him.

Saptavadhi’s entry into the interior of the box was due to the favor of the Aśvins and the words [of the hymn], as is clearly stated in the verse: “Open wide, O Lord of the Forest” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.78.5).
1. Kha, gha, jha, ta, ḷ, ḷh: these are the waters to be attained.
2. Gha: the two Aśvins are the leaders. 3. Kha, gha, ta, na: protect! (Ga: protected.)
4. *ga*—*aśāyata*; *jha*—*aśāyat*; *ta3-4-ma*—*āśāyata*. 5. *kha*—*svasvamirodhakaṃ*; *ga-ta-na-bha-śa*—*svasvamirodhikāṃ*.

Come hither, O possessors of rain-like wealth; hear this my invocation. Your protection is truly near at hand. O possessors of rain-like wealth (*vṛṣaṇvasū*), O Aśvins, come here to this sacrifice. For that purpose, hear this my invocation. Your aid is indeed present nearby.

What is this that is being praised of you two, as if of two ancient, aged men? Your help is indeed near. 11 What? This? Of you two? Like the ancient? As if of two aged [men]? Is being praised. Near. Truly. Be. For you two. Help. 11 O Aśvins, regarding your arrival: "Like the ancient," that is, like two elders; that very thing is expressed by "as if of two aged [men]. It is praised: "Come again and again. "What is this?"—the meaning is: just as in the world an old, decrepit man does not come even when summoned many times, so it seems of you two as well. Thus he speaks because of your non-arrival.

Equal is your common kinship, O Aśvins; equal is your bond. May your protection be near at hand. O Aśvins, between you two there is an identical common kinship (*sajātya*), for both of you are born from the same source—the daughter of the Sun who is in the form of a mare. Likewise, O Aśvins, your bond (*bandhu*)—that which unites you—is one and the same. Or rather, I, the seer, am your sole and common kinsman.

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which traverses the realms, the two worlds (Heaven and Earth)—may its protection be near you. That chariot of yours, O Aśvins, which travels through the realms and across the two worlds, Heaven and Earth—may its protection be close at hand for you both. That chariot of yours, which exists, traverses the worlds and the two worlds, Heaven and Earth; therefore, the ellipsis is: "Come quickly by means of that chariot."

Come to us with thousands of cattle and horses; let your protection be near at hand. (14) "Come to us," [O Aśvins], "with thousands—countless—herds of cattle and herds of horses. Let your aid be present. (14) O Aśvins, come to us with thousands—that is, with immeasurable—multitudes of cattle and multitudes of horses. Come hither. May your protection be close by. (14)

Do not let us be deprived of our cattle, horses, and thousands [of wealth]. Your protection is near, O you who are swift in six ways. (15) 1. *kha-ta-śa*: the nature of the showerer (*varṣaṇadharma*); *ga*: "possessing the wealth of the showerer" (*vṛṣaṇadhanā*). 2. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa*: equal (*samaṃ*). 3. *ga-ta-na-bha-śa*: the word "gavyebhiḥ" is absent.

Do not pass us by with your herds of cattle, your herds of horses, and your thousands; let your small favor be near us. (15) O Aśvins, do not pass us by with your herds of cattle, your herds of horses, and your thousands; let your small favor be near us. (15) The dawn has appeared, touching the red glow; she has made light, the observer of Truth. Let your small favor be near us. (16) O Aśvins, the dawn has appeared, touching the red glow; she has made light, the observer of Truth. Let your small favor be near us. (16) O Aśvins, may [the sun] shine brightly like one who wields an axe upon a tree. Let your small favor be near us. (17) O Aśvins, may [the sun] shine brightly like one who wields an axe upon a tree. Let your small favor be near us. (17) O bold one, break down the stronghold like [an enemy]; driven away by the black [night], enter the dwellings. Let your small favor be near us. (18) O bold one, break down the stronghold like [an enemy]; driven away by the black [night], enter the dwellings. Let your small favor be near us. (18) **Hymn Five: "Viśoviśo vaḥ" (To You, the Guest of Every Clan)** This hymn consists of fifteen verses. The Anukramaṇikā states: "Viśoviśo vaḥ... fifteen verses; addressed to Agni; in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the first four are Gāyatrīs; the last three are Anuṣṭubhs; composed by Śrutavarṇa; a praise of a gift. The seer is Gopavana. In the first three verses, all the first lines are Anuṣṭubhs, while the second and third lines are Gāyatrīs according to the rule regarding Vatsapra. The last three (verses 13–15) are Anuṣṭubhs. The deity of these two hymns is Agni; the other three are a praise of the gift of King Śrutavarṇa. This hymn is used as a Śastra in the Vyoma, Viśvadeva, and Pañcaśāradīya rites. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Viśoviśo vo atithim... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.8). Seeking strength, we praise Agni, the beloved guest of every clan, the lord of the house, with the thoughts of the zealous one. (1)

1. Kha, bha, and śa possess brilliance (*tejaska*). 2. Gha possesses truth and dawn (*satyavyuṣāḥ*). 3. In manuscript *ga*, the word "you" (*tvam*) is absent. 4. In manuscript *gha*: "Afflict [it] from the perspective of sight; just as an enemy afflicts a city, so too [does he]."

O other officiating priests and sacrificers, you who are desiring strength—serve Agni with praise, him who is the guest of every clan (*viśo-viśaḥ*), worthy of honor, and beloved by many. And I, for your sake, praise with hymns of thought the word that dwells in the secret cave, for the attainment of well-being. By what means? By meditations, that is, by hymns worthy of reflection. 1. O other officiating priests and sacrificers, you who are desiring strength—serve Agni with praise, him who is the guest of every clan, worthy of honor, and beloved by many. And I, for your sake, praise with hymns of thought the word that dwells in the secret cave, for the attainment of well-being. By what means? By meditations, that is, by hymns worthy of reflection.

Whom people, bearing oblations, praise with hymns of praise like Mitra who is sprinkled with clarified butter. 2. Whom people, bearing oblations, praise with hymns of praise like Mitra who is sprinkled with clarified butter. 2.

Those people here, who are well-pressed, praise Agni with these oblations, offering sacrifices with uplifted ladles. (6) Those people here, who are "well-pressed" (*subādhaḥ*)—meaning those accompanied by pressure or exertion—praise (*īḷate*) Agni with "pleasing" (*hṛdyebhiḥ*) offerings. What kind of people? Those who are "offering" (*juhvānāsaḥ*), performing the sacrifice, and whose "ladles are uplifted" (*yata-srucaḥ*), holding the handles of the ladles for that purpose. "We have come to him"—this is the syntactical connection.

This newest hymn of yours has been placed before us; O joyous one, well-born, doer of good deeds, unerring, wondrous guest! This newest hymn of yours has been placed before us; O joyous one, well-born, doer of good deeds, unerring, wondrous guest! O Agni, this newest, most recent praise, belonging to you, has been established among us; we offer our hymn to you—this is the meaning. O joyous one, well-born, of noble origin, doer of good deeds, unerring, wondrous, and worthy of honor like a guest—these are the epithets.

O Agni, may this [hymn] of ours be most peaceful, most pleasing, and dear to you. May you, being well-praised, grow strong through it. (8) O Agni, may this hymn being performed by us be most peaceful (*śaṃtamā*), most delightful (*caniṣṭhā*), and dear (*priyā*) to you. Being well-praised (*su-stutaḥ*) by means of that hymn, may you grow strong (*vardhasva*).

May she, rich in splendor through splendors, bestow great fame upon us in the hearing of renown; may she grant abundant food in the victory over Vṛtra. May she—rich in splendor (*yumninī*) through splendors (*yumna*), that is, through shining riches to be bestowed upon us—bestow (*dadhīta*) great (*bṛhat*) fame (*śravaḥ*) upon us in the presence of existing food (*śravasi*). May she maintain it further. Where? It is said: in the battle (*vṛtratūrye*), that is, in the conflict concerning the enemy.

Like one who wins horses, like one who fills the chariot, like the brilliant Indra, the lord of the virtuous—him whose glories you celebrate, and whom every people praise again and again. (10) "Like a horse" (*aśvamit*): *it* is used here in the sense of "just as. It means: "just as one praises a horse, so [one praises him]. "Filling the chariots" (*rathaprām*): the fulfiller of our chariots with wealth. Likewise, "brilliant" (*tveṣam*), like Agni; "lord of the virtuous" (*satpatim*), the protector of the good; "like Indra" (*indram na*): like Indra himself. Him they praise. (10)

1. In manuscript *gha*, [the word] *adhāyi* is present. 2. In manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, the word ‘*stutiḥ*’ is absent. 3. In manuscript *ga*, it is *sukhakarī*; in manuscript *bha*, it is *sukhakaro*. 4. In manuscripts *ta*, *bha*, and *śa*, [it reads] *cūr asmabhyam*. 5. In manuscripts *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, [it reads] *astramyam suśravāsi*; in manuscript *gha*, it is *suśravasi*. 6. In manuscripts *jha*, *ta1*, and *ta2*, [it reads] *vidyamānojai*; in *ta3* and *ta4*, it is *vidyamānoja*; in manuscript *jha*, it is *avidyamānotra*. 7. In manuscripts *ta*, *bha*, and *śa*, [it reads] *upa*. 8. In manuscripts *ga* and *bha*, [it reads] *punar api*. The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) is: “May all people serve [him].”
By the power of that fire, you overcome the glories—that is, the possessions—belonging to the enemy; likewise, whatever wealth worthy of praise exists, that too you utterly destroy.

O Agni, whom Gopavana has most highly praised with song—you, O Angiras, who are the purifier—hear his call! (11) O Agni, you whom Gopavana, the seer, has most highly praised (*caniṣṭat*) with song—that very one, O Agni, O Angiras, who moves everywhere or who is one among the Angirases, O Purifier (*pāvaka*), hear the call of Gopavana. (11)

You whom the people, pressing forward with zeal for the winning of booty, praise—be mindful of us in the overcoming of Vṛtra. (12) O Agni, you whom the people—the worshippers—praise with persistent effort for the sake of obtaining food, may you, being such, be mindful in the slaying of Vṛtra; that is, be aware for the destruction of the enemy or the removal of evil. Alternatively, be mindful in the battle against Vṛtra.

I, being invoked by Śrutarvan, the son of Ṛkṣa, at the exhilarating [sacrifice], plucked off the heads of four [horses] like the bristling hair of woolly sheep. (13) I, the seer, being invoked for the sake of the sacrificial skill by Śrutarvan, a king of this name, the shaker of the pride of enemies—at the exhilarating [rite]—like the bristling hair of woolly sheep (*stukāvin*): *stukāvin* means "woolly"; *stuka* is a mass of hair. Like those bristling hairs (*śardhāṃsi*), which touch [the body], so too the *vṛkṣāḥ*. *Vṛkṣāḥ* means "trees," but here they are "hair" (*keśāḥ*) because they are cut (*vṛśyante*). Possessing those [hairs] are the *vṛkṣāṇi*; *śīrṣā* means "heads. Whose? Of the four horses given by Śrutarvan—the remainder of the sense is that I plucked their heads. Alternatively, *vṛkṣā* is from *vṛkṣa*. Because it is the instrument of eating, *akṣa* is the hand; with that I pluck them.

Four swift horses, wealth-bringers, with beautiful chariots, shall carry me toward the food-offerings of Śaviṣṭha, as birds [carry] you, O Śrutarvan. (14) Me; four; swift; of Śaviṣṭha; wealth-bringers; with beautiful chariots; toward; the food-offerings; they shall carry; like birds; for you. (14) The four swift horses belonging to King Śraviṣṭha, the son of Śrutarvan—who is pre-eminently powerful—horses that are "wealth-bringers" (draviṇavaḥ), meaning they move swiftly, and "with beautiful chariots" (surathāsaḥ); these horses shall "carry toward" (abhivakṣan) me against the food-offerings (prayaḥ) of the enemies. "Like birds for you": just as four ships, impelled by horses, carried Bhujyu to his own home, so it is here.
1. [The syllables] *kha*, *pa*, *ra*, *ca* are accompanied by *ṃ*; [the syllables] *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha* are accompanied by *ṃ*. 2.

[The syllables] *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta* (1–4), *bha*, *śa* are provided with *vadhā*; [the syllables] *ca*, *ba* are provided with *bandhā*; *ta* (3) is provided with *badhā*. 3. The "heads" (*śīrṣā*) of *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa* do not exist.
4. From *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*, [the suffix] *tena* is not elided.

5. For *kha*, *ta* (1–2), and *na*, [the suffix] *tubhyam*; for *ga* and *tu*, [the suffix] *ubhyam*; for *gha*, [the suffix] *tubhyam na*; for *ta* (3–4), [the suffix] *tum*; for *bha*, [the suffix] *ugra*; for *jha*, *śa*, and *ta*, [the suffix] *tubhyam*. [End of section] 3–55.
O great river Paruṣṇī, you have truly revealed yourself as a friend;
these waters are not givers of horses to any mortal other than Śarviṣṭha.
Truly, O great river Paruṣṇī, I have pointed you out from afar. O Waters, you are not the givers of horses; among mortals, there is none more bountiful than Śarviṣṭha. 15.
"O Mahenadī, O Paruṣṇī—by these names—I have truly, indeed as truth, directed my command toward you; I point you out and speak.
Addressing the waters by way of their form as rivers, he addresses them:
'O Waters, there is no mortal whatsoever who is a greater giver of horses than this Śaviṣṭha, the most powerful Śutudrī.'"
On the bank of the Paruṣṇī river, he speaks to awaken the king from his acceptance of the sacrificial fees for the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The sixth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "yuktvā hi," is the work of Virūpa Āṅgirasa; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and addressed to Agni.
Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: "yuktvā hi: sixteen [verses], [by] Virūpa."

This Agni is the lord of thousandfold and hundredfold strength; he is the head, the seer, and the master of riches. (4) This Agni is the lord and master of thousandfold and hundredfold *vāja*—that is, of food—as well as the head, meaning preeminent like a crown, the wise one (*kavi*), and the master of *rayīṇām*, that is, of wealth. The sense is: "May he grant both of these."

O Aṅgiras, bend toward this sacrifice with joint invocations, even closer than the R̥bhus do to the rim of their chariot wheel. 5. O Aṅgiras, with joint invocations—by means of common calls together with other gods—bend toward, that is, incline, this sacrifice which is nearest at hand, just as the R̥bhus [incline] the rim of the chariot wheel. 24.

O Virūpa, of manifold forms, by means of this eternal speech, now indeed impel a beautiful hymn of praise toward that celebrated, radiant, and showering Agni. 6. To him, O Virūpa, with eternal speech, impel a well-fashioned hymn of praise for that radiant showerer. O Virūpa—of various forms, you who bear this name, great seer—do you now, with eternal speech in the form of mantras, impel a beautiful hymn of praise toward that renowned, radiant, and showering Agni; thus the seer speaks to himself, or the sacrificer addresses the Hotṛ priest Virūpa.

Whom indeed, by the army of this Agni who sees from afar, shall we strike down among the cattle—the Paṇi? Whom indeed, by the army of this Agni who sees from afar—of him whose vision is not narrow—by his army in the form of flames, for the sake of the cattle, whom indeed, alas, shall we strike down? "Striking down" means slaying; the meaning is: "Now, let us overcome the powerful one."

May the clans of the gods not abandon us, like cows that have bathed; may the inviolable ones not leave us as they would a weakling. (8) May the *viśaḥ*—the subjects or attendants belonging to all the gods—not abandon (*mā hāsuḥ*) us (*naḥ*). May they not desert us, just as cows (*ustrāḥ*) that have bathed (*prasnātīḥ*) do not leave their calves. Just as those [cows] do not let go, so too may both [the gods and the subjects] not abandon us. How is this? Just as the inviolable cows (*aghnyāḥ*) do not leave (*na hāsuḥ*) their own weakling, small calf (*kṛśam*), even so [may they not leave us].

Who? The people, that is, the human sacrificers. The meaning is: "I too sing [praise] to you. Likewise, with your powers, crush—that is, destroy—the enemy, the adversary. 10 In the event of contact between a domestic fire and a sacrificial fire, an offering to Agni Saṃvarga should be performed. In that rite, "kuvitsu naḥ" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and "mā no asmin" is the offering verse (*yājyā*). Do not abandon us in this great battle, like a burden-bearer who casts off his load; win for us the wealth that is to be gathered from the enemy. "Do not" (*mā*) "abandon" (*vark*) "us" (*naḥ*) "in this" (*asmin*) "great battle" (*mahādhane*). "Like a burden-bearer" (*bhārabhṛd yathā*): just as one who carries a load abandons it at the end, so [do not abandon us]. "Win" (*jaya*) "for our sake" the "wealth" (*rayim*) "to be gathered" (*saṃvargam*) from the enemies.

O Agni, let this distress, which seeks to harm us, pursue another who hates us; and may you increase our powerful might. O Agni, let this distress—the host of oppressors—which seeks to harm us, follow another who hates us for his own destruction. And you, increase our powerful might—our force endowed with strength—in battle.

Whose labor the [gods] have enjoyed—whether that of one who offers salutations or of one who has not performed sacrifice—it is he indeed whom Agni protects with prosperity. (14) Whose—of the one offering salutations (*namasvin*), whose labor (*śamī*) the [gods] have enjoyed, whether it be of one who has performed sacrifice or of one who has not; him alone, that very sacrificer, Agni approaches with abundance in battle. Therefore, the sense is: "May we be possessed of salutations and be performers of sacrifice."
1. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ta, bha, and dūrthyaḥ.

2. [Regarding the phrase] "kha, jha, ta, 1, 2—asmān ādhadhīt mā hiṃsyāt"; gha—"nosmān mā vadhīt mā hiṃsyāt"; ta, 3, 4, na, bha—"āvadhīt mā hiṃsyāt. 3. [In the variant] kha, ga, ta, na, bha, śa, the meaning is "vadhīḥ" (you have killed).
4. gha—well, very well; toward us.

From the furthermost battle-array, cross over toward our own lower ranks; protect those among whom I am present. 15 From the furthermost, from the battle-array, cross over toward our own lower ranks; protect those among whom I am present, the master. 15 O Agni, from the furthermost—that is, from another—battle-array, carry across toward our own lower ranks, that is, those belonging to us; on all sides, overcome them. The meaning is: "Let the enemy army be defeated before our host. Protect those among whom I am present, the master, within the midst of our own attendants.

For indeed, O Agni, we have borne [thee] as of old, even as [one bears] the protection of a father. Now we pray for thy favor. (16) O Agni, just as formerly, so now too—we have borne thee, [thee who art] like the protection of a father. And now we pray for that favor of thine, [that is,] for happiness. Or rather, "as of a father" is a simile: the meaning is, just as a son knows the protection of a father. (16)
The seventh hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "imaṃ nu māthinam," has Kurusuti of the Kaṇva lineage as its seer (ṛṣi) and the Gāyatrī as its meter (chandaḥ).

Indra is the deity. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: ‘This [hymn] consists of twelve verses; Kurusuti Kāṇva is the seer. In the expanded ten-night sacrifice (vyūḍha-daśarātra), this triplet of *āyās* verses is used on the fourth day for the Marutvatīya śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "I now invoke this Māthin; he is yours, the ever-conquering one" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).

I now invoke this Indra, the subduer, who rules by his might, accompanied by the Maruts—him, as it were, for the slaying of Vṛtra. I now invoke this subduing one, Indra, who rules by his own power, the lord of all, accompanied by the Maruts—at this very moment—for the destruction of enemies. I call upon him. *imaṃ māthinam* means "this wise one"; *ojasā īśānam* means "ruling by his own strength," the master of everything; *marutvantam na*—"na" is used here in the sense of "now"—meaning "accompanied by the Maruts at this time"; *indram vṛtrase* means "Indra for the cutting down of foes"; *huve* means "I call."

This Indra, with the Maruts as his companions, split asunder the head of Vṛtra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt. This Indra, having the Maruts as his friends, split apart—that is, severed—the head of Vṛtra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, which possesses a hundred joints.

Growing strong, Indra, with the Maruts as his companions, drove Vṛtra apart, releasing the waters of the ocean. Growing strong, Indra, with the Maruts as his companions, drove Vṛtra apart, releasing the waters of the ocean. This Indra, growing strong—that is, increasing—and having the Maruts as his companions, drove Vṛtra—the cloud—apart; he split it open. What was he doing? Releasing the waters belonging to the ocean; "ocean" here refers to the intermediate space (the atmosphere), and [he released] the waters connected to that.

This very Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, by whom indeed this heaven was conquered—for the drinking of Soma. (4) "This very Indra," indeed, "by whom"—that is, by whom indeed—"accompanied by the Maruts" (marutvatā), by Indra, "this heaven"—meaning this place called heaven, or "this entire world"—was "conquered. For what purpose? "For the drinking of Soma" (somapītaye).

We invoke with songs Indra, who is accompanied by the Maruts, who possesses the *ṛjīṣa*, who is powerful, and who is all-pervading. (5) *Marutvantam*: accompanied by the Maruts. *Ṛjīṣiṇam*: *ṛjīṣa* is the residue remaining after the soma has been pressed; and that is pressed again at the third extraction (*tṛtīyasavana*). We invoke him who possesses that. *Ojasvantam*: *Ojas* is the eighth stage [of life]; it means endowed with physical growth and vigor. *Virāpśinam*: this is a name for "great. We invoke—that is, we call upon—Indra, who is thus great and of such majestic power, with songs, that is, with hymns of praise.

We invoke Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, with an ancient hymn for the drinking of this Soma. (6) We invoke Indra, who is accompanied by the Maruts, with an ancient, venerable hymn for the sake of drinking this Soma.
On the fifth day, for the Marutvatīya [śastra], the triplet beginning with "O bountiful Indra, accompanied by the Maruts" is the insertion-verse (*nividdhānīya*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O bountiful Indra, accompanied by the Maruts... we incite that Indra for strength" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).

O bounteous Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma, O Śatakratu, at this sacrifice, O Puruṣṭuta! (7) O bounteous one—giver of fruit or rain—O Śatakratu, performer of many deeds, O Indra, you who are accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma at this sacrifice, O Puruṣṭuta, you who are invoked by many!

For you alone, O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, these pressed Soma juices, O wielder of the stone, are offered with the heart by those who recite hymns. (8) O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, for you alone—accompanied by the Maruts—the pressed Soma juices are offered with the heart, that is, with the mind and devotion, by those who possess the hymns. They are offered for your sake.
May Indra, the friend of the Maruts, drink the pressed Soma at the celestial rites,
whetting his thunderbolt with might.
1. na-bha-ha ayaṃ | 2. kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa sarvakarma | 3. na-bha-marutvān san | 4. ta³-⁴-na-bha śa; "hṛdā...bhaktyā" is not present.

Drink, O Indra, friend of the Maruts, the pressed Soma during the celestial rites, whetting your thunderbolt with might. O Indra, friend of the Maruts, drink the pressed Soma. For what purpose? During the "diviṣṭis"—that is, for the sake of our great approaches to you or for the attainment of heaven (div). And having drunk, whetting your thunderbolt with *ojas*—the power generated by the drinking of Soma—sharpening it; the sense is that you should slay the enemy.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing, during the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s *śastra*, the triplet beginning with "uttiṣṭhan" is the *utthānapriya* of the *ṣaḍaha*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘uttiṣṭhojasā saha bhindhi viśvā apa dviṣaḥ’ is for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.2).

Rising up with vigor, having drunk, you shook your jaws, O Indra, after drinking the Soma pressed in the vessel. (10) Rising up with vigor, having drunk, you shook your jaws, O Indra, after drinking the Soma pressed in the vessel.

(10) O Indra, this very Indra, as soon as he was born—indeed, at the moment of his birth—being one of a hundred powers (*śatakratu*), possessed of many deeds, thus questioned his mother, his own progenitress.
What [did he ask]?
Who in this world are fierce and possess woolly strength?
Who indeed are heard of for their virtues in Śrīnivara—
that is to say, who are renowned?
May they be your sons, O Niṣṭura: Ārdī, Śavas, Saṃvīda, Aurṇavābha, and Mahīśuva.
Āt īm śavasī abravīt Aurṇavābham Ahīśuvam: "O son, may these be your subduers. ||2||
Questioned by Indra, the mother Śavasī immediately said this to him, Indra: "What is it? She replied:
"The two Asuras named Aurṇavābha and Mahīśūva are standing there."
Having been addressed thus, they replied, "O son, may such cruel people as these be delivered."
With his mace, the slayer of Vṛtra struck down the well-armed [foes] in the sky like spokes;
having grown great, he became the destroyer of the Dasyus.
The slayer of Vṛtra struck them down all at once, as one who expands drives the spokes from their holes with a wedge; he became the destroyer of the Dasyus. 3.
Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, drew them up together at once as they were spoken by their mother.
"Drawing" (kheda) means pulling.
He pulled the spokes—the pegs that are parts of the wheel—out from the *kha*, which is the nave of the chariot wheel, using a cord (*khedya*).
Just as they were drawn out by her,
so Indra, the slayer of the Dasyus and destroyer of enemies, having acted thus, became fully grown.
With a single draught, Indra drank thirty lakes of Soma all at once, out of his desire for it.
With a single resolve, Indra drank thirty lakes of Soma at once, according to his desire.
This Indra, with a single *pratidhā*—that is, with one resolve (*pratijñāna*)—simultaneously [overcomes] even thirty;
that is to say, the cups for the *ukthas*.
Of what kind are they?
He drank—the Mādhyandina-savana—those lakes full of *soma*, filled with the juice of *soma*; lovely (*kāṇukā*) or pervaded by *soma*, or made by *soma*, or full of *soma*.
This is according to the common usage of the ritualists (*yājñika*). But according to the etymologists (*nairukta*), Indra is the personification of time.
There are thirty days and nights of the dark fortnight and thirty of the bright fortnight;
he experiences them as a single form.
All of this is clearly stated in the *Ṛgveda* passage, "He drank it all with a single draught" (*Nirukta* 5.11), and in its commentary.
This should be observed here.
Indra pierced through the Gandharva in the unfathomed realms;
he has grown strong for the sake of the sacred hymns.
Indra pierced the Gandharva within the unfathomed mists, solely for the increase of the sacred prayers.

This Indra pierced through the Gandharva—the Gandharva being the cloud, so called because it holds water (gām udakam dhārayati)—he struck him from all sides. Where? In the *rajasas*, the worlds devoid of a place fit for setting foot, that is to say, in the regions of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). For what purpose? For the very sake of the increase (*vṛdhe*) of the *brahmans*, that is, for the prosperity of the Brāhmaṇas. || 29 ||
From the mountains he struck down and held fast the cooked rice;
Indra [held] the well-aimed *bunda* weapon.
He pierced [it] from the mountains; Indra held fast the cooked rice-mess, the well-pointed spear.
