"Take up the *bunda* (spear) and the arrow, well-strung and extended in every direction"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

With a hundred joints, a thousand leaves, the arrow is indeed one; that which you, O Indra, have made your companion. (7) śatabradhnaḥ | iṣuḥ | tarva | sahasraparṇaḥ | ekaḥ | it | yam | indra | cakṛṣe | yujam || 7 ||
O Indra, that arrow of yours has a hundred broken joints, a hundred points, and is covered with a thousand feathers for swift movement—
or rather, for immeasurable travel.
It is that [arrow].
"He slays the cloud full of water"—this is the ellipsis.
Of what sort is that [cloud]? "Emuṣam.
In place of the word *ā*, there is the vowel *e* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
"Āmuṣam" means the thief of water;
such is the meaning according to the etymological (nirukta) school.
According to the historical (aitihāsika) school, the *Caraka-brāhmaṇa* records the following tradition:
Viṣṇu is the sacrifice;
he made himself invisible to the gods. The other deities did not perceive him, but Indra knew him.
He said to Indra, "Who are you?
Indra replied to him, "I am the slayer of fortresses and of the Asuras; but who are you?

He said, "I am the deliverer from fortresses. But if you are the slayer of fortresses and of the Asuras, then—there is a boar dwelling on the far side of twenty-one fortresses belonging to the Asuras; in it is the desirable wealth of the Asuras. Slay this!"
Indra, having shattered those fortresses, pierced his heart.
Whatever was therein, Viṣṇu carried it away.
This is the ancient legend (itihāsa) established by the two [Ṛgvedic verses]: "At the pressings of his mother... (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.61.7) and "All these, Viṣṇu... (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.61.9).

Between those two, in the verse "asyed u mātuḥ," Viṣṇu says to Indra, "O Indra, you call yourself the slayer of difficulties (durgāṇāṃ hantā). To this, the meaning of the statement "then slay Vāmuṣa, the Varāha demon" is established by the line "avidhyadarāham.

Furthermore, Indra says to Viṣṇu, "O Viṣṇu, you say you are the bringer from difficulties (durgādāhartā). When told, "I have conquered the cities and slain the demon; bring his beautiful wealth (vāmaṃ vasu)," Viṣṇu stole the wealth of that Varāha demon in his form.
That matter is indicated by the line "muṣāyad viṣṇuḥ pacatam."

As for what exactly he brought back, that is now stated: "All these" (*viśvettā*). O Indra, Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of sacrifice, being impelled (*tveṣita*) by you, and you yourself being the one who brings [wealth] from a difficult place—impelled by you, having become one of wide strides (*sabhurukrama*), he brought back (*ābharat*) all those things which were to be brought by you, as mentioned, and whatever else was situated there; he brought them all.
What are those things?
He brought hundreds of immeasurably great and praiseworthy objects—either buffaloes in the form of vehicles for them—or rice cooked with milk, as soon as it was ready to eat.
The meaning stated in the verse "vidhyadvarāham" is expressed by the final quarter-verse:
Indra, however, accepted the boar.
The remainder of the sentence is that he pierced the demon Varāha—who was the essence of all [wealth], who had stolen the wealth of the gods, and who likewise stole the riches of others—in the heart.
Powerful is your well-fashioned bow, easy to handle and golden-hued; your two arms are beautiful, well-formed, and even though soft, they are ever-increasing in strength.
Your bow is firm, well-fashioned, and beautiful; its string is excellent, golden, and strong. Both your arms are delightful and well-formed, even though they are soft, they are yet firm. 11.
This [verse] has been explained by Yāska without leaving out even a single word;

that very [explanation] is written here: "Tuviśram means 'having great range' or 'having great dispersion'; *te* [means] 'your'; *sukṛtam* means 'well-made'; *sumayam* means 'very pleasant'; *dhanuḥ* [means] 'bow'. *Sādhayitā* [means] 'your achiever'; *bṛndaḥ* [means] 'golden'. Both your arms are *raṇyau*, i.e., delightful; *sāṃgrāmyau* [means] 'suitable for battle'; *vadūpe* [means] 'piercing with arrows', or 'striking down', or 'striking at the vital spots', or 'striking as they go'. (Nirukta 6.33).
The ninth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "purolāśa naḥ," has Kurusuti, the son of Kaṇva, as its seer.
The first nine verses are in the Gāyatrī meter, and the tenth is in the Bṛhatī meter.
Indra is the deity.
And thus it is enumerated in the Anukramaṇī: "The *purolāśa* [section] consists of ten [verses], ending with a *bṛhatī*. Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn:
1. kha, ta-1, ba: *jalapūrṇaṃ evaṃ*; ga, na, bha, śa: *jalapūrṇaṃ evaṃ*; jha, ta-3, 4: *jalapūrṇā evaṃ*; tara: *jalapūrṇāṃ*.
2. Kha, Ta, Śa: vāmamuṣaḥ; Ga: vāmamoṣa; Bha₁: nāmanuṣaḥ. 3. Kha, Ga, Ta, Bha, Śa: by twenty-one [syllables] earlier.
4. Kha, Ta: hṛdama°; Ga: hadama°; Śa: hadama°.
5. Those whose forms are food (ga-āhārarūpa). 6. Those who steal the wealth of others (kha-ta-dhanānāmoṣaka); [variant: those who steal the wealth of others (ga-inadhanānāṃ moṣaka)].
7. Those who are engaged in battle (jha-ta-1-na-bha1-saṃgrāmyau).

8. [The arrows] falling by the movement of *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, and *la* are those that fall by sound, those that fall from afar, or those that pierce the vital organs (*marman*), pierce by movement, pierce by sound, or pierce from a distance.
In the two manuscripts *Gha* and *Su*, there exists this commentary on the mantra: "O Indra, your bow is far-reaching (*tuviśraṃ*), of great range, well-crafted, and well-made for ease.
Your arrow is excellent, golden (*hiraṇyaya*), and made of gold (*hiraṇmaya*)."
Both those arms are for the battle, delightful, well-fashioned, and well-made; even in close combat, they do not fail to strike, being soft yet firm strikers that increase the slaying.
[This is] a *laikṣika* [verse]. In the *mahāvrata*, in the *niṣkevalya*, in the *gāyatra-tuca-śīti*, and in the *ādhāstitva*, these are the verses.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'puroḷāśaṃ no andhasaḥ' (Ai. Ā. 5.2.3)."

O Indra, bring us a thousandfold of the *puroḍāśa* from the soma-juice; and, O Hero, bring hundreds of cattle. *puroḷāśam* | *naḥ* | *andhasaḥ* | *indra* | *sahasram* | *ā* | *bhara* | *śatā* | *ca* | *śūra* | *gonām* ||1||

O heroic Indra, having accepted this *puroḷāśa*—this food (*andhas*) known as such—which is being offered before you, bring to us, for our sake, a thousand cows and hundreds of cows; that is, bring them hither. Alternatively, it may be construed thus: "Bring to us, for our sake, the *andhas* (food) being offered before you, as well as a thousand—that is, a number of one thousand—cows."

Bring to us the distinguishing mark, a cow, a horse, and ointment; together with them, bring golden ornaments. 2. ā | naḥ | bhara | vy-añjanam | gām | aśvam | abhi-añjanam | sacā | manā | hiraṇyayā || 2 ||

O Indra, bring to us—unto us—the distinguishing marks of cattle and horses, and the ointment of oil; bring along with you the objects of thought, the golden implements made of gold. Bring them all together!

And bring us many ear-ornaments, O bold one; for you, O Vasu, are renowned as the one who hears us. 3. uta | naḥ | karṇa-śobhanā | purūṇi | dhṛṣṇo iti | ā | bhara | tvam | hi | śṛṇviṣe | vaso iti || 3 ||
Moreover, O bold one, bring to us many, numerous ear-ornaments—ear-rings that beautify the ears. O Indra, O Vasu (dweller), you who clothe all; for indeed, you are renowned as one who hears.
What [is it that you hear]?
"This Indra is sublime."

O Indra, no one else is a better increaser for you than you are; nor is there anyone else who is a better giver or a better bestower of wealth than you, O Hero, for the one who offers worship. 4. No one else, O Indra, is a better prosperer for you, nor a better provider, nor a better giver; indeed, O Hero, none other than you is so for the priest. 4.
O Indra, there is no one other than you who is a *vṛdhīka*—a nourisher—in such a way; nor is there anyone other than you who is a *suṣāh*, a good provider of sustenance in battle and the like;
nor, moreover, is there anyone who is a *sudās*, a liberal giver.
Likewise, O hero, there is no one other than you who is a *vāghat*—that is, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*);
for there is no leader of the sacrificer other than you.

Indra is not to be set aside, nor is the Mighty One to be overcome; he hears and sees everything. 5. Not at all. Indra. To be set aside. Nor. The Mighty One. To be overcome. Everything. He hears. He sees. 5.
Now, Indra cannot be subdued (*nikartum*); indeed, he is not capable of being overcome.
Likewise, Śakra is not capable of being surpassed (*pariśaktave*) or insulted;
yet he hears and sees everything.
He, the undeceivable one, desires to overcome the death of mortals;
before reproach, he desires to act.

1. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the word *‘śūra’* is absent. 2. In manuscript Gha, it reads *somaṃ*. 3. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, and Śa, the phrase *‘naḥ...athavā’* is absent. 4. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the letter *‘ā’* is absent. 5. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, it reads *hiraṇyamānyu0*. 6. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the word *‘hi’* is absent. 7. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, and Bha, it reads *parikartave*.

He, the unassailable one, seeks to suppress the wrath of mortals; before reproach comes, he seeks to suppress it. He, Indra—the unassailable one, being unharmed by anyone—seeks to suppress the *manyu* (wrath) of *martyānām* (mortals). He does not wait until he has encountered that wrath; rather, he seeks to suppress it even before the *nidaḥ* (reproach), that is, prior to censure. The meaning is: as soon as someone desires to revile him, he suppresses that person even before that point.

By his very will, the belly of the swift one, the slayer of Vṛtra, who drinks the Soma, is filled as he performs his rite. (7) By his very will (*kratvaḥ*), the belly of the swift (*turasya*) one—the slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtraghnas*), the drinker of Soma (*somapānaḥ*)—is indeed full (*pūrṇam*) through his ritual action (*kratvā*). Whose? [The swift one’s.]

"This Kruntu" is the tenth hymn, consisting of nine verses. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "This Kruntu; nine [verses]; Kruntu Bhārgava; addressed to Soma; in Anuṣṭubh. The seer (ṛṣi) is Kruntu Bhārgava. It consists of nine verses in the Anuṣṭubh meter; eight [of these] are in the Gāyatrī meter. Soma is the deity. The application (viniyoga) is indicated by the internal characteristics of the text.

This Soma, the all-conquering, the piercer, the seer and sage, has been seized by Kaṇva. 1. This [Soma], the cutter, has been grasped; he is the all-conquering, the piercer—this Soma, the seer and the inspired singer, [has been grasped] by Kaṇva. 1.

We are Soma, the cutter, the maker of all; *gṛbhītaḥ*, seized by others yet unseized [by them]; *viśvajit*, the conqueror of all; and *udbhid*, the uprooter of the fruit—or alternatively, *viśvajit* and *udbhid* are two Soma sacrifices, and we are of that nature because we bring them to completion.
The *vṛṣi* is one who possesses knowledge, a wise sage (*vipra*), intelligent, worthy of special honor like a *vipra*, or a fulfiller.
Such is Soma, of great majesty; the remainder of the sense is that he is to be praised with the hymn of Kaṇva.

He covers what is naked; he heals everything that is injured. He has made the blind see and the cripple walk. 2. He covers what is naked; he heals everything that is injured. He has made the blind see and the cripple walk. 2.
This *soma* covers—that is, it conceals—the sacrificial essence (*yajñama*). It covers that which appears as if fruitless by means of its fruit;
or alternatively, it produces and covers [it] with a garment.
In that manner, he heals—that is, acts as a physician for—the distressed, the afflicted, and the sick; indeed, he heals them all.
Through the gateway of sacrifice, which is both a means to attain heaven and a medicine for achieving bodily perfection, he, though himself bound, perceives clearly even that which is other.
Śroṇa, even a cripple, even one who is lame, goes forth, having emerged from the world.

O Soma, you are the one who extends wide protection against the hostilities caused by ourselves and those committed by others. 3. You, O Soma, [are] from [hostilities] caused by ourselves, from hostilities, from those committed by others, wide, you are, the protector, the refuge. 3.

"O Soma, protect us from those who diminish us—that is, from those who make us emaciated—or alternatively, from those who sever our limbs; from those produced by forest-dwellers; from hostilities created by enemies—that is, from unpleasant things caused by foes;
in other words, from sorceries (kṛtyā)."
"You are a wide-sheltering, excellent protection; you become one who extends wide protection for the singers. "For the *rakṣases* are created by others," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

You are mindful; by your powers, O possessor of the Soma-residue, you have driven away from heaven and from earth even the hatred of the malevolent. 4. You. Mindful. Your. Powers. From heaven. Away. From earth. O possessor of the residue. You have driven away. Of the evil one. Even. Hatred. 4.

O Soma, you who possess the *vṛjīṣa*, by means of that *vṛjīṣa* present at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), and likewise by your own intention (*cittī*), by your wisdom (*cit*), by your skills (*dakṣaiḥ*), and by your powers (*balaiḥ*), from heaven (*divaḥ*) and from earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*), drive away (*vyāvīḥ*)— separate us from— the malice (*dveṣaḥ*) and the sorcery (*kṛtyām*) of our assailant (*ghasya*). Even from the enemy, keep it far apart.
1. At that time, Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, and Śa [had such names].
2. Kha: *sādhanānāmīṣadha*; Ga: *sādhanānāṃ nāmīṣadha*; Gha, Jha, Tara: *sādhanāna īṣadha*; Tā: *sādhanānimauṣadha*; Tā-4, Na, Bha: *sādhanānanauṣadha*; Śa: *sādhanānunīṣadha*. 3.
Kha, Gha, Jña, Tā-1, 2, and Śroṇa: Śroṇa was also [known as] Śroṇa.
4. In manuscripts ga, tā, and 4, there is no "śa-paṃgurapi.
5. In manuscript ga, it is "vārakaṃ.
6. In manuscripts kha, gha, tā, 1, and 2, it reads "yatāsi bahukṛt."

If seekers go for their purpose, let them indeed obtain the gift of the giver; let them fulfill the desire of the one who is satisfied. (5) If seekers—those desiring wealth—go toward their goal, and having gone, they obtain the gift, the giving, of the donor; and among those who have gone, O Soma, you favor him who is satisfied and begging, let them fulfill his desire. That is to say, they satisfy him to that extent. (33)

When he finds that which was lost long ago, he stirs up for this seeker of *ṛta* that which was lost; he extends his life-span beyond what had not yet been crossed. When he finds that which was lost long ago—his own ancient wealth—the one who has lost his wealth stirs up (*ut īryat*) this seeker of *ṛta*, who desires sacrifice for the sake of recovering his lost property; that is to say, he brings about the recovery of the wealth. He extends his life-span (*pra īm āyuḥ tārīt*) beyond what had not yet been traversed.

O Soma, being well-disposed toward us, be gracious, one who brings happiness, whose will is unassailable, and who is free from agitation; be a source of peace for our heart. 7. O Soma, as you are drunk, being well-disposed (*suśevaḥ*)—meaning most pleasant—toward us, abiding in our hearts, be a bringer of joy (*mṛḷayākuḥ*), one whose resolve is unyielding (*adatkratuḥ*), free from agitation (*avātaḥ*), and be a source of peace (*śam*) for our heart. The word *aparaḥ* (another) is used here as a filler (*pūraṇaḥ*). 3.

O Soma, do not cause us to tremble; O King, do not terrify us. Do not strike our heart with your brilliance. (8) O Soma, do not make us shake—that is, do not cause our knowledge to waver. O King Soma, do not frighten us; do not make us afraid. Do not destroy our heart (*hārdi*) with your splendor (*tviṣā*). (8)

When I behold the ill-will of the gods within my own well-disposed [heart], O King, drive away my enemies; O Bounteous One, drive away those who seek to harm me. 9. ava | yat | sve | su-dhasthe | devānām | duḥ-matīḥ | īkṣe | rājan | apa | dviṣaḥ | sedha | mīḍhvaḥ | apa | sirdhaḥ | sedha || 9 ||
1. He avoids the desire for *kha*, he avoids the desire for *gha*, they avoid the desire for *bha*, and he avoids the desire for *śa*.
2. The meaning is that he accomplishes [the goal] by means of *kha*, *jña*, *ta*, and *re*.
Then, may he cause this un-crossed beginning of the sacrifice to cross over—that is, may he cause his life, his existence, to increase preeminently.
3. *kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa-hṛdaye*:

"In one's own abode" (*sve sadhasthe*) means in one's own place or home; "the ill-wills of the gods" (*devānāṃ durmatīḥ*) means evil intentions do not enter there. When I look down upon you, and you look back at me, then, O King, drive away our enemies (*dvipaḥ*).
O you who have poured out the Soma juice, drive away the injurers;
that is, destroy them.

"Na hanyām" is the eleventh hymn, consisting of ten verses. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Na hanyām; ten [verses]; Ekacūnu, the son of Nodhas, is the seer; it is in the Gāyatrī meter, except for the last verse, which is a divine Triṣṭubh.
Thus, Ekacūnu, the son of Nodhas, is the ṛṣi.
The other [verse] is a Triṣṭubh, and it has the gods as its deity; the remaining verses are Gāyatrīs dedicated to Indra.
In the second round (paryāya), the first eight verses belong to the Maitrāvaruṇa recitation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Nahanyam balākaram’—these are eight" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
In the Niṣkevalya hymn of the Mahāvrata, this [verse] is employed as the introductory insertion (ādhā) because of its being in the Gāyatrī meter.
Accordingly, Śaunaka states in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "'Nahanyam balākaram'—with this verse he performs the pratyavadhāna" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.3).

I have not made anyone else my protector and comforter, O Śatakratu; therefore, O Indra, be gracious to us. I have not, by force, made another my comforter—truly, O Śatakratu, I do not. Therefore, O Indra, you must be gracious to us.

O Indra, you who have ever before protected us, the indefatigable, for the winning of booty—such as you are, O Indra, be gracious to us! O Indra, you who have ever before protected us, the indefatigable, for the winning of booty—such as you are, O Indra, be gracious to us! "Yaḥ amṛdhaḥ" means "you, the indefatigable, the non-violent one. "Naḥ" means "us. "Vājasātaye" means "for the obtaining of food. "Purā" means "formerly. "Āvitha" means "you have protected. O Indra, "saḥ tvam" means "you, being such," "naḥ" means "to us," "śaśvat" means "evermore," and "mṛḷaya" means "be gracious; grant us happiness."

O Indra, you who impel the weak, are you not indeed the protector of the one who presses the soma? O Indra, will you not surely grant us strength? (3) O Indra, you are the "impeller of the weak" (*radhracodana*); that is, you are one who urges on the one who is feeble or in need of aid. As such, you are indeed the "protector" (*avitā*) of the one who presses the soma. Therefore, O Indra, "will you not surely" (*kuvit su*) grant us "strength" (*śaka*)? That is, become capable for us; the meaning is: provide us with abundant wealth, or make us prosperous.
O Indra, O wielder of the stone, protect our chariot even if it lags behind; place it for me in the forefront. 4.
1. [The syllables] kha, ta, śa, and da have the gods as their deities.

2. Regarding the manuscript kha-ta-na-bha-1-2, a commentary on this mantra does not exist; O Ga, since you have protected us (naḥ) perpetually and at all times in the past for the sake of obtaining food, may you, as such, be gracious to us (mṛḷaya).

And what kind of person are you? You are *amṛdhaḥ*, meaning unoppressed or unhurt. O Indra, you who previously protected us (*āvitha*) from our adversaries (*mṛdhaḥ*) for the sake of winning booty (*vājasātaye*), that is, for the acquisition of food—be such as you are, O Indra, gracious (*mṛḷaya*) and bring us happiness. Or: O Indra, you who are *amṛdhaḥ* (unoppressed), being unhurt by enemies, and who in former times (*purā*) on many occasions (*śaśvat*) have protected us, may you, for the sake of winning booty—that is, for the giving of food or for the attainment of food—be gracious and bring us happiness.
3. Kha-ta-1-2-bha-abhava: 880 Rigveda.

O Indra, protect our chariot! O wielder of the thunderbolt, even though it be behind us, bring it to the front for me. O Indra, protect (*pra ava*) our chariot (*naḥ ratham*). What kind of chariot? Even though it be behind us (*paścāc cit santam*); *cit* here has the sense of "even" or "also. O wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivaḥ*), O Indra, make this chariot of mine (*enam me ratham*) which is currently behind us, move to the front (*purastāt*). Make it so.

Come now! Why do you sit silent? Make our chariot foremost; [make] us possess the highest fame, O seeker of booty. (5) "Come!"—this and what follows is identical to the address of the chief [priest]. "Come, O Indra! Now indeed, why do you sit silently? To this, if it is asked, "What shall I do?", it is replied: "Make our chariot *prathamam*, foremost—that is, the chief among all. "O seeker of booty (*vājayu*)," [make] our desired "fame" (*śravaḥ*), characterized by the oblation, "upamam"—for that is a word for proximity. The sense is: "Let it remain in your vicinity. Since this is so, therefore, "make this our [chariot] foremost. (35)

Drive our chariot seeking booty; it is easy for you to do. What indeed can hinder you? Make us truly victorious! O Indra, protect our booty-seeking chariot in battle. Everything that must be done by you is easy to perform; there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for you to accomplish. Therefore, make us truly victorious in the fray.

O Indra, be firm; you are a fortress. This auspicious prayer, timely and perfect, approaches your appointed place. O Indra, be firm—be steadfast in battle. You are a fortress (*pūḥ*); like an immovable city, so may you be. Or rather: be firm in our sacrifice; do not desire to go to another's sacrifice. You are a *pūḥ*, a fulfiller of desires. If it is asked what is ordained here, it is said: this auspicious (*bhadrā*) prayer (*dhīḥ*)—whether a hymn of praise or a ritual act—approaches you, the preparer (*niṣkṛtaṃ*), being endowed with the proper season (*ṛtviyāvatī*). The word *ṛtu* indicates time; thus, being possessed of its own proper time, it goes toward you. Or else, it approaches your appointed station (*niṣkṛtaṃ sthānam*).

May she not bring us reproach from every side; may she never partake [of our ill]. May the wide space be our goal, and the wealth placed therein be ours. May the enemies, no longer striving, be cast away. May she (*sīṃ*) not bring us reproach (*avṛdhaḥ*) from every side (*mā... ā*). May she never partake (*ā bhāk*) [of our misfortune]—that is, may it reach us from nowhere. The meaning is: "Make us free from evil. Furthermore, may the wide space (*urvī kāṣṭhā*)—the vast intermediate region extending to the ends—be our goal. Yāska says: "'Kāṣṭhā' refers even to the end-point (*ājyanta*), for it stands having reached its limit" (Nirukta 2.15). Therein, may the wealth (*dhana*) belonging to the enemy, which has been placed (*hitaṃ*) [against us], be for our own stability. May the enemies (*aratnayaḥ*), those who do not strive properly, be cast away (*apāvṛktāḥ*); this is the sense.

1. *ga-he indra*; *gha-haṃto he indra*. 2. *kha-ga-ta-śa-cet*. 3. *gha-vājayuḥ* ... *micchan*. 4. *na-bha-ta-asmād asmān*. 5. *gha-jetṝn asmān kṛdhi*. 6. *kha-ta-tasmāt*. 7. *kha-ta-bha-śa-bhavanti*. 8. *kha-apāvṛttāḥ*; *jha-ta3-4-ma-apāvṛttāḥ*.

When you perform that fourth name which is worthy of sacrifice, we desire that; then indeed you are celebrated as our lord. 9. The fourth name, worthy of sacrifice—when you shall make it, that we desire. From that very moment, you are borne as our lord. 9.

O Indra, when you assume that fourth name which is worthy of sacrifice and connected to the sacrifice, we desire that very thing. Immediately thereafter, O Āditya, as our protector and sustainer, you carry us and lead us forward. There are three names—the secret name, the revealed name, and the name [of the sun]—and the fourth name is "Soma-sacrificer," and that indeed is the name worthy of sacrifice.

He has caused you to grow strong, O immortals; he has gladdened the single-minded gods and those who are goddesses. To him, grant prosperity that is highly praised. May the one rich in wisdom come quickly in the morning. He has caused you to grow strong, O immortals; he has gladdened the single-minded gods and those who are goddesses. To him, grant prosperity that is highly praised. May the one rich in wisdom come quickly in the morning. (10)
This belongs to the Viśvedevas.
O gods, O immortals—those who do not die—he has caused you to increase by means of praise and has gratified you with Soma. I am the one-pointed seer (ekadhur).
And furthermore, O goddesses—O divine wives of the gods—you whom he has caused to increase and gratified.
For him, they two bestow—that is, they provide—praiseworthy, abundant wealth (*rādhas*).
The particle *u* is a filler or has the sense of *eva* (indeed).
May Indra, whose wealth is his ritual action (*dhiyāvasu*), come quickly—meaning at once—at every dawn.
The repetition is for the purpose of highlighting Indra’s superiority due to his lordship over the gods.
In the ninth section (anuvāka), there are thirteen hymns.

Among them, the first hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "ā tū na indra," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Kusīdin, the son of Kaṇva; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: "ā tū na [nine]; Kusīdin, the son of Kaṇva."
In the *mahāvrata* sacrifice, during the *niṣkevalya* chant, there are two hymns beginning with this [verse] in the *gāyatrī* meter.
Śaunaka has likewise prescribed this in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*: "The *sūddohāḥ* [verses] are the two hymns beginning with 'ā tū na indra dyumantam'" (*AiA* 5.2.3).
In the second round (*paryāya*), the first triplet in the *maitrāvaruṇa* litany is the *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, come hither from afar; run toward us with splendor" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
O Indra, do thou grasp for us that resplendent and wondrous prize with thy great right hand. O Indra, do thou grasp for us that resplendent and wondrous prize with thy great right hand.

O Indra, you who have the great hand, the possessor of the great hand—do you at this very moment take hold with your right hand and bestow upon us that resplendent, renowned wealth; "renowned" meaning worthy of praise, "wonderful" meaning admirable, and "grābha" meaning that which seizes or is fit to be grasped. Seize it fully and bring it toward us.

For you, O far-shining one, are indeed possessed of many deeds, many gifts, great wealth, and vast measure, through your saving aids. 2. For you, O far-shining one, are indeed possessed of many deeds, many gifts, great wealth, and vast measure, through your saving aids. 2.
O Indra, we indeed know you as such: what kind [of being]?
One of many deeds (*tuvikūrmi*), one who bestows much (*tuvideṣṇa*), one who possesses abundant wealth (*tuvimagha*), one of great measure (*tuvimātra*), and one endowed with aids (*avobhiḥ*).
Neither gods nor mortals can restrain you, O Hero, when you desire to give; they cannot hold you back, as one might not stop a formidable bull.

1. [The syllables] kha, gha, ta, na, bha, and śa are connected with *yajña*. 2. [The syllables] ta, na, and śa [indicate] one [verse] with *soma*; bha [indicates] one with *māsa*. 3. In kha, ta, na, bha, and śa, the word "atve tu" is absent. 4. In bha, it is read as *stutam i* (with a hiatus). 5. In kha and na, it is *tuvīm agham*. Ka. 3-56: No.
O Hero, neither the gods nor mortals restrain you when you desire to give, like a formidable bull. (3)
O heroic Indra, the gods do not restrain you when you desire to give— that is, when you wish to bestow gifts— nor indeed do mortals restrain you;
[they are like] a terrifying bull that causes fear, set loose upon the pasture.
Just as they are unable to restrain him, so it is in that case.
In the first section of the *Acchāvāka-śastra*, there is the triplet beginning with "eto nv indram.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "eto nv indraṃ stavāmeśānaṃ mā no asmin maghavan" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
Come now, let us praise Indra, the lord of wealth, the self-ruling sovereign;
may we not be deprived of his bounty.
Come now, let us praise Indra, the lord of wealth, the self-ruling one; may we not be deprived of his bounty. 4.
"Come here quickly, you people of ours!
What are we to do? Let us praise Indra!"
Of what sort is he?

He is the lord and master of *vasu*, that is, of wealth; he is self-radiant (*svārāja*), shining by himself, or shining in heaven. May no other wealthy man, through his riches, oppress us who are favored by Indra.
The meaning is: "Having correctly proclaimed the names of those who are being honored, let us praise them."
They have praised him; they have sung unto him. May he hear the Sāman being chanted; may he respond with bounty. ||5||
In the preceding mantra, it was said, "let us praise.
Indra himself shall praise that very hymn;
and having praised it, let him sing it—that is, let him perform the secondary chanting (*upagāna*).
May he hear—that is, listen to—the *sāman* hymn being sung for that purpose;
and endowed with wealth (*rādhas*), may he favor us—that is, graciously accept us.

Bring to us with your right hand; touch us with your left. O Indra, do not exclude us from wealth. 6 ā naḥ bhara dakṣiṇena abhi savyena pra mṛśa | indra mā naḥ vasoḥ niḥ bhāk ||6|| Bring to us with your right hand; touch us with your left. O Indra, may you not deprive us of wealth. 6
"O Indra, bring it to us.
Having brought it, touch it with both hands—the right and the left;
that is to say, bestow it.
Do not exclude us from our wealth; do not exclude me.
In the second section, within the *acchāvāka-śāstra*, there is the triplet beginning with "upa kramasva.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "upa kramasvā bhara dhṛṣatā tadasmai nabhyam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
Step forth boldly, O bold one; bring hither, with courage, the wealth of the people who do not give, even that which is most difficult to attain.
1. In [the manuscripts] kha, ta, na, bha, and śa, the word "devāḥ" is absent.
2. In kha, ta, śa, and bha, it reads "vṛṣṇaṃ bhayajanakam"; in bha, it reads "janabhayajanakaṃ vṛṣṇam". 3. In kha, jña, ta¹, and ta², the word "rājamānam" is absent.
4. In the Ta3-4-śa manuscript, "rājamānaṃ svarge" does not exist. In the Ga manuscript, this mantra is found as follows: "Let the Sotṛ [priest] praise Indra; let him perform the upagāna."
May he hear the Sāman being sung; may he listen.
Endowed with *rādhas*—whether wealth or means of adornment—may he sing toward us, may he accept us.
5. bha3-upagāsiṣt.
6. "Joined with *ta-bha-la-ca*" and "joined with *ga-śa-va-ya*. O Indra, you should approach; go toward the wealth, or rather, proceed to give it.
O bold one, you who daunt the enemies, being joined with a courageous and daring mind, bring it hither—bring it!
Of whose wealth shall you bring it? It is said:
the *veda*, the wealth, of the person among men who is most miserly (*adāśvas*), utterly withholding.
O Indra, whatever strength you possess which is to be won together with the inspired poets—
that, indeed, do you win for us.
O Indra, whatever strength you possess that is to be won by the inspired poets—win that well for us! 8.

O Indra, that strength (*vāja*) which is yours—worthy of being won by us through wise and inspired singers (*vipra*), and worthy of being enjoyed—that strength, having been requested by us, do you truly win for us; grant it to us!
May these swift-winning strengths, all-gladdening, quickly come to us and be brought to maturity through our desires.
May those swift-moving strengths, all-gladdening, quickly come to us with our desires and bring us praise. 9.
O Indra, may those *vājās* (strengths or horses) of yours become swift-moving for us, reaching us instantly.
Of what nature are they? They are *viśvacandrāḥ*: endowed with all gold, or providing delight through many names.
And our people, endowed with many desires under their control, quickly—that is, swiftly—praise [you].
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may Vidyātīrtha Maheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the sixth book in the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa, a commentary on the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the bearer of the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
"Ā pra drava" is the second hymn, consisting of nine verses.
Thus it is enumerated: "Ā pra drava.
According to the metrical rule "The seer is other than [the deity]," the seer is Kusīdhu of the Kaṇva lineage.
By the rule regarding *prāvatsaprīya*, the meter is *gāyatrī*;
by the rule regarding non-specification (*anādeśa*), Indra is the deity;
and its application (*viniyoga*) in the *sūkta* of the *niṣkevalya* at the *mahāvrata* has been stated.
In the second round of the night, during the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra, the triplet beginning with "ā pra drava" is of the *ajurūpa* type.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘ā pra drava parāvataḥ’, ‘nāhyaṃ baḷākaram’—these eight [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
Run hither from afar and from near at hand, O Vṛtra-slayer,
O Maghavan, for the distribution of the sacrificial offering!
O Vṛtrahan, O Maghavan, hasten hither from afar and from near at hand to this offering! 1.
O Vṛtrahan, O slayer of the Asura Vṛtra who obstructed the waters, O Indra, at the *prabharman*—
that sacrifice which possesses *prabharmaṇi*, excellent *bharmāṇi*, that is, excellent sustainments consisting of the accomplishment of the animal-sacrifices (*paśugraha*) and other rites;
or alternatively:
He in whom the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—who are eminent, skilled in their duties, and sustainers of the gods through the offering of oblations (*havis*)—are present, is thus described.
To such a sacrifice, O Maghavan, come quickly and with haste, facing toward the exhilarating Soma juices, from both the far distance (*parāvataḥ*) and the nearby vicinity (*arvāvataḥ*).
Regarding the word *maghava*, the absence of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is due to the rule "optionally in the Vedic language" (*vā chandasi*).
1. Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, Śa, and Tathā; Ga, Tathā, and Taṃ. 2.
Kha, Ga, Bha, Śa, Viśva, and Candrāḥ.
3. Kha, Gha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Kaṇvaḥ.

The Somas are strong; come hither! These pressed juices are exhilarating. Drink, O impetuous one, as you desire! 2. The Somas are strong; come hither! These pressed juices are exhilarating. Drink, O impetuous one, as you desire! 2.

O Indra, these Somas—intense, providing intense exhilaration, meaning they quickly produce intoxication; gladdening, having the nature of delighting or causing delight; these pressed Somas have been prepared for your sake.
Therefore, come— return to our sacrifice—
and having arrived, drink them.
He states the reason for drinking the Soma:
Since you, being bold and confident in your desire, have spoken to them and thus know how to attend upon them, the meaning is:
"therefore, drink them according to your wish.
Regarding the word *dudhry*: from the root *dhṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness" (*prāgalbhya*), the form is derived as a *kin*-suffix ending by the rule "ṛtvigdadhṛk... and so forth.
*Ūciṣe*: from the root *uc*, meaning "to gather" (*samavāye*); Vedic usage.

O Indra, hear my invocation well! Of this pressed soma mixed with milk that belongs to us, grant us the drinking and full satisfaction. 6. O Indra, hear! Well! My! Invocation! To us! Of the pressed! Mixed with milk! Apart! The drinking! Satisfaction! Grant! 6.
O Indra, hear— listen well— to my invocation, that call directed toward you.
Likewise, [be present] for us for the sake of the pressed soma mixed with milk—
that is, mixed with cow's milk.
"Obtain variously (vi-aśnuhi) the drinking—the act of consuming—of such Soma;
through that drinking, attain manifold satisfaction.
[The root] *aś* [is used] in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*).
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of transposition.
In the third turn, specifically in the *acchāvāka* recitation, there is the triplet beginning with "O Indra, that [Soma] which is in the cups" (*ya indra camaseṣu*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘ya indra camaseṣvā’, ‘somaḥ pra vaḥ satām’" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.4).
The third hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "Of the gods" (*devānām*), is the seerly work of Kusīdin of the Kaṇva lineage; it is in the *gāyatrī* meter and addressed to the Viśvedevas.
And thus it is enumerated: "The Vaiśvadeva [hymn] belongs to the gods.
On the eighth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), this hymn is inserted as the *nivid* within the Vaiśvadeva *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Vaiśvadeva [hymn] is 'devānām idam... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.10).

Of the gods, indeed, that great protection we choose for ourselves—of you, the showerers [of blessings], for our aid. (1) O gods! Of the gods—who shine on all sides by their own splendor—that very "vit" (indeed), your "mahat" (great, pervasive, or praiseworthy) protection which exists, that "vavaḥ" (protection) belonging to you, the "vṛṣṇām" (showerers of desires), we, the sacrificers, "ā vṛṇīmahe" (choose, i.e., accept from all sides). For what purpose? "Asmabhyamūtaye"—having first spoken generally as "for us" (*asmabhyam*), he specifies it with "ūtaye": for our protection.

May they—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—be our constant allies; may they, the wise ones, be our increasers. (2) May those gods—Varuṇa, the warder-off of enemies; Mitra, the friend of all; and Aryaman, who ever moves—these three gods, be our allies at all times, in every season. The meaning is that in rites such as the Agnihotra, the gods beginning with Indra should provide assistance from the time of the departure until the completion of the journey and the sacrifice. Furthermore, may those gods, being *pracetasaḥ* (possessing excellent knowledge), or alternatively, being of beautiful praise (*cetaḥ* = hymn of praise), be our *vṛdhāsaḥ* (increasers)—that is, those who cause us to prosper by bestowing wealth and other blessings.

Carry us across the many perils, as one carries water across with boats; you are the charioteers of *ṛta*. O charioteers—leaders of *ṛta* (truth) or of sacrifice, O gods—or rather, because of the connection with *ṛta*, [the word *ṛtasya*] is expected [to modify both]: O charioteers, possessors of chariots, O gods who are the accomplishers of sacrifice! Carry us across (*ati parṣatha*) the many (*puru*), the widely scattered (*viṣpitā*), the extended (*vitāni*) forces of the enemy or the ritual acts (*karman*). The suffix *-sup* has been replaced by *-luk*. Just as a boatman brings water across to the shore by means of boats, so do you carry us to the further bank, to completion, by means of your protections. 3.

May there be for us what is desirable, O Aryaman; may there be for us what is desirable, O Varuṇa, as our praise. For we entreat you for what is desirable. (4) O Aryaman, O God, may that which is desirable—meaning wealth worthy of being sought and honored—be ours. O Varuṇa, may there be for us that which is desirable, namely all that is praiseworthy and worthy of hymns. Why? Because the word *hi* indicates a reason: since we entreat you, O noble ones, for desirable wealth—that is, we pray for it—therefore he hopes, "May it be ours. (4)
For you, O wise Ādityas, are the masters of desirable wealth who ward off injury; none of us shall suffer from evil. 5.

O Pracetasaḥ—those of excellent wisdom or beautiful praise; O Riśādasaḥ—O gods who are the destroyers (asitāraḥ) of enemies (riśatām) who seek to harm; you are the masters (īśānāsaḥ) of desirable wealth (vāmasya).
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis:
you are indeed the masters, the lords.
Therefore, the meaning is that we entreat you; "īśānāḥ" means "rulers," from the root "īśa" in the sense of sovereignty.
It is anudātta.
By the rule "tāsyanudāttet," it becomes udātta on the first syllable due to its accent;
it is not a vocative (saṃbuddhi).
Therefore, O Ādityas—O gods, sons of Aditi—let that wealth not reach me as I entreat it, which wealth belongs to or is connected with *agha*, evil.
O bounteous gods, whether dwelling at home or traveling on the road, we call upon you for protection.

Whether dwelling at home or traveling on the road, O bounteous gods, we invoke you for our prosperity. O bounteous ones (sudānavaḥ), O gods (devāḥ) of excellent gifts: whether we are dwelling (kṣiyantaḥ) in our homes for the sake of comfort, or traveling (yāntaḥ) on the road (adhvan)—the case ending is elided—on our way to gather sacrificial fuel, we invoke (humahe) you alone for the sake of prosperity (vṛdhāya), that we may increase through oblations. Or alternatively: whether in our homes, when setting out from home, or on the paths, we call upon you for prosperity—that is, for the increase of our wealth and other blessings.
Favor us, O Indra and Viṣṇu, among these kinsmen; come also, O Maruts and Aśvins!

Adhi na indra eṣāṃ viṣṇo maruto 'śvinā. (7) O Indra, Viṣṇu, Maruts, and O Aśvins—O gods, Indra and the rest—among these who are *sajātyas* (kinsmen), those born of the same lineage, such as brothers and friends, favor us; come to us for our praise.
O bounteous ones, we now truly bear together our brotherhood and common purpose within the womb of our mother.

And again,

O Ādityas, you who are liberal givers of beautiful gifts: now, immediately after our departure, we—by means of a commonality (*samānyā*;

the substitution of *ḍy* for the case-ending)—having previously [been born] collectively from all the gods, and then in two ways (*dvitā*), in a twofold manner, as born from the womb of Mother Aditi—if that brotherhood of yours truly exists, then we now offer it forth.
*Pradhāraṇa* means utterance or manifestation;
that is, we utter or we manifest [the names].

The birth of all the gods in pairs is clearly stated in the *Taittirīyaka*: beginning with “Aditi, desiring sons, cooked a sacrificial porridge (*brahmaudana*) for the Sādhyas, the gods” (*Tai. Saṃ.* 6.5.5–6), it continues with “From her, Pūṣan and Aryaman were born,” and so forth.
For you indeed, O bounteous givers, with Indra as your chief, are turned toward heaven;
even now I speak of this.

For you indeed are the bounteous givers, with Indra as your chief, reaching unto heaven; therefore, I speak even now to you. [The first half-verse is established: O bounteous ones, O gods of excellent gifts (*sudānavaḥ*), those who have Indra as their chief (*indrajyeṣṭhāḥ*)—meaning all the gods have Indra as their leader—such as you are, reaching unto heaven (*abhidyavaḥ*), you truly are present at our sacrifice. *Hi* (for) indicates a well-known fact. *Adha cit* (therefore, immediately thereafter), I speak to you; that is, I praise you. *Uta* (and also) means that I praise you again and again. 4.

It is thus enumerated: "The *preṣṭham* [hymn] by Uśanas Kāvya is addressed to Agni.
This hymn belongs to the *prātaranuvāka* in the sacrifice dedicated to Agni, in the *gāyatrī* metre, and in the *āśvina-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'gukṣvā hi preṣṭhaṃ vaḥ' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13)."
In the *ābhiprāvika* *ukthya* rites, "preṣṭhaṃ vaḥ" is the optional *stotriya* verse for the *maitrāvaruṇa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "preṣṭhaṃ vo atithiṃ śreṣṭhaṃ yaviṣṭha bhārata" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.8).

I praise for you Agni, your most beloved guest, dear as a friend, to be known like a chariot. (1) O sacrificers, I praise him who is your most beloved (*preṣṭham*), most dear through his bestowing of wealth; your guest (*atithim*), to be honored by you like a guest. Or rather: from the root *at*, "to go continuously"—he is the carrier (*nasaḥ*) characterized by the oblation. As it is said:
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun. (1)
"From the sun rain is born;
from rain come plants; from plants comes fire"—this is the teaching of another sage.

O radiant god Agni, with what kind of speech (*vācā*) shall I bring forth praise (*upastuti*) for you—for you who are desirable (*varāya*), who are to be sought after by all, and who overcome your enemies?
"You are indeed great, while I am small;
for that reason, I shall offer praise"—thus the seer replies to them.

Whose mind shall I serve with the sacrifice, O mighty one, O son of strength? What indeed shall I say as this playful jest? (5) [Whose] service [shall I perform] with [whose] mind at the sacrifice, O powerful one, O young [son of strength]? What indeed shall I utter as this jest? (5)
The seer replies:
"O son of strength!
*Yahu* is a name for offspring."

O Agni, son of strength, because [the sacrifice] is accomplished through power, for what kind of sacrificer—possessing a sacrifice and possessing the gods worthy of worship—do we, being united in mind, offer (*dāśama*) these oblations (*havīṃṣi*) unto you?
The plural number is used for honor.
Furthermore, when (*kad*) and how (*kat*) shall I speak this homage (*namaḥ*)—whether as an oblation or as a salutation—to you? I shall say it.
"U" is used for questioning.
The seer asks the seer, "When shall I sacrifice? When shall I praise? [The other] says, "I shall speak."
This is the form of the substitute *vacya* in the first person singular of the Ātmanepada in the *luṅ* tense.

O Agni, immediately thereafter—*adha* being used here for emphasis—you alone must grant (*karaḥ*) to us; that is, you must give. (The *leṭ* mood of the root *kṛ* takes the augment *aṅ*. To what does this refer? He says: "Our songs"—all our hymns addressed to you—make them such that they become *sukṣitīḥ*. Those two Aśvins are the "Dastras," meaning "the beautiful ones";

The two who cause the decay of all enemies;

Being such, for that very reason, you two—“*mayobhuvā*,” the bringers of *maya*, which is happiness; “*ubhā*,” both, who fulfill the number two with respect to one another; “*ubhā*,” both, you two—you have become connected to the “*vacasaḥ*,” the praise, of “*dakṣasya*,” the Prajāpati known by this name.
Indeed (*hi*) is used as a particle of well-known fact:
in ancient times, you two were indeed praised with sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
‘Tā’—you two who are such, being praiseworthy; ‘viśvakaḥ’, the seer of that name; ‘tanukṛthe’: *tanu* is a son, so called because he extends the lineage;

Therefore, "do not sever" (*mā vi yauṣṭam*)—that is, do not cause to be separated—"our friendships" (*sakhya*), the bonds of companionship that have arisen through mutual sacrifice and worship.
This is the form of the root *yu* in the aorist with the suffix *sic*.
Furthermore, "you two must release us," meaning, standing upon your chariot, release the horses so that we may come.

In the imperative (*loṭ*) form of the root *muc*, there is the elision (*ślau*) of the suffix *śap* according to the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). There is also the augment *ad*.
Here, Viśvaka, the father, speaking of himself, says that he is calling upon you two with reference to his son named Viṣṇāpū.
Or rather, he says: "Kṛṣṇa, the father of Viśvaka, whose son is the seer Viśvaka, invokes you both for the sake of a son."
Surely men of distracted mind have praised you both; they have fixed their thoughts upon you for the sake of attaining wealth.
Viśvaka calls upon you both for the protection of his person; do not sever our friendship, but release us from [this] bond.

Surely the one of distracted mind shall praise you both; they have offered their prayer for the sake of attaining better fortune. Viśvaka invokes you both for the protection of his person; do not sever our friendship, but release us! 2.
The *ṛṣi* named Avimāna [said]: "Surely in former times, how did they praise you two? How did they worship you?
Being thus praised by him, you two [grant] *vasyaṣṭaye*;
*vasyas* means more excellent, highly praiseworthy wealth.

For the sake of attaining—that is, for the acquisition of—that which was desired, or rather, for the attainment of that which is more excellent (*vasīyasa*), they fixed their intellects upon him with focused minds.
Indeed, they bestowed [their devotion].
Regarding the word *vasya*: from the word *vasumat* (possessing wealth), when the suffix *īyasun* is added, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision of *vin* and *matup*."
The elision of the vowel *ī* in the suffix *īyasun* is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
You two, being such, are called upon by "Viśvaka"—this has been explained.
For you two indeed bestowed prosperity upon Viṣṇāpū, who possesses many enjoyments, so that he might attain wealth;

For you two, O lords of many enjoyments, have bestowed this prosperity upon Viṣṇāpū for the sake of seeking better fortune. Viśvaka invokes you both for the protection of his person; do not sever our friendship, but release us from bondage. 3.

We invoke for our protection that very Viṣṇāpū, the Aśvins— who are also the heroic ones, capable in action, the winners of wealth,
and the possessors of the *ṛjīṣa* (the pressed-out Soma)—
even though he is far away, as if lost, we call him hither for our preservation.

For a son indeed protects his father. Furthermore, "of which son or grandson" there is "good-mindedness," meaning excellent praise; it is "most sweet" (svādiṣṭhā), that is, exceedingly sweet-making for the gods.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Just as [the praise] of the Father;
just as the praise of the Father of the universe brings delight to the gods, so too [is this]."
Therefore, "we shall summon him"—this is the ellipsis.
The phrase "mā no" has already been explained.

By the *ṛta* the god Savitṛ has brought peace; the horn of *ṛta* has spread wide across the vast expanse. *Ṛta* has conquered even the great assailant. Do not separate us from our herd; release us both!

By the Eternal Law (ṛta), the divine Savitṛ promotes our welfare. The horn of the Eternal Law has spread wide across the vast expanse. By the Eternal Law he has conquered even those who fiercely attack us. Do not separate us; release us together with our kinsmen. ||5||
The seer offers praise to Truth:
"O Aśvins, the god Savitṛ—the illuminator, the deity who impels all beings toward their respective duties—by means of *ṛta* (Truth), causes his mass of rays to be stilled at evening.
Immediately thereafter, that same Savitṛ, at dawn, spreads wide and far across the vast expanse the very peak, the summit, of *ṛta*, of Truth."
He spreads [his power] everywhere.
Furthermore, the great (*mahi*) strength even of an enemy who is *pṛtanyat*—one desiring an army, one eager for battle—he himself overcomes as *ṛtam*, that is, as truth.
Thus he has become praised.
Therefore, by means of that song, may you two also not sever our friendships; come here quickly, for we are eager to see you.

The Aśvins are the deity.
