Ghunnī! Vām! Stoma! O Aśvins, like a flowing stream, come hither to the libations of the pressed honey-sweet juice. O Heroes, that [juice] is dear to you both; drink it like two wild bulls at a watering hole. 1.

O Aśvins, the Ṛṣi named Ghunīka, whose hymns are inexhaustible, offers this praise to you both; that is, his hymn of praise becomes yours. The meaning is that when your praise is performed, the hymns do not diminish, but rather increase further.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*Kriviṇam*. *Krivi* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
Just as a well (*kūpa*) during the pouring of water—that is, when rain is falling—does not become deficient in water, so it is in this case.
Alternatively:
your hymn—that is, the praise directed toward you—indeed becomes worthy of the *yukthya* rite.
The meaning is that once the hymn has been performed, you must bestow food and other gifts upon him.
Therefore, come both of you to our sacrifice;
come to hear our hymns.

O two heroes (narā), O leaders (netārau), Aśvins! This singer becomes most dear—dear by virtue of his performing praise—to the pressed, well-pressed, intoxicating honey-like Soma at this sacrifice shining in heaven.
Therefore, having come quickly, drink the pressed Soma; you two must drink it.
Herein is an illustration:
just as two thirsty *gaura* deer—deer named *gaura*—come swiftly to a salt-flat (*iriṇa*) for the purpose of drinking water from ponds and such, even so [should you come].
Drink the honeyed *gharma*, O Aśvins; sit upon the sacred grass, O heroes.
Rejoicing in the dwelling of man, protect our vital strength with your wisdom.
Drink the honey-sweet Gharma, O Aśvins; sit upon the sacred grass, O Heroes. Rejoicing in the dwelling of Manu, protect our vital strength with your wisdom. 2.
He [offers] to the two Aśvins the Gharma— sweet,
exhilarating (meaning "causing intoxication"),
and full of essence.
‘The root *nṛ* means to flow or to shine.
Drink the Soma flowing into the vessels;
or rather:
"Sweet. *Madhu* is the intoxicating Soma.
"Drink the *gharma*—the milk contained in the *mahāvīra* vessel—and the Soma," so it is said.

But it is not by way of association, because that is impossible. O men (nara), O leaders (netārau) of all; O Aśvins, sit down (āsīdatam)—that is, take your seats—upon the sacrificial grass (barhiḥ) at the sacrifice (yajñe).
Or else:
Having explained the second quarter-verse previously, the first quarter-verse is now explained:
it is appropriate that the drinking of Soma follows immediately after the *upasada* ceremony.

Furthermore, in the *duroṇa*—the dwelling-place, this sacrificial ground of the gods—of *manuṣ*, meaning of man, you two who are characterized as previously described, rejoicing (*mandasānā*) through the drinking of Soma, having come with *vedas*, the oblation consisting of the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings, drink down (*nipātam*) the food in the form of Soma.
Or rather:
together with *vedas*, wealth, protect (*pātam*) our life-force (*vayaḥ*), that is, our lifespan, thoroughly (*ni*).
With all your aids, Priyamedhas have invoked you both;
do you two come to this sacrifice, which is pleasing and for which the sacred grass has been strewn, during the rites for the gods.
1. In *kha*, *ta*, *bha*¹·², and *vā*, [the waters] become scanty; in *śa* and *vā*, they do not become scanty. 2. In *ta* and *śa*, it is observed. 3.
In *kha*, *jha*, *ta*², and *bha*¹·², there is little water; in *ga*, *ta*¹·³·⁴, there is little water; in *śa*, there is water.
4. *kha-ta-śa* have *devatesmin*; *ga* has *devatābhirasmin*; *bha* has *devātasmin*.
In the *ga-ta-śa* manuscripts, the commentary on the second, third, and fourth mantras is not found.
5. *bha* reads *mandasānā mandasānau*.
6. The Priyamedhas have invoked you both with all your aids, O Gha-soma-lords. Come hither to the sacrifice, which is dear to you, at the rites of those who have strewn the sacred grass. 3.
The Priyamedhas [invoked] those two Aśvins; *medha* means sacrifice;
thus, the sacrificers whose sacrifices are most dear.
Alternatively, "priyamedhāḥ" refers to the seer (ṛṣi) named Priyamedha; the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
They have invoked the sacrificing sages together with all protections—
or, since *avati* is a verb meaning "to entreat," together with all desired petitions. They have called them forth.
He summoned [them] for the purpose of protecting himself;
or rather, they summon the two [deities] to grant what is desired.

O you two, come to the sacrifice—the beloved oblation served by all the gods—belonging to the sacrificer who has trimmed the sacrificial grass for its strewing; come near to that dwelling (*vartiḥ*) at the morning sessions, those sacrifices which are the arrivals of the days. Come hither to accept the offering.
O Aśvins, drinking the honeyed Soma, sit upon the sacrificial grass with favor.
Having grown strong, come from heaven to our excellent praise, like two bulls to the water-trough.
Drink the honey-sweet Soma, O Aśvins; sit upon the sacred grass with favor. Thus strengthened, come to our fair praise from heaven like two wild bulls to a water-hole. 4.
O Aśvins, you two, drink the honeyed, flavorful, or intoxicating Soma.
Then, sit down auspiciously upon the sacred grass (barhis) at the sacrifice.
Thereafter, having grown strong through the drinking of Soma, may you two come hither from heaven to this beautiful hymn of praise being offered by us.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like two wild oxen" (gaurau iva), just as two wild oxen come from another region toward a salt-flat, a pond, or the like for the purpose of drinking water, so too [do they approach].
Come now, O Aśvins, with your horses that are rich in nourishment; O Dastras, whose paths are golden, Lords of Splendor, drink the Soma, you who increase the cosmic order.
Come now, O Aśvins, with your horses that are bright with blossoming manes, O wonder-workers on golden paths, lords of splendor! Drink the Soma, you who increase the cosmic order (ṛta). 5.
O Aśvins, you two [are] with those possessing blossoming forms;
"apsu" is a name for form (rūpa).
[The root] "psu" [is used] in the senses of abandoning, sprinkling, and filling.
"With forms that are smooth"— meaning with forms that are radiant—

with such swift-moving horses, "surely now" (*nūnam*) come hither (*ā yātam*) toward our sacrifice. O *dastrau*— O two destroyers, or rather, O two beautiful ones (*darśanīyau*), or O two who bring near (*upakṣapayitārau*)— O you whose paths are golden (*hiraṇyavartanī*).
That upon which one moves is the *vartanī*, meaning a chariot.

O two lords of beauty (*śubhaspatī*), protectors of water or of prosperity; O two increasers of truth (*ṛtāvṛdhā*), augmenters of the sacrifice or of reality; O Aśvins, having arrived swiftly, drink the Soma.
For we, the inspired singers, invoke you both with our hymns for the winning of booty.
O fair ones, wonder-workers, performers of many deeds, Aśvins, come with your wisdom, being attentive to our call.
For we, the inspired singers, call upon you two for the winning of booty; therefore, O fair ones, O wonder-workers, O doers of many deeds, O Aśvins, listen with your wisdom and come hither! 6.
1. kha-jha-ta¹-²-³-bhara-³-psa; jha⁴-bha¹-sa; śa-apsa | 2. kha-jha-ta¹-bha³-puṣa puṣa | 3. kha-jha-ta¹-²-ṛtasya satyasya |

We, the singers of praise who have failed, and therefore the inspired ones (*viprāsaḥ*), the wise ones—*vayaṃ* meaning "we"—for the sake of winning booty (*vājasātaye*), that is, for the acquisition of food, we invoke you two alone;
*hi* is used here as a particle of emphasis. We call upon you both with hymns of praise.
Then *valū*:
*valgana* means skillful movement.
O you two of many deeds (*purudaṃsāsā*), who possess the nature of skillful movement, being summoned by our prayer—that is, by our hymn—come with readiness (*śruṣṭī*).
*Śruṣṭī* is a name for "quickly.
Come quickly, come hither, to grant us wealth and other gifts.
The hymn beginning with "taṃ vo dasmam" consists of six verses; its seer is Nodhas Gautama.
Accordingly, it is enumerated as: "taṃ vo dasmaṃ nodhāḥ.
Since it has been stated that "the first three [hymns] belong to Pragātha," these three hymns constitute the Prāgatha section.
Indra is the deity.
This hymn occurs in the *bārhatatucāśīti* section of the *niṣkevalya* at the *mahāvrata*.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "taṃ vo dasmamatīṣaham... ā no viśvāsu havyaḥ" (AiĀ 5.2.4).
In the *acchāvāka-śastra* at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) of the *abhiṣṭoma*, there is the *pragātha* beginning with "taṃ vo dasmam. It says:
"Like a mountain, he is surrounded by his powers, by those full of strength and by his glories; he stands like a mass of rocks.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?

*Purubhojasam*: one who must be fed by many sacrificers through the offering of oblations such as *soma*, or rather, Indra, the protector (*pālayitāraṃ*) of many; *kṣumantam*: "the one possessing sound," [derived from] the root *dukṣu* meaning "to sound," thus "possessing sound."
By this, sons and so forth are indicated.

We quickly and immediately beg for one who performs hymns of praise and the like, who possesses hundreds, who possesses thousands—that is, who is endowed with wealth numbering in the hundreds of thousands—who possesses cattle, that is, who is possessed of cows and such, and who possesses *vāja*, which is food.
Or alternatively:
Or, the word *pūrva* may be construed as an adjective qualifying *vāja*.

We pray for that Indra who is radiant, worthy of a beautiful gift, endowed with strength and other virtues, accompanied by many sons, friends, and others, and possessed of sound and other sensory qualities.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, ‘na tvā bṛhantaḥ’ is the optional *anurūpa* verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘na tvā bṛhanto adraya ubhayaṃ śṛṇavacca naḥ’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
The great and firm mountains do not obstruct you, O Indra, when you bestow wealth upon a singer such as I; no one can diminish that gift of yours.
Neither do the great, solid mountains obstruct you, O Indra, when you wish to bestow wealth upon a singer like me; no one can diminish that of yours. 3.

O Indra, even the vast, great mountains—mighty in their strength and therefore firm on all sides—cannot restrain you by force; they do not hold you back. He explains this very lack of restraint in the second half of the verse: whatever wealth you desire to give to a singer like me—one who composes a hymn of praise directed toward you—that gift of yours no one at all can diminish or obstruct.
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*);
[in the sense of] "to perish" (*nigame*), there is a short vowel [by rule].
Thus: *māvate*.

The suffix *vatup* is added [to the stems] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sense of similarity, according to the rule: "There is an addition [of *vatup*] after *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sense of similarity."
You are a warrior by your wisdom, O Śarva, and by your wondrous power you surpass all created beings in might.
May this hymn which the Gotamas have produced turn you hither for our protection.
You are a warrior by wisdom, by power, and by wondrous deed; you surpass all created beings in your might. May this hymn, which the Gotamas have generated, turn you hither for our protection. 4.

O Indra, by your *kratu*—whether by the act of slaying Vṛtra and so forth, or by your wisdom (*prajñāna*)—and by your own *śavas*, your strength, you are a warrior, a striker of enemies. Moreover, by your *daṃsanā*, your own deed, [you are] *majman*.
(The root *maj* signifies sound.)
The root *maj* means "to sound.

By means of a force capable of reviling enemies, you overcome all beings, that is, all classes of living creatures. This meaning has already been expressed in such passages as, "I surpass all beings" (*viśvā jātāny abhy asmi mahaḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.100.4), where Indra is the one who speaks.

Having praised you in this manner, the Sun (arka)—the root *arca* meaning "to worship"—is worthy of worship; or rather, the Sun (arka) is the one who honors the gods. This hymn causes him to turn toward us for our protection, that is, he causes him to return.
The meaning is "he makes [himself] face toward himself.
This is from the root *vṛt* in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, with the frequentative *ślau* reduplication and the augment *aṭ*.
"Thee," whom the *Gotamas*—the sons of Gotama, such as Nodhas and others—"generated," that is, they brought forth at their own sacrifice.
This mantra, the praiser, turns you toward that [state].

1. In kha, na, and na, ‘amādaśāya’ is not present. 2. In ta, bha1, and bha2, it is ‘vastu’. 3. In ga, it is ‘saṃhārakaḥ’. 4. In kha, ta, na, and bha, it is ‘uktārthasya’; in śa, it is ‘uktārthasya’. 5. In ga, it is ‘ātmābhimukhaṃ’. 6. In kha, ta, bha, and śa, it is ‘gautama’. 7. In kha, ta, bha, and śa, it is ‘taṃ tvāṃ vayaṃ’; in na, it is ‘taṃ tvā vayaṃ’. Ṛgveda 3.57:
O Indra, you have indeed surpassed the ends of heaven with your might. The earthly realm could not contain you, O Indra; you have grown according to your own inherent power.
For you have indeed surpassed [all] in might from the very ends of heaven; the earthly realm has not encompassed you, O Indra. You have grown great according to your own inherent power. 5.
O Indra, by your might (*ojasā*), from the very limits of heaven (*divaḥ*), you alone (*hi*)—
the particle *hi* being used for emphasis—
by your own power (*svabalenaiva*), have indeed surpassed (*praririkṣe*) all others, becoming preeminent.
In *ricleṃti*, the suffix *bhlu* is applied according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. It has the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Furthermore, O Indra, the earthly realm (*pārthivaṃ rajaḥ*), that is, the world existing on earth, does not encompass (*na vivyāca*) you with its great body; it does not pervade you.
The meaning is that you become capable through your own power by means of Heaven and Earth (*dyāvā-pṛthivībhyām*).
Being such, you should desire to carry us along our own path (*svadhām*), that is, our way; *anuvavakṣiya* is the form of the desiderative of the root *vah* in the Vedic perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Because it is a mantra, there is a state of non-manifestation.
No one, O Maghavan, can obstruct your bounty when you bestow it upon the one who offers libations.
Be the inspirer of our hymn of praise, you who are most generous for the winning of booty.
None can obstruct thee, O Maghavan, for thy bounty is such that thou bestowest it upon the donor. Be thou the inspirer of our hymn, most liberal one, for the winning of the prize.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, there is no one— no one at all— who can obstruct or restrain your *magha*,
that is, your magnificent wealth, when you bestow it upon the donor, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation; the meaning is that at such a time, there is no one who can withhold it from him.

This being so, you who are impelled—meaning the impeller and sender of riches to the singers, and for that very reason the most generous (*maṃhiṣṭhaḥ*), the giver, or the one worthy of honor (*maṃhanīyaḥ*)—you, as such, take note (*bodhi*) of our *ucatha*, that is, our hymn of praise; [take note] for the sake of winning booty (*vājasātaye*), meaning for the purpose of obtaining food, as it is being performed for that end. The ellipsis is: "Being praised by the hymn, grant us food and the like.
*Bodhi*.
The root *budh* means "to awaken" or "to understand.
It belongs to the *aucādi* group.
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Vedic usage.
The instruction.
With the hymn beginning "bṛhadindrāya," he composed the ninth hymn. Nṛmedha and Purumedha are the seers; since they are not otherwise specified, they belong to the lineage of Aṅgiras.
The first two are *pragāthas*; the fifth and sixth are *anuṣṭubhs*; the seventh is a *gṛhatī*.
Indra is the deity. Thus it is enumerated: “*Bṛhadindrāya sasa*, by Nṛmedha and Purumedha; two *anuṣṭubhs* ending with a *bahvṛc* [verse].”
On the twenty-fourth day, after the original *marutvatīya* *pragātha*, two *marutvatīya* *pragāthas* are to be recited.
The first of these *pragāthas* is "Sing the *bṛhat* for Indra.
This *pragātha* occurs on the second day of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and the *abhiplava* six-day periods.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Sing a great song for Indra; 'None [stops] the chariot of Sudās'—these are the Marutvatīya hymns, following the obligatory one" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.3).
Sing forth a great song for Indra, O Maruts, for the greatest slayer of Vṛtra,
by whom you, as strengtheners, have generated light— the watchful god for the sake of the gods.
Sing forth a great song for Indra, O Maruts, the most effective slayer of Vṛtra, by whom, the increasers of Cosmic Order, you generated the light—the watchful god—for the sake of the god. 1.
He [is] the Maruts.
[The root] *ru* means "to sound.
They are called Maruts because they roar (*ruvanti*) in measured fashion (*mitam*).
O singers who speak with measured words, sing the great *Sāman* for Indra—the slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme destroyer of evil—for the sake of Indra; perform the chanting in our sacrifice. (Note:
*ṛtā-* refers to awakening;
on the second day.)
3. O you who generated—that is, brought forth—the gods for the sake of Indra;

you who are the strengtheners (*vṛdhaḥ*) of true sacrifice (*satyasya yajñasya*); O all-gods (*viśve devāḥ*), sing that *sāman* by which you generated—for the sake of Indra—that god (*devam*), whose nature is to shine (*devanśīlam*), the wakeful (*jāgṛvim*), whose nature is to keep watch over all, the light (*jyotiḥ*) in the sun. Sing that *sāman*.
He blew away the curses; Indra became the slayer of the enemy with his thunderbolt.
O Marut host of mighty power, those gods have striven for your friendship, O Indra.

He blew away the curses; Indra, the slayer of the accusers, became manifest with his splendor, O gods. O Indra, the Marut-hosted one of great fame and great luster, they have striven for your friendship. *Ashastihā*: the slayer of those enemies who are devoid of hymns and praises. *Abhiśastīḥ*: [from the root] *śasu*, "to injure"; those who possess injury on all sides, or rather, the injuries inflicted by enemies. *Apādhamat*: he blew them away completely; the meaning is "drive them out. 2. He blew away the curses; Indra, the slayer of the accusers, became manifest with his splendor, O gods. O Indra, the Marut-hosted one of great fame and great luster, they have striven for your friendship. *Ashastihā*: the slayer of those enemies who are devoid of hymns and praises. *Abhiśastīḥ*: [from the root] *śasu*, "to injure"; those who possess injury on all sides, or rather, the injuries inflicted by enemies. *Apādhamat*: he blew them away completely; the meaning is "drive them out."
O Indra, these waters are our mothers because they are the cause of our birth. How is it that the waters possess motherhood?
From such scriptural passages as, "From the limbs [of the primordial being] came the earth; from the earth, the plants" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
May such waters flow forth with speed—that is, with velocity—and spread out in various directions toward the earth.
If one asks how the waters go, he says:
"Slay Vṛtra"—strike and kill the enemy who obstructs the waters, the cloud.
Then, by the dispersal of the clouds, let the waters vanish;
and once again, may you conquer all that has come into being tomorrow.
In the first [laud], for the *niṣkevalya* [śastra], the *stotriya* verse is "O you of unprecedented power, you were born" (*yajāyathā apūrvya*).
And so it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Their *stotriyas* are 'yajāyathā apūrvya'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.5).
When you were born for the slaying of Vṛtra, O matchless Maghavan,
you then spread out the earth and propped up the sky.
When you were born, O matchless Maghavan, for the slaying of Vṛtra, then you spread out the earth and you propped up the sky. 5.

O matchless one, devoid of any predecessor other than yourself; O bountiful Indra, possessor of wealth that must be gathered, when you were born—that is, when you appeared for the slaying of Vṛtra, the demon—you then spread out the earth, which was previously unextended, making it famous and firm. Moreover, at that very same time, you propped up the sky with the intermediate region, holding it steady.
The word "unprecedented" (apūrva) is used to indicate the meaning that such valor as this is not possible for anyone other than you.
From that the sacrifice was born; from that the hymn and the joyful song;
from that thou art the overlord of all that is sacrificed and all that has life.
From that your sacrifice was born; from that the hymn and the joyful laughter; from that you are the overcomer of all, of whatever has been born and of whatever is yet to be born. 6.
O Indra, when you were born, at that very moment, the sacrifice—such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—was produced for your sake; it came into being for the purpose of drinking the Soma.
Moreover, at that time, there was a loud laugh (*haskṛti*); [the root] *has* means "to laugh."
The mantra known as *arka*—which causes laughter, is performed for the sake of affection, and indicates joy—also came into being.
Furthermore, at that time, whatever was born of the elements (*bhūtajātam*) and whatever was a living creature (*jantvam*) [was produced].
The suffix *tvan* is used here in the sense of the gerundive (*kṛtyārthe*).
Whatever is to be born—that entire universe—you are the conqueror of it all; you have overcome it by your own greatness.
You brought forth the raw milk from the raw cows; you caused the sun to ascend to heaven.
Like a cauldron heated by those sitting around it, we honor with our hymns that which is beloved by the lover of songs—vast and sublime.

Within the raw [cows], you brought forth the cooked; you made the sun ascend to heaven. Like the heat of the *gharma* vessel, heat it with well-fashioned hymns—a lofty song, acceptable to the lover of songs. 7.
O Indra, you have caused the cooked milk to flow within the raw cows and waters;
thus says the mantra: "Even within the raw ones, you placed the cooked" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.62.9).
Furthermore, you made Sūrya ascend in the sky, the world of light.
Formerly, the Asuras named Paṇis, having stolen the cows of the Aṅgirases, placed them on a certain mountain enveloped in darkness.

Then the Aṅgirases, having praised Indra, said to him, "Bring the cows back to us. Being thus addressed, Indra, seeing that the place where the cows were situated was shrouded in gloom, caused the Sun, the illuminator of all, to ascend there in the heavenly realm so that the cows might be seen.
You have established [him] there.
Regarding the rule “*cādilope vibhāṣā*,” the word “*yat*” is absent in the versions marked kha, gha, jña, tta, 1, 2, 3, na, śa, and ṭa of the preceding rule *airaya*.

There is no elision [of the accent]. Now follows the second half-verse, composed in the indirect mode (*parokṣakṛta*). O singers, with *suvṛktibhiḥ*—with beautiful hymns of praise—*tapata* Indra; sharpen him. The meaning is: "Exalt Indra with your praises. Therein lies an illustration: *gharmaṃ na*. Just as they heat the *gharma*, the glowing Pravargya vessel, with *sāman*—"the third case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*"—just as they heat it with Sāmans, so too [exalt Indra]. Then, for *girvaṇase*—for Indra, who is to be praised with songs—sing the *bṛhat* Sāman, which is *juṣṭam*, pleasing or sufficient. 12.
‘Ā no viśvāsu’ is the tenth hymn, consisting of six verses. Nṛmedha and Purumedha are the seers. The verses with an odd number of syllables are Bṛhatīs, and those with an even number are Satobṛhatīs.
Indra is the deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “ā no viśvāsu ṣaṭ.
This hymn is used in the Niṣkevalya Śastra of the Mahāvrata, within the eighty verses in the Bṛhatī meter.
For it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "O Indra, those enjoyments which are to be invoked by us in all [circumstances], bring them hither" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.4).
May Indra, who is to be invoked in all battles, be present for us;
may the slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme victor worthy of praise, attend our prayers and our libations.
May Indra, who is to be invoked in all battles, be present for us; may the slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme victor, equal to the hymns, attend our prayers and the libations. 1.
The Ṛṣi hopes that Indra himself will act thus:

"May such an Indra—one who is to be invoked (*havya*) by all the gods in all battles (*samatsu*), that is, in conflicts with the Asuras, for the sake of protecting the immortals—attend (*upa ā bhūṣatu*) to our prayers (*brahmāṇi*), whether they be hymns of praise or oblations; may he experience them.
The meaning is: "May he serve [them]."
Or rather:
let him adorn these;
by his arrival, the hymns or the oblations become adorned.
Likewise, may he grace the three libations, beginning with the morning libation (prātaḥsavana).
Of what nature is Indra?
He is the slayer of Vṛtra—the Asura or evil—and the supreme archer.
He is so described because his bowstring (*maurvī*) is supremely indestructible for the purpose of slaying enemies in battles;
or alternatively,
he is *paramajyāḥ* because he destroys (*jyā* = *hinasti*) those who are supreme (*paramān*) by their strength (*balena*).
"Ṛcīṣamaḥ" means equal to praise; he is to be brought face-to-face by hymns.
May Indra, being such as this, adorn the songs of praise.
You are the foremost giver of riches; you are the true one who acts as a sovereign lord.
We choose the alliance of the son of great power, possessed of abundant glory.
You are the first giver of riches; you are the true one who acts as a lord. We choose for ourselves the alliance of the son of great power, who possesses abundant splendor. 2.
O Indra, you are the first, the foremost of all; you are the giver of riches (*rādhas*), that is, of wealth (*dhana*).
Or rather, among the givers of wealth, you are the first, the very first.
Likewise, O Īśānakṛt, you who make your worshippers lords (*īśānān*)—that is, endowed with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—you are *satya*, one whose actions are true;
the meaning is that you are one whose deeds correspond to reality.

Since this is so, we therefore choose for ourselves—that is, we partake of—the great riches suitable for union with the son of *tuvidyumna*, who possesses abundant wealth or abundant grain, and whose strength (*śavas*) has arisen as the cause of power for the sake of slaying enemies; for he is indeed *mahaḥ*, the Great One. Thus we seek those appropriate treasures.
O Indra, lover of songs, these unsurpassed hymns are being fashioned for you by Brahmā;
O Lord of bay horses, enjoy them, O Indra, for we have yoked those which are great for you in our devotion.
1. *a-bṛhat* means "not great. 2. *kha-ta-sama*. ... there is no *bṛhat*. 3. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa-āgareti*. 4. *kha-ta-na-bha-śa-īśān*.

O Indra, lover of songs, these hymns of praise (*brahmāṇi*) are being fashioned for you—wonders that cannot be surpassed. O Lord of the tawny steeds (*harivaśva*), accept these prayers (*yojanāni*). O Indra, those which we have meditated upon for you, take pleasure in them. 3.

O Indra, lover of hymns, worthy of praise through songs, your virtues are "un-surpassed" (anatidbhuta); that is to say, they do not cease even when all [other things] have been surpassed, for they pervade the qualities of Indra.
The meaning is that they are consistent with reality.

O Indra, O Lord of bay horses (haryaśva), those hymns which are such Brahmanic praises are being performed by us for your sake; O you who are well-yoked, take pleasure in and enjoy these very hymns. Furthermore, O Indra, all those hymns which we have meditated upon and uttered for your sake—enjoy them all.
For you, O Maghavan, are true and infinite; you have struck down many Vṛtras.
Therefore, O most powerful one, wielder of the thunderbolt, bestow upon the donor wealth consisting of swift horses.
For you, O Maghavan, are true and infinite; you subdue many Vṛtras. Therefore, O most powerful one, wielder of the thunderbolt, bestow upon the donor wealth consisting of swift horses. 4.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, you alone are the true one whose deeds are true; being infinite and unsubdued by anyone, you subdue—meaning you humble and bring low—the many, very many *vṛtras* and *rakṣases*. The particle *hi* is used here for emphasis.
O most powerful one, increased by strength, O wielder of the thunderbolt—
he who has the thunderbolt (*vajra*) in his hand is so described—

O Indra, such as you are, bestow wealth, cattle, and other riches upon the donor, the sacrificer who has offered oblations to you; make that wealth come toward him, turning it hitherward so that it approaches him from all sides.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), in the *śastra* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the *pragātha* "O Indra, you are glorious" (*tvam indra yaśā asi*) is an optional *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, you are glorious; O Indra, bring us the season" (*tvam indra yaśā asi indra kratuṃ na ā bhara*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
O Indra, you are glorious, the drinker of the *ṛjīṣa*, Lord of Might;
you alone, O sustainer of the people, slay the irresistible Vṛtras that have never been overcome before.
O Indra, you are glorious; you are the drinker of the dregs, O Lord of Strength. You alone, the upholder of the people, slay the irresistible Vṛtras that have never been overcome. 5.
O Lord of Might, O Protector of strength, O Indra, you are the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*.
The *ṛjīṣa* is the Soma that has been pressed out, purified, and set aside;
you are possessed of that, and thus you are glorious and renowned.
How does he possess such renown? To this he says:

*apratīni*—unassailable by the powerful, and for that very reason *anuttāni*, unvanquished by others; *vṛtrāṇi*, the demons (rakṣas), you alone (*eka it*), being indeed without companion, *carṣaṇīdhṛtā*—by means of the thunderbolt (*vajra*) which supports men (*manuṣyāṇām dhārakeṇa*) through the slaying of the Asuras—you strike (*haṃsi*), you deal blows.
For this very reason, he possesses such renown.
We now entreat you, O wise Asura, for that gift as if for our share;
like a great deed, O Indra, let your protection be ours, and may your favors reach us.
1. The application of *kha* with *sam*; the application of *jha* with *samyak*; the application of *ta1-2-3-4-sa* with *sa*; the application of *śa* with *sasya*.
2. We pronounce *kha-gha-ta-bha-va*; we pronounce *ga-va*; we pronounce *śa-va*. 3. *Gha*: *vṛtrā vṛtrāṇi*.
4. gha becomes the most increased. 5. kha, ta, bha, and śa go [to their respective substitutes].
6. kha, jha, ta¹, ta², bha, and sa become asi (asi).
To you, O Asura, who are truly wise, we now come for a portion of bounty as if for our own share; like a great, protective work of art, O Indra, may your favors come to us, O possessor of horses. 6.

O Asura, O powerful and vital one, O Indra, we now truly entreat you— him who possesses the aforementioned qualities, the wise one of exalted knowledge— to grant us wealth that is the means for achieving dharma and other goals, even as a father nourishes his son. We pray to you alone.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like a portion.
Just as someone might request wealth that has become the father's share, in that same way, Indra bestows wealth upon the sacrificers and the chanters of praise.
Therefore, we, the sacrificers, beg for wealth that has become our share.
O Indra, it is like a great *kṛti*;
*kṛti* means either a portion or food.
The root *kṛt* means "to cut. The suffix *ktin* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus, [the word] means "that by which one cuts."
Such a "kṛti" (creation/abode) of yours, O Indra, exists as a vast "śaraṇā" (shelter/home) in the atmosphere, in the heavenly world.

Regarding this, Yāska says: "Kṛti is either that which cuts or food; it is like a great creation, a shelter for you, O Indra; it is a very great shelter for you, O Indra, in the atmosphere, like a kṛti" (Nirukta 5.22).
Furthermore, may your own "sumnā" (blessings)—the joys pertaining to sons and other objects—thoroughly "pra abhavan" (come forth and pervade) us.
The augment *ḍa* is applied after the root *abhīta*.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "kanyā vāḥ," belongs to Puṣyapālā, the daughter of Atri;
she praised Indra with this hymn for the sake of removing a skin disease.
Therefore, she herself is the seer (ṛṣi).
The first two verses are *paṅkti*s; the remaining five are *anuṣṭubh*s.
Indra is the deity.
Thus it has been enumerated: “*Kanyā vāḥ sasātreyyapāla*: a historical narrative concerning Indra, in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, beginning with two *paṅkti*s.”
The application [of the mantra] is indicated by its characteristic marks.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:

Formerly, it is said, the daughter of Atri named Apālā, a knower of Brahman, became afflicted with a skin disease for some reason; being truly unfortunate, she was abandoned by her husband and performed penance directed toward Indra for a long time in her father’s hermitage in order to remove her skin disease.
Once, thinking, "The Soma is dear to Indra; I shall give it to him," she went to the riverbank.
Having bathed there, she obtained some Soma on the way back. Taking it with her as she was returning home, she consumed it right there on the path.
At the time of carving, Indra, thinking that the sound produced by the rubbing of the teeth was the sound of the *prāṇas* pressing the *soma*, arrived at that very moment.
Having arrived, he said to her:
"What are the pressing-stones pressing here?"
She replied:

"A maiden comes here for the sake of bathing; having seen the *soma*, she consumes it. The sound produced at that moment is like the sound of a carpenter's axe, not the sound of the *soma* being pressed.
Having been thus answered, Indra turned away.
As Indra was departing, she spoke to him again:
"Why do you turn back? You are going from house to house for the sake of drinking Soma.
Now, drink here as well the Soma pressed by my two fangs, and eat the parched grains and other offerings."
Being disregarded by Indra, she spoke again:

"I did not know that you, O Indra, had arrived here; had I known you had come to my house, I would have shown you great honor. Having thus addressed Indra, and having ascertained that it was indeed Indra who had arrived there and no one else, she said to the Soma placed in her own stomach:
"O Soma, for the sake of Indra who has arrived, first trickle slowly, and then quickly."
Then Indra, having desired her, drank the Soma that had been pressed with his teeth right from her mouth.
When Indra had thus drunk the Soma, Apālā—having been abandoned by her husband due to a burning skin disease—now spoke to Indra upon being united with him:
"What do you desire? I shall do that. Being thus addressed, she chose a boon.

When she was told, "Make my father's head hairless; make his other field devoid of fruit and the like; and make even my private parts hairless—yet make these [other things] possessed of hair and fruit," she removed the baldness from her father’s head and made the field possessed of fruit and the like. To avoid the defect of her own skin, she drew this [skin] three times through the hole in her own chariot and the hole in the yoke of the cart.
Her first discarded skin became a porcupine (*śalyaka*), the second a monitor lizard (*godhā*), and the third a chameleon (*kṛkalāsa*).
Thereupon Indra made even that Apālā resemble the sun; such is the traditional narrative (itihāsikī kathā).
And this has been clearly stated in the Śāṅkhāyana Brāhmaṇa. That Brāhmaṇa will be shown at the appropriate time during the explanation of those respective [passages].
This meaning is set forth in such Ṛgvedic verses as "kanyā vāḥ" and others.

1. [The reading] *ga* has the aforementioned quality (*guṇa*). 2. In *ta*, *bha₁*, and *bha₂*, it is *sapracetasam*; in *śa*, it is *pracetasaṃ*. 3. In *kha*, *ta₁*, *ta₂*, *ta₃*, *ta₄*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa*, it is *dānaṃ*; in *jha* and *bha₁*, it is *dhanaṃ dānaṃ*. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, and *śa*, it is *kṛtaṃ kṛtyāneti*; in *śa*, it is *kṛte kṛtatyaneti*. 5. In *jha*, it is *kṛttireveti*. 6. In *kha*, *ta*, and *śa*, it is *pratyāgamayat*; in *bha₁* and *bha₂*, it is *pratyagamayat*. 7. In *jha*, it is *°dhvaniriti*. 8. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa*, it is *svāmindramiti*. 9. In *ga*, it is *indraḥ somam*. 10. In *ga*, *ta*, and *bha*, it is *°śiraḥsthitāṃ*. 11. In *bha₁*, *bha₂*, and *ya*, it is *eṣo'rthaḥ krameṇa*.
The hunchbacked woman, moving with a low murmur, has pressed the Soma;
she brings it to its place and says: "I shall press you for Indra; I shall press you for Śakra."
The maiden, descending, has found the pressed Soma; bringing it home, she said: "I shall press you for Indra; I shall press you for Śakra. 1.

A maiden named Apālā, going toward the water (*vāḥ*) for the purpose of bathing, found and obtained Soma on the path— [the root] *vid* meaning "to obtain. Carrying that Soma, which was in the form of a creeper, back toward her home, she spoke to the Soma.
"O Soma, I shall press you for Indra; indeed, with my own teeth, I shall crush you.
Again, "O Soma, I shall press you for Śakra—the capable Indra—I shall perform the pressing this very moment.
At the time of consuming the Soma, thinking that the sound of his teeth was the sound of the pressing-stones, he attained the state of Indra.

This matter is clearly stated in the Śāṭyāyanabrāhmaṇa: "While she was descending to the bathing place (tīrtha), she found a shoot of Soma and ate it; his teeth became like pressing-stones (grāvan). Indra rushed toward her, thinking, 'The pressing-stones are surely speaking. She addressed him: 'A maiden, coming down to the water, has found and eaten the pressed Soma; therefore these [teeth] of hers speak like pressing-stones. Having understood this, Indra turned away."
He said to him, "O Vīraka, you who are going there," and so forth.
O you who come as a hero, searching from house to house—
drink this pressed juice of Jambha, accompanied by parched grain, by groats, by cakes, and offered with hymns of praise.
He who, O Vīraka, goes from house to house looking about—drink this pressed juice of Jambha, accompanied by parched grains, by groats, by cakes, and by hymns of praise. 2.
She said to Śakra:
"O Indra, Vīraka is a hero; you are capable, you who have been reflecting thus.
[The root] *kāṣ* means 'to shine' (*dīptau*)."

The form *yalluki* occurs in the *śatari* suffix. Due to Vedic usage, there is the shortening of the vowel of the root. Being thus shining for this purpose, you go—you proceed—to every house, that is, toward the house of the sacrificer, for the drinking of Soma.
Therefore, you too drink this Soma, pressed by my teeth, which is the son of Jambha. Of what kind?
Containing parched grains (dhānāvantam).
*Dhānāḥ* are parched barley grains.

"Drink this very Soma here"—meaning [Soma] which has *karambha* (barley meal) at its end, which has *saktu* (flour) at its end, which has *apūpa* (cakes) and is accompanied by *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cakes), and which is *ukthin*, being joined with hymns (*stotra*) and so forth.
The meaning is that she offered the *dhānā* and other items along with the Soma and performed the hymn of praise.
We do not even consider thee as one who harms, nor do we treat thee with hostility;
O Indu, flow softly, very gently around us, O Indra.
We cannot discern you at all; we do not even perceive you. Flow slowly, very gently, O Indu, for Indra. 3.
Again she said, disregarding him:
"O Indra!"—here *cana* is a combination of particles used for emphasis.
We simply wish to know (*ā cikitsāmaḥ*) you, that is, we desire to understand you.

"Even here on this very path, we do not recognize you who have come; we do not perceive you. Here too, the particle *cana* functions as an emphatic; the meaning is: 'We do not even know that you, who are coming to my house, are Indra.'"

1. The word *asā* does not exist in the versions *kha*, *ta*, and *śa*. 2. In *ta*, *bha₁*, and *bha₂*, it means "booty" (*vāja*) or "wealth" (*dhana*); in *bha₃*, it means "produced by the teeth" (*daṃtairjātam*); in *śa*, it means "while the teeth are being struck" (*daṃtavādyamāne*). 3. In *ga*, it means "the sound of the pressing-stones" (*grāvadhvaniḥ*). 4. In *bha*, it is "or indeed" (*ha vā*). 5. In *kha*, *ta*, and *bha₁*, it is *udhuḥ*; in *bha₂*, *ūdhaḥ*; in *bha₃*, *ūrdhvaḥ*; in *śa*, *ucuḥ*. 6. In *kha*, *ta*, *bha₁*, and *bha₂*, it is *śrutāvidaṃ*.
[Maṇḍala 8, Anuvāka 9, Sūkta 91] End of the Sixth Aṣṭaka, 905. Having spoken thus to Indra, Pālā addresses the Soma that remains in its own place.
O Soma, flow slowly, very gently, for this Indra who has come; flow for his sake first slowly, then more slowly—using *akac* in the sense of censure:
"slowly in a censurable manner," that is, very slowly.
The meaning is "quickly. It means:
"O Soma, being purified by my teeth, flow forth quickly all around.

Similarly, in the sacrifices as well, the Soma, being purified by the woollen filters (*prāvabhiḥ*), first flows around slowly, and then more slowly yet quickly; it is with this intention that it was said.
Then Indra, having heard these words, at that very moment took the Soma thus pressed from the mouth of Apālā herself, who was the site of the sacrifice.
The meaning of what was said is clearly stated in the Śāṭyāyanaka Brāhmaṇa: “Disregarding him, she said: ‘We do not even care for you; we do not even consider you as anything.’”

"In the past, all the guardians of the sacrificial formulas thought, 'He praises me,' and they turned toward him slowly, as it were, very slowly, [saying], 'O Indu, flow around for Indra! Verily, he extracted Soma from his mouth; indeed, one obtains the drinking of Soma here who, knowing this, smells the milk. Thus it is said.
Will he not remove our distress? Will he not do what is beneficial for us? Will he not grant us wealth?
Shall we, as those who go toward their enemies, find union with Indra?
Will he not? Will he not act? Will he not make us more prosperous? Will we not, as those who have been hated by their husbands, come together with Indra? 4.
"Indra has drunk the Soma; may he make us thus," he says.
May that Indra *kvavit*—many times over—*śakat*—make us *śaktān*, capable and competent. Furthermore, may he *kvivit*—abundantly—*karat*, do for us.
Furthermore, may that Indra indeed make us—us here—many times over more prosperous, more wealthy, and exceedingly rich.
[The suffix] *leṭ* is added to the roots *kṛ* (to do) and *śak* (to be able).
Now he says, "I shall do this for Ātreya."

"Previously, indeed, we were much hated by our husbands who were protectors and lords; for many times we were disliked by them, and therefore, being separated from our husbands and not pursued by anyone, we now, together with Indra, shall meet (*saṃgamāmahai*)—that is, we shall come together. The plural number is used everywhere for honor.
By the word 'meeting' (*saṃgama*), it is indicated that Indra desired Apālā."
O Indra, cause these three levels to sprout anew:
his head, this fertile field, and that which is here beneath my belly.
These three worlds—O Indra, cause them to sprout! But let his head be upon this fertile field, and let this [other part] of mine be upon his belly. 5.
When Indra said, "What do you desire? I shall grant it to you," she requested this boon:
"O Indra, these three worlds (viṣṭapāni) exist;
produce (vi sṛja) rice (vrīhayaḥ) in those three places."
What are they?
My father’s head was hairless;
that is to say, it was bald.
And remove that; the meaning is: make it hairy.
Make its upper field, the *vurvarā*, rich in all kinds of crops.
Immediately thereafter, in my own belly— meaning in that place near the belly,
which is a cave— and which, due to the fault of its own nature, has not yet produced heat; [therein...]
Furthermore, by avoiding its own defects, make it hairy.
These are the three places. This matter is explained in detail in the Śāṭyāyanaka: "He said to her, 'O Apālā, what do you desire?'"

She said: "These three worlds," [meaning] his father was bald; he made him non-bald. "The fertile soil" was not born for him; he was indeed born. "In his lap there were no hairs"; they were indeed born. These are the subsequent verses for further explanation: "And she who is ours... and so forth.
1. bha-°mevābhi° | 2. kha-ta-anādriyamāṇe; ga-anādriyamāṇe ca; śa-anādriyamāṇe | 3. kha- tara-karotu tadāhama; jha-bhara-śa-karotu tadāha sa; ta1-tvadāhama |
4. *Bha* is in the navel and the belly.

And that field of ours, and this body of mine, and also that head of my father—make all these hairy. He explains the very meaning already stated by this [verse]: "That field of ours"—this nearby cultivated land—"and immediately after that, this body of mine"—this household site pointed out by you—"and also, moreover, that head of my father" which is hairless—make all these three places hairy. O Śatakratu, through the hole of the chariot, the hole of the cart, and the hole of the yoke, O Indra, having thrice cleansed Apālā, you made her sun-skinned. By this [verse], he says that he made Apālā possess a radiance like the sun: "O Śatakratu"—O performer of a hundred sacrifices, or O one of manifold wisdom—"O Indra, through the hole of your own chariot," in its wider opening; "through the hole of the cart," in its smaller opening compared to that; and "through the hole of the yoke," in its even smaller, subtle opening—in the openings of the chariot, cart, and yoke, for the removal of your own defects, "having thrice cleansed" Apālā by drawing her through them, "you made her sun-skinned," i.e., you made her a possessor of a most beautiful form. This is clearly stated in the Śāṭhyāyana Brāhmaṇa: "She was in the hole of the chariot, then she became a large lizard; she was in the hole of the cart, then she became a large tortoise; regarding this it is recited: 'Through the hole of the chariot, through the hole of the cart. Whatever was the most beautiful of her forms, that form she possessed. Thus, the drawing through the axle and other parts was for the removal of her own defects. This hymn is praised because if one who is defiled by his own defects recites it, Indra removes those defects and makes him possess a splendor like the sun. The thirty-third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with *pāntamā vaḥ*, belongs to Śrutakakṣa or Sukakṣa of the lineage of Aṅgiras; it is addressed to Indra. The first verse is an Anuṣṭubh, the rest are Gāyatrīs. It is thus enumerated: "Pāntam, thirty-three verses; Śrutakakṣa or Sukakṣa; the first is an Anuṣṭubh. In the Mahāvrata, during the Gāyatra-ṛcāśīti, this hymn and the following one are used, excluding the first verse. It is sūtrated in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: "'Puruhūta puruhūtam' is the fault" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.3). In the first night-watch, the first two triplets of the Hotṛ’s recitation are the Stotriya and Anurūpa. It is sūtrated: "'Pāntamā vo andhaso', 'Apādu śipyandhasaḥ'" (Āśva. Śrau. 6.4). Drink of your soma-juice; sing forth unto Indra, the all-conquering, the lord of a hundred powers, the most generous among men. O priests, "drink of your soma-juice"—that which is characterized by the food called Soma—"sing forth unto Indra," who drinks facing toward you. [The root] *pā* means "to drink"; the *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage. "All rules are optional in the Veda. [Note: 1. Ja reads *asau ca yāsā*; 2. Gha reads *tā tānīmāni*; 3. Kha-Ta reads *mabhihitaḥ*; Bhā reads *mabhitā*; 4. Ga reads *yugādi*; 5. Ta-Bhā-1-2-Vikalpyante.]
In the phrase "lokābhyaya," there is no application of the prohibition against the genitive case.
Consequently, in the word "andhasaḥ," the genitive is applied according to the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ... [Pāṇini 2.3.65].
Sing forth with excellence for that Indra, who drinks the soma facing toward him, and who is thus characterized.
Of what sort?

One who is "all-conquering," a subduer of all enemies or of all classes of beings; for that very reason, one of "a hundred powers" (śatakratu), possessing manifold wisdom or manifold deeds; and the most generous (maṃhiṣṭha) among the "showers" (varṣaṇīnām)—that is, the greatest bestower of wealth upon men.
Or alternatively:
The syntactical connection is: "Sing of Indra, who is to be worshipped by the sacrificers as the one to be sacrificed to."
Call him Puruhūta, Puruṣṭuta, Gāthānya, and Sanaśruta; say, "He is Indra. 2. Call him Puruhūta, Puruṣṭuta, Gāthānya, and Sanaśruta; say, "He is Indra. 2.

O officiating priests and sacrificers, you should address that god as "Indra"—him who is invoked by many at sacrifices (*puruhūta*), praised by many through hymns, recitations, and other liturgical forms (*puruṣṭuta*), for that very reason worthy of song (*gāthānya*) and fit to be sung, and renowned from of old as eternal (*sanaśruta*).

[The verb *bravītana* is derived from the root *brūñ* (to speak clearly) in the imperative; by metrical substitution, the ending *-dhvam* is replaced by *-tanap*, and thus the *guṇa* strengthening occurs.]

Indra alone is the giver of great spoils, the dancer of men; as the Great One, he has brought us toward nourishment. 3. Indra alone is the giver of great spoils for us, the dancer; as the Great One, he has brought us toward nourishment. 3.

Indra—indeed, Indra alone, characterized by the previously mentioned attributes—be the giver to us (*naḥ*) of great (*mahānām*) *vājān* (foods), or rather, of great *maghān* (wealthes)—here there is a transposition of letters—or of *vājān* (strengths) or *ajñān* (knowledges). Of what nature is he? *Nṛtuḥ*: the suffix *kū* is applied according to *Uṇādi-sūtra* 1.91 (*nṛtṛśṛbhyoḥ kūḥ*); the short vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). He is the one who causes all to dance. Or alternatively: from the root *nṛ* (to lead), the suffix *tu* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules; the shortening of the root vowel is Vedic. He is the leader of cattle and other things for his worshippers. Therefore, that great Indra, *abhiṣnu*—meaning "approaching our knees"—*ā yamata*: may he restrain [us], may he bestow, may he give. Or rather: may that Indra, coming toward us (*abhiṣṭvat*), take hold of wealth in his own hands and win it for us. The meaning is: having taken the wealth, may he give it to us.

The helmeted Indra drank from the soma-juice—of the well-skilled, the effusing drop—mixed with barley. 4. He drank. Om. The helmeted one. Of the juice. Of the very skillful. Of the effusing. Of the drop. Indra. Mixed with barley. 4.
Śiprī: *śipre* refers to the jaws or the nostrils;
thus, one who has beautiful jaws.
Or alternatively:
*śiprāḥ* refers to those on the head;
[they are] those with beautiful heads.

That Indra [is the one] for *prahoṣiṇaḥ*, those who intensely offer oblations (*havis*) to the gods; [he is the one] for the *yavāśiras* belonging to the seer named Sudakṣas. [The word *yavāśiras* is derived from the root] *śrī* (meaning "to cook") preceded by the prefix *ā*; according to the rule "apaspṛṣedhāmānucuḥ" etc., there is the substitution of *śiras* for the verbal root.
The Soma, characterized as food, mixed with barley and cooked together with barley, flowed from all sides into the vessels;
he drank it— that is, he consumed it— or rather, he drank the portion of this Soma set aside for Indra, a part of the Soma juice.
The particle *u* is used for emphasis.
Sing forth to him, to Indra, for the drinking of the Soma; for that indeed is his strengthener. To him—Om!—sing forth, to Indra, for the drinking of the Soma; for that indeed is his strengthener.

1. [The reading] "kha-ta-na-mara-1-śa-ṣaṣṭhyāḥ" is found; [the reading] "bha1-ṣaṣṭhyā" is found. 2. In manuscript Ga, "kha-ga-ta-bha-śa" does not contain the word "vājānām. 3. In manuscript Ga, [the root] "nṛṇāteḥ" is found.
4. *kha-ta2-1-4bha1-2-śa* reads "somaṃ samapibat"; *ga* reads "somāṃśipabat"; *jha-ta1* reads "somaṃ sāma pibat"; *bha3* reads "somaṃ saṃpibat".
O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), praise—that is, extol with excellence—that very Indra, facing him directly.
For what purpose?

"For the drinking of Soma" means for the purpose of Indra's drinking the Soma here. To specify for what purpose he drinks the Soma, he says: "That very drinking of Soma is indeed his (*indrasya*) *vardhanaṃ*, that is, the cause of his growth."
Therefore, sing forth praises for the sake of joy born from drinking the Soma.
Having drunk of these intoxications, the god, by the power of the god,
has surpassed all worlds.
Having drunk of these exhilarations, the god, by the power of the god, has surpassed all worlds. 6.

By the power and strength born from drinking Soma—of that Soma which is resplendent among the celestial vessels (*devagraha*), or which is playful as a god (*devaśīla*), or which is desired by the gods—he has overcome all beings, that is, all created things.

As in such passages as "In the intoxication of Soma, Indra performed those [deeds]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.15.2), where it is said that he performed all deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra during the intoxication of drinking Soma, so here too it means that he performed all deeds such as the overcoming of all beings.
In the first sequence, in the Hotṛ’s Śastra, the remainder of the hymn beginning with “*atyamu vaḥ satrāsāham*” is used.
This is stated in the Sūtra: “The remainder of the hymn ‘*atyamu vaḥ satrāsāham*’, [and] ‘*abhi tyaṃ meṣam*’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
In the *atiriktoktha* of the Acchāvāka when there is no hymn dedicated to Sūrya, the triplet beginning with “*atyamu vaḥ satrāsāham*” is the optional *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘tyamu vaḥ satrāsāham’ and ‘satrā te anu kṛtye’ are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.11).
On the fourth day of the ten-night *daśarātra* sacrifice when the ritual order is expanded (*vyūḍha*), this very triplet is to be inserted as the *nivid*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'imaṃ nu māthinaṃ huve' and 'tyamu vaḥ satrāsāham'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
Bring hither for our protection that ever-conquering one of yours, who is extended across all songs.
Him, O you [gods], with the syllable "Om"—the ever-conquering one, who has come to all our songs—do you summon hither for our protection. 7.

The sacrificer, addressing the singer, says: O singer, Satrāsāham! The word *satrā* signifies "many"; thus, [Satrāsāham] means "the overcomer of many," or alternatively, "the conqueror of enemies by uniting with his own strength. Among all your songs (*viśvāsu gīrṣu*), that is, in all hymns of praise, he is extended—that is, Indra alone is praised everywhere. Therefore, toward him who is spread throughout them—*tyam* (that one)—the particle *u* being used for emphasis—toward that very Indra, you cause him to move (*ā cyāvayasi*) for our protection (*ūtaye*). [The root] *cyuṅ* [in *cyāvayasi*] means "to go. By means of your hymns, cause him to come forward toward the sacrifice.
The one who is ever-youthful, the warrior, the drinker of soma, the unshakable,
the hero of irresistible will.
The warrior, the most peaceful, the peerless, the drinker of Soma, the unshakable hero whose will is irresistible. 8.

"Bring Indra, who is endowed with such qualities," he says. [Indra is] a fighter (*yudh*), one who strikes down enemies; for that very reason, he is *anarvāṇam*, one who has approached unassailable by others, and therefore *anapacyutam*, not driven away in battles, being unharmed by enemies. He is a drinker of Soma (*somapā*), a protector of Soma; while in the exhilaration (*made*) of this Soma, he possesses *avāryakratum*, irresistible power of action. He is a *nara*, a leader of all. "Bring Indra, who is endowed with such qualities"—this is the connection with what precedes.
O Indra, you who are most wise and worthy of praise, bestow upon us training for wealth; like a steed, lead us toward the prize that protects us.
1. *gha*-vardhana indeed. 2. Not of that which is beautiful (*na-śobhanasya*). 3. *kha-tan-bha1-2-śa*-samprasārakaṃ; *gha*-saṃpratārakaṃ. 4. *jha-ta1-2-3-śa-’rabhivāraṇīya*.
Śikṣā. To us, O Indra, [grant] riches; much, O wise one, O equal to the hymns (*ṛcīṣama*), [grant] to us for the decisive battle, O arbiter of wealth. 9.

O *ṛcīṣama*—equal to praise; or alternatively, from the root *īṣ* (in the sense of "going," "injuring," or "seeing"), with the suffix *am*, meaning "to be gone to by all" or "to be seen by all. O Indra, endowed with the aforementioned qualities, you who are wise (*vidvān*) and possess knowledge of all objects, having brought wealth (*rāyaḥ*) from the enemies, bestow (*śikṣa*) it upon us many times (*puru*). Or rather, *puru* is an adjective qualifying *rāyaḥ*: grant us abundant riches. Furthermore, regarding *pāryai*: *pārāḥ* refers to enemies. In that regard, protect (*ava*) us in the wealth situated there—that is, when the enemy's wealth is sought to be seized. The meaning is: slay the enemies and sustain us with their wealth.
Therefore, O Indra, come to us with food that brings a hundredfold strength, with food that brings a thousandfold strength.
Therefore, O Indra, come hither to us with food that brings a hundredfold strength, with food that brings a thousandfold strength. 10.

O Indra, from this very place—whether from that world of heaven or from this station of the enemy—come toward us, approaching us with full presence. Come endowed with *iṣ*, that is, the essence of food, which possesses a hundredfold strength (*śatavājā*) and a thousandfold strength (*sahasravājā*); for *vāja* means food, and thus you come joined with the nourishment of food known as great power.
O Śakra, wielder of the thunderbolt, may we, through our inspired thoughts and swift steeds, conquer the noble ones in battles for the sake of cattle.
O Śakra, wielder of the thunderbolt, finder of cattle, may we, through our inspired thoughts and with our prayers, conquer in battles those who attack the noble ones. 11.

O Śakra, lord of the capable, possessor of wisdom! By the rule "chandasīraḥ," the suffix *matup* is replaced by *vat*. We, possessing actions (*karmavantaḥ*) through performance of rites, go toward—*ayāma*, that is, we proceed toward—the *dhiyaḥ*, meaning actions for the sake of battle and sacrifice.
Then, regarding *godara*:
[the root] *dṛ* is used in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*). The suffix *i* is applied according to the rule *aca haḥ*.
O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), O possessor of the *vajra*, you who rend the mountains and the cattle;
or alternatively,
the *vajra* is that which moves or goes (*vajanam gamanam*).
The wielder of that [thunderbolt] is the *kuliśa*.
Like that, may we conquer in battles against the enemy with horses given by you—horses that go everywhere (*arbadbhiḥ*)—we shall be victorious through your gift.
O Śatakratu, we cause you to take delight in us, as cattle do in pastures, when you have risen up.
We—O you of a hundred powers!—make you take delight, as cows do in pastures, at our rising-up songs. 12.
O Śatakratu, O Indra of great wisdom and many deeds, we cause you alone to rejoice in every way—in the hymns, the recitations, and so forth;
for "u" is used here as a particle of emphasis. We cause you alone to take delight in these songs and liturgical formulas.
"Idanto masiḥ":
we invoke, we call out;
that is to say, we praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"not like cows.
Just as a cowherd causes the cows—the cattle—to graze (*ramayanti*) on all sides (*ā*) among the pastures (*yavaseṣu*), which are specific types of grass, so it is here.

Regarding the word *gāvaḥ*, because all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is an absence of the substitution of *ā* [for *au*] as prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.93 (*auto'm*).
For all our desires, O Śatakratu, have indeed been fulfilled through your mortal nature; we have come to you, O wielder of the thunderbolt, as those who have not sinned.
For we have indeed attained all our desires through our mortal nature, O Śatakratu, O wielder of the thunderbolt; come hither to us! 13.

1. From *ga*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* [the suffix] *ātṛ*; from *śa* [the suffix] *ātṛ*. 2. From *kha*, *jha*, *tara*, *na*, *bha*, and *āha*; from *ta*, *śa*, and *aha*. 3. In *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, and *śa*, "puru" is not present; in *gha*, it is "āpuḥ". 4. In *ga*, they are "parāḥ". 5. In *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *tara*, [it refers to] the clouds of the mountains. 6. In *kha*, *tara*, *bha*, and *śa*, [it is] "carayitahe"; in *jha*, *ta*, and *ya*, "varayitahe"; in *na*, "carayitahe"; in *bhara*, "darayitahe".
O Śatakratu, O Indra of great wisdom, [addressed as] "martyavanā", [which is] "martyavāni"; the case-ending is replaced by "ā" according to the rule "supāṃ suluk".
The absence of the augment *vṛddhi* occurs because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably obligatory.
For "all" (*viśvā*) means all mortal things indeed; "following desires" (*anukāmā*) means accompanied by desires—that is, possessed of longing.
The meaning is that human beings desire these things.
That being so, O Vajrin—O Indra who wields the thunderbolt—we too have attained (*aganma*), that is, we understand (*avagacchāma*), the *āśasaḥ*, the desires for wealth and other such things;
[this is expressed] by the root *gam* in the *leṭ* mood, with the elision of the suffix *śap* according to the rule "there is frequent elision in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
By the rule "svośca," the letter *m* becomes *n*.
In you, O son of strength, those who fulfill every desire have placed their hopes;
O Indra, no distress surpasses you.
O thou of good sons, O powerful one, they have turned toward thee; O Indra, no one surpasses thee in the fulfillment of desires. 14.
O son of Śavas, because you have arisen for the sake of strength, you are the Son of Strength, Indra. "Kāmakātyaḥ":
[the root] *kai*, *gai*, and *rai* mean "to sound.
Those for whom sounds (*kātyaḥ*) have desire (*kāma*) as their primary object are so described.
Such men, however, have turned well toward you; they conduct themselves properly for the sake of fulfilling their respective desires.
Therefore, it is logical that they possess mortal desires.
[The root] *vṛt* is used in the sense of "turning."

In the *laṅ* [tense], there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by virtue of the rule "the Vedic usage is manifold" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), and the augment *ruṭ* is added. Since this is so, therefore, O Indra, no deity whatsoever surpasses you.
There is no one more powerful or wealthy than he; there is no one capable [of surpassing him].
May he, the bull, come hither with his fierce and impetuous power;
do thou perceive us with thy far-reaching wisdom.
O Bull, with your most bountiful and terrible impulse, hastening with your swift thought, come and find us, you who are mindful of our city. 15.
O Indra, you who are the showerer of desires, O bull; you who possess the previously mentioned characteristics,

through *saniṣṭyā*— [the word] *paṇ* meaning "to give"— by being the most excellent giver of wealth and so forth, [a power] that is formidable and terrifying to rivals, and therefore *dravittvā*, that which must cause enemies to flee, that which must put them to flight.

The suffix *it* is added to the root *dravati*. With *puraṃdhyā*—that is, with the wisdom (*dhī*) that must sustain and nourish many, and with such an action (*karman*), protect us (*naḥ*) completely; that is, preserve us on all sides.
In the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *ava*, the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "there is frequent elision in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Due to the frequent occurrence [of this root], the augment *iṭ* is added to the suffix *sip*.
The meaning is that he protects us by means of the granting of wealth and so forth.
O Indra, O Lord of a hundred powers, that exhilaration of yours which is indeed most glorious—
by means of that exhilaration, do you now truly rejoice.
O Śatakratu, O Indra, that exhilaration of yours which is now most glorious—exhilarate yourself now with that very exhilaration. 16.
Here Soma is praised:
O Śatakratu, you of a hundredfold wisdom, O Indra, most glorious one—[that] intoxication (*mada*). It is called *mada* because by means of it one becomes intoxicated; that is, Soma.

O Soma, that which has now been pressed by us for your sake—both previously and at this moment—with that very Soma being offered by us, when the exhilaration (*mada*) produced by its drinking has arisen in you, do you now exhilarate us as well with the gift of wealth and other riches in that state of exhilaration.
[The root] *mad* means "to rejoice";
here it carries the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) implied within.
"I have received much," thus he cursed.
O Indra, that exhilaration of yours which possesses most wonderful renown, which is the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, and which bestows the most power— [that exhilaration we seek].
1. Those thirty-six [units] consisting of Kha, Ga, Ta-ra, Ma, Śa, and Śai.
2. In the Sṛṣṭaka system, there are four Gs, one Ta, and a gap (chidra) at the end; in the Sṛṣṭaka system, there is one Jha, two Ts, and a gap (chidra) at the end of Bha.
3. Kha, Ga, Ta, Bha-ra, and Śa constitute the Thousand-Sons (Sahasraputra); Bha-1 and Bha-3 are the Thousand-Sons.
4. After *gha*, *bha*, and *su*, [the augment *ṭu* is applied] excellently (*suṣṭhu*).

5. After *kha*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, and *la*, [the augment *ṭu* is applied] when followed by *liṭ*; after *jha*, when followed by *liṭ*; and after *bha*, when followed by *leṭ*. 6. [The augment *ṭu* is applied] to those [consonants] that are endowed with *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *sa*.
7. Kha-ta-na-bha-śa should be protected.
8. Na-bha is not like this.
9. Kha-ta-na-bha is intoxicated; śa is intoxicated.
O Indra, that exhilarating drink which is most renowned, which is the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, and which bestows strength—[that is yours]. 17.
O Indra, that most renowned Soma, possessing manifold fame, which has been pressed by us for your sake;
that Soma which is the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme destroyer of evils;
and furthermore, that Soma which is the bestower of strength, the unsurpassed giver of power.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "May you be exhilarated by this Soma being offered by us."
For that which has been bestowed upon you by the pressing-stone shines forth,
O Wondrous One, among all the peoples.
For that stone which has granted you [the Soma], O true one, drinker of Soma, you have indeed distributed it among all the peoples, O wondrous one. 18.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O wielder of the thunderbolt;
likewise, O truthful one, just as...

Let the drops enter into you, as rivers enter the ocean; O Indra, no one surpasses you. (22) O Indra, let the *indavas*—the flowing Soma juices being offered by us—enter into you (*tvā*); let them enter from all sides. In this regard, there is an illustration: "as rivers [enter] the ocean. Just as flowing rivers enter the ocean, that reservoir of water, from every direction, even so [let the drops enter you]. Since this is so, therefore, O Indra, no deity whatsoever surpasses (*ati ric*) you, whether in strength or in wealth. By implication, the meaning is that there is none superior to you in any respect.

O mighty bull, O watchful one, you have filled yourself with the greatness [of power] for the consumption of Soma, which is within your bellies, O Indra. 23. You have filled yourself; with greatness; O bull; the consumption; of Soma; O watchful one; which...

From afar, O wielder of the stone, let our songs reach you; may we come unto you sufficiently. (27) *parākāttāt*, *cit*, *adrivaḥ*, *tvām*, *nakṣanta*, *naḥ*, *giraḥ*, *aram*, *gamāma*, *te*, *vayam*. (27) O *adrivaḥ*—O wielder of the thunderbolt, O possessor of the discus—let our *giraḥ*, our praises issuing from here, reach (*nakṣanta*) you even from *parākāttāt*, that is, from an exceedingly great distance. How much more so when they are near! This is the form of the root *naś* (to reach) or *naś* (to attain) in the *leṭ* tense with the suffix *sip*. Such being the case, we, the praisers, may *gamāma*—that is, go to—your wealth (*te*), reaching it in full measure (*aram*) and abundance from you. In the hymns of desire during the third pressing, "evā hyasi vīrayuḥ" is the optional *stotriya* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. And likewise the *sumitra*: "evā hyasi vīrayurevā hyasya sūnṛtā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

For thus indeed you are one who desires heroes; thus indeed you are a hero and steadfast. Thus indeed is your mind to be propitiated. (28) For thus indeed you are one who desires heroes (*vīrayuḥ*)—that is, you truly desire to slay heroes capable in the work of battle. "For" (*hi*) indicates a well-known fact. Therefore, you are indeed a hero (*śūraḥ*), possessing prowess. Moreover (*uta*), you are steadfast (*sthiraḥ*)—meaning you possess courage in combat, striking at the enemies while remaining fixed in your place. This being so, your mind (*manaḥ*) is "to be propitiated" (*rādhyaṃ*), meaning it is to be honored with hymns of praise; for by means of this mind, you perform the slaying of enemies and exercise courage in battle. The sense is that your mind alone is to be praised by all.

Thus, O Indra of abundant wealth, your delight has been established by all the foundations; indeed, O Indra, be with me as well. (29) O *tuvimigha*—*tuvi* being a name for "much"—O Indra, possessor of great riches, your *ratiḥ* (delight), consisting of the gift of cattle, horses, wealth, and so forth, has been established (*dhāyi*) by all the *dhātubhiḥ* (foundations)—that is, by all the sacrificial foundations that support the ritual acts, or rather, by all the sacrificers who nourish the gods through the offering of oblations. This is the form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the *luṅ* tense, passive voice. The particle *cit* has the sense of emphasis (*eva*). Therefore, O Indra, such as you are, be *sacā* (with me); that is, be my companion in the performance of rites through the granting of wealth and other gifts.

O Lord of Strengths, do not indeed become like a weary Brahmin; O Lord of Victuals, rejoice in the pressed soma mixed with milk. He who is the Lord of Strengths (*vājānām pati*), whether that means the Lord of foods or the Lord of powers—O Indra, do not indeed become like a weary Brahmin (*brahmava tandrayuḥ*). Following the statement of Yāska, "Now it is also used in that sense" (*Nirukta* 6.31), the term *tandrayukta* is employed here. Alternatively, by abandoning rites such as sacrifice, you might possess the desire for sloth like a Brahmin; therefore, "do not indeed become so" (*mo ṣu bhuvaḥ*)—meaning, "do not be thus," but rather remain always engaged in our ritual acts. This is the prayer. Therefore, rejoice (*matsva*); be exhilarated and joyful by drinking the pressed soma, which is mixed with cow-products such as milk or curd.

O Indra, let not the malevolent intentions of the sun’s daughter reach us; with you as our ally, may we overcome that. 31. O Indra, let not the destructive designs of the daughter of the sun fall upon us; with you as our companion, may we win that [victory]. 31.

1. From *kha-ta-na-ma-śa-nasati* or *nasate*. 2. In the *ṣūkta*s [containing] *jha-ta-2-bha-1-3*. 3. Against the capable enemies (*kha-jha-ta-1-2-na-bha-samarthān śatrūn*). 4. In *kha-ga-gha-ta-na-ma-śa*, there is no *'ca'*. 5. With the *karmadhāraya*s of *kha-ga-gha-bha3*. O Indra, O commanders (*ādiśaḥ*), those who discharge weapons on all sides—[the root] *sṛ* meaning "to go"—those Rākṣasas whose nature is to roam everywhere, may they not come against us (*mā abhi ā yaman*) in the nights (*akuṣu*) nor even by day; may they not become our restrainers (*niyantāraḥ*).
If [the enemies] have come as they did, then with you as our ally and companion, we shall surely overcome—that is, destroy—that host of Rākṣasas.
For the roots *krath*, *krath*, and *kuth* are listed in the sense of "injury," and the root *van* is also taught there in that same sense.

With you as our ally, O Indra, let us answer back against our rivals; you are ours, and we are yours. taryā | it | indra | yujā | vayam | prati | bruvīmahi | spṛdhaḥ | tvam | asmākam | tarva | smasi || 32 || With you as our ally, O Indra, let us indeed speak back against our rivals; you are ours, and we are yours. || 32 ||

O Indra, with you— as *tvayā* here denotes restriction— meaning with you alone as our ally (*yujā*) and companion, may we speak against the rivals (*spṛdhaḥ*), that is, the contending enemies, and repel them.
The response is a refutation.
With the second half-verse, he establishes precisely Indra’s assistance:
"O Indra, you belong to us," meaning you belong to us because you are the one to be praised, the one who praises, and the one to be sacrificed to; "we belong to you" means we are yours.
Likewise, the *Āraṇyaka* says: "You are all this; we are yours; you belong to us.
Therefore, with you as our ally, let us slay the enemies.

For you alone, O Indra, do the singers who long for you, your friends, praise with their songs. (33) For you alone, O Indra, do the singers who long for you, your friends, praise with their songs. (33)

O Indra, immediately after the removal of obstacles to the ritual act, those who desire you (*tvāyavaḥ*)—desiring you for the sake of granting wealth and other boons—and for that very reason, they have praised you repeatedly (*anunotuvataḥ*).
This is a form of the root *nau* (to praise) in the intensive (*yaṅluk*) with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*).
Thus, performing praise again and again in succession, your friends (*sakhāyaḥ*), the poets (*kāravaḥ*) who are your companions, [praise] you.
The word *id* is used for emphasis.
Let them indeed attend upon you alone with hymns of praise;
the particle *hi* signifies well-known fact.
After the root *jvar*, the augment *ñi* is inserted;
due to its connection with *hi*, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
The thirteenth hymn, "Uddhva," consisting of twenty-four verses, is composed by Sukakṣa; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Indra.
However, the other [verses] have Indra-Bṛhaspati as their deity.
Thus it has been declared: "Uddhva consists of twenty-four [verses]; Sukakṣa [composed it], while the other verses are addressed to Indra-Bṛhaspati."
In the second sequence, the *śastra* for the Hotṛ priest is this hymn of Uttama Ārṣeṇya.
And it is stated in the aphorism: "One should extract the best [verse] from these" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.4).
Its application at the Mahāvrata rite has also been mentioned together with the preceding hymn.
In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the first triplet in the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* recitation is as follows:
the Sūtra states—"‘udgṛbhṇāmi’ [etc. are three verses; ‘indra kratuvidam sutam’ is the *yājyā*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.10).
Likewise, in the *maitrāvaruṇa-atirikta-uktha* at the *aso-yāma*, this triplet serves as the *anurūpa*.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Vṛtrahan, whatever today... with all [the hymns]... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11): "Up indeed, O Sūrya, you go toward the famous, the subduer, the bull who performs manly deeds, the archer. (1) *ut | gha | it | abhi | śruta'madham | vṛṣabham | naryā'apasam | astāram | eṣi | sūrya ||1||* "Up indeed, O Sūrya, you go toward the famous, the subduer, the bull who performs manly deeds, the archer. (1)
Sukakṣa stated the qualities of Indra:
"O Sūrya!
Among the twelve rays, Indra is also recited as being of the nature of Sūrya."

Therefore, O Indra, you who possess the solar nature and great vigor, you who are renowned as the giver of wealth— wealth that is famous for being always to be bestowed— you rise up toward such a one of such majesty: one who is a showerer of riches upon those who beg, a bull, whose deeds are for men (*naryāpasaḥ*), who is beneficial to men (*naryaḥ*), whose actions are for the sake of men, a shooter, one who is exuberant in giving, and full of generosity.
The word *it* is used for emphasis;
you alone have risen from the sun as the soul (*ātman*) in his sacrifice.
The word *gha* is used to indicate well-known fact.
1. ga—They were letting go; 2. na-bha—the controllers and the goers;
3. gha—with you as a companion.
4. *ta-hanyāmeti*; *śa-hanyātemeti*. 5. *kha-ga-gha-ta-na-bhara-śa-kurvanti*; *bha1-kurvatī*; *bha3-kurvataḥ*. 6. *kha-yāvānānāṃ*; *ga-yācakānāṃ*; *ta1-na-pāvamānānāṃ*; *tara-3-4-śa-pāvanānāṃ*.

7. You are the high-pitched vowel after *kha*, *jha*, *ta* (1-3), and *na*; you are the high-pitched vowel after *ta* (4), *bha* (1-3), and *rū*. He who by the strength of his arms shattered ninety-nine fortresses, and he, the slayer of Vṛtra, slew the serpent. || 2 || He who, by the might of his arms, shattered ninety-nine fortresses, and the slayer of Vṛtra slew the serpent. || 2 ||
Indra, by the strength of his own arms alone— that is, by the power of his own arms— shattered, for the sake of Divodāsa, the ninety-nine forts of Śambara; he destroyed them.
And so says the mantra: "For Divodāsa, Indra shattered ninety-nine forts of Śambara with his bolts" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.19.6).
He, the slayer of Vṛtra—the destroyer of the demon Vṛtra—that Indra slew Vṛtra, who was like a cloud that could not be pierced by anyone, or rather, the obstructer.
The connection with the following verse is: "May that Indra grant us wealth."

May that Indra, our auspicious friend, yield for us wealth consisting of horses, cattle, and barley, like a cow with a wide-flowing udder. 3. He; for us; Indra; auspicious; friend; possessing horses; possessing cattle; possessing barley; like a wide-streaming [cow]; he milks forth. 3.

That Indra—possessing the characteristics previously described, the most auspicious Śiva, who is our friend through a relationship characterized by being both the one to be worshipped and the worshipper, equal in nature [to us]—has bestowed upon us wealth consisting of horses (*aśvavat*), cattle (*gomat*), and other livestock.
Regarding the form *yava*, there is an absence of the suffix *tup* due to the prohibition in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.2.9, "after words beginning with *yava*.
*Yava* is a specific type of grain.
May she milk—that is, grant to us—wealth joined with grain.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a cow with abundant milk.

At the time of milking, may she who possesses abundant streams of milk—or rather, she who nourishes many, like the cow Gaurī who yields milk for her calf—grant us abundant wealth by milking it [for us].
The suffix *lyap* is applied after the root *duh*.
In the *asoryāma* sacrifice, during the *maitrāvaruṇa-atiriktoktha*, the triplet beginning with "yad agha" is the *stotriya*;
however, this has been cited together with the preceding triplet in the Sūtra.

Whatever exists, O slayer of Vṛtra, and even that which has risen above, O Sūrya—all that, O Indra, is under your control. 4. Whatever exists, O slayer of Vṛtra, and even that which has risen above, O Sūrya—all that, O Indra, is under your control. 4.

O Vṛtrahan, O slayer of Vṛtra—the cloud that obstructs the waters—O Sūrya, O Indra whose essence is the Sun, on this day you have risen up (*udagāḥ*), having turned toward (*abhi*) whatever collection of objects exists (*yat kiñcit padārthajātam*). [The root *iṇ* means "to go";
it is preceded by the prefix *ut*.]
In the *luṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *ga* for that [root].
