When you emerged and became manifest by your own splendor, then this entire world, consisting of the stationary and the moving, came to be under your control;
it became dependent upon you.
When the sun has risen, they perform their preliminary rites and offer oblations for their own sake.

Or rather, O mighty Lord of the Good, that which you think, "I shall not die"—even that is indeed your truth. 5. Or rather, O mighty Lord of the Good, that which you think, "I shall not die"—even that is indeed your truth. 5.

The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Furthermore, O *vpravṛddha*, you who increase by your own power; O *vsarpate*, Lord of the good (*satām pate*); O *svaprakāśādhikyena*, Lord of the stars (*nakṣatrāṇāṃ pate*), O Indra! If you think—that is, if you perceive—“I do not die” (expressed as *na mare* in the manner of humans), [it is because] the root *mṛṅ* means “to give up life. (*mṛṅ prāṇatyāge*)
The augment *leḍyaṅ* is applied;
by the rule *“vaito'nyatra”* (Pāṇini 6.4.135), the vowel *ai* is substituted; and furthermore, the suffix *vun* is also applied.

1. By the *yaṣṭavya* [verse] beginning with *kha-sakhyā*, there is praise through its corresponding characteristics; by the *yaṣṭavya* beginning with *ta-na-bha-ra-śa-ya*, there is praise through its corresponding characteristics; by the *yaṣṭavya* beginning with *bha1-yaṣṭavyānāt*, there is praise through its corresponding characteristics; by the *yaṣṭavya* beginning with *bha3-yaṣṭavyena*, there is praise through its corresponding characteristics.

2. *Kha-gha-ta1-2-na*: that belongs to you (*tatte tava*); *ga*: yours (*tava*); *ta3-4śa*: reality (*tatva*); *bha1-2*: that (*tat*). 3. *Kha-ta-na-bha*: for that purpose (*tadarthā*); *śa*: dependent on that (*tadadhī*).
4. Kha-ta-uta:
The thought that "he is not loved" is [refuted by] the truth, which is the manifestation of things as they are.
Regarding the sense that "Indra is not loved," there is another mantra: "For his husband shall never die of old age" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.86.11).
Those Soma juices which are pressed in the distance and those which are pressed nearby—
you, O Indra, go to them all.
Those Soma juices which have been pressed far away, and those which have been pressed nearby—all of them you reach, O Indra. ||6||
O Indra, those Soma juices— whether the Somas that are pressed in a distant land far away, or those Somas that are pressed in the nearest place;
for in Vedic usage the dual number is optional, there is no use of the dual here—
those Somas which are purified by the officiating priests, you go toward all of them, whether pressed far or near, reaching them simultaneously for the purpose of drinking them.
By this, Indra's omnipresence is indicated.
In the *asuryāma* [chanting] of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin at the *atiriktoktha*, the three-verse hymn (*stotriya*) is "tam indraṃ vājayāmasi.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "tam indraṃ vājayāmasi, mahān indro ya ojasā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11).
Furthermore, on the fifth day of the ten-night *vyūha* sacrifice, this same triplet is to be inserted as the *nivid*.
And it is stated in the *Vyūha* section: "O Maruts, we impel that most bountiful Indra; we urge on Indra for the sake of strength" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.8).
We incite that Indra for the sake of great victory and for the slaying of Vṛtra;
may he become the bull, the showerer of blessings.
We incite that Indra for the sake of great booty, so that he may slay Vṛtra; may he become the bull, the showerer of blessings. 7.
The sacrificers say:
"We cause that Indra, characterized as previously described, to possess vigor; we cause him to be vigorous—either by means of Soma or by means of hymns—we make him full of vigor, full of strength."
For what purpose?
For the sake of the great Vṛtra—that is, to slay the Asura Vṛtra who obstructs the waters.

Being intoxicated by the drinking of Soma or being praised with hymns, may that Indra—the bull, the showerer and giver of riches—be for us, his praisers and givers of Soma, a showerer and giver of wealth and other boons. May he be so.
Indra is made for giving; he is the most powerful, established for exhilaration; he is glorious, worthy of praise, and fit for Soma.
Indra—he was created for the sake of giving; he is the most powerful; he is established in exhilaration; he is glorious, worthy of praise, and fit for Soma. ||8||
That Indra was created by Prajāpati for the sake of giving wealth to his worshippers—that is, for the purpose of bestowing riches.
Furthermore, he is the most powerful (*ojiṣṭha*), the very Indra, in the state of exhilaration (*made*);
*mada* is so called because it causes one to rejoice, namely Soma.
And at that time of creation by Prajāpati, he was established; the meaning is that he was placed there for the purpose of drinking the Soma.
He is glorious (ghumnī).
"May he illuminate his renown, whether by means of *dhī* (insight) or *vāc* (speech). One who possesses fame is therefore a *ślokī*. *Śloka* means praise.
Possessing that, Indra becomes worthy of Soma, one who is fit for Soma.
Like a thunderbolt forged by speech, he is all-pervading and unshakable; lofty and invincible, he has waxed great.
Like a thunderbolt forged by speech, he is powerful, unshakable like the ocean, lofty, and unconquered; he has grown great within.
He is gathered, produced, and sharpened by the singers with speech characterized as praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a thunderbolt (*vajra*).

The "vajra-weapon" is so called because, just as it is sharpened by its makers until it becomes keen-edged, so too is he strengthened by his praisers through their hymns; for that very reason, he is "possessed of strength" (sabala), endowed with power, and therefore "unshakable" (anapacyuta)—not displaced by others.
The meaning is that he is unassailable.
Such a lofty, great, and radiant Indra, unsubdued and invincible by enemies in battle, having been praised, has grown strong; he desires to bring wealth and other blessings to his worshippers.

1. *Na*, *bha*: "in a very distant place. 2. *Kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*: "ending with the great [letter]. 3. *Kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*: "the sprinkler of desires. 4. *Kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *śa*: "*hotṛ* (sacrificial priest). 5. *Kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *śa*: "the first"; *na*, *mā*, *tya*; *bha*, *mā*, *dyā*. 6. *Kha*, *ta*, *ya*, *ka*, *rtṛ*bhiḥ. 7. *Kha*, *ta*, *4*, *bha*, *1*, *2*: "'Not displaced by others' does not exist."

O Indra, lover of songs, being praised by us, make our path easy to traverse even on difficult ground; for you, O Maghavan, are the one who wields power. (10) O Indra, lover of songs (*girvaṇas*), worthy of praise through hymns, being extolled by the singers, make for us a good path (*sugaṃ*) even upon a difficult road (*durge*). Act in such a way! O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, Indra—you—[the word *ca* has the sense of *cet* (if)]; if you should desire it for the sake of drinking the Soma from that giver, then make the path one of beautiful passage. [The suffix *lyap* is added to the root *vaś*]. Due to the connection with the particle *ca*, there is no suppression of the accent (*anighāta*). (22)

Whose command and sovereign rule no one at all violates—not even a god, nor a wealthy man, nor any person. 11. Whose... thee... now... at all... command... not... violate... his own sovereignty... not... a god... nor... a wealthy man... a person.
When the all-gods stepped across the half-light of the serpent, they found the fury of that wild beast. || 14 ||

Furthermore, I declare: when all the gods (*viśve devāsaḥ*), terrified by the breath—which is of the nature of splendor—of Vṛtra, the Asura who was not to be slain; or rather, when they were driven away by his power, took various steps (*vy akramuḥ*), meaning they abandoned their own places and went to other regions—at that time, [they became] like those of a wild beast (*mṛgasya*).
In this way, Vṛtra assumed the form of a deer to terrify them.

Being in that form, he found (√vid)—that is, he encountered—their power, which is characterized by moving everywhere, or the fear born from it; [he found] all those gods. The meaning is that he reached them.
The connection with the subsequent passage is that Indra became the restrainer and slayer of that asura.

Then indeed, may the slayer of Vṛtra, the one against whom no enemy has been born and who is unsubdued, be my protector; he has bestowed manly power upon me. 15. Then indeed; me; nivaraḥ; bhuvat; vṛtrahā; adiṣṭa; pausyam; ajātaśatruḥ; astṛtaḥ. 15.
The particle *ādu* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Immediately after moving everywhere out of fear of the gods, Indra—by means of a relationship characterized as being equal to me, his praiser—became (*abhavat*) my protector; that is, he became the warder-off and slayer of the demon Vṛtra. Thereafter, Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, [attained] his manly power (*pauṣyam*).
The *pauṃsya* of a man refers to his manly deed;
alternatively,
it is derived from the suffix *ñya* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*), according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.1.87 (*strīpuṃsābhyām*).
The letter *y* replaces the letter *n* through a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*). It means "that which exists in Indra, who is masculine.
Alternatively:
He does not diminish his own strength. He has declared that [he] bestows and establishes [it] within his kingdom.

The meaning is that he brought that kingdom under his own control. From that time forward, Indra became "Ajātaśatru"—one whose enemy has not been born—and "Astrita"—one who was not harmed by others in battle.

Hear us, O slayers of Vṛtra, you who are the bold host of the peoples; come for the sake of great and glorious bounty. 16. Hear us! O Vṛtra-slayers! Forward! The host of the peoples! Come! For the sake of [us] to hear! For great bounty! 16.

O priests and sacrificers: [invoke] him who is renowned for his great strength, the supreme slayer of Vṛtra, the powerful one (śardha)—meaning either possessing force or speed—such an Indra, for the sake of your swift attainment among the people (carṣaṇīnām), for you (vaḥ). [The form] *āśuṣe* is derived from the root *aś* with the suffix *leṭ* in the first person plural; the suffix *upratyaya* occurs by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
The augment *aṭ* is applied according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi.
Having gratified that Indra with hymns of praise, I have brought him forth for you;
the meaning is: "I bestow [him] upon you."
For what purpose?
For the sake of great wealth—that is, in order to bestow riches upon you.

With this prayer, O you of many names, much-praised one, who desire cattle—since with every soma libation you have become manifest. 17. With this prayer, and with the desire for cattle, O you of many names, much-praised one, since with each soma you have come hither. 17.
He possesses many names, endowed with various titles such as Śakra, Vṛtrahan, and others;
or rather,
he is one whose praises are manifold.

"Name" (*nāman*) refers to a hymn of praise, because it bends the praiseworthy god and brings him under control. Therefore, O *puruṣṭuta*—O Indra, who art praised by many—when you, with respect to our *soma*s, "were present" (*ābhavaḥ*), that is, when you were fully present for the sake of drinking them, then we [shall offer] "with this" (*ayā*).
Of what kind?
May we be endowed with this wisdom that desires cattle for itself through the cow;
the meaning is: when you have drunk the Soma, may we be released from [the lack of] cattle and other such things.
May this [offering] be for our awakening; may the slayer of Vṛtra be present with abundant libations;
may Śakra hear our prayer for blessings.

1. Of that which is not to be slain; 2. Of Vṛtra, who does not possess such a form; 3. Ga, Na, Bha—“He placed”; 4. Kha, Ta, Bha—thus; 5. Ga—“To the one who quickly drinks with excellence”; “May he whose mind is awakened; indeed; be ours; may the slayer of Vṛtra, the one of abundant draughts, the powerful one, hear us; [the one] with the head [of the sacrifice]. 18.
This is composed in the *parokṣa* (indirect) style:
"The slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of Vṛtra, he for whom abundant libations are prepared.
This means that in many places, the Soma is pressed—that is, extracted—for the sake of Indra.
Or rather:
he is such that many oblations, such as Soma and others, are prepared and offered for the sake of Indra;
he is one whose mind is awakened (bodhinmanāḥ).
The root *budh* means "to understand.
The suffix *it* is added according to the rules of the *uṇādi* class.
He is so described because his mind understands—that is, knows—the desires of those who offer praise.
The word *eva* is used for emphasis.
The meaning is: "May our mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) alone be [present];
may it always know our desired objects."
Or rather:
may such an Indra be present at our sacrifice;
then may Śakra—Indra, who possesses the power to slay enemies in battle—hear our prayer, that is, our hymn of praise or our invocation.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, on the fourth day of the Vaiśvadeva section, during the midday pressing, the triplet beginning with “kayā tvaṃ na ūtyā” serves as the *anurūpa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
This is stated in the Sūtra: “For the Hotrakas: ‘kayā naścitra ā bhuvat’ and ‘kayā tvaṃ na ūtyā’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).

With what aid do you, O Bull, gladden us? With what [aid] do you bring [gifts] to those who praise you? (19) With what aid do you, O Bull, gladden us? With what [aid] do you bring [gifts] to those who praise you? (19)
O Indra, showerer of desires, by what aid (ūti)—

in the sense of protection and other such meanings derived from the root *av* meaning "to go"— do you protect us? The word *ūti* is an irregularly formed noun (*nipātita*) according to the rule beginning with “*atiyutiḥ*.”

By what approach do you gladden us, delighting us intensely from all sides—whether by coming toward our sacrifice for the sake of drinking Soma, or by coming for the sake of hearing your own praise? When will you cause us such delight?
Furthermore, by what approach will you bring wealth to us, the singers; thus the singer asks Indra.

For whom does the bull, accompanied by his team, rejoice at the pressed juice—the slayer of Vṛtra, for the drinking of Soma? (20) For whom? The bull. At the pressed juice. Accompanied. With his team. The bull. Rejoices. The slayer of Vṛtra. For the drinking of Soma. (20)

Indra, the bull, at whose sacrifice—along with whom—at the pressed Soma purified by *ṛc*-verses, does he rejoice? By this, the sacrifice is indicated as the means. At whose sacrifice does he take delight (*raṇat*) for the sake of drinking Soma, for the purpose of consuming the Soma? Of what nature is he? "Accompanied by the *niyuts*. The *niyuts* are the Maruts, so called because they "thoroughly join" or mix with enemies through their own power; he is accompanied by them. Or alternatively, the *niyuts* are the draft-horses of Vāyu. That Vāyu once gave his own horses to Indra in battle; he is accompanied by them. A "bull" (*vṛṣabhaḥ*), a showerer of wealth or waters. Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, at whose sacrifice does he rejoice? Now, let him come toward our sacrifice. Or rather: at whose ritual (*adhvara*) does he rejoice? Not anywhere else, but only at our sacrifice does he sport for the purpose of drinking Soma. (24)

Being exhilarated, do thou indeed bestow upon us thousandfold wealth; be the giver to the one who offers oblations. 21. *Abhi* | *su* | *naḥ* | *tvam* | *rayim* | *mandasānaḥ* | *sahasriṇam* | *pra-yantā* | *bodhi* | *dāśuṣe* || 21 ||
O Indra, you, being exhilarated and rejoicing in the Soma offered by us, bring forth abundantly to us wealth numbering in the thousands.
He says that very thing:
"Be mindful—that is, take heed—that you are the one who bestows wealth and the like upon the donor, the sacrificer who has presented the oblation, or rather, the director of the ritual."
The root *budh* means "to understand.
It belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), which is a Vedic usage.
*Hedhiḥ*:
when *dhi* occurs, there is the elision of the letter *dh*, which is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

1. kha-ta-śa-atha | 2. kha-jha-ta-2-3-stotṛbhiḥ | 3. kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa lacks ‘abhi’. 4. kha-ga-gha-jña-ta-2-na-ma-ṛtvigbhiḥ | 5. kha-ta-na-bha-2-śa reads ‘vāhanāśvās te; bha1 reads ‘vāhanāśvās se; bha3 reads ‘vāhanāśvās taiḥ’. 6. kha-ta-na-bha lacks ‘na’ in ‘nāsmadīyam’. 7. kha-ta reads ‘yajñam’. 8. gha reads ‘rayim dhanam’. 9. ga reads ‘hedhi tve’.

Accompanied by their wives, these pressed [Soma drops], desiring [Indra], go for the enjoyment; they are the goer among the waters, the one who satisfies. (22) *Palīvantaḥ* (accompanied by their wives): the wives are those who must be protected—the *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhana* waters—for the purpose of pouring the Soma. Within them, *ime sutāḥ* (these pressed ones)—these Somas belonging to the household stage of life—*uśantaḥ* (desiring), that is, longing for their own drinking, *yanti* (go), that is, go to Indra. For what purpose? *Vītaye*, for the sake of their own drinking. Furthermore, *nicumpaṇaḥ*: Yāska says, "‘Nicāmtapaṇaḥ’" (*Nirukta* 5.17). From the root *camu* (to eat), *nicāntaḥ* means "eaten," and *paṇaḥ* means "one who gratifies. Alternatively, *nicumanena prīṇāti* ("he gratifies by means of eating"); thus, *nicumpaṇaḥ* means "one who satiates through consumption. Since it is possible for the pressed Soma to be cast into the waters, by implication the Soma in the form of *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs/residue) is understood. Such Soma is *apāṃ jagmiḥ*. Regarding *apām*, the absence of the prohibition of the genitive case (by the rule *na lokāvyaya*) is a Vedic usage; the meaning is "of the waters. Alternatively, *apām* means "into the waters" or "toward the waters"; *jagmiḥ* means "having the nature of going" or "one who goes well. The Soma goes to Indra. He is cast into the waters in the form of *ṛjīṣa*, according to the statement: "At the time of the *śava-mṛtha*, they throw the *ṛjīṣa* into the waters. Therefore, it is said: "He is the goer among the waters."

The sacrificial priests (*hotrāḥ*), having performed the sacrifice, have sent Indra forth with strength toward the *avabhṛtha* bath at the ritual. (23) *iṣṭāḥ* (performed), *hotrāḥ* (the priests), *asukṣata* (have sent forth), *indram* (Indra), *vṛdhāsaḥ* (increasing), *adhvare* (in the sacrifice), *acchā* (toward), *avabhṛtham* (the *avabhṛtha* bath), *ojasā* (with vigor). (23) By implication, it is stated that the *ṛtvij*s perform [the rites] on the very day of the *avabhṛtha*. To avoid digression from that, he says: "In our sacrifice (*adhvare*), the *hotrāḥ*—that is, the officiating priests (*hotrakāḥ*) who have completed the seven forms of the sacrifice (*saptasaṃsthākāḥ*)—having sacrificed (*iṣṭāḥ*), meaning they have performed the rite; increasing Indra with oblations (*havirbhiḥ*), they send him forth (*asukṣata*) with their own splendor (*ojasā*) toward the *avabhṛtha* on another day. Thus, they sacrifice together with the *hotrakāḥ* until the *avabhṛtha*."

"Here, let those two Haris, who feast together, golden-maned, carry Indra toward the prepared food. (24) This verse has been explained [in Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.32.29]. Here too, the meaning of the sentence is enjoined: "Let those two well-known Haris—golden-maned, meaning possessing hair upon their golden shoulders—those two steeds named Haris, which feast together with Indra, being satiated by the oblations, or else feasting together in battle—let them carry Indra here at this sacrifice toward the *prayaḥ*, the food in the form of oblations, which is placed among the vessels or is beneficial; let them bring him. (24)

For you, O Vibhāvasu, these Soma juices have been pressed; the sacred grass (barhis) is strewn. Bring Indra hither for the sake of the worshippers. For you, O Vibhāvasu—O Agni, whose wealth shines forth pre-eminently, or rather, O Agni, in whom the distinguished lights (vibhās), meaning supreme radiances, reside—these Somas have been pressed for you. Likewise, the sacred grass is strewn. Therefore, bring Indra hither for our sake, for the sake of us who are the worshippers, for the purpose of drinking the Soma; that is to say, bring him toward the sacrifice. 25.

1. kha-ta-na-śa-dvāvamṛtha0 | 2. kha-ga-tanna-bha-śa-abhi prati | 3. kha-gha-bha1-3-' svatejasā ' is not present | 4. gha-'mañjamyabhi0 | Maṇḍala 8, Anuvāka 9, Sūkta 93 [Ṣaṣṭho'ṣṭakaḥ 921]: O Indra, bestow skill upon us; distribute radiant splendors and treasures to the donor and to those who praise you. Sing hymns of praise to Indra! ā | te | dakṣam | vi | rocanā | dadhat | ratnā | vi | dāśuṣe | stotṛbhyaḥ | indram | arcata || 26 ||
The seer addresses those performing the priestly office:
"O sacrificer, may Indra bestow upon you—upon you who have offered the oblation to Indra—the *rocanā*, that is, the shining, radiant *dakṣa*, or strength.
Or alternatively: [the same].
"Rocana" means heaven;
may he establish for you the world named Rocana, radiant with divine splendor.
Likewise, may he provide for you jewels and precious gems.

The root *dhā* (from *ḍudhāñ*) means "to hold" and "to nourish. In the *leṭ* mood, by the rule *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*; furthermore, the augment *aṭ* is applied.
May Indra bestow strength, jewels, and other gifts upon you, the praisers—those of you who compose hymns concerning Indra.
Therefore, worship that Indra with oblations and songs of praise.
I bestow upon you your power, O Lord of a hundred powers, all my hymns of praise; O Indra, be gracious to those who laud you. ||27||
O Śatakratu, O Indra, I bestow and accomplish for you all hymns of praise—the entire collection of lauds—for your powerful Soma.
O Indra, be gracious and bring happiness to those who offer praise.

Bring us what is auspicious, bring us what is auspicious—food and strength, O Śatakratu! For when you, O Indra, show us mercy. 28. Auspicious, auspicious; for us; hither; bring; food; strength; O Śatakratu; when; O Indra; you show mercy; to us. 28.

O Śatakratu, O performer of a hundredfold deeds, O Indra of a hundredfold wisdom—whether it be something auspicious, most auspicious, or the best of blessings that produces happiness—bring that wealth to us; accomplish it for us; give it to us! Likewise, grant us food (iṣ), vigor (ūrj)—that is, the essence of food or powerful nourishment—and if you would indeed show us mercy and bring us comfort, then grant us those things as well.
The root *mṛḍ* means "to gladden. This is the *leṭ* [subjunctive] form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) stem, with the augment *āṭ*.
Bring to us all prosperities, O Śatakratu, when you, O Indra, show mercy unto us. 29. Bring to us, O Śatakratu, all prosperities, when you, O Indra, show mercy unto us. 29.
O Śatakratu, O Indra, you who possess the characteristics previously described, [grant] all (viśvāni) auspicious things (suvitāni)—
those things in which one proceeds well (suṣṭīyate) and attains them. The word *suvitāni* is derived from the root *i* preceded by *su*, with the suffix *ka* and the substitution of *uvaṅ*.
Bring all prosperities for us;
O Indra, if you wish to make us happy, then grant us prosperities accompanied by wealth and other such blessings.

We, possessing pressed soma, invoke you alone, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra, so that you, O Indra, may show us mercy. 30. We, possessing pressed soma, invoke you alone, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra; for you, O Indra, will show us mercy. 30.
1. Kha: *idam-viśeṣaṇa*; Jñāta 1–2–3: *indra-viśeṣaṇa*; Ta 4, Na, Bha 1, Śa: *indra-viśeṣaṇa*. 2. In the manuscripts Ta 3, 4, Na, Bha, and Śa, there is no commentary (*bhāṣya*) for this mantra.
3. Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, Śa: *cedanādikaṃ*.
4. Regarding the compound *ga-bha-rūpa-pratyaye*:
O most excellent slayer of Vṛtra—the one who destroys Vṛtra, the obstructer of the waters—O Indra, we, being *sutavantaḥ*, that is, possessing the pressed soma;
[the particle] *id* is used here for emphasis.
We invoke you alone;
having come to our sacrifice, we call you for the drinking of Soma.
O Indra, if you would make us happy, then we call upon you.
In the Niṣkevalya hymn on the sixth day of the ten-day period when it is expanded, the triplet beginning with "upa no haribhiḥ" is to be inserted as the Nivid.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "'ayaṃ ha yena vā idam upa no haribhiḥ sutam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).

Come toward our pressed [juice] with your bay steeds, O Lord of exhilarations; come toward our pressed [juice] with your bay steeds. 31. Come toward our pressed [juice] with your bay steeds, O Lord of exhilarations; come toward our pressed [juice] with your bay steeds. 31.
O Lord of the intoxicants! "Intoxicants" (madāḥ) refers to the Soma juices, because one becomes intoxicated by them.
The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the rule "the suffix *ap* follows the root *mad* when no prefix precedes it."

O Indra, Lord of the Soma-pressings, accompanied by your bay steeds—as in the verses beginning with "with a hundred bay steeds" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.18.6)—come to our sacrifice where the Soma has been pressed;
come quickly for the sake of drinking it.
The repetition of "to us" (*upa naḥ*) is for the sake of emphasis.

Twofold indeed is he who is known as the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, Indra of a hundred powers; may he come with his bay steeds to our pressed soma. 32. Twofold. He. The greatest slayer of Vṛtra. Is known. Indra. Of a hundred powers. Toward us. With his bay steeds. To the pressed [soma]. 32.

The greatest slayer of Vṛtra, the one who destroys Vṛtra beyond measure, the Lord of a Hundred Powers (Śatakratu)—he whose activities are manifold, that Indra is known in two ways (dvitā): as having undertaken the slaying of Vṛtra and other such deeds, and as having his activities stilled during the time of protecting the world; thus he is recognized by all in these two modes. [The root] *vid* means "to know. Regarding the suffix *ta* prescribed for the passive (*karmaṇi*), there is the elision of *t* according to the rule "the *t* is elided in the middle-voice endings" (*lopas ta ābhyanepadeṣu*).
Therefore, O Soma, come together with the bay horses to your son.

For you indeed, O slayer of Vṛtra, are the drinker of these Soma juices; come to our pressed offering with your bay steeds. 33. You indeed, O slayer of Vṛtra, are the drinker of these Somas; come to our pressed juice with your bay steeds. 33.
O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra or of evil!
The word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*);
because you are the drinker, the one who performs the act of drinking, of these our Soma juices.
Regarding the word *eṣām*, when used as a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) for the pronoun *idam*, the substitute *aś* is applied and it is acute-accented (*udātta*).
Therefore, come—approach—to drink the Soma together with these [Maruts].

On the ninth day of the ten-day period (*daśarātra*) when it is expanded, during the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra] of the *abhiplava-pṛṣṭha*, two verses beginning with "May Indra grant us nourishment" (*indra iṣe dadātu naḥ*) and "Bestow upon us jewels" (*no ratnāni dhattana*) are to be recited as introductory.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'May Indra grant us nourishment... bestow upon us jewels'—one and two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).

May Indra grant us nourishment; may he grant us wealth, the lord of the Ṛbhus and the skillful artisan. May Vāja grant us strength and the prize of victory. (34) Indra shall give for our sustenance: the lord of the Ṛbhus, the skillful artisan, and wealth. May the vigorous one grant us that which possesses vigor. (34)
Indra, thus praised and implored by us, [is] R̥bhukṣan— or rather, there is no lengthening of the vowel due to the rule "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*)—
[the one who is] great through the performance of sacrificial rites and so forth, or the most excellent among all his brothers.
Or rather, at the third libation, in the midst of the Prajāpati-savana, because he is a vessel for Soma,
[we invoke] the great one— the Rbhu, the giver, who has attained immortality through the drinking of Soma— such a god as this, for us.

1. *kha-jña-ta* 1-2-3-*na-śa-ihacyoraṇe*; *ta4-bha-ihavayoraṇe*. 2. *gha-mṛḷayāsi* means "you comfort" or "you gladden. 3. *kha-śa-vyūḻahe*; *ga-da2-3-4-bha-vyūḻaha*. 4. *bha-sahasra*. 5. *gha-yaḥ vṛtrahaṃtamaḥ*. 6. *gha-naḥ suta*. 7. *gha-haribhiḥ*. 8. *ga-ārbhava*. 9. *ta4-na-bha-'savanena*.
*^iṣe* has the sense of food (*bhannārtha*); *dadātu* means "may he give" or "may they bestow."
Likewise, may Indra, the powerful and vigorous one, grant us for our pure gain his younger brother named Vāja—who is himself vigorous and full of strength.
In the tenth section (anuvāka), there are ten hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, "gaur dhayati," consisting of twelve verses, belongs to Bindu or Pūtadakṣa of the lineage of Aṅgiras; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and has the Maruts as its deity.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "gaur dhayati [has] twelve [verses]; [the seer is] Bindu or Pūtadakṣa; [it is] addressed to the Maruts."
The application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), when there is an excess of Soma, one *śastra* arises;
therein, the *atha-luc* serves as the *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses], 'asti somo ayaṃ sutaḥ' and 'gaurdhayati marutām,' are the Stotriya and Anurūpa [stanzas]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.7).
The cow of the Maruts, the bounteous lords, yields her milk for glory; she is the immortal one, yoked as the driver of their chariots.
The cow; she suckles; of the Maruts.

This Soma standing before us has been pressed by us for the sake of the Maruts; it exists [is present]. Therefore, for him—referring back to him—the Maruts, who are self-ruling (svarājaḥ), meaning they shine by their own splendor and not by that of another, drink this pressed Soma. Moreover, the two Aśvins also drink the Soma.
Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa drink their fill of the purified juice that flows in three streams from the living plant.

They drink—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—from the *tanā* [filter] of the purified [Soma] that stands in three places, which possesses praise. (5) He says that it is not only the Maruts who are drinkers of Soma, but these [gods] as well: Mitra, because he sets all beings in motion toward their respective duties, is a friend; and Aryaman and Varuṇa, the warder-off of suffering or of enemies. These gods, by name, [drink] from the *tanā*. "Tanā" means the *daśāpavitra* (the woollen filter). By the rule "supāṃ suluk... there is the substitution of *āl* for the third case ending; thus *tanā* is accented on the first syllable. From the *tanā*, they drink the purified [Soma]. "Trisadhasthasya": a place where they stand together is a *sadhastha*; that which has its three places—the *droṇakalaśa*, the *āvanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*—is so called. They drink that Soma which possesses praise (*jāvataḥ*), meaning it is accompanied by hymns. In the second line, the genitive endings have the sense of the accusative.
And may Indra, indeed, for his pleasure, exhilarate himself with this pressed soma mixed with milk,
like the Hotṛ-priest at dawn.
And so indeed, may Indra now take pleasure in this pressed juice mixed with milk; at dawn, he shall exhilarate himself like a Hotṛ priest. 6.

Moreover, O Indra: of this pressed soma, mixed with milk and curds, which has been purified for us by the ten-fingered strainer (*daśāpavitra*), do thou quickly satisfy thyself—that is, perform the service of drinking it—during the morning pressing at every dawn. [The root *mad* means praise and so forth; he praises [thee] face-to-face. Or rather, he desires the enjoyment of the soma. In this regard, there is an illustration: "like the Hotṛ priest. Just as the Hotṛ priest praises the gods during the morning pressing, or desires to praise the gods. || 28 ||
The Sūrya-hymns drive away the obstructors;
those of purified skill cast them far away.
They hasten forth like sunbeams across the firmament; those of pure skill move forward like arrows from a bow.
The seer, having praised the Maruts many times, now reflects upon himself:
"The wise ones are like the sun; they are like waters—just as waters flow crosswise, so too do they possess expansive movements."
When?
At the time of the Aśvins. [The root] *atviṣ* means "to shine."
When do they blaze in the intermediate space?
Furthermore, when do these Maruts—destroyers and slayers of enemies, possessing pure strength and purified power—rush forth?
They come toward our sacrifice.
I choose that which is indeed the highest and most excellent among the great gods,
and that which belongs to those of enduring splendor.
O Agni, I choose the great protection of the gods, and that of those who possess enduring splendor.

O Maruts, when shall I choose for myself the protection (*avaḥ*) of you—of you who are great among the great or the venerable, by your very self even without ornaments, possessing wondrous splendor worthy of being seen, and who are indeed gods, shining ones?
[The root] *vṛ* (in *vṛṇe*) means "to choose" or "to partake";
it belongs to the *krayādi* class.

1. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, Bha, and Śa, "ana" is not present. 2. In manuscript Kha, it is "paraṃśodhitaṃ"; in Jha, Ta¹, Ta², Na, Bha, and Ra, it is "pariśodhitaṃ"; in Gha, it is "pūtaṃ śodhitaṃ"; in Bha¹, it is "pariśodhanaṃ". 3. In Gha¹, it is "tridhasthasya". 4. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, it is "tiṣṭhantyatreti". 5. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, Na, and Śa, it is "pibati"; in Bha and Ra, it is "pibaṃtī". 6. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, and Na, "asya" is not present. 7. In manuscripts Kha, Ta, and Śa, it is "mahanīyānāṃ". [Maṇḍala 8, Adhyāya 10, Sūtra 95] Sixth Aṣṭaka: 925.

Those Maruts who spread out all earthly realms and the luminous regions of heaven—those Maruts, for the drinking of Soma, we summon hither. 9. Those Maruts who spread out all earthly realms and the luminous regions of heaven—those Maruts, for the drinking of Soma, we summon hither. Those Maruts who spread out (*praprathan*)—that is, they caused to extend everywhere—all earthly realms (*pārthivāni*), which exist upon the earth, as well as the luminous regions (*rocanā*) of heaven, the shining lights—the Maruts, for the sake of drinking Soma (*somapītaye*), we invoke. [Grammatical notes: *pratha* means "to make known" or "to spread. In the causative form with the *caṅ* suffix, by Pāṇini 7.4.95 (*atsmṛdṛśvaraprathandastṛspaśām*), the initial vowel of the reduplicated syllable is replaced by *at*. By the rule *caṅyanyatarasyām*, the word is optionally middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). We invoke such Marut deities for the purpose of drinking Soma.

I now call upon you, O Maruts—sons of strength, of pure power, shining with your own splendor from heaven—or rather, dwelling in the heavenly world—for the drinking of this Soma. (10) O Maruts, gods so named because they move measuredly, sons of strength (*pūtadakṣasaḥ*), whose power is purified, and who blaze with your own radiance from heaven (*divaḥ*); or else, those who abide in the heavenly realm (*divaḥ*). I call upon you, those well-known ones (*tyān*), "you" (*vaḥ*), "now" (*nu*)—that is, quickly. For what purpose? For the drinking (*pītaye*) of this our Soma. (10)

I invoke those Maruts who have propped apart the two worlds, heaven and earth; I call them now for the drinking of this Soma. (11) Those Maruts who have propped apart the two worlds—heaven and earth—with their own power, meaning they have made those two worlds firm for their own sake; that is to say, they have brought those two worlds under their own control. I invoke them—those well-known ones—now, quickly. For what purpose? For the drinking of this [Soma], and so forth.

I now call that host of Maruts, dwelling in the mountains, the showerer [of benefits], for the drinking of this Soma. (12) I now call that host of Maruts, dwelling in the mountains, the showerer [of benefits], for the drinking of this Soma. (12) 1. *Tyam*: him, well-known everywhere; *giriṣṭhām*: dwelling in the mountains, in the clouds, or on the peaks; *vṛṣaṇam*: the showerer of waters or of desires; *mārutam*: belonging to the Maruts; *gaṇam*: the host or assembly; *huve*: I, Vindu, call upon. For what purpose? *asya somasya pītaye*: for the drinking of this our Soma. The second hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "Ā tvā," is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and dedicated to Indra. Tiraścīnāṅgirasa is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Thus it is enumerated: "Ā tvā nava tiraścīnānuṣṭubham. In these Ābhiplāvika days, at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the triplet "Ā tvā giraḥ" is an optional *anurūpa* (responsive verse) for the Acchāvāka priest. It is indicated thus: "gāyanti tvā gāyatrina ā tvā giro rathīriva" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.8).

O lover of songs, let our hymns rise up toward you at the libations like a charioteer; they have gathered together around you, Indra, as mother-cows surround their calf. 1. Let our songs stand before you like a charioteer at the pressed juices, O lover of songs! They have gathered around you, Indra, as mother-cows [surround] their calf. 1.
1. [The word] *kha-jha-tara* is with the vowel -3- (e) and the *ḍit*-suffix; *ta1* is without a vowel (*nissvara*). 2.
*kha-ga-gha-ta-śa* [denote] all [the letters]; *bha1* [denotes] "all" (*sarvān*) from every side (*sarvataḥ*).
3. *jha-na-anu-* [denote] the *tiraścīrāṅgirasas*; *ānu* [denotes] the same.

4. Kha-ma-'thūkthepu | O *girvaṇas*, you who are worthy of praise through songs, O Indra, since the *soma* juices have been pressed out, our voices—our words characterized by praise—have risen up toward you (*tvā*); they stand facing you swiftly.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

Like a charioteer: just as a hero possessing a chariot, traveling by means of his chariot, quickly reaches the destination to be attained, even so must we approach you; our hymns of praise come toward you.
Furthermore, O Indra, our songs, directed toward you, resound perfectly together.
The meaning is "they praise. [The root] *stu* is used in the sense of praising; it belongs to the *kuṭādi* class.
The form of that [root] in the *luṅ* tense is as follows;
there is an illustration for it:
"vatsaṃ na mātaraḥ."
Just as two mother cows low with sounds such as "hambhā" when directed toward their calf, so it is in this case.

The bright pressed juices have drawn you hither, O Indra, lover of songs. Drink, indeed, of this soma-plant, O Indra; it has been set before you in all [the vessels]. 2. *Ā tvā śukā acucyavuḥ sutāsa indra girvaṇaḥ | piba tu asyāndhasa indra viśvāsu te hitam || 2 ||*

O *girvaṇas*, you who are to be praised with songs, O Indra—may these pressed *soma* juices, bright within the vessels and cups, which have been extracted by us, cause you to come hither; may they move toward you.
[The root] *cyuṅ-pluṅ* means "to go.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the suffix *śap* is replaced by *śru* according to the rule "there is much variation in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Therefore, quickly drink your portion of the *andhas*—the Soma—being offered by us.
He explains that very point: O Indra, in all directions (*viśvāsu dikṣu*), the sacrificial offerings for you, such as Soma and the *puroḍāśa*, are placed (*hita*) and set down (*nihita*).

Drink the Soma for exhilaration, O Indra, the pressed juice brought by the falcon; for you indeed are the lord and king of all the eternal tribes. 3. Drink the Soma! For exhilaration! O Indra! That which was brought by the falcon! The pressed [juice]! You! Indeed! Of the eternal ones! Lord! King! Of the tribes! You are! 3.
O Indra, you,

drink for exhilaration— that is, for joy— the pressed Soma brought from the heavenly world by the Gāyatrī in the form of a falcon; [in this phrase] the letter *ha* becomes *bha* according to the rule *hagrahor bhaś chandasi*.
*Kam* is a filler [particle], or it has the sense of "happiness.
Drink the *soma* with happiness.
The word *hi* indicates a reason.

For indeed, since you are the lord, protector, and master of the many eternal tribes (viś), of all the hosts of Maruts, and of all the divine hosts; and since you are likewise a king, shining with your own splendor—therefore, you should drink the Soma first.
In the Ukthya sacrifices of the Ābhiplavika series, at the third pressing, the optional *stotriya* for the Acchāvāka is “śrudhī havaṃ tiraścyā” (Hear the call of Tiraścī).
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “śrudhī havaṃ tiraścyā āśrutkarṇaṃ śrudhī havam” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).

Hear the call of Tiraścī, O Indra, he who honors you. Bestow upon him wealth consisting of heroic power and cattle; for you are great. 4. Hear! Call! Of Tiraścī! O Indra! He! You! Honors! Of heroic power! Of cattle! Wealth! Bestow! Great! Are! 4.
1. gha—targeting you (*tvāmabhilakṣya*). 2. kha—*vatsaṃ na ca*; gha—*vatsaṃ na*; na—*vatsaṃ nava*; bha—*vatsamiva*. 3.
kha—*jña-tar-na-bha-piba*; alternatively, since it must be stated that "the action itself is also to be included," [you] are the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
The genitive case is frequently used in the sense of the dative (in Vedic usage).
Therefore, drink this food in the form of soma quickly.
4. [In the presence of] *kha*, *bha*, *bhū*, and *kye*.

O Indra, listen—pay heed—to my invocation consisting of hymns of praise directed toward you, from this one named Tiraścī, who serves you with oblations; the word *saparyati* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class [of roots]. Listen to this call concerning you.
And having heard it, O Indra, you [possess] excellent heroism— meaning the heroism belonging to a father of beautiful valor;
or rather,
the heroism that exists in a heroic son.
O you who possess excellent sons, O you who possess cattle—meaning those who possess livestock such as cows—and wealth: fill us with the gift of riches; that is, satisfy us.
From where does this capacity arise? To this, he says:
You are indeed great, superior in virtues, and the most excellent among the gods.
O Indra, you for whom he has generated this newest, delightful song— a prayer from a conscious mind, swelling with the nectar of immortality— [accept it].
To Indra—[to him] who has generated for you a newest, delightful song, a conscious-minded prayer that is directed toward and overflowing with the Truth (ṛta). 5.
O Indra, that sacrificer who has generated for you— that is, has kindled or produced— a newer, more recent, and exhilarating song consisting of praise,
for your sake; for that singer, you [grant] the ancient [gift] connected with *ṛta*, the Truth.
Or rather,
the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental:
"swollen by truth" (meaning increased by truth).

Regarding the phrase "liḍadha-deśra," it is explained as follows: there is a substitution of *pī* [for the root *pyai*]. Such is one whose mind is possessed of wisdom (*cikitvin-manas*). [The root] *kit* means "to know."
The *kāsa* is the form; the change from *a* to *i* is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). It means "that which knows all born things, the hearts of all."
Since the protection performed by you without guile makes known the heart of all, grant that intellect of yours—known as "protection"—which perceives objects beyond the senses.
Thee, that very Indra, whom songs and hymns have magnified—
desiring to win his many heroic exploits, we shall prevail.
Him—*ūm*!—you, Indra, whom the songs and hymns have magnified; desiring to win his many heroic powers, we pay homage. 6.
The sages said to one another:
"That" refers to the one previously described by those characteristics;
"u" is used for emphasis.
Let us praise that very Indra with hymns;
let us laud him, that Indra whom our songs—our praises and our *uktha* recitations—have magnified and strengthened. Therefore, desiring to win for ourselves his many heroic exploits, we praise him.
The root *paṇ* means "to share" (*saṃbhaktau*).

In the view that the reduplication (*san*) is absent, once the vowel substitution (*ātva*) has been applied, the form *sanoteḥ* becomes *sān* according to the rule "the *na* of *sanoti* [becomes *ta*] in the *saṃhitā*" (*sāṃhitikaṃ tvam*).
Desiring to share those heroic powers (*vīryāṇi*), we approach them (*vanāmahe*).
We honor that Indra with hymns of praise.
Now let us praise Indra with pure song;
may he, who has grown strong through pure hymns, being pure himself, be exhilarated by the pure mixture of soma.
Come hither! Now let us praise Indra, the pure one, with a pure *sāman* chant and with pure hymns; may he, who has grown great through purity and possesses the power of the *āśis*, be exhilarated. 7.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:
In former times, it is said, Indra, having slain the asuras such as Vṛtra and others, considered himself impure due to the fault of killing a brahmin.
Thereupon, in order to remove that fault, Indra spoke to the sages.
"Make me, who am impure, pure by means of your Sāman.
1. kha-ga-ta-na-bha-śa-pravṛddhā | 2. kha-ta-na-bha-śa-nayeti; ja-anayeti |
3. *Kha-ga-ta-bha-indram*; *gha-ya*.
Then they purified it with hymns that produce purity and with weapons.
Afterwards, for the sake of the purified Indra, sacrificial rites such as the *soma* sacrifice and other oblations (*havīṃṣi*) were presented.
This point is established in the Śāṭyāyanaka Brāhmaṇa: "Indra, having slain the Asuras, considered himself as if unpurified and impure.
He desired, 'May they praise me with a pure Sāman while I am indeed pure.
He said to the seers, 'Praise me!'"
Then the seers completed the Sāman; they praised with it, saying, "Hither to Indra.
Thereupon, indeed, Indra became purified, cleansed, and fit for sacrifice.
And thus is the meaning of this verse:
the seers speak to one another,
"Come quickly indeed!"

Having arrived, let us praise—that is, we shall laud—Indra, who is pure and sinless, by means of a pure *sāman* that produces purity, and with pure hymns (*uktha*) and recitations (*śastra*) which are causes of purification.

Then, having caused this Indra—who is increasing through the *sāmans* and recitations and who grows by being free from sin—to increase further, let the pure one, possessing blessings (*āśīrvān*) and taking refuge through the *gadhya* verses and so forth, [worship him]. (In the Vedic language, the suffix *matup* becomes *vat* according to the rule *chandasi iraḥ*.)
May such Soma gladden him; may it exhilarate Indra.
[The substitution of] *bhlu* for the root *mādyati* occurs by Vedic license.

O Indra, come to us pure; pure, with your pure aids. Being pure, bestow wealth upon us; being pure and worthy of the Soma, rejoice. 8. Indra! Pure, come to us! Pure, with your pure aids! Pure, bestow wealth! Pure, O you who are worthy of the Soma, rejoice! 8.
O Indra, you who are pure and purified by our *sāmans* and *śastras*, come (*ā gahi*) toward us; come with your pure protections (*śuddhābhir ūtibhiḥ*).
The Maruts are the protections.
Or, they are so called because they go everywhere; they too are purified by the *sāman* chants and the *śastra* recitations. Together with those Maruts, come pure and free from sin!
And having come, O pure one, bestow wealth upon us; establish it firmly within us.
Furthermore, O pure one, becoming *somya*—worthy of the *soma*—rejoice with the *soma*;
for the root *mad* means "to rejoice."
In the imperative (loṭ), by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision (bhlu) of the suffix śap.

O Indra, for you are pure; as the pure one, grant wealth to us, and as the pure one, grant treasures to the donor. As the pure one, you strike down the Vṛtras; as the pure one, you desire to win the prize of booty. 9. [To] Indra. Pure. For. Us. Wealth. Pure. Treasures. To the donor. Pure. Vṛtras. You strike down. Pure. Prize of booty. You desire to win. 9.
O Indra, you who are pure—
*hi* being used for emphasis—
you are indeed pure; O charioteer, bestow wealth upon us.
Thus, O Pure One, bestow upon the donor—the sacrificer who has offered the oblation—delightful treasures such as wealth and other riches.
Then, O Pure One, being free from sin, you strike down and destroy the *vṛtras*—those enemies who obstruct the waters, who create obstacles to ritual action, or who are evil deeds.
Then, O Pure One, purified by our *sāman*-chants and *śastra*-recitations to avoid the fault of slaying enemies, you desire to grant us *vāja*, that is, food for our sustenance.
"Whenever I slay enemies, then and there you must purify me with conciliatory words and weapons that produce purity"—this is the meaning of verse 5.

The third hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses, begins with “asmai. It is enumerated here as follows: “asmai saikā; Śutānaḥ [is the seer], or the Maruts; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas; the fourth verse is a Virāj; the line beginning with ‘iṣyāmi’ is addressed to the Maruts; and the last two are addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati. The seer is either Śutāna, the son of the Maruts, or Tairaśca, the son of Aṅgiras.
The fourth [verse] is Virāj;
the remaining ones are Triṣṭubhs.
Indra is the deity.
The line “I desire you, O Maruts” has the Maruts as its deity;
the verse beginning with “Then the drop” has Indra and Bṛhaspati as its deities.
The application of the hymn is to be understood from its indicative marks (liṅga).
1. *śa*-paścāt-śuddhādi-indrāya.
2. *kha-śa-tara-3-bhara-śa-stuyur* iti stuyuḥ; *ta1-śastraiḥ stuyur* iti stuyuḥ. 3. *kha-ta-bha-tava*; *ga-ta ete*.
4. I did not see kha, ta, bha, śa, or sā.
5. We would praise gha.
6. In kha, ga, ta, and śa, the word "somyaḥ" does not exist.
7. Kha-ta-dhana-ka-va-dhana-ādi; ga-śa-dhana-kanaka-ādi; na-kanaka-vastra-dhana-ādi; bha-kanaka-va-dhana-ādi. 8. Ga-na-bha-marutaḥ.
To him the Dawns have prolonged their course; for Indra, at night, the waves of well-spoken hymns [have flowed].
For him, the seven mother waters stood ready, the rivers easy to cross for his swift passage.
For him the dawns have lengthened their course; for Indra, at night, the sweet-voiced waves [have risen]. For him the seven mother waters stood still—the rivers easy to cross for men to ford. 1.
Impelled by the power of Indra, the dawns—the periods of dawn—extended their respective courses for this Indra, who is endowed with the previously mentioned qualities.
The root *tṛ* signifies the act of increasing;
they caused them to increase on all sides.
Just as they rose in the past, so too have they risen for him now;
likewise the waves. This is a name for night.
The root *ṛ* means "to go" or "to reach. The suffix *map* is applied according to the rule *atterū ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.484). The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*.
They are to be approached by all,
for at night everyone goes to their own dwelling;
nights are the cause for reaching one's own abode.
At night, during the time of the latter part of the night, they became speakers of beautiful speech (*suvācaḥ*).
For at that time, everyone performs the study of the Vedas and other such activities;
therefore, they became auspicious in their speech.
While Indra was ruling, they became devoted to the study of the Vedas and to inference; likewise, they were like water (āpaḥ),
for the root *āp* means "to pervade."
The Mothers, who pervade everywhere and are the creators of the worlds, are seven in number; they are the flowing rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others—
or rather,
the seven rivers characterized by their habit of flowing.

Because they do not produce the serpent that obstructs them, they became "supārāḥ"—meaning having a beautiful further shore—for this Indra, for the sake of men, so that they might cross over easily; that is, they became fit to be crossed with ease.
The exceedingly wise one, armed with his bolt, has thrice seven times joined together the ridges of the mountains;
neither god nor mortal can undo that which the exalted bull has performed.

Even with his weapon, the utterly ignorant one could not [overcome] the thrice-seven ridges of the mountains joined together by Vidhura. Neither god nor mortal could surpass those things which the fully grown bull performed. 2.
By *vidhura*,
there is a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*). *Cit* has the sense of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
Even with the assistance of Vidhura, [he was struck] by a weapon (*astra*).
[The root] *asu* means "to throw"; the suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of one who habitually performs that action (*tācchīlika*).
By Indra, whose nature is to hurl enemies;
or else,
by the weapon of weapons, the thunderbolt.

The meaning is that the thunderbolt-fall released by him, having pierced through— having struck beyond— the peaks (*sānu*) of seven mountains, which were joined together in groups of three times seven, that is, twenty-one in number, and had been consolidated into a single mass. It passed through them and came forth.
In this regard, the Taittirīyaka Brāhmaṇa states: “Having extracted a blade of Darbha grass and having split the seven mountains, he slew him” (Tait. Saṃ. 6.2.4.3), and so forth.
No one—neither a god distinct from Indra and others, nor a mortal human—could (*turyāt*) or would (*na taret*) perform those deeds of that Indra, such as splitting the mountain peaks and the like;
the meaning is that no one is capable of doing so.

The root *tṛ* means "to float" and "to cross. In the *liṅ* (optative) mood, there is the *ślu* elision of the *śap* suffix by virtue of the rule "the Vedic usage is manifold" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), and there is the substitution of *u* for *i*.
Alternatively:
the root *tur* means "to hasten"; it belongs to the *jauhoty-ādi* class.

The meaning is that Indra—who has grown great through the drinking of *soma* or who has increased by his own power, and who is a bull (*vṛṣabha*) in the sense of being a showerer of desires or waters—performed those deeds which neither a god nor a human is able to perform in such a manner.
1. Kha, gha, and ta increase on all sides; ga, na, and ma increase on all sides; bha increases on all sides. 2.
The study of the Vedas—namely, the study of the *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* [sections]—and the hearing of the treatises (*śāstra*), reflection (*cintanā*), and so forth.
3. The instruction of Indra regarding *kha*, *ga*, and *ta*.
4. Those devoted to the study of the Vedas, logic, and inference;
5. those who have performed [the rites] an equal number of times with the syllables kha, ga, gha, ta, ṭa, bha, ra, śa;
6. those whose peaks are like the letter gha.

7. *Jha* means "he might strike" or "he would be able to strike. In this sense, it is a form of the root *tūr* (as in *tūrī gatihiṃsā-tvaraṇayoḥ*). The absence of the long vowel and the presence of the short vowel are Vedic (*chāndasa*) according to the requirements of the context.
The meaning is that he is not able to act in such a manner. Ka. 1.59, p. 930.
Indra’s thunderbolt is of iron, fashioned by the Unmixed One; in Indra’s two arms is heroism and strength.
From Indra’s head his powers are manifold; they have settled near him, eager to hear his command.

Indra’s thunderbolt is made of iron, well-fashioned; in Indra’s two arms is the greatest strength. In Indra’s head are his mental powers in their excellence; they hasten toward him for the sake of hearing his presence nearby. 3.
The vajra of Indra, who possesses the aforementioned qualities, was made of iron— that is,
fashioned from metal.
That vajra was held firmly in Indra’s own hand, thoroughly integrated and completely joined with it.
For this very reason, Indra possesses the greatest—that is, the most abundant—*ojas*, or heroic power, in his two *bāhvos*, or arms. Likewise, in the word *nireke*:

because of the doubt as to whether it is derived from the root *ric* preceded by *ni* (meaning "to leave" or "to exclude") or from the root *dṛ* preceded by *nis* (meaning "to tear apart"), there is no *avagraha*.

Regarding the departure: when Indra goes forth for the sake of battle, at that time the *kratus*—the ritual acts such as the placing [of oblations] upon the head—are on Indra’s *śīrṣan*, that is, his head.
Alternatively, "head" (*śira*) refers to the upper part of the body beginning from the neck.
In that regard, by means of these two [suffixes], actions such as seeing and impelling occur.
Likewise, from the root *ās*,
there is the substitution of *āsanna*.
And as for those actions performed at the mouth [of the sacrifice], such as harnessing the horses and elephants for the purpose of battle;
furthermore, for the sake of hearing the speech of Indra—who is departing for the fray and giving commands—all his dependents and servants *eṣanta* (strive) *upāke*, that is, nearby.
With the thought, "Where and in what task will this Indra employ us? they come from all sides into his presence.
The root *īṣ* is used in the senses of motion, injury, and seeing;
it belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa.
I deem thee the most worthy of sacrifice among those worthy of sacrifice; I deem thee the shaker of the unshakable.
O Indra, I deem thee the banner of the warriors; I deem thee the bull of the peoples.

I deem you the most worthy of sacrifice among those worthy of sacrifice; I deem you the shaker of the unshakable; I deem you, O Indra, the banner of the warriors; I deem you the bull of the people. 4.
These and others are direct perceptions.

O Indra, I perceive—that is, I recognize—you as the one worthy of sacrifice even before [the other] gods who are themselves worthy of sacrifice; I understand you as such. Likewise, I know—that is, I recognize—you as the shaker, the one who causes even the mountains—which are unshakable and free from falling—to fall apart, the one who cleaves them with the thunderbolt.

Or rather, I know [you] as the one who, by his own power, causes even those powerful heroes— who are unshakable and impossible to drive away by force— to flee. Furthermore, O Indra, [you are the one] of the *satvans*.
The root *vaṇ* means "to share" (*saṃbhakta*).
[The suffix] *kanip* is added.
I consider it to mean "the raised banner of the warriors who are sharing [in the spoils]."
Or rather:

I consider you to be the one who shares [the reward] with living beings through their hymns or oblations, the leader of the mind of the sacrificers, or the one worthy of their worship. Likewise, I consider and know you to be the bull (*vṛṣabha*) among men (*carṣaṇīnām*), raining down their desired fruits.
When you, O Indra, take the most exhilarating thunderbolt into your arms for the sake of slaying [the enemy],
the mountains resounded, the cattle lowed, and the priests approached Indra with their prayers.
When you, O Indra, take the unshakable thunderbolt in your arms to slay the serpent, then the mountains roared aloud, the cows lowed, and the priests approached toward Indra. 5.

1. *kha-gha-jña-ta¹-²-sa* ca; 2. *kha-jña-ta¹-²-atyantasaṃbandhaḥ*; *na-bha-atyantasaṃbandhaḥ*; 3. *kha-ta-nipūrvāddivervā*; 4. *kha-ta-yajñārham iti*; 5. *ga-vyāvayitāram iti*; 6. *gha-bha-indra tvā tvām*; 7. *kha-taṃ-śa-satvanāṃ satvānām*; *ga-gha-satvānām*; *bha-batavāṇām*; 8. *kha-ga-ta-bha-śa-satvānām*.
O Indra, [hold] the thunderbolt, the weapon, in your arm. Of what kind?
"Madacyutam" means the one who causes the intoxication of enemies to fall away; "yat-yadā" means whenever; "ā dhatse" means you bestow [it].
For what purpose?
"Ahave" means for the sake of slaying the Asura named Ahi, or the cloud.
The particle *u* is used for emphasis, meaning "indeed.
[It means] "precisely for the sake of slaying.
Furthermore, when the demon named Ahi was slain by Indra, the mountains—the clouds that fill the world—roared forth.
‘Nu’ means sound;
they made a loud noise,
or rather, when the cows and the waters situated there made a loud sound.

Regarding the phrase "making the waters resound," there is a Vedic citation from the Yajurveda: "When you roared as you struck them down while they were rushing together, for that reason you are called 'Nadyas' (rivers)" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.1.2; Atharvaveda Saṃhitā 3.13.1).
The fourth quarter [of the verse] is cryptic.
At that time, the *brahmāṇaḥ*—the Brahmins—approaching Indra from all sides with hymns and oblations, moved around him.
Alternatively:
*brahmāṇaḥ* [is derived from] the root *bṛh*, meaning "to grow."
The mountains and other beings, having grown great, praised Indra.
May we honor you, the carpenter who begot all these beings that are younger than he;
with songs and prostrations, may we serve Indra as our friend and enter upon the bull.

Let us praise him with the syllable *ūm*, he who brought forth all these creatures that are inferior to him. With Indra we would maintain friendship through our songs; let us approach the Bull with our playful delights. 6.
The worshippers say to one another: "Let us praise, let us perform a hymn of praise, to that very Indra indeed—
who is Indra— that brought forth, who generated these various beings."
Therefore, from this very Indra, all— that is, every class of objects or all worlds—
subsequent things arise at a later time.
By means of this Indra, we [attain] friendship through our songs of praise.
The instruction is by way of the nature of the body:
"May we practice and maintain loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Some say that the verbal root *dhṛp* means "to hold" or "to maintain."
Alternatively,
"mitram" is a Vedic singular form.
"May we become friends and well-wishers together with Indra"— with such words let us call upon Indra. The root *śab* (in the sense of "to call") belongs to the *juhoty-ādika* class.
Here, by way of grammatical anomaly, there is a double conjugation and the substitution of *bhū* for *as*.
Therefore, with prostrations being performed—that is, with salutations or with oblations being offered—we shall approach the Bull, the showerer of desires, Indra; we shall bring him right toward us.
Fleeing from the snorting of Vṛtra, all the gods who were your friends abandoned you;
O Indra, let there be friendship between you and the Maruts, and then you shall conquer all these hostile armies.
Fleeing from the snort of Vṛtra, all the gods who were your friends abandoned you; O Indra, let there be friendship between you and the Maruts, and then you shall conquer all these hostile armies. 7.

"O Indra, all those gods who were previously your friends, let us establish friendship in battle"—thinking thus, all those gods became allies. Seeing them all approaching, the Asura Vṛtra exhaled a breath in order to instill fear in them; [the word] *śvasathāt* is derived from the root *śvas* (to breathe) with the suffix *athan*.
Having seen them all coming, the Asura Vṛtra breathed out to produce terror among them.
Fearing the breath [of the enemy], and therefore trembling and fleeing in every direction, they abandoned you—they deserted you in battle.
This being so, O Indra, let there be friendship—the state of being a friend—between you and the Maruts;
that is, together with those Maruts who do not desert you.
Immediately thereafter, you conquer all these hostile armies; that is, you overwhelm them by your own power.
By this, he refers to Indra as he was slaying Vṛtra.
In this regard, the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "Indra, indeed, being about to slay Vṛtra... (AiB 3.20) should be consulted.
O Maruts, increasing through triple nourishment, like sacrificial rays released from a cord, you who are worthy of worship, come hither;
grant us our portion of glory, and with this oblation we shall honor you.
1. "May I act as a steward. 2. O Viśve (All): all [of you]. Three times.

Sixty. You. The Maruts. Increasing in strength. Like springs. Like heaps. Worthy of sacrifice. Toward you. We have come. Grant us our portion. May it be auspicious for you. With this oblation, let us worship you. 8.
In this context, he states that so many Maruts became his companions:
"O Indra, *tris* means three.
[The form] *jas* [becomes] *su* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
There are sixty-six Maruts;
they are set forth in nine groups of seven each in the Taittirīyaka, beginning with the passage "ihaṃścānyāhaśca" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.6.5.5).
Of these, the first five groups are recorded in the Saṃhitā.
"‘Svatavān, Praghāsī, Sāṃtapana, Gṛhamedhī, Krīḍī, Śākī, and Ujjeṣī’ (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 17.85)—this is the sixth group, consisting of the *khailika* verses.
Following that are the *araṇye-anuvākyās* known as ‘Dhunī, Dhvānta,’ and so forth.
Thus, these sixty groups, like cattle gathered into herds, have strengthened you, increasing you by their own power."
Those Maruts became worthy of sacrifice;
we approach that Indra, who is accompanied by the Maruts.
Therefore, do thou grant us our share—the wealth that is to be enjoyed.
Afterwards, we two also shall "offer" (*vidhema*)— that is, we shall provide— "to you" (*te*) with this oblation characterized by Soma, "splendor" (*śubham*), a power that withers enemies;
[the root] *vidh* means "to provide," thus we provide it.
The meaning is "the tortoise."
The host of the Maruts bears sharp weapons; who, O Indra, has dared to withstand your thunderbolt?
Weaponless are the Asuras, the godless ones; O consumer of the Soma dregs, scatter them with your wheel!

Sharp is the weapon, the host of the Maruts. O Indra, who has dared to withstand your thunderbolt? Weaponless are the Asuras, the godless ones; with your wheel, O consumer of the Soma-residue, strike them down!

O Indra, who indeed—be it a god or a human—has dared to oppose or overcome your own sharp weapon, by which one fights (āyudha), namely the bow; and your host (anīka), the assembly of the sixty-three Maruts who are your allies, as well as your thunderbolt (vajra)? No one has done so.
The meaning is that there is no one who can overcome him. The root *dhṛṣ* means "to overpower";
[the form is] *ā dhṛṣā*.
Thus it has been explained.

In the absence of that [augment], this is the form in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. For this very reason: "O Ṛjīṣin! those Asuras who are weaponless—devoid of weapons such as the bow—and godless—devoid of gods—are the enemies of the gods."
The Soma has been pressed, the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs) has been acquired.

In that same manner, O Śakra, "drive away" (*apa vapa*)—that is, cast off or remove—those Asuras with your "wheel," meaning with a weapon possessing power equal to a wheel, or with the thunderbolt (*vajra*) in the form of a wheel.
The sense is that he should drive them away.
Send forth a well-fashioned hymn to the great, fierce, and powerful one, the most auspicious for our cattle;
offer many songs to Indra, who is fond of praise, for his own body—for will he not surely take notice?

O Mahā, send forth a well-fashioned hymn to the fierce and powerful one, to him who is most auspicious for the sake of cattle; offer many songs to Indra, the lover of praise, for his own body; surely he will know it well. 10.

O singer, direct—urge forward—an excellent hymn (*suvṛkti*) toward Indra, who is great (*maha*) through his qualities, fierce (*ugra*) in strength, powerful (*tavas*), highly exalted (*pravṛddha*), and most auspicious (*śivatama*). (The root *tu* signifies increase. Direct this beautiful praise toward him.
Do it.
For what purpose?
To see [the horse].
Of the animal—
whether two-footed or four-footed—
for my own cow or bull.
Alternatively, impel the praise toward Indra so that he may grant the animal its perceived object beyond the senses—such as wealth—and so that he may bestow happiness and other benefits upon the cow.
This very point is stated:
O singer, "to Indra, who is invoked by songs," "who is praised with hymns," "offer" or "compose" "many" (pūrvīḥ) "songs" (giraḥ), that is, praises.
Then that Indra [thought]: "For the sake of the body; he extends the lineage"—this is the meaning according to the manuscripts kha, ta1, ta2, and bha.
The meaning is that his strength comes about through the drinking of Soma.
2. From the two-footed and the four-footed.
3. ga—°ratīndriyārtham; ta1, bha—°ratīndriyārtham.

**33.** *tanūstanayaḥ* | To that son, or to his own body, [O Indra], grant (*vevat*)—the word *kuvit* is a synonym for "much"—much wealth; indeed, quickly (*aṅga*). [The root] *vid* means "to obtain. The augment *leṭ* is added. Due to its connection with the word *kuvit*, there is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*). **11.** *ukthavāhase vimbai manīṣāṃ duṇā na pāramīrayā nadīnām | ni spṛśa dhiyā tanvi śrutasya juṣṭatarasya kuvidaṅga vedat ||* O singer, for the sake of Indra—who carries the hymns (*ukthavāhas*), who is vast (*vimba*), or rather, the subduer of enemies—urge forth (*īraya*) a prayer (*manīṣā*), a mental impulse of praise. Therein is an illustration: just as a boatman (*duṇā*) brings a traveler to the further shore of roaring rivers by means of a boat, so cause the praise to reach Indra. Furthermore, touch (*ni spṛśa*)—that is, bring—the wealth within yourself or in your son. Of what kind? Belonging to the one who is renowned everywhere (*śrutasya*), the well-known, and the most beloved (*juṣṭatarasya*) Indra. Bring that wealth to yourself through your prayer (*dhiyā*), whether by praise or by ritual action. Then Indra, being invoked by you, will surely (*kuvit*) and quickly (*aṅga*) bestow (*vedat*) much wealth. **12.** *tadviddhi yatta indro jujoṣattuhi suṣṭutiṃ namasā vivāsa | upa bhūṣa jaritarmā ruvaṇyaḥ śrāvaya vācai kuvidaṅga vedat ||* O priest, know (*viddhi*) that Soma-offering or hymn; perform them for the sake of Indra. Whatever offering or hymn belongs to you, may Indra enjoy (*jujoṣat*) it; perform that. [The root] *jupī* means "to please" or "to serve. In the *leṭ* tense, *śap* becomes *śru*; the augment *aṭ* is added. Due to Vedic usage, there is no prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable. O singer, praise (*stuhi*) him who possesses beautiful praise (*suṣṭuti*). Likewise, with reverence (*namasā*)—through hymns or offerings—serve (*vivāsa*) Indra face-to-face. [The root] *vivāsati* means "to serve. This is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*). O singer, adorn (*upa bhūṣa*) yourself. [The root] *bhūṣa* means "to decorate"; be adorned. Do not wail (*mā ruvaṇyaḥ*) due to lack of wealth; do not cry out. He states the reason for the arrival of wealth: O singer, make Indra hear (*śrāvaya*) your voice—that is, make him know your hymn. Then Indra, praised by you, will surely and quickly grant you much wealth. **13.** *ava drapso aṃśumatīmatiṣṭhadīyānaḥ kṛṣṇo daśabhiḥ sahasraiḥ | āvartamindraḥ śacyā dhamantaṃ upa slehītīrmaṇā adhatta ||* The dark drop (*drapsa*), moving along, descended into the *Aṃśumatī* river with ten thousand [followers]. Indra, by his power (*śacyā*), turned back the one who was blowing [the breath of life]; he embraced him with his mind and established him as a source of nourishment (*īrmā*). [In the Pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha rites, during the Ukthya sacrifices, this triplet beginning with "ava drapsaḥ" is used in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s recitation at the third pressing. It is stated in the Sūtra: "ava drapso aṃśumatīm atiṣṭhat... these three verses, and 'acchā ma indram' is the constant daily hymn. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.3) [Note: The provided text contains a mix of commentary and the original verse. The translation above reflects the structure of the verses and their respective commentaries.]

1. For the sake of the meaning of *kha-īra*. 2. According to *kha*, *gha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa*, one should read *gamayet*. 3. According to *kha*, *gha*, *jña*, *ta* (1 & 2), and *aṅga*, [read] *kṣipram*. 4. According to *gha*, [read] *aṅga kṣipraṃ vedat*. 5. According to *kha*, *ta*, and *śa*, [the reading is] *pūkteṣu*; according to *bha* (1), *°pūkteṣu*. Arva. Drapsaḥ. Aṃśumatīm. Atiṣṭhat. Iyānaḥ. Kṛṣṇaḥ. Daśabhiḥ. Sahasraiḥ. Ārvat. Tam. Indraḥ. Śacyā. Dharmantam. Apa. Snehitīḥ. Nuḍmanāḥ. Adhatta. || 13 || The steed, the drop, moving along, stood upon the sun-filled river. The black one, with ten thousand [steeds], ran forth. Him, as he was being heated by power, Indra, with his skillful mind, cast off the oily drops. || 13 ||
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:
An asura named Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by ten thousand asuras, was staying on the bank of a river called Saṃśumatī.
While that Kṛṣṇa was situated in the middle of the water, Indra arrived there together with Bṛhaspati.
Having arrived, he, accompanied by Bṛhaspati, struck Kṛṣṇa and his followers;
some say otherwise,
and the reason for their account is as follows.
The word *drapsa* denotes a drop of water; however, in passages such as "That drop of Soma fell" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.17.11), it is stated with reference to Soma.
Relying on this term, they say: "But Soma, afflicted by fear of Vṛtra, having departed from the gods..."
He stood upon the river named Maṃśumatī, facing toward the Kurus;
there, that planet, along with the others, was eclipsed by Bṛhaspati alone.

*Vāji* means battle; [the phrase] "in that [battle], fight and strike" [is used]. Because there is a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*), there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation). Some read "iṣyāmi vo marutaḥ"; in that case, the meaning becomes "O Maruts, I desire you."

The drop, swelling in might, held his body within the lap of Aṃśumatī; with Bṛhaspati as his ally, Indra overcame all the godless ones who were advancing against him. 15. *ardha*: half; *drapsaḥ*: the drop; *aṃśumatyāḥ*: of Aṃśumatī; *upasthe*: in the lap; *adhārayat*: he held; *tanvam*: his body; *tiviṣāṇaḥ*: swelling in power; *viśvaḥ*: all; *adaivīḥ*: the godless ones; *abhi*: towards; *ā'carantīḥ*: those who were advancing; *bṛhaspatinā*: with Bṛhaspati; *yujā*: as an ally; *indraḥ*: Indra; *sasahe*: he overcame. 15.
Just as a black drop, moving swiftly, having shone intensely in the vicinity— that is, in the lap— of the river Vaṃśumatī, sustains its own body, bearing it so that it cannot be harmed by others;
or rather, for the sake of attaining strength.
He now states that he has slain Śuṣṇa as well:

"With *vadhraiḥ*—weapons that are instruments of striking—you [attacked] Śuṣṇa. The designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) applies here according to the rule: "The mention of the action must be made."
The genitive case is used here according to the rule "caturthyarthe bahulam" (Pāṇini 2.3.62). You struck Śuṣṇa;
you slew him by turning him face-downward for the sake of Kutsa, the royal seer.
And thus says the Nigama: “For Kutsa, you struck down the insatiable Śuṣṇa” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.16.12).
Likewise, O Indra, by means of *śacī*—your own wisdom or action—you found the cattle [of the enemies] after slaying those enemies; that is, you recovered their cattle.
Or else:
Having seized the cattle of the Paṇis from the Aṅgirases, you obtained them.
O Bull among the people, you have indeed become the slayer of Vṛtras and the possessor of great power;
you set free the obstructed rivers and you conquered the waters whose lord was the Dāsa.
O Bull among the peoples, you indeed have become the slayer of Vṛtras and the possessor of great power; you released the obstructed rivers and you conquered the waters whose lord was the Dāsa.

He is the slayer of Vṛtra, Indra, the sustainer of the people; him we shall invoke with fair praise as one to be called upon. He is our protector, the bounteous lord, our advocate; he is the giver of strength that brings renown. 2.
Vṛtrahā, the slayer of Vṛtra, that Indra is the supporter of the people (carṣaṇīdhṛt), the nourisher of human beings through the granting of wealth.
We shall invoke that Indra with a beautiful hymn (sustutyā) at our sacrifices; we call him.
If you ask for what purpose we invoke you, we shall state the reason.
That Indra becomes our protector (*prāvitā*), guarding us preeminently. Furthermore, Maghavan, the possessor of wealth, becomes our advocate (*adhivaktā*), speaking on our behalf with great honor—
or rather, [speaking for us].
He ought to speak of us as superior by means of the gift of wealth;
here the suffix *tṛc* is used according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.169, *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*.
Furthermore, that very Indra [is the master] of *vāja*, which is food, for the sake of *śravasya*, that is, for the sake of *śravas*, or fame.
Or rather:
he indeed becomes a giver for the sake of *śravas*, that is, food, and for the sake of *vāja*, that is, strength.
Therefore, we invoke Indra, who possesses such qualities.

He, the slayer of Vṛtra, Indra, the lord of the Ṛbhus, as soon as he was born, became one to be invoked; performing many manly deeds, like Soma when drunk, he is to be invoked by his friends. 21. He; the slayer of Vṛtra; Indra; the lord of the Ṛbhus; immediately; having been born; became one to be invoked; performing; manly deeds; many; like Soma; when drunk; to be invoked; by his friends. 21.
Ṛbhukṣāḥ is great;
or rather,
the word *ṛbhu* includes its constituent parts (*avayava*).

He dwells together with the Ṛbhus, meaning he resides with them; such is that Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra. Being born—that is, manifesting—at that very moment, he immediately became one to be invoked by all singers and sacrificers.
Furthermore, [he performed] heroic deeds, manly acts.
Men are human beings who lead by means of action (*karman*).

Performing many great deeds (*apāṃsi*) for their benefit—that is, performing them for his friends, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are his allies because they assist him by the offering of oblations—he became one who is to be invoked (*havyaḥ*), or worthy of invocation.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as Soma, when drunk, is to be offered in sacrifice and must be invoked by the gods while producing fruits such as heaven, so it is in this case.
The fourth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "yā indra," is addressed to Indra; it is the seerly composition of Rebha Kāśyapa.
The tenth verse is an atijagatī of fifty-two syllables.
The eleventh and twelfth verses are upariṣṭādbṛhatīs, each having eight syllables followed by twelve.
The thirteenth is an atijagatī;
the fourteenth is a triṣṭubh;
the fifteenth is a jagatī.

And the remaining [verses] are enumerated: "O Indra, those five less [than ten], by Rebha Kāśyapa; the Bṛhatī, the Atijagatī, the Pariṣṭhā, the two Vṛtrahan verses, the Jagatī, the Triṣṭubh, and the final Jagatī.
The application of the hymn is based on its indicative marks (liṅga).
In the Niṣkevalya of the Mahāvrata, the verses beginning with "yā indra" constitute the Bṛhatī-uchvāśīti.
Likewise, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: “*yā indra bhuja ābhara*—these nine are the *sūdadohas* verses” (*Ai. Ā. 5.2.4*).

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), the two optional *anurūpa* verses beginning with “*yā indra*” constitute the second and third [of the set] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
And it is prescribed: “*tamindraṃ johavīmi*, *yā indra bhuja ābhara*—one and two [verses]” (*Āśv. Śr. S. 7.4*).

O Indra, possessor of light, those enjoyments which you brought from the Asuras—O Maghavan, increase the singer of this praise and those who have trimmed the sacrificial grass for you. yā | indra | bhujaḥ | ā | ābharaḥ | svarvān | asurebhyaḥ | stotāram | it | maghavan | asya | vardhaya | ye | ca | tve | vṛktabarhiṣaḥ || 1 ||

The seer prays to Indra: O Indra, possessor of *svar*— whether meaning happiness, heaven, or, alternatively, the word *svar* being a synonym for "all," meaning the entire host of beings, since they have arisen from the Self alone as their source— you, endowed with such qualities,
