brought forth (*ābharaḥ*) those things to be enjoyed (*yāḥ*), namely riches (*bhujaḥ*), from the *asuras*— the powerful Rākṣasas— having slain them, you have taken them away.
By the rule "hraprahoḥ," there is the substitution of *bh* [for *gh*].
Therefore, O *maghavan*, O wealthy Indra, [the word] "asya" [is used];
in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), there is the substitution of *aś*.
By the gift of this unassailable wealth, cause your very praiser—the one who performs your praise—to flourish;
make him prosperous. And those other sacrificers who, for their own sake, have spread the sacrificial grass (vṛktabarhiṣaḥ), cause them also to flourish with wealth.

O Indra, that imperishable portion consisting of horses and cattle which you have held in reserve—bestow it upon that sacrificer who presses the Soma and gives the sacrificial fee, not upon the usurer. 2. yam | indra | dadhiṣe | tvam | aśvam | gām | bhāgam | avyayam | yajamāne | sunvati | dakṣiṇā'vati | tasmin | tam | dhehi | mā | paṇau || 2 ||

O Indra, you— who take away from the enemies the horse (the means of travel), the two bay steeds (harī), the cow (which assists in the Agnihotra rite by providing the path), the undecaying wealth (avyayam bhāgam— wealth that is inexhaustible and worthy of being enjoyed)— place all of these in that sacrificer who presses the Soma, who possesses sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇāvati), and who bestows those fees upon the officiating priests while performing the sacrifice. Grant him all this.
He says: "Do not give wealth and so forth in every case.
Regarding *mā paṇau*: the root *paṇ* means "to bargain" (*vyavahāre*).
A person who deals in goods and the like is called a *paṇin*;
do not give all of this to such a person.

O Indra, that one who sleeps while lacking vows, who is devoid of divine intent through his own ways—drive him far away from there, and bestow upon us wealth that nourishes our household. O Indra, he who sleeps, being lawless, following the sleep of the godless through his own ways—he, O Muru, drive him far away; bestow upon us that wealth which brings prosperity.
O Indra, he who is godless— desiring none among you gods— and having become one who has abandoned his vows and is devoid of ritual action, sleeps a continuous sleep as it were;
[the root] *ṣas* means "to sleep," belonging to the *adādi* class.
May that person, by his own movements alone, cause his own wealth—that which is to be nourished—to perish;

may his riches be destroyed by [the consequences of] not performing sacrifices, such as *amāgaṇ* and *pūtna*, and not by the offering of oblations to the gods. Therefore, you [should punish] that person who does not sacrifice.
Place [it], establish it, in some distant, hidden place, devoid of ritual action.

Whether you are in the distance, O Śakra, or whether you are near at hand, O Vṛtra-slayer, from there may the one who has pressed the soma invite you with songs, O Indra, using long-maned hymns at the proper time. 4. Whether you are in the distance, O Śakra, or whether you are near at hand, O Vṛtra-slayer, from there may the one who has pressed the soma invite you with songs, O Indra, using long-maned hymns at the proper time. 4.

O *Śakra*, O Indra capable of slaying enemies, when (*yat*) you are (*asi*) in the remote, most distant place—the heavenly world—O *Vṛtrahan*, O Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; and when (*yat*) you are in the near place—the intermediate space situated below that and close to it—or even from this world (*ataḥ*), [you come] swiftly (*yugata*). [The root *gam* means "to go"; with the suffix *kvip*, by the rule *gamaḥ kau*, the form *yugata* is derived.]
1. *kha-jha-ta-na-ma*—these [consonants] belong to the *yān* (palatals) and so forth.
2. *khanta-na-ma-dadhiṣe*—he places.
3. *kha-ta-na-ma-śa*—desiring you.
4. He who, having become *gha*; 5. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, and *śa*, the word "he who" (*yaḥ*) is absent;
6. She who is overcome by *ja*, *ca*, *ū*, and *ra*.
Thus, there is the elision of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa). Then the *tuk* augment is applied. Finally, by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*).
With hymns—praises that proceed everywhere like his own radiance, standing as if they were bay horses with manes—the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma seeks to win you over;
he causes you to come toward his sacrifice, or he serves you with these songs of praise. Or rather: "Since you are in the luminous realm of heaven, upon the surface of the ocean."
O slayer of Vṛtra, come from the earthly seat, or come from the intermediate space.
Whether you are in the luminous realm of heaven, upon the surface of the ocean, in the earthly dwelling, O best slayer of Vṛtra, or in the intermediate space—come hither! 5.
O Indra, whether you are in the *rocana*, the luminous place of heaven (*divaḥ*),
or whether you are in the midst of the ocean, having reached (*adhi*) some region (*viṣṭapi*) connected to it.
O supreme slayer of Vṛtra— the demon, or of evil— O Indra, whether you are present in a dwelling on earth belonging to the earthly realm,
or whether you abide in the intermediate space,
in that world; wherever you may be, nevertheless come toward our sacrifice.
O Soma-drinker, Lord of Might, rejoice with us at our pressed libations of Soma; O Indra, bestow upon us wealth abundant in truth and fullness.
O Soma-drinker, Lord of Strength, rejoice with us at our pressed Soma juices; O Indra, you who possess abundance and truth, grant us wealth that is overflowing. 6.

O Soma-drinker (*somapā*), drinker of the Soma; O Lord of Strength (*śavasas-pati*), O Indra, you who possess the previously mentioned characteristics—when the Somas have been pressed by us, do you [favor] us with *rādhas*, that is, with food that is the means of strength, or with that which is endowed with truthfulness (*sūnṛtāvat*), being free from falsehood;
or rather, since *sūnṛtā* is a name for speech, [endowed] with beautiful words.
By this, sons and so forth are indicated;
by the word "putropeta" (endowed with sons),
[the sense is] "parīṇasā" (abundant).
This [phrase] refers to much.
With much *rāyaḥ*—that is, with wealth (*dhana*)—gladden (*mādayasva*) us; that is, cause us to rejoice.
The meaning is: "Grant to us, who are the givers of Soma, food, sons, and so forth."
O Indra, do not turn us away; you are our companion at the feast.
You are our protection, O Indra, you are our kinship; O Indra, do not turn us away.
Do not turn us away, O Indra; you are our companion at the feast. You are our protection, you are our kinship, O Indra; do not turn us away, O Indra. 7.
O Indra, do not exclude us—us who are givers of oblations; do not abandon us.
The root *vṛj* (in the form *vṛṇak*) means "to avoid" or "to exclude";
it belongs to the *raudhādika* class.
This is the form in the *laṅ* tense.
He explains that very point:
"O [Indra], be one who shares the feast (*sadhamādya*) with us through Soma. (*Sadhamādyaḥ* means one whose nature is to feast together.)
Furthermore, O Indra, you alone— by means of your protection (ūtī)— establish us;
or rather,
by your aid (ūtī).
By way of exception, in the active voice (kartari):
1. [The substitution occurs] in the place of *ja*, *bha*, and *sva*;
2. in some editions—namely Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa—the word "someṣu" does not appear.

3. By means of food that accomplishes the strength of *kha*, *jha*, *ta* (1–2), *na*, *bha* (1), and *ba*; by means of food that accomplishes the strength of *ga* and *ba*; by means of food that accomplishes the strength of *ta* (3–4), *śa*, and *ba*. 4.

[The mantra] is provided for one who is devoid of *kha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*; [and] for one who is devoid of *ga* and *ja*. Or, something has been elided (*nipātita*). "You alone are indeed our protector. Thus: "you" (*it*); *id* is used as a particle of emphasis. You alone are our refuge (*āpya*) and kinsman (*jñātaya*); the meaning is that you alone are our relative (*bandhu*). For this very reason, the sense of the verse "O Indra, do not turn us away" (*mā na indra parā vṛṇak*) is already explained.

O Indra, sit down with us at the pressed juice to drink the honey-sweet draught; O Maghavan, grant great protection to the singer; O Indra, come hither with us to the pressed juice. 8. Asme indra sacā sute ni ṣadā pītaye madhu | kudhī jaritre maghavan vau mahad asme indra sacā sute || 8 || O Indra, sit down with us at the pressed juice to drink the honey-sweet draught; O Maghavan, grant great protection to the singer; O Indra, come hither with us to the pressed juice. 8.
O Indra, together with us, sit down at our sacrifice when the soma has been pressed and poured; sit down for what purpose?
For the drinking of the honeyed draught.
The elision of the case-ending *ḍas* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
For the drinking—that is, the act of drinking—of the exhilarating Soma;
furthermore, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, bestow great protection (*avaḥ*) upon the singer (*jaritre*).
When [is it]?
"O Indra, when [the soma] is pressed for us"—this quarter-verse has been explained.

Neither the gods nor mortals have attained you, O wielder of the stone; you surpass all created beings in might—neither the gods nor mortals have attained you. 9. Neither the gods nor mortals have attained you, O wielder of the stone; you surpass all created beings in might—neither the gods nor mortals have attained you. 9.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, all the gods other than you—indeed, all the gods—have not attained you; they do not encompass you through their own deeds or by their own power. Nor do mortals—human beings—encompass you.
From where is this determined? He says:

"O Viśva, you are the overcomer of all (viśvā) created beings (jātāni), that is, of all classes of living things, by your own power (śavasā), that is, by your own strength; you are the one who overcomes."
Therefore, the meaning of the verse "the gods have not attained you" has already been explained.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest, “*viśvāḥ patanāḥ*” is the optional *stotriya*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*viśvāḥ patanā abhibhūtaraṃ naraṃ tamindraṃ johavīmi*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).

All the tribes, acting in concert, have fashioned and begotten Indra, the man who overcomes all attackers, for the sake of sovereignty—him who is most excellent through his power, the chosen one, the son of Asura, the fierce, the strongest, the peerless, and the swift. viśvāḥ | patanāḥ | abhibhūtaram | naram | sajūḥ | tatakṣuḥ | indram | jajanuḥ | ca | rājasai | ṛtvā | variṣṭham | varam | āsurim | uta | ugram | ojiṣṭham | tvasam | tarasvinam || 10 ||

All (viśvāḥ) means every (sarvā). *Dhyāsāḥ* or *patanāḥ*: [the root] *pṛṣṭh* [is used] in the sense of exertion (*vyāyāma*). They are called *patanāḥ* because they are engaged in activity (*vyāpriyante*); that is, the armies (*senāḥ*).
United together, they fashioned Indra—the one who is ever-truthful, the supreme overcomer of enemies, the exceedingly victorious man, and the leader of all.
They sharpened him with weapons and the like;
the meaning is that they made him possessed of arms and endowed with power.

Alternatively, *patanā* is a name for battle; *patanāḥ* refers to battles because they are "places where [warriors] exert themselves. Having come together with one another, the singers made Indra—who overcomes all battles—sharp through their hymns of praise.
When it is praised, it becomes powerful.
Or alternatively:
by the offering of oblations, the sacrificers [attain] vigor (vīrya)—the *ga*-kicca [substitution] being a prior homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*).
2. gha—[it was] ours;
3. kha-ta-na-bha—we were occupied; śa—we are occupied; 4.
kha—the meaning is "they did"; ta-na-bha-śa—the meaning is "they did."
"They make it vomited.
Furthermore, "the praisers [act] for the sake of ruling" (*rājase*);
the suffix *ase* is used in the sense of the infinitive of the root *rāj* (to rule).

For the sake of their own glorification and for the sake of manifestation, they generated Indra, whose essence is the sun; that is to say, they brought forth his hymn of praise at the sacrifice. Moreover, by means of his own deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra, the singers made Indra—the most excellent, the most powerful, and the slayer of enemies who faces them head-on—their choice in the matter of desirable wealth.
The meaning is that they praise him for the sake of obtaining wealth for themselves.

Of what kind? They praise Indra—the fierce one (*ugra*), whose strength is upraised; therefore, the most powerful (*ojiṣṭha*), the mighty (*tavasa*), the increased (*pravṛddha*), and the impetuous (*tarasvin*)—for the sake of wealth, they praise him who possesses speed for the purpose of slaying enemies in battle.
The singers have praised Indra, the lord of heaven, who maintains his vows, for the drinking of the Soma;
may he increase our strength with his aids through his vigor.

The *rebhas* have sung forth together to Indra, for the drinking of Soma—the Lord of Heaven—when they, for his increase, praise him with oblations. For he, whose laws are firm, through his might and by his protections, comes together with the Maruts and his aids. *Rebhas*: from the root *rebh*, "to sound"; those who cause sound, the singers, the praisers. Or, *rebhas* refers to the seers named Rebha, the sons of Kaśyapa. *Īm*: him, this very Indra. *Sam asvaran*: they have sounded forth together; they have praised him fully. For what purpose? For the drinking of Soma (*somasya pītaye*). Furthermore, *svaḥpatim*: the Lord of Heaven, the protector of the celestial realm, or the master of wealth. When they praise this very Indra for his increase (*vṛdhe*) with offerings, then Indra, whose deeds are firm (*dhṛtavrataḥ*), unites with his power (*ojasā*), with the strength of the singers, and with his protections (*ūtībhiḥ*), that is, with the Maruts. The meaning is that through praises Indra gains strength, and through the Maruts, protection.
The inspired poets, with their songs, bow down to the rim of the wheel, to the ram that is the object of their invocation;
your brilliant rays are inexhaustible, reaching even to the ear of the swift one along with the hymns of praise.

The wise ones bow down with their vision to him who is like a felly; the inspired singers, full of splendor and free from malice, praise him with hymns near his ear, O swift one. Just as spokes reach the felly, so he pervades all; to such Indra, whose nature is to bend [toward his devotees], they bow down by mere sight. The Kāśyapas, the Rebhas, or the praisers, offer their salutations. Then the wise ones bow down to Indra in the form of a ram (*meṣam*). Indra, having become a ram, led Medhātithi to heaven; therefore, the inspired singers bow down to Indra who has become a ram, by means of "invoking songs" (*abhisvarāḥ*), that is, through hymns of praise. Now the sacrificer speaks to the praisers: "Moreover, O you of beautiful luster (*sudītayaḥ*), you who are free from malice toward anyone (*aduhaḥ*), you who are swift in action or in hymns (*tarasvinaḥ*), being joined with the *svar* (chant), [you praise] Indra near his ear (*karṇe*) with *arkas*—that is, with mantras joined to worship—or rather, with those liturgical recitations (*śastra*) which contain many *ṛc* verses. The meaning is: "Praise him thoroughly so that Indra hears your hymns and recitations. This very same rule is illustrated in the aforementioned scripture by the optional *anurūpa* verse beginning with "That Indra," etc.; thus the Sūtra is cited.
I invoke that Indra, the bounteous and fierce one, who truly bestows and establishes manifold powers.
May he, the most generous and worthy of sacrifice, being entreated with songs, prepare all fair paths for us; may the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, do so for us.

In the *Āśvamedhika* [section], this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and oblation (*havis*) of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), because it is seen in another *sūtra*: "I invoke that Indra; through Indra's favor... and "He who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin," and so forth. Since its authority regarding the subject matter is established even in other *sūtras*, one should prepare the *caru*.

I call upon that Indra, the fierce subduer of enemies, who truly possesses irresistible powers. May he, the most bountiful and worthy of sacrifice, turn toward us with his songs; may the wielder of the thunderbolt make all paths easy for our wealth. 13.

I repeatedly invoke— that is, I call upon again and again— that Indra who is endowed with the qualities previously mentioned. Regarding the form *hūyate*, the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "and [the reduplication] of a repeated [root]."

Of what sort? I invoke Maghavan, who possesses abundant wealth worthy of being honored; the fierce one, whose strength is aroused; who truly and according to reality maintains powers of might; and for that very reason, who is unassailable and cannot be resisted by enemies.

Furthermore, may Indra—the most worshipful, the greatest giver, or the one worthy of sacrifice—be turned toward us by our songs of praise, and may he turn toward the sacrifices with his face directed hitherward.
The form *vartate* also occurs with the suffix *caṅ*; there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because of the rule "the first word [is unaccented] when joined with *ca* or *vā*.
The accent is determined by the rule "in the case of *caṅ*, optionally [the first syllable is acute]."
Then may Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), make for us all paths indeed easy to travel (*supathā*) for the sake of wealth (*rāye*);
that is to say, may wealth situated in every direction come to us.
O Indra, you have always known how to destroy with your might, O most powerful Śakra;
at your command, O wielder of the thunderbolt, all beings tremble, and both heaven and earth shake with fear.

O Indra, you who are most powerful and mighty, take note of them and destroy them with your strength, O Śakra! Before you, O wielder of the thunderbolt, all beings tremble, and both heaven and earth shake with fear. 14.

O *śaviṣṭha*, most powerful; therefore, O *śakra*, capable of slaying enemies; O *indra*, you—*enāḥ* (referring back to these)—these *puraḥ*, the fortresses of Śambara, you shall *vi nāśayadhyai*, destroy by means of *ojasā*, your own splendor. You are *cikit*, the knower.
The suffix *śatṛ* occurs after a root ending in *naś*.
Furthermore, the capacity [of the word] praises [the Lord]:
O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, all *bhuvanāni*, the multitudes of beings, tremble out of fear of *tvat*, you.
Likewise, in the case of *dyāvāpṛthivī*:
by the rule *divo dyāvā*, *dyāvā* is the substitute for *div*, and it is also acute-accented (*ādyudātta*).
The word *pṛthivī* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because of its status as a *dīpta* (flaming) word.
By the rule *‘devatādvandve ca’*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for both members of the compound;
however, the separation [of the two words] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
And heaven and earth tremble—that is, they shake—out of fear, out of dread of you.
The Vedic citation is: “The two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.31.3).
The meaning is that all things are dependent upon you.
O Indra, O hero, O wonderful one, may that truth protect me; O wielder of the thunderbolt, carry me across many dangers as if across waters.
O King, when will you grant us wealth—wealth that provides for all, wealth that is desirable?

O Indra, Hero, Wondrous One, may that Truth protect us! O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, carry us across many misfortunes as if across waters. O King Indra, when will you grant us wealth—wealth that sustains all and is worthy of longing?
O *śūra* (hero), O *balavat* (mighty one), O *citra* (wondrous)— meaning one who is to be admired or who possesses manifold forms—
since it is seen in such passages as "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 6.47.18);
O Indra of manifold forms, may that *ṛtam* (truth) of yours, which is *praśastam* (praiseworthy), *mām* (me) *pātu* (protect), guarding me from all sides.
Furthermore, O wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrin), O Indra, carry us across— beyond—
the many (bhūri) difficulties (duritā), that is, the numerous evils (pāpāni). Carry us across.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Just as a boatman carries people across the waters, so do you carry us across our sins.
O radiant King, O Indra, [carry us across] that which is all-sustaining.
*Pasa’* is the name for form (*rūpa*). It is derived from the root *pyai* (to swell) with reference to form; the addition of the letter *n* is a Vedic archaism.
That multiform [state] is "desirable" (spṛhayāyya), meaning it is desirable by all;
[this is the sense of] vrāya.
By the rule "kriyāgrahaṇam," the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is applied;
by the rule "caturthyarthe bahulam," the genitive case is used.
To that forest (*vana*), for us (*naḥ*) or for ourselves (*asmabhyam*), when (*kadā*) or at what time (*kasmin kāle*) will you (*tvam*) bestow it (*daśāsye*) directly (*ābhimukhyena*)?
The meaning is: "Then let Your own true nature protect me;
having given me wealth and having caused me to perform the rites, make me free from sin.
May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four goals of human existence.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the sixth book in the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the seventh chapter of the sixth [book] begins.
Therein, the fifth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "indrāya," belongs to Nṛmedha Āṅgirasa.

O Indra, lover of songs, we now indeed offer great desires unto you—hymns that are most desirable—just as those going forth with water sprinkle people standing nearby with their hands full of water for sport. (7) O Hero, O wielder of the thunderbolt, the priests increase you with their prayers, even though you have already grown great, day after day, just as rivers increase the waters of a reservoir. (8)
For you indeed, O Vasu, have become our father; O Śatakratu, you have become our mother.

O Vasu—O indweller, O Śatakratu, O Indra of many deeds—you have become our father, a protector like a father; you have become our mother, a nurturer like a mother. And now, we beg for your *sumna*—your easily attained favor. We beg for your favor. 11.
O impetuous one, much-invoked, lord of a hundred powers, I address you who are eager for the prize;
as such, grant us great heroic strength.
O powerful one, invoked by many, you who are eager for the prize—I address you, O Śatakratu! As such, grant us heroic strength. 12.
O powerful one, O much-invoked, O Indra of a hundred powers and many deeds, I address you—desiring strength, I praise you.
As such, grant us, bestow upon us, wealth consisting of heroic sons.
The sixth hymn, beginning with “tvāmidā hyaḥ,” is a prayer to Indra composed by Nṛmedha.
The odd-numbered verses are Bṛhatīs and the even-numbered verses are Satobṛhatīs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: “tvāmidāhyau prāgātham.”
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), there is for the Acchāvāka the [hymn] beginning with *tvām idā hyaḥ* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
At the Mahāvrata as well, in the Niṣkevalya [laud], there is a Pragātha consisting of Bārhata verses.
Likewise, it is prescribed in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: “He places this Pragātha, *tvām idā hyo naraḥ*, [in its proper position]” (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.4).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the optional *stotriya* *pragātha* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is “śrāyantaiva” [RV 7.60.1–2].
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “śrāyantaiva sūrya baṇ mahā~ asi sūrya” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, [the *uktha*] is “tvam indra pratitiṣu tvam indra yaśā asi” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
On that very day, this Pragātha, which has the Vairāja as its source, is to be recited in the Niṣkevalya;

and it is stated in the Sūtra: “Of those two [Śastras], one should recite the source of the one not being performed, along with the Dhur verses in the Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata meters” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.3).
Yesterday, O Indra, the men, eager for booty and seeking wealth, made you drink [the soma].
Therefore, O Indra, listen here to those who bring hymns of praise; come quickly with your swift steeds.
The zealous men made you drink yesterday; O wielder of the thunderbolt, they have satisfied you. Therefore, O Indra, listen here to those who bring hymns of praise; come hither to our assembly. 1.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, you whom the zealous *naras*— the leaders of rites, the sacrificers— have caused to swell with oblations both today and yesterday; as such, listen here at this sacrifice to our hymn, which brings praise, and [listen] to our dwelling,
for "dwellings" (*svasarāṇi*) are listed among the names for houses.
Come hither; approach.

Rejoice, O fair-jawed one; we implore that golden [splendor] from you. The wise ones attend upon you; O Indra, lover of songs, you possess the highest glories worthy of praise when the juices are pressed.
1. [The syllables] ga, gha, jha, ṭṛ, l, v, na, yaṃ, tvāṃ; ta3-4-yaṃ, tāṃ; śa-yaṃ, taṃ. 2. kha, ta, śa, vā. 3. ga-havirbharaṇa.

O wearer of the golden helmet, O lord of bay horses, we pray for that [favor] from you. To you the wise ones turn their attention; yours are the most exalted and praiseworthy glories, O Indra, lover of songs, when the juices are pressed.

O *suśipra*, you of beautiful jaws or beautiful turban; O *harivas*, possessor of horses; O *girvaṇas*, Indra, worthy of praise with songs—within you, the *vedhasas*, the performers of worship, attend and serve.
Rejoice in the Soma that intoxicates!
Furthermore, we entreat this very thing from you.
To the question "What is to be requested?", he says:
while the Soma juices are being pressed out, may your glories—your foods—which are supreme, that is, comparable to the highest, and which are worthy of praise, be present.
Like the rays in the sun, may all enjoy the riches of Indra; at every birth, we shall hold fast to our portion with vigor.
Like birds toward the sun, may they all enjoy the riches of Indra; at his birth and at his being born with might, we have looked forward to our portion as to a gift.

Just as our people, like rays of light resting upon the sun, partake of the sun, so too do they partake of all the riches of Indra from every side. And whatever treasures he creates by his power for those born, those already living, and those yet to be born—those riches we shall hold fast, as if they were our own ancestral portion.
Or alternatively: [the previous interpretation].

Just as all the rays, having resorted to the sun, wait upon the sun, so too do all the Maruts, desiring to distribute [the wealth], having resorted to Indra, wait upon Indra—this is the sense remaining.

And having waited upon him, the Maruts, by means of their *ojas* (vital power), distribute and bestow the riches characterized by water (*vasūni*) upon the human being who has been born, who is being born, who is currently being born, and who is yet to be born.
And therein, that portion which is ours—that portion [they grant].
"Neti" has the sense of "not. "Pratīti" is used in place of "anviti. "Anu dīdhiima" means "we shall meditate upon."

And thus Yāska says: "They stand near the sun, having taken refuge [in it]. Or rather, it may be used in a figurative sense: 'they stand near Indra, the sun,' meaning they are about to partake of all of Indra's riches."
"Just as he distributes wealth for those already born and those yet to be born, we shall meditate upon that portion" (Nirukta 6.7).
Praise him who grants wealth and whose gifts are free from harm; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. He does not frustrate the desire of the one who serves him, but impels his mind toward giving.

Praise him who is free from malice toward the giver, the bestower of wealth; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. He does not frustrate the desire of the one who honors him, but stirs his mind toward giving. 4.
O singer, [praise him who is] *anarśarāti*, meaning one whose giving is not evil—that is, a giver of what is most free from evil.
And thus Yāska says: "Anarśarāti means one whose gift is not base; 'base' (*aślīla*) means evil (*pāpaka*). (Nirukta 6.23).
Praise Indra, the giver of wealth, the bestower of riches;
for Indra’s gifts are auspicious and beneficial—
meaning they bring about great sovereignty.
And since that Indra, impelling his own mind toward giving—that is, toward the bestowing of desired gifts—does not frustrate, nor does he harm, the desire or wish of this worshiper who serves him.

O Indra, in battles you overcome all adversaries; you are the destroyer of curses, the progenitor [of power], and the subduer of all. O Indra, the crusher of enemies, you overcome those who seek to harm us. O Indra, in the onsets of battle, you prevail over all rival armies. Furthermore, O Indra, the crusher of foes, you are the destroyer of divine curses and the progenitor of power against the Asuras; you are the slayer of every host of enemies and the one who strikes down those who would oppress us.

The two worlds followed after your surging strength, as two mothers follow their child; all your rivals were relaxed before your wrath when you, O Indra, overcame Vṛtra. O Indra, the two worlds—Heaven and Earth—followed after your *śuṣma*, your victorious and crushing power, just as two mother-cows follow their young calf. This is merely a simile for their following. Furthermore, O Indra, because you (*yat*) overcome (*turvasi*) and slay the enemy Vṛtra, therefore (*ataḥ*) all (*viśvāḥ*) your rivals (*spṛdhaḥ*), the armies that wage war, are relaxed (*śrathayanta*); they become weakened and distressed before your fury (*manyave*).

O our people! For your sake—bring hither, that is, place in front, for the sake of protection, Indra: the ageless (ajaram), free from decay; the impeller (prahetāram), the driver of enemies; the unimpelled (aprahitam), not sent by anyone else; the swift (āśum), possessing speed; the conqueror (jetāram) of foes; the sender (hetāram), the goer; the best of charioteers (rathītamam), the most excellent among those who ride in chariots; the unconquered (atūrtam), unharmed by anyone; and the increaser of the waters (tubhyāvṛdham), the one who causes the waters to swell. Bring him from here for your aid. That is to say, honor him.

We invoke for protection the common Indra, the fashioner, the perfecter, the one made of strength, the hundred-formed, the hundred-willed, the possessor of wealth, who bestows wealth. 8. Fashioner. We invoke Indra for protection—for our defense—him who is the overcomer of enemies, the one who is closely joined [to his chariot], the self-fashioned one not adorned by others, the one made by force, the one of a hundred forms (or many protections), the one of a hundred rites (or much wisdom), or the one of many deeds; the one common to many, the possessor of wealth who covers [us] with riches, the impeller of treasures toward the sacrificers, Indra we invoke for our aid. We call upon him.
The seventh hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "atha te," has Nema of the Bhrigu lineage as its seer.

Regarding the two verses beginning with "ayamasmi jaritaḥ," Indra approached Nema and proclaimed his own majesty; therefore, he alone is the seer of that duet, according to the principle: "He whose words [they are], he is the seer" (Anuvāka 2.4).
The sixth verse is in the Jagatī meter.
The first three verses, beginning with the seventh, are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
the remaining ones are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Indra is the deity.

The two verses beginning with "yadvāgvadantī" and "devīṃ vācam" belong to Vāc; the remaining ones belong to Indra. Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "This [hymn] for you consists of twelve verses; [it belongs to] Bhārgava, is in the Triṣṭubh metre, the sixth is in Jagatī, there are three Paṅktis, three Anuṣṭubhs, and two [verses] beginning with 'ayam'; [these] two are addressed to Indra; he praised himself; the last two but one are to be recited for Vāc.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāc, "yadvāgvadantī" is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the omentum (vapā).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "That which the speechless birds utter, the winged one bears in his mind" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
Regarding the aforementioned animal sacrifice, "The divine speech" is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'The gods generated the divine speech,' 'As if desiring a wife,' and 'Now, O singer'—these three [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
At the time of departure, upon hearing unpleasant words from people, one should mutter these [hymns].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should mutter the hymn beginning with 'kanikradajjanuṣaṃ prabuvāṇaḥ' and also the verse 'devīṃ vācamajanayanta devāḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.10.9).

This one, with my body, goes before you; all the gods follow behind me. When, O Indra, you grant me a long-lasting portion, then indeed, together with me, you shall perform heroic deeds. O Indra, this one—myself—with my body, goes before you to overcome the enemies. As I go before you, all the gods follow behind me along with you. When you, O Indra, grant me, the descendant of Bhṛgu, a long-lasting portion—that is, a share held among the enemies—then immediately thereafter, together with me, you shall perform heroic deeds, that is, display manly prowess to conquer my enemies. The sense is: if you intend to give me the wealth held by the enemies, then provide assistance to me as I go forth with my son to defeat those foes.

I place before you a draught of honey; let the pressed Soma be set as your portion. And may you be my friend at my right hand; then we two shall strike down many Vṛtras. O Indra, I place before you first a draught of the intoxicating Soma; let the pressed, enjoyable Soma be set within your heart. Furthermore, being my friend, may you abide at my right side. Then we two—both you and I—shall slay many Vṛtras, our enemies.
Bring forth a beautiful hymn of praise, seeking booty for Indra, if truth indeed exists;
"Indra does not exist"—no one has ever said this, for who has seen him? To whom shall we speak?

O people, you who are *vājayantaḥ*— desiring battle,

for "in the battle for strength" (*pausye vāje*) is listed among the names for combat— bring forth well (*su pra bharata*) a true (*satyam*), that is, a real (*satyabhūtam*), hymn (*stomam*) for Indra.
"If this 'Indra exists' is true," [it would be so]. What doubt could there be regarding Indra's existence? To that, he says:

He shows the reason for this:
"Who has seen him, this Indra?"—that is, who has beheld him?
No one saw [him]. Therefore, whom shall we praise? Whom shall we extol? Him.

All these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at all the Soma-pressings, O Maghavan Indra, which you performed for the one who presses the juice—when you opened up the wealth gathered from afar for Śarabha, the kinsman of the seers.

Seeing Indra who had come into his presence, the delighted seer praises Indra’s various deeds and his generosity with the verse beginning, “*viśvattā te*. O bountiful Indra, whatever deeds you have performed (*cakratha*) for the sacrificer who presses the Soma at the *savanas*—those very deeds of yours are to be proclaimed (*pravācyā*); indeed, they are all infinite (*viśvet*).
Furthermore, you opened up for Śarabha—the kinsman of the Ṛṣis—the wealth belonging to a certain king named Pārāvata;
you made it accessible, so that it was well-accumulated and abundant.
Now run forth in different directions, each toward him who has held you back!
Indra has hurled his thunderbolt down upon the vital organ of Vṛtra.
Run forth now, each in a different direction! He who has held you back here—Indra has driven his thunderbolt down into the vital organ of Vṛtra. || 7 ||

Against that enemy Vṛtra—who now indeed runs away, who stands apart from you here one by one, and who neither covers you nor confuses you—Indra has hurled his thunderbolt, the kuliśa, deep into the vital spot, the very seat of his life-force.
Moving with the speed of thought, he crossed the iron fortress;
having gone to heaven like a well-winged bird, he brought the Soma for the wielder of the thunderbolt.

Suparṇa Garuḍa, swift as thought and possessing the speed of the mind, traveling while approaching, crossed over—that is, he traversed—the iron and golden city, the fortress.
Then, having gone to heaven, the celestial realm, he brought the Soma to Vajrin, Indra.
Within the ocean lies the thunderbolt, enveloped by water;
they bring it tribute, gathered together, as it flows forth.
Within the ocean he lies; the sea-monsters bear him up, surrounded by the thunderbolt. To him, as he stands ready, they bring tribute from the eastward-flowing rivers. 9.

That thunderbolt which lies within the ocean, in the midst of the ocean—that thunderbolt for which the enemies who advance from the front, surrounded by water, bear and offer tribute; for the word *saṃyataḥ* is listed among the names for battle in the sense of "conflict. They bring and maintain this offering.
The meaning is that they become objects to be cut by him.

When Vāk—the sovereign, possessing the nature of a ruler, the delightful one who gladdens the gods—having sat down at the sacrifice, proclaiming and making known those things that are devoid of consciousness and unperceived, then she milked out for the four quarters *ūrj* (nutritive food) and *payāṃsi* (waters), which are the causes thereof.
As for that supreme and most excellent essence belonging to her, the intermediate Speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*), as to where it has gone or goes, it is not seen; such is the meaning.

And thus Yāska says: "Or rather, 'That which they call the unconscious cognitions, the queen of the gods has sat down, the delightful one; the intoxicating [cow] has yielded strength and milk toward the four quarters. Who indeed has reached her highest [abode]? She goes to her own earth, or it is that which the rays of the sun carry away' (Nirukta 11.28)."

The gods generated the goddess Speech; animals of every form speak her. May that cow-like Speech, the delightful one, yielding for us food and vigor, come to us with fair praise. (11) The gods generated the goddess, the radiant Speech belonging to the intermediate region (*mādhyamikā*); she is the proclaimer of *dharma*, pervading all living beings. This verse demonstrates her sovereign power: the gods—the deities of the intermediate region—generated that goddess Speech. Animals of every form (*viśvarūpāḥ*), both those with articulate speech and those with inarticulate speech, speak her; for the activity of speech is preceded by her. That goddess Speech—*mandrā*, meaning exhilarating, praiseworthy, or gladdening through the bestowal of rain—yielding for us *iṣam* (food) and *ūrjam* (vigor, such as milk, clarified butter, and other essences), flowing like a cow, and being well-praised (*suṣṭutā*) by us, may she come to us; that is, may she approach us, intent upon raining. Thus says Yāska: "The gods generated the goddess Speech; animals of every form, both articulate and inarticulate, speak her. May that Speech, the cow, yielding for us exhilaration and essence, come to us with fair praise" (Nirukta 11.29).

"May these rivers, thus released, go forth by the impulse and impulsion of Indra. Summarizing this matter, Śaunaka shows it through verses: "Vṛtra stood obstructing these three worlds with his own destructive power."
Indra was unable to devour him; approaching Viṣṇu, he said to him:
"I shall slay Vṛtra; stand by my side, exerting your prowess."
As he raised his thunderbolt, it left an opening for me;
saying "So be it," Viṣṇu stayed it, and the earth gave him a fissure.
"All this has been declared, O friend Viṣṇu, by the skin," thus [it is said in] Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.121–124.
The eighth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with “ṛdhak,” is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: “*ṛdhak*: sixteen verses; Jamadagni Bhārgava [is the seer]; it is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; it is in the Prāgātha metre, ending with three Triṣṭubhs; from the third verse onwards it is Gāyatrī and Satobṛhatī; it is a Stotra; the two verses concerning the Rājasūya sacrifice are addressed to the Ādityas; the two verses concerning the Aśvins are addressed to Vāyu; the two verses beginning with *bṛhat* are for the purpose of worship; they are either praises of the splendor of the Sun or Pāvamānī verses in prose. Thus, the seer (ṛṣi) is Jamadagni of the Bhṛgu lineage.
The first three verses, beginning with the fourteenth, are *triṣṭubh*s;
the thirteenth is a *bṛhatī*; and among the remaining verses, the odd-numbered ones are *bṛhatīs* and the even-numbered ones are *sato-bṛhatīs*.
The third is a *gāyatrī* verse;

together with the line “Sing the hymn among the kings,” it has as its deity the [verse] beginning with “They urge them on” (*te hinvire*). There are two verses beginning with “To me [come] the words” (*ā me vacāṃsi*), which have the deities as their presiding subjects (*adhidevatāke*).
‘Ā no yajñaṃ divispṛśam’—these two verses have Vāyu and the Viśvedevas as their deities;
‘baṇ mahān asi sūrya’—these two have Sūrya as their deity;
and ‘iyaṃ yā nīcī’—this verse has Uṣas as its deity.
Alternatively,
she is praised by means of the light of the sun;
therefore, she alone is the deity.
The verse beginning with "Three indeed are the progenies" has Pavamāna as its deity;
the two verses beginning with "The mother of the Rudras" have the Cow as their deity;
and the remaining five ṛcs have Mitra and Varuṇa as their deities.
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) is based on the *liṅga* (indicative mark).
For the purpose of equipping a king for battle, he should have the king recite two verses beginning with "pra yo vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He causes him to recite the *abhīvarta* [hymn] and the two verses beginning with 'pra yo vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.12.12).
On the fifth day of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], during the morning litany (*prauga*), the Hotṛ should recite two verses beginning with “ā no yajñam” from the Vāyavya triplet.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘ā no yajñaṃ divispṛśam’—these two; ‘ā no vāyo mahe tane’—this one” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
When about to recite the hymn for the Aśvins, the Hotṛ should offer oblations into the fire with the two verses beginning with “baṇ mahān asi sūrya.”
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*baṇ mahān asi sūrya* and *indra vo viśvatas pari* by two [verses]” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).
At the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), when there is an excess of Soma, one additional *śastra* arises.
Therein, the *pragātha* “*baṇ mahān asi*” is the *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘*baṇ mahān asi sūrya ud gā ājāta darśatam vapuḥ*—these two *pragāthas* are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* [verses]’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.7).
This very *pragātha* is the optional *anurūpa* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin at the midday pressing on the twenty-fourth day.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘*śrāyanta iva sūrya baṇ mahān asi sūrya*’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
Having released the cow at the *madhuparka* offering, one should mutter the verse, "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having muttered, 'The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus,' they release her, saying, 'May they grant us strength'" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 1.24.25).

Possessing most exalted sovereignty, far-seeing, O heroes, kings of most extensive fame—those two, like arms with wondrous power, move upon their chariot together with the rays of the sun. *Varṣiṣṭhakṣatrau*, *uru-cakṣasā*, *narā*, *rājānā*, *dīrghaśrutatamā*, *tā*, *bāhutā*, *na*, *daṃsanā*, *ratheyataḥ*, *sākam*, *sūryasya*, *raśmibhiḥ*. Those two of most exalted sovereignty (*varṣiṣṭhakṣatrau*), meaning those whose strength is preeminently increased; far-seeing (*uru-cakṣasā*), meaning of great vision; *narā*, leaders of actions; *rājānā*, shining ones; *dīrghaśrutatamā*, those of most extensive fame, meaning preeminently wise—those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, like *bāhutā*, as if with arms, together with the rays (*raśmibhiḥ*) or beams of the sun, perform *daṃsanā*, wondrous deeds (since "amaḥ" and "daṃsaḥ" are listed among the names for action). They *ratheyataḥ*, they reach [the sacrifice] on their chariot. The meaning is: just as two arms together perform action, so do Mitra and Varuṇa together reach the sacrifice.

He who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, has run forth to you as a swift messenger—the noble one with a golden head, moving rapidly toward the exhilarating wealth—[he becomes your envoy]. Furthermore, with your arms, protect us from that enemy.

Sing forth for Mitra, sing forth for Aryaman—a serviceable song; O you whose wealth is the Truth (Ṛtāvasu), sing a hymn that provides protection to Varuṇa, a pleasing splendor among the kings. *pra mitrāya pra aryamṇe sacadhyam ṛtāvaso varūthyam varuṇe chandyam varcaḥ stotram rājasu gāyata* || 5 || O *ṛtāvasu*, whose wealth is the sacrifice, sing forth for Mitra a song that is to be served and which provides a protective dwelling (*varūthya*). Sing forth for Aryaman as well. For Varuṇa, sing forth such a word (*varcaḥ*) that is pleasing (*chandyam*), a means of gratification. The plural "sing forth" (*gāyata*) is used for honorific purposes. This very point is shown: "among the kings"—sing and recite the hymn for the kings, Mitra and the others. The collective sense is: "O wise one, praise Mitra and the rest. || 5 ||

The Adhvaryu priest goes forth with the straightest paths to receive the oblations. Now, O Lord of the teams (Niyutvan), drink of both our offerings: the pure Soma mixed with milk. 10. O Vāyu, accompanied by your team of horses called *niyut*, you, the Adhvaryu, go by the straightest paths from the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*). [The verb] *veti* means "he goes. For the sake of enjoyment—that is, for your consumption—he brings the offerings (*havyāni*) to be partaken; this is the ellipsis.
And then, for us, [he brings] the Soma of both kinds belonging to us.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
"Drink"— this shows the dual nature [of the action].
The pure, clean Soma, mixed with the milk of cows—that is, blended with cow's milk.

Truly, O Sūrya, you are great in renown; indeed, O God, you are great. Great among the gods, you are the divine one, the high priest, the pervasive light that cannot be deceived. 12. Truly, O Sūrya, you are great in renown; indeed, O God, you are great. Great among the gods, you are the divine one, the high priest, the pervasive light that cannot be deceived. 12.
O Sūrya, you are indeed great through glory—that is, through renown—and thus preeminent among all; this is truly so (baṭ).
O radiant Deva, Sūrya, you are great through greatness—greater than the midst of the gods; this is certainly true (satrā).
And you are the slayer of the Asuras (asuryaḥ).
Furthermore, you are the *purohita*—the advisor for the welfare—of the gods.
Moreover, your light (*jyotis*) is all-pervading (*vibhu*), great, and invincible (*adāmya*), unassailable by anyone.
This form which was cast downward, fashioned from the red cow— like a marvel, it has appeared visible within the reach of sight, upon the arms.
1. *Gha-śukra*: This one is pure. 2. By the power of *kha*, *gha*, *ta*, *ya*, and *śa*, it is augmented; by the power of *ga*, it is further increased.

This one—*yā* (she who), *nīcīm* (lowly), *arkiṇīm* (praising), *rūpā* (form), *rohiṇyā* (of the red one), *kṛtā* (made)—*citrā* (the bright one) has been seen facing toward us as she approaches, within the sights and the arms. 13.
In this verse, there is praise of either the Dawn (Uṣas) or the radiance of the Sun:

that Dawn, or the solar light, which is directed downward (*nīcī*), possessed of hymns (*arkiṇī*), beautiful in form (*rūpā*), and made manifest through its ruddy glow (*rohiṇyā*); having been produced, she comes forth within the midst of the universe (*antaḥ brahmāṇḍasya*) toward the ten directions—which are like her arms—and is seen by all like a wonderful, variegated cow (*citrā gauriva*).
Three generations have passed away; others have entered around the light.
He has stood firm within the worlds; moving through them, he has entered the golden rays.

Three generations have passed beyond the Ārya; others have settled around the hymn in the triple-layered [sacrifice]. The Great One has taken his stand among the worlds; being purified, he has entered the bay steeds.

Those three classes of beings who have passed beyond this limit, and those others who are passing beyond—these beings have entered toward the *arka*, the one worthy of praise, on every side; having settled around it, they have not perished from there.
Within the worlds, in their midst, is that great one, the Sun;
some say he is Prajāpati.
He stood, illuminating the quarters; the purifying wind entered [and pervaded] them.

Thus says the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa: "Three progenies indeed passed beyond this limit"—those three progenies that passed beyond this limit are these very birds, the Vajravaktras, the Śvāvidhas, and the Erapadas.

"Others have settled around the light (*arka*)," [it says]; these very creatures have settled around this light, namely this very Agni. "The Great One has stood within the worlds," [it says]; that indeed is the Great One within the worlds—this Āditya. "The purifying one (*pavamāna*) has entered the bay horses," [it says]; Vāyu indeed is the purifying one, and he has entered the quarters as the bay horses (AiĀ 2.1.1).

The Vājasaneyins also recite: "He performed austerity; he created offspring. Those offspring of his, once created, perished; they are these very birds. Having begun thus, [the text continues]: "Three classes of offspring passed beyond [the sun]; those offspring which passed beyond entered the *arka* on all sides. The *arka* is indeed Agni; these offspring have settled around him. These are the ones who perished."

"He has stood wide within the worlds"—this was recited with reference to Prajāpati; "the purifying one has entered the quarters"—the quarters are indeed the *harits* (the golden ones), and this purifying one has entered them (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.5.1.1–5).
The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—I declare this now to the discerning person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi!

She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. Now I shall proclaim this to the people who understand: do not slay the innocent cow, the Aditi! 15.
In this hymn, the Cow is praised:

that Cow who is the mother of the Rudras, the progenitress of the Maruts, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel—the dwelling place—of the immortal milk. "Do not slay her," O people; "do not harm" that sinless, faultless, and undepressed Aditi, the goddess in the form of a cow. Thus have I now proclaimed to the attentive person, to those who desire to hear, for the sake of the conscious man. This is the instruction.

1. The light was produced by the dawn (uṣas) or by the sun (sūrya) from *kha*; the light was produced by the dawn or by the sun from *ga*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*; the light was produced by the dawn or by the sun from *ta*. 2.
They entered into (*abhiniviviśre*) from *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa*.
3. They went beyond (*atyāyamāyan*) from *ga*.
4. Kha-ta-śa-anyā; bha-nyā.
5. Of Jha, Bha, and Rudra—of the sons of Rudra—to her who utters speech that knows words, who stands present with all [powers] for the sake of those in fear.
The mortal of feeble intellect has driven away from the gods the divine cow who provides nourishment for them.

The one of feeble intellect has drawn me toward himself by means of mortals—me, who know the word, who utter speech, who stand near with all prayers, a goddess come forth from the gods, a cow who has arrived. 16.

She who knows speech, who causes speech to be obtained, and who utters speech after having drunk milk— just as a hungry person does not utter speech until he has eaten and only utters it afterwards— the dull-witted mortal, one of small intellect, avoids and rejects that radiant goddess, the Cow, who approaches with all her thoughts and voices, coming to me for the sake of the gods.
"Tvam agne"—this ninth hymn, consisting of nine verses in the Gāyatrī metre, is addressed to Agni. Its seer is named Prayoga of the Bhṛgu lineage;
or it is Agni, characterized by the specific epithet Pāvaka, belonging to the Bṛhaspati clan.
Alternatively:
there were two sons of Sahonāman named Gṛhapati and Vidyut;
those two together beheld this hymn.
Therefore, it belongs to him;

or rather, it belongs to one of those two. Thus it has been enumerated: "O Agni, you [consist of] more than three [verses]; [the seer is] Bhārgava, the application is Bārhaspatya, or [it is] Pāvaka, the son of Saḥas; [the deities are] Vāk and Gṛhapati, or [Vāk and] Yaviṣṭhya; or it belongs to either of the two; but the [hymn] addressed to Agni [is as follows]."
In the Āgneya kratu, for the Prātaranuvāka in the Gāyatrī metre, there are eighteen verses from the beginning.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn 'tvamagne bṛhad yaḥ' consists of eighteen verses" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
This verse, "tvamagne bṛhad yaḥ," serves as the invitatory prayer (anuvākyā) for Agni Gṛhapati during the oblations of the Devasū offerings.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, you are the great bearer of oblations, the ageless father of us" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.11).

In the Anvārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi], the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for Agni Bhagineya is this: "At the impulse of Savitṛ... and so forth. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At the impulse of Savitṛ, as he does, so bring us riches" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.8).

In the Ābhilāvika Ukthyas at the third pressing, the optional *stotriya* triplet for the Maitrāvaruṇa is "Agni vo vṛdhantam. This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Agni vo vṛdhantame... yaṃ yajñam adhvaraṃ... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8). On the tenth day, the verse "agne ghṛtasya" takes the place of the second verse of the *stotra-sūkta* beginning with "imaṃ no yajñam."

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In place of the second and third [verses] of the *Stokasūkta*, [one should recite] 'O Agni, with the streams of ghee,' and 'O bright one, of the clarified butter'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.12).

The station (*pada*) of the god Agni—the one who has fulfilled desires and who is radiant—is a place that is to be enjoyed through invincible protections (*ūti*), meaning it is unassailable by enemies.
Likewise, his vision (*upadṛk*), which is like that of the sun, is auspicious (*bhadrā*), meaning it is to be enjoyed by human beings just as the sun is.

O Agni, O God, glowing with the brilliance of your flame through the meditations upon the clarified butter, bring hither the gods and worship them. 16. O Agni! With the meditations upon the clarified butter! Blazing, O God! With your flame! Bring hither the gods! And worship them! 16.
O radiant Agni, heating yourself with the deposits of clarified butter—the means of illumination—bring the gods hither with your flame and offer sacrifice to them. Perform the worship as well.

The divine mothers have generated you, O Aṅgiras, as a seer, the immortal bearer of oblations. 17. Him—*you*—the *mothers* generated, the *seer*, the *divine ones*, O *Aṅgiras*, the *bearer of oblations*, the *immortal*. 17.
O Agni, the Aṅgiras, the seer of performed deeds, the immortal one free from death, the bearer of oblations—him, the renowned one, the gods have generated as you, just as mothers give birth.

O Agni, the wise one, they have established you as the excellent messenger, the bearer of oblations. 18. O Agni, the wise one, O seer, they have established you as the excellent messenger, the bearer of oblations. 18.
O Agni, the wise one of far-reaching deeds, the most excellent, the messenger of the gods, the bearer of oblations—to you, the gods have brought down; they settle down.
I have no axe, nor a hatchet with a polished edge; yet, we bring you such as this. 19. I have no axe, nor a hatchet with a polished edge; yet, we bring you such as this. 19.
O Agni, [this is] for me, Bhārgava Prayoga, the seer (ṛṣi).
"Another cow" (anyā gauḥ);

There is no milk nor clarified butter with which I might sacrifice to you;
furthermore, there is no axe that strikes the wood with which I might kindle you. Therefore, such a milch cow for the Agnihotra and the fuel-wood—this whole [offering], O Agni, I bring unto you.
Whatever logs of wood, O Agni, we place upon you, accept them all, O youngest one. 20. Whatever, O Agni, whatsoever logs of wood we offer unto you, enjoy those, O most youthful one. 20.
This is an exposition of the meaning of what was previously recited.

O *yaviṣṭhya*, most youthful *agne*, when we place (*dadhmasi*) any (*kāni cit*) various kinds of wood (*dārūṇi*) upon you, then (*tadā*) please accept (*juṣasva*) even those pieces that have been cut by axes (*aparaśuvṛktāni*). Accordingly, the Yajurvedic Brāhmaṇa states: "In former times, indeed, one did not burn with fire what had been cut by an axe."

1. [The variants] kha, gha, jña, ta¹·², and dhīti read *nidhāna* with *dīptibhiḥ*; ta³·⁴ read *nidhāna* with *dīptibhiḥ*; śa reads *nidhāna*. 2. kha, jha, ta¹·² read *samidhāya*. 3. gha, bha¹·³ read *te tubhyam*. 4. gha reads *kāṣṭhāniḥ*. Ka 3–61: "In that very application, Agni made the sacrificial food (*ṛdh*) palatable for him with the words, 'O Agni, whatever [woods] there are' (TS 5.1.10.1); he thus places the fuel-stick (*samidh*), and makes it palatable for him as if it were not cut by an axe; everything becomes palatable for him. (TS 5.1.10.1).
Whatever pain the tongue causes, whatever creeps along the palate—may all that be ghee for you. (21)
O Agni, that wood and so forth which is the "upajihvikā"—
it is called *upajihvikā* because it smells at (*upa-jighrati*)—
he eats (*atti*), that is, consumes.
"And that which [is made] of wood and so forth is *vagna*.
It is called *vagna* because it vomits water (*vamati udakam*).
Although the words *upajihvikā* and *vagna* are synonyms, nevertheless, because they are mentioned separately, the word *vagna* refers specifically to a particular type of that."
That [fire] also "creeps over" or "goes beyond";
therefore, may all that be "ghee"—that is, like ghee—for you.
The meaning is that it should become as pleasing to you as ghee is.

Kindling Agni with his mind, let the mortal attend upon the sacred thought; he shall kindle Agni with the radiant ones. 22. Kindling Agni; with the mind; the sacred thought; let him attend; the mortal; he shall kindle Agni; with the radiant ones. 22.
A mortal man, kindling Agni with pieces of wood and placing his faith in him with his very mind, should attend to and partake of the ritual action (*dhī*) at the proper time;
indeed, he kindles Agni himself through the *vivasvat* priests.
The tenth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses, beginning with “adarśi,” is the seer’s work of Sobhari Kāṇva.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: “Aḍarśi; Palgunā Sobhari [composed] a Bārhata hymn; the odd verses beginning with the fifth are Satobṛhatīs; the even verses beginning with the eighth are Kakub-gāyatrīs; and the others are Kakub-anuṣṭubhs.
Thus, the five verses—the fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth—are Satobṛhatīs.
The eighth and twelfth verses are Kakubh; the tenth is Gāyatrī; the fourteenth is Anuṣṭubh;
and the remaining verses are Bṛhatīs.
Since it is stated that "it belongs to Agni," the deity is Agni.
And it is otherwise recited [as *anyathāsvabhimṛta*].
In the *prātaranuvāka* of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, in the *Bārhata* metre, it begins with the *sambharc* [verse].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘adarśi gātuvittama’—this is the *Bārhata* with ‘sa’" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
In the *ābhilāvika* offerings, for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, the verse "pra mahiṣṭhāya" serves as an optional *stotriya*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "pra mahiṣṭhāya gāyata, pra so agne tavottibhiḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).
Furthermore, at the concluding oblation (*maṇḍalāntya-homa*) of the commencement and conclusion of the term (*adhyāyopākaraṇa-utsarjana*), the verse "āgneyāhi" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, do not go [alone]; come as one whose friends are the Maruts; what [is] yours, O King Agni... (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.5.7).

He has been seen, the best finder of the path, in whom they have established their sacred vows. Truly, our songs reach Agni, the well-known strengthener of the noble one. adarśa | gātuvittamaḥ | yasmin | vratāni | ādhuḥ | upo iti | su | jñātam | āryasya | vardhanam | agnim | nakṣanta | naḥ | giraḥ || 1 ||
In that fire wherein the sacrificers have placed their vows and ritual acts—having established them—that Agni, the supreme knower of paths, has become manifest.
Furthermore, our songs of praise, consisting of speech, reach toward this well-born Agni, the increaser of this noble one (the highest caste), who has duly appeared.
The verbal root is *nakṣ*, meaning "to go."
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, and Ta, the phrase "upajihvikā ... kāṣṭhādikaṃ" is absent.
In the manuscripts Na, Bha, and Śa, it reads "tyupajihvikā upadahikā" (in Na and Śa, "upadīhikā").
2. In manuscript Ta₁ (at the end), the fifth [syllable] of the Anuṣṭubh pāda is a Virāj, while the seventh and subsequent odd-numbered [syllables] are [short].
Agni, the son of Divodāsa, has gone forth toward the gods with his might;
he has spread himself across the mother earth and has taken his stand upon the summit of the firmament.
The divine Agni, the servant of the gods, has turned toward the gods with his might; he has spread himself out along the mother earth and stands upon the summit of the firmament. 2.
Agni, being summoned by Divodāsa—the son of Divodāsa—did not turn away from going toward the Mother;
for the Earth is the Mother because she supports the entire world.
Toward that Earth, he did not fail to go forth to meet the gods at the sacrifice of that Divodāsa, in order to carry the oblation to the gods.
Because Divodāsa invoked this Agni with majesty—that is, with power—therefore this Agni stood, remained, in his own abode upon the high-elevated place on the ridge of Nāka, the heavenly realm.
Since the people tremble before him as he performs his glorious deeds, like one who wins thousands in the contest for booty, worship Agni with your own thoughts and prayers.

For the people tremble before him as he performs deeds worthy of praise; like one who wins the prize in a contest for wisdom, they themselves honor Agni with their prayers, the winner of thousands. 3.

Because the other people (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*) tremble before the man who performs the deeds that ought to be done (*carkṛtyāni*), therefore now, O people, worship and serve with your own selves (*ātmanā*) and with the works to be performed through your thoughts (*dhībhiḥ*), Agni, the giver of thousands of cattle and riches, at the sacrifice (*medhasātā*).
The mortal whom you wish to lead toward wealth, O Vasu, whoever offers worship to you—
he gains by himself a hero at the forefront who recites hymns and possesses a thousandfold prosperity.
The mortal whom you wish to lead toward wealth, O Vasu, who offers gifts to you—he, O Agni, gains for himself a hero who recites hymns of praise, one who prospers with a thousandfold nourishment.

O Agni, you who are the dweller and the one who causes others to dwell, you desire to lead forward for the sake of wealth—that is, to guide toward riches—whosoever is your praiser; and that mortal man who offers oblations to you, that man himself bestows and maintains a heroic son who recites hymns, a singer of praises, and one who prospers with a thousandfold wealth.
He pierces even the strongholds with his steed for the sake of booty; he wins imperishable fame.
In thee alone, O Lord of abundant wealth, we ever place all desirable things among the gods.
He overcomes even what is difficult to overcome; he wins booty with his steed. He possesses imperishable fame. In you alone, O God, O Lord of abundant wealth, we ever place all desirable things. 5.

O Puruvasu, that sacrificer who offers oblations to you pierces through even the most firm and impenetrable fortresses of the enemy with his swift horse, seizing the food (vāja). Likewise, O God, O Puruvasu, may we ever place within you all desirable and imperishable glories (śravas) in the dwelling of the gods. 5.

1. In the manuscripts kha, ta, bha, the particle *anu* is absent. 2. In kha, ta, l, 2, and pra, it reads *vavṛte*; in ga, na, 4, bha, and pra, it reads *vavṛte*. 3. In kha, ta, na, it reads *yājanāḥ*; in ga, śa, it reads *yajamānāḥ*. 4. In gha, it reads *stotrāṇāṃ*. 5. In kha, ga, gha, ta, bha, and śa, it reads *arvatā adhenā*.
[He] bestows (*dhatte*) and maintains (*dhārayati*) food (*annaṃ*).

This being so, may we, who offer oblations (*haviṣāṃ pradātāraḥ*) to you, remaining among the gods (*devatrā*) within you, the god (*deva*), always (*sadā*) maintain (*dhīmahi*) all (*viśvā*) desirable (*vananīyāni*) riches (*vāmāni*).
He who bestows all wealth, the joyous invoker of men— for him,
as for the first vessels of honeyed mead, the hymns of praise go forth unto Agni.
He who bestows all wealth, the delightful invoker of men—for him, as for the first vessels of honeyed mead, the hymns of praise go forth unto Agni. 6.

Agni, the invoker of the gods, the delightful one who rejoices—the wise one—bestows all treasures and riches upon the people; to that Agni, the foremost vessels, like those of exhilarating Soma, and the hymns of praise proceed forth.

Like a horse, the pious ones, seeking the gods, groom him with their songs, O bounteous givers. O Agni, may your newest, most recent favor be directed toward us for both our children and our progeny; may it come to us with riches, indeed abundantly.
"Salilam" is listed among the many names [of Agni]. Let him come from afar.

Praise Agni, the most beloved of dear things, the guest, the driver of chariots, the controller. 10. "Most beloved. Om. Of dear things. Praise. O singer! The guest. Agni. Of chariots. The controller. 10. O singer, praise Agni himself—the most beloved of dear things, the guest who has arrived, the driver of chariots, the controller. 14.

The knower, the one worthy of sacrifice, Agni, turns hither the proclaimed and the censured, and the known riches. For him who desires to win booty through his mental power, his flames are as difficult to cross as waves on a downward slope. (11) The knower (*veditā*), the perceiver, the one worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), that Agni turns hither (*ā vavartati*) the proclaimed (*uditāni*) vows and the censured (*nirditāni*) sacred traditions, as well as the known (*vedita*) riches (*vasu*). For him who, through his mental power (*dhiyā*)—that is, through ritual action (*karman*)—desires to win (*siṣāsataḥ*) the prize (*vāja*) or the battle, whose flames are as impossible to cross (*duṣṭarāḥ*) as waves (*ūrmi*) directed down a steep descent (*pravaṇe*) toward the ocean—that Agni, O singer, do thou praise! This is the meaning.

May he not harm us—Agni, the guest, the possessor of wealth, he who is highly praised, the excellent invoker, and the performer of the perfect sacrifice. (12) May he not harm us—Agni, the guest, the possessor of wealth, he who is highly praised by many, that Agni who is the excellent invoker and the performer of the perfect sacrifice. *Vasu*: the dweller; *atithi*: dear as a guest; *purupraśasta*: praised by many; *suhotā*: one who well-invokes the gods; *svadhvara*: one who performs the sacrifice well—that Agni, may he not harm us; may he not be obstructed by anyone. The meaning is: being unobstructed by anyone, may Agni grant us our desired objects.

O Agni, O Vasu, let those men who approach you with hymns of praise not come to harm by any of their ways; for even the poor man, having offered oblations and performing the sacrifice well, prays to you for the office of messenger. O Agni, O Vasu (the dweller), let those men who approach you with *acchoktibhiḥ* (hymns of praise) not be harmed (*mo riṣan*) by any of their *evaiḥ* (ways or approaches). For even the *kīriḥ* (poor or lowly man), having offered the oblation (*rātahavyaḥ*) and performing the sacrifice well (*svadhvaraḥ*), indeed prays to you (*īṭṭe*) for the sake of the office of messenger (*dūtyāya*), characterized by the carrying of the oblation.

4. He causes *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ta*, and *śa* to revolve.
5. *Kha*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* are on the left.
6. One who has offered oblations (*dattahaviṣka*) is a performer of the sacrifice (*svadhvara*) through *gha* and *śa*.
O Agni, come as a friend of the Maruts with the Rudras for the drinking of Soma; come to the excellent praise of Sobhari and rejoice, O Lord of Light. 14.
O Agni, friend of the Maruts, beloved by the Maruts, come hither with the Rudras— the Maruts— to our sacrifice characterized by the Soma-drinking, for the sake of drinking the Soma, O Svarṇara;
and come to this beautiful hymn of Sobhari,
O Sobhari, and rejoice.
Having heard the hymn of praise and having drunk the Soma, intoxicate yourself!
Thus ends the tenth section in the eighth book, and the eighth book is completed.
